Title: Model based analysis of future land-use development in China
Authors: Fischer, G; Sun, LX
Objective: Model-based analysis of future land-use development in China through three complementary approaches: enhanced agro-ecological zones (AEZ) assessment, extended input-output modeling, and dynamic welfare optimization to analyze land-use policy alternatives
LULC Classes: Rain-fed cropland; irrigated cropland; grassland; forestland; land used for industry and mining; transportation; residence and services; cultivated and built-up land
Scenarios: Eight scenarios (A-H) with different combinations of technology levels (2025a and 2025b), population growth, economic development, lifestyle changes, and urbanization patterns
Analysis Methods: Enhanced agro-ecological zones (AEZ) assessment; extended input-output (I-O) modeling; dynamic welfare optimization model; applied general equilibrium (AGE) modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: AEZ provides spatially explicit measure of production potentials; I-O modeling deals with discrete and explicit changes in economic structures rather than instantaneous price responses; integration allows for biophysical and geographical underpinning to economic land-use decisions
Tools/Soft Used: Geographic Information System (GIS); GAMS (General Algebraic Modeling System); RAS technique for matrix adjustment
Predictors: Population growth; urbanization; lifestyle changes; per capita income growth; land productivity improvement; technological progress; climate conditions; soil quality; biophysical factors; economic structural changes
Data Sources: UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO); Ministry of Agriculture (1999); province-level prices and county-level statistical information; land survey data; digital databases for climate, soil, altitude, landform, terrain slope, land cover/use, and administrative boundaries
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Land requirements would exceed availability for cultivated land, grassland, and forestland under most scenarios without optimistic technology assumptions; annual productivity growth of 2% required for cropland, 1.1% for grassland, and 1.2% for forestland; northern regions show highest irrigation potential with 104 MT additional grain production possible
Implications: Moderate grain imports equivalent to 10-15% of current total grain output would significantly reduce pressure on cropland and water resources; sustainable water supply system development essential for northern China's food security; rapid technological progress in land-based sectors necessary
Limitations: Plateau region dropped from multi-regional analysis due to lack of data; fixed trade shares assumption in scenarios; optimization approach may be regarded as too idealistic
Future Directions: Further assessment of policy modifications to food import restrictions; sensitivity analysis for population projections, migration patterns, and climate change scenarios; application of dynamic general equilibrium model for robustness testing
Scalability: The AEZ methodology was extended from tropical/sub-tropical to temperate and boreal climate zones, suggesting adaptability to other regions with similar climatic conditions
Novelty: Integration of three complementary modeling approaches; extension of AEZ methodology to seasonal temperate and boreal zones; incorporation of spatially varied biophysical factors into economic models; multi-regional dynamic optimization framework

Title: Residential construction, land use and the environment. Simulations for the Netherlands using a GIS-based land use model
Authors: Schotten, K; Goetgeluk, R; Hilferink, M; Rietveld, P; Scholten, H
Objective: To apply a GIS-based simulation model in the framework of the Fifth National Physical Planning Report to generate future land use in the Netherlands and assess the effects of land use changes on environmental indicators, with special attention to residential construction as a major driving force in land use changes
LULC Classes: Urban (residential, industrial, roads, railways, airports); Agriculture (pasture, corn, arable land, potatoes, beets, cereals, flower bulbs, orchards, cultivation under glass, other agriculture); Natural areas (wood, nature); Water
Scenarios: Divided Europe (DE) - protectionistic tendencies, low economic growth (1.7% annually), population grows to 16.3 million; European Co-ordination (EC) - accelerated European integration, moderate economic growth (3.0%), population grows to 17.7 million; Global Competition (GC) - market forces dominate, high economic growth (3.3%), population grows to 16.9 million
Analysis Methods: GIS-based land use modeling using Land Use Scanner; logit-type approach for probability determination; doubly constrained spatial interaction model; regression analysis for residential construction determinants
Sim. Method Advantages: Grid-based (covers all 193,399 grid cells of 500x500m); Integrated (provides integration framework for sectoral databases); Exhaustive (considers all grids and land use types); Dynamic (deals with changes taking into account present patterns); Satellite structure (driven by national/regional forecasts); Stochastic (outcomes as expected proportions); Policy oriented (makes sectoral policy implications explicit)
Tools/Soft Used: Land Use Scanner (GIS-based model); FACTS model for car ownership and energy use; LMS-Model for car use calculation; Nature planner model for flora quality; Various environmental impact assessment models
Predictors: Accessibility of work locations; proximity of other residential areas; accessibility of natural areas; distance to highway access points and railway stations; presence of highways and railway lines in grid; soil quality; transition costs; amount of similar land use in neighborhood; government planning regulations
Data Sources: National Institute of Public Health and Environment (RIVM); Dutch Central Planning Bureau scenarios; sectoral models for agriculture, housing, industrial and commercial areas; government policy documents
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Residential construction concentrated near existing urban areas and new towns; accessibility of jobs played important role in most market segments; natural areas (wetlands, forests) stimulated residential construction; infrastructure presence discouraged residential development; environmental quality generally improving by 2020 despite population growth; substantial increase in natural areas (150,000+ hectares) expected; CO2 emissions expected to increase due to increased car use
Implications: Substantial scope for improvement in natural area size despite 15% population increase; mixed results for local environment quality; need to broaden conservation focus to general landscape quality improvement; potential for more quantitative approach to complement qualitative planning practice
Limitations: Assumes unchanged preferences and parameters from 1980-1995 period for future projections; technological developments like ICT-induced telecommuting not considered; difficulty separating private sector preferences from public sector objectives in residential construction analysis
Future Directions: Broaden conservation focus from natural areas to general landscape quality improvement; develop elastic demand functions at aggregate level; investigate alternative assumptions about changing preferences and technological impacts
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integration of GIS-based land use modeling with comprehensive environmental impact assessment; application of doubly constrained spatial interaction model to land use allocation; extensive scenario-based analysis covering demographic, economic and policy variations; comprehensive coverage of 193,399 grid cells at 500x500m resolution

Title: The need for scale sensitive approaches in spatially explicit land use change modeling
Authors: Veldkamp, A; Verburg, PH; Kok, K; de Koning, GHJ; Priess, J; Bergsma, AR
Country: Multiple regions—Costa Rica; Ecuador; Central America; China; Indonesia; Philippines .
Objective: Elaborate on the multi‐scale approach in the CLUE framework for quantitative multi‐scale analysis of actual land use and spatially explicit modeling of land use change scenarios .
LULC Classes: Permanent crops; temporary crops; grassland; natural vegetation; forest; shifting cultivation; paddy fields; dry agriculture; housing and gardens; estates; bananas .
Scenarios: Baseline (growing population, stagnating yields); protection of nature parks; land degradation limitations; market liberalization; domestic food demand changes; regional migration policies .
Analysis Methods: Multivariate statistics (multiple‐regression, stepwise regression); artificial nested scales; Pearson correlation; empirical quantification; cellular automata decision rules .
Sim. Method Advantages: Addresses scale sensitivity; integrates interdisciplinary driving factors; multi‐scale allocation allows top‐down and bottom‐up dynamics; realistic spatial patterns; avoids upscaling problems; captures spatial connectivity .
Tools/Soft Used: Geographic Information Systems (GIS); CLUE modeling framework; remote sensing platforms .
Predictors: Rural population density; total population; agricultural population; agricultural labor; precipitation; temperature; soil fertility; slope; erosion susceptibility; drainage; altitude; relief; infrastructure accessibility; income; illiteracy; urban population .
Data Sources: Agricultural censuses; satellite imagery; existing maps; socio‐economic data (population, income, literacy, market and road networks); biophysical data (soil maps, climate, topography) .
Validation Methods: Comparison of modeled land use change with independent census and survey data at administrative and agro‐ecological zone levels; correlation analysis .
Validation Data Sources: National agricultural census data (Costa Rica, Honduras); agricultural surveys (Java, Indonesia); independent land use change reports .
Key Findings: Natural vegetation persists in biophysically poor areas while agricultural land concentrates in populated, accessible regions; Scale dependencies significantly affect driving‐factor identification; Multi‐scale empirical relations remain robust over ~20 years; Model accurately simulates spatial patterns of land use change across diverse regions .
Implications: Highlights need for interdisciplinary, multi‐scale land use modeling; Enables “what‐if” scenario analysis for policy and planning; Contributes to theoretical development of land use change dynamics .
Limitations: Cannot capture fine‐scale (field/farm) dynamics due to data constraints; Empirical relations lack explicit causality; Time horizon limited to ~20 years; Does not account for future technological or novel land use systems .
Future Directions: Integrate fine‐scale dynamics via nested case studies; Develop economic scaling laws; Apply multi‐agent modeling of human–environment interactions; Validate emerging theories; Extend applications to regions like Venezuela and the Sierra Madre (Philippines) .
Scalability: Applicable globally; tested in Latin America and Asia; adaptable to other regions given comparable data
Novelty: First integration of empirical multi‐scale statistical analysis with dynamic, grid‐based demand‐and‐allocation modeling; Feedback mechanism linking bottom‐up and top‐down scale interactions within a unified framework .

Title: The role of spatially explicit models in land-use change research: a case study for cropping patterns in China
Authors: Verburg, PH; Veldkamp, A
Objective: To present and illustrate a spatially explicit modelling methodology (CLUE framework) for analysing regional land-use and cropping pattern dynamics, and explore near-future changes (1991–2010) in China’s land-use patterns.
LULC Classes: Cultivated land; horticultural land; forest; grassland; built-up land; inland water; unused land; nested crop types: rice; wheat; corn; other grains; cash crops; vegetables; miscellaneous crops.
Scenarios: Baseline scenario projecting trends in land demands, demographic shifts, income growth, crop demands (USDA projections), assuming constant multiple-cropping index and spatial suitability relations.
Analysis Methods: Spatial empirical analysis with multiple regression to quantify land-use–determinant relations; dynamic allocation of land-use change using suitability maps and demand modules within the CLUE modelling framework.
Sim. Method Advantages: Generates spatially explicit trajectories of land-use change, bridging gap between problem identification and design phases; Captures non-linearity and spatial/temporal lags; Links regional patterns with national demand projections; Nested simulation of individual crops for better linkage to economic and agronomic studies.
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Demographic: population density; rural/urban population; rural/agricultural labour force; Socio-economic: illiteracy; distance to city; net income; Climatic: temperature metrics; precipitation metrics; months above threshold temperatures; wet months; Soil: drainage; depth; moisture capacity; texture; fertility; crop-specific suitability; Landform: elevation; slope; physiography; geomorphology; distance to river.
Data Sources: National statistics (US Census Bureau, United Nations urbanisation, USDA crop projections); Smil’s land-use change estimates (1990–2000); Spatial datasets on demographics, environment, and socio-economic factors assembled by Verburg & Chen (2000).
Validation Methods: Not applicable
Validation Data Sources: Not applicable
Key Findings: Cultivated land area projected to decline by ~11 M ha, mainly around urban expansions and degraded regions; Rice share decreases nationally; wheat declines in southern wheat belt; corn and cash crops expand, especially in southern provinces; Vegetable area doubles, concentrated in southern provinces and near urban centres.
Implications: Spatially explicit projections can inform design of land-use plans; identified “hot-spots” guide targeted interventions; nested crop simulations improve policy and economic linkage.
Limitations: Absence of independent validation data for China; Coarse grid resolution (32 × 32 km) limits local-scale detail; Assumes stable suitability relations and constant multiple-cropping index.
Future Directions: Integrate dynamic spatial simulation of productivity change; Link macro-scale CLUE outputs with micro-scale agent-based/local studies for multi-scale integration.
Scalability: Framework applied elsewhere (Ecuador, Burkina Faso, Netherlands); methodology adaptable to other regions given appropriate data and calibration
Novelty: Nested simulation of individual crops within a spatially explicit land-use change model; Bridging of research phases: from problem identification through system description to design planning via dynamic trajectories.

Title: Assessment of interactions between land use change and carbon and nutrient fluxes in Ecuador
Authors: Priess, JA; de Koning, GHJ; Veldkamp, A
Objective: To propose a conceptual dynamic approach (CLUE-Nuts) for modeling the interaction between land use change and nutrient and carbon fluxes, addressing scale-dependent drivers and processes, and including feedback mechanisms
LULC Classes: Annual crops (maize, broad beans, beans, barley, wheat, potatoes, soybeans, rice); Permanent crops (bananas, plantains, cacao, coffee, sugar cane); Grasslands; Natural vegetation
Scenarios: Continuation of actual trends and consumption patterns; scenarios with different combinations of increasing food demands, land degradation, and protection of natural areas
Analysis Methods: Integration of CLUE (Conversion of Land Use and its Effects) model with NUTMON (Nutrient Monitoring) approach; multi-scale spatial statistical analyses; iteration procedures for crop allocation; nutrient balance calculations
Sim. Method Advantages: Accounts for feedback mechanisms between soil nutrient status and land management; includes crop-specific parameters and drivers; handles multi-scale aspects of land use change; calculates annual carbon and nutrient fluxes dynamically rather than static balances
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE model; NUTMON model; MS-ACCESS database; geo-referenced data systems; geographical grids
Predictors: Biophysical factors (soil, terrain, climate characteristics); socio-economic factors (demography, income, infrastructure); agro-ecological conditions; national demand for agricultural products; soil fertility parameters
Data Sources: Agricultural census data (1991); agricultural production data (crop areas, yields, input use, numbers of animals); soil physical and chemical properties; terrain characteristics; infrastructure data; socio-economic indicators
Validation Methods: Backward modeling validation; comparison of modeled and measured areas at administrative levels (cantons and provinces); statistical evaluation of better data for prediction and backward validation
Validation Data Sources: Agricultural census data; demographic census data from different years; administrative level data at canton and province levels
Key Findings: Agricultural land expansion occurred in most scenarios; land use expansion took place in areas with negative nutrient balances; crop-specific nutrient fluxes vary significantly across regions; soil carbon losses from potato fields ranged 0-4.5 Mg C ha⁻¹; banana plantations showed high K exports (maximally 431 kg ha⁻¹); manure N inputs roughly equaled harvest losses but did not compensate for other losses
Implications: CLUE-Nuts provides a tool for predicting crop-specific future land use and related nutrient fluxes; supports risk assessment and development of sustainable agricultural land use; can inform Integrated Nutrient Management (INM) and policy interventions at multiple scales
Limitations: Feedback mechanisms could not be applied to all crops; production functions had low correlation coefficients for some crops; landscape processes like erosion and sedimentation need better representation; validation only possible at administrative levels, not grid cell level; limited data availability for some crops
Future Directions: Further studies needed to evaluate feedback loop contributions to prediction precision; better representation of landscape processes across spatial units; refinement of production functions and crop-specific allocation assumptions; inclusion of more socio-economic parameters at aggregated scales
Scalability: Framework is flexible and can be applied to other regions; approach demonstrated for Ecuador but methodology is transferable; requires region-specific data collection and calibration
Novelty: First integration of land use change modeling (CLUE) with nutrient monitoring (NUTMON); dynamic approach replacing static nutrient balances; inclusion of feedback mechanisms between soil fertility and crop allocation; multi-scale framework addressing spatial and temporal scale dependencies; crop-specific modeling replacing broad land use categories

Title: Modelling land-use change for Central America, with special reference to the impact of hurricane Mitch
Authors: Kok, K; Winograd, M
Country: Central America (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama)
Objective: develop various plausible near-future pathways (1996 until 2010) of landuse change at the national level and to analyse the consequences on spatial patterns in Central America
LULC Classes: annuals (maize, beans, rice, sorghum); bananas; coffee; sugar cane; pasture; natural vegetation
Scenarios: Base scenario; Optimistic scenario; Natural Hazard scenario
Analysis Methods: CLUE (Conversion of Land-use and its Effects) modelling framework; statistical techniques; multiple regression techniques
Sim. Method Advantages: quantifies scale dependencies; incorporates structural complexity and functional complexity; uses multidisciplinary set of land-use drivers; spatially and temporally explicit
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE (Conversion of Land-use and its Effects) modelling framework; grid-based allocation module
Predictors: rural population density, access to nearest port, soil fertility, soil drainage, and climate seasonality
Data Sources: FAOSTAT databases; World Bank; US Census Bureau; UN population projections; CIAT databases
Validation Methods: systematic calibration and multi-scale validation using independent data set
Validation Data Sources: second independent data set
Key Findings: gradual changes at national level translate into spatially explicit hot-spots of change; land-use changes are highly dynamic with large areas of increase and decrease; effects of hurricane on land-use patterns are initially strong but largely disappear within 10 years; land-use system demonstrates resilience though not necessarily stability
Implications: useful for policy makers at various levels; international organisations can gain insight on severity of spatially explicit changes; national authorities can use model to evaluate scenario results; CLUE can be used as tool in recovery planning after extreme events
Limitations: system description at one point in time used throughout model run generating recurring similar patterns; transportation costs through Panama Canal not accounted for in banana cultivation; land tenure and local corporations not considered for permanent crops; results from other disciplines needed to strengthen conclusions
Future Directions: similar studies and spatially explicit models needed from sociology and economics; more modelling efforts needed to unravel long-term effects of extreme events from various disciplines
Scalability: country is the largest organisational unit that should be modelled in Central America; substantial and non-realistic land-use changes could be introduced when scenarios developed for whole region at once
Novelty: first attempt to define realistic scenario based on actual data; multi-scale empirical analysis on drivers of land-use; explicit incorporation of scale dependencies in land-use modeling; integration of extreme event impacts using actual hurricane data

Title: Land-use change and socio-economic metabolism in Austria - Part II: land-use scenarios for 2020
Authors: Haberl, H; Erb, KH; Krausmann, F; Adensam, H; Schulz, NB
Objective: To evaluate the relations between land-use and socio-economic metabolism, particularly socio-economic biomass flows, by constructing four scenarios for Austria in 2020 and highlight the interrelations between socio-economic metabolism and land use, as well as those between resource policy and land-use policy
LULC Classes: Wheat and rye; Fodder cereals; Maize; Pulses; Silo maize; Rape seed; Sunflower; Potato; Sugar beet; Clover; Fallow; Other crops; Gardens; Grasslands; Alpine grasslands
Scenarios: TREND (extrapolation of current trends); GLOB (far-reaching liberalization of agricultural markets); MAX (maximization of biomass production for energy and raw materials); SUST (cascade utilization of biomass without increasing primary extraction)
Analysis Methods: Biomass flow model using spreadsheet calculations; saturation curve fitting using least-square fit; aggregation of primary data to fifteen land-use categories and eight major production zones
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Spreadsheet model
Predictors: Agricultural framework conditions (geomorphology, soil, climate); economic returns for each crop per hectare; projected biomass demand; urban and infrastructure area growth; distribution of crops between major production zones
Data Sources: Austrian Federal Statistical Office (Statistics Austria, ISIS databank) for land-use data 1950-1995; Austrian Federal Environment Agency for urban and infrastructure areas; Austrian Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry for economic returns data; literature sources for technical factors in biomass processing
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Forest areas increase by 2.5% in TREND/SUST/MAX scenarios and 9.4% in GLOB scenario; Grassland areas shrink in all scenarios (-11% to -34%); Cropland decreases in all scenarios (-2% to -20%); Human appropriation of net primary production (HANPP) increases to 52.6-55.3% in TREND/SUST/MAX scenarios but falls to 48.5% in GLOB scenario; MAX scenario leads to reduction in carbon sinks of about 0.73 MtC compared to TREND scenario; Biomass energy potential represents only 3-4 percentage points of total technical primary energy use
Implications: Complicated feedback mechanisms exist between energy policy and land-use policy; Caution needed when developing policies to substitute biomass for fossil energy to reduce CO2 emissions; Biomass energy potential should not be over-estimated; Increases in wood harvest could reduce forest carbon sink function enough to offset CO2 reduction from fossil-fuel substitution; Energy conservation strategies could be more important than biomass substitution
Limitations: Scenarios should not be misinterpreted as forecasts; Reliable forecasts beyond 2006 are impossible; Dramatic changes in world agricultural markets are possible but hard to predict; Considerable uncertainties associated with HANPP calculations; Belowground carbon stocks not considered in carbon accounting
Future Directions: More research warranted on trade-offs and interrelations between fossil-energy use and biomass; Development of more sophisticated models of material flows and biomass flows; Establishment of links between socio-economic metabolism and land-use research fields
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Development of biomass flow model that relates demand and supply of biomass to establish link between biomass flows and land use; Application of socio-economic metabolism approach to land-use studies; Comprehensive scenario analysis combining land-use changes with biomass flow modeling

Title: Carbon dynamics and land-use choices: building a regional-scale multidisciplinary model
Authors: Kerr, S; Liu, SG; Pfaff, ASP; Hughes, RF
Objective: Present an integrated modeling methodology that addresses the needs for forecasts of land use and carbon storage on a large scale over long periods; model the dynamics of the human land-use system and of C pools contained in each ecosystem, as well as their interactions
LULC Classes: Primary forests; secondary forests; pastures; banana plantations; coffee crops; seasonal crops; permanent crops; forest; non-forest
Baseline Years: 1945-1963 (aerial photos available back to 1945 for some areas, 1963 for whole country)
Scenarios: Policy scenarios; baseline scenarios; CDM scenarios; carbon sequestration reward scenarios
Analysis Methods: CENTURY ecological process model; econometric analysis; multinomial logit; Monte Carlo simulations; GIS techniques; revealed preference approach; General Ensemble biogeochemical Modeling System (GEMS)
Sim. Method Advantages: Maintains benefits of detailed process modeling while allowing for heterogeneity in the landscape; explicit use of joint frequency distribution over space; permits explicit uncertainty estimates via ensemble Monte Carlo simulations; forces model to be explicit in beliefs about key distributions
Tools/Soft Used: CENTURY model; GEMS (General Ensemble biogeochemical Modeling System); GIS
Predictors: Land-use and land-cover type; monthly average maximum and minimum air temperature; monthly precipitation; lignin content of plant material; C:N plant tissues; soil texture; initial soil C and N levels; atmospheric N deposition; management practices; lifezone; soil characteristics; crop prices; transport costs; access to markets; road networks; population density
Data Sources: Field measurements; existing literature; remote sensing (satellite images since late 1970s); aerial photos (1945-1963); census data; GIS databases; export price data; industry association data; World Tables (International Monetary Fund)
Validation Methods: Field measurements from 13 sites across five dominant life zones; in-sample fit and prediction of out-of-sample data; comparison with field measurements of aboveground live biomass, large woody debris, fine litter, and soil organic carbon
Validation Data Sources: Field measurements from 13 sites; data from Clark et al. (2001) for net primary production; systematic sampling of variation in edaphic, climatic, and land use conditions
Key Findings: Forest levels will continue to fall slowly and at a decreasing rate; annual payment of $18.50 per tonne C would result in 3.4 million tonnes (1%) more carbon stored by 2020; simulated results of aboveground live biomass, large woody debris, and fine litter agreed well with field measurements; soil organic carbon was well simulated in some life zones but under-estimated in tropical dry forest and over-estimated in tropical moist and wet forests
Implications: Can create baselines and reward sequestration; estimate value in both environmental and economic terms of including C sequestration in tropical forests for climate change mitigation; assess benefits from costly activities to increase accuracy and reduce societal costs of errors; inform future policy makers on comprehensive climate policies
Limitations: Few models have been tested in all dominant life zones in Costa Rica; default maximum decomposition rates in CENTURY were too low for tropical moist and wet forests; uncertainty inherent in predictions of land use and C storage and dynamics; need for region-specific measures of C and N pools
Future Directions: Comprehensive assessment of CENTURY performance in Costa Rica planned; collecting additional field data in different life zones; generalize and apply the integrated modeling system to other regions including non-tropical regions; develop simpler models with reduced input variables for wider application
Scalability: Could be replicated in other developing countries at either regional or national level; ultimate goal to generalize and apply to other regions including non-tropical regions; methods applicable to future models of coupled natural and human land-use systems
Novelty: First known model to explicitly consider interactions where land use affects forest ecosystems on this scale; dynamic interactions and feedback mechanisms between ecosystems and land-use changes previously largely ignored; cross-disciplinary integration of ecological and economic modeling with spatial and temporal explicit information

Title: Constructing land-use maps of the Netherlands in 2030
Authors: de Nijs, TCM; de Niet, R; Crommentuijn, L
Objective: To create spatially detailed land-use maps of the Netherlands in 2030 using the Environment Explorer, a Cellular Automata-based land-use model to construct land-use maps from four scenarios
LULC Classes: 17 land-use types including 10 'active' functions (high and low-density residential areas, industrial areas, commercial services, public services, recreation, greenhouses, three types of forest and nature), 3 'passive' functions (grassland, arable land, other agriculture), and 4 'static' features (airports, fresh water, salt water, foreign land)
Scenarios: Four scenarios based on IPCC scenarios constructed on two axes: 'globalization' versus 'regionalization' and 'individual orientation on material values' versus 'cooperative orientation respecting social and ecological values'. The Individual World scenario was described in detail
Analysis Methods: Cellular Automata (CA)-based land-use modeling using the Environment Explorer; scenario analysis; spatial allocation modeling on 500-m grid-based land-use map
Sim. Method Advantages: Ensures that all relevant aspects of a scenario (economic and demographic developments, zoning policies and urban growth) are integrated systematically into one consistent framework; links future land-use maps to current spatial developments and spatial socio-economic system functioning
Tools/Soft Used: Environment Explorer (CA-based land-use model); ArcGIS
Predictors: Transition potential calculated as weighted sum of neighbourhood potential (NP), policy or zoning map (ZM), and suitability map (SM); CA rules describing relative influence of all 17 land uses; accessibility factors including access roads to motorways; noise levels; soil profitability
Data Sources: 1996 Soil Statistic map of the Netherlands (CBS, 2000); Land-use map of the Netherlands (SC-DLO, 1999); Residential Typology (ABF, 1998); noise map (Dolmans et al., 2000); soil map; policy plans (VROM, 1999, 2001)
Validation Methods: Kappa statistic, K-histo, K-locations, and Fuzzy Kappa statistic; comparison of simulated land use in 1993 with observed land use data
Validation Data Sources: Observed land use data (CBS, 1993, 1997) for 1989-1993 period
Key Findings: 10% of land use will change in the next 30 years; agricultural area decreases by 36% relative to 1996 in the Individual World scenario; the Randstad region urbanizes to a high degree; large residential suburbs develop in green rural areas; huge industrial/commercial complexes develop near motorway access roads; agriculture disappears from less profitable sandy and subsiding peat soils
Implications: The maps provide basis for evaluating potential effects on nature and landscape according to societal trends; demonstrate whether policy objectives can be realized in context of various societal developments; show possible changes in land use under different scenario conditions rather than most probable developments
Limitations: Inconsistency in historical land-use maps affects calibration; spatial allocation has random components making exact location simulation difficult; new land uses like green villages cannot be calibrated on historical data; limited number of comparative studies for model parameter validation
Future Directions: Making causal, consistent and plausible scenarios; utilizing five driving forces (international political developments, economy, demography, technology, socio-cultural); including sensitive variables in scenario definition; improving calibration and validation using satellite-based land-use maps; developing methodology to extract essential CA rules from observed changes
Scalability: The methodology can be applied to other regions with appropriate model calibration and rule adaptation, though more comparable studies for different areas with varying spatial developments are needed
Novelty: First time in the history of Dutch environmental outlooks that consistent, spatially detailed land-use maps for 2030 were constructed from national economic and demographic scenarios; integration of scenario elements into systematic spatial framework using CA-based modeling

Title: Projecting land use transitions at forest fringes in the Philippines at two spatial scales
Authors: Verburg, PH; Veldkamp, A
Objective: Illustrate the use of spatially explicit land use change models in ecological assessments by linking spatial pattern to ecological processes through two case studies at distinct scales .
LULC Classes: Forest; Arable land; Grassland; Plantations; Mixed cropping; Built-up area; Others; Mangrove; Coconut plantations; Wetland rice; Secondary vegetation; Shifting cultivation; Primary forest; Institutional land; Rocky outcrops
Scenarios: Scenario 1: Baseline; Scenario 2: Spatial policies;
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit simulation with the CLUE-s model; logistic regression (logit) for suitability; land use conversion matrices; land requirement extrapolation; spatial metrics (PAC, AI, GISFrag); ROC evaluation .
Sim. Method Advantages: Balances bottom-up suitability and top-down demand; incorporates path-dependence and reversibility; yields non-linear spatial patterns; enables multi-scale complementary insights for environmental management .
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-s model; logistic regression; APACK for spatial metrics; GIS for fragmentation indices .
Predictors: Altitude; Slope; Aspect; Geomorphology; Parent material; Distance to roads; Distance to rivers; Distance to cities; Population density; Spatially lagged population density; Accessibility indices (roads/footpaths) .
Data Sources: NAMRIA/SSC SPOT-based 1987 land use map with field checks; 1:10 000 NIPAP participatory 3-D model; cadastral maps; geological maps; demographic data for population density .
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: National “hot zones” of deforestation at forest fringes (Sierra Madre, Palawan, Samar, Mindanao); spatial policies concentrate deforestation where logging is allowed; strict protection reduces forest loss in many provinces but risks remain in agro-industrial target areas; Sibuyan Island shows valley deforestation for shifting cultivation, limited secondary regrowth, wetland rice expansion, coconut plantation spread on slopes; protected area and buffer enforcement substantially reduce fragmentation; sustainable agriculture can stabilize total forest area but lowland forest loss persists .
Implications: Spatial modeling guides identification of deforestation hotspots and evaluation of land use policies; multi-scale applications inform both macro-level planning and fine-scale ecological assessment; model supports stakeholder decision-making in environmental management .
Limitations: Coarse aggregation limits thematic and spatial detail; remote sensing cannot distinguish primary vs secondary forest at national scale; inability to validate national model; limited representation of reforestation; data availability constraints .
Future Directions: Species-specific landscape impact analyses; multi-scale and process-based ecological assessments (fire, hydrology, soil, carbon); validation with remote sensing time‐series; sensitivity analyses of path dependence and demand scenarios .
Scalability: Model framework configurable for multiple spatial scales and extents, demonstrated from national to island level
Novelty: Integration of spatially specific land use policies; user-defined land use conversion matrices enabling path-dependence; nested multi-scale applications; participatory 3-D mapping for high‐resolution land use data .

Title: Climate change impacts for the conterminous USA: An integrated assessment - Part 6. Distribution and productivity of unmanaged ecosystems
Authors: Izaurralde, RC; Thomson, AM; Rosenberg, NJ; Brown, RA
Objective: To characterize the range in response of unmanaged ecosystems in the conterminous U.S. to 12 climate change scenarios by simulating climatically induced shifts in net primary productivity and geographical distribution of major biomes
LULC Classes: Croplands; grasslands and savannas; forests; wetlands; deserts; tundra; settlements
Baseline Years: Current climate (baseline) - specific years not specified
Scenarios: 12 climate change scenarios including BMRC; UIUC; UIUC + Sulfate scenarios with Global Mean Temperature increases of +1.0°C and +2.5°C; CO2 concentrations of 365 and 560 ppmv
Analysis Methods: Grid-cell modeling using rule-based algorithms; steady-state global natural vegetation pattern prediction; leaf area index optimization for maximum net primary productivity; quasi-empirical rules for succession and disturbance effects
Sim. Method Advantages: BIOME 3 represents improvements over previous empirical approaches; provides realistic and objective baseline of potential distribution of natural vegetation; captures well the potential distribution of major biomes across the U.S. under baseline climate
Tools/Soft Used: BIOME 3 model; EPIC model; HUMUS model; GCAM (Global Change Assessment Model)
Predictors: Growing degree-days; mean temperature of coldest and warmest month; α-moisture index; atmospheric CO2 concentration; photosynthetic active radiation; soil moisture content; precipitation; sunshine hours; soil texture
Data Sources: Climate and soil data for grid cells; Oak Ridge NPP database; Class A vegetation sites data from Olson et al. (2001); Zheng et al. (2001) global database of primary productivity
Validation Methods: Comparison with Küchler (1964) natural biome distribution; comparison with NPP measurements from Class A vegetation sites; comparison with Zheng et al. (2001) grid-cell based global database; regression analysis
Validation Data Sources: Küchler (1964) classification; Oak Ridge NPP database Class A sites; Zheng et al. (2001) global primary productivity database
Key Findings: BIOME 3 captured potential distribution of major biomes reasonably well under current climate; NPP changes would be most severe under BMRC scenario due to significant temperature increases; UIUC and UIUC + Sulfate scenarios would increase NPP especially in the West; CO2-fertilization effect enhanced increases or alleviated losses in NPP; Temperate/Boreal Mixed Forests would lose area under most scenarios; Arid Shrubland/Steppe would expand significantly under BMRC scenario
Implications: Climate change would affect geographic distribution and productivity of unmanaged ecosystems; significant changes in biome distribution would carry severe consequences for ecosystem functioning and people; land use changes would be most dramatic in the West; challenges exist in harmonizing environmental needs and societal development under climatic change
Limitations: NPP projections were reasonable for forests but not for grasslands where simulated values were always greater than observed; results may be overly optimistic because simulations assume soils with nutrients in ample supply; differences in scale between observations and predictions make direct comparisons difficult; native plant response strategies may be hampered by unprecedented rates of climate change and ongoing land use changes
Future Directions: Integration of results through global change assessment model (GCAM) framework; development of consistent scenarios for examining paths to harmonize environmental needs and societal development; consideration of evolutionary response rates to climate change
Scalability: Methods and models employed are useful for identifying range in response of unmanaged ecosystems to climate change and areas where tradeoffs between managed and unmanaged ecosystems would be most likely; approach could be applied to other regions
Novelty: Integration of biophysical and biogeochemical modeling with climate change scenarios; application of BIOME 3 model to conterminous U.S. for climate change impact assessment; overlay analysis of agricultural capacity changes with natural ecosystem distribution projections

Title: Climate change impacts for the conterminous USA: An integrated assessment - Part 7. Economic analysis of field crops and land use with climate change
Authors: Sands, RD; Edmonds, JA
Objective: To demonstrate the impact of potential changes in climate on agricultural production and land use in the United States by placing simulation results from biophysical models into a top-down economic framework of global agriculture and land use
LULC Classes: Crops (food grains, coarse grains, oil crops, other crops); pasture; forests (managed and unmanaged); unmanaged land (primarily unmanaged forest, unmanaged rangeland and grassland)
Scenarios: Twelve climate scenarios derived from three climate models (BMRC, UIUC, UIUC + Sulfates) and two climate sensitivities (1.0°C and 2.5°C global mean temperature increase by mid-century), further distinguished by presence or absence of CO2 fertilization
Analysis Methods: Agriculture and Land Use (AgLU) model; partial equilibrium model of global agriculture and land use; land allocation mechanism based on economic return maximization; reduced-form economic modeling approach
Sim. Method Advantages: Bridges the gap between top-down global economic models and biophysical models with shorter time steps and smaller geographical areas; integrates with compatible model of world energy system; provides global perspective with reduced computational requirements compared to detailed mathematical programming models
Tools/Soft Used: Agriculture and Land Use (AgLU) model; EPIC crop growth model; HUMUS model; BIOME3 model
Predictors: Yield (intrinsic yield for different land uses); prices received for products; non-land costs of production; population; per-capita income; climate scenarios; CO2 fertilization effects
Data Sources: Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations for agricultural data; EPIC crop growth model simulations; HUMUS model results for irrigation constraints; BIOME3 model for unmanaged ecosystem productivity; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) land use and land cover data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Climate change impacts on U.S. agriculture vary significantly by climate scenario; BMRC 2.5°C scenario shows lowest yields relative to baseline; dryland yields with CO2 fertilization exceed baseline yield in all scenarios except BMRC 2.5°C; forest productivity shows dramatic collapse in BMRC 2.5°C scenarios (net primary productivity drops from 5.84 to 0.86-1.34 tons per hectare of carbon); results are sensitive to yield assumptions in rest of world
Implications: Climate change impacts on U.S. agriculture are highly uncertain and dependent on specific climate scenarios; CO2 fertilization effects can offset some negative climate impacts; forest ecosystems may be more vulnerable than agricultural systems under extreme warming scenarios; global agricultural trade patterns may shift significantly
Limitations: Analysis is qualitative and exploratory; detailed results from biophysical models available only for United States; climate impacts outside United States treated on scenario basis; static yield simulations that don't account for future agricultural adaptation; major uncertainties regarding future crop productivity and wide variation in climate scenarios across general circulation models
Future Directions: Need for more detailed biophysical modeling results for countries outside the United States; development of dynamic yield simulations that account for agricultural adaptation over time; improvement in understanding of future crop productivity trends; reduction of uncertainties in climate scenario projections
Scalability: Limited scalability due to sparse availability of detailed biophysical model results for other countries; framework could be applied globally if adequate biophysical data were available for other regions
Novelty: Integration of multiple biophysical models (EPIC, HUMUS, BIOME3) into a global economic framework; development of methodology to bridge gap between detailed biophysical models and top-down economic models; comprehensive assessment of climate change impacts on both agricultural and forest land uses within single analytical framework

Title: Simulating the future of agricultural land use in The Netherlands
Authors: Koomen, E; Kuhlman, T; Groen, J; Bouwman, A
Journal: TIJDSCHRIFT VOOR ECONOMISCHE EN SOCIALE GEOGRAFIE
Objective: To evaluate how expected changes in agriculture will affect agricultural land use in the Netherlands, specifically how much land will be taken out of production and to what use it will be put, using land use simulation modeling under different socio-economic scenarios
LULC Classes: 14 types of land use including 4 kinds of agriculture (arable farming; market gardening; perennial crops; greenhouse horticulture; grassland livestock farming; zero-grazing livestock; mixed types), 2 residential classes (including rural low-density dwellings), commercial, recreational, natural land use, water, and various types of infrastructure
Scenarios: Two opposing socio-economic scenarios: Global Economy (combining globalization with individualism, limited government intervention) and Regional Community (connecting regionalism with cooperation, restrictive spatial policies)
Analysis Methods: Land use simulation modeling using the Land Use Scanner; sector-specific regional models; farm-type oriented micro-simulation approach; logit equation simulating bidding process between competing land users
Sim. Method Advantages: The Land Use Scanner mimics the land market by balancing claims on land from various land-use categories with available suitable land; incorporates government policies through taxes and subsidies in suitability maps; provides spatial visualization of land use changes; allows for 'what if' scenario analysis
Tools/Soft Used: Land Use Scanner (GIS-type computer program); Agricultural Economics Research Institute land-market model
Predictors: Land suitability factors including: quality of land itself (soils for agricultural use); existing land use (representing conversion costs); infrastructure and accessibility; proximity of other land use of the same type; government policies pertaining to the area; economic growth rates; population projections; societal focus; economic orientation
Data Sources: CBS (Central Bureau of Statistics) for historical agricultural area data; Agricultural Economics Research Institute land-market model; sector-specific models from National Nature Outlook study; spatial database containing present land use and land suitability data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Under the Global Economy scenario, dramatic decrease in cultivated area with agriculture almost disappearing in regions surrounding Amsterdam and Utrecht, replaced by urban land use, nature and recreation areas; under Regional Community scenario, less dramatic decline in agricultural land with emphasis on integration of agriculture with nature conservation and maintenance of attractive rural environments
Implications: The shift from government-driven spatial planning to market-oriented spatial policies could lead to virtual disappearance of agriculture in parts of western Netherlands, establishing new park-like landscapes; different policy approaches result in significantly different rural landscape outcomes
Limitations: Results should be regarded as answers to 'what if' questions rather than hard predictions; model predictions depend on parameter values that reflect researchers' assumptions; regions are not predefined but define themselves through generated patterns
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Application of Land Use Scanner model to agricultural land use change; integration of socio-economic scenarios with spatial modeling; comprehensive assessment combining agricultural dynamics, external pressures, and government policies

Title: Developing land use scenario dynamics model by the integration of system dynamics model and cellular automata model
Authors: He, CY; Shi, PJ; Chen, J; Li, XB; Pan, YZ; Li, J; Li, YC; Li, JG
Journal: SCIENCE IN CHINA SERIES D-EARTH SCIENCES
Objective: To develop a Land Use Scenario Dynamics (LUSD) model by integrating System Dynamics (SD) model and Cellular Automata (CA) model to simulate land use scenario changes and assess their potential impacts on ecosystem structure and function; specifically to model land use scenario changes in northern China for the next 20 years
LULC Classes: Urban; cultivated land; grassland; forest land; unused land (including wetland, water area, glacier, bare rock, Gobi and desert)
Scenarios: 6 scenarios based on combinations of GDP growth rates (high/medium/low: 7.5%/7.2%/7.0%), population growth rates (high/medium/low), food supply ratios (1.15/1.0/0.85), and grain productivity levels (maintaining 2000 level vs. advancing)
Analysis Methods: Integration of System Dynamics (SD) model and Cellular Automata (CA) model; SD model for land use scenario demands simulation at national/regional scale; CA model for land use pattern allocation at local scale
Sim. Method Advantages: SD model has advantage to reflect complexity of land use driving forces at national/regional scale; CA model possesses strong ability to represent complexity of land use evolution at local scale; integration improves ability to reflect complex behavior of land use system at different scales
Tools/Soft Used: Stella software from High Performance System (HPS) company; GIS
Predictors: Land suitability (slope, accessibility to transportation networks); inheritance ability; neighborhood effect; population; GDP; market adjustment (food supply ratio); technology advancement (grain productivity); land use policy
Data Sources: Land use/cover maps from 1 km monthly NOAA AVHRR NDVI dataset from National Meteorological Administration of China; Digital Elevation Model (DEM) from USGS EROS data center; GIS data of railroad, road, highway from Chinese Map Publishing House; Statistical data from State Statistical Bureau of China
Validation Methods: Comparison between simulated land use maps and historical land use maps; total accuracy and Kappa coefficient calculation
Validation Data Sources: Historical land use maps in 1994 and 1999; simulation validation using 1989 as starting point
Key Findings: LUSD model achieved total accuracy of about 75% and Kappa coefficient of 0.6; model has ability to reflect complex behavior of land use system at different scales; obvious land use changes will take place in farming-pastoral zone of northern China in next 20 years; cultivated land and urban land are the most active land use types; model is useful tool for assessing potential impacts of land use system on ecological system
Implications: Model can support land use policy and planning; provides methodology for simulating spatial dynamics of land use change; can be used as tool for understanding possible impacts of land use system on terrestrial ecosystem; helps identify 'hot spots' of land use change
Limitations: Model outputs have uncertainty due to ignorance of natural factors such as climate change and water resource shortage; simplification of human driving forces to only several factors (GDP, population, food supply ratio, grain productivity); results should not be interpreted as forecasts but as possible patterns under different scenarios
Future Directions: Further validation by reliable historical data sets; endeavors to represent both human and natural land use driving forces simultaneously; improvement of model to include climate change and water resource factors
Scalability: Model provides methodology that can potentially be applied to other regions; however, specific parameters and driving forces would need to be adapted for different geographical contexts
Novelty: Integration of 'bottom-up' CA model with 'top-down' SD model; addresses limitation of current land use models that are either valid for only one process or lack spatial dimensions; improves simulation ability to reflect complexity of land use system at different scales

Title: Analysis of the effects of land use change on protected areas in the Philippines
Authors: Verburg, Peter H.; Overmars, Koen P.; Huigen, Marco G. A.; de Groot, Wouter T.; Veldkamp, A.
Objective: To discuss the role of land use modeling approaches for assessing the threats and trade-offs of protecting designated nature areas in the Philippines, using spatially explicit land use allocation models at national and landscape scales
LULC Classes: Forest; Grassland; Plantations; Arable land; Mixed cropping; Built-up area; Others; Rice fields; Banana cultivation; Open forest
Scenarios: Scenario 1a (no enforcement of protected areas, no spatial policies for agriculture); Scenario 1b (no enforcement of protected areas, spatial policies for agriculture following NPAAAD); Scenario 2a (strict protection of main protected areas, no spatial policies for agriculture); Scenario 2b (strict protection of main protected areas, spatial policies for agriculture following NPAAAD)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land use allocation modeling using CLUE-s framework; Logistic regression approach for national level; Rule-based modeling for landscape level; Remote sensing image interpretation; Field surveys and structured interviews
Sim. Method Advantages: Models enable identification and quantification of relationships with precision not attained by descriptive approaches; Allow experimentation with different scenarios; Provide visualization of alternative land use configurations; Serve as communication and learning environment for stakeholders; Enable early warning system for future land use changes
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-s modeling framework (version 2.4); Remote sensing techniques; GIS
Predictors: Market accessibility; Altitude; Road access; Population density; Slope; Soil conditions; Neighborhood composition; Current land use; Ethnicity variations; Risk perception
Data Sources: Remote sensing images (SPOT images for 2001 and 2002); Aerial photographs; National-level land use maps; Extensive field work; 155 structured interviews; Collaboration with local institutes (Isabella State University)
Validation Methods: Not applicable; no validation performed for this specific study
Validation Data Sources: Not applicable; no validation performed for this specific study
Key Findings: Deforestation hot spots identified on Mindanao, Samar, Palawan, and along Sierra Madre mountain range; Northern Sierra Madre National Park under high deforestation pressure; Protected areas on Luzon heavily threatened; Different spatial policies show limited impact on protected areas overall; Landscape-level analysis reveals forest patches in agricultural areas are threatened; Population growth and road network upgrading are main threats to parks
Implications: Simple delineation of park boundaries insufficient for ecosystem preservation; Policies providing incentives to change land use conversion activities more efficient than fences-and-fines approach; Understanding of land use change processes essential for efficient park protection strategies; Trade-offs exist between protecting important parks and impacts on other areas
Limitations: High uncertainty in land use simulations; Empirical approach at national level does not guarantee causality; High spatial and thematic aggregation limits identification of forest remnant clearing; Assumption of homogeneous decision-making throughout regions; Poor match between land-based approach and actual agents of land use change
Future Directions: Strengthening of modeling frameworks separately; Development of overarching insights leading to partial integration; Improvement of application approaches in concrete policy contexts; Need for case study-specific validation; Integration of multi-agent modeling approaches
Scalability: The CLUE-s modeling framework is applicable at different scales and capable of simulating different types of land use change trajectories, though actual configuration depends on case study, dominant processes, and available information
Novelty: Multi-scale modeling approach combining national and landscape levels; Use of CLUE-s framework configured differently for each scale; Integration of empirical-statistical methods at national level with process-based rules at landscape level; Combination of quantitative and narrative research techniques including ethnicity considerations

Title: Change of Cultivated Land and Its Implications on Food Security in China
Authors: Bohua, Yu; Changhe, Lu
Objective: To determine to what extent cultivated land can guarantee food security of China under the heavy pressure of population growth and cultivated land loss
LULC Classes: Cultivated land; urban built-up area; rural built-up area; industrial and special land use; forest; grassland
Scenarios: Three scenarios of population growth defined as Max, Min and Mean, corresponding to the maximum, minimum and average decreasing rate of population growth rate from 1990 to 2003; three cases of urban and rural built-up area per capita: 80m² and 120m², 100m² and 150m², 120m² and 200m²
Analysis Methods: Extrapolation trend line based on consistent data of long time series; regression models; coefficient of determination (R²) for accuracy verification; comparison among linear mode, quadratic polynomial, logarithmic curve, exponent curve, and power curve
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Population growth; urban and rural built-up area per capita; natural disasters; ecological conversion of marginal cropland; land consolidation and reclamation; grain output per unit land area; multiple cropping index; quality index of cultivated land
Data Sources: National statistic yearbooks from 1989 to 2003; Ministry of Labour and Social Security of China; Ministry of Land and Resources of China; Planning of Development and Land Consolidation and Reclamation in China (2001-2010)
Validation Methods: Coefficient of determination (R²) was adopted to indicate accuracy and verify models
Validation Data Sources: Time-series data on food production and cultivated land area from 1989 to 2003
Key Findings: China's food supply can only be maintained at a low to middle level of 370-410kg per capita; China has enough land productivity to meet primary demand of food independently; Cannot reach the safe target of 500kg per capita without breakthrough in breeding or remarkable improvement of irrigation works when grain self-sufficiency maintains no less than 80%; Self-sufficiency rate of grain will be above 92.5% if 400kg per capita is the aim of food security
Implications: Policy of family planning should still be one of national basic policies for a long time; intensive land use is an effective way to increase cultivated land productivity; to breed productive crops and to improve land productivity by meliorating low quality cultivated land are appropriate measures to shrink the gap between food demand and supply
Limitations: Many factors affect cultivated land area and food production directly or indirectly; the paper considered only important and direct driving factors, and some uncertain ones were not included, such as severe disasters, and popularity and extension of high yield seeds, possible effects of global environmental change on food production were not taken into consideration, because of interaction complexity among population, change of cultivated land and food production, the results can only provide a general overview
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Construction of quality index of cultivated land according to different land quality; integration of population growth scenarios with built-up area expansion patterns to assess food security implications

Title: A coherent set of future land use change scenarios for Europe
Authors: Rounsevell, MDA; Reginster, I; Araújo, MB; Carter, TR; Dendoncker, N; Ewert, F; House, JI; Kankaanpää, S; Leemans, R; Metzger, MJ; Schmit, C; Smith, P; Tuck, G
Objective: Develop spatially explicit land-use change scenarios for EU15, Norway and Switzerland based on IPCC-SRES storylines
LULC Classes: urban; cropland; grassland; forest land; bioenergy crops; protected areas; surplus (not actively managed) land
Scenarios: A1FI; A2; B1; B2 (IPCC-SRES)
Analysis Methods: Qualitative interpretation of SRES storylines; aggregate land-use change estimation with sector-specific models; spatial allocation rules on 10-min grid; statistical downscaling to 250 m via multinomial logistic regression suitability modeling; integration of IMAGE 2.2 outputs; urban land-use demand model; supply-demand framework for agriculture; country-group rules for forestry; optimisation and opportunity-cost rules for protected areas
Sim. Method Advantages: Combines qualitative and quantitative drivers; produces spatially explicit outputs; captures land-use competition hierarchy; downscaling method needs no time-series or extensive covariates; integrates cross-sector demands and international trade signals
Tools/Soft Used: IMAGE 2.2 integrated assessment model; urban land-use model (Reginster & Rounsevell); ATEAM mapping/statistical downscaling tool; multinomial logistic regression (GIS/statistical software unspecified)
Predictors: population; GDP; transport accessibility; land-use planning restrictions; relative attractiveness of city sizes; competition from other uses; world supply–demand for agricultural and forest products; EU, WTO and environmental policies; climate change; CO₂ fertilisation; technology progress; land cost proxies (urban density, distance to cities, low-value land); species richness distributions
Data Sources: PELCOM 1 km land-cover dataset; REGIO (Eurostat) NUTS2 statistics; CORINE land-cover map; Gaffin et al. population & GDP projections; IMAGE 2.2 model outputs; HadCM3 climate scenarios; Atlas Florae Europaeae species data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Agricultural cropland and grassland decline markedly in A1FI and A2; bioenergy crops and forest land expand; urban growth is modest but spatially divergent; protected areas reach 20% of Europe by 2080 for different motives; technological change is a dominant driver; large areas of surplus land appear in economic scenarios; local-scale spatial patterns differ greatly despite similar continental totals
Implications: Anticipated land-use shifts will affect ecosystem services, biodiversity and carbon stocks; policy levers on technology, trade and planning will strongly shape Europe’s landscapes; spatial pattern detail is essential for impact assessments
Limitations: Subjective storyline interpretations; uncertainties in model process formulations; inability to validate future scenarios; baseline map inaccuracies; potential errors in statistical downscaling; soft-linked model framework lacks feedbacks
Future Directions: Improve process representation and feedbacks; incorporate land-market dynamics; refine technology assumptions; enhance downscaling with additional observations; extend methodology beyond Europe
Scalability: Approach is transferable to other regions with appropriate regionalisation of drivers and data
Novelty: First coherent, multi-sector, spatially explicit SRES-based land-use scenario set for Europe; introduces bioenergy crops and protected-area allocation; downscales to 250 m resolution for local impact studies

Title: Downscaling of land use change scenarios to assess the dynamics of European landscapes
Authors: Verburg, PH; Schulp, CJE; Witte, N; Veldkamp, A
Country: 25 countries of the European Union (EU25), including 15 older member states (EU15) and 10 accession countries that joined in 2004
Objective: To translate European level scenarios into high resolution assessment of changes in land use patterns using a spatially explicit, dynamic land use change model; to downscale European level land use change assessments to the landscape level and bridge the gap between continental scale assessments and local case studies
LULC Classes: Built-up area; non-irrigated arable land; irrigated arable land; pasture; forests, natural grasslands and other natural areas; inland wetlands; abandoned farm land; other stable land use types (beaches, rocky areas, bare land, glaciers)
Scenarios: Four scenarios based on IPCC SRES framework: A1 (Global Economy), A2 (Continental Market), B1 (Global Co-operation), B2 (Regional Communities), distinguished by different degrees of global market integration and policy regulation levels
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land use change modeling using CLUE-s model; logistic regression analysis; hierarchical modeling approach combining macro-economic (GTAP) and integrated assessment models (IMAGE) with spatially explicit downscaling
Sim. Method Advantages: Flexibility in configuration; ability to specify scenario conditions in detail; widely used and validated by different research groups; based on dynamic simulation of competition between land uses; accounts for spatial and temporal interactions; allows specific driving factors for different countries
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-s model (version 2.3); GTAP macro-economic model; IMAGE integrated assessment model; LEITAP model
Predictors: Accessibility variables (travel time to cities, ports, airports); soil characteristics (agricultural limitations, texture, slope); climate variables (temperature, precipitation); topographic variables (elevation, slope); population density and potential; biogeographical regions; protected areas; erosion risk; less favoured areas
Data Sources: Pan-European database (250m resolution); CORINE land cover database; PELCOM database; GTAP macro-economic model; IMAGE integrated assessment model; GISCO database; ELPEN database; USGS GTOPO30; European Soil Bureau database; WCPA protected areas database
Validation Methods: Not specified (validation was acknowledged as an issue not addressed in the paper)
Validation Data Sources: Not specified (authors noted that proper validation would require consistent European land use data for multiple years)
Key Findings: Large impact of agricultural land abandonment and urbanization on European landscapes; spatial policies can contribute to preserving landscapes with high natural/historic values; path-dependence in land use change trajectories has important impact on resulting landscape patterns; tremendous land use dynamics expected (4.7-8.1% of land area changing between 2000-2030); agricultural abandonment most important change in terms of area
Implications: Results support discussions on future of rural areas; help identify hotspots of landscape change needing specific consideration; provide tools for planners to assess implications of alternative decisions and planning strategies at different spatial scales; demonstrate differential impacts of macro-economic changes on regional land use patterns
Limitations: Representation of landscape changes relatively coarse compared to landscape-level case studies; lack of information on land use intensity; method only addresses changes in land use pattern without additional social and economic impact information; limited country-specific spatial policy representation; validity and uncertainty in downscaling procedure not fully assessed
Future Directions: Further downscaling to fundamental determinants of landscapes including field size, structure, management intensity, and landscape elements; linking landscape change trajectory assessments to current downscaling procedure; developing comprehensive toolbox for discussing Europe's landscape and spatial planning policies
Scalability: The approach provides framework to link local case studies and can be used to assess general validity of case studies across Europe; method allows assessment of differential developments and identification of critical regions; however, driving factors are region-specific and context-dependent
Novelty: First comprehensive European-scale (EU25) downscaling of land use change scenarios to 1km resolution; bridging gap between European-level assessments and local case studies; hierarchical modeling approach combining multiple scales; explicit accounting for path-dependence in land use change trajectories; country-specific parameterization for driving factors

Title: Scenario development to explore the future of Europe's rural areas
Authors: Westhoek, HJ; van den Berg, M; Bakkes, JA
Country: EU-25 (expanded European Union, including EU-15 and EU-10)
Objective: Stimulate strategic discussion among national and EU policy makers on the long-term future of Europe’s rural areas by developing and quantifying contrasting scenarios
LULC Classes: Not specified
Scenarios: Global economy; Global co-operation; Continental markets; Regional communities
Analysis Methods: Strategic scenario development (2×2 matrix)
Sim. Method Advantages: Systematic exploration of critical uncertainties via a simple 2×2 scenario matrix; Consistency across global, European, national and local scales; Leverages and extends existing well-known scenario frameworks for credibility and communication
Tools/Soft Used: Worldscan; GTAP; IMAGE; CLUE
Predictors: GDP growth; demographic development (fertility, mortality, migration); trade policy (tariffs, quotas, standards); technology/productivity parameters; policy assumptions (CAP payments, environmental directives)
Data Sources: CPB Four Futures of Europe macroeconomic data; UN demographic projections, Eurostat (urban/rural shares); GTAP agricultural dataset, IMAGE model parameters; UNEP GEO-3, IPCC-SRES, ATEAM, RIVM Sustainability Outlook, GEO-3 Europe
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Scenario study with contrasting worldviews effectively highlights implications of key uncertainties for rural EU up to 2030; Building on existing scenarios accelerates development and improves stakeholder understanding; Model chain enabled quantification of people-planet-profit impacts across scales
Implications: Policymakers gain long-term, multi-scale insight into rural development trade-offs; Need for causal tracing and sensitivity analysis to link drivers to outcomes; Importance of integrating interactive policy-option analysis in future tools
Limitations: CD presentation overwhelming without guided report; Limited insight into individual driver effects, no stakeholder co-creation; No sensitivity analysis, climate change effects marginally addressed
Future Directions: Enhance causal attribution and sensitivity analyses; Incorporate interactive policy-option simulations and stakeholder processes; Expand model chain to cover non-agricultural rural sectors (e.g., recreation, services)
Scalability: Methodology applicable to other regions given appropriate data; first study covering EU-25 with full spatial downscaling
