Title: Scenarios of land cover in China
Authors: Yue, Tian Xiang; Fan, Ze Meng; Liu, Ji Yuan
Objective: Simulate and analyze land cover scenarios in China for 2039, 2069 and 2099 based on climatic change and human–ecosystem interactions
LULC Classes: cultivated land; woodland; grassland; built-up land; water area; wetland; nival area; desert; bare rock; desertification land
Scenarios: HadCM3A1FI (Scenario I); HadCM3A2 (Scenario II); HadCM3B2 (Scenario III)
Analysis Methods: Holdridge Life Zone classification; transition probability matrices; surface modeling of land cover change (SMLC); spatial pattern metrics (ecotope diversity; patch connectivity; mean center shift)
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates both location and quantity of change in a single stochastic framework; Avoids discontinuity between past observations and future projections inherent in global scenarios; Simple construction of transition matrices between HLZ types and land cover types
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: annual mean biotemperature; annual precipitation; potential evapotranspiration ratio; elevation; Holdridge life zone types
Data Sources: 735 meteorological stations; AVHRR remote-sensing; Landsat TM dataset for accuracy assessment; HadCM3 climatic scenarios; digital elevation model of China
Validation Methods: Accuracy assessment by comparison with Landsat TM–derived land cover dataset
Validation Data Sources: Landsat Thematic Mapper land cover data
Key Findings: Cultivated land decreases, woodland expands, grassland declines, desertification spreads slowly, Nival area shrinks, ecotope diversity declines, patch connectivity increases under all scenarios; Mean centers of cover types shift regionally (e.g., cultivated land shifts southeast then northeast)
Implications: Climate change may aid Grain-for-Green policy by promoting woodland expansion; Need for long-term ecological conservation policies to prevent overexploitation beyond ecosystem regulation capacity
Limitations: Simplification of land cover system focusing primarily on climatic attributes; Lack of integration of socioeconomic, political and detailed human activity data
Future Directions: Incorporate a wider range of social, economic and political variables into SMLC framework
Scalability: Applicable at multiple spatial scales given data availability (IPCC, LUCC datasets)
Novelty: Development of SMLC to jointly address location and quantity of land cover change; Use of HLZ–land cover transition matrices downscaled from HadCM3 scenarios in China

Title: Predicted soil organic carbon stocks and changes in the Brazilian Amazon between 2000 and 2030
Authors: Cerri, C. E. P.; Easter, M.; Paustian, K.; Killian, K.; Coleman, K.; Bernoux, M.; Falloon, P.; Powlson, D. S.; Batjes, N. H.; Milne, E.; Cerri, C. C.
Objective: Predict soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and changes in the Brazilian Amazon between 2000 and 2030
LULC Classes: Native vegetation; well-managed pasture; degraded pasture; conventional tillage soybean; no-tillage soybean; abandoned areas
Scenarios: Business-as-usual deforestation at 2 Mha yr⁻¹; Soybean expansion proportions (60% new deforested area in 2015; 70% in 2030); Pasture management splits (well-managed vs. degrading)
Analysis Methods: Century ecosystem model; RothC soil C decomposition model; IPCC regional soil C method
Sim. Method Advantages: Handles >363,000 biotic-edapho-climatic combinations over ~500 Mha; Integrates spatially explicit soils, climate, vegetation, land management; Generates dynamic past, current, and future SOC estimates (unlike static mapping)
Tools/Soft Used: GEFSOC modelling system; GIS linkage via SOTER map
Predictors: Deforestation rate; census land-use time series (1940–2000); management practice (pasture quality; tillage system); climate (precipitation, temperature); soil hydrology; potential natural vegetation
Data Sources: Pluviometric stations (∼1085 stations, CPTEC/INPE/MCT, INMET, CAMREX, ABRACOS); Native vegetation map (IBGE 1988); Soil map (EMBRAPA 1981, SOTER database); Land cover map (JRC-ISPRA radar 2000); Agricultural census (1940–1995, IPEA); FAO projections (2015, 2030)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: SOC stocks (0–20 cm) mostly 60–80 Mg C ha⁻¹, 0–20 cm stocks decline ~7% by 2030 relative to 1990; Projected 4,200 Tg C soil loss (0–20 cm) 1990–2030 under BAU; Soybean no-tillage adoption increases SOC stocks in agricultural expansion areas; Abandoned areas accumulate SOC (217 Tg C in 1990 to 620 Tg C in 2030); Century yields ~18% higher SOC stocks than RothC but all methods agree on decline
Implications: Quantifies CO₂ emissions from Amazon land-use change for greenhouse inventories; Guides management strategies to enhance pasture/agriculture sustainability and slow deforestation
Limitations: Potential overestimation of SOC gains from no-tillage (surface concentration effect); Scenarios are projections, not forecasts, actual land-use developments may differ
Future Directions: Acquire more field data on tropical SOC dynamics across soil types and climates; Integrate remote sensing and GIS to refine current/future SOC estimates
Scalability: Can be applied to other large regions via GEFSOC’s spatially explicit framework
Novelty: First dynamic SOC estimates under actual land use (pasture and agriculture) in Brazilian Amazon; Integration of three distinct SOC modeling methods within a unified GEFSOC system

Title: Spatial sensitivity of species habitat patterns to scenarios of land use change (Switzerland)
Authors: Bolliger, Janine; Kienast, Felix; Soliva, Reto; Rutherford, Gillian
Objective: Assess potential effects of agricultural decline on spatial distribution of seven open-land species under land-use change scenarios
LULC Classes: Forest; Open forest; Scrub; Non-intensively used open land; Intensively used open land; Other
Scenarios: Business as usual; Liberalisation; Lowered agricultural production (moderate); Lowered agricultural production (strong)
Analysis Methods: Generalized Linear Models (logistic regression with logit link); spatial implementation of transition probabilities; FRAGSTATS landscape metrics; species habitat suitability modelling; ROC/AUC evaluation; 10-fold cross-validation
Sim. Method Advantages: Parsimonious regression suitable for large-scale assessment; integrates socio-economic expert judgments; spatially explicit transitions based on observed probabilities
Tools/Soft Used: GIS for spatial modeling; FRAGSTATS v2.0; SimTest (AUC evaluation)
Predictors: Socio-economic drivers (subsidies, regulations, market prices); Topographic variables (elevation, slope); Climatic variables (frost frequency, degree-day sum, precipitation, water budget, global radiation, Gams angle, cloudiness); Neighbourhood composition
Data Sources: Primary: Swiss land-use data (BFS 1979/85, BFS 1992/97), species presence/absence from CSCF and Swiss Ornithological Institute, interpolated climate surfaces, DEM; Secondary: Expert-derived pseudo-absences, tourism statistics, socio-economic policy reports
Validation Methods: ROC plots; AUC and Gini coefficient; 10-fold cross-validation
Validation Data Sources: Observed species presence/absence (CSCF; Swiss Ornithological Institute)
Key Findings: Business as usual yields minor habitat changes, with gains along valley bottoms and losses at higher elevations; Liberalisation causes severe habitat losses (up to 59%) across all regions, minimal gains (<10%); Lowered agricultural production scenarios increase core habitats (up to 41%) on Plateau and Northern Alps, with limited losses at high elevations; Landscape under lowered conservation scenario shows highest patch diversity and fragmentation, liberalisation yields aggregation and homogenisation
Implications: Maintaining non-intensively used open land is crucial for open-land species; policy linking subsidies to agri-environmental schemes can balance agriculture and biodiversity conservation; stakeholder acceptance favors business as usual combined with targeted conservation
Limitations: Temporal dimension of scenario timelines imprecise; regression models omit dynamic biotic interactions and dispersal; scale-invariant socio-economic drivers may mask fine-scale local processes
Future Directions: Incorporate temporal dynamics explicitly; test alternative modeling approaches (e.g., agent-based models); integrate genetic/adaptive responses; stakeholder participatory scenario development
Scalability: Applicable to other European mountainous regions with similar socio-economic and topographic gradients, pending local data calibration
Novelty: Integration of socio-economic expert-driven land-use scenarios with species habitat suitability modeling; spatially explicit implementation of transition probabilities combined with FRAGSTATS analysis for open-land species under diverging policy scenarios

Title: Exploring spatial data uncertainties in land-use change scenarios
Authors: Dendoncker, N.; Schmit, C.; Rounsevell, M.
Journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHICAL INFORMATION SCIENCE
Objective: This paper evaluates errors and uncertainties in representing landscapes that arise from different data rasterization methods, spatial resolutions, and downscaled land-use change (LUC) scenarios
LULC Classes: Urban; cropland; grassland; forest; others (mostly water and bare rocks); bioenergy crops (liquid, non-woody and woody); surplus (abandoned land)
Scenarios: A1 (global, economically oriented world); A2 (regional, economically oriented world); B1 (globalized, but environmentally concerned world); B2 (regional, environmentally concerned world) - based on IPCC/SRES storylines
Analysis Methods: Vector to raster conversion using three cell class assignment methods (point method, majority method, adjusted method); statistical downscaling using multinomial logistic regression (MNLR); landscape metrics analysis using FRAGSTATS; analysis of variance (ANOVA)
Sim. Method Advantages: The statistical downscaling method allows uncertainties arising from the downscaling methodology to be given by probability distributions; the method provides initial probability maps of land-use presence for each LU class
Tools/Soft Used: GIS software for rasterization; FRAGSTATS (Version 3.3) for landscape metrics computation; Microsoft Excel macro 'kappapontius1.xls' for confusion matrix analysis
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: Primary: Occupation Biophysique des Sols du Grand-Duché de Luxembourg (OBSLUX vector); large-scale vector map derived from aerial photographs and ground-truthing, Secondary: ATEAM project LUC scenarios, PELCOM dataset, CORINE land cover datasets
Validation Methods: Confusion matrices comparing original baseline OBSLUX rasters with predicted LU; evaluation of disagreement due to quantity and location; accuracy statistics including User's Accuracy and Producer's Accuracy
Validation Data Sources: Original baseline OBSLUX raster datasets used as reference for comparing predicted land use from MNLR models
Key Findings: Differences in landscape composition and configuration between the three cell class assignment methods and three spatial resolutions were found to be at least as large as the differences between the LUC scenarios; the majority method underestimates minor LU classes by more than 30% as cell size increases; the point method produces much more fragmented landscapes than other methods; rasterization method accounts for 63-93.7% of total variation in landscape metrics while LUC scenarios only account for 3.2-35.7%
Implications: The choice of rasterization method and spatial resolution contributes significantly to uncertainty when developing future LUC scenarios and analyzing landscape structure in ecological studies; maps of future scenarios may reflect data artefacts rather than providing insights into the future; care should be taken when using these methods for policy applications
Limitations: Impossible to disentangle effects of uncertainty from downscaling algorithm from other sources of uncertainty for year 2050; the study did not examine all sources of uncertainty including grid orientation and origin variations; the downscaling method tends to create more aggregated and less fragmented landscape patterns than baseline datasets
Future Directions: Need for full analysis of uncertainty including grid orientation and origin variations; exploration of different downscaling algorithms; development of methods to better quantify uncertainties arising from dataset choice
Scalability: The methodology can be applied to other regions, though the specific findings about rasterization effects may vary depending on landscape characteristics and data quality
Novelty: First comprehensive evaluation of how different rasterization methods and spatial resolutions affect landscape pattern analysis in the context of land-use change scenarios; demonstration that data processing artifacts can exceed actual scenario differences in terms of landscape metrics

Title: Modelling the impact of telecommuting on future urbanisation in the Netherlands
Authors: Muhammad, Saim; Ottens, Henk F. L.; De Jong, Tom
Journal: TIJDSCHRIFT VOOR ECONOMISCHE EN SOCIALE GEOGRAFIE
Objective: To explore how the mass use of ICTs will change people's socioeconomic characteristics and the effects those changes can be expected to have on the pattern of locations for new residential land, analyzing resulting changes in future urbanisation patterns
LULC Classes: Low density residential areas (LDRAs, defined as having population density less than 6,600 inhabitants per square kilometre); High density residential areas (HDRAs, over 6,600 inhabitants per square kilometre)
Scenarios: Physical Space Scenario (PSS) - assumes no tangible effects of ICTs on locational behaviour of employed people; Hybrid Space Scenario (HSS) - assumes ICTs affect spatial residential preferences and spatial policies
Analysis Methods: Hybrid approach combining cellular automata module; weighted overlay module; land-use allocation module; spatial clumpiness index (SCI) for pattern analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: The dedicated approach was developed to overcome limitations of the Environment Explorer (EE) model, particularly its inability to handle detailed job accessibility at 1308 LMS sub-zones level and its restriction to COROP regional allocation which was unsuitable for hybrid space scenario analysis
Tools/Soft Used: Specially designed linked models combining cellular automata, weighted overlay, and land-use allocation modules; spatial statistical methods including spatial clumpiness index
Predictors: Job accessibility (weight 0.6); land-use transition potential (weight 0.2); land-use zoning policies (weight 0.1); physical suitability (weight 0.1)
Data Sources: Netherlands Environment Assessment Agency; Transport Research Centre (AVV); Dutch residential preferences survey commissioned by VROM (2002); LMS transportation model data; existing Environment Explorer application data
Validation Methods: The neighbourhood land-use transition rules were calibrated for changes between 1989 and 1993 and validated for the year 2000
Validation Data Sources: Existing Environment Explorer application operational at Netherlands Environment Assessment Agency
Key Findings: Urban decentralisation and deconcentration are likely to accelerate because of increasing telecommuting; attractive regions at medium distances from large cities will face new urban pressure of sprawling nature; Randstad expansion will occur both inwards into Green Heart and outwards towards south and east; Utrecht-Arnhem-Gorinchem triangle identified as hotspot for future urbanisation
Implications: Urban policies need to be reconsidered to cope with new spatial development trends; complete revision of current urban policies not necessary but awareness and timely adaptation of spatial visions recommended; telecommuting will increase pressure for clustered and sprawling urban deconcentration at local and regional scales
Limitations: The study acknowledges that model-based projections of future effects of telecommuting on Dutch urbanisation patterns had not been carried out previously; the Environment Explorer model had severe limitations for detailed accessibility analysis required for this research
Future Directions: Monitoring and timely adaptation of spatial visions and strategies is highly recommended; need for dedicated planning support systems that fit information needs and available data for particular applications
Scalability: The study suggests the combined approach of modular hybrid allocation model and landscape statistics technique proved useful and could be applied elsewhere, though the specific focus on Dutch spatial planning context may limit direct transferability
Novelty: First model-based projection of telecommuting effects on Dutch urbanisation patterns; development of dedicated residential land-use projection model overcoming limitations of existing Environment Explorer model; integration of virtual space accessibility concepts into land-use modeling; application of spatial clumpiness index for urban pattern analysis

Title: A multi-scale, multi-model approach for analyzing the future dynamics of European land use
Authors: Verburg, Peter H.; Eickhout, Bas; van Meijl, Hans
Objective: Quantify and explore future European land-use dynamics by linking global, national and local scale models in scenario-based simulations
LULC Classes: dryland arable agriculture; irrigated agriculture; grassland; abandoned agricultural land; built-up area; natural vegetation (including production forest, inland wetlands); miscellaneous land types
Scenarios: Global Economy (A1); Continental Markets (A2); Global Co-operation (B1); Regional Communities (B2)
Analysis Methods: Global economy modelling (GTAP CGE); Integrated assessment (IMAGE); Spatially explicit allocation (CLUE-s); Logistic regression for location suitability
Sim. Method Advantages: Addresses processes across global–national–landscape scales; Integrates economic and environmental feedbacks iteratively; High spatial resolution (1 km²) captures hotspots and pattern heterogeneity
Tools/Soft Used: GTAP model; IMAGE model; CLUE-s version 2.4; logistic regression analysis
Predictors: accessibility; soil and geomorphology; climate variables; population density; altitude; proximity to existing land uses; policy-specific suitability rules; neighborhood effects
Data Sources: GTAP input–output tables, OECD Policy Evaluation Model structure; IPCC SRES storylines, Bollen et al. (energy emissions); Demographic and GDP projections, land-cover maps for calibration
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Africa faces major global agricultural expansion by 2030, Europe sees modest decreases overall; EU-25 agricultural area declines in all but Continental Markets (A2); Land abandonment concentrates in marginal/mountainous and high-demand urban regions; Scenario-driven spatial patterns vary markedly, revealing critical “hot-spots”
Implications: Spatially explicit scenarios essential for targeted policy design; Highlights trade-offs between European land use and global impacts; Informs biodiversity, carbon and landscape management strategies
Limitations: Uncertainties and error propagation across linked models; Coarse socio-economic resolution outside Europe; Yield impacts averaged at country scale
Future Directions: Incorporate finer regional climate impacts and ecological models; Enhance coupling and dynamic feedback between modules; Extend methodology to other world regions and land-use sectors
Scalability: Approach is adaptable and transferable to other regions and scales
Novelty: First integration of GTAP, IMAGE and CLUE-s across scales for Europe; combines economic, environmental and spatial allocation in an iteratively coupled framework

Title: Characterising urban concentration and land-use diversity in simulations of future land use
Authors: van Eck, Jan Ritsema; Koomen, Eric
Objective: To present and test functional indicators for assessment of spatial aspects of future land-use configurations as simulated by a land-use model for ex-ante evaluation of spatial planning policies
LULC Classes: water; nature/woodland; agricultural nature management; grassland; arable land; greenhouses; intensive livestock keeping; recreational areas; rural residential land; urban residential land; commercial land; railroads; roads; airports
Scenarios: Individualistic World; Cooperating Region
Analysis Methods: Land Use Scanner model; logit-type approach; discrete choice theory; spatial configuration metrics; patch-size distribution analysis; circularity ratio; Simpson's diversity index
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates and allocates future land-use claims from different sector-specific models rather than forecasting dimensions of change; employs logit-type approach based on economic rationale resembling actual land market functioning
Tools/Soft Used: Land Use Scanner; GIS-based modeling system; FRAGSTATS
Predictors: Location characteristics including physical properties; operative policies; relations to nearby land-use functions; suitability maps for different land-use types
Data Sources: Statistics Netherlands (1996); sector-specific models; expert judgement; Agricultural Economics Research Institute land-market model; policy documents
Validation Methods: Tested indicators in Dutch case study; applied to simulations based on two scenarios
Validation Data Sources: Scenario simulations for Netherlands up to 2030
Key Findings: Urban population density varies significantly between scenarios (24.7 inhabitants/ha in Individualistic World vs 30.0 in Cooperating Region); Cooperating Region scenario shows strongest concentration with smallest number and largest mean size of urban areas; Average circularity of urban areas decreases in both scenarios, more severely in Individualistic World; Combined application of land-use models and indicators produces new and potentially useful information for policy makers; Total urbanised area grows to 17% in Individualistic World vs 15% in Cooperating Region; Urban areas become more monofunctional in cities while agricultural areas become more mixed; Size-independent circularity ratio shows negative correlation with urban area size
Implications: Indicators provide useful tool for ex-ante evaluation of spatial planning policies; Results can inform locally targeted policy measures to counteract negative consequences of general developments; Stronger emphasis on economic development with less restrictive spatial policies may lead to more extensive urbanisation threatening natural and recreational values; Maps show where spatial problems are most likely to occur
Limitations: Model and associated indicators still in development; Scenario simulation results heavily reliant on expert judgement; Validity questionable due to scenario approach; Circularity ratio must be used with caution due to size dependency; Exact implementation may have large influence on results; Scale (spatial, thematic, extent) crucial in application and interpretation
Future Directions: Further development of model and indicators; Policy themes should dictate indicator implementation; Scale considerations should be addressed early in implementation phase
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Combined application of land-use models and functional indicators, Use of heterogeneous grid cells describing relative proportion of land-use types, Non-typical data representation poses special challenges but provides detailed assessment capability; The study represents a significant contribution to spatial planning methodology by developing and testing functional indicators for evaluating future land-use configurations. The research demonstrates the potential of combining land-use modeling with spatial indicators to support evidence-based planning decisions, particularly relevant for compact urbanization policies in the Netherlands.

Title: Internalising the costs of fragmentation and nutrient deposition in spatial planning: Extending a decision support tool for the Netherlands
Authors: Eppink, Florian V.; Rietveld, Piet; van den Bergh, Jeroen C. J. M.; Vermaat, Jan E.; Wassen, Martin J.; Hilferink, Maarten
Objective: Internalise environmental externalities (nitrogen deposition and habitat fragmentation) into the Land Use Scanner decision-support tool to assess their impacts on spatial land‐use allocation
LULC Classes: Landscape management; Arable land; Intensive livestock farming; Bio-industry; Fifteen additional land‐use types (total 19)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit economic‐equilibrium modeling; Probabilistic bid-rent allocation; Discrete grid‐cell allocation; Sensitivity analysis of tax/subsidy rates
Sim. Method Advantages: Emphasises ecological process impacts rather than static species maps; Accounts for competition among multiple land‐use and habitat types in one equilibrium; Discrete allocation maximises summed suitability and yields accurate shadow prices
Tools/Soft Used: Land Use Scanner (LUS)
Predictors: Foregone agricultural revenues; Distance to major transport hubs; Infrastructure noise levels; Groundwater‐table depth; Soil type; Policy weighting parameters
Data Sources: IPCC‐based socioeconomic scenarios (de Mooij & Tang 2003, Lejour 2003); ‘Spatial Impressions’ parameterisation (Borsboom-van Beurden et al. 2005); OPS model source–receptor matrices for N-deposition (van Hinsberg et al. 2004); Management-cost estimates (de Jong et al. 2004); Willingness-to-pay fragmentation values (van der Heide 2005)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: B2 (centralistic/regional) yields lowest fragmentation for four of eight habitat types, A1 (individualistic/global) the highest fragmentation; Rain-fed mires and bogs, peat meadows and coniferous forests are most susceptible to fragmentation under market-oriented scenarios; Internalising N-deposition and fragmentation has limited impact on total land‐use volumes due to binding minimum‐demand constraints; High damage‐cost parameters induce substantial spatial reallocations of agricultural uses, especially between livestock farming and landscape management; Subsidies for reduced fragmentation yield greater net land‐value gains than taxes on N-deposition
Implications: Market‐based instruments can improve land‐use efficiency but must be calibrated to externality magnitudes; Taxing land uses that fragment habitats may be more effective than subsidising habitat agglomeration; Model extension demonstrates feasibility of internalising multiple externalities in spatial planning tools
Limitations: Monetisation of externalities is uncertain (parameter sensitivity); Habitat types are aggregated, species‐specific dispersal not modelled; Model calibration reflects historical contexts without externalities; Only two externalities considered, other impacts (water quality, groundwater) omitted
Future Directions: Incorporate additional externalities (water quality, groundwater impacts); Increase spatial resolution to allow finer habitat typology and species data; Local fine-tuning of policy instruments and suitability weights
Scalability: Can be applied to other regions or countries provided requisite biophysical, socioeconomic and policy data are available
Novelty: Integration of environmental externalities directly into an economic‐equilibrium land‐use allocation model; Emphasis on ecological process impacts (fragmentation, nutrient deposition) rather than static habitat suitability or reserve-selection models

Title: The use of aridity index to assess implications of climatic change for land cover in Turkey
Authors: Onder, Derya; Aydin, Mehmet; Berberoglu, Sueha; Onder, Sermet; Yano, Tomohisa
Journal: TURKISH JOURNAL OF AGRICULTURE AND FORESTRY
Objective: Determine impacts of climate change on aridity and land cover in Turkey
LULC Classes: Evergreen needle-leaf forest; Mixed forest; Deciduous broadleaf forest; Agriculture; Bare-ground; Water surface
Scenarios: SRES A2 scenario
Analysis Methods: Penman–Monteith equation via CROPWAT model for ETo; Aridity index (P/ETo) computation; Kriging and cokriging interpolation (GIS-based geostatistics); Classification tree modelling for land cover
Sim. Method Advantages: RCM provides higher horizontal resolution (25 km) than GCMs for regional climate change projections
Tools/Soft Used: CROPWAT; GIS with kriging/cokriging; Classification tree algorithms
Predictors: DEM; Aspect; Latitude; Distance to sea; Aridity index
Data Sources: Primary: Measured climate data from Turkish State Meteorological Service (DMI); Secondary: RCM outputs (MRI/RCM), MODIS land cover map (Gülbeyaz 2007), DEM layers
Validation Methods: Accuracy assessment via confusion matrix
Validation Data Sources: MODIS-derived reference land cover data
Key Findings: Temperature rise of 2.8–5.5 °C by 2070s; Precipitation decrease of 29.6% in southern Mediterranean coast, increase of 22.0% on Black Sea coast; ETo increase by 17.8% countrywide; Increased aridity across most of Turkey except northeast; Predicted shift from deciduous broadleaf to evergreen needle-leaf forest on northern coasts; Expansion of mixed forest in interior East Anatolia and northwest.
Implications: Risk to crop production and water resources due to higher aridity; Need for long-term vegetation monitoring and adaptation strategies
Limitations: AI does not account for soil variability; Assumes equilibrium of natural vegetation without human interference.
Future Directions: Apply additional global and regional climate models for higher confidence; Develop adaptation strategies for agriculture and ecosystems; Long-term monitoring of vegetation changes.
Scalability: Method can be applied to other semi-arid regions using RCM and aridity index approach
Novelty: Integration of RCM-derived aridity index with classification tree modelling for land cover prediction under climate change conditions

Title: National housing and impervious surface scenarios for integrated climate impact assessments
Authors: Bierwagen, Britta G.; Theobald, David M.; Pyke, Christopher R.; Choate, Anne; Groth, Philip; Thomas, John V.; Morefield, Philip
Journal: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Objective: To develop novel national scenarios of housing density and impervious surface cover that are logically consistent with greenhouse gas emissions storylines for integrated climate impact assessments
LULC Classes: Urban (≤1/4 acre per housing unit); suburban (1/4 acre to 1.68 acres per housing unit); exurban (1.6-40 acres per unit); rural; developed open space; transitional; wildland vegetation; agricultural; wetlands
Scenarios: Base case (BC); A1 (fast economic growth, low fertility, high global integration); A2 (regional focus, high fertility, high domestic migration); B1 (environmental focus, low fertility, low domestic migration); B2 (regional and sustainability focus, medium fertility, low migration)
Analysis Methods: Cohort-component population growth model; spatial interaction model (gravity model); Spatially Explicit Regional Growth Model (SERGoM); regression tree modeling for impervious surface estimation
Sim. Method Advantages: Provides national coverage at 1 ha resolution; incorporates demographic drivers and spatial allocation; consistent with international greenhouse gas emissions storylines; transparent modeling framework
Tools/Soft Used: Spatially Explicit Regional Growth Model (SERGoM) v1.2; regression tree modeling; spatial interaction modeling
Predictors: Population growth rates; fertility rates; international and domestic migration; household size; travel time from urban cores; land ownership patterns; environmental amenities (January and July temperatures, January sunlight, July relative humidity, percent water area); county population growth rates as economic proxy
Data Sources: US Census Bureau projections; National Center for Health Statistics population estimates; Public Use Microdata Sample files; National Land Cover Dataset; Percent Urban Impervious NLCD 2001 dataset; land ownership data; transportation data; groundwater well density data
Validation Methods: Linear regression comparison with ground-truth datasets; tenfold cross-validation for regression tree model; comparison with high-resolution aerial photography data
Validation Data Sources: National dataset of 80 points from 13 major urban centers (2000); 56 watersheds in Maryland (1989); 13 watersheds in Atlanta metro area (1999); Wadeable Streams Assessment reference sites
Key Findings: Urban areas expected to increase by 74-164% and suburban areas by 59-154% by 2100; A2 scenario results in largest changes with >190,000 km² of new residential development; compact development patterns (B1, B2) reduce habitat loss and watershed impairment; number of stressed watersheds projected to increase from 124 (2000) to 193-274 (2100); wetlands most affected by percent area, agricultural lands most affected by total area
Implications: Compact development patterns can reduce habitat loss and number of impaired watersheds; combinations of climate and land use changes important for environmental conditions regulated under Clean Air and Clean Water Acts; development trajectories consistent with A2 make environmental objectives more challenging; B1 patterns more successful for meeting environmental objectives
Limitations: Should not be used at scales below state or multistate region despite 1 ha resolution; scenarios are interpretations, not predictions; fertility rate uncertainty; model based on 1990-2000 growth patterns, doesn't incorporate recent economic recession effects; uncertainty about land protection activities and transportation improvements
Future Directions: Better incorporate direct linkages and feedbacks between land use patterns and climatic processes; analyze combinations of best management practices; extend modeling approach to other countries or globally; develop temporally dynamic demographic parameters for rapidly developing economies
Scalability: Extension to other countries would require simplifying assumptions about growth rates and migration patterns, coarser resolution spatial datasets, and temporally dynamic demographic parameters
Novelty: First national scenarios of housing density and impervious surface cover logically consistent with SRES emissions storylines; integration of demographic modeling with spatial allocation at national scale and 1 ha resolution; transparent modeling framework for integrated climate-land use assessments

Title: Spatially explicit scenario analysis for reconciling agricultural expansion, forest protection, and carbon conservation in Indonesia
Authors: Koh, Lian Pin; Ghazoul, Jaboury
Journal: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Objective: model outcomes of alternative development scenarios to reconcile agricultural expansion, forest protection, and carbon conservation in Indonesia
LULC Classes: airport; barren land; brush; cloud; dry land agriculture mixed with brush; dry land agriculture; estate company; fishpond; mining areas; paddy field; primary dry land forest; primary mangrove forest; primary swamp forest; savanna; secondary dry land forest; secondary mangrove forest; secondary swamp forest; settlement; swamp brush; swamp; timber estate
Scenarios: business-as-usual; food production; forest preservation; carbon conservation; hybrid approach
Analysis Methods: multiple-scenario spatially explicit computer model; GIS overlay of land-cover, carbon, and yield data; matrix-calibrated species-area model; generalized linear model for productivity validation
Sim. Method Advantages: hybrid approach provides a more nuanced, multi-criteria spatial strategy that avoids forest and biodiversity loss while minimizing carbon and food trade-offs compared with single-priority methods
Tools/Soft Used: GIS software; generalized linear models; species-area modeling; custom simulation code
Predictors: potential oil-palm productivity; potential rice yield; habitat quality (forest integrity); biomass carbon stock; peat soil carbon stock; land suitability classes
Data Sources: World Resources Institute land-cover dataset; Sekala/Indonesian Ministry of Forestry peat atlas; Landsat 7 ETM+ imagery; Ruesch & Gibbs biomass carbon map; Fischer et al. (2001) agro-ecological suitability data; Watling & Donnelly and Sodhi et al. biodiversity data; FAO and UN population projections
Validation Methods: generalized linear model fitting of potential oil-palm productivity against current estate locations
Validation Data Sources: Sumatra GIS data on existing oil-palm estates (n = 128,440 polygons)
Key Findings: hybrid scenario allowed doubling oil-palm production on 3.43 M ha of degraded/agricultural lands without forest or biodiversity loss; limited net carbon loss (191.6 Mt) and small rice production loss (1.9 Mt); single-priority scenarios entailed substantial trade-offs in carbon, biodiversity, or food capacity
Implications: demonstrates feasibility of spatially explicit multi-criteria land-use planning to meet production and conservation goals; informs sustainable development policy choices
Limitations: simplifying assumptions on complete carbon loss upon conversion; assumed degraded land sensitivity equal to agricultural; excluded downstream processing and broader ecosystem services; did not model indirect land-use leakages explicitly
Future Directions: integrate valuation of additional ecosystem services; incorporate socioeconomic and land-tenure factors; model indirect land-use change and leakage; extend to other commodities
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: spatially explicit hybrid multi-criteria scenario analysis combining production, food, forest, biodiversity, and carbon objectives into a single simulation framework

Title: CLIMATE CHANGE AND FUTURE LAND USE IN THE UNITED STATES: AN ECONOMIC APPROACH
Authors: Haim, David; Alig, Ralph J.; Plantinga, Andrew J.; Sohngen, Brent
Objective: To project regional and national land-use changes in the United States under two IPCC emissions scenarios using an econometric land-use model driven by county-level measures of net returns to five major land uses
LULC Classes: Crop; pasture; forest; range; urban; cropland enrolled in the Conservation Reserve Program (CRP)
Scenarios: A1 and A2 IPCC emissions scenarios; A1b and A2b for agricultural and forestry yield changes; baseline scenarios with no climate change effects
Analysis Methods: Econometric land-use model; nested logit model; county-level net returns analysis; statistical model of urban net returns; MAPSS ecological model for yield projections
Sim. Method Advantages: Enables regional land-use projections that account for high degree of heterogeneity among determinants of land use; provides critical link between private land-use decisions and IPCC emissions scenarios through county-level net returns
Tools/Soft Used: MAPSS model for ecological projections; three climate models (CSIRO, MIROC, and HADLEY)
Predictors: County-level net returns to five major land uses; land quality rating (Land Capability Class); population and income changes; agricultural prices; agricultural and forestry yields; lagged land use from previous period
Data Sources: National Resources Inventory (NRI) 1992-1997; Woods and Poole Economics county projections to 2030; U.S. Census Bureau; Regional Economic Information System; MAPSS model outputs; various private and public sources for net returns construction
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Large increases in urban land projected under both scenarios (85 to 225 million acres under A1, 183 million acres under A2); largest declines in cropland area; significant regional differences in land-use change patterns; forest expansion in Mountain and Plains regions with declines elsewhere; climate change effects on prices and yields have relatively small influence compared to urbanization
Implications: Future land-use patterns in the U.S. will be shaped largely by urbanization rather than climate change; demographic changes have larger effects on future land use than climate-related changes within agricultural and forest sectors; regional downscaling reveals important spatial heterogeneity masked by national-level projections
Limitations: Unable to account for all potential impacts of climate change on land use; no modeling of feedbacks into global models; not integrated with IAMs used to produce IPCC scenarios; limited representation of extreme temperature events; potential over-prediction of urban area expansion due to lack of endogenous demand-side responses
Future Directions: Full integration of regional models with global climate and economy models; investigation of yield variation effects on land-use decisions; modeling of feedbacks from regional outcomes to Integrated Assessment Models; examination of extreme temperature events impact; refinement for more disaggregated county-level results
Scalability: Methods can be refined to allow for more disaggregated results at finer scales such as counties; downscaling approach represents important step toward coupling global IAMs with regional-scale models
Novelty: Downscaling of IPCC climate change scenarios to regional land-use projections; linking of county-level net returns to global climate scenarios; integration of economic approach with ecological modeling results at disaggregated spatial scale

Title: Dangerous levels of climate change for agricultural production in China
Authors: Tao, Fulu; Zhang, Zhao; Yokozawa, Masayuki
Objective: use water stress index (WSI) and agricultural net primary production (NPP) as indicators to assess where and when projected climate changes may pose dangerous effects for Chinese agricultural production
LULC Classes: cropland
Scenarios: IPCC SRES A2; IPCC SRES B2
Analysis Methods: calculation of WSI via crop-specific water-balance model; estimation of agricultural NPP using Chikugo and Miami models; spatial mapping and inter-annual variability analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: HadCM3 climate model outputs under SRES A2/B2; CRU surface climatology (precipitation, temperature, radiation, vapor pressure, wind speed); FAO/IIASA WSI threshold; crop-specific water-balance model; Chikugo and Miami NPP models
Validation Methods: comparison of NPP inter-annual variability between Chikugo and Miami models
Validation Data Sources: Miami model outputs
Key Findings: the North China Plain–Northeast China Plain region (34.25–47.75°N, 110.25–126.25°E) is most vulnerable; critical drought period projected for 2021–2040 under A2 (GMT + 1.6 °C); agricultural NPP generally increases through 2001–2080 but may decline during 2005–2035 (A2) and 2025–2035 (B2)
Implications: projected climate change can both improve and critically harm water resources for Chinese agriculture, threatening rain-fed crop viability and food security
Limitations: uncertainty in long-term CO₂ fertilization effects; lack of integration of socio-economic and trade modules; extreme event impacts not quantified
Future Directions: develop integrated assessment models incorporating socio-economic, agricultural production, and food-trade modules to identify impact thresholds
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: application of combined WSI and NPP indicators to define spatial and temporal thresholds of dangerous climate impacts on agriculture in China

Title: Measuring and Assessing Urban Sprawl: What are the Remaining Options for Future Settlement Development in Switzerland for 2030?
Authors: Hayek, Ulrike Wissen; Jaeger, Jochen A. G.; Schwick, Christian; Jarne, Alain; Schuler, Martin
Objective: To assess the informative value of new urban sprawl metrics in order to provide planners and decision makers with indications on settlement areas that are particularly exposed to urban sprawl, using Switzerland as an example; analyze by how much settlement will potentially increase in Switzerland by 2030 according to four scenarios and evaluate if the metrics provide useful evidence for characterizing and assessing the nature of settlement dispersion
LULC Classes: Settlement areas; designated building zones; agriculture zones; water bodies; forests; mountainous areas; steep areas; unproductive areas
Scenarios: Four alternative scenarios: A "Spatial Dispersion" (individualistic society with tied back productivity); B "Metropolitan Expansion" (individualistic society with high productivity and global integration); C "Urban and Rural" (regional balance and cohesion with tied back productivity); D "Spatial Equality" (regional balance and cohesion with high productivity and dynamics)
Analysis Methods: Global Business Network (GBS) matrix approach for scenario development; spatially explicit settlement growth model; shift and share approach for job development projection; four urban sprawl metrics calculation (Urban Permeation, Urban Dispersion, Total Sprawl, Sprawl Per Capita); URSMEC (URban Sprawl MEtrics Calculation) tool; step-wise interpretation approach combining quantitative results with qualitative scenario information
Sim. Method Advantages: Major advantages include ability to integrate statistical data, spatially-explicit land-use data, and qualitative expert knowledge; allows for comparison between scenarios using quantitative means; meets 13 suitability criteria ensuring systematic evaluation and understanding of landscape metrics behavior
Tools/Soft Used: URSMEC (URban Sprawl MEtrics Calculation) tool; GIS programs (ArcMap ESRI); settlement distribution tool; Microsoft Excel for calculations; ASCII grid data processing
Predictors: Population size and distribution; number of jobs; settlement area per person and job according to municipality type; people's preferences regarding densification in metropolitan, sub- or peri-urban, and peripheral areas; expert-based index summarizing spatially explicit assumptions about constraints in spatial settlement dispersion
Data Sources: Detailed settlement mapping from Swiss ordnance survey (1:25,000; minimum mapping unit 15m×15m); designated building zones data; population and job statistics from Swiss Federal Statistical Office (BFS 2006) and Ecoplan (2005); harmonised GIS-database of designated building zones from all 26 Swiss cantons
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Overall in Switzerland, urban permeation and dispersion of settlement areas is likely to increase in all scenarios but to different degrees; results differ significantly between settlement types and cantons; individualistic scenarios (A and B) show higher urban permeation than social scenarios (C and D); metropolitan centres and agglomerations show disproportionately high growth in urban permeation; some regions could even experience decrease in urban dispersion; dispersion values indicate continuing trend towards random distribution in all scenarios; different settlement types require different strategies for managing future settlement area growth
Implications: Need for calibration of indicators on regional level to define specific thresholds to limit urban sprawl; various settlement types need different strategies for managing future growth; metrics provide useful evidence on regional characteristics and settlement development pressure; landscape structure, socio-historically evolved settlement forms, and designated building zones greatly influence metric values requiring region-specific calibration
Limitations: Modeling results are not prognosis but images depicting potential alternative spatial layouts; generalized urban growth model does not account for individual development patterns for each municipality; no principles on settlement development shape are integrated; scenarios may be too dispersed and disregard relevant settlement development mechanisms; large number of scenario-related assumptions and generalizations prevent direct policy recommendation derivation
Future Directions: Study landscape conditions through 3D landscape visualizations as next step; combine metrics with additional indicators for view and ecological impairment assessment; integrate visual and non-visual landscape information; combine with indicators of urban growth pressure such as land-market activity measures and other driving forces; test effects of alternative patterns based on societal values
Scalability: Limited explicit discussion, but methodology appears transferable to other regions with appropriate calibration and adaptation to local settlement types and landscape characteristics
Novelty: Application of new urban sprawl metrics that meet 13 suitability criteria; combination of qualitative scenario development with quantitative spatial modeling; integration of expert knowledge with statistical and spatial data; systematic evaluation of urban sprawl using multiple complementary metrics; focus on core phenomenon of urban sprawl considering both amount and dispersion of urban areas

Title: Predicting hot-spots of land use changes in Italy by ensemble forecasting
Authors: Santini, Monia; Valentini, Riccardo
Objective: To predict hot-spots of land use changes in Italy for the end of 21st century using ensemble forecasting through a modified version of the CLUE-S model, evaluating reasonable hot-spots derived from the agreement of a 32 simulation ensemble
LULC Classes: Artificial surfaces; Arable land; Permanent crops; Pastures; Heterogeneous agricultural areas; Land principally occupied by agriculture with significant areas of natural vegetation; Agro-forestry areas; Forests; Natural grasslands, moors and heathland; Sclerophyllous vegetation; Transitional woodland-shrub; Open spaces with little or no vegetation; Glaciers and perpetual snow; Inland wetlands
Baseline Years: 2000 (primary baseline), with historical data from 1990 and 1956-1968
Scenarios: Two climate projections (A2 and B2 emission scenarios by IPCC); Two demographic scenarios (central and high demographic increase); Conservation or not of protected areas; Spatial influence among adjacent land uses; Importance of past/recent LUC trends
Analysis Methods: Modified CLUE-S model (LUC@CMCC); Ensemble forecasting; Stepwise logistic regression; ROC analysis; Markov Chain algorithm for transition probabilities; Spatial and temporal influence modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: Ensemble forecasting allows considering a wide array of possible developments and their implied uncertainties; Each individual simulation may not contain the most likely prospects, but as a whole, simulations suggest the range of possible changes; Overcomes difficulties in single plausible LUC projections relying on robust model calibration/validation
Tools/Soft Used: LUC@CMCC model (developed using Fortran90 programming language); CLUE-S model framework
Predictors: Soil characteristics (carbon content, clay content, density, depth, field capacity, pH, sand content, silt content); Climate variables (mean annual rainfall, mean annual temperature); Socio-economic factors (population density, labor force in agriculture/industry/institutions/commerce); Accessibility factors (distance to cities); Topographic variables (elevation, slope, aspect, topographic index)
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover datasets (1990, 2000); European Soil Database; MARS-STAT database; National Institute of Statistics; SRTM data; River and Catchment database; PRUDENCE project climate data
Validation Methods: ROC analysis (Receiving Operating Characteristic test); Area Under the Curve (AUC) calculation; Stepwise logistic regression validation using split datasets (50% for calibration, 50% for validation)
Validation Data Sources: Split sample validation using CORINE Land Cover datasets; Independent validation using remaining 50% of sample not used in logistic regression
Key Findings: South and Islands are the most LUC-prone areas; Future land use substitution trends will be partially opposite to the past; More than half of future changes (58.5%) forecasted to consist of conversions from scrub/herbaceous vegetation to artificial areas (11.6%) or forests (12.4%), and from arable lands to permanent crops (15.4%) or artificial areas (19.1%); Mediterranean biogeographical region will be most affected (10.8% changes) compared to Alpine (7.9%) and Continental (3.9%) regions
Implications: Results should be considered in landscape and resource planning; Hot-spots can be priority areas for detailed analyses or policy interventions; Planning strategies needed to deal with global change impacts; Different transpositions of directives from high-levels to local scales create fragmented territorial development
Limitations: Limited availability of historical information reduces calibration possibilities; Difficulty in validation without in-depth analysis of past LUCs over comparable time periods; Assumptions about linear relationships between population changes and land-use dynamics may be oversimplified; Climate data resolution is coarsest among input datasets
Future Directions: Need for distinguishing among different types, managements, and levels of protection for protected areas; Requirement for additional relevant datasets and country-level land use data for other periods; Need for more sophisticated socio-economic models rather than simple demographic projections
Scalability: Study is specifically developed for Italy but considered highly representative of the entire Mediterranean region, as many environmental and socio-political processes affecting Italy have also affected or are currently affecting most Mediterranean countries
Novelty: Modified version of CLUE-S with two original factors: (1) component representing mutual influence among adjacent land uses varying for each location; (2) Markov Chain algorithm to build transition probability matrix accounting for recent LUC trends; First evaluation of LUC hot-spot spatial distribution scenarios at different spatial levels within a country

Title: Regional characteristics of climate change altering effects of afforestation
Authors: Galos, Borbala; Matyas, Csaba; Jacob, Daniela
Objective: To investigate climatic effects of forest cover change in Hungary and analyze whether the climate change signal for summer precipitation and probability of droughts can be reduced assuming maximal afforestation for the entire country
LULC Classes: Forests; vegetated areas; agriculture; grasslands; crops
Scenarios: A1B IPCC-SRES emission scenario
Analysis Methods: Regional climate modeling; biogeophysical effects assessment; evapotranspiration analysis; precipitation analysis; surface temperature analysis; drought probability analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Climate modeling with fine horizontal resolution is essential for studying long term climatic feedbacks of land cover change on a regional scale
Tools/Soft Used: REMO (regional climate model at the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology); ECHAM4 physical parameterizations
Predictors: Leaf area index; fractional vegetation cover; background albedo; surface roughness length; forest ratio; plant available soil water holding capacity; volumetric wilting point
Data Sources: REMO regional climate model; AVHRR data at 1 km resolution; International Geosphere-Biosphere Program; US Geological Survey global dataset
Validation Methods: The global dataset of land surface parameters has been validated for application in regional as well as in global climate models
Validation Data Sources: Regional climate models validation; global climate models validation
Key Findings: Afforestation may reduce projected climate change through higher evapotranspiration and precipitation as well as lower surface temperature for the entire summer period; strongest effects visible in northeastern Hungary where half of projected precipitation decrease can be relieved and total number of drought events can be reduced; smallest climatic effect in southwestern region which shows strongest climate change
Implications: Results can help identify areas where forest cover increase should most effectively support alleviation of climate change effects; information about forest-climate interaction is essential for assessment of mitigating effects and development of future adaptation strategies
Limitations: Land use and land cover changes have much weaker influence on atmospheric circulation than changes in greenhouse gas emissions; feedback processes can regionally affect weather and climate conditions only for shorter time periods, in smaller areas or regions with strong land-atmosphere interactions
Future Directions: Development of future adaptation strategies; continued investigation of forest-climate interactions for longer future time periods on regional scale
Scalability: Results indicate potential for application to other temperate regions with similar ecological characteristics, particularly areas at the border zone of closed forests and forest steppe
Novelty: First investigation of climatic effects of forest cover change in Hungary for longer future time periods on a regional scale; assessment of maximal afforestation scenario covering all vegetated areas; regional differentiation of afforestation effects within the country

Title: Simulating the impact of biofuel development on country-wide land-use change in India
Authors: Schaldach, Ruediger; Priess, Joerg A.; Alcamo, Joseph
Objective: To assess the impact of biofuel production on land use change in India up to the year 2030 using spatially explicit simulation modeling, specifically examining the consequences of expanded bioethanol production for the extent of natural land
LULC Classes: Urban area; cropland; pasture; unmanaged natural land; forest; cropland further sub-divided into 10 crop types; natural land includes shrubland; barren land with sparse vegetation cover; open woodlands
Baseline Years: 1990-1993 (early 1990s as starting conditions); 2000 (first time step of simulation)
Scenarios: Order from Strength scenario from Millennium Ecosystem Assessment as baseline; three bioethanol production scenarios to substitute 5%, 10% and 20% of expected petrol demand in 2030
Analysis Methods: LandSHIFT model application; spatially explicit land-use change simulation; multi-criteria analysis (MCA); multi-objective allocation problem solving; MOLA (Multi Objective Land Allocation) heuristic
Sim. Method Advantages: Explicitly addresses competition between land-use activities such as human settlement, biofuel production and food production; spatially explicit simulation capabilities; comprehensive linkage between driving forces and policies; ability to identify regions likely to face major changes
Tools/Soft Used: LandSHIFT model; DayCent agro-ecosystem model; IMPACT agricultural trade model; Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
Predictors: For settlement (METRO): terrain slope; neighbourhood to existing settlement area; For agriculture (AGRO): local crop yields; terrain slope; neighbourhood to settlement area; neighbourhood to cropland
Data Sources: IGBP land-cover dataset from AVHRR satellite imagery; sub-national census data; CIESIN global gridded population datasets; FAO census data; global yield maps from DayCent model; IMPACT agricultural trade model
Validation Methods: Partial validation using two indirect methods; location validation through relative operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, quantity validation by comparing simulated cropland area with census data
Validation Data Sources: FAO census data; initial land-use map from IGBP dataset; country-level crop production data from FAO
Key Findings: Model underestimated crop area by 3.1% and overestimated sugarcane area by 8.8%; two closely linked processes responsible for natural land decrease: overall expansion of cropland due to increasing crop demand and expansion of settlement area displacing existing cropland; natural land conversion associated with additional costs for land preparation and infrastructure
Implications: Need to analyze land-use change dynamics from integrated perspective; findings provide valuable information for evaluating sustainability of biofuel systems; consequences for biodiversity and greenhouse gas emissions need consideration; expansion into natural areas requires additional infrastructure investments
Limitations: Current spatial resolution relatively coarse; does not account for interdependencies between food and bioenergy markets; economic variables considered only indirectly; simplified assumptions about market dependencies; lack of consistent land-cover maps prevented comprehensive validation
Future Directions: Implementation of more detailed model of Indian land-use system; integration of economic and geographic modeling concepts; refinement of suitability assessment and allocation routines; consideration of biodiesel production; integration of methods for environmental impact assessment at landscape level; systematic analysis of model sensitivity and uncertainty
Scalability: Since LandSHIFT uses a global database, the concept can be adapted to other world regions and other biofuel pathways
Novelty: First spatially explicit assessment of biofuel impact on country-wide land-use change in India; comprehensive linkage between driving variables and biofuel policies; explicit modeling of competition between land-use activities; development of new DayCent crop parameter set for sugarcane

Title: Development of flood exposure in the Netherlands during the 20th and 21st century
Authors: de Moel, Hans; Aerts, Jeroen C. J. H.; Koomen, Eric
Journal: GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE-HUMAN AND POLICY DIMENSIONS
Objective: Quantify historical and future trends in flood exposure by combining spatially explicit land-use data with maximum flood inundation information
LULC Classes: residential; industry; infrastructure; grassland; arable land; commercial; greenhouses; three residential subtypes
Scenarios: RC (Regional Communities); GE (Global Economy)
Analysis Methods: GIS grid-based spatial overlay (25 m×25 m, aggregated to 100 m×100 m); Damage Scanner meso-scale damage estimation; Land Use Scanner logit-based land-use allocation
Sim. Method Advantages: Logit-type discrete choice model balances land supply and demand; incorporates economic drivers; offers spatially explicit scenario-based projections
Tools/Soft Used: GIS software; Land Use Scanner; Damage Scanner
Predictors: population; GDP growth; trade regimes; environmental policy; planned developments; location-specific land suitability
Data Sources: primary: HGN historical land use dataset, RWS Waterdienst maximum inundation map, Land Use Scanner outputs, Dutch StatLine (GDP, households), LandScan2008 population data; secondary: CPB socio-economic scenarios, IPCC demographic/economic projections, PBL model configurations
Validation Methods: Model validation against observed land-use patterns; comparison of damage estimates with external study (Van der Klis et al., 2005)
Validation Data Sources: Observed HGN land-use maps; published damage estimates (Van der Klis et al., 2005)
Key Findings: Urban area in flood-prone zone rose from ~20 000 ha (1900) to ~124 000 ha (2000); Projected +30% (RC) to +125% (GE) urban expansion in flood-prone zone by 2100; Potential flood damage increased 16-fold over twentieth century, projected tenfold increase by 2100 (GE) vs. two- to three-fold (RC); Financial coping capacity (damage/GDP) doubled (1900–2000), declines ~20% (RC) vs. increases ~25% (GE) by 2100
Implications: High economic growth may improve coping capacity despite higher exposure; Socio-economic change drives flood risk trends more than hazard change; Planning must account for urban expansion into high-inundation areas
Limitations: No temporal change in flood hazard or defense performance; Excludes indirect, intangible flood impacts, ignores velocity, duration; Inundation map assumes design water levels and no secondary defense failure; Scenario uncertainty, especially for 2100 projections
Future Directions: Incorporate dynamic hazard projections (sea-level rise, defense improvements); Extend damage model to include indirect impacts and hydraulic variables; Develop finer validation data for past/future inundation depths
Scalability: Applicable to other urbanized deltas with spatially explicit land-use and inundation data
Novelty: Integration of long-term historical and future spatial land-use with detailed inundation depths; comparison of flood exposure and coping capacity trends over two centuries

Title: Future flood risk estimates along the river Rhine
Authors: Linde, A. H. Te; Bubeck, P.; Dekkers, J. E. C.; de Moel, H.; Aerts, J. C. J. H.
Journal: NATURAL HAZARDS AND EARTH SYSTEM SCIENCES
Country: Rhine basin across Switzerland; France; Germany; Netherlands
Objective: Estimate current and future fluvial flood risk for the entire Rhine basin in a scenario study
LULC Classes: Residential High Density; Residential Low Density; Commercial; Infrastructure; Construction/mines; Recreation; Nature; Agriculture; Cultivation; Pasture; Inland Water; plus six differentiated urban functions (total 13 classes)
Scenarios: Regional Community (RC); Global Economy (GE); RACMO climate; Wp climate
Analysis Methods: Hydrological modelling (HBV) with resampled climate scenarios; Extreme value analysis (Gumbel/GEV fits); Land Use Scanner downscaling; Damage Scanner stage–damage modelling
Sim. Method Advantages: High spatial (250 × 250 m) and thematic resolution; Detailed urban‐class differentiation; Integration of socio‐economic downscaling with flood‐damage modelling
Tools/Soft Used: Land Use Scanner; Damage Scanner; HBV hydrological model
Predictors: Slope; peat bog/marsh/moor presence; population density (LandScan); Nature2000 sites; flood‐zone designations; distances to metropolitan areas; transport nodes; road network; river courses; neighborhood statistics
Data Sources: CORINE land cover (2000); EUruralis land‐use projections; LandScan population; ICPR Rhine Atlas inundation; Dutch government flood maps; KNMI RACMO and Wp climate outputs; NUTS3 socio‐economic data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Annual expected flood damage may increase by 54 %–230% by 2030; Climate change drives ∼75% of the risk increase; Potential damage highest in Dutch Delta but flood risk highest in Lower Rhine (Germany) and Upper Rhine
Implications: Flood risk is non‐stationary and requires adaptive water‐management strategies; Policy must integrate climate and land‐use change into spatial planning and dike‐management
Limitations: Static inundation maps assumed unchanged in future; Dike failures and wealth increases not simulated; Full inundation of flood‐prone areas assumed; Damage‐model and probability uncertainties not fully quantified
Future Directions: Refine safety‐level mapping via detailed dike‐height and failure analysis; Perform updated 2-D inundation simulations upstream; Assess adaptation measures’ effectiveness under climate scenarios; Incorporate wealth projections into socio‐economic scenarios
Scalability: Scalable to other river basins given similar high‐resolution data and model frameworks
Novelty: First basin‐wide, high‐resolution integration of detailed land‐use downscaling with hydrological and damage modelling for future flood‐risk assessment in the Rhine basin

Title: Modelling of land cover and agricultural change in Europe: Combining the CLUE and CAPRI-Spat approaches
Authors: Britz, Wolfgang; Verburg, Peter H.; Leip, Adrian
Objective: Combine and compare two spatial downscaling approaches (CLUE and CAPRI-Spat) to strengthen geographic–economic integration in modelling EU land cover and agricultural change
LULC Classes: Arable land (irrigated/non-irrigated); pasture; permanent crops; biofuel crops; built-up area; (semi-)natural vegetation; recently abandoned farmland; forest; wetlands; sparsely vegetated areas; water bodies
Scenarios: Baseline (business-as-usual) projections from GTAP-IMAGE; CAPRI medium-term policy scenarios
Analysis Methods: Dynamic spatial competition modelling (Dyna-CLUE); Statistical downscaling with Highest Posterior Density estimator (CAPRI-Spat); Logit-based suitability mapping; Meta-model of DNDC for N and C fluxes
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUE: captures neighbourhood effects, succession, path-dependence, multi-land-cover dynamics; CAPRI-Spat: detailed cropping shares, stocking densities, management practices, direct linkage to agronomic indicators
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE v2.0; CAPRI economic model; CAPRI-Spat; IMAGE; GTAP; DNDC meta-model
Predictors: Soil type; slope; climate; accessibility; administrative region; neighbouring land cover; land cover history; land cover conversion cost; agro-environmental zones
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover 2000; GTAP-IMAGE model outputs; Eurostat LUCAS and Farm Structure Survey 2000; European soil and DEM maps; DNDC model meta-data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Integration of CLUE and CAPRI-Spat adds value by combining dynamic land cover changes with detailed agricultural management; Urban sprawl and natural succession significantly alter regional agricultural shares; Land cover dynamics affect environmental indicators (e.g., N leaching ↓0.8%, NH₃ emissions ↑0.5%)
Implications: Enhanced capacity for ex ante environmental impact assessment of agricultural policies by linking geographic and economic models
Limitations: Incompatibility of underlying data sets (remote sensing vs. statistical); Lack of validation data for large-scale integrated model outputs
Future Directions: Develop mutually consistent multi-scale scenario frameworks; Explore two-way feedbacks between economic and land cover models; Incorporate endogenous land area adjustments in CAPRI
Scalability: Applicable across EU27; methodology transferable to other regions with comparable data
Novelty: First integrated application linking Dyna-CLUE’s dynamic land cover allocation with CAPRI-Spat’s detailed agricultural disaggregation for EU scale

Title: Modelling soil quality changes in Europe. An impact assessment of land use change on soil quality in Europe
Authors: Podmanicky, L.; Balazs, K.; Belenyesi, M.; Centeri, Cs; Kristof, D.; Kohlheb, N.
Objective: Modelling changes in soil quality in Europe by assessing soil water erosion and soil organic carbon content under land use change scenarios
LULC Classes: Forest; Arable land; Grassland; Urban (UR); Other CORINE classes
Scenarios: Baseline scenario (no land use change); CLUE-modelled land use change scenario
Analysis Methods: CLUE-S land use change modelling; Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE); soil organic carbon change via emission factors; GIS spatial aggregation at NUTS-X; comparison to PESERA
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUE: dynamic multi-scale connectivity and competition between land uses; PESERA: process-based, less calibration, suitable for climate and land use impact; USLE: requires widely available parameters
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-S framework; GIS software; USLE model; PESERA model; spline interpolation; digital soil maps
Predictors: Rainfall erosivity (R); soil erodibility (K); slope-length and gradient (LS); vegetation cover factor (C); soil protection factor (P)
Data Sources: CLUE model outputs; CORINE Land Cover (CLC100); JRC-MARS climate database; Thyll’s isoerodent map; Soil Topographical Database of Eurasia; Hungarian Soil Map 1:100 000; SRTM DEM; Schulp et al. (2006) emission factors
Validation Methods: Weighted-average comparison of NUTS-X erosion values; Comparison of SENSOR vs PESERA; Comparison with high-resolution Hungarian USLE map
Validation Data Sources: PESERA pan-European soil erosion database; Hungarian Soil Erosion Map (USLE at 1:100 000)
Key Findings: 65% of NUTS-X regions predicted to have increased erosion (up to 20–31% in Romania, Estonia, Poland); 9% of regions show erosion decline (max −35%); 14 regions exceed 100 t ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ soil loss; PESERA and SENSOR give similar regional erosion rates; USLE at high resolution predicts much higher local erosion; SOC increases in northern/southern Europe, declines in central Europe
Implications: Identification of high-risk regions to guide EU soil protection policies; Need for targeted support and regulation to reduce soil erosion and maintain SOC; Highlight socio-economic impacts of soil degradation
Limitations: Aggregation to NUTS-X hides within-region variability; PESERA ignores channel and gully erosion; Differences in scale and data resolution affect comparability; P factor assumed constant (no mitigation practices)
Future Directions: Refinement of spatial resolution beyond NUTS-X; Upscaling/downscaling methods for different scales; Incorporation of higher-resolution, up-to-date data; Integration of deposition and gully processes
Scalability: Applicable continent-wide and potentially global where data exist; Process-based PESERA suitable for areas lacking calibration data
Novelty: Integration of CLUE land use change outputs with USLE and SOC emission factors at NUTS-X level; Combined modelling of erosion and SOC change under policy scenarios; Comparative validation across three distinct erosion models (SENSOR, PESERA, USLE)

Title: The dimensions of global urban expansion: Estimates and projections for all countries, 2000-2050
Authors: Angel, Shlomo; Parent, Jason; Civco, Daniel L.; Blei, Alexander; Potere, David
Country: Global (all countries; 3 646 metropolitan agglomerations with > 100 000 population in 2000)
Objective: Estimate past and project future global urban land cover (2000–2050), and analyze its drivers
LULC Classes: built-up area; urban land cover; arable land; informal settlements; transport infrastructure; parks & public facilities
Scenarios: Medium, high and low density-change scenarios (based on historical density trends)
Analysis Methods: Satellite imagery (MOD500) for built-up mapping; multiple regression models; U.N. urban population projections; historical map digitizing; Q–Q plots; residual scatter analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS (with Python scripts); statistical software for regression; satellite remote-sensing analysis
Predictors: Total urban population; GDP per capita; arable land per capita; gasoline price; share of urban population in informal settlements
Data Sources: MOD500 global built-up map; U.N. World Urbanisation Prospects; Brinkhoff citypopulation.de; World Bank WDI; WRI Earth Trends; WHO/UNICEF JMP; GTZ fuel price data
Validation Methods: Q–Q plots for normality; scatter plots of standardized residuals for heteroscedasticity and omitted variable bias
Validation Data Sources: Observed urban land cover from MOD500; census data for city populations; measured large-city areas
Key Findings: 20-fold average expansion: 28 of 30 sample cities expanded > 16× during 20th century; Urban land cover grew at 3.66% p.a. (1990–2000) vs. 1.66% p.a. population[Angel et al., 2010]; Elasticities: population 0.93; GDP 0.18; arable 0.21; gasoline price –0.21; Global urban land cover (2000): 300 000 km² in developing countries; projected to 770 000 km² by 2030 and 1 200 000 km² by 2050; Urban land occupies 0.47% of world land in 2000; half the world lived in cities occupying < 0.5% land
Implications: Need realistic land-need projections, metropolitan boundary extensions, arterial road ROW acquisition, selective open-space protection; Gasoline taxation can constrain sprawl, rising fuel prices may naturally compact cities
