Future Directions: Effect of urban land cover on carbon emissions; Projected loss of arable land; Vulnerability of low-lying coastal cities to sea-level rise
Scalability: Global methodology applicable to all countries and urban agglomerations
Novelty: New comprehensive dataset of 3 646 agglomerations’ built-up areas (Mod500); High-explanatory-power regression linking land cover to population, income, land supply, transport cost, informality; Integration of density-change scenarios with U.N. projections for 2000–2050 planning insights

Title: Economic-based projections of future land use in the conterminous United States under alternative policy scenarios
Authors: Radeloff, V. C.; Nelson, E.; Plantinga, A. J.; Lewis, D. J.; Helmers, D.; Lawler, J. J.; Withey, J. C.; Beaudry, F.; Martinuzzi, S.; Butsic, V.; Lonsdorf, E.; White, D.; Polasky, S.
Objective: To construct and parameterize an econometric model of land-use change to project future land use to the year 2051 at a fine spatial scale across the conterminous United States under several alternative land-use policy scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; pasture; range; forest; urban; Conservation Reserve Program
Scenarios: Business-as-usual baseline scenario; afforestation scenario; removal of agricultural subsidies scenario; increased urban rents scenario
Analysis Methods: Econometric modeling using multinomial logit models; National Resource Inventory (NRI) data analysis; 50-year transition probability matrices; stochastic simulation with 500 replicates
Sim. Method Advantages: Can simulate land-use change for broad areas with fine resolution; incorporates economic returns directly; based on underlying economic theory of landowner decision making; can simulate incentive-based scenarios realistically; measures explicit relationship among land-use allocations and inherent productivity of land
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Site's current land use; estimated per-acre county-level net returns to each land use; land capability class rating; county-level net returns defined as average annual profit from each land use
Data Sources: USDA Natural Resources Inventory (NRI) data for 844,000 sampled private land plots; 2001 National Land Cover Classification (NLCD); Soil Survey Geographic (SSURGO) database; Protected Areas Database
Validation Methods: Robustness checking by comparing averages for subsets of 500 simulations with full set; found that averages for more than 200 replicates were almost identical to those for full 500 replicates
Validation Data Sources: Subset comparisons from the 500 simulation replicates
Key Findings: 36% of conterminous United States land area will change land use over 50-year period; urban land projected to increase by 79% (33 million hectares); forest projected to increase by 7% (14 million hectares); cropland projected to decline by 16% (20 million hectares); pasture projected to decline by 13% (7.3 million hectares); differences among policy scenarios were relatively minor except for afforestation scenario
Implications: Any attempts to identify sustainable future or predict climate change effects must account for likely land-use changes; land-use policies can affect trends but basic economic and demographic factors are powerful; even dramatic policy changes showed only moderate deviations from business-as-usual scenario
Limitations: Results not meaningful at single-pixel scale; model artifacts along county borders; lacks neighborhood effects for urban growth; models not dynamic and don't account for endogenous price changes; extrapolates 1990s economic conditions; doesn't account for dramatic biophysical changes; accounts only for land use not land management
Future Directions: Development of data and methods to account for determinants of land-use decisions at fine spatial scales; incorporation of biophysical data to restrict tree growth where not possible; modeling of land management choices and affecting policies
Scalability: The approach represents a major step toward analysis of coupled human-natural systems and opens research avenues to examine ecological implications of different land-use policies for large areas at resolution allowing realistic ecological predictions
Novelty: Large-extent, fine-grain econometric model of land-use change; spatially comprehensive coverage at parcel scale rather than county/state/regional scale; ability to analyze policy levers through net returns modeling; fine spatial resolution (100m pixels) for ecologically meaningful assessments

Title: Scenarios of land use and land cover change in the conterminous United States: Utilizing the special report on emission scenarios at ecoregional scales
Authors: Sleeter, Benjamin M.; Sohl, Terry L.; Bouchard, Michelle A.; Reker, Ryan R.; Soulard, Christopher E.; Acevedo, William; Griffith, Glenn E.; Sleeter, Rachel R.; Auch, Roger F.; Sayler, Kristi L.; Prisley, Stephen; Zhu, Zhiliang

LULC Classes: Developed; Mining; Agriculture (cultivated crops; hay/pasture); Forest harvest; Water; Wetland (herbaceous; woody); Forest (deciduous; evergreen; mixed); Grassland/shrubland (grassland; shrubland); Barren; Snow/Ice; Fire .
Scenarios: IPCC-SRES A1B; A2; B1; B2
Analysis Methods: Scenario downscaling accounting model; integrated assessment with IMAGE 2.2; USGS Trends data; expert-based modifiers; nested ecoregion allocations; FORE-SCE spatial allocation model .

Tools/Soft Used: IMAGE 2.2 model; FORE-SCE spatial model; GIS-based logistic regression; USGS NLCD and VCT datasets .

Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Developed land area increases most under A2 (115%) and A1B (92%); agriculture expands under economic scenarios (up to 48%) and declines under B2; forest cover declines under A2 (8.6%) and A1B (4.5%) but is stable or increases under B1 and B2; regional hotspots identified in Eastern US, Southeastern Plains, Puget Lowlands, Willamette Valley, Central California Valley .
Implications: Downscaled LULC scenarios support carbon and GHG flux assessments; inform ecosystem management; complement downscaled climate data; adaptable for multiple scales and global frameworks .
Limitations: Does not simulate vegetation succession in response to climate; lacks full integration with wildfire and hydrologic modeling; relies on expert modifiers for demand allocation .
Future Directions: Downscale RCP scenarios; backcast LULC to 1850; incorporate vegetation succession models; integrate wildfire and hydrologic simulations; assess impacts on carbon, biodiversity, and water resources .
Scalability: Framework adaptable to downscale other global scenario frameworks and regions .
Novelty: First comprehensive thematic and spatial downscaling of LULC for CONUS; integration of IMAGE, Trends, and expert knowledge; nested ecoregion allocation to 16 classes; coupling with FORE-SCE .

Title: Woodland networks in a changing climate: Threats from land use change
Authors: Gimona, Alessandro; Poggio, Laura; Brown, Iain; Castellazzi, Marie
Objective: To evaluate the vulnerability to land use change of forest habitat networks in Scotland, given scenarios of climate-driven land use change, and identify areas where efforts could concentrate to achieve or maintain landscape-scale woodland connectivity
LULC Classes: Broad-leaved woodland; Bracken; Dwarf shrub heath; Open dwarf shrub heath; Neutral/calcareous/acid grass; Coniferous woodland; Setaside grass; Fen, Marsh, Swamp; Arable cereals; Arable/non-rotational horticulture; Improved grassland; Montane habitat; Supra-littoral/littoral sediment, saltmarsh; Suburban/rural development; Secondary roads; Small lakes; Inland bare ground; Supra-littoral/littoral rocks; Small urban settlements; Primary roads; Secondary rivers; Continuous urban, large urban settlements; Main rivers; Large lakes; Sea/estuary
Baseline Years: Present time (2000 based on Land Cover Map 2000)
Scenarios: Present land use (baseline); Future 1 scenario (all land with potential to become prime agricultural land assumed under intensive agriculture in 2050); Future 2 scenario (as Future 1 but woodland patches on future prime land assumed lost to land use conversion)
Analysis Methods: Circuit Theory integrated with land capability modeling using climatic, soil and land cover data; landscape ecological approach
Sim. Method Advantages: Circuit Theory accounts for multiple dispersal pathways in the landscape and has advantage over least-cost path methods; based on equivalence to random walks making it more easily interpretable; able to highlight multiple dispersal pathways showing degree of redundancy of dispersal pathways in landscape matrix; relaxes assumption that organisms are adapted to movement in fragmented landscapes
Tools/Soft Used: CIRCUITSCAPE software tool; Validation and Quality Assessment
Predictors: Climate; soil properties; landscape resistance to dispersal; land capability for agriculture classification; soil moisture balance; accumulated temperature
Data Sources: Land Cover Map 2000 (LCM2000) produced by UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology; Ordnance Survey Strategy Map; previous modelling studies on land capability; UKCIP02 and UKCIP09 climate scenarios
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Eastern Scotland shows higher connectivity but greater vulnerability to land use change; western landscapes have lower connectivity but lower vulnerability; combination of high food prices and improved land capability could decrease landscape connectivity especially in East and South; woodland loss would cause major reduction in connectivity; areas of future prime agricultural land will come under pressure for conversion; connectivity reduction would be considerable in many areas such as the South
Implications: Planning of ecological networks needs to account for future land use change; adaptation and mitigation strategies across multiple sectors should be reconciled; woodland networks will benefit from minimising creation of new woodlands on future prime agricultural land, protection of existing patches, and creation of wide-scale dispersal pathways along climatic gradients
Limitations: Scenarios are not predictions but tools to explore consequences of contrasting land use patterns; approach uses generic focal species disregarding detailed species-specific habitat requirements; difficult to validate parametrisation method; no firm proof that connectivity leads to viable populations; scenarios represent potential extremes in woodland loss
Future Directions: Dynamic models combining climatic change and land use change could provide more realistic picture of future impacts and adaptation strategies; individual-based simulations could help investigate how results translate into population viability; contribution of direct and indirect effects of climate change should be studied together
Scalability: General approach can be applied to other geographic areas likely to see climatic amelioration of agricultural capability including Northern Europe, parts of Argentina, Finland, Canada, Russia, and especially Siberia
Novelty: Interdisciplinary analysis integrating landscape ecology, soil and land use science; evaluation of indirect effects of climate change on habitat networks mediated by land use change; use of Circuit Theory for woodland connectivity analysis in context of climate-driven land use change

Title: A land-use and land-cover modeling strategy to support a national assessment of carbon stocks and fluxes
Authors: Sohl, Terry L.; Sleeter, Benjamin M.; Zhu, Zhiliang; Sayler, Kristi L.; Bennett, Stacie; Bouchard, Michelle; Reker, Ryan; Hawbaker, Todd; Wein, Anne; Liu, Shuguang; Kanengieter, Ronald; Acevedo, William
Objective: Summarize development and application of a unique land-use and land-cover (LULC) modeling framework to support a U.S. national assessment of carbon stocks, fluxes, and mitigation strategies
LULC Classes: Open Water; Perennial Ice and Snow; Developed (Urban); Barren Land; Surface Mining; Deciduous Forest; Evergreen Forest; Mixed Forest; Clear-cut Forest; Shrub; Grassland; Pasture/Hay; Cultivated Crop; Herbaceous Wetland; Woody Wetland
Scenarios: IPCC SRES A1B; A2; B1; B2
Analysis Methods: Downscaling SRES storylines to EPA ecoregions via expert workshops and IMAGE 2.2 outputs; Demand–supply “prescription” feeding FORE-SCE spatial allocation; Patch-by-patch allocation guided by stepwise logistic regression suitability surfaces; Integration with GEMS biogeochemical models (Spreadsheet, Century, EDCM)
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit, wall-to-wall mapping at 250 m resolution; Modular demand vs. allocation allows flexible scenario inputs; Patch-based allocation yields realistic local and regional patterns; Compatibility with process-based carbon models (Tier 3 IPCC)
Tools/Soft Used: FORE-SCE model; GEMS (Spreadsheet, Century, EDCM); IMAGE 2.2; GIS; spreadsheet accounting model; stepwise logistic regression
Predictors: Compound Topographic Wetness Index; Elevation; Slope; Available Water Capacity; Crop Capability Index; Soil Organic Carbon; Hydric Soils; Annual Precipitation; Average Temperature; January Minimum Temperature; July Maximum Temperature; Population Density; Housing Density; Distance to Road; Distance to Stream; Distance to Surface Water; Distance to City; Urban Window Count; Distance to Rail; X-Coordinate; Y-Coordinate
Data Sources: Primary: 1992 & 2001 NLCD, LANDFIRE Vegetation Change Tracker, USGS Land Cover Trends, USFS FIA, IMAGE 2.2 scenario outputs, IPCC SRES; Secondary: GIS layers for soils, climate, topography, infrastructure
Validation Methods: Quantity disagreement analysis (demand vs. modeled proportions); Qualitative expert review of suitability surfaces and spatial allocations; Spatial diversity mapping across scenarios
Validation Data Sources: USGS Trends data; NLCD change products; expert knowledge
Key Findings: FORE-SCE reliably matches scenario prescriptions with minimal quantity disagreement; Prototype mitigation scenarios increased cumulative carbon sequestration across all biogeochemical models; Spatial hotspots of uncertainty identified where grassland, cropland, and pasture trade-offs occur; Scenario framework bounds LULC uncertainty and informs GHG flux analysis
Implications: Supports national-scale carbon and GHG policy assessments; Informs spatially explicit mitigation strategy planning; Framework extendable to other ecosystem services (biodiversity, hydrology)
Limitations: Scenario bounds not exhaustive of all futures; Lack of Monte Carlo simulations limits within-scenario spatial uncertainty quantification; Formal validation constrained by low historical change rates; Reliance on expert opinion for scenario downscaling and parameter adjustment
Future Directions: Publish regional summaries integrating carbon flux results and mitigation analyses; Complete conterminous U.S. assessment by end of 2012; Extend analyses to additional ecosystem services; Port FORE-SCE to flexible frameworks for external distribution; Incorporate dynamic updating of demand and suitability surfaces; Monte Carlo runs
Scalability: Yes; hierarchical ecoregion approach and modular design support application across other regions and scales
Novelty: First integration of spatially explicit, patch-based LULC modeling with process-based biogeochemical modeling at national scale; Unique downscaling of IPCC SRES scenarios to U.S. ecoregions via combined quantitative and expert methods; High thematic resolution improving linkage to carbon flux models

Title: Forest cover, carbon sequestration, and wildlife habitat: policy review and modeling of tradeoffs among land-use change scenarios
Authors: Rittenhouse, Chadwick D.; Rissman, Adena R.
Objective: Primary objective was to assess forest-relevant climate mitigation strategies in US state plans and evaluate effects of three future land-cover and land-use change scenarios on afforestation, forest loss, carbon sequestration, forest connectivity, and wildlife habitat for Wisconsin.
LULC Classes: Forest; agriculture (cropland, pasture); grassland; shrubland; urban; water.
Scenarios: Static Forest; Dynamic Forest; All Forest
Analysis Methods: Policy review of 35 state climate mitigation plans; Econometric land-use change modeling (Radeloff et al. 2012); ArcGIS spatial assignment of highest-probability land cover; LANDFIRE EVT mapping; FIA-based biomass and age estimation; Carbon sequestration equations (Smith et al. 2006); Morphological spatial pattern analysis (core/connector/patch classification)
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit econometric modeling captures realistic land-use transitions and accounts for additionality and leakage compared to static or purely aspatial approaches.
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; morphological spatial pattern analysis software; econometric modeling framework.
Predictors: Current land use; County-level net economic returns by land use; Conversion costs between land uses; Soil quality and agricultural potential; Land ownership and protection status
Data Sources: Pew Center database of state Climate Action Plans; USGS 2001 National Land Cover Dataset; USGS Wisconsin GAP Stewardship Data (2005); Wisconsin Managed Forest Law data (2009); Radeloff et al. (2012) econometric model inputs; LANDFIRE Existing Vegetation Type layer; USDA Forest Service FIA data; Wisconsin DNR species habitat database; North American Breeding Bird Survey
Validation Methods: Comparison of Dynamic Forest model projections with observed land-cover change trends (1992–2001 net forest gain consistency).
Validation Data Sources: Historical NLCD change (1992–2001); FIA field reference data.
Key Findings: 77% of plans recommended woody biomass, 69% forest loss prevention, 49% afforestation programs.; Dynamic Forest yields 6.0% afforestation, 1.8% forest loss (42.6% total forest), All Forest yields 39.7% afforestation (78.1% total).
Implications: Incorporate spatial/temporal LCLUC dynamics for policy evaluation.; Adapt existing programs (CRP, forest tax laws) for carbon incentives.; Need to balance afforestation with wildlife habitat and leakage prevention.; Southern Wisconsin private lands crucial for mitigation.
Limitations: Assumed no tree harvest or mortality.; All Forest scenario ignores productivity variation and competing land uses.; Dynamic model based on past trends may not capture future market or policy shifts.
Future Directions: Integrate climate variability and economic changes into LCLUC projections.; Evaluate leakage at broader socio-economic scales.; Incorporate biodiversity valuation into cost-effectiveness analyses.; Engage stakeholders in spatially explicit policy development.
Scalability: Methods applicable to other regions with available land-cover, economic, and forest inventory data.
Novelty: Combined national policy review with spatially explicit scenario modeling linking carbon, connectivity, and wildlife habitat tradeoffs.

Title: How accurately may we project tropical forest-cover change? A validation of a forward-looking baseline for REDD
Authors: Sloan, Sean; Pelletier, Johanne
Journal: GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE-HUMAN AND POLICY DIMENSIONS
Objective: Develop and validate a national, spatially explicit, forward-looking baseline of forest-cover change for REDD+
LULC Classes: Forest; non-forest; young fallow (80% canopy closure)
Scenarios: Projected business-as-usual baseline; null model (no change baseline)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit pixel-based modelling with GEOMOD; driver weighting via ArcGEOMOD; accuracy assessment using ROC statistic, quantity/allocation disagreement, Figure of Merit, multi-resolution analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Simplicity; institutional familiarity; moderate data demands; user control; transparency; optimal weighting of drivers via empirical fit
Tools/Soft Used: GEOMOD model (Idrisi, ArcGIS); ArcGEOMOD driver-weighting algorithm
Predictors: Agricultural capacity; elevation; life zone; soil pH; soil texture; distances to asphalt/Earth/highway roads; slope; protected areas; cattle density; settlement density; rural male unemployment; farm forest percentage; farm title percentage; pasture predominance; agricultural employment; agricultural sales; female employment; farm machines per farm; off-farm income; rural income per agricultural area; rural population per agricultural area; rural income
Data Sources: ANAM Landsat-derived forest-cover maps (1990, 2000); CATHALAC 2008 forest-cover map; SRTM DEM; IDIAP soil and agri-capacity GIS; IGNTG road GIS; 1990/2000 population, housing, agricultural censuses from Panama’s Dept. of Statistics
Validation Methods: Comparison of projected vs. actual 2008 forest maps; ROC statistic; partitioning total disagreement into quantity and allocation disagreement; Figure of Merit; assessment at multiple spatial resolutions
Validation Data Sources: CATHALAC 2008 Landsat-derived forest-cover map
Key Findings: Projection accuracy 85.2% at 100 m resolution; total disagreement 14.8% (6.2% quantity, 8.6% allocation); projection less accurate than null model; allocation error larger where regeneration; rate of forest-cover change most critical parameter
Implications: Spatially projected baselines offer limited value for REDD+ where change small/complex; simpler retrospective or historical-adjusted baselines recommended; spatial projections still useful for sub-national targeting
Limitations: Complexity and non-linearity of drivers; small change relative to landscape; two-way change (deforestation and regeneration); temporal misalignment of mosaic maps; spatial heterogeneity; limitations of one-way projection
Future Directions: Probabilistic area prediction; simultaneous two-way projections; finer-scale driver data; smaller empirically delimited strata; simpler aggregation or quasi-spatial approaches; institutional harmonization of reference levels
Scalability: Methodology relevant to other tropical countries but accuracy likely limited where forest-cover change is minor or complex; more suitable in contexts of simple deforestation
Novelty: First national-scale empirical validation of a spatially explicit forward-looking REDD+ baseline; integration of ArcGEOMOD driver-weighting; multi-resolution partitioned accuracy assessment

Title: Lowering environmental costs of oil-palm expansion in Colombia
Authors: Garcia-Ulloa, John; Sloan, Sean; Pacheco, Pablo; Ghazoul, Jaboury; Koh, Lian Pin
Objective: Model trade-offs and impacts of projected oil-palm expansion in Colombia under multiple scenarios to identify low-impact development pathways
LULC Classes: Forests; natural grasslands and shrublands; secondary vegetation; mosaics; annual crops; perennial crops; pasture lands; forest plantations; human-disturbed areas; existing oil-palm plantations
Scenarios: Production-oriented; Agroindustrial development; Ecosystem protection; Carbon conservation; Hybrid (multipriority)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit scenario modeling; GIS overlay; buffer analysis; species-area modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: Enables integration of spatial data layers (land cover, carbon, yield potential, profitability, accessibility); Accounts for conversion-priority indices reflecting multiple priorities; Allows repeated iteration (10,000 runs) to quantify variability
Tools/Soft Used: GIS software (unspecified); spatial database construction; matrix-calibrated species-area model
Predictors: Distance to roads; distance to existing plantations; oil-palm yield potential; suitability indices for rice, maize, sugarcane; above- and belowground biomass carbon; land profitability; elevation; protected areas; ethnic territory boundaries
Data Sources: Primary: Landsat TM/ETM+ 2001 land-cover (IDEAM et al. 2007), IPCC Tier-1 biomass carbon map (Ruesch & Gibbs 2008), Fedepalma 2008 plantation maps; Secondary: FAO yield data (2009), municipality agricultural revenue/costs
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated land-conversion patterns with existing plantation locations; sensitivity analysis over 10,000 simulation runs
Validation Data Sources: Fedepalma plantation thematic maps; municipality production statistics
Key Findings: Production-oriented yields lowest land area (∼730,000 ha) but highest carbon loss (4.36 Mt C); Carbon-conservation requires double land area, reduces carbon loss by 87%; Agroindustrial minimizes crop losses but converts ∼795,000 ha forest and loses 15.8 Mt C; Ecosystem protection spares forests but sacrifices 1.2 M ha pasture and reduces rice/maize by 3 Mt and sugarcane by 48 Mt
Implications: Directing expansion to degraded pasture lands can mitigate environmental and food security trade-offs; Policy incentives may be needed to offset land-purchase costs; Hybrid planning can reconcile productivity, conservation, and socio-economic goals

Future Directions: Incorporate social well-being and human-rights metrics; Include irrigation and climate-change effects on yield potentials; Evaluate policy incentive mechanisms and market dynamics; Extend model to dynamic demand projections and ecosystem services beyond carbon
Scalability: Applicable to other tropical regions with available spatial datasets; requires adaptation of scenario indices and local data
Novelty: First spatially explicit multi-priority scenario analysis of oil-palm expansion in Colombia; Integrates biomass carbon, biodiversity, food security, profitability, and accessibility into conversion-priority indices; Uses high-resolution GIS buffers around roads and plantations in hybrid scenario modeling

Title: Spatial and Temporal Responses to an Emissions Trading Scheme Covering Agriculture and Forestry: Simulation Results from New Zealand
Authors: Kerr, Suzi; Anastasiadis, Simon; Olssen, Alex; Power, William; Timar, Levente; Zhang, Wei
Objective: perform simulations using the integrated Land Use in Rural New Zealand (LURNZ) model to analyze the effect of various New Zealand emissions trading scheme (ETS) scenarios on land use, net greenhouse gas emissions and agricultural output
LULC Classes: dairy farming; sheep-beef farming; plantation forestry; unproductive scrub
Scenarios: baseline (no ETS); ETS without agriculture (forestry-only ETS); full ETS (forestry and agriculture)
Analysis Methods: integrated LURNZ simulation; dynamic national land-use share econometric model; static geographic land-use allocation model; revealed-preference econometric modeling; multinomial choice model; spatial allocation algorithm; emissions decomposition
Sim. Method Advantages: direct econometric estimation of land-use responses; accounts for geophysical characteristics, location and tenure; spatially explicit at 25-ha resolution; captures regional economic and ecosystem service impacts better than agent-based or optimization models
Tools/Soft Used: LURNZ model
Predictors: commodity prices; real carbon price; geophysical characteristics; location; land tenure; regional carbon stocks; discount rate; productivity trends; fertilizer intensity
Data Sources: MAF carbon stock look-up tables; SONZAF commodity price projections; Livestock Improvement Corporation Dairy Statistics; Statistics New Zealand trade and slaughter data; MAF emissions factors; national inventory; 2007 Agricultural Census; Beef & Lamb and DairyNZ sector data; Scion forestry data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: ETS policies reduce net greenhouse gas emissions via land-use change; forestry component has far larger impact than agriculture; afforestation under ETS projected to sequester an additional 6–7 Mt CO₂ by 2024 (17.6–20.5% of 2008 agricultural emissions); sheep-beef land share declines; dairy output largely unchanged across scenarios; including agriculture in ETS yields only small incremental land-use and emissions effects
Implications: ETS can substantially reduce future harvest liabilities; rewarding forestry is more cost-effective than taxing agriculture; point of obligation at processor level provides little incentive for on-farm mitigation; policy design should prioritize forestry sequestration
Limitations: on-farm mitigation and intensive-margin adjustments not modeled; emissions per output held constant; conservative valuation of carbon returns; sensitive to parameter assumptions and commodity price projections; policy uncertainty not fully captured
Future Directions: assess farm-level point of obligation and on-farm mitigation; incorporate climate-driven pasture productivity changes; model endogenous rotation lengths; include multiple carbon price expectations
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: first use of a spatially explicit dynamic partial-equilibrium econometric model integrating forestry and agriculture in ETS analysis; simultaneous simulation of land use, emissions and production; direct econometric estimation of land-use responses at fine spatial resolution

Title: Spatiotemporal land use modelling to assess land availability for energy crops - illustrated for Mozambique
Authors: van der Hilst, Floor; Verstegen, Judith A.; Karssenberg, Derek; Faaij, Andre P. C.

Key Findings: BAU scenario: available land declines from 9.1 Mha (2005) to 7.7 Mha (2030), 95% CI: 6.1–8.2 Mha, remaining areas are remote, low-productivity regions.; Progressive scenario: available land increases from 9.1 Mha to 16.4 Mha by 2030, requires 0.4 Mha plantation to offset wood demand without deforestation.; Uncertainty mapping reveals highest ambiguity at land use expansion edges.

Title: Evaluation of Spatiotemporal Dynamics of Simulated Land Use/Cover in China Using a Probabilistic Cellular Automata-Markov Model

Title: Past and future impacts of land use and climate change on agricultural ecosystem services in the Czech Republic
Authors: Lorencova, Eliska; Frelichova, Jana; Nelson, Edward; Vackar, David
Objective: To provide spatially explicit information at a national level on climate and land use change impacts in order to assess changes in the provision of ecosystem services; specifically providing qualitative and quantitative analysis of impacts on selected ecosystem services (carbon sequestration, food production and soil erosion) in the agricultural sector of the Czech Republic
LULC Classes: Agricultural land consisting of arable land; grasslands (pastures and meadows); permanent cultures (orchards, gardens, vineyards and hop-fields); built-up; forest; other land uses
Scenarios: BAMBU (Business As Might Be Usual) - policy driven scenario based on A2 IPCC SRES scenario; GRAS (Growth Applied Strategy) - liberal, free-trade, globalization scenario corresponding to IPCC SRES A1FI scenario; SEDG (Sustainable European Development Goal) - backcasting normative scenario using IPCC SRES B1 scenario
Analysis Methods: Index of change analysis; ALARM scenarios application; Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) for erosion assessment; ecosystem services assessment using specific indicators; spatially explicit analysis using GIS mapping
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Climate change; land use change; socio-economic changes; agricultural policies; greenhouse gas emissions
Data Sources: Czech LUCC database; Czech Statistical Office (CZSO) data; ALARM scenarios; Corine Land Cover 2000 (CLC 2000); Central Land Survey and Cadastre Archive files; Department of Irrigation, Drainage and Landscape Engineering of the Czech Technical University in Prague
Validation Methods: Data compliance testing between different databases; control of land use categories and data comparability assessment

Key Findings: Historical land use trends and projected climate scenarios show shared spatial patterns with significant decrease of arable land in border fringes replaced by grasslands; net carbon sequestration shows negative values due to arable land dominance; food production of wheat and barley dropped while maize production increased; soil erosion rates decreased from 1948 levels but remain significant with 50% of arable land under water erosion risk
Implications: Results can be used as support tool for local land use management and evidence-based policy decisions; climate change impacts cannot be considered in isolation but must be set against socio-economic trends; ecosystem services provide measurable indicators of land system functioning and change
Limitations: Simplification through indicators introduces bias; combination of different data sources with varying accuracy levels; ecosystem size considered as only forcing variable while other factors like crop type, soil conditions, and management practices also influence services; linear assumption of ecosystem services delivery while reality is non-linear; substantial uncertainties in climate scenarios utilization
Future Directions: Further research on development and implementation of adaptation options in Czech agricultural sector under changing climate; development of more comprehensive approaches considering multiple forcing variables beyond ecosystem size
Scalability: The approach of applying spatial trend data to climate scenarios could be applied to other socio-economic sectors (urban areas, forestry, aquatic environments) and other countries, especially those that have undergone socio-economic changes in land ownership and management

Title: A Comparison of Two Land Use Simulation Models under the RCP4.5 Scenario in China
Authors: Wu, Feng; Zhan, Jinyan; Xu, Qian; Xiong, Yihui; Sun, Zhongxiao

Future Directions: Develop dynamic, region-specific parameter optimization methods; Incorporate policy intervention impacts explicitly; Disaggregate forest land types; Extend calibration framework to other regions
Scalability: Calibration approach is transferable to other regions with adjustment of socioeconomic and biophysical parameters
Novelty: First comparative calibration of global GCAM and GTAP-AEZ models under RCP4.5 for China, demonstrating improved accuracy through region-specific parameter adjustment

Title: A decision support tool for sustainable planning of urban water systems: Presenting the Dynamic Urban Water Simulation Model
Authors: Willuweit, Lars; O'Sullivan, John J.
Objective: Primary objective of the study is to develop and present the Dynamic Urban Water Simulation Model (DUWSiM), a decision support tool for sustainable long-term planning of urban water systems that links urban water balance concepts with land use dynamics and climate change scenarios.
LULC Classes: CORINE-based classes including residential (high, medium, low density), commercial, industrial, public open space, agricultural
Baseline Years: 2006 (actual land use), 2007–2012 (calibration period for water demand and runoff)
Target Years: Up to 20 years into the future (simulation scenarios to 2026 and beyond; example simulated land use for 2026)
Scenarios: Business-as-usual urbanisation scenario from MOLAND; Climate change scenarios from GCMs downscaled via LARS-WG
Analysis Methods: Cellular automata land use dynamics (MOLAND); Stochastic weather generation and downscaling (LARS-WG); Urban water balance modeling (DUWSiM-WB) with daily water balance equations and multi-scale spatial aggregation
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates dynamic land use change with climate scenarios; Modular and user-friendly; Captures long-term socio-economic and climatic impacts on urban water cycle; Allows evaluation of centralized and decentralized options under changing conditions
Tools/Soft Used: MOLAND (cellular automata land use model); LARS-WG (weather generator); DUWSiM-WB (C# urban water balance model); InfoWorks CS (GDSDS runoff reference model); GIS software; Microsoft Excel for output interface
Predictors: Population projections; Job market projections by economic sector; Accessibility maps; Suitability maps; Zoning maps; Neighbourhood effects; ; Historical daily rainfall; temperature; solar radiation
Data Sources: GIS land use polygons from satellite imagery, aerial photography; Population and economic data for Dublin Region; Historical daily weather data (Dublin Airport); DMA flow data from Dublin City, South Dublin, Dun Laoghaire Rathdown and Fingal councils; GDSDS model outputs for runoff calibration
Validation Methods: Calibration and validation of water demand using Nash–Sutcliffe coefficient (E); Calibration and validation of stormwater runoff against GDSDS model outputs; Visual comparison and efficiency metrics
Validation Data Sources: Observed DMA water consumption data (263 DMAs, 2007–2012); GDSDS hydrodynamic model runoff outputs for Santry and Dublin City Centre (2010–2011)
Key Findings: DUWSiM predicts water demand with Nash–Sutcliffe E = 0.710 (calibration) and E = 0.421 (validation); Stormwater runoff predictions achieve E = 0.953 (Santry) and E = 0.961 (City Centre); Cellular automata approach yields comparable performance to static models; Model can assess feasibility of centralized vs decentralized supply and demand options under urbanisation and climate change
Implications: DUWSiM enables sustainable water management planning by integrating land use dynamics and climate scenarios; Supports decision making on infrastructure investments and decentralized systems; Facilitates comparison of options based on life-cycle cost, energy, and water recycling potential
Limitations: Does not model daily fluctuations of water demand or feedback from water resources to urban development; Evapotranspiration simplified; No groundwater or contaminant transport modeling; Seasonal index fluctuations and extreme leakage events not explicitly captured
Future Directions: Incorporate groundwater and contaminant balance modules; Develop disaggregated water demand module capturing daily variability; Implement feedback loop between DUWSiM-WB and MOLAND; Test and apply DUWSiM in other jurisdictions
Scalability: Potentially scalable to other urban jurisdictions due to generic framework and modular design, but requires calibration with local land use, climate, and water data
Novelty: First integrated tool linking urban land use dynamics (MOLAND), stochastic climate scenarios (LARS-WG), and urban water balance in a single decision support model; Dynamic (annual) land use change rather than static urban representation; Multi-scale spatial aggregation from cell to city level.

Title: Assessing spatial uncertainties of land allocation using a scenario approach and sensitivity analysis: A study for land use in Europe
Authors: Verburg, Peter H.; Tabeau, Andrzej; Hatna, Erez
Objective: Assess how uncertainty in national‐level macro‐assumptions (GDP and population) translates into spatial uncertainties in future agricultural land allocation in Europe
LULC Classes: Arable land; Pasture land; Forest land; Urban areas; Other semi‐natural land uses
Scenarios: Marketeer; Musketeer
Analysis Methods: Conditional probabilistic (input‐constrained) scenario approach; Systematic Sensitivity Analysis (SSA) via Gaussian quadrature; Random resampling (50 runs) for spatial downscaling; Coupled multi‐scale modelling (LEITAP + Dyna-CLUE)
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates global economic feedbacks with local spatial allocation; Captures compound uncertainty propagation from macro to grid scale; Distinguishes quantity vs. locational uncertainty
Tools/Soft Used: LEITAP (GEMPACK); Dyna-CLUE; GEMPACK SSA module; R (mvtnorm package)
Predictors: GDP growth; Population size; Land suitability factors (biophysical & socio‐economic); Spatial policy restrictions
Data Sources: World Bank World Development Indicators (1967–2003); CPB Worldscan macro‐economic projections; IPCC SRES demographic assumptions; GTAP database (LEITAP calibration); European land use maps (remote sensing & statistics)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: GDP uncertainty has larger impact on agricultural land projections than population uncertainty; Musketeer (lower GDP) yields higher land‐use uncertainty than Marketeer; Spatial hotspots exist where land change is highly certain vs. highly uncertain; Agricultural abandonment dominates in Western/Southern Europe, expansion limited to parts of Eastern Europe
Implications: Spatially explicit uncertainty mapping aids targeted adaptation and policy communication; Aggregate assessments risk masking location‐specific risks
Limitations: Focused only on GDP and population uncertainties; Model structure and input data uncertainties (e.g., land suitability, remote sensing errors) not assessed; Validation of simulated patterns not conducted
Future Directions: Incorporate additional uncertain drivers (soil, climate, infrastructure); Assess uncertainty in model structure and parameters; Perform empirical validation with observed land‐change data
Scalability: Methodology applicable to other regions, land‐use types, and scenario variables
Novelty: First combined use of probabilistic SSA with spatial downscaling to translate macro‐level scenario uncertainty into high‐resolution land‐use allocation uncertainty maps

Title: Current and Future Land Use around a Nationwide Protected Area Network
Authors: Hamilton, Christopher M.; Martinuzzi, Sebastian; Plantinga, Andrew J.; Radeloff, Volker C.; Lewis, David J.; Thogmartin, Wayne E.; Heglund, Patricia J.; Pidgeon, Anna M.
Objective: Evaluate current and future (2051) land use around U.S. National Wildlife Refuges
LULC Classes: Natural (NLCD 41,42,43,52,71); Agriculture (NLCD 81,82); Urban (NLCD 21–24); Open water; Wetlands; Barrens; Non-natural woody cover
Scenarios: Business-as-usual; Preserve-natural-habitats; Restricted-urban-growth
Analysis Methods: Econometric land-use modeling; Buffer analysis at 5 km, 25 km, 75 km; County-level transition probability estimation; Endogenous price feedback incorporation
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows evaluation of policy scenarios via adjustment of economic returns; Incorporates endogenous feedbacks on commodity prices and net returns
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Observed land-use change (1992–97); Soil productivity; County-level net economic returns; Metropolitan status (for urban restriction)
Data Sources: National Land Cover Dataset (2001); National Resources Inventory (1992–97); USFWS Cadastral database; County economic return data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Forest/range dominant around refuges (57.4%) in 2001; By 2051, urban use grows fastest (28.5–57.0% rate), crop/pasture declines, forest/range increases under conservation/restriction scenarios; Restricted-urban-growth yields urban increase nearly 50% lower than other scenarios; Regional variation: Upper Midwest most dynamic, substantial forest/range loss in regions 4 and 5
Implications: Regional policy and budget allocations needed to address encroachment; Urban containment policies could rival habitat‐preservation taxes in conserving natural land
Limitations: “Business-as-usual” based on 1990s trends, may not reflect current economic climate; No confidence intervals reported; Excludes wetlands/open water dynamics
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Applicability to other regions limited by region-specific economic, demographic, ecological forces
Novelty: Incorporation of endogenous price feedbacks in land-use projections and comparison of urban‐growth restriction versus habitat‐preservation scenarios

Title: Impact of Climate and Land Use Changes on Water and Food Security in Jordan: Implications for Transcending “The Tragedy of the Commons”
Authors: Al-Bakri, Jawad Taleb; Salahat, Mohammad; Suleiman, Ayman; Suifan, Marwan; Hamdan, Mohammad R.; Khresat, Saeb; Kandakji, Tarek
Objective: Assess the risks of climate change, population growth and land use change on water resources and food productivity in Jordan
LULC Classes: Urban; mixed rainfed areas; irrigated areas; forests; rangelands/non-cultivated; water bodies
Baseline Years: 1994–2008 (climate data); 1978–2010 (land use time series); 2010 (land use map)
Scenarios: Temperature change +1 °C (2030) and +2 °C (2050); Precipitation change –5% to –20% or +5% to +20% depending on basin
Analysis Methods: Trend analysis (linear, Mann-Kendall); GIS remote sensing classification (ASTER, Landsat TM/ETM+); FAO-56 Penman-Monteith evapotranspiration; Crop simulation (process-based and statistical models); Regression analysis; Risk assessment via SSD and water budget
Sim. Method Advantages: Statistical and process-oriented crop simulation models capture local climate–yield relationships and allow prediction under varied CC scenarios, offering mechanistic and empirical insight superior to simple yield trend extrapolation
Tools/Soft Used: GIS (unspecified packages); image classification tools; FAO-56 model; regression software
Predictors: Air temperature; rainfall in critical months; accumulated rainfall; cultivated area; basin location
Data Sources: Department of Statistics; Ministry of Water and Irrigation; FAO; ASTER and Landsat imagery; national communication reports to UNFCCC; published literature
Validation Methods: Map verification against existing land use maps and Google Earth high-resolution images
Validation Data Sources: Previous land use studies; Google Earth imagery
Key Findings: Temperature rise and reduced rainfall will exacerbate water scarcity and reduce crop yields (barley –35% by 2050, wheat –21%); Irrigated area to decline ~20% by 2050, rainfed by 11–18%, urban area to more than triple by 2050; Water deficit to reach 488 MCM (2030) and 769 MCM (2050) under CC; Self-sufficiency degree declines for most food items, vegetables remain above 100% SSD
Implications: Need for adaptive measures: cropping pattern modification; irrigation efficiency improvement; treated wastewater reuse; supply augmentation (Red-Dead project)
Limitations: Not specified
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Framework applicable to other arid/semiarid countries with limited water resources
Novelty: Integration of land use change, climate scenarios and water–food security risk assessment in a unified GIS-crop simulation framework

Title: Key areas for conserving United States' biodiversity likely threatened by future land use change
Authors: Martinuzzi, S.; Radeloff, V. C.; Higgins, J. V.; Helmers, D. P.; Plantinga, A. J.; Lewis, D. J.
Objective: Quantify potential consequences of future land use changes on the nation’s Areas of Biodiversity Significance (ABS) and identify regions where ABS are likely threatened by future land use expansion
LULC Classes: Forest; natural grasslands/rangelands; crop; pasture; urban; water; wetlands
Scenarios: Business-as-usual; Avoided Deforestation (US$100/acre forest tax, REDD-type); High Crop Demand (2% annual crop price increase + CRP maintained); Urban Containment (urban expansion limited to metropolitan counties)
Analysis Methods: Econometric land use change model based on National Resources Inventory observations; endogenous price elasticities for economic returns; spatial aggregation to ecoregions and ABS
Sim. Method Advantages: Empirical projection from observed landowner decisions; accounts for economic returns and conversion costs; explores multiple policy and price scenarios under uncertainty
Tools/Soft Used: Econometric modelling framework; Marxan (spatial optimization for ABS design)
Predictors: Economic returns to each land use; conversion costs; soil quality (SSURGO); price elasticities for commodities; county-level economic data
Data Sources: Primary: 2001 National Land Cover Dataset (NLCD), National Resources Inventory (NRI), SSURGO soils, Protected Areas Database (PAD-US), TNC ABS maps; Secondary: Lubowski et al. (2006) county-level returns, Marxan outputs (for ABS delineation)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Under Business-as-usual, 128 000 km² (7%) of natural habitats in ABS lost by 2051; High Crop Demand yields highest loss (159 741 km², 8%), Urban Containment lowest (98 161 km², 5%); Range losses driven mainly by crop/pasture expansion, forest losses equally by urban and crop/pasture; Strong regional variation (0–30% loss), highest in Southeast, South-Central, parts of Upper Midwest and Northwest; Fourteen ecoregions show >15% habitat loss across scenarios
Implications: Conservation strategies must address future urban and agricultural expansion; national-scale policies (zoning, subsidies/taxes) have regionally variable effects; targeted actions (easements, land acquisition, management on private lands) required
Limitations: Habitat loss measured only by area, not fragmentation or connectivity; No differentiation among natural vs. managed vs. plantation forests; Wetlands held constant, so wetland impacts uncertain; Excludes potential habitat gains; Coarse resolution unsuitable for pixel-level targeting
Future Directions: Incorporate fragmentation and connectivity metrics; Model wetland dynamics; Evaluate habitat gains and afforestation policies; Compare with alternative land use datasets (e.g., Sohl et al. 2012)
Scalability: Yes; approach applicable to other ecoregions and global assessments
Novelty: Integration of TNC’s ABS with an econometric land use model under multiple policy/price scenarios to spatially forecast habitat loss within priority conservation areas

Title: Scenario-Based Analysis on the Structural Change of Land Uses in China
Authors: Xu, Qian; Jiang, Qunou; Cao, Kai; Li, Xing; Deng, Xiangzheng
Objective: Scenario‐based analysis of how land use change affects CO₂ emissions and to identify the land use structure most suited for climate change adaptation
LULC Classes: cultivated lands; forest lands; grasslands; unused land; built-up areas
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU); Rapid economic growth (REG); Coordinated environmental sustainability (CES)
Analysis Methods: AgLU module of GCAM (logit‐based land share allocation); ERB module for CO₂ emissions
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates socioeconomic drivers with land-use allocation; Captures both land-use and fossil fuel emissions in one framework
Tools/Soft Used: GCAM model (AgLU and ERB modules)
Predictors: population; per-capita income growth rate; proportion agricultural population; urbanization ratio; GDP; energy price indices (oil, gas, coal, hydropower)
Data Sources: TM/ETM Landsat imagery (1990–2010) from Resources and Environment Data Center, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Statistical Yearbook of China; provincial statistical data (population, GDP, urbanization); Energy Statistics Yearbook (fuel price indices)
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated vs. observed land use areas in 1990, 2005, 2010
Validation Data Sources: Real land‐use statistics for 1990, 2005, 2010
Key Findings: BAU: CO₂ emissions peak ~2065 then decline very slowly; remain high long term; REG: Continuous CO₂ increase; highest emissions of all scenarios; CES: CO₂ emissions decline from ~2030; return near 1990 levels by 2070; CES scenario best balances economic growth and emission control
Implications: CES scenario offers a “double win” of environmental protection and steady economic development; informs sustainable land use planning
Limitations: Socioeconomic drivers oversimplified in scenario design; Only three broad scenarios; lack detailed sub-scenario variation
Future Directions: Incorporate more socioeconomic factors in scenarios; Design additional scenario variants under CES framework
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integration of GCAM’s AgLU and ERB modules to link land‐use structural change directly with CO₂ emission trajectories under multiple socioeconomic scenarios

Title: Urbanization and climate change impacts on future urban flooding in Can Tho city, Vietnam
Authors: Huong, H. T. L.; Pathirana, A.
Objective: Quantitatively assess future urban flood hazards in Can Tho city under combined influences of climate change (sea-level rise, increased river runoff) and urbanization-driven local hydrological and microclimatic changes
LULC Classes: Open water; Developed areas (low-intensity; medium-intensity; high-intensity); Infrastructure; Shrub and grassland
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU); Rapid economic growth (REG); Coordinated environmental sustainability (CES)
Analysis Methods: Land-use simulation with Dinamica EGO; Mesoscale atmospheric modelling (WRF coupled with Noah LSM); Coupled 1D/2D urban flood modelling (EPA-SWMM5 + Brezo)
Sim. Method Advantages: Dinamica EGO: spatially explicit cellular automata captures complex transition patterns using thematic drivers; WRF-Noah: resolves urban heat island impacts on extreme rainfall at 1 km resolution; SWMM-Brezo coupling: simulates storm-sewer surcharge and surface inundation depth dynamically
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica EGO; WRF; Noah LSM; EPA-SWMM5; Brezo
Predictors: Road network; water bodies; elevation; slope; protected/restricted areas
Data Sources: Landsat imagery for land-use maps; NCEP-FNL global analyses for atmospheric boundary conditions; USGS land-use dataset; DEM (15 m) from Dept. of Geodesy and Cartography; Engineering drawings from Can Tho Water Supply Company; Rainfall observations (Can Tho met station); Hydrological station data (river levels); Climate projections from MONRE/IMHEN report (ECHAM4, PRECIS, MAGICC/SCENGEN)
Validation Methods: Simulation of historical flood events (October 2000, October 2009); Comparison of simulated vs observed inundation depths and rainfall totals
Validation Data Sources: Can Tho meteorological station (rainfall); Can Tho hydrological station (river levels); observed maximum flood depth at Pham Ngu Lao Street
Key Findings: Urbanization alone increases maximum inundation depth by ~21% and area by 18% by 2050; Climate change drivers (100 cm SLR + increased runoff) alone raise depth by ~60%; Combined worst-case scenario yields ~80% increase in inundation depth (to ~1.51 m)
Implications: Adaptation measures must target localized inundation drivers; Urban drainage planning should integrate future climate and urban growth impacts; Urgent infrastructure upgrades and sustainable urban drainage needed
Limitations: High model uncertainty from GCM downscaling and statistical assumptions; “Business-as-usual” urban growth assumption may not hold; Limited calibration/validation data; Exclusion of some climate drivers and vulnerability/damage assessment
Future Directions: Probabilistic analysis of joint flood drivers; Inclusion of green-infrastructure and adaptive design evaluations; Expanded calibration with detailed inundation observations; Assessment of vulnerability and damage impacts
Scalability: Methodology transferable to other deltaic/coastal cities with similar data availability
Novelty: Integration of urban heat island–induced extreme rainfall changes with large-scale climate impacts and coupled 1D/2D urban flood modelling within a unified scenario framework

Title: Analysis and Projection of the Relationship between Industrial Structure and Land Use Structure in China
Authors: Jin, Qin; Deng, Xiangzheng; Wang, Zhan; Shi, Chenchen; Li, Xing
Objective: To analyze the relationship between industrial structure and land use structure in China using computable general equilibrium (CGE) modelling method and project future changes from 2010 to 2020
LULC Classes: Cultivated land (crop); grassland (wool); other agriculture land; manufacturing land (secondary industry); construction land; service industry land
Baseline Years: 2000-2011 (for historical data and model calibration); 2010 (for projection baseline)
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU) scenario; Rapid Economic Growth (REG) scenario; Coordinated Environmental Sustainability (CES) scenario
Analysis Methods: Multi-regional Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) model; nested production functions combined with CES production function and Leontief production function; Bayesian estimation using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods (MCMC); sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Can quantitatively describe relationships and interdependencies among components of various economies within a complex social system; reflects structure of systematic equilibriums through market mechanism; depicts both supply and demand of commodities and services in unit pricing system
Tools/Soft Used: Multi-regional CGE model; Bayesian estimation; Markov chain Monte Carlo methods (MCMC)
Predictors: Labor force growth rate; investment growth rate; total factor productivity (TFP) growth rate; natural disaster impact factors; land use constraints; agricultural production impact function
Data Sources: China Statistic Yearbook 2001-2012; China Agricultural Statistic Yearbook 2001-2012; time series data of land use and demand changes; national land use plan 2006-2020
Validation Methods: Sensitivity analysis testing robustness of optimum solution; 1000-times simulation runs under 2% growth scenario; elasticity of substitution parameter validation within 95% confidence interval
Validation Data Sources: Historical data from 2000-2011; elasticity parameters distributed in range (0.1, 2.5) for CES production function
Key Findings: Industrial proportion in each province increasing from 2010-2020 with agriculture and service industries shifting to secondary industry; land use of secondary and tertiary industries increasing while agricultural land use decreasing; cultivated land will decrease but remain within acceptable limits (not below 120.33 million ha by 2020); built-up area expansion will remain within limits; productivity of cultivated and service industry land may decrease
Implications: Need to promote smooth economic structure transformation; adjust land management pattern toward market-oriented distribution; strengthen regional surveys of industrial and land use structure changes; focus on increasing land use efficiency for cultivation and service industries
Limitations: Less land use data availability; slow updating of data which influences industrial structure analysis; limited to 31 provinces (excluding Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macao due to lack of statistical data)
Future Directions: Strengthen regional surveys of industrial structure and land use structure changes; improve data collection and updating systems; focus on increasing economic efficiency of land use for cultivation and business services
Scalability: The model framework could potentially be applied to other regions, but specific parameters and constraints would need to be adjusted based on local conditions and data availability
Novelty: Integration of land use constraints into CGE model; incorporation of natural disaster impact functions; nested production function structure combining CES and Leontief functions; multi-regional dynamic approach for analyzing industrial-land use relationships

Title: Downscaling global land cover projections from an integrated assessment model for use in regional analyses: results and evaluation for the US from 2005 to 2095
Authors: West, Tristram O.; Le Page, Yannick; Huang, Maoyi; Wolf, Julie; Thomson, Allison M.
Objective: To develop and apply a new method for downscaling global land cover projections directly from an integrated assessment model for use by sub-regional and Earth system models using a land class nomenclature consistent with the Community Land Model plant functional types.
LULC Classes: Evergreen needleleaf forest; evergreen broadleaf forest; deciduous needleleaf forest; deciduous broadleaf forest; shrubland; grassland; cereal cropland; fiber crops; oil crops; other croplands; urban and built-up; snow and ice; barren or sparse vegetation.
Scenarios: Reference scenario; mitigation pathway 4.5; mitigation pathway 2.6.
Analysis Methods: Spatial downscaling using MODIS PFT Type 5 baselines; reconciliation of GCAM and MODIS land classes and areas; allocation driven by a priority conversion hierarchy; kernel density distance-weighted indices; integration with climate regime delineations.
Sim. Method Advantages: Direct translation of IAM outputs to high-resolution gridded products; retention of IAM scenario detail; consistency with CLM PFT nomenclature; improved alignment with Earth system models without intermediate conversion steps.
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Kernel density of existing plant functional types (distance and density); climate suitability variables (precipitation; temperature; growing degree days); pre-existing land-cover distribution.
Data Sources: GCAM regional land-cover outputs; MODIS MCD12Q1 Type 5 plant functional type data; agro-ecological zones from Monfreda et al.; climate data from New et al.; MODIS Vegetation Continuous Fields from Hansen et al.; global cropping data from Ramankutty and Foley.
Validation Methods: Statistical correlation of downscaled 2010 land realizations with observed MODIS PFT changes; comparison of grid-cell transitions between 2005 and 2010.
Validation Data Sources: MODIS PFT land-cover data for 2005 and 2010.
Key Findings: Net replacement of grassland by cropland in the western US and by forest in the eastern US under mitigation pathways; the downscaling method reproduces recent land-cover change patterns; annual gridded land-cover realizations for CLM PFT classes were successfully generated.
Implications: Provides spatially explicit inputs for regional and global climate and ecosystem models; informs potential impacts of socioeconomic and environmental drivers on future land-cover change; enhances regional analyses of climate–land interactions.
Limitations: Reliance on baseline MODIS data quality; assumption of a fixed priority conversion hierarchy; potential mismatches in class reconciling; absence of explicit land-cover transition data; coarse resolution constraints.
Future Directions: Application to other regions and scales; refinement of priority rules and transition algorithms; integration with finer-scale environmental datasets; coupling with high-resolution CLM simulations.
Scalability: Applicable to other regions using the same downscaling framework, though not explicitly tested.
Novelty: First direct downscaling of IAM land-cover outputs to 0.05° resolution using MODIS PFT baselines and CLM-compatible nomenclature; integration of kernel density indices with a priority conversion hierarchy; preservation of IAM scenario information in spatial realizations.

Title: Expansion of Protected Areas under Climate Change: An Example of Mountainous Tree Species in Taiwan
Authors: Lin, Wei-Chih; Lin, Yu-Pin; Lien, Wan-Yu; Wang, Yung-Chieh; Lin, Cheng-Tao; Chiou, Chyi-Rong; Anthony, Johnathen; Crossman, Neville D.
Objective: This study aims to predict whether or not the distributions of two high-mountain tree species, Abies (Abies kawakamii) and Tsuga (Tsuga chinensis var. formosana), will significantly shift upward due to temperature change, and whether current protected areas will be suitable for conserving these species
LULC Classes: Land-use types; forest types; timber; animal resources; soil types from the Third Forest Resources and Land Use Inventory
Scenarios: 15 different future scenarios produced from five global climate models (CSIRO-Mk3.5, GFDL-CM2.1, MIROC3.2, MPI-ECHAM5, MRI-CGCM2.3.2a) combined with three greenhouse gas emissions scenarios (B1, A1B, A2)
Analysis Methods: Species distribution models (SDMs) using maximum entropy model; bootstrap resampling technique; Wilcoxon nonparametric statistical test; systematic conservation planning approaches using Zonation software
Sim. Method Advantages: Maximum entropy model provides high accuracy predictions with AUC values ranging from 0.8 to 0.96 for Abies and 0.85 to 0.95 for Tsuga; bootstrap method provides easy-to-implement tool to assess uncertainty without assumption of statistical distribution
Tools/Soft Used: SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences); maximum entropy model; Zonation conservation planning software
Predictors: Average annual temperature; average spring monthly temperature; average summer monthly temperature; elevation
Data Sources: Third Forest Resources and Land Use Inventory in Taiwan (TFRLUI) published by the Forestry Bureau; Taiwan Climate Change Projection and Information Platform (TCCIP); Central Weather Bureau weather station networks; high resolution digital elevation model
Validation Methods: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) value calculation; bootstrap method with 1000 iterations; 80% of presence records used for training, 20% for validation
Validation Data Sources: Presence-only dataset of Abies and Tsuga from the Third Forest Resources and Land Use Inventory
Key Findings: Significant differences in suitable habitat distributions for Abies and Tsuga under seven of the 15 scenarios; mountainous ecosystems will be substantially impacted by climate change; uncertainty from GCMs and SDM parameters contribute most to overall variability; existing protected areas remain adequate with proportions of suitable habitat protected ranging 87.2%-90.9% for Abies and 85.3%-88.7% for Tsuga
Implications: Protected area networks may need modification to mitigate climate change impacts; additional conservation areas determined by systematic planning approaches will be necessary to offset loss of suitable habitat; policy makers should take projections of future species distributions into account
Limitations: Significant limitations exist in projecting future species distribution using SDMs; inherent uncertainty due to variability of both SDMs and projected future climatic models under different emission scenarios presents challenges
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: The bootstrap approach and systematic conservation planning framework could be applied to other mountainous regions facing climate change impacts, though specific adaptation would be required for different species and environmental conditions
Novelty: Integration of uncertainty analysis from multiple sources (SDM parameters, GCMs, GESs) using bootstrap resampling technique; combination of species distribution modeling with systematic conservation planning approaches; quantification of relative contributions of different uncertainty sources to overall variability in species distribution projections

Title: Integrated spatiotemporal modelling of bioenergy production potentials, agricultural land use, and related GHG balances; demonstrated for Ukraine
Authors: van der Hilst, Floor; Verstegen, Judith A.; Zheliezna, Tetiana; Drozdova, Olga; Faaij, Andre P. C.
Objective: To develop a modeling framework that enables the spatially and temporally specific assessment of bioenergy potential and agricultural intensification, including land-use change and related GHG emissions
LULC Classes: Arable land; Mosaic cropland-pasture; Pasture land; Bioenergy crops; Forest; Grassland; Shrubland; Natural vegetation
Scenarios: Business As Usual (BAU) scenario representing continuation of historic trends in agricultural productivity; Progressive scenario representing convergence of yield levels in Ukraine with Western Europe by 2050; Progressive scenario with sustainable agriculture measures including reduced tillage, increased carbon input, and fertilizer type improvements
Analysis Methods: PCRaster Land Use Change (PLUC) model for spatiotemporal land-use change modeling; GHG emissions modeling including CO2, N2O, and CH4 emissions; IPCC approach for calculating CO2 emissions related to changes in carbon stocks; Spatial modeling on 1 km² grid resolution
Sim. Method Advantages: Enables spatially and temporally specific assessment taking into account variability in land use, soil, and climate; Allows for integrated modeling of total GHG emissions of bioenergy production and intensification of agricultural sector; Provides detailed spatial resolution (1 km²) compared to aggregated assessments
Tools/Soft Used: PCRaster Land Use Change (PLUC) model; MITERRA-EUROPE model framework; Tension spline interpolation method; Expert consultation for weighting suitability factors
Predictors: Agro-ecological suitability; Accessibility (distance to infrastructure); Population density; Land conversion elasticity; Neighborhood characteristics; Number of villages; Changes in population density and unemployment; Land rent prices as proxy for areas where cropland and pastures will not be abandoned easily
Data Sources: FAO outlook for Eastern European Countries; National trends in population size; Dietary intake and export data; NOAA weather stations database; Spatial data on soil characteristics from Batjes; Ukraine country report of UNFCCC; State Statistic Service of Ukraine
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: In BAU scenario, little land becomes available for bioenergy crops; In progressive scenario, 32.1 Mha could become available by 2030; Potential production of 3.6 EJ/yr wheat or 5.0 EJ/yr switchgrass by 2030; Cumulative GHG emission reduction potential of 0.8 Gt CO2-eq for wheat and 3.8 Gt CO2-eq for switchgrass in progressive scenario; Changes in carbon stocks due to land-use change are main contributor to overall GHG balance
Implications: Bioenergy potential without expanding agricultural land depends on agricultural intensification rate; Spatiotemporal assessment shows different results than aggregated assessments; Model framework allows identification of best areas for agricultural intensification and bioenergy crop production; Longer timeframes favor second-generation biofuels over natural vegetation regrowth
Limitations: Lack of detailed and accurate spatial data for Ukraine; Inconsistencies between data sources; Simplifications in both LUC and GHG emission modeling; Use of default emission factors; Linear modeling of soil organic carbon and biomass carbon gains and losses; Application of rudimentary scenarios uniformly across Ukraine
Future Directions: Obtaining more detailed and accurate spatial data on land use and biophysical factors; Applying more process-based modeling; Performing extensive analysis of error propagation and uncertainty; Finer modeling resolution for ex-ante assessment, monitoring and certification of biomass production
Scalability: The modeling framework approach can be applied to other regions, though country-specific drivers and suitability factors would need to be adapted
Novelty: Integration of spatiotemporal land-use change modeling with dynamic GHG emission assessment; Spatial differentiation of GHG emissions at 1 km² resolution; Linking agricultural intensification with bioenergy potential assessment; Temporally explicit modeling of carbon sequestration and GHG emissions over time

Title: Integrating global socio-economic influences into a regional land use change model for China
Authors: Xu, Xia; Gao, Qiong; Peng, Changhui; Cui, Xuefeng; Liu, Yinghui; Jiang, Li
Objective: Develop an integrated modeling system that links a global socio-economic model (GLOBFOOD) with a regional spatial allocation model (modified CLUE) to examine how global market and economic drivers influence land-use changes in China.
LULC Classes: CROP (crop fields); GRAS (grassland); FORE (forest land); BUIL (buildings); WATE (water bodies); OTHE (other land use).
Baseline Years: 2000 and 2005 (land-use maps used to derive transition probabilities).
Scenarios: Scenario A: Regional environmental protection; Scenario B: Sustainable global economic development.
Analysis Methods: Global socio-economic model (GLOBFOOD within SIMILE framework); Regional spatial allocation model (modified CLUE); Terrestrial ecosystem simulation model (TESim); Markov transfer matrix for land-use transitions; Weighted suitability index (site, expert, stability, demand factors)
Sim. Method Advantages: Links cross-scale interactions; integrates socio-economic and ecological drivers; simulates multi-factor competition among land-use types; iteratively balances demand and allocation.
Tools/Soft Used: SIMILE modeling framework; ArcGIS for spatial resampling; modified CLUE and TESim models; GLOBFOOD model.
Predictors: Slope; elevation; mean annual temperature; cumulative growing-season temperature; annual precipitation; growing-season precipitation; expert fuzzy membership factors; land-use stability (Markov loss likelihood); socio-economic demand constants.
Data Sources: Land-use maps (2000–2005) from Chinese Academy of Resources and Environment Science Data Center; DEM (50 m) from State Bureau of Surveying and Mapping; Daily weather records (2000–2007) from 685 National Weather Service stations; GDP, production, population, trade data from national statistical departments.
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Scenario A yields slight decreases in cropland (–1.43 %) and grassland (–0.72 %), and a forestland increase (+1.05 %) by 2020.; Scenario B projects significant increases in cropland (+11.55 %), grassland (+52.38 %), and built-up areas (+19.66 %), with major losses in forest (–28.76 %) and other lands (–29.22 %).; Built-up expansion concentrates in high-quality cropland regions of eastern China.
Implications: Environmental protection policies can mitigate natural land loss; global economic growth pressures necessitate balancing food security and ecological objectives; policy should prioritize high-productivity cropland conservation.
Limitations: Assumes stationarity of driver–land-use relationships; expert-based parameters introduce uncertainty; scenario outputs indicate possibilities, not forecasts.
Future Directions: Compare simulations with and without global-regional coupling feedbacks.; Integrate soil fertility and ecosystem nutrient cycling for low-input agricultural systems.; Extend coupled framework to other land-intensive sectors (e.g., global logging).
Scalability: Approach is adaptable to other regions and processes involving global drivers and regional land-use impacts (e.g., logging, biofuel demand).
Novelty: First integration of a global socio-economic model (GLOBFOOD) with a regional spatial allocation model (CLUE) and ecosystem model (TESim) via iterative coupling to assess cross-scale land-use change dynamics.

Title: Projected land-use change impacts on ecosystem services in the United States
Authors: Lawler, Joshua J.; Lewis, David J.; Nelson, Erik; Plantinga, Andrew J.; Polasky, Stephen; Withey, John C.; Helmers, David P.; Martinuzzi, Sebastin; Pennington, Derric; Radeloff, Volker C.
Journal: PROCEEDINGS OF THE NATIONAL ACADEMY OF SCIENCES OF THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
Objective: To project land-use change in the contiguous United States to 2051 under two plausible baseline trajectories of economic conditions and analyze policy alternatives designed to encourage forest cover and natural landscapes and reduce urban expansion
LULC Classes: Cropland; pasture; forest; range (grasslands and shrublands); urban (includes developed open space and low- to high-intensity urban lands)
Scenarios: Two baseline scenarios: 1990s trend (continuation of land-use change trends from 1992 to 1997); High crop demand (10% increase in crop prices every five years relative to the 1990s trend); Three policy scenarios: Forest incentives; Natural habitats; Urban containment
Analysis Methods: Econometric model to predict spatially explicit land-use change; ecosystem service provision models for carbon storage, food production, timber production, and wildlife habitat; integration of land-use change analysis with ecosystem service models
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows simulation of effects of future policies that modify relative returns to different land uses; estimates probability of conversion based on observations of past land-use change, land parcel characteristics, and economic returns while accounting for endogenous feedbacks from policies into commodity prices; incorporates price feedbacks resulting from induced changes in land use
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: County-specific net returns to each land use; soil type; starting land use; characteristics of land parcels; economic returns
Data Sources: USDA National Resource Inventory (NRI) for observed land-use changes between 1992 and 1997; National Land Cover Database (NLCD) for initial 2001 land-use map; Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) estimates; Bliss et al. soil carbon stock estimates; USDA National Nutrient Database
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Large increase in croplands (28.2 million ha) under high crop demand scenario compared with loss of cropland (11.2 million ha) under 1990s trend; projected land-use changes result in increases in carbon storage, timber production, food production from increased yields, and >10% decreases in habitat for 25% of modeled species; 47 out of 194 species projected to lose more than 10% of their habitat under 1990s trend scenario; policy interventions need to be aggressive to significantly alter underlying land-use change trends
Implications: Differences in underlying drivers of land-use change can have large impacts on projected land-use change with cascading effects on ecosystem services; there are inevitable tradeoffs among ecosystem services; powerful underlying trends drive land-use change that are difficult for policies to overcome; market price feedbacks limit policy effectiveness
Limitations: Does not include analyses of changes in land management; represents changes among land uses but not changes in intensity of uses; spatial grain mismatch between net returns data and land use map; does not explicitly model spatial processes; cannot anticipate all market and biophysical forces that will influence land use over the next four decades; species modeled are generally common species with relatively large ranges
Future Directions: Extension to allow land-use intensity to change endogenously; inclusion of spatial variables such as distance to cities and land-use choices of neighboring parcels; analysis of climate change effects on scenarios and policies
Scalability: Model results can be compared with other relatively fine-grained model projections of regional land-use change scenarios; approach is not a true general equilibrium model but accounts for critical market feedbacks; most spatially detailed local-scale land-use analyses suitable for ecosystem service analysis
Novelty: Builds from empirical analysis of landowner decisions based on relative returns to predict land-use change and its impact on ecosystem services with illustrative and implementable policies; combines endogenous price modeling approach with detailed local-scale analysis of land-use change; accounts for influence of aggregate land-use change on commodity prices while maintaining spatial detail

Title: Spatially explicit modeling of 1992-2100 land cover and forest stand age for the conterminous United States
Authors: Sohl, Terry L.; Sayler, Kristi L.; Bouchard, Michelle A.; Reker, Ryan R.; Friesz, Aaron M.; Bennett, Stacie L.; Sleeter, Benjamin M.; Sleeter, Rachel R.; Wilson, Tamara; Soulard, Chris; Knuppe, Michelle; Van Hofwegen, Travis
Objective: The primary objective of the study was to produce spatially explicit, thematically detailed scenario-based land-use and land-cover projections and to model forest stand age for the conterminous United States from 1992 through 2100 .
LULC Classes: Water; Urban; Clearcut (National Forest); Clearcut (Other Public); Clearcut (Private); Mining; Barren; Deciduous Forest; Evergreen Forest; Mixed Forest; Grassland; Shrubland; Cropland; Hay/Pasture; Herbaceous Wetland; Woody Wetland .
Scenarios: IPCC-SRES: A1B; A2; B1; B2
Analysis Methods: Forecasting Scenarios of Land-Use Change (FORE-SCE) model; hierarchical downscaling by 84 Level III ecoregions; stepwise logistic regression to generate suitability surfaces; patch-based spatial allocation; scenario storylines consistent with IPCC SRES; use of VCT and NLCD data .
