Sim. Method Advantages: Combined top-down scenario demand with bottom-up spatial allocation; produced annual, spatially explicit, thematically detailed LULC maps; captured gross change rather than only net change; tracked forest stand age to inform cutting-cycle realism .
Tools/Soft Used: FORE-SCE modeling framework; logistic regression (statistical software unspecified); GIS for spatial data processing .
Predictors: Climate variables; soil characteristics; topographic factors; socioeconomic variables; vegetation change tracker (VCT) disturbance data; PAD-US protected-area masks .
Data Sources: National Land Cover Database (NLCD) 1992/2001/2006; USGS Land-Cover Trends; Vegetation Change Tracker (VCT); PAD-US protected-areas database; IPCC SRES storylines and IMAGE data; US Forest Service FIA; ancillary climate, soils, topography, and socioeconomic datasets .
Validation Methods: Comparison to 1992–2001 NLCD retrofit change data; calculation of quantity disagreement and allocation disagreement metrics; county-level comparisons of urban growth and clearcuts .
Validation Data Sources: 1992–2001 NLCD retrofit change data; USGS Land-Cover Trends data .
Key Findings: Natural land covers generally declined except under B2; anthropogenic lands (urban, agriculture, mining) increased in all scenarios except modest decline of agriculture in B2; fragmentation of natural covers increased; B2 maintained more stable natural cover and fragmentation; forest stand age was lowest under high-cutting scenarios (A1B) and higher on protected lands .
Implications: These spatially explicit projections can inform carbon and GHG flux modeling, biodiversity assessments, hydrologic change studies, and ecosystem management under multiple futures .
Limitations: Climate-change effects handled primarily top-down with limited dynamic suitability updates; lack of natural vegetation succession modeling; absence of integrated hydrologic or disturbance (fire, pests) modules; data inconsistencies among NLCD versions hinder formal validation .
Future Directions: Integrate dynamic climate-driven suitability surfaces; incorporate natural succession and disturbance regimes; link hydrologic models to account for water availability; extend framework to other regions .
Scalability: The modeling framework is flexible and transportable to other spatial extents, thematic resolutions, and geographic settings .
Novelty: First nationwide, annual LULC projections from 1992 to 2100 at 250 m resolution with scenario-based demand; integration of top-down IPCC SRES with bottom-up spatial allocation; explicit tracking of forest stand age .

Title: Using Changes in Agricultural Utility to Quantify Future Climate-Induced Risk to Conservation
Authors: Estes, Lyndon D.; Paroz, Lydie-Line; Bradley, Bethany A.; Green, Jonathan M. H.; Hole, David G.; Holness, Stephen; Ziv, Guy; Oppenheimer, Michael G.; Wilcove, David S.
Objective: To quantify how the agricultural utility of South African conservation lands may be altered by climate change and develop a framework for classifying their current and future vulnerability to agricultural conversion
LULC Classes: Maize cropland; wheat cropland; protected areas; priority conservation areas; natural ecosystems
Baseline Years: 1979-1999 (period for which historical weather data were available)
Scenarios: 36 different climate-crop response scenarios using 18 downscaled climate scenarios run twice - once with crop growth simulated under projected future CO2 concentration levels and once under 1979-1999 CO2 concentrations
Analysis Methods: DSSAT4.5 crop modeling; logistic regression; topographic ruggedness index; break-even yield analysis; agricultural utility calculation; vulnerability framework adaptation
Sim. Method Advantages: The 2-predictor model is accurate in distinguishing between farmed and unfarmed areas, and its lower complexity makes it more generalizable compared to more complex models
Tools/Soft Used: DSSAT version 4.5.0.047 (Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer); topographic ruggedness index calculations; logistic regression models
Predictors: Potential crop yield (maize and wheat); topographic ruggedness (local elevational variation)
Data Sources: DSSAT4.5 model; 92m resolution shuttle radar terrain mapping (SRTM) digital elevation model; point observations for crop presence (SIQ 2007); remotely sensed yield proxies
Validation Methods: Area under curve (AUC) of receiver operating characteristic curve; binary classification error assessment; comparison with remotely sensed yield proxies; accuracy assessment for delineating suitable growing regions
Validation Data Sources: Remotely sensed yield proxies; observed farm locations; point observations for crop presence and absence
Key Findings: Most conservation lands (89% of area) have negative agricultural utility now and in the future, placing them in low conversion pressure category; 8% of protected areas and 3% of priority areas in maize region classified as urgent; median utility of conservation lands strongly negative (-92 to -166 tons) while majority of current farmland has positive utility (27-28 tons median)
Implications: Several conservation lands classified as urgent require immediate conservation action, particularly priority areas northeast and east of Lesotho (high altitude grasslands) and coastal areas in wheat region (fynbos biome); areas with increasing agricultural utility may become future conversion targets; some areas with decreasing utility may become easier to protect
Limitations: Did not simulate potential agricultural management adaptations beyond altering planting density and sowing date; did not account for changing commodity prices, market accessibility, land ownership, transportation costs; did not consider alternative land uses like livestock ranching or tree plantations; large variations in crop yield projections created classification uncertainties
Future Directions: Developing estimates based on outputs of multiple crop models; building more detailed land-use models that factor in crop prices, subsidies, market growth, and alternative land uses; better understanding of agricultural utility shifts under climate change
Scalability: The approach provides a useful case study for other regions where significant biodiversity, extensive agricultural development, and substantial climate exposure overlap, such as the Brazilian cerrado; offers a readily transferable method for incorporating potential human responses to climate change into conservation planning
Novelty: First study to systematically quantify agricultural utility changes in conservation lands under climate change; novel adaptation of Margules and Pressey's vulnerability framework by replacing irreplaceability dimension with projected agricultural utility; innovative integration of crop modeling with conservation planning using break-even yield analysis

Title: Combined speeds of climate and land-use change of the conterminous US until 2050
Authors: Ordonez, Alejandro; Martinuzzi, Sebastian; Radelo, Volker C.; Williams, John W.
Objective: measure combined speeds of climate and land-use change and identify areas most vulnerable to biodiversity and ecosystem impacts
LULC Classes: forests; rangelands; pasture; cropland; urban
Scenarios: RCP 6.0; RCP 2.6; RCP 8.5; 1990s land-use trends; high crop-demand; restricted urban growth
Analysis Methods: univariate velocity (temporal anomaly / spatial gradient); multivariate speed via standardized Euclidean distance; analogue-based methods; econometric land-use projections
Sim. Method Advantages: integrates climate and land-use exposures; multivariate, species-independent index; accounts for local spatial heterogeneity vs regional displacement vectors
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: climate: mean annual temperature, potential evapotranspiration, total annual precipitation, annual water deficit, winter minimum temperature; land use: forest, rangeland, pasture, cropland, urban; economic incentives driving land-use projections (e.g., commodity prices, urban policy)
Data Sources: downscaled CMIP3/CMIP5 ensemble climate projections; US Natural Resources Inventory land-use scenarios; IPCC 5th Assessment RCP data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: climate speeds ≈ order of magnitude higher than land-use speeds; highest combined speeds in central USA swath and intermountain west; significant positive correlation between climate and land-use speeds (ρ = 0.45, p < 0.001); spatial patterns driven by topography and regional land-use trends
Implications: need for integrated, region-specific adaptation and conservation planning; prioritization of land acquisition/protection in high-exposure areas; recognition that multivariate assessments alter prioritization vs single-factor analyses
Limitations: dependent on availability of spatiotemporal data; no directional component in multivariate metric; uncertainties in scenarios and habitat matrix composition; species-specific traits not incorporated
Future Directions: apply framework to other regions; extend to indices of ecosystem intactness and adaptive capacity; characterize spatial rates of other stressors (e.g., pollutants)
Scalability: general approach adaptable to other regions given suitable data
Novelty: first integrated multivariate speed metric combining climate-velocity and analogue-based methods; normalization by local spatial dissimilarity for local exposure indexing

Title: Grassland production under global change scenarios for New Zealand pastoral agriculture
Authors: Keller, E. D.; Baisden, W. T.; Timar, L.; Mullan, B.; Clark, A.
Objective: Adapt and integrate Biome-BGC and LURNZ models to project New Zealand’s pastoral pasture production under land-use, intensification, and climate change scenarios
LULC Classes: Dairy pasture; sheep/beef pasture; plantation forestry; regenerating natural forest (scrubland)
Scenarios: Baseline; intensification; elevated CO₂; dynamic land-use change under ETS carbon prices (NZD 0, 50, 100 / t CO₂e); climate change (IPCC AR4 A2) mid-range (MPI) and upper-end (GIEH, CCC)
Analysis Methods: Process-based simulation across ∼5 km grid; decoupled land-use change sampling; statistical downscaling of GCMs; major axis regression; spatial aggregation in ArcGIS
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures CO₂ fertilisation and N-cycle feedbacks absent in simpler climate-index approaches; Intermediate complexity avoids farm-scale data overload of full system models; Flexible decoupled approach enables rapid re-sampling for varied land-use scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: Biome-BGC v4.2; LURNZ v2; PEST v12.0; ArcGIS 9.3; R (lmodel2 v1.7-2)
Predictors: Biophysical grid inputs: daily climate variables (Tₘₐₓ/min, precipitation, radiation, humidity, VPD corrected for wind); soil texture and rooting depth; N fixation rates; pasture utilisation; land-use class from LURNZ
Data Sources: NIWA VCSN daily weather (1972–present); IPCC AR4 GCM outputs downscaled via PLS regression; New Zealand Fundamental Soil Layers (FSL); LURNZ land-use maps (2008 baseline, 2020/2050 projections)
Validation Methods: Calibration of NPP against measured pasture clipping data at 6 sites (PEST optimization); Validation at 22 additional sheep/beef sites, comparison of daily and monthly averages, major axis regression; Dairy proxy validation via national milk solids production correlation
Validation Data Sources: Landcorp Farming and DairyNZ clipping data, South Island Dairying Development Centre, Beef + Lamb NZ, published studies (Rosser & Ross 2011, Smith et al. 2012); National milk solids production records (2006–2012)
Key Findings: Intensification yields ~10% national production increase by 2020, elevated CO₂ alone ~0.5%; Land-use trends: dairy area +18–19%, sheep/beef −4% by 2050, net +1.5% production; Climate change mid-range 2050: +2% national, upper-end: +1%; Dairy systems more resilient: increase or slight decline under all scenarios, sheep/beef decline under extreme warming
Implications: High-fertility dairying more adaptable to future climate and CO₂ changes; Policy planning should consider combined land-use and climate effects on feed supply and GHG emissions
Limitations: Potential biases in absolute production estimates, uncertainty not fully quantified; Underestimation of peak growth, poor fit at northern C₄ grass regions; No explicit irrigation modeling, dairy proxy validation indirect
Future Directions: Extend validation with additional spatially varying data, including C₄ grass regions; Incorporate irrigation and farm management practices; Quantify uncertainty bounds of model outputs
Scalability: Approach can be applied cost-effectively to other national or regional pastoral systems
Novelty: First national-scale integrated simulation of climate change, CO₂ fertilisation, and N-cycle feedbacks on NZ pastoral systems; Decoupled land-use change sampling method enabling rapid scenario analysis

Title: Integrated models, scenarios and dynamics of climate, land use and common birds
Authors: Ay, Jean-Sauveur; Chakir, Raja; Doyen, Luc; Jiguet, Frederic; Leadley, Paul
Objective: Present an integrated bio-economic modeling framework linking climate projections, private land‐use decisions and common bird abundances to evaluate direct and indirect effects of climate change and land‐use dynamics
LULC Classes: annual crops; perennial crops; pastures; forests; urban areas
Scenarios: S0: constant land use + climate; S1: extrapolated LUC trends + climate; S2: climate-induced LUC (Ricardian returns) + climate; S3: S1 + uniform pasture payments; S4: S2 + uniform pasture payments
Analysis Methods: Species distribution models (negative-binomial GAM); Econometric LUC model (multinomial logit); Ricardian model of land returns; Principal component analysis; Scenario simulations
Sim. Method Advantages: Simultaneous integration of direct climate effects and indirect climate-mediated land-use changes at fine (8×8 km) spatial resolution; Capability to evaluate incentive-based conservation policies over decades
Tools/Soft Used: R packages mgcv (GAM), glmmADMB, pscl (zero-inflation), nnet (multinomial logit)
Predictors: Climatic variables (2 PCA axes); habitat variables (including fragmentation index); topographic PCA axes; spatial coordinates; economic returns; biophysical variables (elevation, slope, land quality); previous land-use dummy
Data Sources: French Breeding Bird Survey (FBBS); TERUTI land-use survey; French Ministry of Agriculture land prices; regionalized climate data (Météo-France); IGN; INRA InfoSol
Validation Methods: Alternative SDMs (mixed models, zero-inflated hurdle models); Pearson correlations among model projections; Score tests for homoscedasticity; Hausman-McFadden IIA tests
Validation Data Sources: Online Resources (alternative SDM outputs); TERUTI land-use data; simulated cross-scenario comparisons
Key Findings: Climate change effects on bird abundances exceed land-use change impacts by mid-century; Climate-induced LUC amplifies negative climate impacts on most bird groups; Uniform pasture payments yield limited localized benefits, insufficient to offset climate effects
Implications: Policy must address both direct climate and climate-mediated land-use changes; Simple uniform incentives are inadequate, targeted spatial or regulatory measures are needed
Limitations: Single climate projection (IPCC A1B, relatively dry); truncated bird niche data (France-only); common birds as biodiversity proxy; IIA assumption in multinomial logit
Future Directions: Extend framework to European scale; incorporate broader climate scenarios; add spatial autocorrelation in LUC model; explore spatialized payments and quota-based regulations
Scalability: Potentially scalable to other regions with analogous data, but requires expanded biodiversity and land-use datasets
Novelty: First integrated framework simultaneously coupling direct climate impacts, indirect land-use adaptations and incentive policies on biodiversity at fine spatial resolution

Title: Land Use Dynamics, Climate Change, and Food Security in Vietnam: A Global-to-local Modeling Approach
Authors: Rutten, Martine; van Dijk, Michiel; van Rooij, Wilbert; Hilderink, Henk
Objective: To analyze impacts of uncertain and complex futures on Vietnam’s economy via changes in land use patterns using a global-to-local modeling approach
LULC Classes: Paddy rice; other agriculture (wheat; other cereal grains; vegetables, fruits & nuts; oil seeds; sugar cane & beet; plant-based fibers; other crops); production forest; non-production forest; shrub & grass land; built-up land; other land
Scenarios: Business as Usual (BAU); High Climate Impact (HCI); High Economic Growth (HEG)
Analysis Methods: Soft-linked global CGE modeling (MAGNET) with spatial land‐use allocation model (CLUE)
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures global-to-local trade linkages in a developing country; Produces spatially explicit land‐use maps at 1×1 km resolution; Integrates macroeconomic and landscape-level determinants
Tools/Soft Used: MAGNET CGE model; CLUE‐S land‐use model; GIS for spatial data; IMAGE flood module
Predictors: Bio-physical: soil type, slope, elevation, proximity to infrastructure and populated areas, flood risk maps; Socio-economic: population growth, urbanization rates, protected area status, land supply, yields, productivity growth
Data Sources: Primary: 2007 FIPI land use map, IMAGE flood maps (ECHAM4 scenario), Vietnamese National Institute of Agricultural Planning and Projection, UNDESA urbanization projections; Secondary: GTAP v8 database (2007), FAO yield projections, USDA-ERS macroeconomic projections
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Services (>50% GDP) and manufacturing (~30%) dominate by 2030, agriculture declines; Commercial forest expands (44%→54% of commercial land), paddy rice falls (28%→21%); Built-up land rises (3%→5% BAU, up to 8% HEG); HCI reduces GDP growth (6.6%→6.4%/yr), lowers food security, HEG boosts growth (8%/yr) and food security; 57% of paddy rice, 32% built-up land, and 13% other agriculture at flood risk by 2030
Implications: Need for agricultural R&D and yield‐boosting investments; Improve land‐market functioning for smoother reallocation; Implement climate change mitigation/adaptation and forest conservation policies
Limitations: Excludes extreme weather event impacts and livestock heat stress; No feedback loops from land‐use change to emissions and further climate impacts; Relies on land‐use base map with classification inconsistencies
Future Directions: Model land‐market dynamics and forest growth more explicitly; Incorporate extreme weather and livestock vulnerability; Quantify crop losses by flood depth and frequency; Enhance feedback between land‐use change and GHG emissions
Scalability: Framework applicable to other developing countries given adequate data
Novelty: First global-to-local dynamic land‐use modeling application for a developing country, integrating MAGNET and CLUE for spatially explicit scenario analysis.

Title: Threats and opportunities for freshwater conservation under future land use change scenarios in the United States
Authors: Martinuzzi, Sebastian; Januchowski-Hartley, Stephanie R.; Pracheil, Brenda M.; McIntyre, Peter B.; Plantinga, Andrew J.; Lewis, David J.; Radeloff, Volker C.
Objective: Evaluate potential consequences of future land use changes on freshwater ecosystems by comparing projected patterns of land use change with current patterns of freshwater biodiversity and water quality impairment
LULC Classes: Urban; Crop; Pasture; Forest; Rangeland; Natural grassland; Natural shrubland
Scenarios: Business As Usual; Forest Incentives; High Crop Demand; Urban Containment
Analysis Methods: Econometric multinomial logit land use model; Rarity-weighted richness calculation; Overlay of land use change and water quality threat maps
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows scenario testing of policy-induced and market-induced changes; Accounts for endogenous economic returns and ‘slippage’ effects
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Net economic returns for each land use; Soil characteristics; County-level commodity prices; Conversion costs
Data Sources: National Land Cover Database 2001; Soil Survey Geographic Database; USDA Natural Resources Inventory; NatureServe; IUCN species distribution; Brown & Froemke water quality threat ratings; USGS HUC watershed boundaries
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Widespread urban expansion projected in eastern watersheds, doubling watersheds with >20% urban cover under Business As Usual; Forest Incentives scenario increased natural vegetation in Midwest and reduced slippage via endogenous pricing; High Crop Demand scenario projected 23% increase in watersheds with >30% crop cover, threatening high-biodiversity areas; Urban Containment markedly reduced urban expansion in biodiversity hotspots but had limited effect in California
Implications: Policy and market forces can significantly alter future land use pressures on freshwater ecosystems; Incentives for afforestation and urban containment can mitigate threats; Crop price trends present windows for conservation easements
Limitations: Focus solely on land use threats; Does not account for spatial configuration, connectivity, climate change, invasive species, or land-use legacy; Global-scale amphibian range data may lack local accuracy
Future Directions: Incorporate climate change, invasive species, hydrological connectivity, spatial arrangement, and updated land-use and biodiversity data into scenario analyses
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with available land use and biodiversity data, pending model adaptation to local economic and policy contexts
Novelty: Coupling econometric land use projections with freshwater biodiversity and water quality threat assessments to evaluate policy and market scenario impacts for freshwater conservation

Title: Effects of Governance on Availability of Land for Agriculture and Conservation in Brazil
Authors: Sparovek, Gerd; de Oliveira Pereira Barretto, Alberto Giaroli; Matsumoto, Marcelo; Berndes, Goran
Objective: To analyze the influence of public and private environmental protection on nature conservation and agricultural production in Brazil, and to advance understanding of how governance systems addressing nature conservation and agricultural production may influence Brazilian land use depending on the relative priority of conservation and production objectives
LULC Classes: Natural Vegetation (NV); Pasture (PA); Cropland (CR); Intensive Cropland (CR+); Intensive Pasture (PA+)
Baseline Years: 2008 (reference date for Forest Act compliance rules established before July 22, 2008)
Scenarios: Three scenarios: Conservation scenario (prioritizing nature protection); Production scenario (prioritizing high agricultural production); Neutral scenario (balancing agricultural production and environmental protection objectives)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land-use modeling; two-step land allocation process; first step reserves land for nature conservation under legal command and control frameworks; second step allocates unreserved lands based on agricultural suitability and governance mechanisms
Sim. Method Advantages: The spatially explicit modeling approach complements economic equilibrium modeling by taking a finer approach to land use/land cover, legislation, and other aspects influencing land use decisions; grounded in empirical data and scientific analysis; well-suited for showing development pathways that deviate from historic experiences
Tools/Soft Used: Spatially explicit land use model; GIS-based analysis with process polygons averaging 3,729 hectares
Predictors: Land use/cover type (NV, PA, CR); land suitability class (Very High, High, Medium, Low, Very Low); legal compliance frameworks; agricultural land suitability; available technology and management options; local and market-driven land use regulations
Data Sources: Brazilian Forest Act (FA); Atlantic Forest Law (AFL); Terra Legal land titling initiative; National Framework for Conservation Units policy (SNUC); Indian Reservations data from FUNAI; military areas data; spatially explicit land use data with 228,250 process polygons
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: About 80% of existing natural vegetation in Brazil is under private or public command and control legal protection; roughly one-third of natural vegetation on private land (20% of total NV) is not protected by legal frameworks; Terra Legal program adds roughly 28% of natural vegetation to existing Legal Amazon public conservation network; 114 million hectares of natural vegetation on private lands without legal obligations rely on non-command and control mechanisms for protection
Implications: Future natural vegetation protection beyond legal requirements depends on incentives influencing the balance between conservation and production objectives; achieving incentive-based natural vegetation protection requires far-reaching changes in the beef sector including major productivity improvements; direct investments in conservation are strategically important for protecting natural vegetation in Brazil
Limitations: The model does not include logistic or other constraints for land use changes; results should not be understood as possible near-term land use change but as indicative of longer-term dynamics; uncertainty regarding the hierarchy of Forest Act rules addressing legal deficits in the Amazonian biome; volatile situation following shift from command and control governance toward market-based intervention
Future Directions: Need for improved private sector compliance with legislation; better alignment with global environmental policies; promotion of relevant public institutions and monitoring/enforcement frameworks; support for civil society activism and surveillance; coordination with ongoing societal processes influencing governance in poverty, economic development, health care, education, and food security
Scalability: The spatially explicit modeling approach may be applicable to other regions, but the specific governance frameworks and legal structures analyzed are particular to Brazil's context
Novelty: First study to include projections for the Terra Legal program; comprehensive analysis combining multiple governance frameworks (Forest Act, Atlantic Forest Law, Terra Legal); integration of command and control mechanisms with market-based and voluntary governance approaches; spatially explicit modeling at high resolution with over 228,000 process polygons

Title: Effects of land use planning on aboveground vegetation biomass in China
Authors: Sun, Xiaofang; Yue, Tianxiang; Wang, Meng; Fan, Zemeng; Liu, Fengqiao
Objective: To assess how land use change will influence the size and spatial distribution of vegetation biomass in China, specifically evaluating the impact of national level land use planning on the spatial configuration of vegetation biomass for the period 2005–2030
LULC Classes: Built-up land; cultivated land; grassland; shrub; forest; water area; other land use types (including bare land, rocky areas, glaciers and wasted land)
Scenarios: Trend scenario (extrapolation of land use trends for 1985–1995 before implementing national ecological restoration program); planning scenario (projected using a set of land use policies including forest coverage goals, grassland restoration, and cultivated land protection)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land use change model (Dyna-CLUE); biomass density approach; logistic regression to correlate land use patterns with driving factors; Kappa statistics for validation
Sim. Method Advantages: The Dyna-CLUE model can well capture the land use dynamics with spatial allocation rules determined by integrating empirical analysis, user-specified decision rules, and neighborhood characteristics; enables downscaling of national-scale scenarios to land use patterns with high spatial resolution (2×2 km)
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE model; logistic regression; receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis
Predictors: Population density; GDP; distance to nearest main road; average percentage of sunshine; total precipitation; average temperature; elevation (DEM); slope; aspect index; topsoil pH; soil texture; soil depth; soil drainage; soil organic carbon
Data Sources: Land use maps produced by Chinese Academy of Sciences through human-machine interactive interpretation based on Landsat TM data; China's national forest inventory data (2004–2008); China Rural Statistical Yearbook; province-specific biomass densities from published literature
Validation Methods: Kappa statistics to validate allocation algorithm and evaluate relationships between land use types and driving factors; comparison of simulated and observed land use patterns of 2005
Validation Data Sources: Land use distribution data for 1985 and 2005; observed land use data in 2005 for comparison with simulated results
Key Findings: Under planning scenario, vegetation biomass would be 15.47 Gt in 2030, showing increase by 0.11 Gt compared to 2005; under trend scenario, biomass would be 14.62 Gt in 2030, 0.02 Gt higher than 2005; planning scenario shows 7.66% increase in biomass (1,100 Tg) than in 2005; Kappa coefficient for location validation was 0.85; ROC values ranged between 0.81 and 0.98 for different land use types
Implications: Land use planning measures can significantly impact biomass variation; vegetation biomass can increase due to afforestation and restoration of grassland under planning scenario; young forests have high potential to increase biomass and can become carbon sinks; carbon sequestration in biomass change would regulate atmospheric carbon dioxide and impact climate change
Limitations: Changes of climatic and socioeconomic factors not considered due to trivial effects over timeframe and data availability; biomass densities for grassland, shrub and cultivated land assumed constant over 25 years; built-up land, water area and other land use types assumed to have zero biomass; some deviation might be introduced by extrapolating climatic and socioeconomic conditions for 2030
Future Directions: Studies using same scenarios and land use type classification in different simulation methods should be performed to better compare results; assessment of other aspects like species composition and distribution, phenology should be considered to evaluate global warming containment effects
Scalability: The spatially explicit analytical methods can facilitate policy makers and scientists to evaluate impacts of national-scale land use policies on landscape, identify critical regions for biomass change and develop sound regional-scale policies and planning; similar assessments are possible for other ecological and social indicators
Novelty: Few spatially explicit assessments have been undertaken to assess the influence of land use change on biomass in China; this study provides nationwide estimation of biomass changes fully accounting for land use changes; method contributes to multi-scale assessment of future biomass under wide range of land use types

Title: Forest forecasting with vegetation models across Russia
Authors: Shuman, Jacquelyn K.; Tchebakova, Nadezhda M.; Parfenova, Elena I.; Soja, Amber J.; Shugart, Herman H.; Ershov, Dmitry; Holcomb, Katherine
Objective: To test and compare results between two vegetation models (RuBCliM and UVAFME) for both present-day and future climatic conditions, specifically examining forest response to changing climate across Russia
LULC Classes: Tundra; forest-tundra; dark-needled forests (northern, middle, southern taiga); light-needled forests; subtaiga; forest-steppe; steppe; mixed conifer-broadleaved; broadleaved forest; desert-semidesert
Scenarios: IPCC A2 (business as usual with steadily increasing CO2 emissions); A1B (stabilizes CO2 emissions at 720 ppm)
Analysis Methods: Bioclimatic envelope modeling (RuBCliM); individual-based gap modeling (UVAFME); kappa statistics for concordance assessment; Monte Carlo simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Gap models can project forest response across large regions in terms of species composition and structural properties; bioclimatic models provide correlation-based envelope-style matching of climax vegetation with climate; using two disparate modeling techniques provides more reliable and robust results
Tools/Soft Used: NCAR's Community Climate System Model (CCSM); Hutchinson's thin-plate splines; IDRISI; ESRI ArcGIS version 9.3
Predictors: Growing degree-days above 5°C (GDD5); negative degree-days below 0°C (NDD0); annual moisture index (AMI); presence/absence of continuous permafrost; monthly temperature and precipitation variables
Data Sources: National Climate Data Center weather station data (1941-2001); Russian weather station records (1900-1964); Stolbovoi and McCallum (2002) soil data; forest inventory maps; biome classification maps
Validation Methods: Kappa statistics for spatial comparison; comparison with independent observation-based maps; model concordance assessment between RuBCliM and UVAFME
Validation Data Sources: Isaev (1990) forest inventory map of species distribution; Isachenko et al. (1988) landscape map of forest biomes
Key Findings: Both models show good agreement (kappa values 0.76-0.69) and project a shift from coniferous to deciduous species dominance; UVAFME projects 43% increase in deciduous species area, RuBCliM projects up to 50% increase; carbon losses of 0.678-1.347 Pg C projected under different scenarios
Implications: Transition from conifers to deciduous species has implications for energy budget, carbon cycle, and land cover feedbacks in boreal system; albedo shifts may affect regional warming patterns; economic impacts due to different values of coniferous versus deciduous species
Limitations: UVAFME constrained by current species range limitations while RuBCliM allows unlimited migration; neither model explicitly simulates species migration under climate change; carbon projections don't account for soil organic carbon or permafrost thaw effects
Future Directions: Need for continued investigation of this landmass due to its size and influence on regional and global climate; investigation of permafrost dynamics and soil carbon stocks; studies incorporating active disturbances like fire and insect outbreaks
Scalability: Models have been tested along altitudinal gradients in northern China, Australia, central Europe, Sierra Nevadas, and applied to reconstruct pollen chronologies in Europe, central Asia, and North America
Novelty: First comprehensive comparison between bioclimatic envelope model and individual-based gap model across entire Russian territory; integration of permafrost considerations in vegetation modeling; validation against multiple independent observation-based maps

Title: Future landscapes of Switzerland: Risk areas for urbanisation and land abandonment
Authors: Price, Bronwyn; Kienast, Felix; Seidl, Irmi; Ginzler, Christian; Verburg, Peter H.; Bolliger, Janine
Objective: To define scenarios of future land-use for Switzerland and identify locations for key land use transitions, specifically risk areas for urbanisation and agricultural land abandonment by 2035
LULC Classes: Closed forest; Open forest; Overgrown areas; Pasture agriculture; Intensive agriculture; Settlement and Urban areas
Scenarios: Five scenarios along axes of Globalisation to Regionalisation and Market-driven developments to high policy intervention: Trend; A1; A2; B1; B2
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land-use allocation modelling using Dyna-CLUE framework; scenario-based approach incorporating socio-economic and bio-geographical variables; suitability modelling
Sim. Method Advantages: Incorporating socio-economic as well as bio-geographical variables into suitability modelling allowed improvement on biogeographical-only approaches; spatially explicit framework enables identification of hotspots and risk areas
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE (Conversion of Land Use and its Effects) modelling framework
Predictors: Climate variables (continentality index, moisture index, solar radiation, precipitation); Relief variables (slope, elevation, aspect); Soil characteristics (permeability, stoniness, suitability); Infrastructure variables (distance to roads, forest proximity); Socioeconomic factors (taxable income, employment sectors, public transport accessibility)
Data Sources: Swiss land use statistics (SFSO 2013a); Swiss Federal Statistical Office demographic and economic data; MeteoSwiss climate data; Swiss topographical landscape model; soil suitability maps; municipal taxation data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Large areas of the Swiss Plateau and Alpine valley bottoms face strong urbanisation pressure, Much of the mountainous pasture agriculture continues to face risk of abandonment without policy intervention, Key drivers of urbanisation vary spatially; public transport and employment in secondary/tertiary sectors important on Plateau, while primary sector employment and environmental factors more important in Alpine areas
Implications: Knowledge of spatial locations and magnitude of likely land use changes is key for enabling policy makers to make informed decisions; Strong policy interventions would be needed to change current underlying land use trends; Agricultural abandonment and reforestation can have negative implications for open land and wetland species
Limitations: Modelling future land use change is subject to large uncertainty, particularly in future socio-economic and policy trajectories; Land use processes driven by management and policy decisions are generally more difficult to model accurately than those driven by physical environmental processes; Lack of nation-wide tourism data was not explicitly considered as a driver
Future Directions: Scenarios will provide key base information for future work including assessing conflicts and synergies in land-use planning and assessing impacts of land-use change on landscape function and ecosystem health
Scalability: The methodology demonstrates the importance of considering regional variations in drivers in land use modelling, which could be applied to other regions with similar biogeographical diversity
Novelty: First comprehensive spatially explicit scenario study for Switzerland incorporating both urbanisation and agricultural abandonment processes; Integration of socio-economic and bio-geographical variables in a multi-scenario framework; Identification of spatial differences in land use change drivers across biogeographical regions

Title: Modelling Australian land use competition and ecosystem services with food price feedbacks at high spatial resolution
Authors: Connor, Jeffery D.; Bryan, Brett A.; Nolan, Martin; Stock, Florian; Gao, Lei; Dunstall, Simon; Graham, Paul; Ernst, Andreas; Newth, David; Grundy, Mike; Hatfield-Dodds, Steve
Objective: Demonstrate the importance of high resolution land heterogeneity representation in understanding local impacts of future global scenarios with carbon markets and land competition influencing food prices; investigate how food price feedbacks from land use competition may impact land use change in aggregate and locally at high resolution; assess the significance of food price feedback relative to other significant land use drivers
LULC Classes: Agriculture (24 irrigated and rain-fed agricultural commodities); Carbon plantings (fast-growing Eucalyptus monocultures); Environmental plantings (local native tree and shrub species); Biofuels (wheat grain and residue for transport fuel); Bioenergy (short rotation Eucalypt for biomass-based electricity)
Scenarios: Three global outlooks from Australian National Outlook (ANO): L1 (very strong global abatement effort, peak at 3.0 W m⁻² then decline to 2.6, 445 ppm CO₂); M3 (strong abatement effort, 4.5 W m⁻², 650 ppm CO₂); H3 (no action, 8.5 W m⁻², 1360 ppm CO₂)
Analysis Methods: Australian continental Land Use Trade-offs (LUTO) model with bottom-up parcel scale granularity; linear programming optimization model; partial equilibrium food price impacts modeling; global sensitivity analysis using extended Fourier amplitude sensitivity test (eFAST)
Sim. Method Advantages: Methodologically unique in modelling high resolution land use and ecosystem service processes interacting with macro level impacts of land use competition influencing agricultural commodity prices; provides substantially more detail than previous models in accounting for within-region, parcel-scale spatial differences in land attributes influencing economic returns and ecosystem service productivity diversity
Tools/Soft Used: Australian Land Use Trade-offs (LUTO) model; Global Trade and Environment Model (GTEM); 3-PG2 forest growth model; Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM); Energy Sector Model for Australia; Australian Water Resources Assessment Landscape Model; extended Fourier amplitude sensitivity test (eFAST)
Predictors: Carbon price; agricultural commodity prices; agricultural productivity; adoption hurdle rate parameter; climate conditions; soil conditions; land suitability; global demand for crops and livestock; energy prices
Data Sources: Australian Bureau of Statistics (2006); Marinoni et al. (2012) for current national mapping of agricultural land use; Global Trade and Environment Model (GTEM) outputs; Australian National Outlook (ANO) integrated assessment; published 3-PG2 forest stand growth and carbon sequestration modeling; Agricultural Production Systems Simulator (APSIM); Energy Sector Model for Australia; Australian Water Resources Assessment Landscape Model
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Food price feedbacks produce modest aggregate national land use and ecosystem service supply changes; high resolution results show amplified land use change and ecosystem service impact in some places and muted impacts in other areas relative to national averages; price feedback effects only have modest influence on land use change and ecosystem services at the aggregate national level; locally-unique, highly spatially variable, and scenario-dependent impacts of agricultural commodity price feedback were observed at high resolution
Implications: Small aggregate impacts at national scale can be highly concentrated in local areas; failure to appreciate local effects may threaten success of community-based natural resource management; objections from disaffected local areas may hinder realization of large-scale policy benefits; need for nested evaluation process to assess both aggregate large-scale impacts and focus on particularly impacted regions
Limitations: Validation is fundamentally problematic for long horizon futures; lack of representation of opportunity to expand agricultural area could lead to overestimation of land competition impacts on food prices; simple rational choice approach based on expected utility that generalizes complex land use change decision factors; assumes land use change from agriculture to tree-based uses is irreversible
Future Directions: More general formulation could incorporate energy price feedback from bioenergy and biofuel production; general equilibrium representation of global and local land and food demand supply linkages; representation of opportunity to expand agricultural area; more realistic behavioral representations including asymmetric risk valuation, bounded rationality, heuristic-based decision-making
Scalability: The approach points toward nested evaluation processes that could be applied to other regions, though the specific findings are context-dependent on local environmental and economic conditions
Novelty: First study to combine traditional market dynamics with fine resolution economic and environmental heterogeneity in modeling land use change; methodologically unique Australian continental model with bottom-up parcel scale granularity and partial equilibrium food price impacts; novel integration of high spatial resolution (0.01° grid cells) with macro-economic price feedback mechanisms

Title: Modelling the combined effects of land use and climatic changes: Coupling bioclimatic modelling with Markov-chain Cellular Automata in a case study in Cyprus
Authors: Louca, Marianna; Vogiatzakis, Ioannis N.; Moustakas, Aristides
Objective: To quantify the combined effects of climatic and land use changes on two endemic plant species (Crocus cyprius and Ophrys kotschyi) in Cyprus by coupling climate change scenarios and land use change models with species distribution models
LULC Classes: Artificial surfaces; non-irrigated arable land; sclerophyllous vegetation; natural grasslands; broad-leaved forest; mixed forest; coniferous forests
Scenarios: A1B; A2; B1; B2A climate change scenarios derived from IPCC reports
Analysis Methods: Bioclimatic modelling using classification trees; Markov-chain Cellular Automata for land use prediction; Species Distribution Models (SDMs)
Sim. Method Advantages: Markov chain combined with Cellular Automata solves the lack of spatial dimension problem of Markov chain alone, providing accurate information on transition probabilities and spatial distribution of changes
Tools/Soft Used: SPSS version 20 for statistical analysis; CA_MARKOV in Idrisi Selva software for land use prediction; ArcGIS version 8 for mapping
Predictors: For Crocus cyprius: mean temperature of wettest quarter; max temperature of warmest month; precipitation seasonality. For Ophrys kotschyi: precipitation of wettest month; mean temperature of warmest quarter; isothermality; precipitation of coldest quarter; annual precipitation
Data Sources: Red Data Book of the Flora of Cyprus for species distribution data; Worldclim database version 1.4 for bioclimatic data; CORINE database for land use data 2000 and 2006; GCM HadCM3 for future bioclimatic data
Validation Methods: Cohen's Kappa and "area under the curve" (AUC) of receiver operating characteristic plot (ROC plot)
Validation Data Sources: Current species distribution data from Red Data Book of the Flora of Cyprus
Key Findings: All scenarios predict disappearance of C. cyprius' main occurrence area in Troodos Mountains; 34 to 68 out of 102 current C. cyprius sites excluded from future potential distribution; O. kotschyi potential distribution declines in all scenarios with 111 to 116 out of 117 current sites excluded; inclusion of land use change causes additional reduction for O. kotschyi but not significant changes for C. cyprius
Implications: Results demonstrate the importance of including both land use and climatic changes in predictive species modelling; maps can guide adaptation and mitigation measures for climate change; provides useful tool for policy and decision makers
Limitations: Spatial and temporal resolution mismatches; possibility of sampling bias; quality and accuracy of Worldclim and CORINE data; unrealistic SDM assumptions including equilibrium with environment; ignoring biotic interactions and evolutionary changes; scale-specific predictions; uncertainty from creation of theoretical presences and absences
Future Directions: Use of individual based models to model both land use and climatic changes; comparison of model outputs in identical grid size; disentangling interaction effects between land use and climate changes
Scalability: The procedure developed can be used for any species where data is available and provides a valuable and transferable method for understanding potential shifts in species distributions
Novelty: First study to couple bioclimatic modelling with Markov-chain Cellular Automata for endemic species in Cyprus; dynamic model coupling of climate models and land use models; integration of both climatic and land use variables in species distribution modelling for Mediterranean island ecosystems

Title: Oil palm for biodiesel in Brazil-risks and opportunities
Authors: Englund, Oskar; Berndes, Goran; Persson, U. Martin; Sparovek, Gerd
Objective: To determine the net present value (NPV) of establishing new oil palm plantations for biodiesel production under different climate and energy policy regimes in order to map areas in Brazil where production would be profitable; estimate the associated biodiesel production and LUC; and investigate whether pricing of carbon emissions from LUC could make oil palm production unprofitable on lands with high carbon stocks
LULC Classes: Forest; pastures; cropland; mosaic cropland; natural vegetation (excluding forests); protected areas (natural parks, indigenous land, military purposes)
Scenarios: 18 main scenarios based on three energy scenarios from the 2012 World Energy Outlook (WEO): 'Current policies' (CP), 'New policies' (NP), and '450 ppm'; combined with three different levels of LUC carbon price ($22/tC mid, $64/tC high for 2013; $43/tC mid, $125/tC high, $249/tC high for 2025); two different establishment years (2013 and 2025)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit modelling; Net Present Value (NPV) calculations; GIS-based spatial analysis; algebraic and statistical operations on NPV results
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS
Predictors: Land price; timber revenue; plantation establishment cost; mill establishment cost; LUC carbon emissions cost; palm oil and residues revenue; cultivation cost; transport cost; N2O emissions cost; climate and soil conditions; potential yield; willingness to pay for biodiesel and residues
Data Sources: FAO (2013); IIASA and FAO (2012); FNP (2012); Baccini et al (2012); IEA (2012) World Energy Outlook; SUFRAMA (2003); Peters-Stanley et al (2013); Busch et al (2009); EMBRAPA (2010)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Oil palm was found to be profitable on extensive areas, including areas under native vegetation where establishment would cause large LUC emissions; 40-60 Mha could support profitable biodiesel production corresponding to approximately 10% of the global diesel demand without causing direct LUC emissions or impinging on protected areas; pricing of LUC emissions at $125/tC or higher could make oil palm production unprofitable on most lands where conversion would impact native ecosystems and carbon stocks; without LUC carbon pricing, establishment would be profitable on 360-390 Mha; forest conversion could emit up to 50 Gt of carbon to the atmosphere
Implications: Large-scale oil palm expansion could provide significant biodiesel production but poses substantial environmental risks if not properly managed; LUC carbon pricing could effectively discourage forest conversion; policy measures are crucial for directing oil palm development to appropriate lands; intensification of cattle production could free up pasture land for oil palm without additional deforestation
Limitations: Results do not account for dynamic effects of large-scale biodiesel production on global oil prices; main uncertainties include oil price projections and discount rate assumptions; calculations assume constant costs that may increase faster than inflation; indirect LUC effects not fully considered
Future Directions: Need for effective LUC carbon pricing schemes or REDD+ mechanisms; requirement for comprehensive policy measures applied to all agricultural activities; monitoring of enforcement effectiveness; assessment of international leakage effects
Scalability: The methodology could potentially be applied to other regions, but the study focuses specifically on Brazil's conditions, policies, and geographical characteristics
Novelty: High-resolution (100m) spatially explicit modelling of oil palm profitability across entire Brazil; comprehensive integration of multiple policy scenarios with LUC carbon pricing; detailed analysis of opportunities to achieve substantial biodiesel production without forest conversion

Title: Scenarios and Modeling of Land Use and Cover Changes in Portugal from 1980 to 2040
Authors: Santos, Sara; Cabral, Pedro; Zamyatin, Alexander
Journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF AGRICULTURAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION SYSTEMS
Objective: To analyze land use and cover changes in continental Portugal, test the hypothesis that land cover changes are generated by a first-order Markov process, and provide multi-decadal land cover projections using spatially explicit modeling approaches that combine Markov chains with cellular automata
LULC Classes: Agriculture; Agro-forestry; Artificial; Water bodies; Forest; Non-cultivated; Wetlands (7 simplified classes from 32 original Landyn classes)
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU); Environmental sustainability; Gross Domestic Product (GDP); Desertification
Analysis Methods: First-order Markov chains; Cellular automata combined with Markov chains; Chi-square statistical tests; Chapman-Kolmogorov equation; Transition matrix calculations
Sim. Method Advantages: Markov chains provide legitimate projections if changes are stationary in time; Cellular automata overcome the limitation of non-spatial explicit projections from Markov chains alone; Combined approach provides both quantitative and spatially explicit information
Tools/Soft Used: ESRI ArcGIS; IDRISI Selva software; CA_Markov module; ETRS89-LAEA 52N 10E reference grid
Predictors: Previous land use/cover state; Transition conditional probabilities; Neighborhood filter (5x5 cell window); Suitability maps
Data Sources: Landyn research project dataset; Portuguese Territory General Directorate (DGT); Random sample units based on Eurostat LUCAS guidelines (499,596 ha, 6% of territory, 1,279 samples); Corine Land Cover (CLC) maps for 1990-2000
Validation Methods: Quantity and allocation disagreement measures; Comparison of estimated 2010 results with real 2010 map
Validation Data Sources: Real map of 2010 matching sample units for validation decade
Key Findings: LUCC follows Markovian behavior in continental Portugal; Agriculture class will decrease from 39.3% (1980) to 30.1% (2040); Forest and artificial classes show significant increases; Water bodies increased 29.3% between 1995-2010 due to dam construction; All 5 NUTS 2 regions exhibited Markovian behavior; Validation showed 9.7% quantity disagreement and 22.4% allocation disagreement
Implications: Results enable better understanding of land cover change tendencies; Useful for territorial planning and management; Scenarios provide powerful tool for understanding tradeoffs between different land use strategies; Can engage discussions with land use planners and policy-makers
Limitations: Use of transition matrices over time periods can lead to wrong short-term projections or lack spatial continuity; Important drivers not considered include cyclic economic factors, specific development policies, natural catastrophes, new infrastructures; Factors like proximity to roads, slope, aspect were not included due to long time span; Requires stationary element for successful modeling
Future Directions: Include additional factors such as proximity to roads, slope, aspect to improve predictive power; Consider cyclic economic factors, development policies, and natural catastrophes; Adapt scenarios to reflect different strategies
Scalability: Results can be extrapolated for the total study area within confidence limits of sampling method; Methodology could be applied to other regions with similar characteristics
Novelty: Extends LUCC analysis period back to 1980s for Portugal; Combines Markov chains with cellular automata for spatially explicit projections; Develops concept-driven scenario building approach; Tests Markovian hypothesis for Portuguese LUCC using statistical methods

Title: Will Passive Protection Save Congo Forests?
Authors: Galford, Gillian L.; Soares-Filho, Britaldo S.; Sonter, Laura J.; Laporte, Nadine
Objective: To examine whether passive protection of Democratic Republic of Congo forests is sufficient for conservation and to simulate future land-use change under different policy scenarios from 2010 to 2050 using the SimCongo model
LULC Classes: Forest types (forest and woodland savanna); cleared lands; croplands; plantations (including forest crops and oil palm)
Scenarios: Historical Trends (passive forest protection); Conservation (active protection with REDD+ implementation); Agricultural Development (increased agricultural activities with concomitant deforestation)
Analysis Methods: Cellular automata modeling using Bayesian Weights of Evidence (WofE) method; linear regression modeling; spatially explicit land-use change modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica-EGO platform; LabFit Pro freeware; Google Earth imagery
Predictors: Distance to roads; distance to rivers; distance to towns and villages; slope; distance to croplands; distance to railroads; biomass; soil types; vegetation sub-types
Data Sources: Potapov et al. forest and cleared land maps; geo-wiki.org croplands map from International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis; Woods Hole Research Center plantation mapping; MODIS Vegetation Continuous Fields; Baccini et al. aboveground biomass map; FAO agricultural data
Validation Methods: Fuzzy logic validation using exponential decay function at multiple increasing windows; comparison of simulated 2010 land use map with observed 2010 land use map
Validation Data Sources: Historic deforestation observations from 1990-2010 used to validate model predictions
Key Findings: Historical Trends trajectory will result in average emissions of 139 million t CO2 year-1 by 2040s (15% increase over current emissions); Conservation scenario would result in 58% less clearing than Historical Trends; Agricultural Development scenario leads to emissions of 212 million t CO2 year-1 by 2040s; passive protection is insufficient to reduce deforestation
Implications: Passive protection of DRC's forest and woodland savanna is insufficient to reduce deforestation; enactment of REDD+ plan or similar conservation measure is needed to actively protect Congo forests, their unique ecology, and their important role in the global carbon cycle
Limitations: Minor errors in Potapov et al. dataset required corrections; woodland savannas not mapped prior to 2000 requiring ratio-based estimates; agricultural expansion probability map could not be validated due to single time period data availability
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Development of SimCongo model specifically tailored for the DRC using Bayesian statistical methods; first comprehensive spatially explicit modeling of land-use change scenarios for Congo forests combining policy interventions with carbon emission projections

Title: A travel time-based variable grid approach for an activity-based cellular automata model
Authors: Crols, Tomas; White, Roger; Uljee, Inge; Engelen, Guy; Poelmans, Lien; Canters, Frank
Journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF GEOGRAPHICAL INFORMATION SCIENCE
Objective: Integrate travel time–based distances into an activity-based variable grid cellular automata model to assess transport network impacts on land-use and activity change
LULC Classes: Active: discontinuous urban fabric, continuous urban fabric, industrial/commercial units; Passive: agricultural, natural land-cover states; Static: water, parks
Scenarios: Euclidean; road-based; congestion; train only; choice (multimodal)
Analysis Methods: Variable grid CA; distance-decay influence functions; Dijkstra shortest-path for network times; accessibility index
Sim. Method Advantages: Higher resolution than external transport models; faster run times; easy parameter modification; integrates long- and short-distance interactions without full coupling to transport model
Tools/Soft Used: Custom CA software (64-bit implementation); Dijkstra algorithm
Predictors: zoning status; transport accessibility; land-use suitability; neighbourhood effect (activity potentials); diseconomies of agglomeration; inertia; random perturbation
Data Sources: Primary: CORINE 2000 land-cover, NAVSTREETS road network, Belgian rail OD travel-time matrix (2013), population and employment maps from White et al. (2012); Secondary: Flemish Traffic Study Centre congestion report (Hoornaert et al. 2014)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Transport scenarios produce distinct land-use and population patterns; congestion reduces suburban growth; rail-accessible areas densify; multimodal choice scenario similar to road-only due to modal weightings
Implications: Model can test effects of congestion and public transport on sprawl; supports sustainable land-use planning and transport policy analysis
Limitations: Centroid representation for supercells may misrepresent activity distribution; asymmetric access/egress legs not implemented; static network; limited train OD matrix
Future Directions: Calibrate with historical data; represent supercell activity centres; incorporate evolving networks; couple directly with transport models; conduct full sensitivity analysis; use generalized cost measures
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with appropriate transport and land-cover data; computational efficiency suitable for large areas
Novelty: Dual Euclidean/local and network/time-distance influence rules within variable grid; fixed ‘network grid’ for efficient travel-time storage; multimodal travel-time integration without full transport model coupling

Title: Analysis of deforestation and protected area effectiveness in Indonesia: A comparison of Bayesian spatial models
Authors: Brun, Cyrille; Cook, Alex R.; Lee, Janice Ser Huay; Wich, Serge A.; Koh, Lian Pin; Carrasco, Luis R.
Journal: GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE-HUMAN AND POLICY DIMENSIONS
Objective: Analyze spatial patterns of deforestation and evaluate protected area effectiveness in Indonesia using Bayesian spatial models
LULC Classes: Mangrove; Peat swamp forest; Lowland forest; Lower montane forest; Upper montane forest; Plantation/regrowth; Lowland mosaic; Montane mosaic; Lowland open; Montane open; Urban; Large-scale palm plantation
Scenarios: Scenario 1 (20% agricultural price increase); Scenario 2 (20% price decrease); Scenario 3 (25% transport cost and 4% price increase)
Analysis Methods: Autologistic regression; Von Thünen spatial-autoregressive Bayesian models with MCMC
Sim. Method Advantages: Accounts for spatial autocorrelation explicitly; Allows mechanistic interpretation of drivers; Integrates prior knowledge and estimates parameter dispersion; Handles non-standard error distributions and missing data flexibly
Tools/Soft Used: ESRI GIS; Bayesian MCMC computational framework (software not specified)
Predictors: Agricultural rent; Transport cost; Elevation; Illegal logging hotspots; Logging concessions; Industrial timber plantations; Protected area category status
Data Sources: Remote sensing land-cover maps (MODIS, ALOS; Miettinen et al.); World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA); Illegal logging hotspot maps (Forest Watch Indonesia, WRI); Logging concession and timber plantation maps (WRI); Global crop distribution (Monfreda et al.; Ramankutty et al.)
Validation Methods: Ten-fold cross-validation; Matthews correlation coefficient thresholding
Validation Data Sources: Land-cover maps from 2000 and 2010
Key Findings: Categories Ia and V protected areas did not slow deforestation; Higher transport costs and elevation reduce deforestation; Greater agricultural rents and proximity to illegal logging hotspots increase deforestation; Forest concessions and timber plantations buffer against deforestation
Implications: Prioritize enforcement and monitoring in illegal-logging hotspots; Integrate road‐planning to avoid protected and biodiverse areas; Use logging concessions as buffers around protected areas; Expand high-risk protected areas (e.g., Sebangau, Sungai Kayan)
Limitations: Possible “paper park” protected-area boundaries; Incomplete private‐road maps, especially in Papua; Exclusion of land-tenure regimes and forest regrowth dynamics
Future Directions: Ground validation of category Ia degradation processes; Incorporation of topographic ruggedness metrics; Improved mapping of private and concession roads; Inclusion of land‐tenure data
Scalability: Methods adaptable to other regions with single or repeat high-resolution land‐cover datasets; model choice depends on data availability
Novelty: First nationwide comparison of autologistic and von Thünen Bayesian spatial models for Indonesia; Integration of a protected-area liability cost component into a mechanistic von Thünen framework

Title: Approach to the Analysis of Land Cover Dynamics using Change Detection and Spatial Stochastic Modeling
Authors: Zamyatin, A. V.; Afanasyev, A. A.; Cabral, P.
Objective: Develop a multi-step approach combining change-detection and spatial stochastic modeling to rapidly analyze and predict land cover dynamics.
LULC Classes: Agricultural land; Agroforestry; Urban land; Water bodies; Woodland; Unused land; Wetland
Scenarios: Basic (usual) scenario; Environmental sustainability; Accelerated industrial development
Analysis Methods: Image difference; Change vector analysis; Principal component analysis; Chi-square analysis; Markov chain; Cellular automata
Sim. Method Advantages: Enables stochastic representation of complex land-cover processes; Supports reproducibility and automated multi-step processing; Selects large-scale changes efficiently for expert review
Tools/Soft Used: IDRISI Selva GIS and image processing software
Predictors: Historical land cover transitions (matrix Ma); Transition probabilities (matrix P); Expected transitions (matrix Mexp)
Data Sources: Landsat TM and ETM+ multi-temporal images; ESRI shapefile samples from DGT; Portuguese Science Foundation LANDYN project archive
Validation Methods: Chi-square test of Markov property via Chapman–Kolmogorov equation; Expert review by DGT and Portuguese Science Foundation
Validation Data Sources: Contingency tables of land-cover transitions (1980–2010); LANDYN project expert assessments
Key Findings: Identified 98 large-scale change areas (~645 km², 0.7% of Portugal); Woodland loss of 8% (1980–1995) and gain from unused land of 17% (1995–2010); Urban land grew 63.1% (1980–2010); Projected agriculture decline to 30.1% by 2040, woodland and urban expansion under basic scenario; Environmental sustainability scenario ↑ woodland by 23%, ↓ agriculture by 13%; Industrial development scenario ↑ agriculture by 21%, ↓ woodland by 26%
Implications: Facilitates rapid selection of significant change areas for detailed monitoring; Informs territorial planning and greenhouse-gas assessments; Supports conditional scenario planning for sustainability or development
Limitations: Threshold (t) and window size (r) parameters chosen empirically; Parallel computing implementation not evaluated within this study
Future Directions: Develop and assess distributed parallel computing for large archives; Refine parameter-selection methods for change-detection thresholds; Extend application to other regions and longer time series
Scalability: Approach designed for large archived datasets; Potentially transferable to other territories with multi-temporal imagery
Novelty: Original eight-step procedure integrating change detection with spatial stochastic modeling; Introduction of concentration-based scale parameter (Md) for automated selection of significant change areas

Title: Change in agricultural land use constrains adaptation of national wildlife refuges to climate change
Authors: Hamilton, Christopher M.; Thogmartin, Wayne E.; Radeloff, Volker C.; Plantinga, Andrew J. .; Heglund, Patricia J.; Martinuzzi, Sebastian; Pidgeon, Anna M.
Objective: Evaluate changes in land use surrounding National Wildlife Refuges under economic scenarios and inform conservation adaptation
LULC Classes: forest; range; crop (including CRP); pasture; urban
Scenarios: business-as-usual; pro-agriculture
Analysis Methods: multinomial logit econometric land-use model; transition-matrix projection with 5-year time steps; ArcGIS spatial analysis (100-m resolution)
Sim. Method Advantages: permits evaluation of economic and policy scenario effects on transition probabilities; accounts for land-use change costs, soil capability, and county-level returns
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.x (ESRI)
Predictors: current land use; soil capability; county-level net profit for each land use
Data Sources: Primary: USGS National Wildlife Refuge boundaries, NLCD 2001, USDA NRI 1990s, county-level economic returns, land capability data; Secondary: CRP enrollment data (USDA NRI classification)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Forest and urban use increase, range and pasture decrease under both scenarios; Crop decreases under BAU but increases (+10.2%) under pro-agriculture; Pro-agriculture yields half forest gain and double range/pasture loss; Urban growth largest rate (50–52%); Number of refuges with >20% natural cover stable under pro-agriculture (299→300) but increases under BAU (299→319)
Implications: Agricultural profitability may undermine refuge connectivity and climate adaptation; Urban containment policies needed to curb irreversible urban expansion; Regional policy flexibility crucial for targeted conservation
Limitations: No population trend inclusion; Wetland and urban transitions assumed static; CRP treated as cropland; Assumes private lands only; No validation presented
Future Directions: Incorporate population projections and wetland dynamics; Validate model predictions with observed change; Assess specific corridor planning applications per refuge
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with econometric transition data and GIS capability
Novelty: Use of econometric model to simulate land-use change under economic scenarios at refuge buffer scale; integration of pro-agriculture subsidy scenario to assess impacts on protected areas.

Title: Effects of land-use-change scenarios on terrestrial carbon stocks in South Korea
Authors: Lee, Dong Kun; Park, Chan; Tomlin, Dana
Objective: Model effects of land-use-change scenarios on terrestrial carbon stocks in South Korea
LULC Classes: Forest; Paddy field; Upland field; Grassland; Other areas
Scenarios: IPCC's SRES (A1; A2; B1; B2)
Analysis Methods: Land-change Modeler with multilayer perceptron neural network; Markov chain transition matrices; Cellular automaton simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures spatially explicit land-use dynamics and integrates socioeconomic and physical drivers more effectively than simpler statistical or aggregate approaches
Tools/Soft Used: Land-change Modeler; GIS conversion tools
Predictors: Legal/policy zones (greenbelts, conservation areas); GRDP; scenario-specific population; elevation; slope; distance to roads; distance to built-up areas
Data Sources: Landscape Ecology Level-1 land-cover maps (1989, 1999); Korean Ministry of Environment; South Korea Forest Service inventory; KFRI literature values
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated 1999 land-cover to observed 1999 map (calibration with historical data)
Validation Data Sources: Korean Ministry of Environment 1999 land-cover map
Key Findings: All scenarios show net carbon uptake (12.4–14.1 MtC yr⁻¹) by 2030; A1 yields net source of –19.8 MtC; B1 yields highest sequestration benefit; Soil carbon stock responds rapidly to land-use conversion, reaching equilibrium in ~20 years
Implications: Land-use policy strongly influences carbon sinks; afforestation of abandoned cropland can contribute up to 8.3% of 2005 CO₂ emissions; scenario B1 aligns best with low-carbon goals
Limitations: Linear growth assumption may misestimate young vs. old forests; Soil carbon dynamics simplified by fixed equilibrium stocks; Excludes impacts of future climate change on growth rates
Future Directions: Incorporate climate-dependent growth models; Assess economic feasibility of policy scenarios; Extend analysis beyond 2030
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with available land-cover maps and socioeconomic data
Novelty: First high-resolution, scenario-based coupling of LUC modeling and carbon-stock calculations for South Korea

Title: Filling the gap between Earth observation and policy making in the Black Sea catchment with enviroGRIDS
Authors: Lehmann, A.; Giuliani, G.; Mancosu, E.; Abbaspour, K. C.; Soezen, S.; Gorgan, D.; Beel, A.; Ray, N.
Country: Black Sea catchment (23 countries of the Black Sea drainage basin)
Objective: Perform a gap analysis and build capacity for Earth observation data sharing, develop regional scenarios, model hydrology of the entire Black Sea catchment, and implement a distributed observation system
LULC Classes: Cropland; Grassland; Forest; Urban; Wetlands; Water bodies; Bare soil
Scenarios: R-E: Regional governance & environmental priority; R-Ec: Regional governance & economic priority; G-E: Global governance & environmental priority; G-Ec: Global governance & economic priority
Analysis Methods: Gap analysis; Climate delta downscaling; Demographic geostatistical downscaling; Metronamica land-use modeling; SWAT hydrological modeling; SUFI2 calibration; Grid and cloud–enabled processing
Sim. Method Advantages: Semi-distributed SWAT allows integrative modelling of water quantity and quality with widely available inputs; Grid-enabled SWAT (gSWAT) accelerates calibration of large complex models
Tools/Soft Used: SWAT; SWAT-CUP SUFI2; Metronamica; OGC web services (WMS, WFS, WCS, WPS); gSWAT; Greenland; BASHYT; eGLE; enviroGRIDS geoportal
Predictors: Climate deltas (temperature, precipitation); Demography (urban/rural density); Land-use transition rules; Elevation; Soil type; Crop management practices
Data Sources: Meteorological station time series; PRUDENCE RCM outputs; United Nations demographic projections; CORINE land-cover; Soil maps; DEM
Validation Methods: Calibration against gauged flow and water quality observations; Cross-validation of land-use scenarios with historical satellite imagery; Metadata service interoperability tests
Validation Data Sources: River gauging stations (flow, NO₃, PO₄); Remote-sensing imagery; National land-cover statistics
Key Findings: Identified major gaps in regional Earth observation infrastructures; Developed four coherent climate-land use-demography scenarios; Successfully calibrated SWAT for 12,000+ sub-catchments; Demonstrated impacts of combined climate, land-use, and demographic changes on water resources; Established a distributed Black Sea Catchment Observation System
Implications: Informs policy for Water Framework and Marine Strategy directives; Supports decision-making via interoperable web services; Provides template for regional SDI development and transnational data sharing
Limitations: Political and institutional barriers to data sharing; Delta-method downscaling does not capture extreme event dynamics; Demographic projections constrained by administrative census boundaries
Future Directions: Integrate dynamic population mobility models; Enhance downscaling with stochastic weather generators; Expand SDI uptake in non-EU Black Sea countries
Scalability: Yes; framework can be applied to other large transboundary catchments
Novelty: First hydrological modelling of entire Black Sea catchment at high resolution; Coupling of climate, land-use, and demographic scenarios in a unified pipeline; Grid-enabled SDI and processing workflows for environmental modelling

Title: Future Land-Use Changes and the Potential for Novelty in Ecosystems of the United States
Authors: Martinuzzi, Sebastian; Gavier-Pizarro, Gregorio I.; Lugo, Ariel E.; Radeloff, Volker C.
Objective: Understand how alternative scenarios of future land-use change may affect novelty in ecosystems across the conterminous United States
LULC Classes: Urban; Crop; Pasture; Forest; Natural rangelands (natural grasslands and shrublands)
Scenarios: Business-as-Usual; Forest Incentives; Native Habitat; Urban Containment; High Crop Demand
Analysis Methods: Linking spatially explicit land-use change projections (1 ha resolution) to drivers of novelty; Multinomial logit econometric modeling of land-use conversions; Spatial summarization on 10 km grid; mapping patterns of expansion and abandonment
Sim. Method Advantages: Ability to simulate effects of policy and economic changes on land-use probabilities; based on observed landowner decisions and soil/economic predictors
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Land-use type; Soil characteristics (soil quality); County-level economic returns for different land uses
Data Sources: USDA National Resources Inventory (∼800,000 observations, 1990s); Lawler et al. (2014) land-use change scenarios; Lubowski et al. (2006) econometric model parameterization
Validation Methods: Hypothesis tests within econometric estimation framework
Validation Data Sources: USDA National Resources Inventory observations used in Lubowski et al. model validation
Key Findings: Total area of land-use expansion plus abandonment by 2051 ≈ 73–95 million ha; Eastern U.S. and West Coast projected hotspots of change; Conservation-policy scenarios yield somewhat less expansion but still large areas; Traditional conservation policies may have limited ability to prevent increases in novelty
Implications: Future land-use changes will likely facilitate widespread novel ecosystems; Environmental management and biodiversity conservation require novel approaches in the Anthropocene
Limitations: Did not incorporate climate change or non-land-use drivers; Did not map actual novel ecosystems; Model holds public lands constant; Restoration efforts not modeled; Coarse spatial configuration and forest management practices not distinguished
Future Directions: Incorporate other drivers (climate, invasive species); Map future levels of ecosystem novelty; Model urban-to-natural transitions and restoration; Refine fine-scale spatial patterns and management practice distinctions
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Focus on well-documented drivers of novelty (land-use expansion and abandonment); Use of econometric-based spatially explicit scenarios; Broader definition of novelty allowing gradients and reversibility

Title: Methods used to parameterize the spatially-explicit components of a state-and-transition simulation model
Authors: Sleeter, Rachel R.; Acevedo, William; Soulard, Christopher E.; Sleeter, Benjamin M.
Objective: To describe the methods and input parameters of LUCAS, a customized state-and-transition simulation model utilized to assess the relative impacts of LULC on carbon stocks for the conterminous U.S.
LULC Classes: Water; Developed; Barren; Forest; Agriculture; Grassland/Shrubland; Wetlands; Perennial Ice/Snow
Scenarios: IPCC-SRES (A1B, A2, B1, B2); Representative Concentration Pathways (8.5, 6.0, 4.5, 2.6); business as usual; drought; random
Analysis Methods: State-and-transition simulation; Monte Carlo simulation methods; harmonization process; spatial multipliers; distance-decay theory
Sim. Method Advantages: Combination of stochastic, deterministic and empirical methods; age-dependent transitions make it non-stationary; tracks age and time-since-transition for every simulation cell; suitable for capturing variability in future projections
Tools/Soft Used: ST-Sim software package (APEX Resource Management Solutions); LUCAS (Land Use and Carbon Scenario Simulator)
Predictors: Distance to existing land uses; soil condition; protected areas; population density; historical harvest and fires; forest age; crop capability; ecoregions
