Data Sources: Over 20 national LULC datasets; National Land Cover Database; LANDFIRE; Cropland Data Layer; National GAP Land Cover; Forest Inventory and Analysis data; North American Carbon Program data
Validation Methods: Comparing input area targets with modeled output at 5-year time-steps; R² correlation analysis
Validation Data Sources: Input area targets from A1B scenario
Key Findings: Near perfect correlation (R²) between input area targets and modeled output; primary change is increase in developed/urban area; Oak Woodlands had largest amount (~19,000 km²) of land transition to developed; agricultural intensification occurs along eastern edge of Central Valley
Implications: Spatially-explicit results link local, regionalized change to national and global change estimates; contributes to transferability of data and modeling methods to various scales; enables assessment of carbon dynamics under multiple scenarios
Limitations: Formal validation of spatial accuracy is needed; spatial accuracy of change projections are difficult to validate due to future time period and scenario assumptions
Future Directions: Improve accuracy measures to promote visibility; formal validation of spatial accuracy; continue to explore transferability and scalability
Scalability: Adaptable modeling environment that can implement data from various disciplines at any scale, local-to-global; transferability to other regions
Novelty: Unique harmonization method to converge wide range of temporal, spatial and classification schemes; integrated approach where LULC changes and carbon stocks operate synchronously; spatially-explicit state-and-transition simulation at 1-km resolution

Title: Quantifying climate change mitigation potential in the United States Great Plains wetlands for three greenhouse gas emission scenarios
Authors: Byrd, Kristin; Ratliff, Jamie; Bliss, Norman; Wein, Anne; Sleeter, Ben; Sohl, Terry; Li, Zhengpeng
Journal: MITIGATION AND ADAPTATION STRATEGIES FOR GLOBAL CHANGE
Objective: Assess future opportunities for climate change mitigation via avoided loss of wetland carbon stocks under agricultural expansion scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; hay/pasture; development; grassland; herbaceous wetlands; woody wetlands
Scenarios: IPCC-SRES A2; A1B; B1
Analysis Methods: Linkage of FORE-SCE land-use change model to EDCM biogeochemical model; spatial analysis by EPA Level III ecoregions; wetland carbon map reclassification; avoided loss sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit projection of LULC change consistent with IPCC-SRES; accounts for biophysical and socioeconomic drivers; integrates probabilistic allocation for high regional realism
Tools/Soft Used: FORE-SCE; EDCM; GIS raster processing (resampling, reclassification)
Predictors: Slope; elevation; soil carbon; climate; distance to roads; distance to cities; land capability class; cropland rent value; aboveground biomass
Data Sources: USGS national carbon sequestration assessment; NLCD 1992 baseline; SSURGO/STATSGO2 soils data; USDA NASS cash rent survey; USDA Forest Service FIA biomass data; IMAGE land-use projections; EPA ecoregions shapefiles
Validation Methods: Comparison of FORE-SCE outputs against Land Cover Trends historical data; model calibration statistics
Validation Data Sources: USGS Land Cover Trends project; FIA field measurements
Key Findings: Temperate Prairies lose most wetlands (341,964 ha in A1B, 165,589 ha in A2); Highest SOC in herbaceous peatlands of Northern Glaciated Plains & Lake Agassiz Plain (160–210 MgC ha⁻¹); Average SOC loss ~6 MgC ha⁻¹ over 30 yr; Average annual SOC loss 0.20–0.21 MgC ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹; Economic scenarios show Western Cornbelt Plains has high carbon but high land rent
Implications: Prioritize avoided loss in regions with high SOC and lower land costs (Northern Glaciated Plains, Lake Agassiz Plain); Incentive design must account for competing agricultural demand and land value
Limitations: Wetland mapping resolution (250 m) may miss small wetlands; Scenario uncertainty beyond 2050; 1% pixel sampling in EDCM; Assumed conservation tillage may understate SOC loss
Future Directions: Field-based site-level assessments of carbon stocks and land value; Extend projections through 2100; Evaluate restoration and creation scenarios; Incorporate methane flux in freshwater wetlands
Scalability: Framework applicable to other U.S. ecosystems (forests, grasslands) and regions with suitable LULC and carbon data
Novelty: Integration of probabilistic LULC scenarios with spatially explicit wetland carbon mapping; Avoided loss sensitivity analysis combining carbon and economic criteria for prioritization

Title: Scenarios of future land use change around United States' protected areas
Authors: Martinuzzi, Sebastian; Radeloff, Volker C.; Joppa, Lucas N.; Hamilton, Christopher M.; Helmers, David P.; Plantinga, Andrew J.; Lewis, David J.
Objective: Quantify future land-use changes around U.S. protected areas and compare effects of alternative land-use scenarios
LULC Classes: Urban; crop/pasture; natural vegetation (forests, grasslands, shrublands); other (water/wetlands)
Scenarios: Business As Usual; Forest Incentives; High Crop Demand; Urban Containment
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit econometric projections; multinomial logit model; 10-km buffer analysis; comparative scenario analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows simulation of tax and subsidy–based policies by endogenizing economic returns; does not require assumptions on future population or GDP trends
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Initial land use; soil type; county-specific net returns for urban, crop, pasture, range, forest; conversion costs
Data Sources: National Land Cover Database 2001; Soil Survey Geographic Database; National Resources Inventory; county net return data (Lubowski et al.); PAD-US protected areas; cadastral data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Urban cover projected to expand 67% (4 M ha) around protected areas under business-as-usual; Natural vegetation declines (−1.4 M ha) and crop/pasture declines (−2.6 M ha) overall; Refuges and Forests most affected, Parks and Wilderness least; Forest Incentives boosts vegetation only in some regions, High Crop Demand offsets vegetation gains, Urban Containment halves urban growth
Implications: Need for regional and multi-agency coordination; Smart-growth zoning can mitigate urban threats; Carbon incentives may aid habitat recovery in agro-landscapes; Tailored management (corridor protection, land-use regulations) by region and PA type
Limitations: Single 10 km buffer may not suit all ecological processes; Combined crop and pasture masks differences in land-use intensity; Model not suited for fragmentation/connectivity metrics; Does not address underlying causes of designation-specific patterns
Future Directions: Incorporate climate projections; Assess fragmentation/connectivity impacts; Evaluate finer land-use classes (separate pasture vs crop); Expand analysis to state protected areas and easements
Scalability: Summary at national scale; model summaries reliable only at ≥10 km or county scales; could apply to other regions with comparable data
Novelty: Combined econometric land-use projections with protected-area buffer analysis; simulated policy-driven returns (tax/subsidy) without relying on population or GDP trends; first broad assessment across four major PA types rather than only Refuges.

Title: An examination of historical and future land use changes in Uganda using change detection methods and agent-based modelling
Authors: Li, Jingjing; Oyana, Tonny J.; Mukwaya, Paul I.
Objective: To analyse historical land use/land cover changes beginning from 1996 to 2013 and apply an agent-based model to simulate potential agricultural land use change scenarios in Uganda
LULC Classes: Waterbodies; wetlands; urban; agricultural lands; forest lands; grasslands
Scenarios: Business as Usual Scenario (BAU); Deforestation Scenario
Analysis Methods: Agent-based modelling (ABM); change detection methods; Geographic information system tools; satellite image analysis; supervised and unsupervised classification methods
Sim. Method Advantages: ABM is advantageous in integrating decision-making processes into land use change contexts; enables using ABM as a micro-simulation technology for a wide range of spatial applications; agents can represent human behaviour more accurately and offer better assessments based on empirical findings; facilitates the incorporation of subsets of different ancillary data and discrete variables
Tools/Soft Used: Geographic information system tools; ERDAS Imagine® (Signature Editor); Principal Component Analysis (PCA); United States Geological Survey land use/cover classification system
Predictors: Biophysical and socioeconomic factors; physical constraints; policy scenarios; economic factors; distance to roads; slope information; farmers' decision-making processes
Data Sources: Land use datasets from land cover database of Uganda-Africover (FAO Africover, 2013); Landsat 8 OLI satellite images; Digital terrain elevation data from Advanced Space borne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) Global Digital Elevation Model Version 2; Google aerial photography; Wetland Inventory Reports and Maps; Biomass study reports
Validation Methods: Accuracy assessment using error matrix; overall accuracy; kappa statistics; commission error; omission error; cross-tabulation image comparison between simulated and observed land use data
Validation Data Sources: Google aerial photography as reference; 75 random points for each class selected in the classified image; total sample of 450 reference data for accuracy assessment
Key Findings: Agricultural lands increased from 37% in 1996 to 43% in 2013; forest lands dropped from 25% in 1996 to 13% in 2013; 91% of regions experienced reductions in forest cover except Teso region which gained 62%; 82% of regions experienced salient expansions in wetlands; overall accuracy score of simulation is 83.73% with kappa coefficient of 0.67
Implications: Conversions of land uses to agricultural land will continue unabated given population growth; immediate economic returns to individuals outweigh costs to wider society associated with loss of important ecosystem benefits; if deforestation process continues progressively, agricultural land will increase substantially in the future
Limitations: Errors inherent in simulation results attributed to incomplete driving forces in the model; lack of continuous time series data; external variables do not contain economic factors such as crop prices; lack of relevant demographic data; parameters such as largest parcel size and physical constraints probability threshold affect simulation results; agricultural land set as developed and did not revert back to other land types in iteration process
Future Directions: Improve simulation model using more comprehensive biophysical and socioeconomic factors at district level; extend concept of Markov chains with specified transition probabilities; take additional socioeconomic factors using household survey data; add market force factors like distance to towns and crop prices; add national agricultural and land use policies; scale agents for high-performance computing platform
Scalability: The ABM approach enabled exploration of land use heterogeneities within a spatially explicit agent structure across the study area, suggesting potential for application to other regions with similar characteristics
Novelty: Development of an ABM to systematically represent historical and future land use dynamics at national scale in Uganda; incorporation of farmers' decision-making processes into biophysical and socioeconomic factors; spatially explicit representation of interactions between farmers and land cover systems

Title: Deforestation scenarios for the Bolivian lowlands
Authors: Tejada, Graciela; Dalla-Nora, Eloi; Cordoba, Diana; Lafortezza, Raffaele; Ovando, Alex; Assis, Talita; Aguiar, Ana Paula
Objective: To explore an innovative land use modeling approach to simulate how the growing demand for land could affect future deforestation trends in Bolivia, and to discuss the social and environmental implications related to different land use change scenarios
LULC Classes: Natural vegetation (includes forests, chaco, cerrado, savannas/wetlands, and puna/andean scrublands); Others (including water, no natural vegetation, and clouds); Deforestation or LCC (natural vegetation converted to other land cover classes)
Scenarios: Scenario A (Sustainability); Scenario B (Middle of the road); Scenario C (Fragmentation)
Analysis Methods: Top-down modeling approach using LuccME framework; spatial autoregressive modeling; multi-resolution analysis for validation
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: LuccME framework; Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) data
Predictors: Spatial autoregressive coefficient; connectivity index via road network to regional markets; Euclidean distance to closest paved or unpaved roads; percentage of cell area covered by flat slope; percentage of cell area covered by protected areas and indigenous territories
Data Sources: Noel Kempff Mercado Museum of Natural History (NKMMNH) for land cover change data; INE for population data; ABC for road data; SERNAP and CI for protected areas; FAN for indigenous territories; SRTM for elevation data
Validation Methods: Multi-resolution analysis comparing model results with observed deforestation during 2001-2008 period
Validation Data Sources: Land cover change data from Killeen et al. (2012) for 2008
Key Findings: In Sustainability scenario, deforestation reaches 17,703,786 ha by 2050; in Middle of the road scenario, 25,698,327 ha; in Fragmentation scenario, 37,944,434 ha. Model performance showed 69% spatial adjustment at first level, 75% at fifth level, and 81% at tenth level
Implications: These deforestation scenarios show how current and future decisions by neo-extractivist practices of MAS government could affect deforestation and carbon emission trends. Recognizing land use systems as open and dynamic systems is central to designing efficient land use policies
Limitations: The lack of pertinent information such as multi-temporal land cover change data limits efforts, as many LCC datasets have only been available since 2012
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Innovative land use modeling approach for Bolivian lowlands; adaptation of AMAZALERT scenarios for Bolivia; use of LuccME framework combining exploratory and normative scenario approaches

Title: From local scenarios to national maps: a participatory framework for envisioning the future of Tanzania
Authors: Capitani, Claudia; Mukama, Kusaga; Mbilinyi, Boniface; Malugu, Isaac O.; Munishi, Pantaleo K. T.; Burgess, Neil D.; Platts, Philip J.; Sallu, Susannah M.; Marchant, Robert
Objective: To present a novel framework for participatory development of spatially explicit scenarios at national scale that model socioeconomic and environmental dynamics by reconciling local stakeholder perspectives and national spatial data
LULC Classes: Natural forest; Closed woodland; Open woodland; Bushland; Grassland; Thicket; Wetlands; Mangrove forest; Cultivated land; Mixed cultivated-wooded land; Paddy rice in wetlands
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU) with two patterns (BAU1 and BAU2); Green economy (GE) scenario
Analysis Methods: Four-step participatory framework including scenario setting; stakeholder-driven scenario development at subnational scale; modeling using composite indicators; synthesis and consensus building at national scale
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures perspectives and knowledge across diverse stakeholders and regions; strengthens participation of stakeholders in linking socioeconomic trajectories to LULCC; disentangles complexity of socioeconomic drivers; captures and reconciles subnational perspectives at national scale; eases transfer of knowledge to inform decision making
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.2; R statistical software
Predictors: Population density; Proximity to protected areas borders; Distance to roads; Cost distance to Dar es Salaam; Distance from major food markets; Distance from cultivated areas; Grazing impact; Distance to mining sites; Crop suitability; Distance to irrigated sites; Elevation; Slope
Data Sources: AfriPop Alpha version 2010; Tanzania National Census 2012; WDPA 2014; Global roads dataset; NAFORMA LULC map; Gridded Livestock of the World v2.0; MIRCA2000; SRTM 90m Digital Elevation Model; Multi-stakeholder workshops with 240 participants
Validation Methods: Visual validation of preliminary scenario output maps by national stakeholders; Feedback questionnaires from workshop participants; Synthesis workshop for consensus building
Validation Data Sources: National-level workshop with 60 stakeholders from public institutions, research institutions, CSOs, agribusiness, and media
Key Findings: Under BAU scenario, cultivated land expands by ~2% per year reaching 88,808 km² with large impacts on woodlands and wetlands; Additional wood demand leads to degradation of up to 80,426 km² of wooded land; Under GE scenario with 10% productivity increase, cropland expands by 44,132 km² with degradation limited to 35,778 km²; Spatial patterns show highest likelihood of change in northern and southern development corridors
Implications: Results can inform national level planning and policy implementation for sustainable development, especially REDD+ climate mitigation strategy; Framework provides basis for ex-ante assessment of development trajectories and policy implementation impacts; Outputs support spatial priority setting for specific interventions
Limitations: Challenges in representativeness and replicability; Low women attendance especially in governmental organizations; Limited control over participant characteristics; High logistical costs; Framework requires expert facilitation and modeling skills; Limited number of scenarios due to resource constraints
Future Directions: Exploring how to address competing perspectives between customary and ordinary rules; Tackling socioeconomic and environmental trade-offs directly in scenario formulation; Reducing implementation costs and improving self-assessment capacity; Greater integration with local scale scenarios work
Scalability: Framework has wide applicability in developing countries where local communities participate in collaborative actions for sustainable natural resource management and livelihood improvement
Novelty: First methodological framework for participatory development of spatially explicit scenarios reconciling subnational perspectives at national scale; First country-wide, stakeholder-driven assessment of potential socioeconomic and environmental trajectories for Tanzania; Novel approach to identify and quantify region-specific patterns of causality behind LULCC; Differentiation of habitat degradation versus whole-scale conversion processes

Title: Land-use and sustainability under intersecting global change and domestic policy scenarios: Trajectories for Australia to 2050
Authors: Bryan, Brett A.; Nolan, Martin; McKellar, Lisa; Connor, Jeffery D.; Newth, David; Harwood, Tom; King, Darran; Navarro, Javier; Cai, Yiyong; Gao, Lei; Grundy, Mike; Graham, Paul; Ernst, Andreas; Dunstall, Simon; Stock, Florian; Brinsmead, Thomas; Harman, Ian; Grigg, Nicola J.; Battaglia, Michael; Keating, Brian; Wonhas, Alex; Hatfield-Dodds, Steve
Journal: GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE-HUMAN AND POLICY DIMENSIONS
Objective: Understanding potential future influence of environmental, economic, and social drivers on land-use and sustainability to guide strategic decisions that can help nations adapt to change, anticipate opportunities, and cope with surprises through comprehensive, detailed, integrated, and quantitative scenario analysis of land-use and sustainability for Australia's agricultural land from 2013–2050
LULC Classes: Winter cereals; Summer cereals; Rice; Winter legumes; Summer legumes; Winter oilseeds; Summer oilseeds; Sugarcane; Pastures and crops for hay; Cotton; Other non-cereal crops; Vegetables; Apples; Pears and other pome fruit; Stone fruit excluding tropical; Tropical stone fruit; Nuts; Plantation fruit; Grapes; Citrus; Dairy; Beef; Sheep; Carbon plantings; Environmental plantings; Biofuels cropping; Bioenergy
Scenarios: Four global outlooks (L1, M3, M2, H3) with varying carbon prices and emissions abatement efforts; Two domestic policy focuses (Carbon focus, Biodiversity focus); Multiple uncertainty dimensions including productivity growth rates, adoption hurdle rates, capacity constraints, and climate models
Analysis Methods: Land-Use Trade-Offs (LUTO) model - integrated, environmental-economic model implemented as constrained, partial equilibrium, linear mathematical programming model; Global Integrated Assessment Model (GIAM); Energy Sector Model (ESM); Scenario analysis; Global sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures trends over time and space at much higher resolution than other comparable continental or global scale models (annual time step and ~1.1 km grid cells vs typical 5–10 year time steps and 10–50 km grid cell resolution); Strongly linked to global dynamics in environmental, economic, and energy systems; Uniquely able to capture important localised processes of economic and environmental sustainability; Incorporates land-use competition between multiple land-uses; Assesses multiple indicators of environmental and economic sustainability
Tools/Soft Used: Land-Use Trade-Offs (LUTO) model; Global Integrated Assessment Model (GIAM); Energy Sector Model (ESM); Mathematical programming optimization; Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
Predictors: Climate (rainfall, temperature); Carbon prices; Oil prices; Electricity prices; Crop and livestock demand; Productivity growth; Land-use change adoption behavior; Capacity constraints; Water use costs; Fire and drought risk; Soil quality; Geographic suitability
Data Sources: ABARES (Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences); Australian Bureau of Statistics; CSIRO datasets; Global Integrated Assessment Model outputs; Energy Sector Model outputs; Multiple spatio-temporal models and data layers from various sources
Validation Methods: Model evaluation through comparison with previous work; Sensitivity analysis of model parameters; Robustness testing under uncertainty; Comparison against other national-scale analyses for carbon sequestration, biodiversity, and energy
Validation Data Sources: Previous national-scale studies; Regional studies; Government carbon price modelling; Agricultural production data; Carbon sequestration studies
Key Findings: Substantial potential for land-use transition from agriculture to carbon plantings, environmental plantings, and biofuels cropping under certain scenarios; Carbon price was the strongest influence on land-use change; With strong global abatement incentives, land-use responses can substantially increase and diversify economic returns to land; Agricultural production tended to increase despite reductions in agricultural land area due to productivity improvements; Land-sector abatement potential could exceed Australia's total current greenhouse gas emissions by 2040 under very strong global emissions abatement action
Implications: Transformational economic opportunities for Australia's regions through new income streams from carbon and biodiversity payments; Need for sustained productivity growth and investment in agricultural research and development; Requirement for stronger water governance due to increased water resource use under extensive reforestation scenarios; Potential for significant contributions to emissions abatement targets; Need for policy mechanisms to reduce behavioral inertia and capacity constraints
Limitations: Scenarios are modeled projections, not forecasts or predictions; Did not consider competition between agricultural land-uses or intensification of land management; Did not assess effects on regional communities; Excluded Northern Australia development issues; Did not account for societal constraints or social licence for large-scale land-use change; Trajectories based on mean parameter values without considering variability over time
Future Directions: Extension to Northern Australia; Assessment of impacts on ecosystem services such as soil carbon, land degradation, sedimentation, water quality, and amenity values; Incorporation of deforestation as a major land change issue; Consideration of time-variant parameters and price volatility; Assessment of regional community impacts
Scalability: Directly applicable to other regions with similar social-ecological contexts (e.g., Europe, the US); Greater modification required for different socio-ecological systems (e.g., tropical subsistence agriculture, African smallholder cropping); Template for comprehensive, integrated, quantitative, and high resolution scenario analysis can support other nations in strategic thinking and decision-making
Novelty: Most comprehensive and detailed continental-scale quantitative scenario analysis of land-use and sustainability; Assessed multiple potential land-use options and land-use competition; Multiple indicators of environmental and economic sustainability; Intersecting global change and domestic policy responses under uncertainty; Higher spatial and temporal resolution than comparable models; Strong linkage between global dynamics and local processes; Comprehensive synthesis providing basis for national strategic decision-making

Title: Projected climate change impacts on upland heaths in Ireland
Authors: Coll, John; Bourke, David; Hodd, Rory L.; Skeffington, Micheline Sheehy; Gormally, Michael; Sweeney, John
Objective: To model the impacts of climate change for wet heath and alpine and boreal heath Annex I habitats for the island of Ireland using climate and elevation variables as predictors in a bioclimatic envelope modelling framework
LULC Classes: Northern Atlantic wet heaths (4010); alpine and boreal heaths (4060)
Scenarios: A1B scenario from HadCM3-Q16 global climate model projecting temperature rise of 1.3 to 1.8°C, decrease in summer precipitation by 5 to 10%, and increase in autumn and winter precipitation by 5 to 10%
Analysis Methods: Seven bioclimatic envelope modelling techniques implemented in the BIOMOD modelling framework including generalised linear models (GLMs), generalised additive models (GAMs), artificial neural network (ANN), random forest (RF), generalised boosting method (GBM), classification tree analysis (CTA), and flexible discriminant analysis (FDA)
Sim. Method Advantages: Consensus methods decrease predictive uncertainty of single models by combining their predictions; provide advantage of combining forecasts to give a probability distribution per pixel as opposed to a single value; BIOMOD ensemble prediction reduces uncertainty associated with individual model types
Tools/Soft Used: BIOMOD modelling framework; R-based routines; ArcGIS 10.2 software; digital elevation model (GTOPO30)
Predictors: For wet heath models: annual temperature range, mean winter precipitation, mean winter temperature, elevation range, mean elevation; For alpine and boreal heath models: same covariates except maximum elevation replaced mean elevation
Data Sources: Irish National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) habitat and species distribution maps on 10 × 10 km grid; Joint Nature Conservancy Council database (JNCC) for Northern Ireland; quality-controlled 1961-1990 baseline climate data from 560 precipitation stations and 70 temperature stations; HadCM3-Q16 global climate model data dynamically downscaled via regional atmospheric model RCA3
Validation Methods: Area under the curve (AUC) from receiver operating characteristic plots; true skill statistic (TSS); Cohen's kappa
Validation Data Sources: Same as primary data sources; observed habitat distribution data for comparison with model predictions
Key Findings: Wet heath models showed good performance with TSS (0.648-0.713), kappa (0.652-0.714) and AUC (0.874-0.929) values; Alpine and boreal heath models had TSS (0.671-0.737), kappa (0.670-0.738) and AUC (0.858-0.936) values; Mean winter precipitation and elevation emerged as key variables; Projected climate space losses of -40.84% (limited expansion) and -10.38% (full expansion) for wet heath; -18.31% (limited expansion) and +28.17% (full expansion) for alpine and boreal heath
Implications: Projected decline and fragmentation of climate space would have significant implications for ecology of upland ecosystems and associated species; Loss of unprotected high-quality upland habitats will result in direct loss of upland biodiversity; Climate change-driven degradation may cause secondary impacts through increased isolation and fragmentation; Upland ecosystem degradation has ecosystem service implications for downstream communities
Limitations: 10 × 10 km grid resolution loses important topographic and environmental heterogeneity and fine-scale microclimatic controls; Projected changes in climate space not same as projecting changes in actual habitat distribution; Baseline models may not fully capture climate envelope reflecting sustainable conditions due to historical grazing and burning modifications; Important environmental information omitted including slope angle, aspect, soil conditions
Future Directions: Incorporating more detailed information into BEMs including habitat type and species composition at finer scale; Adding more topography and land cover variables; Using different GCM and RCM outputs from range of scenarios; Work using new representative concentration pathways (RCPs) and multiple GCMs; Expanded framework to identify adaptation strategies robust to climate change uncertainties
Scalability: The distribution models should be applicable to areas of wet and montane heath distribution outside Ireland, so long as data for evaluation of estimates are available
Novelty: First application of bioclimatic envelope model ensemble modelling framework to heathland habitat data; Novel use of BEMs for habitats with only limited number of previous studies applying these methods to landforms and habitats

Title: Scenarios for Australian agricultural production and land use to 2050
Authors: Grundy, Michael J.; Bryan, Brett A.; Nolan, Martin; Battaglia, Michael; Hatfield-Dodds, Steve; Connor, Jeffery D.; Keating, Brian A.
Objective: To explore the response of Australian land use and agricultural production to changes in productivity rates, resource scarcity and degradation, greenhouse gas abatement policy, climate change, and global demand from 2013 to 2050 using an integrated systems modelling approach
LULC Classes: Winter cereals; Summer cereals; Rice; Winter legumes; Summer legumes; Winter oilseeds; Summer oilseeds; Sugarcane; Pastures and crops for hay; Cotton; Other non-cereal crops; Vegetables; Citrus; Apples; Pears and other pome fruit; Stone fruit excluding tropical; Tropical stone fruit; Nuts; Plantation fruit; Grapes; Dairy; Beef; Sheep; Carbon plantings (Eucalyptus monocultures); Environmental plantings (mixed local native species); Wheat biofuels; Wheat food/biofuels; Wheat food/bioenergy; Woody perennials bioenergy; Woody perennials biofuels
Scenarios: L1 (low emissions RCP 2.6, low population); M2 (moderate emissions RCP 4.5, medium population); M3 (moderate emissions RCP 4.5, high population); H3 (high emissions RCP 8.5, high population)
Analysis Methods: Integrated systems modelling approach using multiple coupled models; Partial equilibrium land use change modelling; Economic profitability analysis; Spatial grid cell resolution modelling (~1.1 km); Sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Novel integration of multiple systems models linking global, national, and local scales; Ability to explore interactions between climate change policy, productivity changes, and land use competition; Incorporation of adoption behavior and capacity constraints; Spatial resolution allowing detailed landscape analysis
Tools/Soft Used: LUTO (Land Use Trade-Offs) model; GIAM.GTEM (global trade and environment model); GALLM (Global and Local Learning Model); Simple Carbon Climate Model; ESM (Energy Sector Model); MMRF·H2O (Monash multi-regional economic model); NIAM.Flow (rainfall and runoff analysis model); Biodiversity model; MEFISTO (resource and material flows model); Max Planck Institute Earth System Model (MPI-ESM-LR)
Predictors: Global population projections; Greenhouse gas emissions trajectories; Climate change scenarios; Food demand projections; Carbon prices; Energy prices; Agricultural productivity rates; Adoption hurdle rates; Infrastructure capacity constraints; Biodiversity payments
Data Sources: National Land Use Map of Australia Version 4 (ABARES, 2010); National Vegetation Information System (ESCAVI, 2003); Global Trade Analysis Project data; Representative Concentration Pathways data; Australian National Outlook stakeholder engagement
Validation Methods: Model evaluation against historical data; Comparison with other agricultural model intercomparisons
Validation Data Sources: Historical agricultural productivity data; Previous model validation studies referenced (Dong et al., 2015; Gao and Bryan, accepted for publication; Gao et al., in review)
Key Findings: Potentially large transitions in spatial and temporal patterns of land use, agricultural production, output rates, and profitability; New land uses competed with food and fibre production, reducing its area; Agricultural production increased under most settings despite competition for land; Agricultural profits increased due to higher prices and output rates; Negligible land use change observed with carbon payments below $50 per tCO2-e; Significant change did not occur before 2030 except in unconstrained, high-abatement scenarios; Transformative land use change is plausible but high levels of food/fibre production can co-exist with non-food land uses
Implications: Australian land sector can continue significant contribution to global food security while responding to new economic opportunities; Policy settings can influence outcomes through reducing infrastructure constraints, enhancing adoption strategies, and research and development in agricultural technology; Sustained agricultural productivity increases required to maintain production levels; Need for national conversation on potential changes and policy instruments
Limitations: Only minor negative impact on production due to climate change modeled; Does not capture impacts of extreme events or increased climate variability; Thresholds in agricultural systems not captured; Did not model Australian land use change outside existing intensive land use footprint; Did not model indirect effects of changes on global land use patterns; Did not consider social and community responses to land use change
Future Directions: Need for better knowledge of infrastructure deployment efficacy; Economic and market incentives and mechanisms research; Role of information, extension, and advisory systems; Research into coping with shocks and volatility; Integration of social and community responses
Scalability: Limited scalability acknowledged; extrapolating beef results to whole of Australia inappropriate, Northern Australia agricultural development not modeled, Model framework could potentially be adapted to other regions with similar data availability
Novelty: Novel integration of multiple systems models linking global, national, and local scales; Complex interaction analysis between productivity and rate/timing of land use change; Incorporation of adoption behavior through hurdle rates; Integration of capacity constraints in land use change modeling; Comprehensive scenario analysis combining climate, economic, and policy drivers

Title: Scenarios of land system change in the Lao PDR: Transitions in response to alternative demands on goods and services provided by the land
Authors: Ornetsmuller, Christine; Verburg, Peter H.; Heinimann, Andreas
Objective: To implement a modelling approach to represent land system changes in the context of Laos and simulate future transitions in land systems for three different scenarios; to address methodological challenges in simulating land system regime shifts and complex mosaic landscapes while accounting for societal demands for different types of goods and services from land systems
LULC Classes: Shifting cultivation systems; smallholder permanent agriculture; large-scale commercial plantations; forest (multiple types); National Protected Areas; permanent agriculture; concessions and leases
Scenarios: Three scenarios: (1) different degrees of international market integration, (2) sustainable growth objectives, (3) alternative socio-economic development trajectories with varying orientation of markets and land governance
Analysis Methods: CLUMondo land change model; spatially explicit representation of land systems by mapping agricultural and forest systems; integration of different datasets including land cover maps, inventory maps of concessions and leases, and village level data on land use from agricultural census
Sim. Method Advantages: Uses land systems as units of simulation rather than land cover types; captures differences in intensity of land use and land management; distinguishes shifting cultivation, smallholder permanent agriculture, large-scale commercial plantations and forest that have similar land cover but represent very different land uses; addresses methodological challenges in simulating complex mosaic landscapes; uses demands for different types of goods and services as drivers of land system change
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo model
Predictors: Location factors important for the spatial distribution of land systems; societal demands for different types of goods and services provided by land systems; international market integration; land governance orientation; sustainable growth objectives
Data Sources: Land cover maps; inventory maps of concessions and leases; village level data on land use from agricultural census; datasets providing complementary insights into land systems
Validation Methods: Authors acknowledged validation difficulties due to absence of consistent data for two historical time periods and noted that validation of land change models is a difficult issue, especially those operating at large spatial scales
Validation Data Sources: Not applicable; no validation performed
Key Findings: All scenarios show a decline of shifting cultivation systems; different orientation of markets and land governance resulted in strongly different land change trajectories; land system changes are strongly location dependent with different trajectories found in different parts of the country; some scenarios show clear elements of land sparing with intensification of land management in valleys and regrowth of forest on sloping land; other scenarios show elements of enhanced multi-functionality
Implications: Simulation results contribute to debate about desired future land use on national scale including environmental and socio-economic implications; scenarios can help discuss what land use futures are wished for in Laos and what conditions would be needed to achieve these; different mixes of demand led to different land system changes as each land system supplies different mix of goods and services
Limitations: Validation difficulties due to absence of consistent data for two historical time periods; processes determining land systems in Laos have changed considerably making historic processes very different from those addressed in scenarios; transitions lead to land system configurations unprecedented in Laos; validity for historic conditions does not necessarily mean valid model for very different future conditions
Future Directions: Future scenarios could include demands for other services, particularly regulating ecosystem services such as carbon sequestration and those regulating disaster risk such as flooding and landslides; however this would largely increase model complexity and may be limited by available data
Scalability: Comparison with case study results from Indonesia, Vietnam and Southern China shows the model is capable of replicating regime shifts described for the South-East Asian region; different trajectories found by studies across Southeast Asia case-studies are also found within simulation results at different places within Laos
Novelty: Novel simulation approach focusing on simulating changes in land systems rather than land cover; novel feature of using demands for different types of goods and services as drivers of land system change; land systems approach facilitates going beyond land cover to land systems representations as these better reflect socio-economic and land use realities; allows addressing land use as being part of a socio-ecological system rather than only addressing its land cover appearance

Title: Simulation and Evaluation of Urban Growth for Germany Including Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation Measures
Authors: Hoymann, Jana; Goetzke, Roland
Objective: To analyze conflicts in urban area management and develop integrated sustainable land use strategies for Germany by simulating alternative scenarios of land use change for 2030, evaluating measures for climate change mitigation and adaptation objectives
LULC Classes: 13 land-use classes total, including 6 urban land-use classes; built-up and transport areas; forestry; agriculture; biomass areas
Baseline Years: Current conditions (approximately 2014-2016 based on publication date and data references)
Scenarios: Reference scenario assuming continuation of observed demographic and economic development trends; Alternative policy scenarios implementing measures for climate change mitigation and adaptation
Analysis Methods: Multi-criteria analysis; spatially explicit land use change modeling; scenario comparison; indicator-based evaluation; optimization algorithm for land allocation
Sim. Method Advantages: Land Use Scanner provides spatially explicit simulation with 100m resolution; incorporates planning regulations; uses optimization algorithm for optimal land allocation; produces reproducible results; integrates regional demand for sub-regions; capable of simulating large countries with high spatial resolution
Tools/Soft Used: Land Use Scanner model (GIS-based land use change model); linear programming optimization algorithm
Predictors: Current land use; physical conditions; planning regulations; accessibility of infrastructures; regional demographic and economic development; location factors evaluated through statistical analysis
Data Sources: External models for global trends and demographic/economic development; planning regulation data; accessibility infrastructure data; suitability maps; location characteristic data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Built-up and transport area development can be influenced in magnitude and spatial distribution to contribute to climate mitigation and adaptation; strengthening inner-urban development is particularly effective in reducing built-up and transport area development; possible to reduce development to approximately 30 ha per day by 2030, matching German Federal Government sustainability objective for 2020; inclusion of extreme flood events in spatial planning may reduce damage potential
Implications: Settlement structures need adaptation to climate change impacts; climate change mitigation measures can reduce greenhouse gas emissions from land use changes; synergies and conflicts exist between mitigation and adaptation measures; active restructuring opportunities exist in regions facing demographic and industrial decline
Limitations: Not specified
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: The Land Use Scanner model framework is potentially scalable to other regions, as it has been applied to simulate large countries with high spatial resolution
Novelty: Integration of climate change mitigation and adaptation measures in land use planning for Germany; application of Land Use Scanner model to German context; development of multi-criteria analysis framework for evaluating conflicts between mitigation and adaptation objectives

Title: Spatial Analysis of Cultural Heritage Landscapes in Rural China: Land Use Change and Its Risks for Conservation
Authors: Yu, Huirong; Verburg, Peter H.; Liu, Liming; Eitelberg, David A.
Objective: To systematically analyze the spatial distribution of designated cultural heritage landscapes (cultural villages) across China and assess the threats these traditional landscapes face under current and future urbanization and other land use pressures
LULC Classes: Built-up land use; agricultural land use; forest and (semi-)natural land use; densely built-up landscape; agricultural landscape; forest and (semi-)natural landscape; mosaic landscape
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU) scenario; planned scenario; optimum scenario
Analysis Methods: Rural typology analysis based on economic density and accessibility; landscape typology based on spatial pattern of land cover; neighborhood analysis using focal function; risk assessment combining recent and future land use changes
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUE-S model used for land use simulations; advantages not explicitly detailed in the paper
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-S model for land use simulations; focal function for neighborhood analysis; cost-distance function for accessibility calculations
Predictors: Economic density; accessibility (weighted average travel time-cost to cities and county capitals); spatial pattern of land cover
Data Sources: Global Land Cover 2000 (GLC2000) dataset; CCI Land Cover (CCI-LC) 2010 data from ESA; 1-km resolution economic density map of China (2010); OpenStreetMap data for transport network; land use simulation results by China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development (CCICED)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Most cultural villages located in rural (49.7%) and peri-urban regions (36.0%); cultural heritage landscapes predominantly in Central and South China; high urbanization risks in Southeast China along sea coast and near cities along Yangtze River; high pressures from other land use changes in Southwest China especially Yunnan and Guizhou provinces; 67.8-75.5% of cultural villages facing risk from land use changes
Implications: Results provide guidance for selection of most threatened cultural villages for detailed investigation and additional protection measures; help target management strategies to protect cultural heritage landscapes; facilitate identification of high-risk villages needing urgent investigation
Limitations: Uncertainty in rural and landscape typologies that change over time; sensitivity to arbitrary choice of thresholds; variation in village boundaries; sensitivity to neighborhood size selection; spatial aggregation effects; loss of small patches upon data aggregation; higher resolution data needed for nuanced changes
Future Directions: More detailed investigations regarding comprehensive causes and consequences of land use change; assessment of other pressures like erosion, earthquakes, landslides; evaluation of subtle land use changes affecting cropping structure and landscape elements; exploration of more cultural villages beyond the current 2555 designated ones
Scalability: Rural and landscape typology methods were adapted from European approaches showing potential for application to other regions; methodology sufficiently generic for broader application
Novelty: First systematic national-scale analysis of distribution and characteristics of cultural heritage landscapes in China; combination of characterization with risk analysis using alternative scenarios; integration of recent observed changes with future projections up to 2050

Title: The effects of future nationwide forest transition to discharge in the 21st century with regard to general circulation model climate change scenarios
Authors: Mouri, Goro; Nakano, Katsuhiro; Tsuyama, Ikutaro; Tanaka, Nobuyuki
Objective: To qualitatively assess future changes in runoff including the effects of variation in forest type across Japan and understand how future climate changes will affect average rainfall distribution and temperature and their effects upon forest types across Japan
LULC Classes: Paddy field; Cultivation; Forest; Bare ground; Urban region; Empty field; River, lake; Evergreen broad-leaved forest; Deciduous broad-leaved forest; Evergreen needleleaf forest; Coniferous forest; Arable land; Plantation forest
Scenarios: Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5) using four General Circulation Models: MIROC (Model for Interdisciplinary Research on Climate), MRI-GCM (Meteorological Research Institute Atmospheric General Circulation Model), HadGEM (Hadley Centre Global Environment Model), and GFDL (Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory) climate model
Analysis Methods: Catchment Simulator modelling framework based on MATSIRO (Minimal Advanced Treatments of Surface Interaction and Runoff) model; Species Distribution Models (SDMs) using multivariate regression tree model; Semi-distributed hydrodynamic modeling approach
Sim. Method Advantages: Semi-distributed approach has physically interpretable parameters and combines the parametric efficiency of a combined approach with links to physical theory; provides area-averaged values while covering all important aspects of catchments by selecting appropriate landscape units
Tools/Soft Used: MATSIRO model; Catchment Simulator modelling framework; TOPMODEL scheme; Digital elevation model (DEM); Global geographic information system (GIS) data sets
Predictors: Four climatic variables for Species Distribution Models; rainfall distribution; temperature; hydrological factors; topographic structure; infiltration rates; overland and channel flow velocities; soil hydrological characteristics
Data Sources: Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5); Automated Meteorological Data Acquisition System (AMEDAS) of the Japanese Meteorological Agency; Phytosociological Relevé Database (PRDB); Digital National Information (DNI) framework; FAO-UNESCO global digital soil map; Forestry and Forest Products Research Institute (FFPRI); Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT)
Validation Methods: Scatterplots of observed and estimated rainwater discharge with 95% confidence intervals; comparison with observed river data
Validation Data Sources: Observed data for 21 first-order rivers throughout Japan provided by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism (MLIT)
Key Findings: Annual runoff will increase above present-day values by the 2090s; increases in annual variation in runoff predicted to be around 14.1% using MRI-GCM data and 44.4% using HadGEM data; largest increases in runoff related to evergreen forest types; proportion of evergreen broad-leaved forest typically increasing by approximately 4-21.7%; discharge particularly high in September (typhoon season); ratio of discharge variation increased by approximately 14-44%
Implications: Increased runoff can have negative effects on both society and the environment, including increased flooding events, worsened water quality, habitat destruction and changes to the forest moisture-retaining function; high discharge rates can create problems such as water cloudiness due to high concentrations of suspended sediment; process-based models have great potential for application to ecologically based river basin management planning strategies
Limitations: Model was able to identify hot-spot areas for future discharge but could not give detailed spatial information on slope processes; landscape unit simplification in 10×10-km grids can cause errors; the discharge estimated represents potential value rather than absolute amounts leaving the grid; study focused on Japanese discharge patterns and variation trends rather than absolute runoff amounts
Future Directions: Variations in forest type should be considered in future plans to ameliorate projected climate changes; need to improve water retention and storage capacities, enhance flood protection function of forests, and improve human health; prediction of impacts of future climate change on water generation is crucial for effective environmental planning and management
Scalability: Limited; the model was specifically developed for Japan using Japanese-specific data sources and calibrated for Japanese conditions, however, the methodological approach could potentially be adapted to other regions with appropriate local data
Novelty: Integration of forest transition effects with hydrological modeling at national scale; use of ensemble approach with multiple GCMs and RCP scenarios; incorporation of Species Distribution Models to project forest type changes; assessment of both climate change and forest transition impacts on discharge patterns

Title: Cross-sectoral impacts of climate and socio-economic change in Scotland: implications for adaptation policy
Authors: Holman, Ian P.; Harrison, Paula A.; Metzger, Marc J.
Objective: Understanding cross-sectoral impacts of climate and socio-economic change in Scotland and implications for adaptation policy
LULC Classes: Arable; Intensive grassland (dairying); Extensive grassland (sheep & beef); Managed and unmanaged forest; Urban/suburban; Unmanaged land
Scenarios: Tartan Spring; Mad Max; The Scottish Play; MacTopia; UKCP09 climate percentiles (A1FI-90th, A1FI-50th, A1FI-10th; B1-90th, B1-50th, B1-10th for temperature & precipitation)
Analysis Methods: Participatory scenario development; Fuzzy set translation of narrative to quantitative drivers; Integrated Assessment via CLIMSAVE IA Platform with reduced-form metamodels; Box-and-whisker statistical analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Fast, interactive web-based exploration under deep uncertainty; Captures cross-sectoral interactions; Transparent linkage of qualitative narratives to quantitative models; Enables stakeholder engagement in “what-if” testing
Tools/Soft Used: CLIMSAVE IA Platform; Regional Urban Growth (RUG) metamodel; MetaGOTILWA?; CFFlood; WaterGAP metamodel (WGMM); ROIMPEL crop models; SFARMOD metamodel; SPECIES ANNs
Predictors: GDP growth; Population change; Food import ratio; Protected area extent; Oil price; Household size; Climate variables (temperature, precipitation); Soil properties
Data Sources: UKCP09 climate projections, Vertical land movement data (Bradley et al. 2011); Soil data (Panagos et al. 2012); Observed species distributions (empirical European & North African records); Baseline land-cover maps, RUG, GOTILWA?, WaterGAP3, ROIMPEL, SFARMOD-LP, SPECIES model outputs
Validation Methods: Comparison of metamodel outputs against full model runs; Baseline observations comparison; Sensitivity analyses of linked models
Validation Data Sources: Outputs of full models (GOTILWA?, RUG, WaterGAP3, SFARMOD-LP, ROIMPEL); Observed baseline climatology and land-cover data
Key Findings: Significant spatial variability and uncertainty in direction of change across indicators under climate & socio-economic futures; Only 6 of 13 indicators robust in direction nationally, only 3 robust regionally (artificial surfaces, forest area, irrigation usage); Climate change alone increases intensive/extensive farming, reduces forest area, impacts on water stress, biodiversity vulnerability vary locally; Socio-economic scenarios amplify uncertainty and can reverse trends (e.g., land-use diversity, water exploitation)
Implications: Conventional prediction-based adaptation insufficient under deep uncertainty; Need for robust policy options beneficial across all scenarios; Participatory integrated assessment essential for framing adaptation in institutional contexts
Limitations: Reduced-form models may omit fine-scale processes; Indicator set limited to 13 measures; Excludes non-modeled sectors (e.g., energy beyond biofuels)
Future Directions: Expand indicator suite and regional downscaling; Incorporate additional sectors and social dynamics; Refine metamodels with updated climate projections (e.g., UKCP18)
Scalability: Framework and platform architecture transferable to other European regions via CLIMSAVE European version
Novelty: Integration of participatory scenario narratives with quantitative metamodels in an interactive web platform; Application of fuzzy set methodology to link stakeholder stories to model inputs; Emphasis on cross-sectoral interactions and robust adaptation under deep uncertainty

Title: Potential impact of land use change on ecosystem services in China
Authors: Wang, Meng; Sun, Xiaofang
Objective: Predict spatially explicit land use changes across China using Dyna-CLUE model; develop an improved method for estimating ecosystem service values based on value transfer with biomass adjustment; simulate how ESVs change under different land use scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; grassland; woodland; water area; built-up land; unused land
Scenarios: 2000s trend scenario; planning scenario
Analysis Methods: Dyna-CLUE spatial allocation; logistic stepwise regression for location suitability; biomass-adjusted value transfer for ESV; quantity and allocation disagreement metrics
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit downscaling of land use change; Ability to integrate user-specified policy constraints; Incorporates dynamic driving factors and conversion elasticity; Produces spatially detailed projections vs. aggregate accounting
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE model; logistic regression (ROC analysis); custom GIS-based biomass adjustment
Predictors: Elevation; slope; soil texture; temperature; precipitation; traffic (roads, railways); population; GDP; natural reserve distribution; development policy constraints
Data Sources: Institute of Remote Sensing and Digital Earth land use maps (2000,2005,2010); China Statistical Yearbook, Agricultural Statistics Yearbook, national forest inventory (2009–2013); Province-specific biomass densities from literature (Fang et al.1996,1998, Piao et al.2007,2009); Physical and socioeconomic driving factor datasets (Sun et al.2015); Natural reserve data (Fan et al.2013); National General Land Use Planning Outline (2008)
Validation Methods: Quantity disagreement; allocation disagreement
Validation Data Sources: Observed 2010 land use data from Chinese Academy of Sciences land use maps
Key Findings: Total ESV in 2010: RMB 18,766.94 billion; 60% from woodland; ESV increase 2010–2020: * 2000s trend: +RMB 1,798 billion * Planning: +RMB 2,215 billion; High ESV areas: northeastern and southern China; low (< 5,000 RMB ha⁻¹ a⁻¹) in northwest; Woodland expansion drives ESV gains; water area declines under trend but recovers under planning
Implications: Biomass-adjusted ESV maps aid sustainable land use planning; Supports green GDP accounting and policy evaluation; Highlights importance of forest conservation and restoration
Limitations: Value transfer method ignores some spatial heterogeneity (species, landscape); Assumes constant ESV coefficients over space/time except biomass; Built-up land ESV set to zero, neglecting urban ecosystem services; Future driving factor projections may be uncertain
Future Directions: Incorporate primary data-based ESV models (InVEST, ARIES) for higher accuracy; Integrate urban ecosystem service valuation; Refine biomass-age relationships and include other heterogeneity factors; Apply to other countries or finer scales
Scalability: Yes; method transferable to other regions with available land use, biomass, and socioeconomic data
Novelty: First study in China to adjust ESV valuation with spatially explicit biomass data integrated into Dyna-CLUE projections

Title: The importance of uncertainties in scenario analyses - A study on future ecosystem service delivery in Flanders
Authors: Landuyt, Dries; Broekx, Steven; Engelen, Guy; Uljee, Inge; Van der Meulen, Maarten; Goethals, Peter L. M.
Country: Belgium (specifically the Flemish region in Northern Belgium)
Objective: To assess future ecosystem service delivery and associated uncertainties in Flanders, Belgium by combining cellular automaton land use change modeling with Bayesian belief networks, specifically investigating the importance of accounting for land use allocation uncertainty in scenario analyses
LULC Classes: 37 possible land use classes including agricultural land (54% of territory), urban areas (30%), forests, natural areas, and managed nature areas
Scenarios: Four socio-economic development scenarios: Strong Europe (SE), Global Economy (GE), Regional Communities (RC), and Transatlantic Market (TM) based on two axes - international cooperation vs national sovereignty and private responsibility vs public responsibility
Analysis Methods: Cellular automaton land use change modeling coupled with Bayesian belief networks (BBNs) for ecosystem service delivery modeling; Monte Carlo simulation approach with 25 model runs per scenario; uncertainty propagation analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: BBNs can easily account for uncertainties and explicitly handle intrinsic variability of natural processes; ability to deliver predictions even when input variables are uncertain or unknown; can represent both epistemic and stochastic uncertainty; facilitates uncertainty propagation through the model
Tools/Soft Used: Constrained cellular automata model developed by White and Engelen (1993); Bayesian belief networks; grid-based BBN models
Predictors: Land use; soil type; hydrology; spatial interactions with neighborhood (circular area with radius of 8 cells); accessibility; physical suitability; zoning status; distance-dependent repulsion and attraction among land uses
Data Sources: Published technical reports; meta-analyses; regionally available datasets; expert knowledge; regionally calibrated models; national forecasts of the Belgian Federal Planning Bureau; EU NATURA2000 Directive data
Validation Methods: Model calibration and validation by comparing predicted growth trends at EU NUTS 3 regions level with national forecasts
Validation Data Sources: National forecasts of the Belgian Federal Planning Bureau (achieved 96% accuracy)
Key Findings: Taking into account uncertainties may affect policy recommendations from scenario analysis; uncertainties in ecosystem service models were dominant, reducing importance of land use allocation uncertainty; regional ecosystem service delivery relatively certain for specific scenarios despite land use change prediction uncertainty; three out of four services showed increased delivery between 2010-2050 for some scenarios; mean probability of newly assigned pixels ranged 10-70% depending on land use type
Implications: Future ecosystem service delivery highly uncertain and depends on realized socio-economic developments; while decrease in agricultural land may increase national ES delivery, it potentially leads to lower ES delivery in developing countries; more services need integration for reliable policy recommendations; global scale studies needed to reveal complete impacts
Limitations: Only land use change considered while ES delivery sensitive to other changes (climate change, management practices); spatial interactions not fully accounted for in BBN models; temporal interactions limited; incomplete set of services considered; potential effects of biodiversity changes not quantified
Future Directions: More services need to be integrated requiring more data; need to quantify effects on biodiversity and soil formation; include climate change effects and management practice changes; account for spatially explicit interactions; develop scenarios including climate change and biodiversity changes; gather more data on factors like soil type, climate, and biodiversity
Scalability: Model has been applied in different regions based on past applications mentioned; approach can be adapted to other regions but requires region-specific calibration and data; transferability depends on availability of regional datasets and expert knowledge
Novelty: First study to assess sensitivity of scenario outcomes to alternative land use configurations; novel approach combining cellular automaton with BBNs for uncertainty propagation in ecosystem service assessments; introduction of random component to represent land use allocation uncertainty; use of posterior probability certainty index (PPCI) for uncertainty assessment

Title: Assessing the impact of historical and future climate change on potential natural vegetation types and net primary productivity in Australian grazing lands
Authors: Liu, Xiaoni; Zhang, Baisen; Henry, Beverley; Zhang, Jinglan; Grace, Peter
Objective: Assess the historical and future impact of climate change on potential natural vegetation (PNV) types and net primary productivity (NPP) in Australian grazing lands
LULC Classes: Twenty-eight vegetation classes classified using the Comprehensive and Sequential Classification System (CSCS), with four major classes corresponding to Australian rangelands: VIA (subtropical extra-arid subtropical desert), VIIA (tropical extra-arid tropical desert), VIB (subtropical arid subtropical desert brush), and VIIB (tropical arid tropical desert brush)
Scenarios: Three climate change scenarios for 2050: cool-wet scenario (T20R80), average scenario (T50R50), and warm-dry scenario (T80R20)
Analysis Methods: Comprehensive and Sequential Classification System (CSCS) model for vegetation classification; Miami model for NPP calculation; spatial raster analysis; change detection analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: CSCS model uses only climate parameters making it useful for assessing climate change impacts on vegetation; Miami model is simple but widely used and considered reasonable choice given that mechanistic models provide no greater accuracy; empirical relationship between NPP and climate is robust
Tools/Soft Used: Python scripts with Nio, NumPy, and GDAL modules; ArcGIS 10.1; OzClim methodologies
Predictors: Annual humidity index (K) calculated from annual total precipitation and annual cumulative temperature >0°C; annual cumulative temperature >0°C (degree-days); annual precipitation
Data Sources: SILO climate database (Queensland Department of Science, Information Technology and Innovation); 19 General Circulation Models (GCMs) based on three emission scenarios (A1FI, A1B, B1) and three model sensitivities (high, medium, low)
Validation Methods: Comparison with other climate-oriented vegetation classifications including World Wildlife Fund ecoregions and modified Köppen climate classification by Australian Bureau of Meteorology; comparison with published NPP estimates for Australia
Validation Data Sources: World Wildlife Fund ecoregions classification; Australian Bureau of Meteorology Köppen climate classification; published NPP estimates from previous studies
Key Findings: Substantial shift in vegetation classes from 1931-70 to 1971-2010 due to increased rainfall; by 2050, many vegetation classes with intensive land use projected to decrease; NPP projected to increase in central and northern Australia and decrease in southern and eastern coastal areas; average NPP in 2050 projected to be higher than 1931-70 period; rangeland vegetation classes mostly had increased NPP projections
Implications: Australian vegetation, particularly rangeland vegetation, will likely be a net carbon sink rather than carbon source by 2050 (except under warm-dry scenario); projected changes may have significant impact on grazing industry and biodiversity conservation; decrease in forest vegetation classes would affect habitats of vulnerable species; projected decrease in precipitation and NPP in densely populated areas may impact land use, water supply, and agricultural production
Limitations: Modelling of PNV minimizes human-caused disturbances but actual response will be affected by human management activities, fire, and extreme events; vegetation changes resulting from deforestation and land use changes not fully considered; empirical nature of Miami model may have concerns for extrapolating future climate scenarios
Future Directions: Need to consider human activities, fire, and extreme events in future assessments; investigate complex dynamics of vegetation changes under varied climate-change projections and land-management practices
Scalability: The CSCS model has been widely used for management of grassland vegetation resources and assessment of climate change impacts in other regions, suggesting potential scalability; however, climate-specific parameters may need regional calibration
Novelty: First national-scale assessment of climate change impact on PNV types and NPP in Australian grazing lands; use of CSCS model for Australian vegetation classification; integration of historical and future climate projections with vegetation and productivity modeling at continental scale

Title: Climate impacts on agricultural land use in the USA: the role of socio-economic scenarios
Authors: Mu, Jianhong E.; Sleeter, Benjamin M.; Abatzoglou, John T.; Antle, John M.
Objective: Examine how climate variability and future climate-change scenarios affect crop and livestock net returns and, in turn, drive agricultural land-use change across the contiguous USA
LULC Classes: cropland; marginal land (idle/failed/CRP etc.); pastureland; woodland
Scenarios: RCP4.5; RCP8.5; SSP1; SSP2; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5; climate-only case (“CC”) and combined climate + SSP cases
Analysis Methods: two-stage approach; hedonic regression of net returns; fractional multinomial logit land-use share model with correlated random effects (extended Chamberlain–Mundlak); weighted regression; within/out-of-sample RMSE comparison; Wald tests
Sim. Method Advantages: semi-reduced form preserves structural economic response while simpler than full structural models; allows explicit coupling of climate projections with socio-economic scenarios; shows better predictive accuracy than reduced-form alternative
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: growing-season precipitation; growing-season degree-days; precipitation intensity index; drought index (PDSI); lagged weather variables; per-capita income; population density; irrigation rate; soil characteristics; government payments; annualized crop net return; annualized livestock net return; 30-year mean precipitation; 30-year mean degree-days; time trend; latitude
Data Sources: US Census of Agriculture; US Bureau of Economic Analysis; National Resource Inventory; 4-km gridded meteorological dataset (Abatzoglou 2013); MACA-downscaled CMIP5 outputs for 20 GCMs; Palmer Drought Severity Index; IIASA SSP population & GDP projections
Validation Methods: robustness checks with lagged variables and weighted regressions; within-sample vs. leave-one-census-year-out RMSE; Wald joint significance tests
Validation Data Sources: same agricultural, economic and climate datasets used for model estimation
Key Findings: crop net returns are more heat-sensitive and less moisture-sensitive than livestock; future climate alone modestly raises livestock returns more than crop returns, but adding SSPs reverses this; cropland area is projected to expand while marginal and pastureland contract, with large spatial heterogeneity; incorporating socio-economic scenarios greatly amplifies uncertainty and changes the direction/magnitude of land-use shifts
Implications: ignoring future socio-economic pathways can misrepresent climate-driven land-use change; policy design for adaptation, biofuel expansion and GHG mitigation must account for economics and SSP uncertainty
Limitations: price projections consistent with SSPs not included; only agricultural land uses analysed (development and forest excluded); assumptions on livestock stocking rate, irrigation change and government payments require sensitivity checks; potential unobserved factors remain
Future Directions: integrate commodity price scenarios; extend to forest and urban land conversion; evaluate policy instruments that steer land-use shifts under combined climate-socio-economic futures
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: first U.S. national study coupling a semi-structural land-use model with both RCP climate projections and full SSP socio-economic narratives to quantify climate-and-society-driven agricultural land-use change

Title: Climatically-mediated landcover change: impacts on Brazilian territory
Authors: Zanin, Marina; Tessarolo, Geiziane; Machado, Nathalia; Albernaz, Ana Luisa M.
Journal: ANAIS DA ACADEMIA BRASILEIRA DE CIENCIAS
Objective: Describe and quantify the effects of future climate change on the distribution of native landcover in Brazil, using native landcover as a surrogate for biodiversity, and map vulnerable areas at the biome level to inform conservation strategies.
LULC Classes: Closed forest (closed to open broadleaved evergreen and/or semi-deciduous forest); open vegetation (closed to open shrubland, open broadleaved deciduous forest, mosaic forest/shrubland/grassland); closed to open vegetation on regularly flooded or waterlogged soil.
Baseline Years: Current climate scenario (baseline not explicitly dated, but WorldClim current data, typically ~1970–2000).
Scenarios: Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 4.5 (medium-low emissions, optimistic); RCP 8.5 (high emissions, pessimistic).
Analysis Methods: Decision tree analysis for landcover classification; random forest for variable importance; ecological niche modeling (ENM) using nine algorithms (BIOCLIM, Gower distance, Mahalanobis distance, GLM, GAM, MARS, MaxEnt, GARP, random forest); ensemble forecasting; systematic sampling; cross-validation.
Sim. Method Advantages: MaxEnt provided the best performance, with high accuracy and robustness compared to ensemble forecasting, which can be affected by low-performing models and tends to underestimate distributions, leading to omission errors.
Tools/Soft Used: R software (rpart and randomForest packages); BIOENSEMBLE platform for ensemble forecasting.
Predictors: Isothermality; minimum temperature of the coldest month; mean temperature of the wettest quarter; annual precipitation; precipitation of the wettest month; precipitation of the wettest quarter; precipitation of the driest quarter; precipitation of the coldest quarter.
Data Sources: GlobCover map (landcover, European Space Agency); WorldClim database (climate variables); HadGEM2 ES model (future climate projections); literature and supplementary datasets for validation.
Validation Methods: Cross-validation (1000 replicates for decision tree; 10 replicates for ENM); systematic sampling; evaluation metrics: sensitivity, specificity, True Skill Statistic (TSS), Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC).
Validation Data Sources: Randomly selected grid cells from GlobCover and WorldClim datasets, partitioned into calibration and validation sets.
Key Findings: Closed forest is predicted to contract by up to 50% by 2070, especially in the Amazon and Atlantic Forest biomes; Open vegetation is predicted to expand, particularly in drier biomes (Cerrado, Caatinga); Vulnerability is highest in the Amazon’s eastern edge and the Atlantic Forest, with significant risk to biodiversity; Expansion of open vegetation may be limited by anthropogenic barriers and the rapid pace of climate change.
Implications: Climate change poses a severe threat to Brazilian biodiversity, especially in closed forest biomes; Conservation and management plans must prioritize vulnerable areas and consider restoration in climatically stable or expanding regions; Results provide guidance for ecological and economically efficient conservation strategies.
Limitations: Only climatic variables were considered; anthropogenic landcover (urban, agriculture) and other environmental factors (topography, soil) were excluded; Some landcover classes with small geographic extent were underrepresented or excluded; Pantanal and Pampas biomes were not well characterized due to limited data.
Future Directions: Include finer-scale studies for sparsely distributed landcover types; Incorporate additional predictors such as topography and soil; Develop approaches tailored to small or unique biomes (Pantanal, Pampas).
Scalability: Potentially scalable to other regions with available landcover and climate data, but methodology may need adaptation for local landcover types and finer resolution.
Novelty: Use of native landcover as a biodiversity surrogate to overcome species data scarcity; Integration of decision tree and ecological niche modeling to classify and predict landcover change at a national scale; Identification of climatically mediated landcover groups and mapping of biome-level vulnerability.

Title: Enhanced land use datasets and future scenarios of land change for Slovakia
Authors: Pazur, Robert; Bolliger, Janine
Objective: To develop enhanced land use and cover (LUC) datasets for Slovakia and create spatially explicit future scenarios of land change for 2040 using improved CORINE datasets and multiple development pathways
LULC Classes: Artificial surfaces (continuous urban fabric, discontinuous urban fabric, low-density urban fabric); Industrial, commercial and transport units; Agricultural areas (non-irrigated arable land, vineyards, fruit trees and berry plantations, pastures); Forests (broad-leaved forest, coniferous forest, mixed forest); Shrub and herbaceous vegetation; Open spaces with little vegetation; Wetlands; Water bodies
Scenarios: Five scenarios including TREND scenario based on recent development trends, and four IPCC scenarios (A1, A2, B1, B2) developed along axes of globalisation vs. regionalisation and low vs. high policy intervention
Analysis Methods: Raster processing using R software; overlay analysis of LUC datasets; integration of multiple data sources including CORINE Land Cover, Urban Atlas, soil sealing layer, and Reference Spatial Database (ZB GIS); step-wise refinement approach maintaining original CORINE nomenclature
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: R software with raster package for data processing and analysis
Predictors: Not specified in detail, but mentioned spatial policies and restrictions, land use conversion settings, land use demand, and local suitability assessments as scenario parameters
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover dataset (2006, 2012); Urban Atlas; Pan-European High-Resolution Layers including soil sealing layer; Reference Spatial Database (ZB GIS); European waterbody map; European Environmental Agency (EEA) data; Global Change Institute (GCI) data; national and European predictions
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Enhanced LUC datasets provide most detailed and accurate temporal layers available for Slovakia at national level; spatial resolution improvement from 25 ha minimum mapping units to 20 m resolution; most urbanised areas were converted to permanent crops in refined dataset, indicating allocation of gardens within cities; small settlement structures negatively influenced agricultural land amounts; refinement revealed linear features not captured in original CORINE dataset
