Implications: Improved datasets provide important baseline information for researchers and practitioners for implementation into management practice; scenarios provide insights into likely magnitudes and locations of future land change; enhanced spatial resolution enables better representation of landscape heterogeneity and small-scale land use changes
Limitations: Not specified
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Methodology appears applicable to other Central European countries using similar data sources and classification systems, though specific transferability assessment not provided
Novelty: Enhanced spatial resolution approach combining multiple high-resolution datasets (Urban Atlas, soil sealing layer, ZB GIS) with traditional CORINE classification; development of spatially explicit future scenarios for Slovakia using IPCC storylines; substantial improvement in minimum mapping units from 25 ha to 20 m resolution while maintaining original nomenclature

Title: Integrating Climate Change and Land Use Impacts to Explore Forest Conservation
Authors: Choe, Hyeyeong; Thorne, James H.
Objective: To estimate the impacts of climate change and land use policy on the biodiversity of existing forest areas by exploring the spatial results of different forest conversion and climate models; to stratify current forest areas into four categories of future conditions based on the integration of forest conversion and climate models; and to suggest options in forest policy and conservation strategies that address both biodiversity conservation and climate mitigation
LULC Classes: Eight categories; water, urban use, barren land, wetlands, grass, forest, rice paddies, and fields (later combined into seven categories: water, urban use, barren land, wetlands, grass, forest, and agriculture)
Baseline Years: 1995 and 2000 for model building; 2009 for model validation and scenario projection base
Scenarios: Four climate scenarios (HadGEM2-ES RCP 4.5, HadGEM2-ES RCP 8.5, NorESM1-M RCP 4.5, NorESM1-M RCP 8.5) combined with four forest conversion scenarios: (1) forest loss continues at current rates; (2) forest loss at same rate but with conservation in climatically suitable areas; (3) 50% reduction in forest loss rates; (4) combination of conservation in suitable climates and 50% reduction in deforestation rates
Analysis Methods: Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines (MARS) multiresponse species distribution models for 1031 climate vulnerable species; multinomial logistic regression models for forest conversion prediction; scenario-based spatial modeling approach combining climate and land use projections
Sim. Method Advantages: MARS multiresponse SDMs are appropriate for datasets with large numbers of species with few records; they combine all species data and use information on presence of other species to supplement information for modeled species by considering locations of other species as pseudo-absences; suitable for handling the study's data characteristics
Tools/Soft Used: R software (version 3.1.1) with packages: 'raster' for extracting predictor values; 'nnet' for multinomial logistic modeling; 'caret' for confusion matrix calculations
Predictors: Four criteria for forest conversion modeling: proximity to roads; distance from urban areas (both log-transformed); slope (classified into four categories: flat, 1-25%, 25-90%, >90%); binary map of national protected areas
Data Sources: Primary: 65,491 species occurrence records from South Korean second and third national ecosystem survey (ECObank); Secondary: WorldClim climate data; HadGEM2-ES and NorESM1-M global climate models; 1995 and 2000 land use maps from Korean Water Management Information System (WAMIS); 2009 land use map from Environmental Spatial Information Service; road data from Korea Transport Database; protected areas data from ProtectedPlanet website; 2000-2010 Forest Service statistics
Validation Methods: Spatial accuracy assessment by comparing predicted forest conversion to observed 2009 land use map; cross-tabulation of observed and predicted land use classes using confusion matrices; overall accuracy calculated as total number of correctly classified grid cells divided by total number of grid cells originally forested in base year
Validation Data Sources: 2009 land use map from Environmental Spatial Information Service used for validation against predictions made from 2000 base year
Key Findings: Climate-suitable forest areas declined sharply and moved northward as future temperatures increase; species richness loss due to forest conversion could be reduced significantly by preserving forest areas climatically suitable for climate vulnerable species; forest conversion scenarios preserving climatically suitable areas in Gangwon province were nearly as effective as reducing deforestation rates by 50%; protecting forests with future suitable climates emerged as leading forest conservation policy; four forest categories identified (FI, FD, CI, CD) with varying conservation priorities
Implications: Climate refugia (existing forests with suitable future climates) should be protected from land use conversion to preserve forest biodiversity; forest conservation strategies should consider biogeographic climate dynamics; protecting forests in Gangwon province is as important as reducing national deforestation rates; different management strategies needed for each forest category; policy should redirect rather than necessarily reduce forest conversion
Limitations: Species distribution models used only climate parameters without considering species interactions; did not consider species' capacity to reach future suitable regions; stacking species ranges may overestimate species richness; assumed future forest conversion patterns similar to recent changes; used limited time steps for model development; did not include all potential land use change drivers; only considered two levels of forest conversion scenarios
Future Directions: Studies on interaction between climate change and land use changes and their interrelated impacts on biodiversity; analysis of impacts on other species beyond climate vulnerable species; consideration of multiple time steps and additional parameters explaining forest conversion by region; development of more diverse land use conversion scenarios; creation of more realistic land use scenarios once forest policy direction is established
Scalability: Methods may be applicable to other forested regions, but planners should consider assumptions and uncertainties of climate projections, species distribution models, and land use trends when addressing forest biodiversity conservation in different contexts
Novelty: Integration of climate change and land use impacts through scenario-based spatial modeling; development of four-category forest classification system (FI, FD, CI, CD) for policy guidance; demonstration that protecting climatically suitable areas can be as effective as reducing overall deforestation rates; spatially explicit approach linking species distribution modeling with forest conversion prediction for policy development

Title: Land changes in Slovakia: Past processes and future directions
Authors: Pazur, Robert; Bolliger, Janine
Objective: Determine past and current land-use trajectories in Slovakia (1980–2012) and quantify institutional effects; assess potential spatial development to 2040 using scenario-based modelling
LULC Classes: Urban fabric (11); Industrial, commercial and transport units (12); Mine, dump and construction sites (13); Artificial non-agricultural vegetation (14); Arable land (21); Permanent crops (22); Pastures (23); Heterogeneous agricultural areas (24); Forests (31); Scrub/herbaceous vegetation (32); Open spaces with little/no vegetation (33); Inland wetlands (41); Inland waters (51)
Scenarios: A1 (globalised, low intervention); A2 (regionalised, low intervention); B1 (globalised, high intervention); B2 (regionalised, high intervention); TREND (business as usual extrapolation)
Analysis Methods: Boosted regression trees for past LUC transitions; CLUmondo spatial allocation for future scenarios; scenario-based demand modelling (VOLANTE SRES)
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures linear and nonlinear predictor–response relationships; High predictive accuracy and interpretability; Handles both frequent and rare transitions without overfitting
Tools/Soft Used: R (version 3.2.2) for BRT; ArcGIS 10.1 for friction and distance mapping; CLUmondo framework for allocation; boosted regression trees; path distance tool
Predictors: Georelief subgroup; Protected areas; Slope; Soil quality; Topographic Wetness Index; Rainfall; Solar radiation; Temperature; Distance to forest/shrubland; Distance to LAU-2 centres; Distance to 3/8 regional capitals; Distance to roads; Distance to settlements; Distance to towns; Age index; Agricultural activity share; Economic activity share; Number of flats built; GDP per capita; Net migration rate; Population density
Data Sources: Primary: CORINE Land Cover (1980–2012), Digital Elevation Model, EU Urban Atlas, ZB GIS, climate station records, Slovstat census, MARD reports; Secondary: World Bank GDP data, VOLANTE project scenarios, Ramsar and national protected-area datasets
Validation Methods: 10-fold cross-validation for model calibration; split-sample testing; performance metrics AUC and Pearson correlation
Validation Data Sources: Randomly selected presence/absence samples from CORINE change data; held-out test subsets from same datasets
Key Findings: Late socialism (1980–1990) saw highest rates of urbanisation, agricultural intensification, extensification, and forest disturbance; Postsocialism (1990–2000) marked sharp decline in agricultural intensification/extensification and rise in afforestation; EU accession/membership periods featured continued forest disturbance and renewed urban growth; Future scenarios uniformly predict afforestation as dominant process, extensification exceeding intensification, and urban expansion in city hinterlands
Implications: Afforestation and agricultural extensification trends may compromise cultural‐heritage landscapes; Spatially explicit scenario outputs support national policy planning and early warning for land‐system vulnerabilities; Urban sprawl control requires stringent planning in suburban zones
Limitations: CORINE resolution (20 m) overlooks small landscape features (e.g., hedgerows, small fields); Agricultural intensification underestimation due to lack of farm‐level data; Scenario demands linearly interpolated from heterogeneous sources
Future Directions: Integrate farm‐type and parcel‐level datasets for refined intensification modelling; Incorporate dynamic socio‐economic feedbacks beyond linear projections; Apply higher-resolution remote sensing to capture small‐scale land‐use changes
Scalability: Applicable to other post-socialist and EU‐member states using analogous data and modelling frameworks
Novelty: First national‐level integrated assessment combining long-term CORINE data, boosted regression trees, and spatially explicit scenario modelling (CLUmondo) for past and future land-use dynamics in Slovakia

Title: MODELING LAND USE AND THE EFFECTS OF CLIMATE CHANGE IN BRAZIL
Authors: Faria, Weslem Rodrigues; Haddad, Eduardo Amaral
Objective: To develop a computable general equilibrium (CGE) model with detailed specification for land use and integrate it with an econometric model to analyze the economic effects of climate change on land allocation among 13 different land uses in 27 regions of Brazil
LULC Classes: Paddy rice; Corn grain; Wheat and other cereals; Cane sugar; Soybean; Other crop products and services; Cassava; Tobacco; Cotton; Citrus fruits; Coffee beans; Forestry; Livestock
Scenarios: IPCC AR4 A2 scenario; IPCC AR4 B2 scenario
Analysis Methods: Computable General Equilibrium (CGE) modeling; Econometric modeling; Normalized quadratic function; Iterative Seemingly Unrelated Equations (ISUR) estimation; Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) technology; Constant Elasticity of Transformation (CET) technology
Sim. Method Advantages: Systematically captures effects of changes in land use patterns; Considers role of relative prices in land allocation; Captures backward and forward linkages; Addresses spatial and sectoral linkages in general equilibrium framework; Includes price effects; Captures systemic economic effects of interaction between agricultural activities and land allocation
Tools/Soft Used: BLUE (Brazilian Land Use Energy) model; B-MARIA-27 model; ENERGY-BR model; PRECIS model
Predictors: Temperature; Precipitation; Product prices; Input costs; Land allocated to each activity; Agro-climatic variables
Data Sources: Agricultural Census 2006 (IBGE); Climatic Research Unit (CRU/University of East Anglia) database; PRECIS regionalized model from National Space Research Institute; Household Budget Survey; National Survey for Household Sample; Annual Survey of Services; Annual Industrial Survey; IBGE Sistema de Recuperação Automática; ALICEWEB System; Second National Communication of Brazil to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change; Energy and Emissions Balance
Validation Methods: Systematic sensitivity tests; Robustness testing regarding variations in parameter values and elasticities; Testing with ±20% parameter value range using triangular and symmetric distribution; Confidence intervals construction using Chebyshev inequality
Validation Data Sources: Not explicitly specified for validation procedures
Key Findings: Negative changes in real GDP ranging from -0.0054% to -0.0198% depending on scenario; Climate change reduces activity levels in most productive regions; Sugar cane and cotton show positive variations in specific states; Increased land use intensity and competition among uses; Negative deforestation indicator indicating conversion of forest to agricultural use; Equivalent variation decreases of R$5,336.6-8,157.8 million by 2070-2099; Four states show positive activity variations: Acre, Maranhão, Piauí, and Mato Grosso do Sul
Implications: Climate change threatens Brazil's agricultural competitiveness but heterogeneous climatic profiles may help adaptation through interregional production reallocation; Need for ongoing research to improve crop yields and reduce greenhouse gas emissions; Land becomes more intensively used with increased competition among uses; Economic activity generally reduces with negative effects on aggregate demand
Limitations: Model specification influences deforestation results; Conversion of protected forest areas legally limited to 20%; Comparative static analysis rather than recursive dynamic; Average climate values cannot capture extreme events effects; Limited to climate variables only in integration strategy
Future Directions: Ongoing research required to improve crop yields; Reduce greenhouse gas emissions; Develop new agricultural technologies; Recursive dynamic analysis would be more appropriate with annual climate projections
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First CGE model for Brazil with detailed land use specification on both demand and supply sides; Integration of CGE and econometric models for climate change analysis; Classification of land use according to agricultural use rather than agro-ecological zones; Detailed specification of 13 land uses across 27 Brazilian regions; Novel approach to land supply modeling using constant elasticity of transformation technology

Title: Modeling the spatial distribution of crop cultivated areas at a large regional scale combining system dynamics and a modified Dyna-CLUE: A case from Iran
Authors: Mesgari, Iman; Jabalameli, Mohammad Saeed
Objective: Assessing the demand of different crops at country-level and for predicting the spatial distribution of cultivated areas at provincial scale
LULC Classes: Wheat; barley; rice; maize
Scenarios: Population growth (medium); economic growth (4.9%); precipitation amount (212 mm)
Analysis Methods: System Dynamics (SD) and modified Conversion of Land Use and its Effects (CLUE) modeling framework
Sim. Method Advantages: Strong foundation in agricultural economics through SD approach; enables rapid testing of wide range of scenarios; suitable for large provincial scale with limited data availability typical in developing countries
Tools/Soft Used: Vensim software
Predictors: Population growth; economic development; climatic changes; policy rules; GDP; international agricultural price index; precipitation; groundwater resources; land suitability
Data Sources: World Bank database; FAO statistical database; Iran Meteorological Organization; Iran Water Resource Management Company; Annual Agricultural Statistics of Iran; Statistical Center of Iran; Ministry of Agriculture Jihad database
Validation Methods: Structural validation and behavioral validation; comparison with historical trends; R-squared regression analysis
Validation Data Sources: Historical data from 2007-2014; data from 2006-2014 for integrated model verification
Key Findings: Change in spatial distribution of cultivated areas; increase in rice proportion in northern Iran; wheat proportion increasing in mountainous western areas; wheat and barley becoming dominant crops; total cultivated area shows stable growth for wheat and barley; rice and maize areas remain approximately constant
Implications: Provides theoretical and technical support for agriculture management in Iran; useful for policy formulations, land use change modeling, and agricultural management; enables rapid testing of scenarios for policy making
Limitations: Need for improving the prediction accuracy and field level interactions within the system; base scenario was limited without detailed climate change and government policies consideration
Future Directions: Improving prediction accuracy; studying field level interactions within the system; considering climate change and detailed government policies in scenarios; developing more integrated models for agricultural systems
Scalability: Yes; model can be applied to other countries due to Iran's diversity in climate, natural and socioeconomic conditions serving as a representative case
Novelty: Dynamic integration of System Dynamics with modified Dyna-CLUE framework; combination of socioeconomic and spatially explicit data; large provincial scale approach suitable for developing countries with data limitations

Title: Predictive modelling of the spatial pattern of past and future forest cover changes in India
Authors: Reddy, C. Sudhakar; Singh, Sonali; Dadhwal, V. K.; Jha, C. S.; Rao, N. Rama; Diwakar, P. G.
Objective: To simulate the forest cover changes in India using Land Change Modeler and predict the spatial pattern of past and future forest cover changes
LULC Classes: Forest; Non-forest
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU) scenario
Analysis Methods: Land Change Modeler (LCM); Multi-layer perceptron neural network; Markov chain analysis; Cellular Automata-Markov (CA-Markov) model; Change detection analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Multi-layer perceptron neural network is capable of modelling complex relationships between variables and allows prediction of output for given input objects; CA-Markov improves accuracy of LULC prediction because it considers driver data; LCM combines temporal and spatial pattern simulation
Tools/Soft Used: IDRISI Selva software; Land Change Modeler (LCM)
Predictors: Elevation; Slope; Distance to roads; Distance to settlements; Distance to water bodies
Data Sources: Multi-temporal classified forest cover data from National Remote Sensing Centre; Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) data; Advanced Wide Field Sensor of Resourcesat 1 (AWiFS); Historical archives at district and state levels
Validation Methods: Kappa statistic comparison; Confusion matrix analysis; Comparison of simulated forest cover maps for 2013 with actual remote sensing derived forest cover map
Validation Data Sources: Actual remote sensing derived forest cover map for 2013
Key Findings: Predicted forest cover in 1880 was 1,042,008 km² (31.7% of India's geographical area); About 40% of forest cover lost during 1880-2013; Northeast states and Andaman & Nicobar Islands showed annual gross deforestation rate >0.3 from 2005-2013; Model predicted further decrease of 2305 km² forest area by 2025; Protected areas mostly successful in forest protection except Manas, Sonai-Rupai, Nameri and Marat Longri
Implications: Results provide useful inputs for effective resource management, biodiversity conservation, and climate change mitigation; Support for UNFCCC REDD+ Programme implementation; Can guide declaration of new protected areas and regional planning
Limitations: Model focused only on selected states/union territories with high deforestation rates; Limited to forest/non-forest classification; Historical reconstruction relies on non-spatial records for validation
Future Directions: Projections can support biodiversity conservation planning; Declaration of new protected areas; Regional planning and adoption of climate change mitigation measures
Scalability: Model approach can be applied to other regions with similar deforestation patterns and data availability
Novelty: First comprehensive spatial reconstruction of India's forest cover back to 1880; Integration of multi-layer perceptron neural network with Markov chain analysis for forest cover prediction; Long-term temporal analysis spanning 145 years (1880-2025)

Title: Projections of Future Land Use in Bangladesh under the Background of Baseline, Ecological Protection and Economic Development
Authors: Hasan, Shaikh Shamim; Deng, Xiangzheng; Li, Zhihui; Chen, Dongdong
Objective: To predict land use and land cover changes from 2010 to 2030 under baseline, ecological protection priority and economic growth scenarios in Bangladesh using the Dynamics of Land Systems (DLS) model
LULC Classes: Cultivated land; Forest area; Grassland; Water area; Built-up area; Unused land
Scenarios: Baseline scenario; Ecological protection priority scenario; Economic growth scenario
Analysis Methods: Dynamics of Land Systems (DLS) model; Logistic regression analysis; Spatial regression analysis; Scenario analysis; Spatial allocation module
Sim. Method Advantages: Two special features: provides scenario analysis of land demand at regional level and spatial integration of land uses at pixel level; can consider the interactions among influencing factors of land use and neighboring pixels
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.1; SPSS software; Dynamics of Land Systems (DLS) model
Predictors: Soil pH; Elevation (DEM); Air temperature; Hours of sunshine; Average rainfall; Distance to divisional head quarter; Distance to nearest highways; Distance to nearest secondary highways; Population density; GDP; Urban population density
Data Sources: www.globallandcover.com for land use data; Bangladesh Agricultural Research Council (BARC) for climatic data; International Soil Reference and Information Center (ISRIC) World Soil Information Service for geophysical data; Ministry of Agriculture Bangladesh; Statistical Year Book of Bangladesh; The World Population Organization
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient to assess agreement between actual and simulated land use patterns
Validation Data Sources: Land use data from 2000 used as base data for simulating 2010 land use data, then compared with actual 2010 land use data
Key Findings: Cultivated land declines and built-up area expansion is common under all three scenarios; Under ecological protection priority scenario, forest area and grassland will increase more; Under economic growth scenario, built-up area will expand dramatically; Kappa statistic value of 0.667 indicating substantial agreement between actual and simulated results
Implications: Results furnish meaningful decision-making information for planners to conserve and/or exploit land resources in Bangladesh in a more sustainable manner; Rapid spatial expansion of cities will exert huge pressure on cultivated land conversion to built-up areas; Need for sustainable land management due to annual cultivated land loss of 1%
Limitations: Forest area and built-up area were poorly simulated and under-predicted by the DLS model; Kappa coefficient has bottlenecks such as being affected by skewed distributions of categories and bias problems
Future Directions: Further studies incorporating relevant factors such as physical, socioeconomic and policy factors that might affect land use change; Need for integrated action plan based on simulation results
Scalability: The DLS model can be applied to simulate land use changes at any region, suggesting potential scalability to other areas
Novelty: Application of DLS model to Bangladesh for future land use prediction under multiple scenarios; Integration of multiple data sources and driving factors; Scenario-based approach considering ecological protection and economic growth priorities

Title: Simulating Block-Level Urban Expansion for National Wide Cities
Authors: Long, Ying; Wu, Kang
Objective: Develop a mega-vector-blocks cellular automata model (MVB-CA) to simulate urban expansion at the block level for 654 Chinese cities
LULC Classes: Rural; Urban
Scenarios: Business-as-Usual (BAU); Urban Agglomeration Oriented Scheme (UAO); New Type of Urbanization (NTU)
Analysis Methods: Automated Identification and Characterization of Blocks (AICP framework); logistic regression; mega-vector-blocks cellular automata; scenario analysis; GIS-based processing
Sim. Method Advantages: Irregular polygons align with real-world entities; direct correspondence to blocks; avoids raster CA cell-size sensitivity; enhances policy relevance; facilitates stakeholder engagement; enables intra-city comparison; supports spatial interaction analysis
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; Python; ESRI File Geodatabase; CartoDB
Predictors: SIZE_LN (log block size); COMPACT (perimeter²/area); CENTER (air distance to city centre); DENSITY (standardized POI density)
Data Sources: 2011 ordnance survey road network; 2011 POIs dataset; MOHURD urban land area statistics (2007–2012); administrative boundaries; DEM (90 m slope); NFGIS hydrological data; Beijing block maps; OpenStreetMap for AICP
Validation Methods: Inter-model comparison with BUDEM; online crowdsourced feedback; statistical accuracy assessment (overall precision; spatial overlap; zone-wise correlation)
Validation Data Sources: BUDEM model outputs for Beijing; user feedback via Sina Weibo
Key Findings: Total urban land in 2017 under BAU = 62,835 km² (+38.5%); under UAO = 58,394 km² (+28.7%); under NTU = 58,930 km² (+29.7%); (2) Logistic regression explanatory power = 81.9%; CA model precision = 83.2% in Beijing; (3) Spatial policies (UAO; NTU) significantly curb sprawl relative to BAU
Implications: Enables linking national policies to local block-level outcomes; Supports urban planning in cities lacking local expansion models; Facilitates stakeholder engagement via block-scale results; Provides infrastructure for ecological and social impact assessments
Limitations: Calibration restricted to Beijing weights; Block subdivision not implemented; Data constraints and potential biases from Beijing-based parameters; Unrealistic large blocks in small cities without subdivision
Future Directions: Integrate spatial equilibrium module with provincial input-output analysis; Incorporate local development policies and spatial plans as model factors; Enhance block subdivision techniques; Include global land cover and nighttime light data for block generation
Scalability: Applicable to other countries with road network and POI data
Novelty: First national-scale block-level urban expansion CA model; Use of irregular vector blocks via AICP; Linking macro-scale policy scenarios to block-level simulations

Title: The effect of forest owner decision-making, climatic change and societal demands on land-use change and ecosystem service provision in Sweden
Authors: Blanco, Victor; Holzhauer, Sascha; Brown, Calum; Lagergren, Fredrik; Vulturius, Gregor; Lindeskog, Mats; Rounsevell, Mark D. A.
Objective: To explore future ecosystem service provision, land-use change, and changes in land owner objectives in the Swedish forestry sector under combined socio-economic and climatic scenarios using an agent-based model that incorporates forest owner decision-making and behavior
LULC Classes: Pine forest; spruce forest; pine-spruce forest; pine-boreal broadleaf forest; spruce-boreal broadleaf forest; boreal broadleaf forest; nemoral broadleaf forest; agriculture; protected areas; non-productive forests; semi-natural vegetation; wetlands; open spaces; other unmanaged land; artificial surfaces; water bodies
Scenarios: SSP1-RCP4.5 (Sustainability and lower emissions); SSP3-RCP4.5 (Regional rivalry and lower emissions); SSP3-RCP8.5 (Regional rivalry and higher emissions); SSP4-RCP4.5 (Inequality and lower emissions); SSP5-RCP8.5 (Fossil-fuelled development and higher emissions)
Analysis Methods: Agent-based modeling; cluster analysis for forest owner typology validation; Cobb-Douglas production function; linear regression for climate impact projections; sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Incorporates land owner behavior and decision-making; represents multifunctional land use; handles trade-offs between various ecosystem services; accounts for diversity of human behavior; capable of large-scale applications; represents long-term forest allocation dynamics
Tools/Soft Used: CRAFTY-Sweden (agent-based modeling framework); ProdMod model; LPJ-GUESS ecosystem model; R statistical software; EC-Earth-RCA4, IPSL-RCA4, and NorESM-RCA4 climate models
Predictors: Forest productivities (pine, spruce, boreal broadleaf, nemoral broadleaf); grassland productivity; transportation infrastructure; forest age; owner objectives and management practices; climatic change effects on productivities; societal demands for ecosystem services
Data Sources: SLU Forest Map; Swedish Forest Agency statistics; CORINE land cover data; Nationally Designated Areas; LPJ-GUESS climate projections; FAO production data; Survey data from 872 Swedish forest owners; EURO-CORDEX climate models; IIASA SSP data
Validation Methods: Cluster analysis validation of forest owner typology using empirical data; comparison of theoretical typology with empirical forest owner survey data; sensitivity analysis
Validation Data Sources: Survey data from 872 Swedish forest owners; National Forest Inventory data
Key Findings: Substantial increase in timber harvesting in coming decades due to uneven forest age distribution; decoupling between supply and demand for forest ecosystem services; climate change influence may be less important than socio-economic change or behavioral differences; variability in land owner behavior has substantial role in determining land-use change direction and impact; accelerating timber harvesting may negatively affect biodiversity, recreation, and carbon sequestration
Implications: Challenge of continuously meeting demands for ecosystem services over long periods; need for top-down mechanisms using national-scale information to regulate forestry processes; potential trade-offs between forest services and agricultural expansion; importance of considering voluntary set-asides and certification requirements in forest management
Limitations: Difficulty in estimating ecosystem service demands; coarse spatial resolution for climate change effects in mountainous regions; fixed management effects throughout forest life; lack of voluntary conservation set-asides; overestimation of middle-aged forest and underestimation of old/young forest in age distribution; no consideration of improved planting material from seed orchards
Future Directions: Include voluntary set-asides for conservation; account for certification requirements; incorporate improved planting material effects; develop more evenly distributed forest age distributions; include services provided by protected natural systems; consider uptake of innovations through forest owner networks
Scalability: Model framework is designed to be flexible and applicable across a wide range of empirical or theoretical settings and geographical scales
Novelty: First large-scale application of agent-based modeling incorporating forest owner behavior and decision-making for ecosystem service provision; integration of multiple ecosystem services beyond timber; incorporation of forest owner typology validated with empirical data; simultaneous consideration of climate change and socio-economic scenarios in forestry sector modeling

Title: The importance of socio-ecological system dynamics in understanding adaptation to global change in the forestry sector
Authors: Blanco, Victor; Brown, Calum; Holzhauer, Sascha; Vulturius, Gregor; Rounsevell, Mark D. A.
Objective: To explore adaptation to global change in the forestry sector using an agent-based model (CRAFTY-Sweden) that represents large-scale land-use dynamics based on demand and supply of ecosystem services, and to evaluate the competitiveness and coping ability of different forest management strategies under future climatic and socio-economic conditions
LULC Classes: Timber production (pine, spruce, boreal broadleaf, nemoral broadleaf); carbon sequestration; biodiversity; recreation; cereal production; meat production
Scenarios: Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP4.5, RCP8.5) combined with Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSP1, SSP3, SSP4, SSP5); three climate models (EC-Earth-RCA4, IPSL-RCA4, NorESM-RCA4)
Analysis Methods: Agent-based modeling; ecosystem service supply and demand analysis; competitiveness assessment; coping ability evaluation; scenario analysis; Monte Carlo simulations
Sim. Method Advantages: Process-based models account for system states and dynamics that determine state changes; better exploration of future adaptation processes; representation of individual behavior and socio-ecological interactions; ability to simulate autonomous adaptation over time; incorporation of behavioral and cognitive factors in adaptive decisions
Tools/Soft Used: CRAFTY-Sweden agent-based model; LPJ-GUESS ecosystem model; ProdMod forest growth model
Predictors: Land productivity; climate-induced productivity changes; ecosystem service demands; agent objectives; management practices; capital levels; infrastructure availability; giving-up and giving-in thresholds
Data Sources: Swedish Forest Agency (2015); Swedish Board of Agriculture (2009); Institute of Environmental Studies (2015); FAO (2015); ProdMod model (Eko, 1985); LPJ-GUESS ecosystem model; EURO-CORDEX climate projections
Validation Methods: Model calibration to produce minimal short-term changes under constant conditions; 32 simulation runs for stochasticity assessment; reference scenario comparison
Validation Data Sources: Current Swedish forest management data; baseline agricultural production data; FAO production statistics
Key Findings: Multi-objective management strategies provide better adaptation capacity; substantial forest felling will occur before 2050; competitiveness and coping ability are dynamic and context-dependent; socio-economic conditions more important than climate change for forest owner competitiveness; boreal broadleaf forests alone not suitable for adaptation; combination of management strategies advisable across large regions
Implications: Large-scale felling events represent windows of opportunity for incorporating new management strategies; top-down institutional measures needed during these periods; autonomous adaptation alone insufficient to meet societal demands; planned adaptation through policies and incentives essential; need for advance planning to avoid vulnerability from uneven age distributions
Limitations: Model assumptions about free conversion between management strategies; absence of climate change effects on biodiversity; no agent learning or interaction capabilities; parameter uncertainties; scenario representation limitations; process omissions including voluntary set-asides
Future Directions: Better understanding of multi-service production synergies; incorporation of more comprehensive ecosystem services in models; improved representation of agent learning and interaction; development of adaptive management throughout stand rotation periods; better incorporation of behavioral barriers to strategy transitions
Scalability: Results specific to Sweden's biophysical and socio-economic conditions; approach applicable to other regions but findings may differ; methodology transferable to other forest sectors globally
Novelty: First application of agent-based modeling to assess forest management strategy suitability for climate adaptation; integration of socio-ecological implications beyond economic considerations; dynamic assessment of adaptive capacity evolution over time; novel approach combining autonomous adaptation simulation with ecosystem service provision

Title: Data Descriptor: A web platform for landuse, climate, demography, hydrology and beach erosion in the Black Sea catchment
Authors: Lehmann, Anthony; Guigoz, Yaniss; Ray, Nicolas; Mancosu, Emanuele; Abbaspour, Karim C.; Freund, Elham Rouholahnejad; Allenbach, Karin; De Bono, Andrea; Fasel, Marc; Gago-Silva, Ana; Baer, Roger; Lacroix, Pierre; Giuliani, Gregory
Country: Black Sea catchment (covering parts of 15 countries)
Objective: Develop and share an integrated web-based platform delivering modeled datasets on land-use, climate, demography, hydrology, water vulnerability/scarcity, and beach erosion for the entire Black Sea catchment to support science and policy‐making.
LULC Classes: forest; grassland; cropland; built-up area; scrubland; crops/natural vegetation; barren or sparsely vegetated; water; snow and ice; permanent wetlands
Scenarios: BS-HOT; BS-ALONE; BS-COOP; BS-COOL land-use/demography storylines; HB1 (B2) & HS1 (A2) climate scenarios; sea-level-rise 0.5 m, 0.82 m, 1 m
Analysis Methods: statistical downscaling & spatial allocation (Metronamica); INLA interpolation & Delta method for climate; SWAT2009 agro-hydrological modeling; SUFI-2 sensitivity/uncertainty calibration; water-scarcity indices (Hoekstra, Smakhtin); ensemble of six 1-D beach-erosion models
Sim. Method Advantages: Continuous, process-based SWAT enables climate-land-use coupling; INLA yields high-accuracy gridded climate fields; Metronamica’s stochastic yearly allocation captures spatial dynamics; ensemble beach modeling reduces single-model bias; grid computing accelerates large-scale calibration
Tools/Soft Used: Metronamica v4.2.2; R with R-INLA; SWAT2009 rev 528; SWAT-CUP/SUFI-2; MATLAB (beach models); GeoNode 2.0; Linux grid cluster
Predictors: elevation; slope; soil quality; mean temperature; annual precipitation; accessibility by major/secondary roads & rail; protected areas; fire & flood risk layers; historical land-use change probabilities
Data Sources: MODIS 2001/2008 land-use; WorldClim climate surfaces; GHCN & ECA&D station data; PRUDENCE RCM outputs; UN population variants; Eurostat & national statistical offices; GRDC river discharge; ICPDR nitrate; FAO, World Bank water-use statistics; satellite imagery for beaches
Validation Methods: climate cross-validation against thin-plate splines; land-use Kappa, Klocation, Fuzzy-Kappa plus stakeholder review; hydrology multi-site calibration/validation with SUFI-2; comparison of Delta-method climate surfaces; visual inspection of beach digitization
Validation Data Sources: withheld meteorological stations subset; MODIS observed land-use maps; 144 river-discharge gauges; 37 nitrate stations; crop-yield statistics; satellite imagery accuracy checks
Key Findings: Produced 400 000 km² coastal and 2.2 million km² catchment datasets accessible via interoperable web services; nearly 50% of Black Sea beaches already require artificial protection; water-scarcity and agricultural vulnerability highly heterogeneous; platform demonstrates GEOSS-compatible data sharing
Implications: Enables regional environmental assessments, supports EU directives and Black Sea/Danube commissions, and guides prioritization of protection investments under plausible future changes
Limitations: Coarse spatial resolution unsuitable for local planning; model and scenario uncertainties; beach inventory limited by variable image dates and geolocation shifts
Future Directions: Increase spatial, temporal and thematic resolution as computing capacity grows; establish long-term monitoring to refine beach-erosion dynamics; extend scenario analyses
Scalability: Approach and open-standards platform are readily transferable to other large transboundary basins
Novelty: First basin-wide integration of land-use, climate, demographic and hydrological scenarios with beach-erosion modeling delivered through an open GeoNode platform under GEOSS principles

Title: Integrated modelling of urban spatial development under uncertain climate futures: A case study in Hungary
Authors: Li, Sen; Juhasz-Horvath, Linda; Pedde, Simona; Pinter, Laszlo; Rounsevell, Mark D. A.; Harrison, Paula A.
Objective: To provide fundamental decision support information for climate risk assessment in Hungary, an urban spatial development model of land cover change and population age structure dynamics was developed and applied to local integrated scenarios of climate change and stakeholder-derived socio-economic change
LULC Classes: Residential (Urban fabric, CLC class 111-112); Commercial/industrial (Industrial or commercial units, CLC class 121); Urban green/leisure (Green urban areas, CLC class 141 and Sport and leisure facilities, CLC class 142)
Scenarios: SSP1 x RCP4.5; SSP4 x RCP4.5; SSP3 x RCP8.5; SSP5 x RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Integrated modeling using ALLOCATION model with three sub-models: economic change sub-model, urban land cover change sub-model, and population distribution sub-model
Sim. Method Advantages: Fine resolution projections over large area; generates variety of outputs including extents of multiple urban land cover types and age-structured populations
Tools/Soft Used: R version 3.2.0; ArcGIS version 10.2; Repast Simphony version 2.1
Predictors: GDP and population (for demand estimation); per capita GDP and extent of existing urban land cover; proximity to social amenities; attractiveness of territorial types; planning regulations
Data Sources: CORINE land cover datasets (2000, 2006, 2012) from EEA and FOMI; Hungarian Central Statistics Office (KSH) census data; SSP Database from IIASA; Climate projections from HadGEM Earth System Model
Validation Methods: Coefficient of Determination (R-squared) analysis; Visual and distance-density plot comparisons; Qualitative evaluation by stakeholders
Validation Data Sources: CORINE land cover observed data; NUTS5 level population data; Stakeholder feedback
Key Findings: Peri-urbanisation around Budapest occurs under all scenarios; Decline in working age population in centres of capital and major towns; Temperature rises cause up to 2.18% and 7.91% GDP damage by 2100 under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 respectively; Climate change impacts on urban development patterns were marginal
Implications: Future urban planning needs to consider potential for underutilised urban infrastructure in capital centre and pressures for social service provisioning in outskirts; Model can be used to test effectiveness of inter-sectoral policy responses
Limitations: Model lacks explanatory power on complex underpinning processes; Climate change impacts approximated through GDP damage only; Limited to top-down approach; Requires optimization of stakeholder engagement levels
Future Directions: Link bottom-up agent-based modelling framework; Build wider range of localised sectoral scenarios; Include more scenario drivers; Apply to smaller geographical regions at finer scales
Scalability: Yes; modeling framework has considerable flexibility and can be easily applied elsewhere with open access land cover and census data
Novelty: Integration of multiple disciplines; stakeholder engagement in scenario and model development; integration of scales from national to local levels; fine resolution projections over large area with multiple output types

Title: Land-use-change induced dynamics of carbon stocks of the terrestrial ecosystem in Pakistan
Authors: Chen, Dongdong; Deng, Xiangzheng; Jin, Gui; Samie, Abdus; Li, Zhaohua
Journal: PHYSICS AND CHEMISTRY OF THE EARTH
Objective: Analyze the impact of land use change on ecosystem service of carbon sequestration in Pakistan under alternative scenarios
LULC Classes: Forest; cultivated land; grassland; water; built-up; unused land
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU); Investment priority oriented (IPO); Ecological conservation oriented (ECO)
Analysis Methods: DLS model for land use simulation; InVEST carbon module for carbon stock estimation
Sim. Method Advantages: System-level integration of exogenous/endogenous drivers; Quantitative spatial statistical modeling at grid level; Minimization of subjective bias in land system dynamics
Tools/Soft Used: GIS platform; DLS model; InVEST model
Predictors: Elevation; slope; distance to river; distance to road; annual mean temperature; annual mean precipitation; diurnal temperature range
Data Sources: Land use/cover (ESA Global Cover; USGS TM imagery revision); Elevation/slope (SRTM-3); Climate (WorldClim); Rivers (Digital Chart of the World); Roads (OpenStreetMap); Population (national statistical yearbooks; Nordpil)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Total carbon stocks declined from 10.34 Tg C (2006) to 9.49 Tg C (2009); 2020 carbon stocks under BAU: 9.08 Tg C/IPO: 10.24 Tg C/ECO: 11.94 Tg C; Only BAU scenario shows continued decline; IPO and ECO yield increases, with ECO highest
Implications: Infrastructure investment (IPO) can enhance carbon storage while fostering development; ECO scenario maximizes sequestration but is less feasible under Pakistan’s socioeconomic constraints
Limitations: Land use data limited to two periods; only seven driving factors considered; InVEST carbon module simplifies carbon cycle processes
Future Directions: Incorporate multi-period land use data and additional socioeconomic drivers; Refine carbon pool transformations and classification granularity
Scalability: Methodology applicable to other terrestrial—and potentially marine—ecosystems
Novelty: Integration of land-system DLS model with InVEST carbon module across CPEC context; Scenario linkage of large-scale infrastructure investment to carbon service dynamics

Title: Will rapid urban expansion in, the drylands of northern China continue: A scenario analysis based on the Land Use Scenario Dynamics-urban model and the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Authors: He, Chunyang; Li, Jingwei; Zhang, Xiaoling; Liu, Zhifeng; Zhang, Da
Objective: Systematically assess past (1992–2015) and projected (2015–2050) urban expansion in the drylands of northern China under alternative socioeconomic pathways
LULC Classes: Cropland; woodland; grassland; water; built-up land; unused land; urban land
Scenarios: SSP1 (sustainability); SSP2 (middle of the road); SSP3 (regional rivalry); SSP4 (inequality); SSP5 (fossil-fueled development); Business-as-usual
Analysis Methods: AGU and AGR indicators for quantifying expansion; Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs) framework; Land Use Scenario Dynamics–urban (LUSD-urban) model (CA + system dynamics); Adaptive Monte Carlo calibration
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates macro- (system dynamics) and micro- (cellular automata) drivers; Spatially explicit simulation under alternative scenarios; Flexible incorporation of ecological and policy constraints
Tools/Soft Used: GIS; LUSD-urban model; Monte Carlo simulation; Excel/ArcGIS (implicit)
Predictors: Elevation; slope; distance to highways; distance to railways; distance to city centers; population density (HYDE); ecological constraints (nature reserves); planning constraints (protected areas); neighborhood effect; inheritance attribute
Data Sources: Xu et al. (2016) time-series urban land (1 km); Landsat TM land-cover (1990) via Liu et al.; HYDE population data (10 km); SRTM DEM (90 m)
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated vs. observed urban maps (2000, 2010, 2015) using kappa index
Validation Data Sources: Observed urban land maps for 2000, 2010, 2015 (Xu et al., 2016)
Key Findings: Urban land grew from 4 110 km² (1992) to 20 969 km² (2015) at 7.34% yr⁻¹.; Dry sub-humid zone accounted for ~68% of expansion.; Under SSP1/5, urban land reaches ~31 066 km² by 2050 (1.13% yr⁻¹), under BAU it reaches ~43 522 km².; BTH agglomeration leads expansion (5 785 → 8 563 km² by 2050 under SSP1).; Divergence between BAU and SSP1 emerges after 2030.
Implications: Urgent need for sustainable urban-management measures in DNC.; Policy focus on SSP1-type transformation before 2030 to curb sprawl.; Framework applicable for assessing ecological impacts and guiding regional planning.
Limitations: 1 km resolution limits fine-scale detail.; Model ignores household purchase capacity and detailed socioeconomic behavior.; SSPs designed at global scale, regional implementation gaps.; Scenario projections not forecasts.
Future Directions: Use 500 m NPP-VIIRS nighttime lights for finer mapping.; Enhance LUSD-urban with agent-based components for resident behavior.; Link with ecological models (e.g., InVEST) to assess water stress, habitat loss.
Scalability: Model and scenarios transferable to other large dryland regions globally
Novelty: First integration of IPCC SSPs with the LUSD-urban model for region-wide, multi-scale scenario simulation of urban expansion in DNC

Title: Adaptation with climate uncertainty: An examination of agricultural land use in the United States
Authors: Mu, Jianhong E.; McCarl, Bruce A.; Sleeter, Benjamin; Abatzoglou, John T.; Zhang, Hongliang
Objective: Examine adaptation responses to climate change through adjustment of agricultural land use, distinguishing inter-annual variability and long-term climate normals, and projecting future land-use shifts
LULC Classes: Cropland; Other cropland (idle, failed, cover, summer fallow, conservation reserve); Grazing land (pasture, rangeland, woodland for forage); Woodland (non-pasture)
Scenarios: RCP4.5; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Fractional Multinomial Logit (FMLOGIT) with Chamberlain-Mundlak correlated random effects; average partial effects; RMSE validation; Wald tests
Sim. Method Advantages: Distinguishes short-run vs long-run adaptive responses; Accounts for endogeneity and unobserved heterogeneity via correlated random effects; Uses full ensemble of 20 CMIP5 models for unbiased distribution of future projections
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Inter-annual climate variability: total precipitation; growing season degree-days; precipitation intensity index; drought index; Long-term climate normals (10-year moving averages): precipitation; degree-days; precipitation intensity; Economic/socio-economic: annualized revenue-cost ratios (crop, livestock); per-acre government payments; population density; irrigation share; latitude; time trend; Soil conditions: clay fraction; sand fraction; flood-prone fraction; K-factor; slope length; permeability; wetlands; moisture capacity; salinity
Data Sources: U.S. Census of Agriculture; U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis; Abatzoglou gridded meteorological data; Abatzoglou & Brown downscaled CMIP5 projections; National Resource Inventory (NRI)
Validation Methods: Within-sample and out-of-sample RMSE; Wald tests of joint significance
Validation Data Sources: Census of Agriculture panel data; CMIP5 downscaled projections
Key Findings: Long-term climate normals have impacts on land-use shares as large as inter-annual variability; Predicted hill-shaped responses of cropland share to degree-days and precipitation; Projected 5–15% increase in cropland share and 4–10% decrease in grazing share by 2085; Spatially, cropland expands in northern/interior West; grazing expands in southern regions and Inland Pacific Northwest
Implications: Inform food-security adaptation planning; Guide ecosystem and habitat management under land-use shifts; Highlight infrastructure and crop-breeding policy needs for shifting production zones
Limitations: Excludes urban and forest land-use change; Holds non-climate variables at historical means (no future socio-economic projections); Ignores CO₂ fertilization effects on land-use decisions
Future Directions: Integrate broader land-use types (urban, forest); Include future socio-economic and market-risk projections; Assess CO₂ fertilization impacts on land allocation
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Differentiates farmers’ responses to inter-annual vs long-term climate drivers; Employs full CMIP5 ensemble for land-use projection uncertainty rather than a limited subset of models

Title: An integrated and dynamic approach to agricultural land-use change modeling at country-level to regional scale: Application to Iran
Authors: Mesgari, Iman; Jabalameli, Mohammad Saeed
Objective: Predict demand for agricultural land use at the national level and simulate its spatial distribution at regional scale using an integrated dynamic modeling approach
LULC Classes: Agricultural; Pasture; Forest; Desert; Non-agricultural
Scenarios: Medium fertility rate; GDP growth 4.9%; annual precipitation 212 mm (2015–2040)
Analysis Methods: Dynamic simulation model; Multicriteria LUC model; AHP; MADM; Sensitivity analysis; Empirical validation
Sim. Method Advantages: Systemic integration of macro-level demand with spatially explicit allocation; Top-down and bottom-up feedback loops; Ability to test “what-if” socioeconomic and environmental scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Population; GDP growth; International agricultural price index; Precipitation; Land-pattern optimality; Location suitability factors (precipitation, temperature, soil fertility, elevation, groundwater depth); Change elasticity
Data Sources: World Bank; FAO statistical database; Iran Meteorological Organization; Annual Agricultural Statistics of Iran; General Census of Agriculture; Iran Water Resource Management Company; Statistical Center of Iran; Ministry of Agriculture Jihad
Validation Methods: Structural validation via expert focus groups; Behavioral validation via sensitivity analysis; Verification using R-squared comparison to historical data
Validation Data Sources: Annual Agricultural Statistics of Iran; General Census of Agriculture (2014); FAO; World Bank; Statistical Center of Iran; Ministry of Agriculture Jihad; Iran Meteorological Organization; Iran Water Resource Management Company
Key Findings: Total agricultural area rises from 16.7 M ha to 19.9 M ha by 2025 then stabilizes; Increase concentrated in north & southwest provinces (Khuzestan, Gilan, Mazandaran, Golestan); Decline or stagnation in east & northeast provinces (Razavi, South, North Khorasan); Water availability is the most determining factor; Land-pattern optimality improves from 0.85 (2015) to 0.96 (2040)
Implications: Provides decision-support for land-use planning and water resource management; Highlights need for sustainable water supply investments in east/northeast regions
Limitations: Spatial resolution limited to province level; Assumes continuation of past trends; Scenario results sensitive to exogenous variable uncertainty
Future Directions: Develop additional scenarios; Apply higher spatial resolution; Explore alternative suitability analysis methods
Scalability: Scalable from local to regional scales without altering model structure
Novelty: Integrated dynamic top-down and bottom-up modeling framework; Combination of national-level dynamic simulation with regional multicriteria LUC allocation; Inclusion of feedback between spatial pattern optimality and demand projections

Title: Analyzing the relationship between urbanization, food supply and demand, and irrigation requirements in Jordan
Authors: Koch, Jennifer; Wimmer, Florian; Schaldach, Ruediger
Objective: Analyze how urbanization affects food supply and demand and irrigation requirements in Jordan
LULC Classes: Urban area; Irrigated farmland; Rainfed farmland
Scenarios: Baseline; FS1 (Urban Expansion); FS2 (Climate Change); FS3 (UE + CC); FD1 (SocioEconomic change); FSD1 (UE + SE); FSD2 (CC + SE); FSD3 (UE + CC + SE)
Analysis Methods: Chain of simulation models including downscaled climate projections; GEPIC crop-productivity simulations; LandSHIFT.R spatially explicit land-change modeling; scenario analysis; ensemble modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: High spatial resolution (30 arc sec) and explicit mapping of land‐use changes; Soft coupling of crop productivity and land‐change models allows endogenous feedbacks; Ability to isolate effects of urban expansion, climate change, and socioeconomic change; Use of multiple downscaled climate datasets to quantify uncertainty
Tools/Soft Used: GEPIC; LandSHIFT.R; MM5 regional climate model (ECHAM5 and HadCM3 outputs); GIS; cellular automata approach
Predictors: Urban population growth; Climate projections (temperature, precipitation); Crop yields; Water productivity; Population-driven food demand; Dietary composition; Technological yield improvements
Data Sources: Climate projections from Smiatek et al. (2011) (SRES A1B, GCM–RCM ensemble); Crop-productivity input data from Koch et al. (2012a); Population and water-use scenarios from “Modest Hopes” (Anonymous, 2011); FAOSTAT, FAO freshwater data; MODIS land-cover data, UN Population Division
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Farmland displacement by urban expansion has negligible effects on cropland area, yields, and irrigation needs; Climate change alone increases cropland area by ~147 km² by 2025 and irrigation requirements by 19 MCM; by 2050 increases of 265 km² and 64 MCM; Socioeconomic change (population + diet + tech) doubles irrigated farmland and nearly doubles irrigation by 2050 (618 MCM); Combined CC + SE nearly triples irrigation requirements (≈439 MCM by 2050)
Implications: Urgent need for investment in water infrastructure (e.g., Red Sea–Dead Sea canal) and irrigation planning; Spatially explicit projections critical for regional water planning strategies; Managing dietary and technological trends more important than urban‐land displacement
Limitations: Results depend on scenario assumptions and do not predict actual futures; Exclusion of lifestyle-driven demand changes and microclimate/impervious surface effects; Single SRES A1B scenario; no RCP inputs
Future Directions: Integrate future water-availability projections with land-use demands; Incorporate RCP-based climate data and additional socioeconomic scenarios; Model urban microclimate and impervious-surface impacts
Scalability: Model framework adaptable to other semi-arid regions with regional calibration
Novelty: First spatially explicit, high-resolution analysis of isolated and combined effects of urbanization, climate change, and socioeconomic demand on Jordan’s land and water resources; Soft coupling of downscaled climate, crop-productivity, and land-change models for uncertainty assessment

Title: Future environmental and agricultural impacts of Brazil's Forest Code
Authors: Soterroni, Aline C.; Mosnier, Mine; Carvalho, Alexandre X. Y.; Camara, Gilberto; Obersteiner, Michael; Andrade, Pedro R.; Souza, Ricardo C.; Brock, Rebecca; Pirker, Johannes; Kraxner, Florian; Havlik, Petr; Kapos, Valerie; zu Ermgassen, Erasmus K. H. J.; Valin, Hugo; Ramos, Fernando M.
Objective: Quantify future environmental and agricultural impacts of Brazil’s 2012 Forest Code through 2050, assessing combined and isolated effects of deforestation control, obligatory restoration, and environmental reserve quotas
LULC Classes: Cropland; pasture; forestry; bioenergy; short-rotation plantations; non-productive land
Scenarios: NoFC; IDCAmazon; IDCBrazil; IDCImperfect1; IDCImperfect2; IDCImperfect3; FC; FCnoCRA
Analysis Methods: Partial equilibrium economic modeling (GLOBIOM-Brazil); spatially explicit land-use change simulation; scenario analysis; EPIC crop modeling; RUMINANT livestock modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: Endogenously computes deforestation based on agricultural demand-feedback; integrates market feedback and regulatory constraints; provides spatially explicit projections without historical calibration; detailed sectoral representation
Tools/Soft Used: GLOBIOM-Brazil; EPIC; RUMINANT
Predictors: GDP growth; population growth; dietary trends; biophysical constraints (soil fertility; climate); transport infrastructure costs; productivity (crop yields; livestock productivity); policy/regulatory variables (Forest Code enforcement); land tenure/legal reserve data
Data Sources: Official agricultural statistics; satellite imagery (PRODES/INPE); rural Environmental Cadastre (CAR); protected area maps; biomass maps (Third Emissions Inventory; Ruesch and Gibbs; Havlík et al.)
Validation Methods: Comparison of model projections (2000–2010 deforestation and land use) against PRODES/INPE data and official statistics
Validation Data Sources: PRODES/INPE deforestation dataset; official crop and livestock production statistics
Key Findings: Rigorous enforcement prevents net loss of 53.4 Mha of forest by 2050 (81% in the Amazon); cropland area reduced by 4% and cattle herd by 8%; cattle productivity must increase by 56%; obligatory restoration creates 12.9 Mha; environmental reserve quotas protect 5.8 Mha; enforcement contributes up to 1.03 PgCO₂e reduction by 2030; imperfect enforcement yields limited benefits and leakage to other biomes
Implications: Full enforcement reconciles agricultural growth with conservation; critical for Brazil’s NDC commitments; environmental reserve quotas essential for conserving native vegetation; requires political will, resources, and rapid CRA regulation; model applicable to other developing countries
Limitations: Passive restoration assumed with no costs; no enforcement cost modeling; uncertainties in public land tenure and CRA assumptions; 50 km resolution; omission of biodiversity and enforcement costs
Future Directions: Evaluate restoration costs and active restoration strategies; model CRA market design; quantify enforcement costs; integrate biodiversity outcomes; property-level analysis; CRA regulation scenario modeling
Scalability: Applicable as a model framework for other developing countries facing land-use and policy challenges
Novelty: First spatially explicit nationwide assessment of Brazil’s 2012 Forest Code using a global partial equilibrium model; disentangles impacts of illegal deforestation control and obligatory restoration; integrates endogenous market feedback with biophysical constraints

Title: Fuzzy definition of Rural Urban Interface: An application based on land use change scenarios in Portugal
Authors: Amato, Federico; Tonini, Marj; Murgante, Beniamino; Kanevski, Mikhail
Objective: Propose and apply a fuzzy set theory–based framework integrated with Multilayer Perceptron and Markov Chain models to map and forecast the Rural-Urban Interface (RUI) in Portugal without fixed buffer parameters.
LULC Classes: Urban fabric; Other artificial surfaces; Industrial, commercial and transport units; Mine, dump and construction sites; Artificial non-agricultural vegetated areas; Irrigated agricultural areas; Arable land; Permanent crops; Pastures; Heterogeneous agricultural areas; Forest and semi-natural areas; Shrub/herbaceous vegetation; Open spaces with little/no vegetation; Inland wetlands; Coastal wetlands; Inland waters; Marine waters
Scenarios: Business-as-usual future scenario for 2030 based on quadratic regression of Markov Chain transition matrices
Analysis Methods: Multilayer Perceptron neural network; fuzzy set theory (large and near membership functions); Markov Chain; Evidence Likelihood; Kappa statistics; ROC/AUC; TOC
Sim. Method Advantages: Handles non-linear processes (urban growth, rural development); Higher predictive accuracy than other models (LCM MLP vs. alternatives); Produces continuous probability maps (non-categorical); Eliminates reliance on rigid, user-defined buffer parameters; Requires no expert rule-based parameterization
Tools/Soft Used: Land Change Modeler™ (ArcGIS extension); ESRI ArcGIS®; R (TOC package)
Predictors: Elevation (DEM); slope; aspect; population census; agricultural census; distance to primary roads; distance to cities >50 000 inhabitants; soil thickness; soil pH; soil texture; ecological value; proximity to Protected Areas & Natura 2000; NUTS II/III administrative units; dynamic distance from land-cover classes
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover (1990, 2000, 2012); Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (DEM, slope, aspect); Instituto Nacional de Estatística (agricultural & population census); OpenStreetMap (roads, cities); EPIC WebGIS Portugal (soil properties, ecological value); Portuguese Natura 2000 network (Law 2008/142); NUTS II/III boundaries; Instituto Português do Mar e da Atmosfera (climate data)
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient (overall, location, histogram); Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) and Area Under Curve (AUC); Total Operating Characteristic (TOC)
Validation Data Sources: Observed CLC 2012 land cover map; Reference RUI map based on 1 km buffer intersection (Tonini et al., 2017a); RUI point dataset (≈15 000 points)
Key Findings: Overall Kappa 0.8227 for LULCC simulation vs. CLC 2012; Fuzzy Gamma overlay outperformed OR/Sum (mean AUC 0.811); High-possibility RUI expansion along Braga-Porto-Aveiro-Lisbon corridor and Algarve coast; Scattered inland hotspots driven by rural abandonment ≥88.8% of pixels in 1–2 km buffer had RUI possibility >90
Implications: Supports fire-prevention policy with flexible risk thresholds; Enhances decision-support by accounting for spatial uncertainty; Enables adaptive planning without fixed buffer distances
Limitations: Dependence on CLC misclassification (notably 1990 map errors); Single scenario (no alternative socioeconomic storylines); No future population or socioeconomic projections; Binary multi-label approaches not explored
Future Directions: Extend to alternative uncertainty frameworks (e.g., multi-label classification); Incorporate multiple socioeconomic scenarios and population forecasts; Apply defuzzification for policy-specific thresholds: Test in other Mediterranean and non-Mediterranean regions
Scalability: Methodology generalizable to other regions and other urban-interface vulnerable areas
Novelty: Integration of fuzzy set theory with MLP-based transition potential modeling; Continuous non-categorical RUI possibility mapping without fixed buffers; Spatio-temporal forecasting of RUI with uncertainty assessment

Title: Grassland futures in Great Britain - Productivity assessment and scenarios for land use change opportunities
Authors: Qi, Aiming; Holland, Robert A.; Taylor, Gail; Richter, Goetz M.
Objective: Estimate current and future dry matter yields (DMYs) of grassland types across Great Britain; assess biomass availability; identify productivity gaps; evaluate impacts of land use change scenarios
LULC Classes: Temporary grassland; Permanent grassland; Rough-grazing grassland
Scenarios: A: PG→RG (Abandonment);
Analysis Methods: Process-conservative meta-models for DMY; spatial upscaling to 1 km² and 2 km² grids; UKCP09 climate projections; CO₂ fertilisation and technology progress adjustments; stochastic land-use transition algorithm with biophysical and policy constraints; GIS overlay
Sim. Method Advantages: Meta-models are as robust as process-based models but require fewer input data
Tools/Soft Used: R (stochastic algorithm implementation)
Predictors: Monthly temperature; Precipitation; Global radiation; Soil available water capacity; Nitrogen application rate; Atmospheric [CO₂]; Technological progress factor
Data Sources: Experimental DMY data (1970s–1980s); UKCP09 climate projections; European Soil Database; Defra Agricultural Census (2010); Mauna Loa atmospheric CO₂ records; BERN model CO₂ projections; Defra Fertiliser Manual; National Statistics
Validation Methods: Calibration and validation of meta-models against observed experimental DMYs; comparison with long-term experiments
Validation Data Sources: Park Grass Long-term Experiments; experimental DMY datasets from 1970s–1980s
Key Findings: Current benchmarks: TG 12.5 t/ha; PG 8.7 t/ha; RG 2.8 t/ha in 2010s; By 2050s, TG↑24%; PG↑14%; RG unchanged; Yield gaps of 45% (TG) and 39% (PG) due to sub-optimal N use (~21 Mt DM unused); Closing gaps could add ~21 Mt DM (rising to 30 Mt by 2050); Scenarios C and D could each add ~18 Mt DM under realistic constraints; Scenario E shows upland reversion and lowland intensification can maintain total DM
Implications: Significant scope to enhance grassland productivity via improved agronomy and technology; informs post-Brexit land-use policy; potential feedstock for livestock and bioenergy; supports ecosystem service planning
Limitations: Irrigation ignored; conservative CO₂ fertilisation assumption; simplifies socio-economic drivers; excludes Northern Ireland; on-farm DMY data sparse
Future Directions: Refine scenarios with biodiversity and ecosystem-service priorities; incorporate regional socio-economic factors; include irrigation potential; gather detailed on-farm yield data
Scalability: Yes; approach adaptable to other regions with comparable climate, soil, land-use and data availability
Novelty: First spatially explicit integration of climate, CO₂ fertilisation and technological progress in grassland DMY modelling at national scale; use of meta-models and stochastic, constraint-based land-use transition scenarios

Title: Identifying effects of land use cover changes and climate change on terrestrial ecosystems and carbon stocks in Mexico
Authors: Mendoza-Ponce, Alma; Corona-Nunez, Rogelio; Kraxner, Florian; Leduc, Sylvain; Patrizio, Piera
Journal: GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE-HUMAN AND POLICY DIMENSIONS
Objective: Identify which natural covers are most vulnerable to land use cover change (LUCC) and quantify carbon stock losses under two socioeconomic and climate change scenarios
LULC Classes: temperate forests; scrublands; tropical dry forests; tropical evergreen forests; natural grasslands; cloud forests; hydrophilic vegetation; other vegetation; rain-fed agriculture; irrigated agriculture; pastures; urban covers; barren land
Scenarios: Business as Usual (SSP2-RCP4.5); Green (SSP1-RCP2.6)
Analysis Methods: Weights of Evidence; correlation analysis; transition probability mapping; short-term simulation; long-term projections; Monte Carlo analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit fine-resolution LUCC modeling; integrates RCP and SSP scenarios; captures hotspots across 13 land-cover categories; outperforms coarse global models by including detailed natural covers
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica EGO; R v2.14; R packages fitdistrplus, mc2d
Predictors: distance to roads; distance to human settlements; distance to cities; population size; GDP; protected areas; slope; altitude; soil type; annual mean temperature; temperature range; temperature seasonality; precipitation; precipitation seasonality
Data Sources: INEGI land cover maps; WorldClim; National Forest Inventory (CONAFOR 2004–2009); allometric equations dataset; IASA socioeconomic projections; SNIM; four GCMs (CNRM-CM5, GFDL-CM3, HADGEM2-ES, MPI-ESM-LR); FAO
Validation Methods: Spatial validation using exponential and multiple-window constant decay function; quantitative comparison of observed vs. simulated 2011 maps at multiple resolutions
Validation Data Sources: INEGI 2011 land cover map
Key Findings: 83% of deforestation (1993–2007) occurred in tropical dry forests, scrublands, temperate forests, tropical evergreen forests; under BAU anthropogenic cover rises from 26% to 37% by 2050; Green scenario reduces to 21%; BAU C stocks decline from 2.13 PgC (1985) to 1.76 PgC (2100); Green scenario raises to 2.15 PgC by ~2080; main drivers are proximity to roads and settlements
Implications: Target conservation and restoration in vulnerable ecosystems; reduce deforestation and enhance regeneration to maintain carbon stocks
Limitations: Scenario assumptions uncertainty; excluded climate feedback on crops and CO₂ fertilization; did not incorporate migration, market trade, policy effects (bioenergy, REDD+), land tenure, violence, corruption
Future Directions: Integrate climate change impacts on crops and C flux feedbacks; include rural-urban migration; assess policy and market drivers (bioenergy, REDD+); incorporate land tenure, violence, corruption influences; improve socioeconomic and biophysical data accuracy
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First national fine-resolution LUCC model in Mexico incorporating 13 detailed land-cover classes under RCP and SSP scenarios to identify hotspots and carbon stock changes

Title: Land use projections in China under global socioeconomic and emission scenarios: Utilizing a scenario-based land-use change assessment framework
Authors: Dong, Na; You, Lan; Cai, Wenjia; Li, Gang; Lin, Hui
Journal: GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE-HUMAN AND POLICY DIMENSIONS
Objective: To develop a scenario-based land-use change assessment framework integrating GCAM and FLUS to evaluate potential land use projections of China under global socioeconomic (SSP1–SSP5) and emission (RCP2.6, RCP4.5) scenarios from 2010 to 2100
LULC Classes: crop; forest; pasture/grass; shrub; urban; other
Scenarios: S1 (SSP1 no climate policy); S2 (SSP2 baseline); S3 (SSP3 no climate policy); S4 (SSP4 no climate policy); S5 (SSP5 no climate policy); S6 (SSP2 + RCP2.6 + Universal Carbon Tax); S7 (SSP2 + RCP4.5 + Universal Carbon Tax); S8 (SSP2 + RCP2.6 + Fossil Fuel & Industrial Carbon Tax)
Analysis Methods: Integration of Global Change Assessment Model (GCAM) and Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS); artificial neural networks; cellular-automata self-adaptive inertial and competition mechanism; multi-regression for urban calibration; spatial downscaling
Sim. Method Advantages: FLUS integrates top-down system dynamics and bottom-up CA with ANNs, enabling fine-resolution downscaling under macro demands, long-term simulation of multiple land use classes, and user-defined scenario assessments
Tools/Soft Used: GCAM 4.0; FLUS model; ArcGIS
Predictors: DEM; slope; population density; GDP; distance to urban areas; distance to rivers; distance to roads; mean annual temperature; annual precipitation; dominant soil; historical land use
Data Sources: CLUM land use dataset; FAO/GTAP; SAGE; HYDE; SSP database (IIASA); GAEZ v3.0; Landsat TM/ETM; Chinese Statistical Yearbook; UN population & urbanization data; World Bank GDP; RESDC population/GDP grids; Natural Earth; Harmonized World Soil Database; IUCN/UNEP-WCMC protected areas
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient; figure of merit; relative error analysis for urban calibration
Validation Data Sources: CLUM maps; Chinese Statistical Yearbook built-up areas; UN population & urbanization data
Key Findings: Under varying socioeconomic pathways, population and GDP dynamics drive food and bioenergy demands, leading to biomass expansions at the expense of cropland, forest, and pasture; Afforestation occurs under low-growth scenarios (S3, S4); Under emission scenarios, Universal Carbon Tax regimes favor forest gains while Fossil Fuel & Industrial Carbon Tax drives high bioenergy–crop expansion
Implications: Provides a quantitative framework for national mitigation strategy and land-use planning; highlights trade-offs among food security, bioenergy, and carbon sequestration; informs policy design under alternative futures
Limitations: Static representation of bioecological and hydrological feedbacks; coarse AEZ-scale assumptions; fixed neighborhood weights; 5-year time steps may miss finer dynamics
Future Directions: Incorporate dynamic bioecological and hydrological interactions; tighter iterative downscaling with smaller time steps; refine neighborhood weighting; extend framework to other regions
Scalability: Yes—to other regions given local land-use, socioeconomic, and environmental data
Novelty: First integration of GCAM and FLUS with fine-resolution (1 km) spatial downscaling calibrated to national land-use data; simultaneous analysis of SSP–RCP combinations with detailed scenario-based spatial allocation

Title: Modelling Farm Growth and Its Impact on Agricultural Land Use: A Country Scale Application of an Agent-Based Model
Authors: Beckers, Veronique; Beckers, Jeroen; Vanmaercke, Matthias; Van Hecke, Etienne; Van Rompaey, Anton; Dendoncker, Nicolas
Objective: Introduce and apply an agent-based model (ADAM) to simulate farmer population dynamics and land use change at national scale
LULC Classes: Arable land with temporary crops; Permanent crops; Grassland; Greenhouses; Agricultural buildings; Residential conversion
Scenarios: Business-as-usual scenario
Analysis Methods: Agent-based modelling; ODD-protocol framework; Linear regression for profitability; Stochastic decision processes; RRMSE calibration and validation
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures individual farmer decision mechanisms; Spatially explicit parcel-level simulation; Represents emergent dynamics; Allows exploration of policy scenarios beyond statistical models
Tools/Soft Used: Java 8 (Javac 1.8.0_51) for ADAM code; GIS parcel datasets
Predictors: Farm size; Farm type; Farmer age; Profitability (area × slope); Regional succession rate; Parcel proximity; Land suitability (soil fertility, infrastructure, topography); Crop rotation probabilities; Expected yields; Crop prices; External market and policy factors
Data Sources: National agricultural surveys (NIS); SIGEC and Landbouwgebruikspercelen parcel datasets; Corine Land Cover; FAO producer price data; Belgian mortality statistics; Expert interviews
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated vs observed farmer counts; Relative root mean square error (RRMSE); Scatterplots; R² at national and municipality levels
Validation Data Sources: Agricultural surveys (2000–2010) from National Institute of Statistics of Belgium
Key Findings: ADAM reproduces observed national farmer decline and farm size increase; BAU scenario predicts continued farmer loss and farm growth, with spatial heterogeneity; Model underperforms in densely populated municipalities due to unmodelled urbanisation pressures
Implications: Need for policies addressing urbanisation impacts on agriculture; ABM offers a tool for evaluating socio-ecological and subsidy scenarios; Upscaling farms may reduce landscape diversity and ecological value
Limitations: Excludes mixed-farm typology; Urbanisation processes not modelled; Land ownership vs rental omitted; Limited farm types; Region-specific assumptions; Lower accuracy in urban areas
Future Directions: Refine agent decision rules and farm typologies (e.g., peri-urban, eco-farming); Integrate urbanisation data and rental tenure effects; Assess ecosystem service impacts; Simulate climate change and subsidy policy scenarios; Apply to other regions with recalibration
Scalability: Applicable to other EU countries using EU-required datasets, subject to data availability and recalibration
Novelty: First real-world, country-scale ABM of farmer population and parcel-level land use dynamics capturing individual decision-making aýd agent interactions

Title: Modelling future impacts of urban development in Kuwait with the use of ABM and GIS
Authors: Alghais, Nayef; Pullar, David
