Objective: To model disaggregate future changes in land-use patterns given forecast population estimates and planning policies using Agent Based Modelling (ABM) and Geographical Information Systems (GIS), specifically focusing on housing shortage and traffic congestion impacts in Kuwait
LULC Classes: Residential districts; mixed use districts; other non-urban areas (industrial, agricultural, ports, desert)
Scenarios: Business-as-usual scenario following historical trends with fixed land policy; adaptive growth scenario where government is more reactive to solve housing shortage
Analysis Methods: Agent Based Modelling (ABM) integrated with Geographical Information Systems (GIS); spatial model using disaggregate spatial data; suitability model; regression analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: ABM allows examination of interactions between autonomous units at disaggregate level which evolves via simulation to reveal emergent macroscopic land use patterns; bottom-up modeling approach; enables evaluation of decisions by different groups based on settlement patterns and interactions with future plans
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS Agent Analyst extension; ArcGIS for GIS operations; Java for encoding rules; Google Earth for satellite images
Predictors: Infrastructure proximity (distances to major street networks, CBD, coastline); urban area proximity; weighted proximity to facilities (hospitals, shopping malls, governmental offices, company offices, factories, universities); land costs of houses or apartments for developable parcels
Data Sources: Kuwait Institute for Scientific Research (KISR) for population projections; Kuwait Central Statistical Bureau and Public Authority for Civil Information (PACI) for socio-economic, transportation and demographic variables; Public Authority of Housing Welfare (PAHW) for housing data; Interior ministry for accident data; Kuwait Finance House (KFH) for land cost data
Validation Methods: Model calibrated by running with 1995 data to predict spatial pattern of urban growth to 2015 and comparing with actual growth pattern; run over 50 times with different parameters to achieve best match
Validation Data Sources: Historical land use data from 1995 and 2015; real urban development patterns
Key Findings: Continued city-centric growth will aggravate problems with more than 50% increase in housing shortage and congestion unless government intervenes; housing shortage will increase from 108,000 applications in 2015 to 180,000 by 2050 under business-as-usual scenario; adaptive government reaction could reduce pending applications to only 11,676 by 2050; traffic accidents projected to increase to 136,000-154,750 by 2050
Implications: Current planning processes inadequate for dealing with urban growth impacts; need for more adaptive planning approach that triggers changes in public housing releases; housing and traffic congestion problems will dramatically worsen without significant changes to urban plans and growth policies
Limitations: Assumption that infrastructure remains unchanged over simulation period; particular agent interactions such as competition between land development agents not included; use of suitability model and historical allocation weights not adequate for representing policies that encouraged land use conversion over time
Future Directions: Obtain further data on public opinion for traffic congestion and housing problems; conduct interviews and surveys with decision makers, private sector, and residents for better understanding of behaviors; enhance validity by adding dynamic infrastructure changes; propose changes to current center-focused approach for urban expansion
Scalability: The proposed approach for disaggregating national demographic data and using ABM could be used to assess alternative urban plans and growth policies in other contexts; methodology applicable to other Gulf cities with similar characteristics
Novelty: First clear process for modeling urban development and its impacts in Arabian Gulf cities; integration of ABM with GIS for Gulf region urban modeling; disaggregation of existing land use and census data suitable for modeling future urban growth; focus on housing shortage and traffic congestion as primary social impacts for Gulf cities

Title: Modelling the impact of urban growth on agriculture and natural land in Italy to 2030
Authors: Martellozzo, F.; Amato, F.; Murgante, B.; Clarke, K. C.
Objective: Analysis of past land use changes in Italy and spatially explicit modelling of urban growth and LUCC under contrasting policy-oriented scenarios to 2030
LULC Classes: agricultural land; natural areas (forests; shrubs; sparsely or poorly vegetated areas); built-up areas; water bodies; wetlands; glaciers; perennial snow
Scenarios: Diffusion scenario (economic interest prevails); Conservation scenario (emphasis on environmental conservation)
Analysis Methods: cellular automata modelling (SLEUTH); analytic hierarchy process (AHP); multi-criteria decision making; past trend data analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: ease of implementation; ability to input high-resolution multi-temporal data at national scale; spatially explicit coupling of local and global criteria; statistically robust realistic projections
Tools/Soft Used: SLEUTH model within a GIS environment (unspecified software)
Predictors: Slope; land use; exclusion layer (socioeconomic; ecological; landscape planning criteria); urban extent; transportation network; hill-shade
Data Sources: Corine Land Cover; digital elevation model; OpenStreetMap; national census; ancillary economic data; Code of Cultural and Landscape Heritage (CBCP); thematic maps; topographic slope; transport network data
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: significant urban expansion up to 2030; 80% increase under Diffusion vs. 71% under Conservation; agricultural land most affected; natural areas loss lower under Conservation; potential reduction in agricultural productivity by 27% (Diffusion) and 23% (Conservation); urban sprawl increases habitat fragmentation
Implications: need for sustainable spatial planning; support policy makers in balancing development and conservation; implications for food security; habitat quality; GHG mitigation; use of scenario outputs for further analyses
Limitations: static one-dimensional exclusion layer; limited integration of dynamic socioeconomic factors; uncertainties in LUCC classification; potential biases from data preparation; sensitivity to boom-bust parameters
Future Directions: integrate dynamic socioeconomic variables into modelling; deeper agronomic analyses for productivity forecasts; apply scenario maps to habitat quality and land surface temperature studies; research on enhancing CA model flexibility
Scalability: Framework demonstrated at full country scale; applicable to other regions with requisite data
Novelty: first high-resolution national-scale application of SLEUTH coupled with AHP-derived policy scenarios providing spatially explicit comparative forecasts

Title: PAST AND FUTURE LAND USE/COVER FLOWS RELATED TO AGRICULTURAL LANDS IN ROMANIA. AN ASSESSMENT USING CLUE-S MODEL AND CORINE LAND COVER DATABASE
Authors: Popovici, Elena-Ana; Kucsicsa, Gheorghe; Balteanu, Dan; Grigorescu, Ines; Mitrica, Bianca; Dumitrascu, Monica; Damian, Nicoleta
Journal: CARPATHIAN JOURNAL OF EARTH AND ENVIRONMENTAL SCIENCES
Objective: to provide a regional-level (Development Regions) assessment of past changes in the agricultural land use pattern during the 1990–2006 period and to simulate future changes (2007–2050) in order to detect the main potential agricultural flows and their regional differences
LULC Classes: built-up areas; arable lands; permanent crops; pastures; scrub and/or herbaceous vegetation association; forests; open spaces with little or no vegetation; heterogeneous agricultural areas; natural grasslands; agricultural complex cultivation patterns
Scenarios: S1 (linear trend 1990–2000 extrapolated to 2007–2050); S2 (linear trend 2000–2006 extrapolated to 2007–2050)
Analysis Methods: logistic regression with forward stepwise; land cover flows analysis; ROC analysis; cross-classification overlay; confusion matrix
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUE-S is an advanced empirical-statistical multi-scale model integrating location suitability analysis with dynamic spatially explicit simulation of land use/cover changes at regional extent
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.4; Dyna-CLUE v2.0
Predictors: elevation; slope declivity; precipitation; temperature; horizontal relief fragmentation; total organic matter content in topsoil; population density; population growth; employees; unemployment rate; tertiary sector employment; large livestock units; built/non-agricultural ratio; settlement density; distance to nearest main towns; distance to nearest main roads; secondary roads density; distance to settlements
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover (1990, 2000, 2006, 2012); EU-Hydro River Network; DEM (30 m); National Meteorological Administration; population census (1992, 2006); ESRI Romania database; Soil quality and electricity transmission atlas; National Institute of Statistics
Validation Methods: cross-classification overlay; confusion matrix; overall accuracy; producer’s accuracy; user’s accuracy; Kappa index; ROC
Validation Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover 2012 (reference); CLC 2006 (baseline)
Key Findings: internal agricultural changes (intensification and extensification) dominate; permanent crops decrease; heterogeneous agricultural areas increase by 10.7% under S1 and decrease by 32.3% under S2; forest losses mainly in plains and gains in mountains; built-up expansion near main towns; spatial accuracy OA ≈ 86%, Kappa ≈ 0.8
Implications: informs sustainable land use strategies and policy-making; aids in anticipating negative impacts and land use conflicts; supports agricultural decision-making
Limitations: limited predictor datasets; coarse spatial data resolution; CLC minimum mapping unit constraints; socio-economic data only at LAU2; post-2006 dynamics and political factors not considered; input data and calibration uncertainties
Future Directions: integrate additional demographic and economic predictors; include dynamic political and climatic scenarios; improve explanatory factor sets; refine scenarios for specific areas
Scalability: preliminary work suggests applicability to other regions with improved predictor integration; suitable at regional scale
Novelty: first application of CLUE-S to simulate future agricultural land use flows in Romania; adaptation of land cover flows methodology to modelled categories

Title: Population-Based Simulation of Urban Growth: The Italian Case Study
Authors: Cosentino, Claudia; Amato, Federico; Murgante, Beniamino
Objective: Analyze the importance of population dynamics in urban growth using the FUTURE Urban-Regional Environment Simulation model in Italy
LULC Classes: undeveloped; developed; forests and woodlands; water bodies; protected areas; agricultural areas
Scenarios: high population-growth scenario (of three ISTAT projections)
Analysis Methods: multilevel logistic regression; linear regression; Monte Carlo robustness tests; Patch-Growing Algorithm; global Moran’s I and Geary’s C; Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA)
Sim. Method Advantages: open-source integration with GRASSGIS; user-friendly GUI for planners; no programming required; accommodates regional heterogeneity; stochastic patch growth
Tools/Soft Used: FUTURES model in GRASSGIS; r.grow.distance; GIS spatial-analysis tools
Predictors: development pressure; slope; percentage of forests; distance from nodes; travel time
Data Sources: CORINE land cover (1990, 2000, 2012), ISTAT 2011 census and projections; Copernicus DTM, Italian National Geoportal (protected areas, road network)
Validation Methods: Monte Carlo analysis of variable selection; spatial autocorrelation (global and local Moran)
Validation Data Sources: CORINE land cover maps; spatial weight matrices derived from municipal boundaries
Key Findings: Population dynamics alone cannot explain observed urban growth patterns; Model predicts 3 316 km² new urban area by 2035, concentrated in Tuscany, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna, Veneto, Piedmont; Southern regions with population decline show negligible simulated growth; Metropolitan Rome leads municipal growth (59.17 km², 4.60% of area)
Implications: FUTURES can guide revision of master plans by aligning development zones with real housing demand; supports strategic planning and infrastructure optimization
Limitations: considers only demographic trend as main driver; excludes other socioeconomic factors; requires homogeneous data; model stochasticity; hard classification overlooks uncertainty
Future Directions: develop composite indices of social/economic drivers; incorporate ecosystem-service variables; test alternative constraint scenarios (e.g., protected areas); apply framework to master-plan updates
Scalability: Applicable to other regions (especially Mediterranean contexts) given availability of consistent data and GRASSGIS integration
Novelty: First application of FUTURES to Italy; deep integration with GRASSGIS; user-oriented GUI; focus on demographic drivers; adoption of soft-classification uncertainty layer

Title: Representing large-scale land acquisitions in land use change scenarios for the Lao PDR
Authors: Debonne, Niels; van Vliet, Jasper; Heinimann, Andreas; Verburg, Peter
Objective: The primary objective of the study is to represent the characteristics that distinguish large-scale land acquisition (LSLA) dynamics in a land change modeling framework and use this model to explore different LSLA development trajectories as they interact with smallholder land use dynamics.
LULC Classes: 15 land systems
Scenarios: High LSLA (quadruple LSLA area); Moratorium (no new LSLA); No target (no LSLA policy target)
Analysis Methods: CLUMondo land system model with a multi-cell allocation algorithm; hierarchical decision-tree classification
Sim. Method Advantages: captures multi-scalar land change processes via multi-cell allocation of contiguous patches; includes an explicit policy-driven demand for LSLA effects in addition to commodity demands; preserves detail of smallholder dynamics while simulating large-scale acquisitions
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo land system model; GIS for data aggregation and mapping; hierarchical decision-tree algorithm
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: national land cover maps; census data; Land Matrix database and national concession inventories; FAO; World Bank; literature on LSLA in Laos
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: High LSLA impedes smallholder engagement in rubber and cash crops; Moratorium scenario increases smallholder cash cropping and rubber production; swidden extent decreases under Moratorium, increases under High LSLA; commodity demands are met mainly through cropland expansion, driving forest loss; LSLA and smallholder systems are spatially segregated yet strongly linked
Implications: policy stance on LSLA critically shapes land use futures and rural livelihoods; including LSLA dynamics in land change models is essential for realistic projections; provides a framework for government decision‐making on LSLA policies
Limitations: limited empirical data on LSLA location choice and plantation delineation; potential over-/underestimation of commodity production values; regression overfitting due to autocorrelated plantation patches; exclusion of economies of scale and LSLA–smallholder synergies; legal land change may not equate to actual land cover change
Future Directions: fine-tune model parameterization with detailed LSLA delineation and empirical data; assess discrepancies between legal concessions and actual land cover change; explore indirect land use impacts and LSLA–smallholder contract farming synergies; conduct local-scale case studies to validate and refine scenario outcomes
Scalability: Scalable to other regions using the CLUMondo framework given appropriate LSLA and smallholder data
Novelty: first land change model to explicitly simulate LSLA via a multi-cell allocation algorithm; integration of a policy-driven demand driver for LSLA in addition to commodity demands; explicit modeling of interactions between LSLA and smallholder agriculture

Title: Climate-induced Land Use Change in France: Impacts of Agricultural Adaptation and Climate Change Mitigation
Authors: Lungarska, Anna; Chakir, Raja
Objective: Assess impacts of climate change adaptation and GHG mitigation policy on land use competition in France
LULC Classes: Agriculture (crops and pasture); Forest; Urban; Other
Scenarios: IPCC A2; IPCC B1; CTL (current climate)
Analysis Methods: Sector-specific bio-economic models (AROPAj, FFSM++); Spatial econometric land use share model (SDEM)
Sim. Method Advantages: Combines bio-ecological crop (STICS) and forest (GAM-based) outputs with economic optimization and spatial econometrics; Accounts for farmer adaptations; spatial autocorrelation; land-use feedbacks

Predictors: Agricultural land rent; Forestry revenues; Population density; Household revenues; Slope; Soil texture; Spatial lags of these variables

Limitations: Excludes price feedbacks; animal number variation limited; soil-carbon flux from LUC roughly estimated

Scalability: Method transferable to other regions with comparable data

Title: Dramatic cropland expansion in Myanmar following political reforms threatens biodiversity
Authors: Zhang, Yuchen; Prescott, Graham W.; Tay, Rebecca E.; Dickens, Borame L.; Webb, Edward L.; Htun, Saw; Tizard, Robert J.; Rao, Madhu; Carrasco, Luis Roman
Objective: Develop a modelling framework to (i) understand factors explaining current cropland and forest distribution in Myanmar, (ii) project spatial patterns of cropland expansion under multiple economic scenarios, and (iii) identify Key Biodiversity Areas (KBAs) most vulnerable to cropland expansion
LULC Classes: Forest; Cropland; Miscellaneous land-use types (excluded)
Scenarios: Baseline; Potential yield; Agricultural value (+50%); Transportation cost (+35%); Stability (end civil war); Combined (agricultural value + stability)
Analysis Methods: Generalized linear mixed-effects models (logit link); Extended von Thünen rent framework; Model selection via Akaike Information Criterion
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures dynamic, spatially and temporally heterogeneous threats; integrates socio-economic and conflict factors; flexible application for conservation planning
Tools/Soft Used: ArcMap 10.2; R 3.4.1 (lme4 package)
Predictors: Agricultural value; Transportation cost; Elevation; Socio-political stability; PA status
Data Sources: Primary land-use: GLC2009 (Global Land Cover 2009); Alternative land-use: IIASA-IFPRI cropland map; Crop yields: Global potential yield maps; Prices and costs: FAO Food Price Index, IEA transport cost outlook; KBAs: Wildlife Conservation Society Myanmar; Protected areas: National PA database; Elevation: Digital elevation models; Conflict proxy: Ethnic-majority state boundaries
Validation Methods: Robustness tests using alternative cropland dataset; model diagnostics (variance inflation factors; heteroscedasticity checks)
Validation Data Sources: IIASA-IFPRI cropland percentage map
Key Findings: Elevation and socio-political stability most strongly predict cropland presence, higher elevation and conflict zones inhibit expansion.; Under combined scenario, 48.5% of land projected to convert, export crops (maize, pigeon pea) drive greatest expansion.; 28 KBAs face >50% conversion risk, freshwater KBAs disproportionately vulnerable.; Protected areas significantly slow deforestation but current PA coverage insufficient to meet Aichi Target 11.
Implications: Guides spatially explicit conservation planning in transition countries; prioritizes vulnerable KBAs (especially freshwater); informs PA expansion and zoning; supports integration of socio-political factors in land-use policy
Limitations: Assumes rational farmers with perfect information; potential yields fully realized; binary conflict proxy conflates ethnicity and governance; lacks temporal land-use panel data; coarse global input layers
Future Directions: Obtain multi-temporal land-use maps for panel analysis; Refine spatial conflict intensity data; Incorporate governance and tenure complexity; Test framework in other conflict-affected countries
Scalability: Can be applied to other tropical nations with dynamic conflict and market liberalization contexts (e.g., DRC, Colombia, Rwanda)
Novelty: First integration of dynamic von Thünen rent framework with conflict and PA factors for cropland expansion modelling; Scenario ensemble across multiple crops to assess biodiversity threats in Key Biodiversity Areas

Title: Land-use change may exacerbate climate change impacts on water resources in the Ganges basin
Authors: Tsarouchi, Gina; Buytaert, Wouter
Objective: Quantify how future projections of land-use change and climate change affect the hydrological response of the Upper Ganges river basin
LULC Classes: Broadleaf trees; Needleleaf trees; C₃ grasses; C₄ grasses; Shrubs; Urban; Water; Bare soil; Ice
Scenarios: RCP4.5; RCP8.5; 15 Markov-chain land-use pathways; eight extreme 100% single-cover experiments
Analysis Methods: Delta-change climate downscaling; JULES land-surface model simulations; Markov-chain simulation of land‐use transitions; CMIP5 multi-model ensemble analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Relatively simple to apply; computationally efficient; applies uniformly to all variables (fluxes scaled by relative change, state variables by absolute change)
Tools/Soft Used: JULES v3.4; Landsat image classification (maximum likelihood); Markov-chain modelling; delta-change method
Predictors: Historical land-use transition probabilities derived from six Landsat-based maps (2000–2010)
Data Sources: CMIP5 GCM outputs; TRMMv7 precipitation; Princeton hydrology reanalysis; Landsat 7 ETM+ imagery; Sapkota et al. (2013) water‐demand data; Amarasinghe et al. (2007) water‐demand projections
Validation Methods: Generated 2010 land-use maps from pre-2010 transition matrices, compared to observed 2010 map
Validation Data Sources: Historical 2010 land-cover map from Landsat classification
Key Findings: High-flow extremes (Q₅) projected to increase by 41% (RCP4.5) and 60% (RCP8.5) under climate-only, by 42% and 63% when combined with land-use change; Low-flow extremes (Q₉₅) slightly decrease under climate-only, small increases/decreases when combined; Spatial evapotranspiration and soil-moisture changes largely cancel at catchment scale; Climate change is dominant driver, land-use change adds ~2% effect
Implications: Winter water demands may not be met; Need for adaptation strategies and regional land-use planning in northern India
Limitations: Large inter-model GCM uncertainties; Delta-change ignores variability and sequence changes; Inconsistencies among climate, land-use and water-demand projections; Irrigation practices and hydropower impacts not explicitly modelled
Future Directions: Incorporate irrigation dynamics and hydropower dam effects; Refine downscaling methods; Extend analysis beyond 2035; Reduce GCM uncertainty through bias correction
Scalability: Applicable to other large monsoon-dominated river basins
Novelty: First quantitative integration of 15 land-use pathways with CMIP5-driven JULES simulations to assess combined impacts of land-use and climate change on hydrology

Title: Potential environmental benefits from woodfuel transitions in Haiti: Geospatial scenarios to 2027
Authors: Ghilardi, Adrian; Tarter, Andrew; Bailis, Robert
Objective: Assess potential environmental benefits of woodfuel transitions in Haiti by modeling impacts of current and alternative household energy pathways on above-ground biomass and non-renewable biomass extraction.
LULC Classes: Forest; woodland; shrubland; agroforestry woodlots; trees outside forests; cropland; grassland; barren; urban
Scenarios: BAU; urb_1; urb_2; urb_3; rur_1; rur_2; rur_3; rur_4; rur_5; kiln
Analysis Methods: Dynamic spatiotemporal landscape modeling using MoFuSS; Monte Carlo simulations; geospatial accessibility mapping
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures spatial heterogeneity of supply and demand; Models both regeneration and harvest dynamics at pixel level; Integrates accessibility, land cover, and demographic drivers
Tools/Soft Used: MoFuSS v1.0 platform; GIS software for mapping; Monte Carlo simulation routines
Predictors: Population distribution; fuel type prevalence; land cover class; transport infrastructure proximity; elevation; accessibility to markets; biomass growth parameters (rₘₐₓ, K)
Data Sources: 2003 Haitian census; 2003 gridded population map; LULC map; FAO forest data; expert-identified charcoal production hotspots; transport network data; literature yield and efficiency estimates
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Under BAU, above-ground biomass may decline 4%±1% by 2027, emitting 555±54 kton CO₂ yr⁻¹; BAU yields fNRB ~12%±2%; Aggressive urban-focused interventions (urb_1–3) could reverse degradation and increase AGB; Rural-only interventions have smaller impacts; Improved kilns alone reduce demand modestly
Implications: Demand-side interventions in urban areas most effective for mitigating biomass loss; Policies must balance charcoal demand reduction with rural livelihood impacts; Improved charcoal kiln adoption provides moderate benefits
Limitations: Uncertainty in biomass growth parameters and initial stocks; Excluded cross-border charcoal trade and industrial demand; No field validation or high-resolution change detection
Future Directions: Field assessments of coppice system productivity; High-resolution land cover classification; Quantification of Haiti–DR charcoal trade; Remote sensing or field validation of modeled hotspots
Scalability: Methods and MoFuSS platform adaptable to other data-poor woodfuel-dependent regions
Novelty: Integration of accessibility-based harvest allocation with dynamic biomass growth modeling; Spatially explicit fNRB at fine resolution; Scenario-based assessment linking urban and rural energy transitions to landscape outcomes

Title: Simulated Impacts of Soy and Infrastructure Expansion in the Brazilian Amazon: A Maximum Entropy Approach
Authors: Frey, Gabriel P.; West, Thales A. P.; Hickler, Thomas; Rausch, Lisa; Gibbs, Holly K.; Boerner, Jan
Objective: Identify areas in the Brazilian Legal Amazon likely to undergo conversion to soy plantations and simulate how potential infrastructure improvements affect those probabilities.
LULC Classes: Forest; Planted Forest; Coastal Zone Forest; Unobserved; Non-Forest Vegetation; Pasture; Agriculture; Other; Water
Scenarios: 2014 (current infrastructure); Scenario 1 (unpaved → paved roads; railroads operational); Scenario 2 (Scenario 1 + planned roads finalized); Scenario 3 (Scenario 2 + new storage/crushing facilities)
Analysis Methods: Maximum Entropy modeling (MaxEnt); Jackknife sensitivity analysis; ROC/AUC; map-comparison metrics (Figure of Merit; Kappa Simulation; Fuzzy Kappa Simulation)
Sim. Method Advantages: Incorporates presence-only data under Maximum Entropy Principle; Handles continuous and categorical predictors; Establishes complex relationships via machine learning; Requires only one time-slice of occurrence data
Tools/Soft Used: MaxEnt 3.3.3; R (packages: raster, maptools, GDAL); Insensa-GIS 0.3.9; Map Comparison Kit 3.2.3
Predictors: Bioclimatic variables (bio1–bio19); Soil quality/type; elevation; slope; Distance to cities, ports, storage facilities, crushing facilities; Roads; railroads; waterways; ports; terminals; Land-use/cover maps (2008–2014); Settlements; protected areas; military areas; Municipal land price appreciation (forest, cropland, pasture)
Data Sources: MODIS and Landsat-based soy maps (Gibbs et al. 2014, Rudorff et al. 2013); WorldClim (bioclimatic); EMBRAPA (soil); SRTM (elevation); CSR-UFMG (roads, railroads, waterways, ports, storage, crushing facilities, settlements, protected areas); MapBiomas (land-use/cover 2008–2014); FNP Consultoria (land prices 2007–2012); IBGE (urban areas)
Validation Methods: Figure of Merit; Kappa Simulation (KTransition; KTransLoc); Fuzzy Kappa Simulation with moving windows (2, 4, 8, 16 pixels)
Validation Data Sources: Observed soy expansion map 2017 (MODIS imagery, unpublished by H. Gibbs); Satellite-based soy maps
Key Findings: Cross-validated test AUC = 0.757 (± 0.005), indicating good predictive power; Distance to storage facilities was most important predictor, followed by pasture land price and distance to crushing facilities; 14.7 Mha high-risk area for soy expansion in 2014 (in addition to 2.3 Mha planted); Infrastructure improvements increase high-risk area by 2.5% (Scenario 1), 13% (Scenario 2), and 14.6% (Scenario 3); High-risk forests area rises by 9.6%–51.4% across scenarios, pastures by 1.8%–11.4%; At least 4.8 Pg CO₂ could be released if high-risk forests are cleared
Implications: Infrastructure development amplifies deforestation risk; Conservation policies (e.g., Soy Moratorium, protected areas) should target identified high-risk zones; Monitoring and enforcement needed outside protected areas and settlements
Limitations: MaxEnt lacks built-in temporal quantity forecasting, linear extrapolation used for area projections; Resolution may understate slope importance; Settlements variable had low predictive power, smallholder dynamics require further study
Future Directions: Apply more sophisticated forecasting methods for area projections; Explore trade-offs between biophysical suitability and infrastructure access; Assess smallholder impacts and food security implications
Scalability: Method can be adapted to other regions with presence-only occurrence data and similar predictor layers
Novelty: First use of Maximum Entropy approach for land-use/cover change modeling of soy expansion; Integration of future infrastructure scenarios via travel-cost projections and new facility location modeling

Title: The threat of political bargaining to climate mitigation in Brazil
Authors: Rochedo, Pedro R. R.; Soares-Filho, Britaldo; Schaeffer, Roberto; Viola, Eduardo; Szklo, Alexandre; Lucena, Andre F. P.; Koberle, Alexandre; Davis, Juliana Leroy; Rajao, Raoni; Rathmann, Regis
Objective: Explore how weakening of environmental governance affects Brazil’s ability to meet Paris Agreement CO₂ targets via integrated assessment of deforestation and other sectors
LULC Classes: Annual crops (soy; sugarcane; corn; cotton; wheat; beans; rice; manioc; tobacco); perennial crops (Arabica coffee; Robusta coffee; oranges; bananas; cocoa); plantation forests; native vegetation
Scenarios: Weak environmental governance (WEG); Intermediate environmental governance (IEG); Strong environmental governance (SEG); sensitivity budgets (LB; HB)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land-use modelling (OTIMIZAGRO); Energy and land-use system optimization IAM (BLUES); Integrated assessment modelling (CD-Links ensemble)
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows coupling of spatial land-use dynamics with energy-sector optimization under CO₂ constraints; captures spillovers across regions and sectors; perfect-foresight least-cost framework
Tools/Soft Used: OTIMIZAGRO (Dinamica EGO platform); MESSAGE-based BLUES IAM; CPLEX solver
Predictors: Distance to roads; proximity to previously deforested areas; crop demand; policy indicators (protected area status; licensing requirements); agricultural profitability
Data Sources: Brazil rural environmental registry; IBGE micro-regions; CD-Links IAM outputs; national crop and land-cover statistics; model parameter databases (Supplementary Table 5)
Validation Methods: Comparison of modelled deforestation rates against observed trends; calibration of land-use transitions to historical data
Validation Data Sources: PRODES deforestation monitoring; IBGE land-cover maps
Key Findings: WEG yields 23.1 Gt CO₂ from deforestation (2010–2030), exceeding Brazil’s 24 Gt budget; SEG limits cumulative emissions to 9.6 Gt CO₂ (deforestation) and 14.4 Gt CO₂ (other sectors); IEG still fits budget but at double investment cost vs SEG; Weak governance forces reliance on immature, costly technologies and external compensation
Implications: Strengthening deforestation control is lowest-cost strategy; rollback of environmental policies jeopardizes NDC; costs fall disproportionately on energy sector or external partners
Limitations: Uncertainties in Brazilian CO₂ budget estimates; reliance on model assumptions for technology maturity; exclusion of non-CO₂ GHGs beyond cost proxy
Future Directions: Refine carbon budget allocation methods; incorporate non-CO₂ gases explicitly; assess socio-economic impacts of governance shifts; evaluate policy instruments for governance strengthening
Scalability: Applicable to other tropical deforestation contexts with adaptation of model parameters and scenarios
Novelty: Integration of spatial land-use modelling with national energy-economy IAM under governance scenarios; quantification of political bargaining impacts on mitigation pathways

Title: A Scenario-Based Simulation of Land System Changes on Dietary Changes: A Case Study in China
Authors: Huang, Jincheng; Liu, Yueyan; Zhang, Xiaoying; Wang, Yu; Wang, Yisong
Objective: To explore how dietary changes influence future land systems and their environmental impacts in China through scenario-based simulation using the CLUMondo model
LULC Classes: settlement systems; bare systems; water systems; cropland; mosaic cropland; grassland; forest; mosaic natural systems
Scenarios: trend scenario; balanced scenario
Analysis Methods: scenario-based simulation using CLUMondo model; logistic regression for suitability; land system classification; life cycle assessment
Sim. Method Advantages: Reflects land use intensity and multifunctional land; Integrates supply–demand interactions; Simulates land cover, land use, and intensity more intuitively than earlier CLUE models
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo model; logistic regression
Predictors: mean annual temperature; annual precipitation; sand content; silt content; clay content; soil erosion modulus; elevation; slope; NDVI; distance to city; distance to water; distance to road; distance to railway; population density; economic density
Data Sources: Provincial crop yield statistics (National Bureau of Statistics); FAO livestock density maps; REDCP land cover maps; FAOSTAT food supply data; UN World Population Prospects; National Land Planning Outline; LCA database; national boundary data (Surveying, Mapping & Geoinformation); regional boundary data (Fang et al.)
Validation Methods: ROC analysis of logistic regressions; Simulation of 2000–2010 land system changes; Confusion matrix and Kappa statistic
Validation Data Sources: Land system map 2000; land system map 2010; provincial statistical data
Key Findings: Dietary trends drive cropland expansion and intensification; Trend scenario increases livestock density, carbon/water/ecological footprints; Balanced scenario reduces cropland area, de-intensifies land use, lowers footprints
Implications: Promoting balanced diets can align health and environmental goals; Supports policies for returning croplands to grassland and forests; Demand-side dietary measures crucial for sustainable land management
Limitations: LCA database based on global (Euro-American) production chains, not China-specific; Assumed import/export change rates mirror aggregate demand changes
Future Directions: Develop local LCA database for China; Investigate non-linear dynamics of future food trade
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integrated land system classification combining cover, use intensity, and livestock density; Scenario-based dietary change impact modeling on land systems; Coupling land system simulation with lifecycle environmental footprints

Title: Assessing Land Use/Land Cover Dynamic and Its Impact in Benin Republic Using Land Change Model and CCI-LC Products
Authors: Guidigan, Meminvegni Landry Gildas; Sanou, Charles L.; Ragatoa, Dakega Saberma; Fafa, Cham O.; Mishra, Varun Narayan
Objective: Assess LULC dynamics and impacts in Benin Republic using ESA CCI-LC products within a GIS environment and predict future LULC scenarios for 2025 and 2037
LULC Classes: Cropland; forest land; Savannah; wetland; urban; bare land; water bodies
Scenarios: Future LULC “business-as-usual” projections for 2025 and 2037
Analysis Methods: Change detection with reclassified CCI-LC maps; Transition matrix and class statistics; Transition potential modeling using multi-layer perceptron artificial neural network (MLP-ANN); Simulation via MOLUSCE plugin in QGIS
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: QGIS (MOLUSCE plugin); ArcMap
Predictors: Distance to major roads
Data Sources: ESA CCI-LC maps (2001–2013); SRTM DEM; UN population reports; INSAE-Benin demographic data; USGS EROS LULC change reports
Validation Methods: Kappa index statistics (overall kappa “Kovr”; kappa histogram “Khisto”; kappa location “Kloc”)
Validation Data Sources: Observed ESA CCI-LC map of 2013
Key Findings: Cropland increased by 1,970 km² (1.8%) and became dominant by 2013; Savannah declined by 3,272 km² (2.9%) over 2001–2013; Forest land gained 1,093.5 km² (1.0%); urban areas gained 223.3 km² (0.2%); Validation kappa ≈ 0.90447, indicating high predictive accuracy; Projection to 2025 shows slight cropland decline (–96 km²) and Savannah gain (+107 km²); to 2037 shows further cropland decline (–287 km²) and Savannah gain (+320 km²)
Implications: Results signal continued loss of natural vegetation, potential biodiversity decline, altered carbon sinks, and increased runoff intensity—highlighting need for sustainable land-use planning
Limitations: Low spatial resolution (300 m) of CCI-LC data; model accuracy limited by input data quality and omission of additional physical and socio-economic variables
Future Directions: Incorporate higher-resolution imagery and additional predictors (e.g., economic drivers, demographic projections, slope, soil) to improve simulation accuracy
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First application of ESA CCI-LC products combined with QGIS-MOLUSCE MLP-ANN modeling to assess and predict LULC change dynamics in Benin Republic

Title: Deforestation and secondary growth in Costa Rica along the path of development
Authors: Stan, Kayla; Sanchez-Azofeifa, Arturo
Objective: Study the areal extent and spatial pattern of Costa Rican forests between 1960 and 2013; project future changes to 2069
LULC Classes: Forest; Non-forest
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU); Deforestation increase 1% (DF1); DF2; DF5; Regrowth increase 1% (RF1); RF2; RF5
Analysis Methods: Cellular automata modeling via Dinamica EGO; Bayesian weight-of-evidence; landscape metrics (patch size, distances); t-tests
Sim. Method Advantages: Applicable to time-series LCC modeling; replicates quantity and spatial patterns; integrates biophysical, socioeconomic, and legislative drivers; high adaptability and inter-scale communication
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica Environment for Geoprocessing Objects (Dinamica EGO); GIS preprocessing; Landsat and SPOT image classification
Predictors: Geology; Topography; Slopes; Rivers and water routes; Biological corridors; Geomorphology; Watershed delineation; Fire risk; Population change; Distance to roads; Land usability; Protected areas; Indigenous zones; Biological reserves
Data Sources: Historical forest maps (1960 aerial photographs; Landsat 1979–2013; SPOT 2010); Biophysical shapefiles and rasters from SINAC, CCT/MAG, GEOTECNOLOGIAS, Atlas Digital; Census district-level data; Legal boundaries of protected areas
Validation Methods: Spatial agreement with observed maps using moving window (1–13 pixels); accuracy assessment within 600 m/2.5 pixels; t-tests on patch metrics
Validation Data Sources: Independent field control points (1500); classified Landsat maps for 1997, 2005, and 2013
Key Findings: High deforestation from 1960–1986 followed by net regrowth up to 2013; mean forest patch size declined ~98.8%; BAU projections recover 1960 forest extent by 2040; extreme scenarios alter stabilization extents; Puntarenas and Guanacaste most at risk; only 13 protected areas show >40% deforestation probability without protection
Implications: Continued forest regeneration possible; need targeted monitoring in hotspot provinces; improved protected area selection and community management; optimized forest inventory and funding for payments for ecosystem services
Limitations: Binary forest/non-forest classification limits land-use differentiation; national model hindered by intraprovincial variability; climate change not considered; data quality variability
Future Directions: Develop detailed land-use classifications (e.g., pasture vs cropland); integrate explicit plantation extraction databases; incorporate climate change; hotspot-based mapping and monitoring; leverage WAVES 2017 land cover maps
Scalability: Method applicable to other tropical regions with provincial calibration; requires intraregional driver consideration
Novelty: Long-term historical analysis (1960–2013) integrated with socioeconomic and legislative variables; first projections to 2069 using Dinamica EGO; combined patch metric analysis and protected area severity index

Title: Development of land-use scenarios using vegetation inventories in Japan
Authors: Shoyama, Kikuko; Matsui, Takanori; Hashimoto, Shizuka; Kabaya, Kei; Oono, Akiko; Saito, Osamu
Objective: Develop land-use scenarios using detailed LULC maps derived from national vegetation inventories to enable assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services at the national scale
LULC Classes: Residential area; Paddy field; Cropland; Other agricultural land; Bush, grassland, and other vegetation; Natural forest; Secondary forest; Plantation forest; Others
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BaU); Natural capital-based compact society (NC); Natural capital-based dispersed society (ND); Produced capital-based compact society (PC); Produced capital-based dispersed society (PD)
Analysis Methods: Change analysis; Transition potential modeling via multi-layer perceptron neural network; Markov chain change prediction; Empirical likelihood mapping; Linear programming for demand matrix adjustment; Cramer’s V; ROC/AUC validation
Sim. Method Advantages: MLPNN robustly models nonlinear relationships among drivers; Cellular automata–based approach provides spatially explicit land-change projections
Tools/Soft Used: IDRISI Land Change Modeler
Predictors: Elevation; Slope; Annual temperature; Precipitation; Distance to stream; Distance to main paved road; Population density; Empirical likelihood of change
Data Sources: National Land Numerical Information (NLNI) LULC and population data; National vegetation surveys (Ministry of the Environment) for 1978–2014; Satellite imagery (Landsat, AVNIR-2); National population census and 2050 projections (National Institute of Population and Social Security Research); Government policy reports (National Spatial Strategy; National Forestry Plan); Housing and Land Survey; Census of Agriculture and Forestry
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated 2014 LULC with observed 2014 map; calculation of hits, misses, false alarms, null successes; figure of merit; ROC curve and AUC
Validation Data Sources: LULC map 2014 derived from national vegetation surveys (time-3 dataset)
Key Findings: BaU: Agricultural land decreases by ~2%, bush/grassland increases, plantation forest expands, residential area maintained; NC/ND: Minimal overall change; paddy fields and forests largely maintained, slight cropland increase; PC/PD: Substantial land change; plantation forest and paddy fields decline, secondary forest and bush/grassland expand; Spatial hotspots: Paddy loss in Hokuriku and Kyushu; plantation-to-secondary shifts in Chubu–Kyushu; Model validation shows low FOM (1.56%) but high AUC (0.97)
Implications: Scenario-based LULC maps inform spatially explicit assessments of ecosystem service impacts; Intervention to maintain rural livelihoods can curb land abandonment; Policy design should consider regional hotspots of land change
Limitations: Coarse 1 km resolution limits detection of fine-scale abandoned farmland; LULC inputs only cover 1987–1998; lacks post-2010 change trends; Stationary driver assumption; climate change not incorporated
Future Directions: Local-scale validation and refinement of models; Integration of process-based approaches and climate change drivers; Development of higher-resolution and more timely LULC datasets via multi-source observation systems
Scalability: Approach applicable to other countries with complex land-use systems and socio-ecological landscapes
Novelty: Use of detailed national vegetation-inventory–derived; LULC dataset aggregated into nine classes; Integration of MLPNN-based transition potential modeling with empirical likelihood and linear programming for demand-driven scenario adjustment; Generation of five national-scale land-use scenarios linked to demographic and policy narratives

Title: Exploring the impacts of biofuel expansion on land use change and food security based on a land explicit CGE model: A case study of China
Authors: Weng, Yuwei; Chang, Shiyan; Cai, Wenjia; Wang, Can
Objective: Explore impacts of biofuel expansion on land use change and food security based on a land-explicit computable general equilibrium model; quantify direct and indirect LUC and food security impacts under China’s E10 ethanol mandate
LULC Classes: rice; wheat; corn; other grains; non-grain feedstocks (sweet sorghum, cassava); other cropland; forest; grassland; marginal land (levels I and II)
Scenarios: Baseline (S1); Non-deforestation (S2); Marginal land (S3); Enhanced target scenarios (150% ET, 200% ET, 250% ET, 300% ET)
Analysis Methods: Computable general equilibrium model with explicit land allocation module; comparative static scenario analysis; sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: integrates heterogeneous land use types with market mechanisms; captures both direct and indirect LUC via economic interactions; simulates land conversion among alternative uses endogenously; provides national/regional specificity beyond global models
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: land profit (rent); transformation elasticities; land productivity; marginal land availability; share parameters; exogenous bioethanol demand
Data Sources: 2012 Input-Output table (NBS China); NDRC Costs & Benefits Compilation; USDA FAS China biofuels reports; FAO database; China Statistical Yearbook; Ministry of Agriculture marginal land survey
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: in S1, land for wheat +0.119%, corn +0.213%, non-grain feedstocks +0.182%; rice −0.015%, forest −0.023%, grassland −0.023%; in S2, cropland competition intensifies; rice −0.016%, other grains −0.398%, other crops −0.043%; in S3, marginal land use eases competition; rice −0.009%; saves 0.217% cropland vs S1; non-grain feedstocks share rises to 26.97%
Implications: planting energy crops on marginal land can diversify feedstocks, reduce cropland loss, protect forests and food security; policy should encourage non-grain feedstocks on marginal land and avoid deforestation while setting bioethanol mandates
Limitations: static, closed-economy CGE lacks temporal dynamics and spatial detail; relies on parameter values (elasticities) with uncertainty; highly aggregated production functions omit conversion technology details
Future Directions: develop dynamic, multi-region CGE with higher spatial resolution; integrate spatially explicit biophysical models; incorporate detailed bioenergy conversion technologies; assess economic costs and ecological impacts of marginal land reclamation
Scalability: Methodology (land-explicit CGE + scenario approach) is transferable to other national/regional cases
Novelty: first national CGE augmented with explicit land allocation nest including marginal land; combined DLUC and ILUC quantification under varied land-conversion scenarios; scenario design comparing existing cropland, protected forests/grasslands, and reclaimed marginal land

Title: Future governance options for large-scale land acquisition in Cambodia: Impacts on tree cover and tiger landscapes
Authors: Debonne, Niels; van Vliet, Jasper; Verburg, Peter
Objective: To assess how different large-scale land acquisition (LSLA) governance options in Cambodia affect future tree cover, natural area integrity, and the potential for successful tiger reintroduction by 2040
LULC Classes: Water, Floodplain/Mangrove, Urban, Converted annual crops LSLA, Converted forestry LSLA, Converted perennial crops LSLA, Forested unconverted LSLA, Other unconverted LSLA, Evergreen forest, Deciduous forest, Cropland, Cropland; Evergreen forest mosaic, Cropland; Deciduous forest mosaic
Scenarios: Hands-off (noninterventionist); Penalization (interventionist); Proactive Granting (preventive)
Analysis Methods: Mapping of LSLAs and land systems using remote sensing (Google Earth, Landsat) and decision‐tree classification; CLUMondo land system change model simulations; Logistic regression of suitability using socio-economic and biophysical predictors; Overlay analysis of tree cover; Core area delineation (5 km buffer from disturbances)
Sim. Method Advantages: Explicitly models land cover, land use, and management regimes (LSLAs vs. smallholders); Integrates multiple commodity and service demands in a spatially explicit, forward-looking framework; Allows comparison of alternative policy scenarios to 2040
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo model; GIS and remote sensing platforms (Google Earth; Landsat); logistic regression tools
Predictors: Eighteen socio-economic and biophysical factors used in logistic regressions (not detailed in main text)
Data Sources: 2015 land cover map (Miettinen et al., 2016); Forest classification and tree cover map (Open Development Cambodia, 2016a); LSLA spatial database (Open Development Cambodia, 2016b); High-resolution Google Earth imagery; Landsat time series; Protected area delineations (Open Development Cambodia, 2018; World Bank, 2018); Supplementary literature for demand quantification and tiger ecology (Wikramanayake et al., 2011; Gray et al., 2017)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: In 2015, 68% of LSLA areas were underused (only 32% converted); Hands-off: LSLA area rises to 3.03 Mha with 43% remaining unconverted; tiger habitat in Eastern Plains lost; potential for only 310 tigers by 2040; Penalization: LSLA declines to 1.80 Mha with 6% unconverted; highest total tree cover (7.6 Mha) but strong fragmentation; supports 586 tigers; Proactive Granting: LSLA increases to 2.30 Mha with 7% unconverted; protects all mapped protected areas; preserves core natural areas; supports 920 tigers
Implications: LSLA governance critically affects tree cover, habitat integrity, and tiger reintroduction success; Preventive policies combined with effective protected-area enforcement best reconcile LSLA with conservation goals; Cambodia may need to shift reintroduction focus to more stable areas (Cardamom, Virachey) or boost protection capacity
Limitations: Socio-economic and livelihood impacts not quantified; Assumes constant tree cover within land systems; excludes plantations outside official LSLAs; Leakage effects of commodity demand uncertain; assumes perfect enforcement of protected areas; Does not model poaching, prey densities, or finer ecological processes
Future Directions: Apply landscape genetics and population viability analyses for finer tiger reintroduction assessment; Quantify livelihood impacts and distributive outcomes of LSLA policies; Explore full cancellation and redistribution of converted LSLAs
Scalability: Potentially scalable to other LSLA-affected countries (e.g., demonstrated for Laos in related work)
Novelty: First rigorous national-scale mapping of LSLA productive use in Cambodia; Integration of LSLA governance scenarios with land system change modeling and tiger reintroduction potential; Explicit differentiation of converted vs. underutilized concessions in scenario analysis

Title: Future land use/cover changes in Romania: regional simulations based on CLUE-S model and CORINE land cover database
Authors: Kucsicsa, Gheorghe; Popovici, Elena-Ana; Balteanu, Dan; Grigorescu, Ines; Dumitrascu, Monica; Mitrica, Bianca
Objective: To assess past land use/cover dynamics during 1990-2006 and simulate future changes (2007-2050) to identify main land use/cover change processes and their potential environmental and land management implications
LULC Classes: Built-up areas; arable lands; permanent crops; pastures; scrub and/or herbaceous vegetation association; forests; open spaces with little or no vegetation; heterogeneous agricultural areas; natural grasslands; agricultural complex cultivation patterns
Scenarios: Two scenarios: S1 based on annual rates of change between 1990-2000; S2 based on historical land use/cover dynamics in interval 2000-2006
Analysis Methods: CLUE-S model; logistic regression using stepwise method; statistical and spatial validation using ROC method and cross-classification maps; GIS and statistical analyses
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUE-S is a process-based modeling framework that allows development of spatially explicit future land use/cover datasets based on multiple scenarios; combines statistical analyses and decision rules; has been widely used and validated across different regions
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE (version 2.0) modeling framework; GIS software
Predictors: Elevation; slope declivity; precipitation; temperature; horizontal relief fragmentation; total organic matter content in topsoil; population density; population growth; employees; unemployment rate; large livestock units; employment in tertiary sector; built-up/nonagricultural ratio; settlement density; distance to nearest main town; distance to settlement; secondary road density; distance to nearest main road
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover (CLC) database (1990, 2000, 2006, 2012); Digital elevation model; National Meteorological Administration; EU-hydro river network; Romania soil quality data; Population census (1992, 2006); National Institute of Statistics; ESRI Romania
Validation Methods: ROC (receiver operating characteristic) method; cross-classification maps; confusion matrix; overall accuracy; producer's accuracy; user's accuracy; kappa index
Validation Data Sources: CLC 2012 dataset used as reference to evaluate spatial accuracy
Key Findings: Changes will affect 7.0% of total study area under S1 and 15.2% under S2; increases expected in built-up areas (5.3%), arable lands (0.6%), open spaces with little or no vegetation (48.7%), and agricultural complex cultivation patterns (1.2%); decreases expected in permanent crops (15.2%), scrub and/or herbaceous vegetation association (18.3%), forest cover (0.2%), heterogeneous agricultural areas (6.2%), and natural grasslands (1.1%)
Implications: Potential environmental and economic implications due to expansion of unused lands; transition of agricultural land types from higher-intensity to lower-intensity use; tendency for abandonment of agricultural lands; intensification of deforestation process; impacts on landscape fragmentation, biodiversity, and ecosystem services
Limitations: Unavailability of some relevant factors like land tenure or economic activities; scenarios do not consider demographic tendencies, economic development, and climate change indicators; limitations related to spatial accuracy and resolution of CLC database; coarse resolution of some spatial data; extrapolation of short historical trends to longer simulation period
Future Directions: Examination of consequences of land use/cover changes on landscape diversity and biodiversity; interaction between land use/cover changes and natural hazards; implications for ecosystem services; assessment of landslide hazard scenarios; implementation of improved scenarios with updated driving factors
Scalability: The approach can be applied to other regions with similar data availability and biophysical conditions; methodology is transferable but requires region-specific calibration and validation
Novelty: Regional application of CLUE-S model for Romania; integration of biophysical and socioeconomic explanatory variables; comprehensive analysis of six main land use/cover change flows; application for disaster risk assessment within RO-RISK project

Title: High-resolution national land use scenarios under a shrinking population in Japan
Authors: Ohashi, Haruka; Fukasawa, Keita; Ariga, Toshinori; Matsui, Tetsuya; Hijioka, Yasuaki
Objective: Develop high‐resolution national land use scenarios under a shrinking population in Japan by applying a population‐projection‐assimilated predictive land use modeling (PPAP-LM) approach and evaluate the effects of spatial population distribution on future land use structure
LULC Classes: paddy field; forest and wasteland; built-up area; other agricultural land; other artificial land
Scenarios: centralization; decentralization
Analysis Methods: population‐projection‐assimilated predictive land use modeling (PPAP-LM); Classification and Regression Trees (CART)
Sim. Method Advantages: accommodates complex spatially heterogeneous relationships; high predictive ability; interpretable hierarchical rules; robust to multicollinearity and non-normal variable distributions; identifies processes beyond simple mechanism models
Tools/Soft Used: QGIS v2.10.1-Pisa
Predictors: Pop1 (population within focal TMU); Pop1_p (previous step); Pop5; Pop5_p; Pop10; Pop10_p; Elv (elevation); Slp (slope); Rlf (relative relief); Gm (geomorphologic class); Lon (longitude); Lat (latitude); pEx (legacy of artificial land)
Data Sources: Land Utilization Tertiary Mesh Data (National Land Numerical Information); grid-based national population census (Statistics Bureau & National Land Information Division); Japan Engineering Geomorphologic Classification Map; municipal-level population projections (National Institute of Population and Social Security Research)
Validation Methods: 10-fold cross-validation; withheld 10% test dataset; error-propagation simulation; accuracy metrics (Pearson’s r; MAE; MSE; RMSE)
Validation Data Sources: Longitudinal land use maps and population census data (1985–2010)
Key Findings: population centralization promotes built-up compaction and forest/wasteland expansion; population decentralization maintains mixed forest-agricultural landscapes; paddy and other agricultural land decline more under centralization; built-up area decreases more under centralization; other artificial land increases more under centralization
Implications: spatial distribution of population strongly influences land use and related ecosystem services; centralization may enhance carbon storage via forest expansion; decentralization may preserve cultural agricultural landscapes; findings inform balanced rural and urban development strategies
Limitations: excludes future economic and climatic change drivers; focused solely on Japan; sequential predictions may propagate error
Future Directions: integrate economic and climate change scenarios; assess biodiversity and ecosystem service impacts; apply PPAP-LM to other regions
Scalability: Applicable at national scale; framework transferable to other countries with shrinking populations
Novelty: First national‐scale land use scenarios under depopulation incorporating spatially explicit population projections via the PPAP-LM framework

Title: Identifying hotspots of land use cover change under socioeconomic and climate change scenarios in Mexico
Authors: Mendoza-Ponce, Alma; Corona-Nunez, Rogelio O.; Galicia, Leopoldo; Kraxner, Florian
Objective: Contextualize the drivers of land use cover change and determine hotspots of LUCC under socioeconomic and climate change scenarios for Mexico
LULC Classes: Temperate forest; scrubland; hydrophilic vegetation; agriculture; tropical evergreen forest; tropical dry forest; other vegetation; natural grasslands; other covers (urban, barren)
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU, SRES B2); Pessimistic (high population growth, low economic growth, SRES A2)
Analysis Methods: Weights of Evidence; transition probability matrices; Markov chain modelling; categorization of predictor variables; Reciprocal similarity (jFuzzy); figure of merit; allocation and quantity disagreement metrics
Sim. Method Advantages: Unifies socioeconomic and climate storylines via SRES scenarios for consistency; Weights of Evidence coupled with Markov chain yields spatially explicit transition probabilities and quantifies individual driver influence; Better predictive performance with fewer input variables than large non-processed climate datasets
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Distance to human settlements; distance to roads; distance to protected areas; marginalization index; GDP; population density; altitude; slope; aridity index; potential evapotranspiration; temperature seasonality
Data Sources: National land cover maps (vector, 1993/2002/2007); Climate data from four GCMs (HadCM3, CGCM2, MK2, Nies 99, bioclimate variables from Metzger et al. 2013); Socioeconomic datasets (marginalization index, GDP, population density); Protected areas layers
Validation Methods: Reciprocal similarity (modified fuzzy Kappa); figure of merit; allocation and quantity disagreement analysis
Validation Data Sources: Observed 2007 land cover map
Key Findings: Agricultural expansion drove 49–65% of ecosystem conversions (1993–2007) at 16 000–28 000 km²·yr⁻¹; By 2050 grassland and tropical evergreen forest lose 20–33% (BAU) or 43–46% (pessimistic) of 1993 extent; Agriculture increases from 24.4% (1993) to 30% (BAU) or 34% (pessimistic) by 2050; Distance to roads and settlements strongest predictors; socioeconomic forces outweigh climate change in hotspot location
Implications: Inform spatial prioritization for conservation and protected area expansion; Guide policies to reduce deforestation by integrating urbanization, industrialization, and food-consumption feedbacks; Highlight need for sustainable agricultural intensification and water-management strategies
Limitations: Use of older SRES scenarios rather than newer SSP–RCP combinations; Uncertainty in GCM projections for some regions (Yucatán, Pacific Coast); Under-representation of some ecosystems (dry forest, scrubland) in protected areas; Lack of explicit future population distribution maps
Future Directions: Regional/local studies incorporating migration, land abandonment, and ecosystem regeneration; Analyze yield-climate-LUCC relationships for semiarid and temperate ecosystems; Evaluate socioeconomic driver causality (e.g., roads vs. agricultural expansion); Integrate updated SSP–RCP scenarios
Scalability: Method transferable to subnational, regional, and other tropical country contexts with spatially explicit LUCC modelling
Novelty: First national-scale integration in Mexico of socioeconomic and climate drivers using Weights of Evidence–Markov approach across multiple GCMs to identify LUCC hotspots under consistent SRES storylines

Title: Investigation of Future Land Use Change and Implications for Cropland Quality: The Case of China
Authors: Wang, Meng; Sun, Xiaofang; Fan, Zemeng; Yue, Tianxiang
Objective: assess the implication of land use change on cropland quality and crop production of China between 2015 and 2030
LULC Classes: built-up land; cropland; grassland; forest; water area; unused land
Scenarios: trend scenario; planned scenario; cropland protection scenario
Analysis Methods: Dyna-CLUE model; Markov model; Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZ) model; spatial logistic regression; overlay analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: spatially explicit scenario parameterization; accounts for driving forces, spatial policies and restrictions, and land suitability; simulates spatial distribution better than statistical models; more detailed than CA and ABM
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE model; lulcc R package
Predictors: elevation; slope; aspect; soil depth; soil texture (silt, clay, sand); soil pH; soil drainage; soil organic carbon; annual average temperature; annual radiation; total precipitation; population density; distance to main roads; GDP
Data Sources: land use data (2000, 2015) from Resource and Environment Data Cloud Platform, Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research, CAS; DEM; climate data from National Meteorological Information Center of China; soil data from National Earth System Science Data Sharing Infrastructure of China; railway and road maps and socio-economic data from national websites; natural reserve map from previous studies; potential yield data from GAEZ model
Validation Methods: Figure of Merit (FOM) components via lulcc package; ROC analysis
Validation Data Sources: land use maps of 2000 and 2015
Key Findings: Trend scenario decreases high- and medium-yield cropland, increases low-yield cropland, crop yield decreases; Planned scenario decreases high- and medium-yield cropland, increases low-yield cropland, crop yield stable; Cropland protection scenario slight reduction in high-yield cropland, increases in medium- and low-yield cropland, crop yield increases; Built-up land tends to occupy high-quality cropland
Implications: land use policies must consider both quantity and quality of cropland; Farmland Requisition-Compensation Balance policy should require quality balance; medium- and low-yield cropland upgrades critical; implement payment systems for high-yield cropland protection; scenario-based decision-making
Limitations: only two time periods for trend scenario; mixed-pixel errors at 1 km resolution; driving factor fluctuations not considered; potential omission of relevant driving factors
Future Directions: apply finer spatial-temporal resolution land use data; integrate Dyna-CLUE with production efficiency model (GLOPEM-CEVSA) and machine learning to assess yield gaps
Scalability: method easily applied to other regions with specific development scenarios
Novelty: integration of Dyna-CLUE with Markov and GAEZ for national-scale spatially explicit cropland quality simulation; scenario-based assessment of future cropland quality and crop production

Title: Large changes in Great Britain's vegetation and agricultural land-use predicted under unmitigated climate change
Authors: Ritchie, Paul D. L.; Harper, Anna B.; Smith, Greg S.; Kahana, Ron; Kendon, Elizabeth J.; Lewis, Huw; Fezzi, Carlo; Halleck-Vega, Solmaria; Boulton, Chris A.; Bateman, Ian J.; Lenton, Timothy M.
Objective: Combine state-of-the-art, high-resolution climate scenarios with a process-based land surface model (JULES) and an empirically-derived agricultural land-use model (ECO-AG) to evaluate future vegetation productivity, agricultural land-use, and irrigation demands in Great Britain under unmitigated climate change (RCP8.5)
LULC Classes: Arable farming; grassland (livestock); broadleaf trees; needleleaf trees; temperate (C₃) grasses; tropical (C₄) grasses; shrubs; urban; lakes; bare soil; land-ice
Target Years: End of century (2100; 11-year future RCM period)
Scenarios: Baseline (ECO-AG, present climate, no CO₂, no irrigation); Baseline (JULES, present climate, present CO₂, no irrigation); Climate only (ECO-AG, future climate, no CO₂, no irrigation); Climate only (JULES, future climate, present CO₂, no irrigation); Irrigation only (JULES, present climate, present CO₂, irrigation); Climate & Irrigation (ECO-AG, future climate, no CO₂, irrigation); Climate & CO₂ (JULES, future climate, future CO₂, no irrigation); Climate & CO₂ & Irrigation (JULES, future climate, future CO₂, irrigation)
Analysis Methods: Land surface modelling with JULES v4.9; Spatially-explicit econometric binomial logit model (ECO-AG); High-resolution (1.5 km) RCM climate projections; Net primary productivity simulation; Bias correction of RCM data
Sim. Method Advantages: Unprecedented 1.5 km spatial resolution enabling fine-scale land-use change assessment; Explicit resolution of convective storms in RCM; Combination of process-based and empirical models for cross-validation; High-resolution, spatially-explicit econometric land-use predictions
Tools/Soft Used: JULES v4.9; ECO-AG econometric model; AppEEARS; Regional Climate Models; Monsoon2 HPC system
Predictors: 30-year growing-season (April–September) averages of temperature; 30-year growing-season rainfall; soil type; terrain; policy variables; output and input prices; yearly fixed effects
Data Sources: Regional Climate Model outputs (Kendon et al. 2012, 2014, Chan et al. 2018); Harmonized World Soil Database; June Agricultural Census data (1972–2010); MODIS NPP (Zhao & Running 2010, AppEEARS 2019); CRU TS4.02 precipitation/temperature; ESA Climate Change Initiative land cover; JULES parameter repository (u-ao645, branch ‘full_UK’); Met Office MASSdataarchive
Validation Methods: Comparison of JULES NPP with MODIS remote-sensing NPP; Agreement of ECO-AG-predicted arable shares with agricultural census observations; Reference to prior JULES carbon-cycle evaluations
Validation Data Sources: MODIS NPP (2000–2008); June Agricultural Census (observed land-use); ESA CCI land cover; observational climate data (1960–1989)
Key Findings: Unmitigated climate change alone reduces grassland and arable productivity; CO₂ fertilisation largely counteracts productivity declines; Westward expansion of arable farming; Reversion from arable to grassland in south-east GB under drying; Irrigation could sustain arable use but demands ∼200 mm per season; CO₂ fertilisation effect remains a crucial uncertainty
Implications: Large-scale seasonal and geographic water redistribution may be required; Irrigation adaptation has potential but could strain water resources; Policy and water-management interventions needed; Uncertainty in CO₂ fertilisation must be constrained for reliable projections
Limitations: JULES likely overestimates CO₂ fertilisation; ECO-AG applied outside its historical climate estimation range; ECO-AG omits CO₂ effects and uses fixed 2010 prices; Nitrogen limitation and growing-season length changes not modelled; Extreme events impacts not included
Future Directions: Assess feasibility of large-scale water redistribution; Develop econometric models including CO₂ effects and extreme events; Constrain CO₂ fertilisation responses; Incorporate growing-season shifts and nitrogen dynamics
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First high-resolution (1.5 km) multi-model analysis of GB vegetation and land-use under RCP8.5 to 2100; Integration of process-based and empirical models at fine spatial scale; Explicit evaluation of irrigation demands under unmitigated climate change

Title: Projecting Australia's forest cover dynamics and exploring influential factors using deep learning
Authors: Ye, Long; Gao, Lei; Marcos-Martinez, Raymundo; Mallants, Dirk; Bryan, Brett A.
Objective: Project continental-scale, time-continuous forest cover dynamics in Australia’s intensive agricultural region and quantify influential factors using Long Short-Term Memory deep learning networks
LULC Classes: forest; non-forest
Scenarios: Not specified
Analysis Methods: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) deep learning neural networks; spatial-econometric modelling (for comparison)
Sim. Method Advantages: 44% RMSE improvement; 12% pseudo R² improvement; captures long-term, continuous dynamics; handles complex spatiotemporal relationships; spatially explicit ensemble “plug-and-play” per grid-cell
Tools/Soft Used: High-performance computing cluster; deep learning frameworks (not specified)
Predictors: forest cover index; neighborhood forest indices (fidx3NN; fidx10NN); agricultural output price (priceRec); timber price index (timberPI); maximum temperature; rainfall; rolling statistics of temperature and rainfall (temp5MA; temp5SD; rain5MA; rain5SD); distance to protected areas (dist2prote); State-jurisdiction variables
Data Sources: Australian National Carbon Accounting System; Land Cover Change Program (NCAS-LCCP), National Forest Inventory, climatic data, socioeconomic data (Australian Bureau of Statistics), physiographic data, State-jurisdiction datasets
Validation Methods: Comparison of projected vs observed forest cover using RMSE and pseudo R-squared metrics
Validation Data Sources: NCAS-LCCP forest cover data for 2011–2014
Key Findings: Deep learning LSTM outperformed spatial-econometric model by 44% (RMSE) and 12% (pseudo R²); Neighborhood effects and agricultural output prices were most influential predictors; Model remained robust under exclusion of variables (average RMSE 0.0687–0.0785, pseudo R² 0.9399–0.9537); Errors >±30% limited to 2.1% of grid-cells in deforestation hotspots
Implications: Supports site-specific land management and conservation planning; Enables identification of forest cover hot-spots for targeted intervention; Informs design of policy and resource allocation based on influential drivers
Limitations: Exclusion of non-temporal spatial variables; limited performance in grid-cells with sudden changes; underperformance in non-agricultural/coastal regions; lack of uncertainty quantification
Future Directions: Incorporate non-temporal spatial variables; include regulation and spatial-temporal drivers for sudden change areas; extend model to coastal and other regions; develop Bayesian deep learning framework for uncertainty estimation
Scalability: Ensemble LSTM approach is scalable to other regions via plug-and-play grid-cell sub-models but requires region-specific variables and high-performance computing resources
Novelty: First application of LSTM deep learning networks for continental-scale, time-continuous forest cover projection; bottom-up ensemble of ~1.38 million grid-cell sub-models; variable influence quantified via exclusion experiments

Title: Projecting the Spatial Distribution of Possible Planted Forest Expansion in the United States
Authors: Wade, Christopher M.; Baker, Justin S.; Latta, Gregory; Ohrel, Sara B.; Allpress, Justine
Objective: Estimate a spatially explicit logistic regression function to assess the likelihood that forest plots in the United States will be planted based on physical, climate, and economic factors, and project the potential spatial distribution of planted forests at both intensive and extensive land-use margins across illustrative future scenarios
LULC Classes: Planted forest; Naturally regenerated forest; Other land-use types
Scenarios: BAU Predicted; Low expansion (16 million acres); Medium expansion (32 million acres); High expansion (64 million acres)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit logistic regression; Spatial econometric modeling; Probability-based scenario simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures spatial heterogeneity at the forest-plot level; Provides plot-specific probabilities for planting decisions; Offers more spatial detail than regionally aggregated structural models
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Physical factors (e.g., slope); Climatic factors; Economic factors (e.g., expected rents, product markets); Spatial attributes (location); Stand age; Species group (softwood vs. hardwood); Ownership category
Data Sources: Primary: U.S. Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) data; Secondary: Climate data, Economic/market data, Topographic data (slope)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Historical drivers of planting include higher productivity sites, gentler slopes, and favorable economic conditions; In low and medium expansion scenarios, most new planting occurs in the Southeast, on naturally regenerated stands; Under high-expansion, Oregon (3.9 M acres) and Washington (2.8 M acres) contribute substantially; Other states (California, Maine, Arizona) show large extensive-margin potential under strong incentives
Implications: Enables policymakers to identify spatial “hotspots” for incentivizing or limiting planting; Informs conservation planning and carbon-sequestration program targeting; Improves parameterization of economic and land-use models
Limitations: Slope treated categorically, potentially masking within-plot variability; Data limitations in plot-level attributes and policy contexts; Spatial bias toward regions with existing plantation concentration
Future Directions: Adapt framework for region-specific analyses; Integrate results into spatially explicit economic optimization models; Incorporate projected climate change impacts on planting suitability
Scalability: Yes; framework can be readily applied to other regions or subnational analyses
Novelty: First application of spatially explicit logistic regression to project both intensive and extensive margin forest planting in the U.S.; Combines plot-level probability modeling with scenario-based spatial projections to inform policy and management decisions

Title: Simulation of Spatiotemporal Land Use Changes for Integrated Model of Socioeconomic and Ecological Processes in China
Authors: Jiang, Honglei; Xu, Xia; Guan, Mengxi; Wang, Lingfei; Huang, Yongmei; Liu, Yinghui
Objective: to develop an integrated model coupling land use allocation, socioeconomic influences, and dynamic ecological processes to simulate future land use patterns under two grain-yield scenarios in China
LULC Classes: Cropland (CROP); Grassland (GRAS); Forest (FORE); Built-up land (BUIL); Other land (OTHE)
Scenarios: Scenario A: grain yield continues to rise at current rate; Scenario B: grain yield remains constant after reaching current level
Analysis Methods: Global Food System model (GLOBFOOD); Terrestrial Ecosystem Simulator (TESim); CLUE spatial allocation model; logistic regression; fuzzy expert membership functions; Markov chain transition analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Integration of socioeconomic demand, dynamic ecological suitability (SOM and SON) and spatially explicit allocation; addresses both “quantity” and “position” problems; uses dynamic ecosystem outputs instead of static soil databases
Tools/Soft Used: GLOBFOOD model; TESim; CLUE model; ArcGIS 10.2
Predictors: population density; elevation; slope; mean annual temperature; mean annual precipitation; cumulative growing-season temperature; growing-season precipitation; soil organic matter (SOM); soil organic nitrogen (SON)
Data Sources: land-use maps (Chinese Academy of Resources and Environment Science Data Center); DEM (State Bureau of Surveying and Mapping); meteorological records (China National Weather Service); socioeconomic data (National Statistics Department; FAO)
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated vs monitored land use areas for 2010; spatial pattern verification based on previous studies by Xu et al.
Validation Data Sources: land-use map for 2010 (Chinese Academy of Resources and Environment Science Data Center)
Key Findings: In Scenario A, cropland area declines by ~27.4% (2020–2080) while forest, grassland, and built-up areas increase; In Scenario B, cropland expands by ~29.4% with losses in forest, grassland, and built-up land; Scenario A aligns with ecological restoration goals (e.g., Grain for Green) and supports sustainable land use
Implications: Enhancing yield through technology can free land for ecological restoration and urban development; Strict environmental policy and yield improvements are critical for balancing food security and ecosystem protection; China’s import–export dynamics have global sustainability impacts
