Limitations: Assumes stability of driving-factor relationships over time; Excludes food-stock buffering effects; Parameterization relies on expert knowledge with inherent uncertainty
Future Directions: Incorporate medium- to high-resolution remote sensing for finer LULCC quantification; Add more ecological variables (e.g., soil moisture, net primary production) for suitability assessment; Use IMAGE model to evaluate trade-mediated land-use impacts
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Coupling of global socioeconomic modeling (GLOBFOOD), dynamic ecosystem simulation (TESim), and spatial allocation (CLUE) with use of dynamic SOM and SON outputs for site suitability assessment

Title: Tele-connecting China's future urban growth to impacts on ecosystem services under the shared socioeconomic pathways
Authors: Chen, Yimin; Li, Xia; Liu, Xiaoping; Zhang, Yuangying; Huang, Min
Objective: Integrate an urban cellular automata (CA) model with a multi-region input-output (MRIO) model to quantify how future urban land expansion in one Chinese province drives ecosystem services degradation in distant provinces under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenarios.
LULC Classes: cropland; forest; grassland; water; urban land; unused land
Scenarios: SSP1; SSP2; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: Multi-region input-output (MRIO) modeling; cellular automata (CA) simulation; Random Forest calibration; provincial regression for non-agricultural consumption; Total Operating Characteristic (TOC) validation; Figure of Merit (FoM) accuracy assessment
Sim. Method Advantages: MRIO captures direct and indirect environmental impacts along global supply chains; CA offers spatially explicit modeling of urban growth and a controlled experimental environment for scenario testing
Tools/Soft Used: Weka (Random Forest calibration)
Predictors: distance to capital cities; distance to prefectural cities; distance to towns; distance to provincial/national roads; distance to highways; distance to railways; slope (from digital elevation model); neighborhood effect
Data Sources: 2010 China Inter-regional IRIO tables (Liu et al., 2014b); 2000 and 2010 1 km land use from Chinese Academy of Sciences; 2010 1 km ecosystem services from Ouyang et al. (2016); administrative city locations; provincial/national roads, highways, railways; DEM; 2010–2050 SSP population scenarios (Jiang & O'Neill 2017; Jones & O'Neill 2016)
Validation Methods: 10-fold cross-validation for RF classifier; Total Operating Characteristic (TOC) for development potential; Figure of Merit (FoM) comparing simulated vs observed urban expansion
Validation Data Sources: 2000 and 2010 CAS land use maps; observed urban gain from overlay analysis
Key Findings: Coastal provinces (e.g., Shanghai, Tianjin) import large shares of urban land, interior provinces (e.g., Hebei, Henan) are net exporters of embodied urban land; China’s urban land peaks between 2030–2040 at 240–333 × 10³ km² depending on SSP; Direct loss of ecosystem services (2010–2050) under SSPs:; food production 1.14–5.42%; carbon sequestration 0.06–0.44%; soil retention 0.09–0.59%; sandstorm prevention 0.05–0.29%; water retention 0.12–0.80%; habitat provision 0.19–1.04%
Implications: Provide quantitative basis for payment-for-ecosystem-services schemes to internalize ecological costs of inter-regional urban land tele-connections; inform balanced compensation strategies to align stakeholder rights and responsibilities in ecological protection
Limitations: Does not account for international (overseas) urban land trade due to data gaps; focuses solely on direct losses from urban land expansion and ignores potential positive urbanization impacts and cascading land-use changes
Future Directions: Develop an integrated framework capturing both negative and positive urbanization effects on ecosystem services; incorporate global trade data to extend tele-connection analysis beyond China
Scalability: Approach applicable to other regions sharing comparable MRIO data and land-use/SSP projections, enabling cross-regional tele-connection studies
Novelty: First integration of spatially explicit urban CA with MRIO analysis under SSP scenarios to quantify domestic tele-connections between urban land consumption and ecosystem services degradation in China

Title: Using spatial multi-criteria decision analysis to develop new and sustainable directions for the future use of agricultural land in Denmark
Authors: Vogdrup-Schmidt, Mathias; Olsen, Soren Boye; Dubgaard, Alex; Kristensen, Inge Toft; Jorgensen, Leif Bach; Normander, Bo; Ege, Christian; Dalgaard, Tommy
Objective: Develop a spatially explicit multi-criteria decision analysis model to rank Danish agricultural land by societal value (land rent vs. ecosystem services) and identify optimal areas for land use change under alternative 2050 scenarios
LULC Classes: Arable land; Permanent grass; Energy crops; Afforestation
Scenarios: Baseline; Green growth; Urban and rural; Bio-based society; Rich nature
Analysis Methods: Spatial multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) using weighted linear combination; Scenario analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Straightforward and intuitive; Easy to communicate to decision makers; Incorporates spatial dependencies and geographic information; Facilitates transparent trade-off visualization
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS (ESRI, 2012); ILWIS spatial MCDA software (University of Twente, 2013)
Predictors: HNV Index; Field size; Organically farmed area; Livestock density; Retention capacity; Area in crop rotation; Peat soil in crop rotation; Reduction requirements; Dexter index; Ruminant emissions; Land rent; Employment
Data Sources: National high-resolution geo-database (soil type maps, carbon content, nutrient‐loss sensitivity, HNV scores, farm production statistics); Statistics Denmark; Danish Action Plan for the Aquatic Environment (Vandmiljøplan 2004); EU Biodiversity Strategy 2020; Brunbjerg et al. (2016) HNV index; Schjønning et al. (2012) Dexter index
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Baseline map reveals low-value areas suited for land use change; Green growth & Urban and rural scenarios concentrate measures in NW Denmark; Bio-based society scenario yields no clear regional pattern; Rich nature scenario identifies few high-priority patches
Implications: Spatial MCDA provides detailed, transparent decision support for agricultural land-use policy; can inform national/EU biodiversity and climate strategies; emphasizes need to articulate societal preferences
Limitations: Weights selection is subjective and may not reflect broader societal preferences; Limited to five criteria (excludes other ecosystem services); Score functions partly arbitrary; Model indicates where but not how much land to convert; No dynamic feedback or demographic factors considered
Future Directions: Sensitivity analysis of weighting schemes; Incorporate additional ecosystem service criteria; Develop interactive stakeholder preference elicitation; Extend model to dynamic land-use simulations; Apply approach at EU or other national scales
Scalability: Applicable to other regions or EU level where comparable high-resolution spatial data are available
Novelty: First national-scale application of spatial MCDA for agricultural land use in Denmark; Integration of land rent and multiple ecosystem service indicators; Scenario-specific weighting to explore trade-offs under different futures

Title: Assessing potential landscape service trade-offs driven by urbanization in Switzerland
Authors: Gerecke, Madleina; Hagen, Oskar; Bolliger, Janine; Hersperger, Anna M.; Kienast, Felix; Price, Bronwyn; Pellissier, Loic
Objective: Assess potential future landscape service trade-offs driven by urbanization by coupling land use change models with landscape service quantification
LULC Classes: Few-family houses; Multi-family houses; Manufacturing & service infrastructure; Arable land; Grasslands & meadows; Orchards, vineyards & horticulture; Forest; Alpine agricultural land
Scenarios: Business-as-usual extrapolation of past trends (no alternative socio-economic or policy scenarios)
Analysis Methods: Generalized linear models; External and split-sample validation; True-Skill-Statistics; Moran’s I; Adjusted deviance; Ensemble projections (100 runs)
Sim. Method Advantages: Improved regional specificity by hard regionalization; Integration of statistical land change drivers enables both explanation and projection; Spatially explicit probabilistic sampling captures uncertainty
Tools/Soft Used: R (version 3.3.3); “ecospat” R package
Predictors: Natural/spatial (elevation; slope; solar radiation); Technological (distance to roads; public transport accessibility); Cultural (not explicitly separated); Political (distance to economic centers); Economic (employee density in primary, secondary, tertiary sectors; population change); Climatic (mean annual temperature); Landscape state metrics (distance to urban centers; neighborhood land use composition)
Data Sources: Primary: Swiss Land Use Statistics (100 m grid, 72 categories), Swiss Federal Statistical Office hazard maps; Secondary: SFSO population and living space data, Cantonal agricultural production stats
Validation Methods: External validation using first transition to predict second; Split-sample (70:30) internal validation; True-Skill-Statistics thresholding; Moran’s I for spatial residuals
Validation Data Sources: Population and living space per person (Häne 2014, SFSO 2017a,b); Employment statistics (SFSO 2017c); Cantonal agricultural production (SFSO 2016)
Key Findings: Grassland→forest transitions decelerate; Grassland→few-family houses transitions accelerate (+115% by 2057–2081); Built-up area doubles by 2081; Crop production declines (~25% Plateau, ~80% Western Alps); Recreation provisioning plummets (–195% Plateau); Biodiversity & reared animals decrease; Forest area increases modestly (+6%) with upward shift; Housing and jobs provisioning increase dramatically
Implications: Business-as-usual urban sprawl threatens agricultural supply and recreational access; Need for densification policies and green infrastructure planning; Trade-offs highlight necessity of including built-up services in landscape service assessments
Limitations: LSS quantification relies on proxy formulas and look-up tables; Lack of data for some services prevented validation; Business-as-usual scenario omits potential policy shifts (e.g., densification regulations)
Future Directions: Develop socio-economic and policy scenarios; Improve service quantification methods with independent data; Standardize ESS/LSS assessment frameworks; Validate more services with observed data
Scalability: Approach generalizable to other countries experiencing urban sprawl
Novelty: Integration of built-up area services into landscape service assessment; Combined explanation and long-term projection using statistical land change models at regional scale

Title: Assessing the potential impacts of climate and population change on land-use changes projected to 2100 in Japan
Authors: Fujita, Tomohiro; Ariga, Toshinori; Ohashi, Haruka; Hijioka, Yasuaki; Fukasawa, Keita
Objective: Project proportional changes in 6 land-use types under climate and population change scenarios
LULC Classes: Paddy fields; Croplands; Forests; Wastelands; Built-up areas; Other artificial land cover
Scenarios: Climate: RCP2.6; RCP4.5; RCP8.5 (averaged over 26 GCMs); Population growth: High birth; Intermediate birth; Low birth; Population distribution: Centralization (C); Decentralization (D)
Analysis Methods: Random forest regression models
Sim. Method Advantages: More stable error rates than single CART; Captures non-linear interactions; Ensemble averaging reduces overfitting
Tools/Soft Used: R 3.3.1; ‘h2o’ package
Predictors: Climate: Warmth index; Coldest-month minimum temperature, Summer precipitation, Winter precipitation; Demography: Pop1km, Pop5km, Pop10km; Geography: Longitude, Latitude, Average elevation, relief, average slope, GEOMnames; Historical: pBltOth (previous 5-yr built-up+other artificial cover)
Data Sources: Land use: National Land Information Division (3rd-order mesh); Climate: Mesh Climatic Data 2010 (JMA); Population: National Census (1985–2005), Population projections (2012 NIPSSR); Geography: Japan Engineering Geomorphologic Classification Map
Validation Methods: Out-of-bag (OOB) MSE and R²; Observed vs. predicted comparison
Validation Data Sources: OOB samples from 1985–2005 dataset
Key Findings: Forest and wasteland areas driven mainly by climate change; Paddy fields, built-up, other artificial cover driven mainly by population distribution; Cropland affected by both, stronger climate influence; Regional variation pronounced (e.g., Hokkaido paddy increase under RCP8.5 +95.7%)
Implications: Climate mitigation critical for protecting forests and croplands; Urban planning and demographic policies influence paddy and artificial land trends; Region-specific strategies needed
Limitations: No land-use–climate feedbacks; Coarse GCM resolution; Data limited to 1985–2005; Lack of qualitative metrics (connectivity, heterogeneity); Assumed constant future relationships and domestic rice consumption
Future Directions: Incorporate land-use–climate feedbacks; Use finer resolution RCP and land-use data; Extend historical data pre-1985; Include qualitative landscape metrics; Model socio-economic factors (trade, industry)
Scalability: Potentially scalable using 3rd-order mesh framework, but requires compatible data and scenario adaptation
Novelty: Integration of climate and population distribution scenarios at 1 km mesh; Use of random forest for proportional land-use forecasting; Inclusion of artificial land legacy predictor (pBltOth)

Title: Cross-sectoral and trans-national interactions in national-scale climate change impacts assessment-the case of the Czech Republic
Authors: Papadimitriou, Lamprini; Trnka, Miroslav; Harrison, Paula; Holman, Ian
Objective: Assess systemic impacts of future climate and socio-economic change on the Czech Republic
LULC Classes: Arable land; Grassland (intensive; extensive); Managed forest; Unmanaged forest; Urban
Scenarios: RCP2.6; RCP4.5; RCP8.5; SSP1; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: Integrated modelling using IMPRESSIONS IAP2; Scenario-neutral sensitivity via Impact Response Surfaces; Combined scenario runs; Sensitivity analysis (110 runs)
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures cross-sectoral interactions; Includes trans-national feedbacks; National-scale focus within European modelling domain; Scenario-neutral and scenario-based approaches combined
Tools/Soft Used: IMPRESSIONS Integrated Assessment Platform 2 (IAP2)
Predictors: Temperature change; Precipitation change; Population; GDP; Dietary preferences; Technological innovation; Water-saving behavior; Environmental regulation
Data Sources: CRU climatology; CORINE land-cover; Czech Statistical Office; CMIP5-RCM projections; European SSP quantifications; Stakeholder estimates
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated vs observed:; Land-cover (CORINE, national statistics); Crop areas; Crop yields (13 NUTS3 regions)
Validation Data Sources: CORINE 2000; Yearbook national land-cover 2010; Czech Statistical Office (2000–2017)
Key Findings: Expansion of arable land at expense of grassland and forestry; Increased water scarcity and irrigation demand; Reduced biodiversity with species loss under warming/drying; Czech Republic gains competitive advantage as crop-growing region
Implications: Need for national adaptation policies accounting for cross-sectoral and trans-national interactions; Importance of socioeconomic drivers in adaptation planning; Support sustainable transitions to protect ecosystems
Limitations: Does not account for adaptation (except autonomous land-use change); Does not address interannual variability; Local factors (ownership, topography) not modelled
Future Directions: Incorporate local land-ownership and topography constraints; Model interannual climate variability; Assess adaptation measures within IAP2
Scalability: Yes—to other European nations via trans-national integrated modelling
Novelty: First national-scale integrated cross-sectoral and trans-national climate-socioeconomic assessment for the Czech Republic; Combined scenario-neutral and scenario-based approach using IAP2

Title: Exploring future scenarios of ethanol demand in Brazil and their land-use implications
Authors: Uba de Andrade Junior, Milton Aurelio; Valid, Hugo; Soterroni, Aline C.; Ramos, Fernando M.; Halog, Anthony
Objective: Explore future scenarios of ethanol demand in Brazil towards 2030 and estimate their land-use implications
LULC Classes: Sugarcane; Other crops; Planted forest; Native vegetation; Non-productive land; Pasture
Scenarios: Renewable Fuels Oriented (RFO); Business as Usual (BAU); Fossil Fuels Oriented (FFO)
Analysis Methods: Panel regression analysis of transport demand; Logistic regression for fuel-blend choice; Partial equilibrium land-use modeling (GLOBIOM-Brazil)
Sim. Method Advantages: Grid-cell level competition optimization maximizing consumer and producer surplus under policy and resource constraints; endogenous adjustment of productivity and management systems
Tools/Soft Used: GLOBIOM-Brazil; EPIC model; RUMINANT model
Predictors: GDP per capita; Population growth; Fleet composition; Fuel blend mandates; Relative fuel prices; Vehicle fuel-consumption efficiency
Data Sources: World Bank; OECD; COPPE/EPE; ANP; MMA; CETESB; Sindipeças/Abipeças; EPE; FAO; GFEI
Validation Methods: Comparison of 2010 model outputs with official statistics on deforestation, agricultural production, and land-use
Validation Data Sources: PRODES/INPE; Brazilian government land-use and agricultural production statistics
Key Findings: Ethanol demand by 2030 could range from 37.4 to 70.7 billion L depending on scenario; Sugarcane area expands by 1.6–5.4 Mha (2010–2030); Expansion occurs predominantly on pasture (72%) with minimal native vegetation loss (0.05 ha per ha sugarcane)
Implications: Brazil can meet increased ethanol demand with limited impacts on food production and native vegetation if sugarcane AEZ is enforced
Limitations: Reliance on AEZ compliance and governance assumptions; use of SSP2 for other agricultural demand; exclusion of CNG and second-generation biofuels; partial equilibrium model constraints
Future Directions: Assess impacts of corn and second-generation ethanol; Explore varied governance and illegal-deforestation control scenarios; Incorporate international sugar-market shifts
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integration of macroeconomic and policy drivers into ethanol-demand scenarios; application of GLOBIOM-Brazil with sugarcane AEZ for land-use implications

Title: Fires, Smoke Exposure, and Public Health: An Integrative Framework to Maximize Health Benefits From Peatland Restoration
Authors: Marlier, Miriam E.; Liu, Tianjia; Yu, Karen; Buonocore, Jonathan J.; Koplitz, Shannon N.; DeFries, Ruth S.; Mickley, Loretta J.; Jacob, Daniel J.; Schwartz, Joel; Wardhana, Budi S.; Myers, Samuel S.
Objective: To develop an integrative framework that connects land use decisions with fire activity and public health outcomes, specifically to assess the health benefits of peatland restoration and other land management strategies in reducing fire-related mortality across Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore
LULC Classes: Intact primary forest; degraded primary forest; nonforested areas; combined tree plantations and secondary forest; peatlands; nonpeatlands
Baseline Years: 2005-2010 for land use and land cover analysis; 2005-2009 for fire emissions analysis
Scenarios: Business-As-Usual (BAU) scenario; blocking fires in all peatland areas; blocking fires in industrial oil palm, wood pulp, and logging concessions; blocking fires in existing conservation areas; BRG (Peatland Restoration Agency) priority restoration sites
Analysis Methods: Integration of land use science, atmospheric modeling, and public health modeling; GEOS-Chem adjoint sensitivities; spatially explicit land use change modeling; health impact assessment using concentration-response functions; population-weighted PM2.5 exposure calculations
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica EGO Version 3.0.17; GEOS-Chem adjoint model v8-02-01; MODIS Collection 6 fire radiative power observations; online decision support tool
Predictors: Landform type; soil type; elevation; slope; protected areas; oil palm, logging, and wood fiber industrial concessions; population density; distance to roads; distance to rivers; distance to oil palm mills; distance to each individual LULC class
Data Sources: Global Fire Emissions Database version 4s (GFED4s); MODIS Collection 6 fire radiative power observations; Margono et al. (2014) land use dataset; Hansen et al. (2013) Global Forest Change; UN-adjusted GPW population data; Global Burden of Disease (GBD) project; GEOS-5 assimilated meteorology; various spatial datasets for industrial concessions, protected areas, and infrastructure
Validation Methods: Forward simulation validation using spatial correlation coefficient (r = 0.84) and mean bias calculation (-27%) for PM10 observations; multicollinearity checks for input variables (variance inflation factor <5)
Validation Data Sources: PM10 observations from 50 sites in Malaysian Peninsula and Borneo
Key Findings: Business-As-Usual scenario would lead to 36,000 excess deaths per year across the region from air pollution exposure; protecting peatlands could reduce fire-related mortality by 66% (preventing 24,000 excess deaths per year); fires in peatlands contribute disproportionately to total emissions despite having relatively small total areas; most emissions occur during July-October with highest activity during El Niño conditions
Implications: Land management strategies can significantly reduce public health impacts from fire emissions; peatland restoration is highly effective due to peatlands' location upwind of densely populated areas and high fuel content; the framework can support evidence-based policy decisions for fire reduction strategies; current trends without intervention will lead to substantial preventable mortality
Limitations: Use of 2005-2010 LULC maps may not reflect recent changes; GFED4s fire emissions inventory may underestimate small fires; uncertainty in emissions factors from tropical peatland burning; health impact estimates based on studies from developed countries rather than local epidemiological data; population data do not reflect changes over time; climate change effects on fire-atmospheric transport relationships not explored
Future Directions: Incorporating newly available data on health outcomes and other input datasets; exploring climate change impacts on fire and atmospheric transport relationships; potential for primary epidemiological studies in the region
Scalability: The integrative framework is applicable to other fire-prone regions around the world to develop strategies that reduce negative health outcomes associated with biomass burning
Novelty: First integrated approach combining land use science, atmospheric modeling, and public health for fire policy evaluation; development of publicly available online decision support tool; use of adjoint sensitivities to prioritize restoration locations based on health benefits; quantification of health impacts from different spatial fire reduction strategies

Title: High resolution predictive modelling of potential natural vegetation under recent site conditions and future climate scenarios: Case study Bavaria
Authors: Fischer, Hagen S.; Michler, Barbara; Fischer, Anton
Country: Federal State of Bavaria, Southeastern Germany
Objective: develop a model to simulate the distribution of potential natural vegetation (PNV) units under current and future climate scenarios
LULC Classes: 26 phytosociological forest types (PNV units); agricultural and abandoned lands characterized by corresponding PNV
Scenarios: +1 K, +2 K, +3 K, +4 K, +6 K temperature increases; each combined with –10%, no change, +10% precipitation (15 total)
Analysis Methods: discriminant analysis; correlation analysis; Generalised Linear Models (GLM); Generalised Additive Models (GAM); MaxEnt predictive modelling
Sim. Method Advantages: dynamic, high spatial resolution (50 m x 50 m) mapping; phytosociological PNV units yield finer habitat differentiation than species‐level models; enables pixel‐level scenario comparisons
Tools/Soft Used: R (packages “raster”, “dismo”); MaxEnt software
Predictors: Total pore volume; available water capacity; water conductivity coefficient; air capacity; hygroscopic water; base saturation (0–30 cm); cation exchange capacity; exchangeable Ca²⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺; organic matter; soil depth; depth of decalcification; potential evapotranspiration; annual precipitation; solar radiation; annual temperature; May–Sep water balance; de Martonne aridity index; growing degree days (>5 °C); floodplain index; aspect index; slope
Data Sources: primary: National Forest Inventory (NFI, BWI II) sampling points, National Forest Soil Inventory (NFSI), Bavarian General Soil Map 1:25 000 expanded by LfU/LWF, digital climate grids from DWD and LWF, digital terrain model from LDBV; secondary: regional ecograms, indicator‐species checklists, forest‐type fact sheets
Validation Methods: independent split of calibration (NFI) and evaluation (NFSI) datasets; AUC (ROC) statistics; threshold maximizing sum of true positive and negative rates
Validation Data Sources: National Forest Soil Inventory sampling points (NFSI)
Key Findings: AUC > 0.9 (“excellent”) for all 26 forest‐type models; base saturation, precipitation, floodplain index, water balance and temperature most influential predictors; future scenarios produce non-analogue site conditions on 36% (+2 K) to 94% (+4 K) of Bavaria; montane and colline-submontane PNV units shift upslope or contract; some wet-forest types remain stable while oak–hornbeam expand under warming
Implications: equips policymakers and land managers with local-scale hot-spot maps of site-condition change; informs adaptive forestry, agriculture, conservation planning
Limitations: inability to predict PNV under non-analogue climate beyond training range; no dynamic successional processes; rare PNV units excluded due to sample size or resolution constraints
Future Directions: extend calibration via space-for-time substitution from European PNV maps; develop interactive version incorporating novel climates; integrate sky-view factor for ravine forests
Scalability: approach can be transferred to other regions using equivalent high-resolution site data (e.g., European PNV map)
Novelty: first fine-scale (50 m) dynamic PNV mapping under multiple climate scenarios for Bavaria; quantitative ecological preference functions for 26 phytosociological units; integrated thresholding to derive crisp and fuzzy distribution maps.

Title: Impacts of Urban Expansion on Terrestrial Carbon Storage in China
Authors: Liu, Xiaoping; Wang, Shaojian; Wu, Peijun; Feng, Kuishuang; Hubacek, Klaus; Li, Xia; Sun, Laixiang
Objective: Coupling the Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) model and the InVEST model to quantify impacts of historical and future urban expansion on terrestrial carbon storage in China
LULC Classes: Second‐level land use types reclassified into seven first‐level types: cropland; woodland; grassland; water bodies; built‐up (urban) land; unused land; reclaimed land
Scenarios: Baseline Development Scenario (BDS; SSP2-RCP4.5); Fast Development Scenario (FDS; SSP5-RCP6.0); Slow Development Scenario (SDS; SSP1-RCP2.6); Harmonious Development Scenario (HDS; SSP3-RCP4.5)
Analysis Methods: Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs (InVEST) carbon storage module; Cellular Automata–based Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) with ANN probability estimation and SD demand module; Zonal statistics of climatic zone × land use carbon densities
Sim. Method Advantages: ANN within FLUS captures nonlinear spatial drivers more effectively than traditional CA; InVEST requires fewer inputs and directly maps land‐use change to carbon impacts, avoiding complex biogeochemical parameterization
Tools/Soft Used: FLUS model (http://www.geosimulation.cn/FLUS.html); InVEST carbon module; GIS software for spatial overlay; SD demand module
Predictors: Distance to provincial capital; jurisdictive city/county town; rivers; provincial roads; national roads; railways; expressways; spatial variables of land‐use conversion costs
Data Sources: Land use maps (1980, 1990, 2000, 2010) from Data Center for Resources and Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences; Climatic zoning map (Köppen–Geiger) from internet; Biomass carbon density tables from literature (Hou 2001, Pan 2009, Song 2005); Soil organic carbon density tables from literature (Song 2005, Pan 2009); Spatial data on roads, rivers, administrative boundaries from national agencies
Validation Methods: ROC curve and AUC evaluation for ANN land‐use probability modeling; Comparison of simulated 2010 land‐use patterns against observed 2010 maps
Validation Data Sources: Observed land‐use map of China in 2010 (Data Center for Resources and Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences)
Key Findings: Carbon storage loss accelerated from 0.72 TgC/y (1980–1990) to 8.72 TgC/y (2000–2010); Cropland-to-urban conversion accounted for > 50% of loss; woodland-to-urban share rose to ~28% (2000–2010); Future annual loss (2010–2050) projected at 9.31–12.94 TgC/y, 2.6–3.7× historical rate; Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei, YRD, PRD agglomerations to contribute ~17% of future national loss
Implications: Ongoing urbanization risks undermining China’s Paris Agreement targets; Need for ecologically friendly urban policies (green roofs, forest protection, permeable surfaces)
Limitations: InVEST’s assumption of fixed carbon densities ignores regrowth and aging periods; Scenario‐only uncertainty analysis; input‐parameter uncertainty not quantified
Future Directions: Incorporate carbon sequestration dynamics and aging in models; Conduct Monte Carlo analysis for input‐parameter uncertainty; Evaluate effects of green infrastructure interventions
Scalability: Applicable to other regions given global availability of FLUS and InVEST, but requires localized carbon‐density calibration and climatic zoning
Novelty: Nationwide, climate‐zone‐specific coupling of FLUS and InVEST for both historical and four SSP-RCP future urbanization scenarios; Detailed classification of land use × climatic zone to improve carbon‐density estimation

Title: Modeling different urban change trajectories and their trade-offs with food production in Jiangsu Province, China
Authors: Wang, Yuan; van Vliet, Jasper; Pu, Lijie; Verburg, Peter H.
Objective: Analyze alternative trajectories of changes in human settlements and agricultural systems in Jiangsu Province under different population scenarios and cropland protection policies
LULC Classes: Dense urban landscape; Peri-urban landscape; Clustered industrial town; Clustered traditional town; Spread industrial town; Spread traditional town; High-yielding agricultural system; Med-yielding agricultural system; Low-yielding agricultural system; Forest; Reclaimed area; Wetland
Scenarios: S1: Planned population, no cropland policy; S2: Trend-extrapolated population, no cropland policy; S3: Planned population + no net loss of cropland area; S4: Trend-extrapolated population + no net loss of cropland area; S5: Planned population + no net loss of crop production; S6: Trend-extrapolated population + no net loss of crop production
Analysis Methods: Classification tree for land systems; CLUMondo land use modelling; logistic regression for suitability; iterative land allocation
Sim. Method Advantages: Represents multiple settlement types and intensities rather than a single urban class; Simulates both area change and intensity change for urban and agricultural land; Allows multiple land systems to fulfill demands simultaneously
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo model; Logistic regression analysis
Predictors: Share of built-up land; Number of built-up clusters; Share of population employed in industry and services; Cropland productivity (annual crop production and multi-cropping frequency); Biophysical and socio-economic variables
Data Sources: GHS human grid; Land cover datasets; Town-level crop production data; Multi-cropping frequency; Socio-economic data; National and provincial planning documents
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Without cropland policies, urban expansion causes cropland loss and reduced crop production; Area-protection policies prevent cropland loss but reduce production by converting high-quality land to low-quality reclaimed land; Production-protection policies maintain crop output while allowing cropland area loss and urban expansion; Settlement changes occur incrementally (town → peri-urban → urban)
Implications: Protecting crop production is more effective for food security and urban development; Policy focus on high-quality cropland and intensification can reconcile urban expansion with food production
Limitations: Yields assumed constant (no rising yield trends); Wealth and non-population drivers of urban growth not included; Classification may conflate expansion and intensification transitions
Future Directions: Incorporate economic growth and housing demand; Use additional intensity metrics (floor area, economic activity); Apply classification and modelling approach in other regions
Scalability: Approach transferable to other regions with diverse settlement trajectories
Novelty: First urban land use model representing multiple settlement intensity classes; Simultaneous simulation of area and intensity changes for urban and agricultural land

Title: Modelling population structure in the context of urban land use change in Europe
Authors: Terama, Emma; Clarke, Elizabeth; Rounsevell, Mark D. A.; Fronzek, Stefan; Carter, Timothy R.
Objective: Link national‐scale SSP population projections with sub‐national population distributions and integrate into a regional urban growth (RUG) model to assess how age‐structure and population dynamics drive urban land‐use change in Europe.
LULC Classes: Residential artificial surfaces (city, suburban/town, rural); Non‐residential (industrial) artificial surface
Scenarios: SSP1; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: Downscaling of age‐specific national projections to NUTS-2 regions; Regional Urban Growth (RUG) model with spatial allocation on a 10′ grid; Boxplot analysis of regional change rates
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates thematic (age) and spatial (regional) resolution; Captures divergent regional trends versus uniform national approaches; Links demographic structure directly to residential preferences and land‐use demand
Tools/Soft Used: Regional Urban Growth (RUG) model; Eurostat databases; SSP database
Predictors: Age‐group population projections; Baseline regional age distributions; Scenario‐defined residential preference parameters; Population density regulations; Spatial autocorrelation of artificial surfaces
Data Sources: Wittgenstein Centre SSP population database (IIASA); Eurostat 2010 age‐specific population; Eurostat 2016 urban/residential population distributions; European storylines (Kok & Pedde 2016)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Regional total‐population change rates vary widely within countries due to baseline age‐structure differences; SSP1 and SSP5 drive substantial artificial surface expansion (up to ~9% land area by 2100 in SSP5); SSP3 and SSP4 show limited demographic‐driven urban growth; Low‐fertility countries (e.g., BG, RO, LT, LV, MT) exhibit little new sprawl under SSP5
Implications: Accounting for sub‐national age structure is critical for accurate urban land‐use projections; Policymaking on housing, infrastructure, and climate adaptation must consider regional demographic heterogeneity
Limitations: Assumes no sub‐national migration between NUTS-2 regions; Age‐group change rates spatially uniform within each country; Existing artificial surfaces treated as static (no conversion)
Future Directions: Incorporate sub-regional migration dynamics; Link RUG outputs with impact/adaptation models (CCIAV); Extend downscaling to finer spatial units
Scalability: Applicable to other European regions given data availability; Potentially transferable to other continents with comparable SSP and sub‐national data
Novelty: Novel integration of age‐specific population downscaling with a spatially explicit urban growth model; Thematic resolution of demographic drivers linked directly to land‐use demand.

Title: On projected hydrological scenarios under the influence of bias-corrected climatic variables and LULC
Authors: Sahoo, Satiprasad; Dey, Saumava; Dhar, Anirban; Debsarkar, Anupam; Pradhan, Biswajeet
Objective: Assess the effect of climate change on projected streamflow and groundwater recharge in the Dwarakeswar-Gandheswari basin
LULC Classes: Crop Land; Forest Cover; Barren Land; Fallow Land; Water Bodies; Shrub Land; Built-up Land
Scenarios: RCP 2.6; RCP 4.5; RCP 6.0; RCP 8.5
Analysis Methods: Bias correction (LS, LOCI, PWTR, DM, VARI) of RCM data; Dyna-CLUE logistic regression land-use simulation; SWAT hydrological modeling; Statistical performance metrics (NSE; PBIAS; MAE; R²); Sensitivity and uncertainty analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE; SWAT; MIROC5 RCM; GIS
Predictors: Aspect; Elevation; Slope; Rainfall; Temperature; Soil depth; Geology; Distance from road; Distance from rail; Distance from river; Distance from built-up; Distance from cropland; Distance from forest cover
Data Sources: Landsat imagery from Earth Explorer & GloVis; RCP data (CMIP5 AR5) via MIROC5; Observed precipitation & temperature (NCEP CFSR); Soil maps (National Bureau of Soil Survey); DEM (SRTM); Discharge data (Irrigation and Waterways Directorate); Groundwater data (Central Ground Water Board)
Validation Methods: Streamflow calibration/validation (1990–2006, 2007–2016); Groundwater recharge validated against observed groundwater levels and field soil-moisture
Validation Data Sources: Observed discharge (2007–2016); Groundwater level records (2002–2011); Field soil-moisture measurements
Key Findings: Monsoon (Jun–Sep) streamflow increases, non-monsoon (Oct–Dec) decreases; Groundwater recharge rises in most sub-watersheds for 2016–2030, less so for later periods; LS best for precipitation bias correction, DM best for temperature
Implications: Results can guide irrigation planning and water resources management
Limitations: Use of a single RCM (MIROC5) limits the representativeness of climate projections
Future Directions: Incorporate multiple GCM datasets for broader analysis of hydrological impacts
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Combined framework linking bias-corrected climate data, Dyna-CLUE land-use simulation, and SWAT hydrology under multiple RCPs

Title: Projecting Global Urban Area Growth Through 2100 Based on Historical Time Series Data and Future Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Authors: Li, Xuecao; Zhou, Yuyu; Eom, Jiyong; Yu, Sha; Asrar, Ghassem R.
Objective: Provide a global projection of urban area growth through 2100 based on historical time series data and future Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
LULC Classes: Urban vs. non-urban extents
Scenarios: Five Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1 Sustainability; SSP2 Middle-of-the-road; SSP3 Regional rivalry; SSP4 Inequality; SSP5 Fossil-fueled development)
Analysis Methods: Country-specific sigmoid growth models relating per capita urban area to per capita cumulative GDP; time series fitting (1992–2013)
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures three urbanization phases (initial, middle, mature) with a single four-parameter function; Consistent application across all countries; Requires only historical urban extent and socioeconomic data versus region-specific multiregression or system-dynamics models
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Per capita cumulative GDP; population (to derive per capita urban area and total urban area)
Data Sources: Historical urban extents from 1-km nighttime-light satellite data (1992–2013); Population and nominal GDP (World Bank, adjusted via PPP and deflator); Future population and GDP projections (IIASA SSP database)
Validation Methods: Goodness-of-fit (R²) between modeled and observed per-country urban extents
Validation Data Sources: Observed urban extents derived from nighttime light data
Key Findings: Global urban area grows 40–67% by 2050 and more than 200% by 2100 relative to 2013; SSP3 and SSP4 yield lower growth due to slower GDP/population trajectories; Developing countries (e.g., China, India) drive most growth but show different temporal patterns (China plateaus ~2050, India continues increasing); Mature countries exhibit modest growth (<50% by 2100)
Implications: Provides first country-level SSP-variant urban area projections for modeling urban sprawl, assessing SDG progress, evaluating ecological and health impacts, and integrating into Earth system models for climate and resource studies
Limitations: Does not include other quantitative inputs (natural resources, technology, investment) or qualitative narratives (policy, institutions, lifestyle, settlement pattern); Lower model performance in countries with poor population/GDP data (e.g., parts of Africa)
Future Directions: Integrate spatial allocation models (e.g., cellular automata) for explicit sprawl simulation; Incorporate additional drivers and qualitative narratives consistent with SSP indicators; Improve data quality in low-income regions
Scalability: Demonstrated global applicability across 171 countries; extensible to regional and subnational studies
Novelty: First use of long-term (1992–2013) satellite-derived urban time series for country-specific sigmoid growth modeling; First global, country-level urban extent projections under five SSP scenarios through 2100

Title: Remote sensing as the foundation for high-resolution United States landscape projections - The Land Change Monitoring, assessment, and projection (LCMAP) initiative
Authors: Sohl, Terry; Dornbierer, Jordan; Wika, Steve; Robison, Charles
Objective: Produce high-resolution, parcel-based landscape projections for U.S. Great Plains to evaluate feasibility and suitability compared to existing datasets
LULC Classes: Corn; Soybeans; Cotton; Wheat (dryland, winter, spring); Sorghum; Barley; Oats; Rice; Peanuts; Potatoes; Other crops; Hay; Alfalfa; Perennial grass; Urban/Developed; Grassland; Shrubland; Deciduous forest; Mixed forest; Evergreen forest; plus additional minor classes
Scenarios: BAU; BTU40; BTU60; BTU80; GCAMRef; GCAM4.5; GCAM2.6; SRES A1B; SRES A2; SRES B1; SRES B2
Analysis Methods: Logistic regression for suitability; parcel-based FORE-SCE spatial allocation; CCDC time-series analysis; object-based image segmentation; ROC analysis; quantity/exchange/shift disagreement metrics
Sim. Method Advantages: Parcel-based framework ensures realistic landscape pattern; 30 m resolution matching NLCD/CDL; dynamic suitability surfaces responding to climate and water availability; integration with remote sensing for parameterization
Tools/Soft Used: FORE-SCE model; CCDC algorithm; TimeSync; object segmentation (Jones et al.); logistic regression routines; GIS software
Predictors: Soils; climate variables (RCP projections); elevation; transportation networks; biofuel feedstock productivity; groundwater saturated thickness; protected area mask; pixel history (Time Since Last Change)
Data Sources: Primary: LCMAP monitoring products, NLCD, USDA CDL, USDA CLU parcels, Global scenarios (BTU, GCAM, SRES); Secondary: Protected Areas Database (PAD-US), EPA ecoregion boundaries, well-head groundwater data, Sentinel-Landsat harmonized imagery
Validation Methods: ROC (suitability model fit); quantity and allocation disagreement analysis; comparison of urban growth metrics to theoretical trends; evaluation of demand matching
Validation Data Sources: NLCD historical change data; Cropland Data Layer; LCMAP reference sample points; literature-derived landscape metrics
Key Findings: Feasible to produce high-resolution, parcel-based projections at national scales; Strong variability among scenarios in cropland, perennial grass, and rangeland trends; New urban model better captures sprawling patterns (increased patch density, edge density); Dynamic suitability allows climate/water impacts (grassland-to-shrubland transitions); FORE-SCE met scenario demand within ±5% for most ecoregion–scenario combinations
Implications: Enables researchers and land managers to assess uncertainties in future landscapes; facilitates integration into existing workflows using NLCD/CDL; informs interdisciplinary applications (water, biodiversity, hazards, carbon)
Limitations: Parcel data availability inconsistent nationally; challenges in quantitative validation of unprecedented long-term projections; exogenous scenarios may be unrealistic at regional scales
Future Directions: Develop national-scale parcel datasets for all land uses; integrate improved forest parcelization; refine scenario downscaling; extend LCMAP temporal analysis
Scalability: Demonstrated across three Great Plains megaregions; methodology adaptable to conterminous U.S. pending parcel/data availability
Novelty: First high-resolution (30 m), parcel-based national projections aligned with NLCD/CDL; dynamic suitability surfaces incorporating future climate and groundwater; new urban allocation replicating leap-frogging and sprawl patterns

Title: Scenarios of Land Use and Land Cover Change and Their Multiple Impacts on Natural Capital in Tanzania
Authors: Capitani, Claudia; van Soesbergen, Arnout; Mukama, Kusaga; Malugu, Isaac; Mbilinyi, Boniface; Chamuya, Nurdin; Kempen, Bas; Malimbwi, Rogers; Mant, Rebecca; Munishi, Panteleo; Njana, Marco Andrew; Ortmann, Antonia; Platts, Philip J.; Runsten, Lisen; Sassen, Marieke; Sayo, Philippina; Shirima, Deo; Zahabu, Elikamu; Burgess, Neil D.; Marchant, Rob
Objective: Assess potential interacting impacts on carbon stock, biodiversity and water yield of alternative land-use and land-cover change scenarios in Tanzania
LULC Classes: Closed forest; open woodland; bushland; grassland; mangrove forest; cultivated land; mixed cultivated wooded land; degradation classes
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU); Green economy (GE)
Analysis Methods: Participatory scenario development; spatial allocation of LULCCs using likelihood layers; Biomass and soil carbon stock estimation; BRRI calculation for biodiversity; WaterWorld V2 hydrological modelling; Multi-dimensional RGB overlay of impacts
Sim. Method Advantages: Participatory mixed qualitative–quantitative approach ensures stakeholder legitimacy and local representativeness; Spatially explicit, demand-driven scenarios capture non-detectable deforestation fractions
Tools/Soft Used: WaterWorld V2; GIS spatial resampling; participatory GIS mapping
Predictors: Likelihood spatial layers for cultivated land demand; wood biomass demand; baseline land-cover map; protected area distribution
Data Sources: NAFORMA forest inventory; WorldClim climate data; MODIS VCF 2010; IUCN Red List distributions; Soil and Terrain Database (SOTER); World Database on Protected Areas
Validation Methods: National- and regional-level stakeholder workshops; secondary data comparison; workshop-based feedback and refinement
Validation Data Sources: MNRT land-cover map 2010; IUCN & UNEP-WCMC protected area database; secondary literature cited in workshops
Key Findings: BAU yields 296 MtC loss by 2025, GE yields 133 MtC loss, BAU reduces endemic species habitat by 20% on average, GE reduces by 4%, BAU increases mean water balance by 3.9 mm yr⁻¹, GE by 1.9 mm yr⁻¹,; High simultaneous impacts concentrate in Eastern Arc and south-western forests under BAU, GE reduces these hotspots
Implications: Effective REDD+ implementation (GE) can halve carbon losses and limit biodiversity and water impacts; Protected and community-managed forests crucial but insufficient alone; broader landscape integration needed
Limitations: Uncertainty from spatial resampling and index choices; pixel-based analysis omits connectivity; static climate inputs; limited temporal horizon (to 2025)
Future Directions: Incorporate climate change disturbance; include social dimensions; extend temporal scope beyond 2025; integrate connectivity metrics
Scalability: Framework transferable to other tropical countries with participatory calibration and local data
Novelty: First multi-dimensional, participatory, spatially explicit scenario assessment of carbon, biodiversity and water yield in Tanzania; Demand-driven modelling capturing deforestation not detectable by satellite alone

Title: Spatio-temporal evolution scenarios and the coupling analysis of ecosystem services with land use change in China
Authors: Sun, Yongxiu; Liu, Shiliang; Dong, Yuhong; An, Yi; Shi, Fangning; Dong, Shikui; Liu, Guohua
Objective: quantifying the spatial distribution and temporal trends of ecosystem service (ES) supply, demand and balance under four future land use scenarios; clarifying sensitivity mechanisms of how land use change influences ES supply and demand; exploring the coupling coordination between land use intensity and ES balance
LULC Classes: water; forest; grassland; farmland; urban; barren
Scenarios: I (low population–high urban expansion); II (high population–high urban expansion); III (low population–low urban expansion); IV (medium population–low urban expansion)
Analysis Methods: LULC matrix method for ES supply, demand and balance; linear regression analysis of slope trends; ecological sensitivity index calculation; coupling coordination model
Sim. Method Advantages: efficient and simple; suitable for data-scarce regions; provides credible guidance for land and ES management under future scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: GIS for mapping; statistical software for regression and sensitivity analyses (specific software not specified)
Predictors: land use comprehensive intensity; ES supply and demand values (derived from expert-based LULC matrices)
Data Sources: Li’s database of future land use/land cover scenarios; Burkhard’s supply-demand balance matrices
Validation Methods: coefficient of sensitivity (CS) analysis
Validation Data Sources: sensitivity adjustment of ES quantitative values by ±50% (no external dataset)
Key Findings: ES supply, demand and balance exhibit significant spatial–temporal variation under different scenarios; high population and urban expansion scenarios lead to decreases in ES balance in most provinces; approximately 90% of provinces show low ecological sensitivity to land use change under all scenarios; coupling coordination degree remains stable in most provinces but degrades or improves in some regions
Implications: results provide guidance for targeted land use planning and ES management; highlight provinces requiring ecological restoration or improved coordination
Limitations: expert-based assessment method with high subjectivity and uncertainty; semi-quantitative matrix cannot capture all ecological and social drivers; reliance on global LUCC predictions may not reflect regional policy changes
Future Directions: improve temporal resolution of land use simulation; incorporate additional ecological and social variables; refine scenario modeling to account for regional policy and demographic changes
Scalability: method is applicable to data-scarce regions and larger spatial scales; can be promoted in other regions
Novelty: integration of ES supply, demand and balance under four future land use scenarios; combined ecological sensitivity and coupling coordination analyses linking land use change with ES evolution

Title: Towards an integrated assessment of climate and socio-economic change impacts and implications in New Zealand
Authors: Ausseil, A. G. E.; Daigneault, A. J.; Frame, B.; Teixeira, E., I
Objective: To conduct a site-specific assessment of future scenarios by combining global assumptions from the IPCC scenario framework with local conditions, using a spatially explicit integrated assessment that combines economic and biophysical models to quantify potential impacts of climate-induced changes coupled with regional environmental and land-use policy
LULC Classes: Grassland (47,000 ha); dairy farming; sheep and beef farming; exotic forestry; indigenous forest; kiwifruit horticulture (6,000 ha); maize cropping; freshwater wetlands; native forests
Baseline Years: 2015; 1980-1999 for sea-level rise; 1985-2005 for pasture production reference
Scenarios: Three scenarios: 'Unspecific Pacific' (RCP 8.5/SSP3/SPA A), 'Kicking, screaming' (RCP 4.5/SSP3/SPA A), and 'Clean leader' (RCP 4.5/SSP5/SPA F)
Analysis Methods: Integrated assessment modeling approach combining economic and biophysical models; spatially explicit analysis; coupled component modeling approach; Story and Simulations (SAS) approach combining narrative stories with quantitative model simulations
Sim. Method Advantages: Loose coupling preserves the integrity of specialized models and maintains control over data interpretation between models; enables exploration of complex interactions between sectors in lowland environments where climate change impacts productivity and global economic trends influence land use
Tools/Soft Used: NZFARM; CliMAT-DGE; CLIMEX; APSIM; Biome-BGC; CenW; OVERSEER; WATYIELD; NZEEM
Predictors: Climate variables from RCP scenarios (primary production, pests and disease, sea-level rise); socio-economic variables from SSP scenarios (demographics); commodity prices; yield changes; land use change constraints
Data Sources: IPCC RCP and SSP databases; IIASA database; Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) version 8 data set; six GCMs (BCC-CSM1.1, CESM1-CAM5, GFDL-CM3, GISS-E2-R, HadGEM2-ES, NorESM1-M); LCDB3 and Agribase for land use mapping
Validation Methods: GCMs were selected because they validated well against New Zealand climate; model parameters were calibrated against New Zealand pasture growth data and validated for both dairy and sheep systems
Validation Data Sources: New Zealand climate data (Tait et al., 2016b); New Zealand pasture growth data for model calibration
Key Findings: Strong influence of policies on regional economic output and ecosystem services relative to just accounting for physical impacts of climate change; commodity price changes more influential for land-use change than yield changes from climate; projected conversion from sheep/beef and dairy farms to forest plantations under carbon pricing scenarios
Implications: Quantitative modeling results can be used to identify adaptation options in light of climate change implications; socio-economic context mainly drives changes in ecosystem services through land-use change effects
Limitations: Uncertainties inherent to integrated modeling approach; main sources include data inputs (different GCMs), model parameters for biophysical, economic, and ecosystem services models; not all O'Neill et al. (2014) elements could be modeled quantitatively
Future Directions: Future research needed to test hard coupling of key models in the integrated system; more sensitivity analyses required to understand how outcomes and narratives are affected; need for dynamic adaptive pathways approach
Scalability: Framework designed for transferability to other areas through participatory approach with stakeholders; methodology provides guiding principles for combining global assumptions with local conditions
Novelty: First framework combining global assumptions with local conditions for site-specific assessments; integration of diverse models to quantify complex climate-induced impacts with regional policy; demonstration of policy influence on regional outcomes relative to physical climate impacts

Title: Abandonment and Recultivation of Agricultural Lands in Slovakia-Patterns and Determinants from the Past to the Future
Authors: Pazur, Robert; Lieskovsky, Juraj; Buergi, Matthias; Mueller, Daniel; Lieskovsky, Tibor; Zhang, Zhen; Prischchepov, Alexander, V
Objective: Quantify patterns and determinants of agricultural land abandonment and recultivation in Slovakia from 1985 to 2010 and project future agricultural land use to 2060
LULC Classes: Cropland; grassland; forest; built-up
Scenarios: Scenario assuming continuation of observed agricultural land change trends and a future climate-change projection to 2060
Analysis Methods: Multi-seasonal Landsat-based land cover mapping; random forest classification; boosted regression trees; pixel-based image compositing; cost-distance accessibility analysis; scenario modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: High spatial resolution and long temporal coverage capture small-scale changes omitted in coarse datasets; synergetic use of satellite data and land-use modeling enhances land planning and anticipation of environmental and policy effects
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS Desktop 10.3; Land Facet Corridor Designer; random forest classifier; Boosted Regression Trees algorithm
Predictors: Distance from Bratislava; settlement cost-distance; distance to forest edges; slope; topographic position index; topographic wetness index; soil fertility; mean temperature; precipitation; sun radiation; mountainous region dummy; protected area status
Data Sources: 30 m multi-seasonal Landsat imagery; 30 m DEM from civil contour maps; soil maps from Slovak National Agriculture and Food Center and National Forest Center; CHELSA climate dataset; Natura 2000 and Ramsar protected area databases; Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic; Carpathian ecoregion land cover dataset
Validation Methods: Accuracy assessment including overall accuracy, user’s and producer’s accuracies from confusion matrices
Validation Data Sources: Reference data from previous land cover classification and validation datasets used in the Carpathian ecoregion study
Key Findings: Cropland abandonment affected 11% of agricultural land during 1986–2000 and 6% during 2000–2010; recultivation affected ~2% in both periods, abandonment more prevalent in plains but with twice the rate in mountainous areas; abandonment likelihood increased with distance from capital, cooler temperatures, proximity to forest and steeper slopes; recultivation driven by opposite factors, future changes projected to be largely determined by climate and terrain rather than proximity to economic centers
Implications: Satellite-based high-resolution mapping combined with land-use modeling informs land planning and anticipation of environmental and policy impacts
Limitations: Soil depth data unavailable for entire region; assumption of stable protected areas; reliance on continuation of past trends; potential classification inaccuracies
Future Directions: Explore alternative policy and socioeconomic scenarios; incorporate dynamic socioeconomic projections; extend scenario modeling to varied land use pathways
Scalability: Applicable to other Central and Eastern European regions and the broader Carpathian ecoregion with appropriate spatial data
Novelty: First wall-to-wall 30 m Landsat-based mapping of agricultural land use change in Slovakia capturing small-scale changes; synergetic integration of satellite data with boosted regression trees; scenario-based projection to 2060

Title: Agricultural Development and Land Use Change in India: A Scenario Analysis of Trade-Offs Between UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Authors: Hinz, R.; Sulser, T. B.; Huefner, R.; Mason-D'Croz, D.; Dunston, S.; Nautiyal, S.; Ringler, C.; Schuengel, J.; Tikhile, P.; Wimmer, F.; Schaldach, R.
Objective: Analyze pathways of agricultural productivity, land use, and land-cover changes in India until 2030 and their impacts on terrestrial biodiversity and carbon storage
LULC Classes: Cropland (12 crop types); pasture (intensive grazing; man-made pasture); forest; other natural land; set-aside (mosaic subsistence farming and natural vegetation); urban; water
Scenarios: REF_NoCC; REF_HGEM (RCP8.5); MED (intermediate CGIAR R&D + RCP8.5); HIGH+RE (high + efficiency R&D + RCP8.5)
Analysis Methods: Coupled economic–spatial modeling (IMPACT → LandSHIFT); Empirical biodiversity modeling (Biodiversity Intactness Index/GLOBIO MSA factors); IPCC Tier 1 carbon stock change method (soil + vegetation)
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit allocation captures land-cover heterogeneity at ~9 × 9 km cells; Linear coupling of socioeconomic and environmental models enables assessment of trade-offs; Integrates economic drivers, climate impacts, land use, biodiversity, and carbon in one framework
Tools/Soft Used: IMPACT model; LandSHIFT model; DSSAT/MINK crop models; GIS analysis (30 m→5′ raster)
Predictors: Country-level crop and livestock production; crop-specific yield changes; cell-level suitability (potential yields, slope, population density, infrastructure, protected areas)
Data Sources: FAO statistics (harvested area, livestock, GDP, labor force); GlobCover 2009, regional land-cover (Roy et al. 2015); IPCC (soil C stocks), JRC, Ruesch & Gibbs; Jenkins et al. (2013) species richness, GLOBIO MSA factors, HadGEM2-ES climate outputs
Validation Methods: Comparison of LandSHIFT outputs with observed land-cover data; previous model applications for India and other regions
Validation Data Sources: GlobCover 2009; Roy et al. (2015) regional 30 m land-cover
Key Findings: Crop yields ↑41–54% and production ↑43–55% by 2030 across scenarios; Cropland expands 0.9–2.1% and pasture ↑100–155%, largely into set-aside land; BII declines 3.1–5.8% by 2030 (largest loss under HIGH+RE); Agricultural soils become net carbon sink (−35 to −247 MtCO₂/a), especially under HIGH+RE
Implications: Sustainable intensification is crucial to meet food demand while limiting land expansion; Policies must minimize biodiversity losses during intensification and support soil C sequestration
Limitations: Excludes non-vertebrate taxa and functional biodiversity aspects; Neglects CH₄ and N₂O emissions from rice and livestock; Simplified assumptions on intensification pathways and constant cropping intensity; No systematic uncertainty propagation across models
Future Directions: Extend to additional SDGs (water, urbanization, eutrophication); Incorporate insects, plants, soil biota, multiple biodiversity indicators; Process-based ecosystem or feedback coupling between IMPACT and LandSHIFT; Ensemble climate and crop models, systematic sensitivity/uncertainty analysis
Scalability: Framework adaptable to other country-level and global studies, with region-specific data inputs
Novelty: Integrated economic, spatial, biodiversity, and carbon modeling for India’s SDG trade-offs; Scenario analysis combining RCP8.5 climate impact with varied CGIAR R&D investment paths; Use of set-aside mosaic lands as primary conversion domain for agriculture expansion

Title: Assessing the Potential Future Forest-Cover Change in Romania, Predicted Using a Scenario-Based Modelling
Authors: Kucsicsa, Gheorghe; Popovici, Elena-Ana; Balteanu, Dan; Dumitrascu, Monica; Grigorescu, Ines; Mitrica, Bianca
Objective: Analyse the potential future forest-cover change in Romania as a result of land-use/cover scenario in 2007-2050 period, projected according to historical changes registered in 1990-2006 period
LULC Classes: 10 categories aggregated from CORINE Land Cover (CLC) 44 classes: forests; shrub/herbaceous vegetation; pastures; grasslands; arable lands; built-up areas; open spaces; water bodies; wetlands; other categories
Scenarios: Baseline scenario based on extrapolation of linear trend of change registered in 1990-2006 period
Analysis Methods: CLUE-S (Conversion of Land Use and its Effects at Small regional extent) modelling framework; Binary logistic regression; ROC/AUC analysis; Kappa simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Spatially explicit simulation; Combines empirical analysis with dynamic simulation; Multi-scale approach; Widely validated; Handles competition and interactions between land-use systems
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-S model; SPSS (Statistical Package for the Social Sciences); GIS software for spatial analysis
Predictors: 18 biophysical and socio-economic factors including: elevation; slope declivity; precipitation; temperature; horizontal relief fragmentation; total organic matter content; population density; population growth; employment factors; unemployment rate; large livestock units; settlement density; distance to main towns; distance to settlements; secondary roads density; distance to main roads
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover (CLC) database; Digital Elevation Model (DEM); National Meteorological Administration; Population census data; EU-Hydro River Network; ESRI Romania; National Institute of Statistics
Validation Methods: K Simulation (extension of Kappa Index); ROC/AUC analysis; Pixel-based comparison; Contingency table analysis
Validation Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover 2012 dataset as reference data
Key Findings: Projected slight increase in forest-cover area of about 82,000 ha; Widespread deforestation mainly related to agricultural land expansion; Forest gains higher than losses by 21% in baseline period; ROC/AUC values 0.83-0.88 indicating good predictive power; K Simulation scores 0.69-0.79 showing model performance
Implications: Useful inputs for effective forest resource management and environmental policies; Spatial data can contribute to exploring future environmental implications; Assessment of landslide and flood hazard scenarios; Forest biomass dynamics and carbon allocation impacts; Impact on ecosystem services
Limitations: Errors associated with the model and accuracy of spatial/statistical data; Uncertainties related to conversion type and position of forest-cover change; Assumption of constant determinant factors over time; Limited incorporation of social, political and economic factors due to data availability
Future Directions: Examine interaction of forest-cover change and carbon allocation; Evaluate impact on landscape diversity and biodiversity; Assess implications for ecosystem services; Implement more accurate scenarios by integrating other significant determinant factors; Upgrade data according to biophysical and socioeconomic changes
Scalability: High; CLUE-S model has been extensively used across wide range of scales and applications globally, Method applicable to other regions with similar data availability and post-socialist transition contexts
Novelty: First comprehensive forest-cover change projection for Romania at development region level; Application of CLUE-S framework to post-socialist land-use transitions; Integration of 18 biophysical and socio-economic factors; Long-term projection (2007-2050) based on post-1990 transition dynamics

Title: Climate Change Policy Implications of Sustainable Development Pathways in Korea at Sub-National Scale
Authors: Chae, Yeora; Choi, Seo Hyung; Kim, Yong Jee
Objective: To investigate the climate change policy impact of socio-economic development pathways by developing three Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSPs) at the sub-national level in Korea and analyzing their implications for climate change mitigation and adaptation policies using quantitative scenarios
LULC Classes: Urban; agriculture; forest; others
Baseline Years: 2013 (reference year for population); 2010 (reference year for economic indicators)
Scenarios: Three Shared Socio-economic Pathways - SSP1 (low carbon adaptation-ready society), SSP2 (business as usual), SSP3 (high carbon adaptation-unready society); combined with Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP2.6, RCP4.5, RCP8.5)
Analysis Methods: Cohort component method for population projections; time-series economic modeling based on demand-supply system; Cellular Automata (CA) for land-use projection; PAGE-ICE integrated assessment model for climate impact analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Cellular Automata enables spatially explicit modeling of land-use change patterns based on neighborhood interactions and transition rules; provides high-resolution (30m × 30m) grid-based simulations with approximately 169,000,000 cells
Tools/Soft Used: PAGE-ICE (Policy Analysis of Greenhouse Effect) integrated assessment model; Cellular Automata simulation model; cohort component method; time-series economic models
Predictors: Population (fertility rate, mortality rate, migration rate); economy (GDP, productivity, industrial structure); land use (growth coefficient, transition possibility, transition rules); climate scenarios (RCPs)
Data Sources: National statistical data; recent national economic projections; stakeholder participatory workshops; past trend analyses; expert opinions; sector-specific models
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Economic damage from climate change varies significantly across scenarios (0.67% GDP in RCP2.6-SSP1 to 5.47% GDP in RCP8.5-SSP3); population decreases in all scenarios by 2100 (22% in SSP1, 45% in SSP2, 60% in SSP3); GDP increases most in SSP1 (4908 trillion KRW by 2100); tertiary industry share increases most in SSP1 (68.8% by 2100); urban area expansion occurs primarily in SSP3 (18.1% by 2100)
Implications: Sustainable development pathways can reduce mitigation and adaptation policy burden; SSP3 requires more ambitious mitigation policies with higher costs; achieving SDGs generates additional incentives for governments as it reduces climate policy requirements; socio-economic development pathways are key components for determining future climate change impact levels
Limitations: Extended proxies required for sectoral vulnerability assessment; long-term endogenous relationships among variables not sufficiently considered; more systematic scenario development needed for both adaptation and mitigation capacity; limited quantification of sector-specific socio-economic proxies for exposure and adaptation capacity
Future Directions: Identification and quantification of extended proxies for adaptation and mitigation policies; development of sector-specific socio-economic proxies for exposure and adaptation capacity; systematic scenario development considering synergies and trade-offs between adaptation and mitigation policies; coherent scenarios with various perspectives for multifunctional policy development
Scalability: Framework can be applied to other regions with appropriate contextualization; demonstrates importance of regional customization considering local circumstances; methodology transferable but requires region-specific assumptions and data
Novelty: First quantitative development of sub-national SSPs in Korea reflecting Korean contexts; translation of global storylines to national level with region-specific assumptions; integration of climate and socio-economic scenarios using PAGE-ICE model; comprehensive analysis of policy implications across multiple development pathways

Title: Disclosing contrasting scenarios for future land cover in Brazil: Results from a high-resolution spatiotemporal model
Authors: Fendrich, Arthur Nicolaus; Barretto, Alberto; de Faria, Vinicius Guidotti; de Bastiani, Fernanda; Tenneson, Karis; Guedes Pinto, Luis Fernando; Sparovek, Gerd
Objective: Construct a model to evaluate the possible consequences of policy actions on land cover dynamics in the near-future at a high-resolution scale
LULC Classes: Natural vegetation (NV); Pasture (PA); Croplands (CR)
Scenarios: Three scenarios based on Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP): S1 (aggressive/RCP8.5-based); S2 (intermediate); S3 (environmentally oriented/RCP4.5-based)
Analysis Methods: Spatiotemporal Generalized Additive Model (GAM) with multinomial distribution
Sim. Method Advantages: Computational efficiency allowing scaling calculations; Captures neighborhood effects and spatial autocorrelation; Handles non-linear relationships between variables
Tools/Soft Used: R (for Generalized Additive Models implementation)
Predictors: Topography (terrain slope and height); Soil properties (cation exchange capacity); Climate data (annual maximum temperature); Distance to transportation corridors; Protected Areas and Indigenous Lands designations
Data Sources: MapBiomas Project collection 3.1 (30m resolution land cover maps); USGS (topography); Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (transportation); Ministry of Environment (Protected Areas)
Validation Methods: Predictive accuracy validation in unobserved locations; Forecasting performance validation using 1985-2007 data to forecast 2017; Separate validation for unchanged and changed pixels
Validation Data Sources: Half of the sampled dataset (33,000 points) reserved for validation
Key Findings: Considerable threat to natural vegetation in aggressive scenario (S1) with large impacts on remote Amazonian areas; Historical threats to natural areas could not be stopped in any scenario; High variability of land cover changes despite short period; Environmental degradation cannot be prevented without coordinated agency efforts
Implications: Environmental gains cannot be achieved without coordinated efforts between public agencies with conflicting development views; Need for science-based decision-making for conservation actions; Results can guide licensing guidelines and new legislation
Limitations: Need for disaggregation into more detailed land cover categories; Unavailability of detailed remote-sensed data at high resolution; Computational costs requiring data sampling
Future Directions: Disaggregate land cover classes into more detailed categories; Improve incorporation of equilibrium models; Better model economic responses to policy changes; Overcome theoretical challenges for scalable disaggregation
Scalability: Model framework can be applied to other regions with appropriate data and spatial drivers
Novelty: High-resolution (30m) spatiotemporal modeling at national scale, Use of bivariate splines for spatial autocorrelation, Probabilistic approach rather than categorical land cover mapping, Integration of policy scenarios with land cover modeling; This study represents a significant contribution to land use modeling by providing high-resolution forecasting capabilities that can inform policy decisions regarding Brazil's environmental future. The research demonstrates that even environmentally oriented scenarios cannot fully prevent natural vegetation loss, highlighting the critical need for coordinated conservation efforts across multiple government agencies with often conflicting development priorities.

Title: How Effective Is Spatial Planning for Cropland Protection? An Assessment Based on Land-Use Scenarios
Authors: Tobias, Silvia; Price, Bronwyn
Objective: To assess whether the new spatial planning regulations (revised planning act 2014) would better protect dedicated prime cropland from conversion to urban areas using land-use suitability models and land-use scenarios
LULC Classes: Urban area; arable agricultural land; prime cropland; construction zones
Scenarios: Trend Scenario (linear extrapolation of observed trends); small urban extension (12.5% population growth, 407 m² per capita); medium urban extension (12.5% population growth, 407 m² per capita with regionalization); large urban extension (25.2% population growth, 509 m² per capita); B1 scenario (excluded from analysis)
Analysis Methods: Land-use suitability models; GLM (Generalized Linear Models) modeling; Dyna-CLUE spatially explicit land-use allocation modeling framework; scenario modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows ex-ante exploration of consequences of potential policy interventions; enables visualization of planning decision consequences; can incorporate existing and potential policy interventions; key tools for understanding potential trajectories of change and managing uncertainty
Tools/Soft Used: Dyna-CLUE modeling framework; GLM modeling
Predictors: Climate (continentality index, yearly moisture index, precipitation, solar radiation); topography (altitude, inclination); soil (suitability for agricultural management, permeability, stoniness); infrastructure/neighborhood (distance to forest and roads); socio-economic parameters (public transport accessibility, percentage of residents in primary sector)
Data Sources: Swiss land-use statistics; Swiss Federal Statistical Office population growth scenarios; cantonal comprehensive plans; vector data 1:200,000 and 1:25,000
Validation Methods: Figure of merit calculation; ability to reproduce observed land-use changes over period 1985-2009 with figure of merit of 0.902
Validation Data Sources: Swiss land-use statistics for observed land-use changes 1985-2009
Key Findings: New planning regulations reduce potential consumption of prime cropland by six times compared to past trends; 10 out of 26 cantons could drop below mandatory prime cropland quota; conflicts most likely near urban areas; compensation possible through undeveloped construction zones with high arable suitability (19,548 ha available, four times larger than potential new construction zones on prime cropland)
Implications: Risk to food security and agricultural self-sufficiency; need for strict implementation of planning measures; potential for trans-cantonal compensation mechanisms; effectiveness of spatial planning in reducing urban growth rate; need for restrictive assignment of new urban areas to safeguard fertile soils
Limitations: Assumption that new constructions will be located according to highest urban suitability may not be realistic due to political, financial, and social factors; models based on rough resolution soil data; extrapolation of past trends does not address causal relationships; assumptions of population growth and land-take per capita may differ from cantonal plans
Future Directions: Further development of land-use scenarios for policy evaluation; need for detailed large-scale soil mapping campaigns (1:5000 scale); development of exchange markets for prime cropland quota and development rights; determination of distinct regions for tradeable development rights
Scalability: Model can be applied for a whole country including urban and rural areas; approach uses open data which simplifies application to other regions; method transferable to other countries with similar spatial planning challenges
Novelty: Development of approach to a priori evaluate spatial planning measures; method to compare potential performance of spatial plans with past urbanization trends; integration of land-use suitability models with scenario modeling for policy evaluation; first comprehensive assessment of Switzerland's revised spatial planning act effectiveness

Title: Modelling the impact of climate change on Tanzanian forests
Authors: John, Elikana; Bunting, Pete; Hardy, Andy; Roberts, Osian; Giliba, Richard; Silayo, Dos Santos
Objective: Climate change is pressing extra strain on the already degraded forest ecosystem in Tanzania. However, it is mostly unknown how climate change will affect the distribution of forests in the future. We aimed to model the impacts of climate change on natural forests to help inform national-level conservation and mitigation strategies.
LULC Classes: Montane forest; Lowland forest; Mangrove forest; Closed woodland; Open woodland; Thicket
Scenarios: RCP 4.5; RCP 8.5
Analysis Methods: Maximum entropy (MaxEnt) modelling; Habitat suitability modelling
Sim. Method Advantages: Successfully predicts forest species habitat suitability under current and future climate scenarios; Relies on detecting shared patterns of environment response for sparsely recorded species
