Tools/Soft Used: MaxEnt software version 3.4.1; QGIS 3.6; Remote Sensing and GIS software library (RSGISLib)
Predictors: Mean annual precipitation; Rainfall driest month; Mean annual temperature; Elevation; Terrain ruggedness index; Soil types; Potential evapotranspiration; Annual moisture index
Data Sources: National Forest Resources Monitoring and Assessment (NAFORMA) 2015; KITE dataset (AFRICLIM); Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM); World Soil Information (ISRIC)
Validation Methods: Area under the curve (AUC) of receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves; Cross-validation (75% calibration, 25% validation); Overall accuracy; F1 score index; Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)
Validation Data Sources: Independent forest tree species data removed during spatial rarefication process (57,901 points)
Key Findings: Climate change will threaten forest communities, especially montane forests; Montane forests projected to almost halve by 2085; Microhabitat forests (thickets) face losses exceeding 70%; Mangroves predicted to expand by 40%; Lowland forests and woodlands will decrease
Implications: Need for shift in conservation efforts; Enhanced management of existing protected areas; Expanding conservation efforts to newly suitable regions; Effective land use planning and land reclamation; Preserving forest connectivity between fragmented patches
Limitations: Uncertainties of data and climate models; Results should be interpreted at national scale rather than regional or local scale; Does not consider sea-level rise impact on mangroves; Limited anthropogenic factors consideration
Future Directions: Consider spatial patterns of change including proximity to urban centres and road networks; Include population growth projections; Explicitly consider sea-level rise and geomorphology impacts on mangroves; Incorporate anthropogenic factors
Scalability: Methodology is scalable and tractable for national, regional, and global decision-making
Novelty: First comprehensive national-scale modeling of climate change impacts on Tanzanian forests using National Forest Inventory data; Integration of MaxEnt modeling with 19,000+ forest observations; Comprehensive assessment of multiple forest types simultaneously

Title: Projections of land use changes under the plant functional type classification in different SSP-RCP scenarios in China
Authors: Liao, Weilin; Liu, Xiaoping; Xu, Xiyun; Chen, Guangzhao; Liang, Xun; Zhang, Honghui; Li, Xia
Objective: To generate a high-resolution land use product with the newest integrated scenarios of SSP-RCPs for regional climate studies in China using the FLUS model and PFT classification
LULC Classes: Forest; Grassland; Cropland; Urban; Barren; Water (six major classes), further expanded to 17 Plant Functional Types (PFTs)
Scenarios: Eight SSP-RCP scenarios: SSP1-1.9; SSP1-2.6; SSP2-4.5; SSP3-7.0; SSP4-3.4; SSP4-6.0; SSP5-3.4-OS; SSP5-8.5
Analysis Methods: Future Land Uses Simulation (FLUS) model; Cellular Automata (CA) approach; Artificial Neural Networks (ANN); Self-adaptive inertia mechanism; Roulette selection mechanism; Plant Functional Type (PFT) classification
Sim. Method Advantages: Overcomes complexity of multi-type land use transitions; Combines bottom-up CA and top-down demand projection; Incorporates natural and human effects; Uses self-adaptive inertia mechanism for auto-adjustment; Implements roulette selection for uncertainty reflection; Handles nonlinear relationships between driving factors
Tools/Soft Used: Future Land Uses Simulation (FLUS) model; Artificial Neural Networks (ANN); Cellular Automata (CA) framework
Predictors: Natural forces: DEM; Slope; Soil quality; Temperature (annual mean, seasonality, annual range); Precipitation (annual, seasonality); Socioeconomic forces: Population; GDP; Distance forces: Distance to cities; Distance to roads; Distance to rivers; Distance to ocean
Data Sources: Primary: LUH2 datasets; MODIS Land Cover Type Product (MCD12Q1); Secondary: LandScan 2010 Global Population Project; GDP data; Climate data; Soil quality data; DEM data; Roads data; Rivers and ocean data
Validation Methods: Figure of Merit (FoM) index; Historical simulation validation (2001-2015); Comparison with observed land use maps; Model accuracy assessment using Mean Square Error (MSE) for ANN training
Validation Data Sources: 2001 and 2015 MODIS land use maps; Historical land use change observations
Key Findings: Land use dynamics under different SSP-RCP scenarios are jointly affected by global assumptions and national policies, Improved spatial resolution better captures spatial heterogeneity, Different scenarios show distinct patterns; SSP1 emphasizes eco-friendly development with forest increase, SSP3 shows higher agricultural land demand, SSP5 shows rapid urban expansion, China's trends sometimes differ from global trends due to national policies
Implications: High-resolution land use projections have strong potential for reducing uncertainty in regional climate model simulations; Can better assess mitigation effectiveness at regional and local scales; Provides crucial input for climate, hydrological, and biogeochemical models; Enables more accurate evaluation of land use management practices and policies
Limitations: Mapping relation for PFT disaggregation is based only on historical datasets and not temporally dynamic; Urban shrinkage is difficult to observe at 1-km spatial scale; Distribution of vegetation species changes under climate change not fully considered; Land use simulations treat China as whole region rather than sub-regional differences; Actual policy factors not directly incorporated into simulations
Future Directions: Develop more comprehensive links considering spatial changes of vegetation species under dynamic climate feedbacks; Use actual models (e.g., GCAM) to create simulations for specific policy factors; Consider sub-regional differences within China; Improve temporal dynamics of vegetation distribution mapping
Scalability: The methodology can be applied to other regions with appropriate regional data and scenario adaptations; FLUS model has been successfully applied globally; Framework transferable with region-specific driving factors and land use demands
Novelty: First to generate land use projections over China based on PFT classification for eight SSP-RCP scenarios, High-resolution (5 km) land use projections with temporal resolution of 5 years, Integration of newest SSP-RCP scenarios with advanced FLUS model, Bridging gap between land use simulation and climate models through PFT classification; This comprehensive analysis reveals a significant methodological advancement in land use projection modeling for China, addressing the critical gap between coarse-resolution global datasets and the fine-resolution requirements of regional climate models. The study's integration of SSP-RCP scenarios with the FLUS model and Plant Functional Type classification represents a novel approach that enhances the spatial and temporal resolution of land use projections while maintaining compatibility with Earth System Models.

Title: Spatially-explicit modeling and intensity analysis of China's land use change 2000-2050
Authors: Feng, Yongjiu; Lei, Zhenkun; Tong, Xiaohua; Gao, Chen; Chen, Shurui; Wang, Jiafeng; Wang, Siqin
Objective: Project and analyze long-term land use scenarios critical for land use planning and policymaking; Address three critical questions regarding land use change in China (2000-2050): (1) long-term projections at high resolution (2) land conversions among cultivated, forest and built-up lands (3) urbanization impacts on cultivated land and CLRLR policy
LULC Classes: Cultivated; Forest; Grass; Wetland; Water; Built-up; Other
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU)
Analysis Methods: LandCA model; Cellular Automata (CA); Intensity Analysis; Logistic regression; Markov chain; Built-up Expansion Intensity (BEI)
Sim. Method Advantages: (1) simulating change of each land use category using different drivers in single model calibration; (2) reporting detailed logistic regression statistics not available in other CA tools; (3) determining land use conversion using roulette method based on transformation probability; (4) employing Markov chain for macro projections
Tools/Soft Used: LandCA model; Cellular Automata (CA)
Predictors: Distance to provincial cities, Distance to prefecture-level cities, Distance to roads & railways, Elevation, Slope, Population density (PPP; persons per pixel)
Data Sources: GlobeLand30 (30m resolution); National Geomatics Center of China; SRTM global terrain data; WorldPop project; Consortium for Spatial Information
Validation Methods: Overall accuracy (94%) and Kappa coefficient (0.92)
Validation Data Sources: GlobeLand30 data (2000-2010)
Key Findings: Land Exchange intensity more than 3 times greater than Quantity intensity (2000-2050); Overall land use change rate will decelerate from 2010-2050; Built-up land growth rate 3.4 times larger during 2000-2010 than 2010-2050; Cultivated land continuously decreases but will not violate CLRLR by 2050; Government's 26% forest cover goal by 2050 may not be achieved
Implications: Provides evidence for land use policy adjustment and amendment; Critical for ensuring food self-sufficiency through high-quality cultivated land protection; Guides sustainable urban development; Supports assessment of long-term environmental impacts
Limitations: Complex to simulate long-term land use change due to multiple drivers; Limited to seven factors which may compromise predictive ability; Challenging to provide statistical significance of spatial forecasts; Based on BAU scheme only; Lack of anthropogenic activities and climate change factors
Future Directions: Develop new methods to examine significance level of projections; Conduct multi-scenario projections considering anthropogenic activities and climate change; Include more comprehensive driving factors
Scalability: Yes; modeling workflow can be applied to land use projections in other geographic contexts, yielding insights for urban governors and regulators
Novelty: Novel LandCA model integrating remote sensing images and vector datasets; New land-use-change CA model with enhanced functionality; Contributes new evaluations of long-term land use change in China; First to conduct long-term spatially-explicit modeling with Intensity Analysis for China

Title: The impact of urbanization on agricultural dynamics: a case study in Belgium
Authors: Beckers, Veronique; Poelmans, L.; Van Rompaey, A.; Dendoncker, N.
Objective: To look at the impact on the agricultural population in the urban fringe of both direct and indirect urbanization
LULC Classes: Residential; Commerce and services; Industry; Unregistered arable land (hobby farming); Agricultural land; Natural areas
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU); Global Economy (GE); Regional Communities (RC)
Analysis Methods: Agent-based modeling; Cellular automata; Constrained cellular automata (CCA); ADAM (Agricultural Dynamics through Agent-based Modelling); Spatially explicit modeling
Sim. Method Advantages: Agent-based models allow looking into the evolution of a population at the level of the agent in a spatially explicit way, keeping track of decisions of farming population with changing characteristics over time; goes beyond simple land take procedure by considering farmer characteristics, farm structure and regional characteristics
Tools/Soft Used: GIS; CCA-based land-use model; ADAM model; Cellular automata modeling; Raster-GIS format processing
Predictors: Farm size; farm type; farm location; farmer age; succession rates; farm profitability; urbanization pressure; land fragmentation; demographic factors
Data Sources: Statistics Belgium; Agricultural census data (2013 and 2016); Corine land cover data; Cadastral information; SIGEC dataset (Wallonia); Landbouwgebruikspercelen dataset (Flanders); Federal Planning Bureau projections
Validation Methods: RRMSE (Root Relative Mean Square Error) validation; Historical data comparison for 2000-2010 period
Validation Data Sources: Historic agricultural data (2000-2010)
Key Findings: Continuous decline of farmers in all scenarios until 2035; Aging farming population and low succession rates drive decline; Higher declines expected in rural-urban fringe areas; Increasing average farm size despite farmland loss; Over 50% loss of farmers expected by 2035 in all scenarios
Implications: Social challenges including farmer bankruptcy and poverty; Environmental challenges including biodiversity loss and landscape simplification; Economic upscaling and consolidation of farming sector; Need for policy interventions to support farm succession
Limitations: Need for improved economic model; Limited behavioural mechanisms; Does not consider changes in crop choices; Does not include yield changes; Linear relationship assumptions may not hold for very long-term simulations
Future Directions: Future research on model improvements; Combination with external economic models; Including farmland abandonment mechanisms; Extension to other regions; Incorporation of crop choice changes and yield variations
Scalability: Mentioned for extension to other regions with similar characteristics
Novelty: Combination of agent-based modeling with cellular automata; Considers both direct and indirect urbanization impacts; Spatially explicit approach; Integration of demographic, economic and spatial factors in agricultural modeling

Title: The Urbanization Run-Up in Italy: From a Qualitative Goal in the Boom Decades to the Present and Future Unsustainability
Authors: Romano, Bernardino; Fiorini, Lorena; Marucci, Alessandro; Zullo, Francesco
Objective: To overcome the information gap on the evolution of urbanized surfaces in Italy between 1950 and 2000 by reconstructing land take dynamics during the post-World War II economic boom period and develop an inferential scenario to 2050
LULC Classes: Urbanized areas; parking areas; streets within neighborhoods; goods storage and handling areas; various other structures; residential buildings; production buildings; commercial buildings; office buildings
Scenarios: Two growth trend scenarios: 1950-1980 rapid growth scenario; 1990-2010 slower growth scenario; 2050 inferential projection scenario based on current trends
Analysis Methods: Digitization of paper maps; geo-referencing of raster maps; building census data processing; mathematical modeling using equations linking urbanized areas to building construction; chronological distribution analysis; ten-year average urban growth rate calculations
Sim. Method Advantages: Novel approach to fill historical data gaps; uses only available data sources; provides unprecedented information on transformation speed during economic boom decades; enables geographical indications previously lacking on national scale; allows for reliable scenario development over longer time periods
Tools/Soft Used: Geographic Information System (GIS) for digitization and geo-referencing; digital mapping technologies; statistical analysis software for demographic and building data processing
Predictors: Number of buildings per construction decade; building construction chronology; cover ratio between built surfaces and private land property; demographic data; urban density; land property sizes
Data Sources: Italian Military Geographic Institute (IGMI) paper maps at 1:25,000 scale (1949-1962); Regional Land Use Maps (LUM) from aerial photos (2000-2008); ISTAT building census data (1918-2011); ISTAT demographic data (1861-2011); ISPRA-SNPA data for validation
Validation Methods: Comparison with ISPRA 2018 estimates; statistical convergence analysis with different scenario approaches; cross-validation with long-term statistical scenarios developed by ISPRA
Validation Data Sources: ISPRA (Higher Institute for Environmental Protection and Research) data and reports; ISPRA-SNPA monitoring data; European and United Nations land protection guidelines
Key Findings: Land take reached peaks of almost 100 ha/day between 1960-1980; current rate is approximately 40 ha/day; urbanization continues despite population stability; per capita urbanization index has steadily increased; 2050 scenario projects additional 700,000 ha of urbanized land; only mountain and economically weak provinces will retain urbanization density below 2% by 2050
Implications: Italy faces territorial emergency due to excessive urbanization pressure; urgent need for national and regional legislation; current municipal-level planning is insufficient; need for centralized monitoring and control systems; risk of reaching 13% national urbanization density without intervention
Limitations: Significant approximations in matching building-covered surfaces with urbanized areas; cover ratio variations over time and geography; lack of detailed building type differentiation; reliance on fragmented historical data sources; tolerance issues in regional data compatibility
Future Directions: Need for more detailed building/urbanized area type data; implementation of standardized regional monitoring systems; development of national legislation framework; creation of regional control rooms for planning coordination; extension of methodology to other territorial levels
Scalability: Methodology could be applied to other countries experiencing rapid urban growth; requires systematic data collection on urbanized surfaces; applicable at various territorial levels with appropriate data standardization; transferable to regions with similar data availability constraints
Novelty: First study to reconstruct comprehensive land take scenario between 1950s-2000 with seven temporal sections; unique methodology linking building census data to urbanized area evolution; unprecedented historical analysis of Italy's post-WWII urbanization boom; novel approach to overcoming data availability limitations for historical urban development analysis

Title: Using a hybrid demand-allocation algorithm to enable distributional analysis of land use change patterns
Authors: Brooks, Evan B.; Coulston, John W.; Riitters, Kurt H.; Wear, David N.
Objective: To develop a technique to translate coarse-scale land use change projections to a finer spatial grain in support of the RPA assessment, specifically to generate multiple spatial realizations for distributional analysis of land use change patterns
LULC Classes: Developed; Forest; Agriculture; Water; Other
Scenarios: 20 curated scenarios combining climate influence and socioeconomic storylines from IPCC; baseline scenario with fixed climate and single socioeconomic storyline used for demonstration
Analysis Methods: Hybrid demand-allocation algorithm; Random forest models; Seeding algorithm with stochastic patch generation
Sim. Method Advantages: Model continuum from simple random allocation to contagious allocation allowing user control over conversion strictness; Efficiently generate multiple spatial realizations for distributional analysis; Tunable stochastic process for creating library of projected allocations rather than single outcomes
Tools/Soft Used: Random forest algorithm; FORE-SCE (referenced); Custom demand-allocation algorithm
Predictors: T1 land use state; geophysical variables; land use pattern variables; legal variables; elevation; slope; percent land use in 3x3 windows
Data Sources: National Land Cover Datasets (NLCD) 2001, 2006, 2011; US Census Bureau; USDA Forest Service; RPA assessment data
Validation Methods: Comparison of forest fragmentation patterns from realizations with observed 2011 forest fragmentation; Coverage assessment of observed values by distribution of realizations at multiple spatial scales
Validation Data Sources: NLCD 2011 land use data; Observed forest fragmentation patterns at county, state, and regional scales
Key Findings: Realizations based on seeding sample sizes n ≤ 256 generally covered observed forest fragmentation at regional scales for approximately 70% of assessed cases; Algorithm successfully generates multiple spatial realizations for distributional analysis; Approach enables separation of scenario-based vs. allocation-based variability; Coverage was ~83% when excluding rare forest cases
Implications: Enables fine-scale analysis of ecosystem services and ecological indicators; Supports distribution-based analyses of projected land use patterns; Provides uncertainty quantification for land use projections; Informs land use policy and ecosystem service assessments; Facilitates analysis of timing and variability of landscape patterns
Limitations: Algorithm realizations best used when pattern metrics are aggregated to county or coarser scales; Simplified assumptions made for computational efficiency; Stability of transition models over time unknown; Some cases did not cover observed fragmentation (especially rare forest class); Higher miss rate in Great Plains subregion
Future Directions: Compare transition models across different time periods using NLCD 2016 data; Explore bootstrapping approach for patch size selection; Develop data-driven methods for selecting seeding sample size; Explore multiple random forest models for additional variation; Investigate model stability over time
Scalability: Yes; approach designed for national scales and expected to be applicable globally, demonstrated at continental scale with computational tractability
Novelty: First algorithm specifically designed to generate multiple realizations for distributional analysis rather than single outcomes; Tunable continuum from random to contagious allocation; Hybrid seeding approach with data-driven patch growth; Focus on within-scenario variability in addition to between-scenario differences

Title: A simple grid-based framework for simulating forest structural trajectories linked to transient forest management scenarios in Fennoscandia
Authors: Majasalmi, Titta; Allen, Micky; Anton-Fernandez, Clara; Astrup, Rasmus; Bright, Ryan M.
Objective: Present a simple grid-based framework (F2S2) for predicting time-dependent forest structural trajectories compatible with land models employed in regional climate and hydrological research
LULC Classes: spruce, pine, and deciduous; Four forest development classes (1-4)
Scenarios: Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP4.5, RCP8.5); Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSP1, SSP5); Two management intensities (BAU, H)
Analysis Methods: Four-dimensional k-means clustering; Ordinary least squares regression; SiTree single tree simulator; Simple Forest Dynamics (SFD) models
Sim. Method Advantages: i) the initial mapping if forest structure is based on high resolution (i.e. pixel resolution of ~ 30 m) MSNFI data, ii) the 0.0028° resolution of our map product allows spatial allocation of forest management actions (e.g. for 61.1° N and 10.5° E in Norway, pixel size of our product is 4.7 ha whereas using 0.5° map products commonly applied in LSMs, the respective pixel size would be 14,939 ha), iii) the use of simplified forest dynamics models (SFD), which combine the effects of forest management and temperature, are quick to adapt to new regions and classifications, as they can be calibrated using data simulated from NFI inputs.
Tools/Soft Used: SiTree; R statistical software; F2S2 (Fennoscandic Forest State Simulator)
Predictors: maximum leaf area index (LAI, m /m ), Lorey's height (m), tree crown length (m), and volume density (m /ha)
Data Sources: Norwegian National Forest Inventory (NNFI); Multi-source National Forest Inventory (MS-NFI); European Space Agency's CCI Land Cover product; EURO-CORDEX regional climate model simulations
Validation Methods: Statistical validation using R² values; Model significance testing (p < 0.005)
Validation Data Sources: Norwegian National Forest Inventory (NNFI) data; SiTree simulation results
Key Findings: Climate has the strongest influence on forest structural development; Higher harvesting intensity decreases the area of most-developed class (c4) across all species; Warming climate results in faster forest development class transitions; Management effect has larger influence on pine than spruce dominated areas
Implications: Forest management plays important role in shaping forest structures; Need for strategies to increase forest area and flexibility in species harvest demands; Climate warming affects forest LAI development patterns
Limitations: it cannot be used in regions without established NFI inventories due to the need for regional calibration.
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Limited to regions with established NFI inventories; Suitable for regional climate modeling studies; Not applicable for global modeling studies
Novelty: First method to dynamically map forest structure in space and time compatible with land surface or hydrological models employing sub-grid tiling

Title: Agricultural expansion in Uruguayan grasslands and priority areas for vertebrate and woody plant conservation
Authors: Brazeiro, Alejandro; Achkar, Marcel; Toranza, Carolina; Bartesaghi, Lucia
Objective: To study the vulnerability of vertebrate and woody plant diversity to the loss of grassland areas, driven by agricultural and forestry expansion, to identify priority areas for conservation in Uruguay
LULC Classes: Cultivated and managed terrestrial areas; artificial surfaces and associated areas; artificial waterbodies, snow, and ice; cultivated aquatic or regularly flooded areas; natural and seminatural vegetation; natural and seminatural aquatic or regularly flooded vegetation; bare areas; natural waterbodies, snow, and ice. Main focus on croplands (especially soybean) and exotic forest plantations (Eucalyptus and Pinus)
Baseline Years: 1990, 2000, 2008, 2011, 2015 (with 2015 as primary baseline for current assessment)
Scenarios: Single target scenario for 2030 based on national production goals proposed by Office of Planning and Budget (OPP) of Uruguay, projecting expansion of soybean crops and exotic forest plantations
Analysis Methods: Vulnerability index calculation as weighted sum of grassland species richness (40%) and focal grassland species richness (60%); spatial prioritization using 17% threshold following Aichi Target 11; two-phase land-use modeling approach with downscaling procedure; geoprocessing and spatial analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: QGIS 2.18
Predictors: Soil suitability for agriculture (highly suitable, suitable, marginally suitable, unsuitable); proximity to consolidated agricultural regions; forestry priority areas; proximity to established forestry regions; proximity to cellulose pulp plants; international commodity prices (soybean, wood pulp)
Data Sources: Official agricultural census (1990, 2000, 2011) from DIEA; National forest inventories (1990, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015) from Forest Department; Land-cover maps (2000, 2008, 2011, 2015) from Ministry of Environment (MVOTMA); LANDSAT 5TM scenes; Species database from Brazeiro et al. (2015b) with 853 species; Soils Map of Uruguay (1:1,000,000)
Validation Methods: Field verification of land-cover classification
Validation Data Sources: Field surveys and ground-truthing for land-cover classification accuracy assessment
Key Findings: 36.2% of Uruguay's original territory was converted by 2015 (27.5% croplands, 7.9% exotic forest plantations, 0.8% urban); 51 priority cells (17% of territory) identified for conservation; 27% of priority cells already transformed by 2015; Projected 48.7% habitat loss by 2030 with 45% of priority cells affected; Half of vertebrate and woody plant species (431 of 853) use grassland habitats; 95 focal species of conservation concern identified
Implications: Urgent need to develop strategies to reduce grassland loss rate; Conservation efforts should focus on prioritized cells with no protection status and high conversion likelihood; Need to expand public and private protected areas; Promote wildlife-friendly agricultural alternatives like sustainable beef production; Integrate agricultural and environmental policies; Need private sector involvement in conservation
Limitations: Study focused only on woody plants and terrestrial vertebrates, excluding herbaceous flora which is a representative component of grassland ecosystems; Unknown extinction thresholds for individual species; Limited economic resources for protected area system expansion; Difficulty in promoting sustainable practices in soybean sector due to short production cycles and tenant farming
Future Directions: Incorporate herbaceous flora in future vulnerability analyses; Expand National System of Protected Areas; Develop wildlife-friendly agricultural practices; Promote beef production certification under sustainability protocols; Implement private reserves in forestry areas; Find strategies for sustainable soybean production; Integrate agricultural and environmental policies through Watershed Management Committees
Scalability: Methodology applicable to other regions of the Río de la Plata Grasslands (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay); Approach relevant for other temperate grassland regions globally facing agricultural expansion pressures
Novelty: First comprehensive vulnerability assessment of vertebrate and woody plant diversity to agricultural expansion in Uruguay; Integration of biodiversity vulnerability with spatial prioritization for conservation planning; Projection of future land-use scenarios based on national production goals; Focus on grassland ecosystem conservation in context of agricultural intensification

Title: Alternative pathways to a sustainable future lead to contrasting biodiversity responses
Authors: Martins, Ines S.; Navarro, Laetitia M.; Pereira, Henrique M.; Rosa, Isabel M. D.
Objective: Quantify future changes in breeding bird species richness including changes in richness of three functional species groups (forest species, farmland species and species with affinity for other natural habitats) under distinct positive land-use change scenarios; compare national and grid cell level species responses; evaluate which species groups will experience the most changes across regions; identify regions where changing management strategy could have largest effects
LULC Classes: Intensive agriculture; intensive forest; extensive agriculture; extensive forest; other natural
Scenarios: Pathway A (technological improvements/land-sparing approach); Pathway B (societal transformation/land-sharing approach); Pathway 0 (business-as-usual/historical trends)
Analysis Methods: Countryside species-area relationship (cSAR) model; spatially-explicit land-use projections; biodiversity modeling using functional species groups
Sim. Method Advantages: Accounts for species' ability to persist in human-modified habitats; outperforms traditional SAR approaches in describing species numbers in human-modified landscapes; considers differential habitat affinities
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.2 (ESRI, 2014); countryside SAR model; spatially-explicit land-use change model
Predictors: Socio-economic dynamics; presence of roads; topographic features; climatic features; land-use transitions based on pathway assumptions
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover Map 2012; forest tree species distribution map from 2010 national forest inventory; national statistics on agricultural areas; National Forest Inventory (1990-2010); national Agricultural Census; EU FP7 PATHWAYS project narratives
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Alpha and gamma diversity projected to increase in Pathways A and B, decrease in Pathway 0; Pathway A shows highest biodiversity change rates (+0.73 sp. local, +1.54 sp. national); Pathway B shows moderate changes (+0.33 sp. local, +0.63 sp. national); Different pathways favor different species groups with strong regional differences; Pathway A: forest and other species increase, farmland species decrease; Pathway B: farmland species increase, forest and other species decrease; Baseline 2010: 60.9% extensive use, 20.8% intensive use, 18.3% natural areas

Future Directions: Future studies should aim for more integrative approaches capturing changes in abundance and community structure; need to account for climate change interactions; consider fragmentation effects; develop approaches that capture temporal biodiversity changes
Scalability: Framework could be used to assess biodiversity-friendly land-use decisions in other countries; could support prioritization exercises and conservation actions at larger scales; approach applicable for cross-country analyses and coordination efforts
Novelty: Use of countryside SAR model that accounts for species persistence in human-modified habitats; spatially-explicit cross-scale approach; consideration of multiple sustainable pathways with different transformational changes; focus on functional species groups rather than total richness only

Title: Brazilian Cerrado and Soy moratorium: Effects on biome preservation and consequences on grain production
Authors: Magalhaes, Iara Barbosa; Aona de Paula Pereira, Alexia Saleme; Calijuri, Maria Lucia; Alves, Sabrina do Carmo; dos Santos, Vitor Juste; Lorentz, Juliana Ferreira
Objective: To study the comparison of the Soy Moratorium influence for two scenarios: a temporal analysis of change trends prior to the implementation of this policy for 2012; and an impact analysis on the Cerrado policy extension for 2028
LULC Classes: Vegetation; Pasture; Agriculture; Forest Plantation; Urban Infrastructure; Rivers, Lakes and Ocean; Mosaic of Agriculture and Pasture
Scenarios: Real scenario vs. modeled scenario without Moratorium for 2012; Business as usual scenario (maintaining current conditions without Cerrado Moratorium extension); Extension of the moratorium to the Cerrado with 100% conservation of Vegetation class
Analysis Methods: Land Change Modeler (LCM); Crosstab Algorithm; Kappa coefficient; Evidence Likelihood tool; Hard prediction; Polynomial trend surface analysis (5th degree equation)
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Land Change Modeler (LCM); Evidence Likelihood tool
Predictors: Land use transitions; Burned Areas; Deforestation; Open Land Value mapping (OLV in R$/ha); Soybean yield (ton/ha by municipality); Fire areas; Anthropogenic disturbances

Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient; Accuracy calculation; Crosstab Algorithm
Validation Data Sources: 2006 prediction map validation; 2012 prediction validation; 2017 validation analysis
Key Findings: The Soy Moratorium influenced the spatial distribution of agricultural transitions rather than quantity; In a No-Moratorium scenario, agricultural areas in Mato Grosso would increase by 18.08% (0.955 million hectares); The focus of agricultural change shifted from Amazon border regions to Matopiba region; Agriculture and Pasture classes contributed majorly to vegetation suppression (over 500,000 ha); Extension of Cerrado Moratorium is feasible while meeting 2028 production goals; Both conservation scenarios exceed OECD 2028 estimates for soybean production
Implications: Biome vegetation preservation is possible without disregarding economic importance of soybean for Brazil; Reconciling interests between agribusiness and natural resource conservation is one of Brazil's main challenges; Extension of Cerrado Moratorium can contribute to sustainable development of Brazilian soybean production; Need for discussion of public policies addressing deficiencies in current agreements and existing laws
Limitations: Model presented limitations in future projections; Lower explanatory power of variables for transitions modeled; Local trends cannot be ignored but global analysis is less suited for local cases; Limited comprehension of variable behavior on local cases; Brazil has sparse data context with limited resources and data quality

Novelty: Not specified

Title: Costs and Carbon Sequestration Assessment for REDD plus in Indonesia
Authors: Liu, Guifang; Liu, Qing; Song, Mengxiao; Chen, Junsheng; Zhang, Chuanrong; Meng, Xing; Zhao, Jincai; Lu, Heli
Objective: To evaluate the impacts of carbon sequestration from plantations on opportunity costs of avoided deforestation under REDD+ program implementation, examining two scenarios (with and without consideration of carbon sequestration in plantations)
LULC Classes: Dense forest; Peatland; Sparse forest; Cropland; Road; Water
Scenarios: Scenario A: without consideration of carbon sequestration in plantations; Scenario B: with consideration of carbon sequestration in plantations
Analysis Methods: Cellular automaton technique for business-as-usual simulation; Gain-loss method for carbon emissions measurement; Opportunity cost assessment; Sensitivity analysis; Maximum likelihood classification (MLC) technique for land use classification
Sim. Method Advantages: Cellular automaton model can capture reasonable spatial patterns of land use change under business-as-usual conditions; Comprises four elements (X, S, N, R) and one important condition allowing for comprehensive spatial modeling of deforestation patterns
Tools/Soft Used: Remote sensing image processing; NDVI data analysis; Supervised classification; Band combination technique; Cellular automaton model
Predictors: Aspect; Elevation; Slope; Soil type; Distance to previously deforested land; Distance to rivers; Distance to roads; Distance to villages
Data Sources: Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus/Thematic Mapper (ETM+/TM) remote sensing images; Field surveys (189 randomly chosen households); In situ forest inventories from Rahajoe; Studies on rubber plantations from Wauters et al.; Oil palm plantation studies from Khasanah et al.; Parameters for carbon pools from Ramankutty et al.
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient calculation; Comparison of simulation results with actual land-use map
Validation Data Sources: Actual land-use map for comparison with simulation results
Key Findings: Opportunity costs in Kalimantan, Indonesia range from 3.5/tCO2 to 19.6/tCO2 with average value of USD 8.56/tCO2; Carbon sequestration from plantations affects opportunity costs less than social discount rates; Oil palm plantations have greater impact on opportunity costs than rubber plantations; Oil palm and rubber plantations generate USD 15.2 million and USD 10.5 million in revenue over 25 years, respectively
Implications: Carbon sequestration contribution from plantations to REDD+ remains limited; Opportunity costs in Southeast Asia will likely increase due to future oil palm expansion; Oil palm plantation expansion significantly increases opportunity costs while rubber plantations have smaller effect; Forest conversion for economically viable plantations puts carbon-rich ecosystems at risk
Limitations: Results yield only opportunity costs of carbon emissions in north Palangka Raya, Kalimantan; Local parameters limit broader applicability; Resolution limitations of satellite sensors required field surveys; Exclusion of carbon sequestration from remaining forest area; Long-term uncertainty about climate change and mitigation costs
Future Directions: Application of the framework to other regions for evaluating plantation carbon sequestration impacts; Development of locally adaptive regulatory frameworks for various climate objectives; Further research on spatially explicit modeling frameworks for REDD+ implementation
Scalability: The study provides a case that can be applied to other regions for evaluating impacts of plantation carbon sequestration and insights that can help local policymakers design financially attractive REDD+ programs in other tropical forests worldwide
Novelty: First study to focus on carbon sequestration impact from agroecosystems on opportunity costs for REDD+; Development of spatially explicit modeling framework capturing reasonable payments under two scenarios reflecting plantation carbon sequestration concerns; Integration of cellular automaton technique with gain-loss method for comprehensive assessment

Title: Detecting changes in irrigation water requirement in Central Asia under CO<sub>2</sub> fertilization and land use changes
Authors: Tian, Jing; Zhang, Yongqiang
