Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; CropWat model
Predictors: precipitation; temperature; DEM; slope; distance to rivers; population density
Data Sources: CMIP5 Global Climate Models; European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative (ESA CCI); Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO); Climatic Research Unit (CRU); Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM)
Validation Methods: Kappa index (achieved 0.84)
Validation Data Sources: Land use data 2015 (predicted vs actual comparison)
Key Findings: Without considering CO2 fertilization leads to large errors in IWR estimation; IWR tends to increase in 2020s-2040s but decrease in 2060s-2080s under RCP2.6; Change magnitude is less than 5% in most areas; Maximum increases of 5-15% for cotton occur in Tajikistan; Maximum increase of more than 50% for winter wheat occurs in Tajikistan
Implications: Severe water security pressure predicted in Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan; Helps decision makers for sensible water management; Important for maintaining sustainable development of agriculture
Limitations: Potential changes of crop growing periods not considered; Fertilizer impacts on IWR not considered; Extreme assumption that either cotton or winter wheat is grown in the whole region
Future Directions: Address limitations regarding crop growing periods and fertilizer impacts
Scalability: Method can be applied at global and regional scales
Novelty: First study to quantify IWR changes in Central Asia under CO2 fertilization; Considers bias correction for regional IWR estimation

Title: Disentangling the potential effects of land-use and climate change on stream conditions
Authors: Maloney, Kelly O.; Krause, Kevin P.; Buchanan, Claire; Hay, Lauren E.; McCabe, Gregory J.; Smith, Zachary M.; Sohl, Terry L.; Young, John A.
Objective: To predict stream biological conditions using the Chesapeake Basin-wide Index of Biotic Integrity (Chessie BIBI) under a suite of land-use and climate projections for the Chesapeake Bay watershed, and determine the percent of stream length improvement needed under different scenarios to improve health and function of 10% of stream miles over a 2008 baseline
LULC Classes: Developed land; agriculture (24.5% of watershed in 2011); hay/pasture; cropland; forest; wetlands; mechanically disturbed land (MechDist); 12 land-cover categories total from 17 original classes
Scenarios: Four IPCC Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES): A1B, A2, B1, and B2 for land-use; Climate scenarios included quartiles of CMIP5 (25th, 50th, 75th percentiles) and Lynch2016 uniform scenario; 72 total future scenarios combining land-use and climate projections
Analysis Methods: Random forests analysis; Geographic Information System (GIS) procedures; Statistical downscaling of climate models; Bootstrap approach for Chessie BIBI calculation
Sim. Method Advantages: Random forests are well suited for predicting stream condition scores because they can use continuous and categorical predictors, often perform exceptionally compared to other methods, are relatively insensitive to correlated covariates, and account for nonlinear relationships and complex interactions among predictors
Tools/Soft Used: R Statistical Software Package version 3.6.0; randomForest R package; ArcGIS 10.6; NHDPlusV2 Catchment Attribute Allocation and Accumulation Tool (CA3TV2)
Predictors: 36 predictors total including: upstream cumulative watershed area; elevation; seven soil predictors (water depth, organic matter content, permeability, depth to bedrock, clay content, sand content, soil erodibility); three geochemical measures (calcium oxide, hydraulic conductivity, compressive strength); runoff and baseflow index; topographic wetness index; 12 land-use/land-cover categories; seasonal temperature and precipitation; dominant bioregion
Data Sources: Chesapeake Basin-wide Index of Biotic Integrity (Chessie BIBI) from 21,343 sampling events; National Hydrography Dataset Version 2 (NHDPlusV2); StreamCat database; PRISM climate data; FORE-SCE land-use projections; CMIP5 climate projections; National Land Cover Database (NLCD)
Validation Methods: Model divided into training (75%, n=2,775) and test (25%, n=925) datasets; Percent correctly classified (PCC) and Kappa statistic calculated; Temporal consistency testing using separate models for 2000-2005 and 2006-2011 periods
Validation Data Sources: Same Chessie BIBI dataset split into training and test portions; separate temporal validation using 2000-2005 and 2006-2011 data subsets
Key Findings: By 2090, watershed-wide conditions may exhibit degradation ranging from 16.2% (A2 CMIP5 25th percentile) to 1.0% (B2 Lynch2016) of stream kilometers; Combined land-use and climate scenarios showed interactive effects with less degraded conditions than additive effects alone; Meeting and sustaining the 10% stream improvement goal may require improvement in 11.0%-26.2% of stream kilometers depending on scenario
Implications: Restoration costs to reach 10% improvement goal would range between 82.7 and 197.0 million US dollars; Different scenarios require different spatial targeting approaches; Early climate and population changes in this region make it an important test case for global freshwater impacts; Results highlight need for adaptive management strategies
Limitations: Coarse resolution of land-use (250m) and climate (800m) data; Limited to four SRES scenarios; Temporal aggregation of seasonal data is oversimplified; Novel climate conditions in future may exceed model training data range; Contemporary relationships assumed to hold in future; Lack of biologically relevant instream temperature and flow metrics
Future Directions: Need for longer-term data to test temporal consistency; Development of spatially explicit RCP and SSP scenarios for the watershed; Integration of more biologically relevant climate metrics; Investigation of interactive effects across different abiotic conditions
Scalability: High; the Chesapeake Bay watershed serves as an early case study for other regions given expected relatively early temperature changes and population growth, Results provide framework for other regions facing similar land-use and climate uncertainties
Novelty: First study to simultaneously investigate land-use and climate change interactions on stream conditions using multiple scenarios in the Chesapeake Bay watershed; Novel application of random forests to predict stream biological conditions under future scenarios; Comprehensive multi-scenario approach capturing range of potential future conditions; Integration of downscaled climate projections with spatially explicit land-use scenarios

Title: Downscaling of Long-Term Global Scenarios to Regions with a Forest Sector Model
Authors: Eriksson, Ljusk Ola; Forsell, Nicklas; Eggers, Jeannette; Snall, Tord
Objective: Evaluate the use of a forest sector model to downscale global scenario results to regional level
LULC Classes: Productive forest (NFI plots); sawlogs; pulpwood; residues
Scenarios: RCP4p5.SSP3; RCP2p6.SSP4; RCP2p6.SSP5
Analysis Methods: Partial equilibrium forest sector modelling; downscaling global scenarios with SweFor; two specifications (MaxNSP, MaxNPV)
Sim. Method Advantages: Maintains consistency with global market conditions; Captures economic drivers and spatial detail via NFI plots; Enables regional framework conditions grounded in national/global models
Tools/Soft Used: SweFor (AIMMS); Gurobi solver; Heureka (PlanWise); IIASA GLOBIOM model
Predictors: Harvest volumes; market prices; forest management programs; standing stock; transport distances; facility capacities
Data Sources: GLOBIOM global scenarios; Swedish National Forest Inventory (2012); Heureka/PlanWise for management regimes; facility data from SLU; FAOSTAT (for elasticities)
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: MaxNSP yields smoother national and regional harvest trajectories; MaxNPV better matches imposed national scenario volumes but shows greater temporal variation; Smaller regions exhibit high variation due to limited NFI plots; FSM-based downscaling deviates from constant-share assumption, highlighting regional heterogeneity
Implications: Choice of formulation (MaxNSP vs. MaxNPV) affects regional harvest profiles; Need sufficient plot density or smoothing for small regions; FSM allows more realistic regional framework conditions than simple proportional methods
Limitations: Sparse NFI plot density for small regions leading to volatile results; model inconsistencies between GLOBIOM and SweFor definitions; binding ending-stock constraint
Future Directions: Increase NFI plot sample size or use master areas with matching forest attributes; Introduce smoothing or anchoring constraints for first-period harvests; Enhance harmonization of scenario and national model definitions
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with sufficient inventory data and model harmonization; Requires adaptation of plot network and facility data
Novelty: First investigation of using a forest sector partial equilibrium model to downscale global SSP/RCP scenarios to regional level with explicit economic-forest management linkage

Title: Estimation of Future Changes in Aboveground Forest Carbon Stock in Romania. A Prediction Based on Forest-Cover Pattern Scenario
Authors: Dumitrascu, Monica; Kucsicsa, Gheorghe; Dumitrica, Cristina; Popovici, Elena-Ana; Vrinceanu, Alexandra; Mitrica, Bianca; Mocanu, Irena; Serban, Paul-Razvan
Objective: model potential changes in aboveground forest carbon stock based on a simulated 2050 forest-cover pattern scenario
LULC Classes: forest-cover; agricultural lands; built-up/artificial areas; other CORINE land-cover categories
Baseline Years:
2015 (aboveground forest biomass)
2006 (forest-cover map initial year)
1990; 2000; 2006; 2012 (historical CLC)
Scenarios: forest-cover pattern change scenario simulated by CLUE-S for 2050
Analysis Methods: allometric equations based on dbh–height models; GIS spatial and statistical analysis; Conversion of Land Use and its Effects at Small regional extent (CLUE-S) model; binomial logistic regression for location suitability
Sim. Method Advantages: spatially explicit; integrates biophysical and socio-economic drivers; handles small regional extents with empirical calibration
Tools/Soft Used: SPSS; GIS software (unspecified)
Predictors: elevation; slope declivity; annual precipitation; annual temperature; relief fragmentation; topsoil organic matter; population density; number of employees; unemployment rate; tertiary-sector employment rate; livestock units; built-up/non-agricultural ratio; population growth; settlement density; distance to settlements; distance to main towns; secondary road density; distance to main roads
Data Sources: Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (Forest Type 2015, Tree Cover Density 2015); NASA Carbon Monitoring System (Global Forest Height); CORINE Land Cover (1990, 2000, 2006, 2012); EU-Hydro River Network; Digital Elevation Model (30 m); National Meteorological Administration (1961–2015 climate); Romanian soil atlas (topsoil organic matter); National Institute of Statistics (population, employment); ESRI Romania (road network)
Validation Methods: test-area correlation of predicted vs. observed tree density; pixel-based comparison of observed vs. simulated forest-cover change; Kappa Simulation, Kappa Transition, Kappa TransLoc decomposition
Validation Data Sources: Google Earth high-resolution imagery (tree counts); CORINE Land Cover datasets (1990–2012)
Key Findings: 4% overall increase in aboveground forest carbon stock by 2050; significant regional variation with higher accumulation in mountain regions and losses in plains
Implications: informs ecological and socio-economic policy; guides forest management and climate-mitigation strategies; supports land-use planning
Limitations: uncertainties in biomass estimation and scenario simulation; spatial errors from allometric models; unvalidated remote-sensing biomass map
Future Directions: further validate models with field data; assess ecological, socio-economic, and management responses; refine allometric coefficients; incorporate dynamic disturbance regimes
Scalability: applicable to national-scale assessments in other European temperate/boreal regions
Novelty: first integration of national aboveground biomass model with spatially explicit CLUE-S scenario to project future carbon stock changes in Romania

Title: Modeling changes in China's 2000-2030 carbon stock caused by land use change
Authors: Feng, Yongjiu; Chen, Shurui; Tong, Xiaohua; Lei, Zhenkun; Gao, Chen; Wang, Jiafeng
Objective: Propose a cellular automata (LandCA) model to predict future land use scenarios and estimate China’s terrestrial ecosystem carbon stock change from 2000 to 2030
LULC Classes: Agricultural; Forest; Grass; Shrub; Wetland; Artificial surfaces; Others (tundra, barren land, permanent snow and ice)
Scenarios: Future land use scenarios projected to 2020 and 2030 using the LandCA model
Analysis Methods: Cellular automata modeling; Markov chain; Logistic regression; Inverse distance weighted interpolation; Pearson correlation
Sim. Method Advantages: Includes Markov chains for macro quantitative predictions; models different land‐use types with distinct driving factors; reports detailed logistic regression statistics; uses roulette selection based on transition probabilities
Tools/Soft Used: LandCA tool (built with GDAL); IDW interpolation; Markov chain; GIS processing
Predictors: Distance to provincial capital; Distance to prefecture-level cities; Distance to railways; Distance to road networks; Altitude; Slope; Gross domestic product; Population density
Data Sources: SOC, AGBC, BGBC point data from Xu et al. (2004–2014); GlobeLand30 land use maps (2000, 2010); terrain, administrative boundaries, railways, roads, gridded population from RESDC; policy program records (e.g., Grain-for-Green)
Validation Methods: Cell-by-cell comparison of simulated 2010 land use against actual GlobeLand30 2010; confusion matrix yielding overall accuracy and Kappa coefficient
Validation Data Sources: GlobeLand30 2010 land use dataset
Key Findings: Total carbon stock ≈98 Gt, decreasing by 0.2% from 2000 to 2030; Annual carbon emissions from land use change decline from 13.5 Mt yr⁻¹ (2000–2010) to 2.4 Mt yr⁻¹ (2010–2030); In developed regions, urban expansion causes >25% of regional carbon emissions; In other regions, grassland and forest loss account for >50% of regional carbon emissions; Environmental policies (e.g., Grain-for-Green) increase carbon stock in some subregions
Implications: Findings inform government land use policies and carbon emission reduction strategies; support regulation design to mitigate land use–driven carbon losses
Limitations: Macro land prediction relies solely on historical patterns via Markov chain; omits explicit socioeconomic, policy, and institutional dynamics
Future Directions: Incorporate climatic, socioeconomic, policy, and institutional factors into macro predictions; extend assessment to intercontinental and global scales
Scalability: LandCA framework is transferable to other regions for projecting land use and carbon stock scenarios
Novelty: First study to spatially predict future carbon stock under land use change in China using a bottom-up CA model; integrates Markov chain, per-type driving factors, logistic statistics, and roulette selection mechanism

Title: Modelling Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) in response to climate change scenarios for the SAARC nations
Authors: Singh, Ram Kumar; Sinha, Vinay Shankar Prasad; Joshi, Pawan Kumar; Kumar, Manoj
Country: Afghanistan; Bangladesh; Bhutan; India; Nepal; Maldives; Pakistan; Sri Lanka
Objective: Project future Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use (AFOLU) for SAARC nations under climate change scenarios
LULC Classes: Agriculture; Forestry; Other Land Use
Scenarios: RCP 2.6; RCP 4.5; RCP 6.0; RCP 8.5
Analysis Methods: Markov Chain transition modelling (Land Change Modeler); Multilayer Perceptron Neural Network (MLP-NN) with backpropagation; Cramer’s V for driver explanatory power
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures nonlinear complex relationships between drivers and land-use transitions; Performs better with non-normal data distributions than simple regression; Optimizes transition potential via evidence likelihood maps
Tools/Soft Used: TerrSet Land Change Modeler (Clark Labs)
Predictors: BIO1–BIO19 (annual/seasonal temperature & precipitation metrics); PC-1 of elevation, slope, aspect, curvature (TOPO)
Data Sources: MODIS NDVI (NASA Earth Explorer); WorldClim bioclimatic data; SRTM DEM; NR-Census Land Use–Land Cover (India); IGBP land cover (South Asia, 2016); FAO, IPCC, World Bank, national reports
Validation Methods: Total Operating Characteristic (TOC) / AUC comparison with observed AFOLU
Validation Data Sources: Mnlogit-classified AFOLU (2007 India; 2016 SAARC); Debella-Gilo & Etzelmüller (2009); Seto & Kaufmann (2005)
Key Findings: Agricultural land increases across all SAARC nations under RCP 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, most extreme gain under RCP 8.5 for Sri Lanka and Bangladesh at the expense of forests; Forestry land declines in all scenarios except slight gains in India under moderate RCPs; “Other” land use remains nearly constant
Implications: Informs nation-specific strategies for sustainable land allocation; Supports food security planning under climate uncertainty
Limitations: Coarse 250 m resolution may miss local hotspots (e.g., small afforestation/deforestation patches); Annual AFOLU maps do not distinguish permanent vs. temporary transitions; Anthropogenic drivers (e.g., planned land conversions) not explicitly modelled
Future Directions: Incorporate finer-resolution data and additional human-activity drivers; Differentiate permanent land-use transitions; Extend modelling framework to include socioeconomic variables
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with appropriate local calibration of drivers and training data
Novelty: First comprehensive MLP-NN–based AFOLU projection for all SAARC nations integrating multiple topographic and bioclimatic drivers under four RCP scenarios

Title: Projecting China's future water footprint under the shared socio-economic pathways
Authors: Xu, Xiaocong; Zhang, Yuanying; Chen, Yimin
Objective: Project future water footprint patterns of China at fine resolution under SSP scenarios
LULC Classes: Built-up land; Rural residential land; Urban residential land; Industrial land; Agriculture land; Other land-use types (implicit in conversion cost matrix)
Scenarios: SSP1; SSP2; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: MRIO analysis; Log-transformed linear regression; CA-based Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) model; Artificial Neural Network (BP-ANN); Leontief inverse; Regression significance testing
Sim. Method Advantages: Enables fine-scale spatial heterogeneity; Integrates top-down demand with bottom-up local evolution; Captures nonlinear suitability via ANN; Models stochastic leapfrog growth via roulette mechanism
Tools/Soft Used: ArcMap (ESRI) for driving factor generation; FLUS model implementation; BP-ANN calibration; Statistical software for regression
Predictors: Population; Urbanization rate; Built-up land area
Data Sources: Primary: Interregional Input-Output Tables of China (2007, 2010, 2012), Water resource bulletins, Bulletin of First National Census for Water, China Statistical Yearbook, CAS land use maps (2008, 2010, 2013), NASA SRTM DEM, NCAR SSP population projections; Secondary: Distance to cities/railways/rivers, Expert-assigned conversion costs
Validation Methods: Historical simulation (2008–2013) comparison; Figure of Merit (FoM) metric
Validation Data Sources: CAS land use map for 2013; Stratified sampling of observed land-use change
Key Findings: China’s water footprint rose 35.5% (2007–2012); Projected 2050 footprint up to ~400 billion m³ under SSP1/4/5 (~40%↑); Eastern provinces (Shandong, Henan, Hebei) increase 100–130%; Western provinces (Xinjiang, Ningxia, Qinghai) decrease; Similar hotspot patterns across SSPs in BTH, YRD, PRD
Implications: Future water scarcity and spatial inequality will intensify; Urgent need for targeted water management policies
Limitations: Outdated IO tables (up to 2012); Scale-transfer bias from province to pixel; Aggregated sectoral footprint—sectoral breakdown absent
Future Directions: Incorporate updated IO data (post-2014); Develop pixel-scale regression calibration; Project sector-specific water footprints
Scalability: Applicable to other regions sharing SSP framework, given availability of IO and land-use data
Novelty: First fine-resolution (0.125°) future water footprint projection under SSPs in China; Integration of MRIO, regression, and CA-based land-use simulation with ANN suitability modeling

Title: Projecting the future impacts of China's cropland balance policy on ecosystem services under the shared socioeconomic pathways
Authors: Li, Xia; Chen, Yimin
Objective: Explore future impacts of China’s cropland balance policy on ecosystem services under shared socioeconomic pathways
LULC Classes: Cropland; built-up land; forest; grassland; water bodies; unused land
Scenarios: SSP1–SSP5 under two objectives: quantity balance (QNB) and quality balance (QLB)
Analysis Methods: Cellular automaton modeling; machine learning classifiers (decision tree, random forest, rotation forest); zonal statistics; total operating characteristics; Figure of Merit
Sim. Method Advantages: Combines CA’s spatial allocation with machine learning for calibrated suitability; Higher predictive accuracy and flexibility compared to pure CA or regression methods; Captures spatial patterns under globally consistent SSPs
Tools/Soft Used: WEKA (decision tree, random forest, rotation forest)
Predictors: Elevation; slope; distance to roads; distance to built-up land; population density; GDP; precipitation; temperature
Data Sources: Land use maps (1 km resolution) for 2000 and 2010; SSP socioeconomic data (CMIP6 SSPs); Ecosystem service coefficients from regional spatial datasets; Built-up land expansion projections from Chen et al. (2019b)
Validation Methods: 10-fold cross-validation; Total Operating Characteristics (AUC); Figure of Merit
Validation Data Sources: Empirical land use data for 2000 and 2010
Key Findings: Reclaimed cropland has inferior physical conditions (higher slope) and only offsets 28–31% of lost productivity under QNB; QLB requires 1.93–2.38× more area, causing 3× larger ecosystem service losses; Cropland reclamation leads to substantial declines in carbon sequestration, soil retention, sandstorm prevention, and water retention
Implications: Quantity balance policy fails to secure productivity and harms ecosystems; Focus should shift to improving existing cropland quality and yield intensification; Reuse of abandoned cropland and advanced technology investments are critical
Limitations: 1 km resolution misses fine-scale fragmented cropland; Model lacks multi–land use interactions and grain-for-green impacts; Does not represent local vs. central government policy feedbacks
Future Directions: Incorporate grain-for-green policy impacts; Represent local–central governance dynamics; Use finer resolution land use data
Scalability: Applicable to other regions under SSP frameworks but requires region-specific calibration of suitability and ecosystem coefficients
Novelty: First national-scale CA application assessing China’s cropland balance policy impacts on ecosystem services under CMIP6 SSPs with machine-learning–derived suitability modeling.

Title: Agricultural and Forestry Land and Labor Use under Long-Term Climate Change in Chile
Authors: Melo, Oscar; Foster, William
Objective: To analyze the expected impacts on agricultural land and labor use in Chile under projected climate-change scenarios in 2040 and 2070, modeling farmers' land allocations based on relative profitability of activities in specific agroclimatic zones
LULC Classes: Field crops (wheat, corn, oats, potatoes, rice, beans, beats); Fruits and vines (table grapes, avocados, apples, plums, peaches, walnuts, olives, cherries, oranges, pears, vines); Pastures and forage (natural pastures, managed pastures, fallow land, alfalfa); Forestry (radiata pine, eucalyptus)
Scenarios: Four climate-change scenarios: A240 (severe scenario for 2040); A270 (severe scenario for 2070); B240 (moderate scenario for 2040); B270 (moderate scenario for 2070) based on IPCC's A2 and B2 emission projections
Analysis Methods: Farmland allocation model using multinomial logistic regression; Two-stage allocation process (first to broad activities, then to specific crops); Econometric estimation of land-use sensitivities to relative net-income changes
Sim. Method Advantages: Requires considerably less production-level data than optimization-based programming models; More practical for developing countries where detailed farm-level data is limited; Based on observed historical land allocations and market responses
Tools/Soft Used: Hadley Centre Coupled Model version 3 (HadCM3); Precis model for climate projections; Agronomic simulation models for yield projections
Predictors: Relative net incomes per hectare; Per-hectare yields; Output prices; Production costs; Water availability constraints; Agroclimatic zone characteristics
Data Sources: Chilean Agricultural Census (1997 and 2007); Standardized crop budgets from Agrogestión (Fundación Chile), Ministry of Agriculture, and Department of Agriculture Economics at Catholic University of Chile; Ten-year average annual national prices; Hadley Center's Precis model climate projections
Validation Methods: Parameters estimated using historical land allocations and price data from two census periods (1997 and 2007); Econometric validation through multinomial logistic regression analysis
Validation Data Sources: Historical land allocation data from Chilean Agricultural Census; Historical price and yield data
Key Findings: Climate change impacts will be mitigated by land-use adaptation with main export crops moving south; Agricultural employment will decrease in all climate scenarios; Total land use changes for broad activity categories are relatively small due to farmer adaptability; Forestry land expected to increase by 2-3% under all scenarios; Fruit production most affected with 76% revenue decline under severe scenarios by 2070; Total agricultural labor demand decreases 18% under severe 2070 scenario
Implications: Farmer adaptability and land-use responses provide important mitigation effects; Spatial redistributions will have significant local welfare consequences; Need for targeted policies to address uneven adaptive capacity between different farmer types; Investments in climate-appropriate technologies will be necessary in favored agroclimatic zones
Limitations: Ceteris paribus assumption that factors other than climate remain unchanged; Cannot anticipate all possible future changes in international prices, technologies, trade agreements; Climate projections may not match either hypothetical regime; Limited ability to reflect full range of changes at community and individual farmer levels
Future Directions: Examine in more detail how different population strata linked to agriculture will be affected; Develop nexus between land, water use, and food security for policy recommendations; Address decision model to allow more dynamic climate adaptation process; Incorporate political-economic model of land policy changes; Use cost data from farm surveys rather than activity budgets when available
Scalability: Limited discussion of direct scalability, but methodology could be applied to other countries with similar data availability and agricultural systems
Novelty: Development of practical economic model for farmer-decision-based land allocation changes among 25 different activities; Application of two-stage multinomial logistic approach to land allocation modeling; Integration of climate projections with economic decision-making at municipal level; Focus on labor demand implications of climate-driven land use changes

Title: Assessment of Land-Use Scenarios at a National Scale Using Intensity Analysis and Figure of Merit Components
Authors: Shoyama, Kikuko
Objective: To address the impacts of future land changes on biodiversity and ecosystem services by developing and validating national-scale land-use scenarios in Japan, with focus on improving the accuracy of model predictions to better inform policymakers during the decision-making process
LULC Classes: 10 categories: (1) residential area; (2) paddy field; (3) cropland; (4) other agricultural land; (5) abandoned farmland; (6) bush and grassland; (7) natural forest; (8) secondary forest; (9) plantation forest; (10) others
Scenarios: Five scenarios: Natural capital-based compact society (NC); Natural capital-based dispersed society (ND); Produced capital-based compact society (PC); Produced capital-based dispersed society (PD); Business-as-usual (BaU)
Analysis Methods: Intensity analysis and figure of merit components (hits, misses, and false alarms); Land Change Modeler; Multilayer perceptron neural network; Markov chain method
Sim. Method Advantages: Land Change Modeler empirically models relationships of explanatory variables of observed land changes and simulates future scenarios; enables spatially explicit modeling with transition potential modeling capabilities
Tools/Soft Used: Land Change Modeler (IDRISI software); GIS-based products from National Land Numerical Information
Predictors: Physical factors: elevation, slope, annual temperature, precipitation; Socio-economic factors: distance to stream, distance to main paved road, population density; Empirical likelihood of change for each category
Data Sources: GIS-based vegetation maps from Biodiversity Center of Japan, Ministry of the Environment; National Land Numerical Information; National Population Census; PANCES projected population data
Validation Methods: Intensity analysis and figure of merit components to distinguish quantity disagreement from allocation disagreement; Visual and quantitative comparison of changes during calibration and validation intervals
Validation Data Sources: LULC map at time-3 (2014) for validation; 26% incomplete data in the latest vegetation map resulted in 1,393,165 cells for validation
Key Findings: Low figure of merit accuracy was revealed; Quantity disagreement was more important than allocation disagreement in simulation; Gains in abandoned farmland targeted only paddy fields in simulation, whereas all types of agricultural land and bush/grassland were targeted in reference; Model improvements needed to reduce mismatch between simulation and validation
Implications: Need to improve accuracy of model predictions to better inform policymakers; Importance of aligning underlying spatial vegetation maps; Need to reduce disagreement between simulation and reference maps; Critical for National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan
Limitations: Low accuracy of national scale land-use scenarios; Transition modeling limited in describing transitions relating to land abandonment; 1 km spatial resolution too coarse to detect land transitions; 26% incomplete data in latest vegetation map; Potential lack of updated datasets to detect current land change trends
Future Directions: Need for updated datasets to detect current land change trends; Improve model to reduce quantity and allocation disagreement; Align underlying spatial vegetation maps; Develop finer spatial resolution models for agricultural land abandonment detection
Scalability: Methods and approaches could be applied to other regions experiencing similar land-use changes, depopulation, and aging society challenges; Intensity analysis and figure of merit components are transferable validation techniques
Novelty: First comprehensive validation of national-scale land-use scenarios in Japan using intensity analysis and figure of merit components; Novel approach to distinguish quantity disagreement from allocation disagreement in land-use scenario validation; Development of 500m resolution land-use maps from vegetation inventory data for national-scale ecosystem service assessment

Title: Changes in land use and ecosystem services values in Pakistan, 1950-2050
Authors: Aziz, Tariq
Objective: To quantify ecosystem services delivered by ecosystems at different temporal scales in Pakistan and assess how government-driven land-use policies have changed ecosystem services, the consequences of future land-use changes, and the effects on water and climate services
LULC Classes: Water; Forest; Grassland/shrubland; Cropland; Urban; Desert/bare areas
Scenarios: Four IPCC emission scenarios - A1B (low population growth, sprawling urban expansion, balanced energy sources); A2 (medium economic growth, high population growth); B1 (low population, high economic growth, compact urban expansion); B2 (medium economic and population growth, emphasis on local solutions)
Analysis Methods: Value transfer method (benefit transfer approach) using equation TV = Σ(Ak × UVk) where TV is total value, Ak is area, and UVk is unit value for land-use category k
Sim. Method Advantages: Value transfer method is fast, relatively inexpensive, commonly used for large spatial scale valuation; becomes more effective when dealing with changes in ecosystem service values; useful for data-scarce regions like Pakistan
Tools/Soft Used: GIS services provided by the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of Waterloo, Canada
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: Goldewijk's dataset (1950); Global Land Cover 2000 project (GLC 2000) (2000); Copernicus Global Land Service Dynamic Land Cover Map 2015 (CGLS-LC100) (2015); Future Land-Use Simulation (FLUS) system by Li et al. (2017) (2050); Global unit value datasets from Costanza et al. (2014), de Groot et al. (2012), Chen et al. (2014), Jahanifar et al. (2017), Taylor et al. (2017)
Validation Methods: Sensitivity analysis to show the impact of mixing urban and agricultural areas on ecosystem services values
Validation Data Sources: Land use data for 1950 with varying urban area percentages (0.1% to 0.5%)
Key Findings: Ecosystem services value increased $87 billion (1950-2000) due to dam construction and agricultural expansion; sharp decline of $70 billion (2000-2015); future scenarios show 12-21% decline except B2 scenario; climate services continuously decrease; water services increased (1950-2000) but declined afterward; per capita values decreased from over $5000 to below $1000 (1950-2050)
Implications: Results can inform land-use planning for efficient provision of ecosystem services; need for national land-use policy; importance of protecting high-valued ecosystems; B2 scenario (compact urbanization, medium economic growth) yields highest future value; critical need to address declining water and climate services
Limitations: Unit values not readily available for all of Pakistan and would vary considerably within the country; global datasets may not be strictly applicable at local level; lumping different land-use categories creates uncertainty; large scale makes it impossible to account for local variations; transfer error of 62-86% for domestic studies and 166% for international studies
Future Directions: Local unit values need to be developed for more accurate assessment; spatially explicit analysis required to identify ecosystems whose services are actually used by people; development of optimal land-use scenario for the country
Scalability: Limited scalability due to reliance on global datasets and Pakistan-specific conditions; however, methodology could be applied to other countries with similar data constraints
Novelty: First study to account for changes in ecosystem services values at national level for long-term land-use changes in Pakistan; considers land use changes at long temporal scale (100 years); depicts values for four future land uses under IPCC emission scenarios; employs both regional and global values making analysis more locally relevant

Title: Coupled SSPs-RCPs scenarios to project the future dynamic variations of water-soil-carbon-biodiversity services in Central Asia
Authors: Li, Jiangyue; Chen, Xi; Kurban, Alishir; Van de Voorde, Tim; De Maeyer, Philippe; Zhang, Chi
Country: Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan)
Objective: To project the future dynamic variations of water-soil-carbon-biodiversity services in Central Asia under the combined effects of future climate change and socioeconomic development using coupled SSPs-RCPs scenarios
LULC Classes: Forestland; Grassland; Barren; Cropland; Urban areas; Water areas
Scenarios: SSP126; SSP245; SSP585
Analysis Methods: Future land-use simulation (FLUS) model; Integrated valuation of ecosystem services and trade-offs (InVEST) model; Spearman correlation analysis; Multimodel ensemble (MME) technology; Artificial neural network (ANN); Cellular automata
Sim. Method Advantages: FLUS model has two main advantages: (1) ANN-based probability of occurrence estimation module that can continuously fit complex relationships between training targets and input data; (2) Adaptive inertial competition mechanism of roulette selection that combines conversion rules and neighborhood weight
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.2; FLUS model; InVEST model; R version 3.5.2
Predictors: Natural forces (elevation, slope, aspect, annual mean temperature, precipitation); Socioeconomic forces (population density, GDP); Distance forces (distance to roads, cities, water bodies)
Data Sources: Climate data: Climatologies at high resolution (1 km × 1 km) for historical data, CMIP6 four GCMs (CanESM5, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MRI-ESM2-0) for future projections; Land use: ESA-CCI (300m) for historical, LUH2 (0.25°) for future; Topographic: WorldClim v2.1; Soil: HWSD; Population: GPW v4; GDP: Kummu et al. 2018; Roads: Global roads open access dataset
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient; Figure of Merit (FoM)
Validation Data Sources: Comparison of simulated 2015 land use map with actual 2015 land use map based on 1995 land use map
Key Findings: Cropland degradation (-4.11% to -19.93%) and urban (+33.14% to +127.96%) and forestland (+5.31% to +25.52%) expansion will be the main forms of future land-use change; Four ecosystem services (water yield, soil conservation, carbon storage, habitat quality) will exhibit different decreasing trends across Central Asia; Risk of soil erosion will increase in mountainous areas of Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan; Weak pairwise correlations between habitat quality, soil conservation and carbon storage will be strengthened (R = 0.22–0.58) in Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan
Implications: Different management strategies should be designed in accordance with major interactions among water, soil, carbon and biodiversity services; Spatial optimization of proportional allocation of different land-cover types is crucial for balancing multiple service relationships; Need for payment for ecosystem services (PES) policies including 'Returning Grazing Land to Grassland'
Limitations: Transition rules assumed to be fixed in FLUS simulation while they may change in 20-50 years; Only four GCMs used creating uncertainty; Limited scenarios selected (SSP126, SSP245, SSP585); InVEST model limitations including ignoring eco-hydrological processes from snow/glacier melt and not considering changes in carbon storage based on each land-use type
Future Directions: Need to integrate more land surface ecological process models such as arid ecosystem models (AEM) and Biome-BGCs; Open up the black box underlying the model tool; Address uncertainties from different GCMs and scenario limitations
Scalability: The research framework coupling SSPs-RCPs, FLUS and InVEST models provides powerful support for future ecosystem protection and sustainable development and can be applied to other regions
Novelty: First framework integrating SSPs-RCPs scenarios with FLUS and InVEST models for projecting multiple ecosystem services; Comprehensive assessment of trade-offs and synergies among water-soil-carbon-biodiversity services under combined climate change and socioeconomic development scenarios

Title: Forest management can mitigate negative impacts of climate and land-use change on plant biodiversity: Insights from the Republic of Korea
Authors: Choi, Yuyoung; Lim, Chul-Hee; Chung, Hye In; Kim, Yoonji; Cho, Hyo Jin; Hwang, Jinhoo; Kraxner, Florian; Biging, Gregory S.; Lee, Woo-Kyun; Chon, Jinhyung; Jeon, Seong Woo
Objective: To quantitatively evaluate and map the combined impacts of climate change, land-use/cover change, and qualitative change in habitat on biodiversity in the Republic of Korea through an integrated approach to create an effective conservation strategy
LULC Classes: Urban; Croplands; Forests (classified into 4 naturalness grades: 1st-grade, 2nd-grade, 3rd-grade, 4th-grade); Pastures; Wetlands; Bare land; Water; Semi-natural pasture; Farmland; Natural pasture; Artificial bare land; Rice paddy; Other cropland; Natural bare land
Scenarios: SSP3 scenario (regional rivalry); RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 climate scenarios; Forest management scenarios with logging for timber production; Land cover only change scenario
Analysis Methods: Generalized Dissimilarity Modeling (GDM); Biodiversity persistence (BP) modeling; Species-area relationship; Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network; Land Change Modeler (LCM); Markov chain analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: GDM measures and predicts dissimilarity in species composition based on environmental variables; converts proportional loss of habitat into expected loss of species; integrates climate change with habitat conditions; provides spatially-explicit scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: TerrSet 18.31; Land Change Modeler (LCM); ArcGIS 10.3; Multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network
Predictors: 23 bioclimatic variables including Warmth Index, Minimum Temperature of Coldest Month Index, Precipitation Effectiveness Index, Growing Degree Days, and 19 standard bioclimatic variables; altitude; slope; aspect; distances to cropland, forests, urban areas, and roads; effective soil depth; Environmental Conservation Value Assessment Map
Data Sources: 3rd National Ecosystem Survey dataset (2006-2013); 5th National Forest Inventory; CHELSA climate dataset; National Environment Information Network System; Korean Soil Information System; Ministry of Environment land cover maps; Forest type maps from National Institute of Forest Science; Korean Database on Protected Areas
Validation Methods: Comparison with vegetation conservation grade map; Classification of BP results into 5 grades based on distribution ratio; Quantitative analysis of BP values within each conservation grade
Validation Data Sources: Grade map of vegetation conservation from national environmental survey (2006-2013) by Ministry of Environment
Key Findings: Continuous forest management had positive impact on biodiversity persistence by offsetting negative effects of urbanization; forest habitat quality improvements can effectively reduce negative impacts of climate change; biodiversity persistence increased from 89.95% in 1960s to 91.43% in 2010s; net effect of forest management was 1.66% increase in biodiversity persistence; current forest management insufficient to fully offset future decline from climate change
Implications: Economic development and urbanization can be parallel with biodiversity enhancement; forest management is efficient strategy for climate change mitigation and biodiversity conservation; developing countries can achieve economic development without biodiversity loss; quality enhancement of limited habitat areas can contribute to biodiversity persistence
Limitations: Forest naturalness grade classified only based on origin and age class without considering tree species diversity or forest structure; only macroscopic forest management considered; model-dependent predictions require additional verification with independent datasets; focused only on flora; limited to national scale
Future Directions: Diversification of scenarios including longer future periods (2070s) and various SSP-RCP combinations; subdivision of habitat types considering intensity of use and surrounding environment; extension beyond flora to include other taxonomic groups; site-level forest management assessment; development of optimal strategies to minimize biodiversity decline
Scalability: High scalability to other developing countries where forest degradation is occurring or has occurred; applicable to countries with high proportion of well-managed forests; methodology can be adapted using detailed national datasets
Novelty: First quantitative and spatial assessment of reforestation impact on biodiversity at national level in Korea; development of new Habitat Condition Index based on national survey datasets; integration of climate change, land-use change, and qualitative habitat changes in single framework; demonstration of successful forest restoration effects on biodiversity during economic development

Title: Future Scenarios for Land Use in Chile: Identifying Drivers of Change and Impacts over Protected Area System
Authors: Benavidez-Silva, Cesar; Jensen, Magdalena; Pliscoff, Patricio
Objective: To describe the current state of LULC in Chile, project future dynamics of change at high spatial resolution (1 km) in different time steps (2030, 2050, and 2080) under four IPCC AR5 scenarios, relate these dynamics to ecosystem distribution on a national scale, and analyze LULC dynamics inside the protected area network to identify potential effects on ecosystem representativeness and network integrity
LULC Classes: Natural areas; Agricultural areas; Forest plantations; Urban areas; Mining areas; Water bodies; Permanent snow
Baseline Years: 1992 (base time T0); 1997-2008 (intermediate years T1); 2011 (final calibration date T2)
Scenarios: Four IPCC AR5 scenarios - RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5
Analysis Methods: Land Change Modeler (LCM); Bioclimatic modeling approach using biomod2; Multilayer perceptron (MLP) method; Transition probability matrices; Spatial analysis using QGIS; Statistical analysis using R
Sim. Method Advantages: Not specified
Tools/Soft Used: Land Change Modeler (LCM); QGIS 3.4.4; R Core Team software; biomod2 package; lulcc library; raster library
Predictors: Distance to hydrological network; Distance to urban centers; Distance to mining fields; Distance to forest fields; Distance to agricultural fields; Distance to disturbances; Distance to protected areas; Distance to road network; Temperature; Precipitation; Elevation; Slope; Aspect; Hillshade; Evidence likelihood; Protected area network; Indigenous settlements
Data Sources: Forest cadastre by CONAF; Climate surface dataset for 1950-2000 period; CCAFS climate scenarios; IPCC AR5 scenarios; Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) Project data; National System of State Protected Wildlife Areas (SNASPE) data
Validation Methods: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis; Kappa index; True Skill Statistic (TSS); Comparative analysis with Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) Project global projections; Cramer's coefficient for driver evaluation

Key Findings: Forest plantations increased by 1.1 million ha (1992-2011) at ~75,000 ha/year; Natural areas decreased by 642,500 ha; Agricultural areas decreased by 607,800 ha; Future projections show continued increase in forest plantations (>50% increase) and urban areas (>55% increase); Natural and agricultural areas expected to continue decreasing; Anthropogenic disturbances expanding within protected areas; Vegetational formations in center and south could decrease while northern formations could expand
Implications: Chile's protected area network at risk of becoming biological islands; Reduced functionality and effective area of conservation spaces; Increased exposure of protected area borders to anthropic pressures; Need for mitigation and adaptation strategies for protected area management; Potential consequences for biodiversity conservation and ecosystem functions
Limitations: Restrictions in temporal consistency of information; Need for individual regional processing due to forest cadastre temporal variations; Lack of experiments at similar scale in Chile; Spatial resolution (1 km) may affect detection of smaller farms; Difficulty in interpreting and incorporating diverse factors acting as driving forces
Future Directions: Understanding of driving forces essential for LULC change dynamics; Generation of public policies for relevant decisions about country development; Effective maintenance of Chilean protected areas; Need for studies incorporating socioeconomic variables; Integration of different factors in LULC change processes
Scalability: Limited scalability mentioned; study focused specifically on Chile's unique geographic and climatic conditions, Methods could potentially be adapted to other regions with similar data availability and environmental characteristics
Novelty: High spatial resolution (1 km) modeling for entire country; Integration of LULC change models with ecosystem distribution models; Analysis of protected area network impacts; Combination of multiple climate scenarios with land use projections; Comprehensive evaluation of drivers across different geographic zones of Chile

Title: Future scenarios impact on land use change and habitat quality in Lithuania
Authors: Gomes, Eduardo; Inacio, Miguel; Bogdzevic, Katazyna; Kalinauskas, Marius; Karnauskait, Donalda; Pereira, Paulo
Objective: To study the impacts of LULC changes under different scenarios: business as usual (A0), urbanisation (A1), land abandonment and afforestation (A2) and agriculture intensification (A3) in 2050, and assess their effects on habitat quality (HQ) using Cellular Automata (CA) method and InVEST model
LULC Classes: 1-urban; 2-cropland; 3-grassland; 4-woodland and forest; 5-heathland and shrub; 6-sparsely vegetated areas; 7-wetlands; 8-marine inlets and transitional waters; 9-rivers and lakes
Scenarios: A0 (business as usual); A1 (urbanisation); A2 (land abandonment and afforestation); A3 (agricultural intensification)
Analysis Methods: Cellular Automata (CA) method; Integrated Valuation of Ecosystem Services and Trade-offs (InVEST) model; Moran's I index for spatial autocorrelation; Getis Ord* hotspot analysis; Weights of Evidence method; Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; Spearman correlation coefficient
Sim. Method Advantages: CA has been one of the most widely used methods for LULC dynamics studies; powerful method to study complex analysis, exploring principles of system evolution and self-organisation over a restricted set of simple rules; well established when coupled with GIS for creating complex spatial models
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica EGO 5.0; InVEST model; ArcGIS 10.7; Statistica 12.0; SAGA GIS
Predictors: Population density; dwellings density; farms density; utilised agricultural area density; workers in agriculture density; distance to main roads; distance to urban areas; distance to building areas; distance to agricultural areas; distance to woodland and forest; distance to grasslands; distance to coastline; distance to rivers and water bodies; slope; topographic wetness index; industrial soil pollution; land fragmentation; natural susceptibility to soil compaction; available water capacity; soil erosion by water; mean annual temperature; mean annual precipitation; flood areas; turbines buffer zones; protected areas; national parks
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover (CLC) from European Environment Agency; Official Statistics Portal (OSP); European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF); European Soil Data Centre (ESDAC); IPCC climate projections; National geodata repositories
Validation Methods: Reciprocal Similarity Comparison method using fuzzy comparison function; Multiple resolution windows (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11); Regression analysis for HQ model validation
Validation Data Sources: Tree density data; Imperviousness data; Reference land use map of 2018
Key Findings: The LULC model achieved 80% accuracy; A2 scenario showed highest HQ while A3 scenario had lowest HQ; Between 1990-2018, urban areas increased by 3.41% mainly at expense of cropland (-4.2%) and grassland (-6.9%); Under A1 scenario, urban areas will increase by 28.7% (4628 ha) in 2050; A2 scenario shows 375,820 ha increase in woodland and forest; A3 scenario projects 884,030 ha increase in croplands; HQ model validation was better with tree density data (r²=0.67) than imperviousness (r²=0.26)
Implications: A2 scenario most promising for sustainable future and biodiversity recovery; A3 scenario poses greatest challenges for achieving European biodiversity strategy 2030 and other environmental targets; Urban sprawl threatens achievement of EU recommendations and SDGs; Results can support policy-makers in assessing impacts of future LULC changes and developing appropriate land management strategies
Limitations: Data quality and resolution limitations; Different data resolutions inducing processing errors; Point data interpolation errors; Future scenario uncertainty; Limited expert survey size for HQ model weights; Information loss when aggregating HQ data at eldership level; Extrapolations should be done with prudence
Future Directions: Use high-resolution data; Apply other LUCC models such as agent-based models for better household decision-making representation; Assess impacts on different ecosystem services with proper model validation; Develop better validation approaches for ES mapping and assessments
Scalability: The methodology can be applied to other regions with similar socio-economic and environmental conditions, particularly post-communist Eastern European countries that experienced similar political regime transitions and land use transformation patterns
Novelty: Few studies have addressed the impact of political regime change on future LULC changes and their effects on ecosystem services in ex-soviet countries; Comprehensive validation of both LULC and habitat quality models; Integration of expert knowledge through surveys for habitat quality assessment; Application of multiple spatial analysis techniques for comprehensive assessment

Title: High-resolution urban change modeling and flood exposure estimation at a national scale using open geospatial data: A case study of the Philippines
Authors: Johnson, Brian A.; Estoque, Ronald C.; Li, Xuecao; Kumar, Pankaj; Dasgupta, Rajarshi; Avtar, Ram; Magcale-Macandog, Damasa B.
Objective: To present an approach for simulating future urban land-use changes and evaluating potential flood exposure at a high spatial resolution (30 m) and national scale to support climate resilient urban planning efforts
LULC Classes: Urban/built-up areas (commercial, residential, industrial areas); defined as artificial impervious surfaces from GAIA dataset
Scenarios: Three population growth scenarios: low, medium, and high population growth based on UN-DESA projections
Analysis Methods: Logistic regression cellular automata (logistic-CA) model; trend-based logistic-CA method; flood exposure assessment by overlaying land-use simulation results onto global floodplain map
Sim. Method Advantages: Clear physical meaning and ease of interpretation; logistic regression provides intuitive weights of spatial proxies; trend-based CA approach weights areas with recent urban expansion higher than traditional CA approaches
Tools/Soft Used: WEKA data mining software version 3.9.3 (Logistic model with ridge estimator)
Predictors: Distance to nearest existing urban area; Distance to nearest highway; Distance to nearest other roads; Slope in degrees
Data Sources: Global Artificial Impervious Areas (GAIA) dataset; Global Roads Inventory Project (GRIP) version 4; Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) version 4.1; Joint Research Council (JRC) global water maps version 1.2; GFPlain250m global floodplain map
Validation Methods: Figure of Merit (FOM) metric; Land-use Hazard Estimation Bias (LHEB) metric (newly proposed); 10-fold cross-validation for logistic regression
Validation Data Sources: GAIA dataset (2009-2018 period used for validation); GFPlain250m for flood hazard validation
Key Findings: Approximately 6040-13,850 ha of urban land conversion likely in flood prone areas by 2050; affecting 2.5-5.8 million additional urban residents; 10-11% of total projected urban conversion in flood-prone areas; FOM validation accuracy of 0.201; LHEB value of +0.218 (21.8% overestimation)
Implications: Need for climate resilient land-use planning; flood mitigation measures particularly important for Mindanao Island; existing local planning policies already reducing urban flood exposure to some degree
Limitations: No future climate projections included; unable to capture effects of increased impervious surface area on flood hazards; conservative urban land demand projections; errors in geospatial datasets (GAIA ~89-97% accuracy; SRTM-DEM ~4.28m RMSE)
Future Directions: Incorporate future climate projections; include effects of impervious surface changes on flood hazards; conduct site-specific hydraulic modeling; use downscaled climate projections; assess exposure to other hazards (landslides, storm surge)
Scalability: High; methodology uses openly available global/near-global datasets, intended for replication in other countries experiencing urban expansion, all datasets are freely available
Novelty: First high-resolution (30m) national-scale urban change modeling for Philippines; new Land-use Hazard Estimation Bias (LHEB) metric for flood hazard assessment; trend-based cellular automata approach using high temporal resolution data

Title: How to halve the carbon and biodiversity impacts of biofuel-driven land-use change in Brazil
Authors: de Andrade Junior, Milton A. U.; Watson, James E. M.; Williams, Brooke A.; Allan, James R.; O'Bryan, Christopher J.; Maxwell, Sean L.
Objective: Minimising the environmental impacts of biofuel production by integrating future ethanol demand scenarios in Brazil within a spatially-explicit planning framework aimed at minimising impacts of ethanol-driven agricultural expansion on aboveground carbon stocks and 453 species of immediate conservation concern
LULC Classes: Native forests; grasslands; sugarcane; cropland; pastureland
Scenarios: Conservation-considered planning scenario; Conservation-blind planning scenario
Analysis Methods: Zonation spatial prioritization software; spatially-explicit planning framework; core-area zonation planning unit removal rule
Sim. Method Advantages: Core-area Zonation method minimises biological loss by selecting planning units with smallest occurrence for most valuable features; iteratively ranks planning units in order of priority; accounts for landscape condition and anthropogenic influence
Tools/Soft Used: Zonation spatial prioritization software; ArcMap (ESRI, 2017)
Predictors: Aboveground carbon stocks; species geographic distributions; agricultural suitability; proximity to roads; Human Footprint; landscape condition values
Data Sources: Mapbiomas (2019); Brazilian land-cover data, IUCN Red List (2019); species distributions, BirdLife (2018); bird species data, Englund et al. (2017); aboveground carbon dataset, Zabel et al. (2014); agricultural suitability dataset, Venter et al. (2016); Human Footprint data, Meijer et al. (2018); roads data

Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Conservation-blind agricultural expansion would release 44.9 MtCO₂eq and impact habitat for 273 species; Conservation-considered expansion reduces emissions by 87% (5.8 MtCO₂eq) and avoids impacts on 113 species; Only 9% overlap in grassland expansion and 1% in forest expansion between scenarios; 75% of emissions would come from grassland conversion
Implications: Results are immediately relevant to policy makers seeking to guide ethanol-driven land-use change; Safeguarding carbon stocks helps Brazil meet climate change pledges like Paris Agreement; Findings contribute to efforts to address global extinction crisis; Highlights need for integrated land-use planning

Novelty: Integrated land-use approach combining carbon and biodiversity values; Spatially-explicit planning framework for ethanol-driven expansion; Comprehensive analysis of 453 terrestrial vertebrate species of conservation concern; First study to quantify trade-offs between conservation-considered and conservation-blind biofuel expansion scenarios

Title: How will land degradation neutrality change future land system patterns? A scenario simulation study
Authors: Schulze, Katharina; Malek, Ziga; Verburg, Peter H.
Objective: The aim of this study is to demonstrate how LDN can be implemented in land system modelling and how achieving LDN alongside sufficient supplies of food, timber and shelter could affect future land system patterns, using the Republic of Turkey as a case study.
LULC Classes: Annual cropland; permanent cropland; grassland; forest systems; urban land; extensive and intensive systems
Scenarios: Business-as-usual scenario (without LDN); LDN scenario (with full implementation of LDN guidelines); sensitivity analyses on different LDN principles
Analysis Methods: Land system modelling; scenario simulation; sensitivity analysis; comparison of land conversion matrices; spatial analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Capability to match demand and supply for a range of goods and services; ability to test different LDN principles; provides virtual laboratory for testing impact of different principles in LDN framework
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo model; Trends.Earth tool; spatial analysis software
Predictors: Land suitability; current land system conditions; market pressures; policy targets; climate change projections (aridity index); soil organic carbon (SOC); net primary productivity (NPP); land cover changes
Data Sources: FAO soil organic carbon data; AppEEARS Team NPP data; Turkey's biogeographical regions (EEA 2016); aridity index projections (Trabucco and Zomer 2018); Trends.Earth methodology; WOCAT database
Validation Methods: Comparison with Turkey's voluntary LDN targets from pilot project; comparison with historical irrigation trends
Validation Data Sources: Turkey's voluntary LDN targets (Ministry of Forest and Water Affairs 2016); historical irrigation data (Rufin et al. 2021)
Key Findings: Although it is possible to achieve LDN in the context of increasing demands for resources and housing, it might require considerable re-organization of land systems; intensification of annual cropland systems was the main driver of new land degradation; to achieve no-net-loss, about 20% of Turkey's territory was afforested; afforestation mainly claimed extensively used annual cropland (~70%) and grassland (~30%); SOC indicator mostly drives the observed land system projections; like-for-like principle has large impact on results
Implications: Pursuing LDN under growing demands could stimulate land sparing approach with trade-offs; need for local support and new solutions for rural areas to avoid poverty and migration; large-scale afforestation would be challenging and very costly (over 26 billion USD estimated); demand-side solutions needed to reduce counterbalancing requirements
Limitations: Did not include water availability restrictions; did not include economic restrictions; did not distinguish between different types of intensification; used average values per land system without accounting for spatial variation; did not account for smaller management changes within same land system; rough implementation of like-for-like principle using biogeographical regions
Future Directions: Include participatory scenario development; consider sustainable intensification and climate-smart agriculture; include demand-side solutions; develop people-centered restoration approaches; improve monitoring of soil carbon stocks; validate satellite trends with ground-truth data; include economic feasibility assessments
Scalability: Approach can be applied to other countries and regions; methodology provides framework for implementing LDN in land system modelling; principles can be adapted to different geographical and socio-economic contexts
Novelty: First scenario assessment of future land system change with LDN embedded as core principle; novel implementation of LDN framework in land system modelling; first comprehensive sensitivity analysis of different LDN principles; innovative approach to testing impact of individual LDN components

Title: Impact of land cover changes on carbon stock trends in Kenya for spatial implementation of REDD plus policy
Authors: Nyamari, Nicodemus; Cabral, Pedro
Objective: Analyze spatial and temporal trends of carbon stock as an indicator of climate-regulation ecosystem services between 2004 and 2028 under Business-As-Usual (BAU) and REDD+ scenarios based on land cover changes
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forests; Non-forest vegetation; Built-up areas; Bare areas; Water
Scenarios: Business-As-Usual (BAU); REDD+
Analysis Methods: Random Forest decision trees algorithm; One-versus-All encoding; Neighborhood proximity functions; InVEST carbon model; Cross-validation (10-fold); Confusion matrix; ROC curve analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Non-parametric ensemble reduces over-fitting and improves prediction accuracy; Permutation–based variable importance measurement; Spatially explicit “what-if” scenario mapping for policy implementation
Tools/Soft Used: QGIS 3.4; RStudio; Python 3.6 (GDAL, NumPy, scikit-learn, Keras); ArcMap 10.6; InVEST carbon model
Predictors: 2004 land cover (six binary vectors); Soil type (five binary vectors); Slope; Distance to roads; Distance to cities; Distance to major towns; Neighborhood proximity to each land cover class
Data Sources: GlobCover 2004 and 2009 (ENVISAT MERIS, 21 classes); Africa Land Cover 2016 (Sentinel-2A, 10 classes); USGS SRTM DEM; WRI Kenya road network; ILRI cities and town centers; ILRI soil type map
Validation Methods: Confusion matrix (overall accuracy, user’s/producer’s accuracies, kappa); ROC curves
Validation Data Sources: ‘Actual’ 2016 land cover map (Africa Land Cover project)
Key Findings: 8% decline in carbon stock 2004–2016, projected 8.4% further decline by 2028 under BAU; BAU yields US$ –21 billion loss 2004–2028; REDD+ scenario reverses trend with 1.6% gain in carbon stock and US$ 1 billion avoided cost by 2028; Forest cover drops from 15.7% (2004) to <2% (2028 BAU); Cropland increases from 8.6% (2004) to ~17% (2028)
Implications: Urgent reinforcement of REDD+ policies; spatial planning to balance resource use; incentivize forest conservation to mitigate carbon losses
Limitations: Carbon pool values sourced from Ugandan study (extrapolation risk); Land cover maps’ low classification accuracy (65–73%); Mixed spatial resolutions (20 m vs. 300 m) and resampling errors; Aggregated land cover legend induces misclassification; Climatic seasonality not explicitly modelled
Future Directions: Socio-economic and demand vs. supply analysis of carbon services; Region-specific case studies (e.g., urban Nairobi, Mount Elgon); Improved, regularly updated high-accuracy land cover datasets; Incorporation of additional drivers and advanced algorithms
Scalability: Methodology is flexible and cost-free—applicable to other countries using open data and software
Novelty: First spatial implementation of REDD+ policy via land cover modelling; Integration of Random Forest with InVEST for spatiotemporal carbon stock estimation; Use of free, open-access data and tools for national-scale analysis

Title: Linking land change model evaluation to model objective for the assessment of land cover change impacts on biodiversity
Authors: Sangermano, Florencia; Pontius, Robert Gilmore, Jr.; Chaitman, Jamieson; Meneghini, Aaron
Objective: Evaluate land cover change simulations in Bolivia at both pixel level and biodiversity-relevant grain to inform model selection for biodiversity impact assessments
LULC Classes: Forest; nonforest (deforested areas)
Scenarios: national-level; department-level; province-level; municipality-level; ecoregion-level; carbon-stock-level
Analysis Methods: Transition potential modeling; demand-for-land modeling; allocation modeling; error decomposition (quantity, stratum, pixel); stratified evaluation; Jaccard similarity index for species impacts
Sim. Method Advantages: Stratified evaluation aligns model selection with biodiversity assessment objective by ignoring irrelevant within-grain errors, unlike pixel-level metrics alone
Tools/Soft Used: TerrSet (with Python plug-in for regional allocation)
Predictors: Cost distance to populated places; cost distance to Santa Cruz; precipitation seasonality; Euclidean distance to roads; Euclidean distance to previously deforested areas
Data Sources: Primary: Killeen et al. (2007) land cover 2001, Hansen et al. (2013) Global Forest Change 2000–2014, IUCN Red List species range polygons, BirdLife International ranges; Secondary: Nelson (2008) global accessibility layer
Validation Methods: Pixel-level Figure of Merit (PFOM); Stratum Figure of Merit (SFOM); decomposition of hits, misses, false alarms; Jaccard similarity index
Validation Data Sources: Reference land cover 2014; IUCN/BirdLife species range data
Key Findings: Province-level simulation best balanced allocation and biodiversity error; Pixel-level accuracy (PFOM) favored carbon-level model but misrepresented biodiversity impacts; Linear extrapolation underpredicted quantity due to policy-driven deforestation increases; Error decomposition revealed meaningful vs. irrelevant errors
Implications: Model evaluation must align with impact assessment grain; Stratified metrics improve selection for biodiversity applications; Future deforestation projections require multiple demand scenarios
Limitations: Assumed no reforestation/regeneration; Transition potential model dominated by distance to Santa Cruz (spatial non-stationarity unaddressed); IUCN range grain uncertainty (100 km grid)
Future Directions: Develop province-specific transition potential models; Incorporate multiple demand-for-land trajectories; Assess configuration-based metrics for other objectives
Scalability: Methodology applicable to other regions by defining evaluation strata relevant to specific impact objectives
Novelty: Linking error decomposition to model purpose; Stratified evaluation grain based on biodiversity data validity; Integration of quantity vs. allocation errors to guide model selection

Title: Major United States Land Use as Influenced by an Altering Climate: A Spatial Econometric Approach
Authors: Cho, Sung Ju; McCarl, Bruce
Objective: Examine how climate and socioeconomic factors influence U.S. land use changes and project future land use allocations under climate scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; Pastureland; Grassland; Forest; Urban; Other
Scenarios: RCP 2.6; RCP 4.5; RCP 8.5
Analysis Methods: Spatial linearized fractional multinomial logit; Spatial lag model; Two-step estimation; Partial effect estimation
Sim. Method Advantages: Controls for spatial dependence across adjacent regions without specifying exact common factors; Captures fine-scale (10 km×10 km) interactions; Allows nonlinear climate impacts and identification of inflection thresholds
Tools/Soft Used: MATLAB (sparseinv); Stata (spmat); ArcGIS (fishnet)
Predictors: Annual mean temperature (5-year average & SD); Annual precipitation (5-year total & SD); Elevation; Slope; Land capability class; Farm income; Nonfarm income; Population density; Irrigation rate; Lagged land use shares
Data Sources: NLCD/MRLC satellite-based land cover, USDA gSSURGO soils, PRISM climate; US BEA personal income, USDA Quick Stats irrigation, TIGER grid mapping; Downscaled CMIP5 BCSD climate projections
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Significant spatial dependence for cropland, pasture, grass (negative for forest, urban irreversible); Nonlinear temperature and precipitation effects with inflection points (~10–16 °C, 0.86–2.56 m); Temperature above thresholds reduces cropland/forest, increases pasture/grass; Precipitation effects invert above inflection; Economic, topographic, soil, irrigation, and socioeconomic factors significantly influence land shares; Projected southerly cropland losses and northerly gains under RCP scenarios; Greater sensitivity under RCP 8.5
Implications: Regional tailoring of mitigation/adaptation policies (e.g., carbon sequestration incentives, sustainable land management, livestock emissions strategies, forest species shifts); Attention to food supply shifts and carbon sequestration potential by region
Limitations: Omission of policy drivers, crop/livestock prices, enterprise incomes at fine scale; No feedback from land allocation changes to climate
Future Directions: Include market factors and panel spatial modeling; Incorporate explicit policy variables (carbon price, sequestration incentives); Develop integrated global land-climate feedback models
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with high-resolution spatial data and similar econometric frameworks
Novelty: Simultaneous incorporation of spatial econometrics, fine-scale (10 km) gridded data, and combined climate–socioeconomic drivers; Use of linearized spatial fractional multinomial logit for land use shares

Title: Modeling Future Land Use Development: A Lithuanian Case
Authors: Mozgeris, Gintautas; Jukneliene, Daiva
Objective: Test methodological principles for land use development scenario modeling for use in GHG accounting and management
LULC Classes: forest land; producing land; grassland and pastures; wetland; built-up areas; other land
Scenarios: Reference 2005–2010; Reference 2010–2015; producing land to forest; grassland to forest; no grassland to producing land
Analysis Methods: land use change analysis; multilayer perceptron neural network; Markov chain analysis; Cramer’s V statistic for variable selection
Sim. Method Advantages: Compatible with EFDM and official GHG accounting workflows; Models multiple transitions simultaneously; Utilizes publicly available GIS data and standard GIS software without custom development
Tools/Soft Used: TerrSet 18.21 Land Change Modeler; standard GIS software; EFDM referenced
Predictors: distance to nearest agricultural block; distance to nearest built-up block; distance to nearest forest block; distance to nearest road block; distance to nearest linear hydrographic feature; distance to nearest areal hydrographic feature; proportion of agricultural land; proportion of built-up land; proportion of forest land; proportion of road blocks; proportion of linear hydrography; proportion of areal hydrography; proportion of protected areas; proportion of nature heritage areas; proportion of protective zones; proportion of abandoned agricultural land; proportions of land from land declaration (producing land; berry fields; orchards; other producing land; forest land; pastures and meadows; natural grassland; other pastures and meadows; waters and wetlands); average soil productivity grade; population density
Data Sources: Lithuanian National Forest Inventory; GRPK, GDR50LT, AZ_DRLT, SŽNS_DR10LT, Dirv_DR10LT, KŽS, National Paying Agency farmland/cropland dataset, 2011 housing census
Validation Methods: Calibration of 2005–2010 change to predict 2015; accuracy assessment by confusion between classes
Validation Data Sources: Lithuanian National Forest Inventory data for 2015
Key Findings: Prediction accuracy >80% for major LULUCF classes; forest and built-up >96%; Producing land vs grassland most challenging (misclassification ~12–16%); All scenarios project net CO₂ accumulation in LULUCF sector, driven by forests; Afforestation and preventing grassland conversion most effective to reduce emissions
Implications: Prioritize increasing forest and grassland areas to improve GHG balance; Direct EU CAP payments to maintain permanent grassland and support afforestation; National policy can meet 2030 forest area targets under tested scenarios
Limitations: Use of point-based rather than wall-to-wall land use data; Limited number of driver variables in TerrSet LCM; Lack of land ownership data; Static driver variables, challenges in grassland subtype differentiation
Future Directions: Develop wall-to-wall mapped land use inputs for scenario modeling; Implement spatially explicit cellular automata and agent-based models; Integrate digital inventory and decision-support technologies
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integration of NFI point data with TerrSet LCM for national-scale GHG scenario modeling; First test of methodological principles for Lithuanian LULUCF land use change scenario modeling compatible with official frameworks

Title: Modelling drivers of Brazilian agricultural change in a telecoupled world
Authors: Millington, James D. A.; Katerinchuk, Valeri; Bicudo da Silva, Ramon Felipe; Victoria, Daniel de Castro; Batistella, Mateus
Objective: To develop and empirically calibrate CRAFTY-Brazil, a spatially-explicit land use/cover change model representing multiple commodity productions (soybean, maize, beef) to examine future scenarios of global-to-local “telecoupled” drivers under political, economic and environmental uncertainties
LULC Classes: Cropland; Pasture; Nature; Other
Scenarios: BAU (MAPA standard projections); EXT (MAPA upper projections, RCP4.5 & RCP8.5 climate); EXT-NP (EXT plus removal of protected area designations)
Analysis Methods: Empirical calibration; sensitivity tests (+/–20% demand, yield, climate); spatial allocation comparison; scenario simulation using CRAFTY framework
Sim. Method Advantages: Agent-functional approach allows broad-scale (national) spatially explicit modeling; Computationally efficient “agency-based” aggregation versus fine-scale agent-based required for continental extents; Integration of exogenous capitals (climate, transport, technology, land value) and endogenous dynamics (agglomeration, contagion, regeneration, debt)
Tools/Soft Used: CRAFTY framework (custom code); scripts available via GitHub; Docker deployment
Predictors: Moisture-Main; Moisture-Second; Transport; Land Value; Conservation; Tech-Soy-Maize; Tech-Pasture; Protection-Soybean; Protection-Maize; Protection-Beef; Protection-OCrop; Access-Nature; Access-Soy-Maize; Access-OCrop
Data Sources: MapBiomass Project
Validation Methods: Comparison of simulated aggregate area & production time-series; municipality-level land cover proportion comparison (modal class accuracy)
Validation Data Sources: MapBiomas LULC; IBGE commodity production; municipality land cover proportions
Key Findings: Calibrated model reproduces aggregate trends in cropland expansion, pasture decline, soybean & maize production increases; Spatial allocation accuracy lower (modal municipality misclassification rose from 9.8% in 2009 to 16.4% in 2018); Model outputs most sensitive to demand & yield changes (land sparing/intensification effects), least to climate; Scenario EXT-NP yields highest production but conversion not confined to de-protected areas; Climate variability drives inter-annual production variability but limited short-term land cover change
Implications: Empirically-grounded CRAFTY enables exploration of policy (e.g., moratoriums, protected area removal), economic and climate uncertainties on land systems; Highlights potential for land abandonment under demand/yield shifts (land sparing); Suggests infrastructure and market developments crucial for future land expansion
