Limitations: Coarse AFT aggregation (“agency-based”) limits representation of individual decision-making and debt/regeneration history; Uncertainty in MapBiomas reclassification (Grassland, mosaic classes); Endogenous demand not modeled (assumed market clearing); Invariant infrastructure in scenarios may understate feedbacks in newly de-protected areas
Future Directions: Dynamic coupling with System Dynamics global trade model for endogenous demand; Finer-scale agent-based modeling for individual decision processes; Improved demand projections for ecosystem services; Inclusion of infrastructure development feedbacks
Scalability: Model structure and calibration approach adaptable to other broad-scale regions given appropriate LULC, climate, socio-economic data
Novelty: First empirically-calibrated application of CRAFTY at national scale; Integration of multiple exogenous and endogenous drivers including debt, agglomeration, contagion and regeneration; Agency-based adaptation enabling simulation over ~4 million km² with empirical validation of both aggregate and spatial outputs

Title: Predicting land cover changes using a CA Markov model under different shared socioeconomic pathways in Greece
Authors: Gemitzi, Alexandra
Objective: To develop a land change model for Greece based on historical remotely sensed land cover data, determine dominant land cover changes and their driving variables, and predict future land cover projections up to 2030 under different Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
LULC Classes: Based on International Geosphere-Biosphere Program (IGBP) classification: Evergreen Needleleaf Forests; Evergreen Broadleaf Forests; Deciduous Needleleaf Forests; Deciduous Broadleaf Forests; Mixed Forests; Closed Shrublands; Open Shrublands; Woody Savannas; Savannas; Grasslands; Permanent Wetlands; Croplands; Urban and Built-up Lands; Cropland/Natural Vegetation Mosaics; Permanent Snow and Ice; Barren; Water Bodies
Scenarios: SSP126 (sustainable development/sustainable future); SSP585 (worst case scenario/fossil-fueled development)
Analysis Methods: CA Markov model coupled with Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) neural network; transition probability matrix analysis; Cramer's V analysis for variable selection; classification accuracy assessment using Producer's Accuracy, User's Accuracy, Overall Accuracy, and Kappa Coefficient
Sim. Method Advantages: CA Markov models coupled with MLP offer the strongest capabilities among other approaches; reliable tools to simulate successfully multiple and complex patterns of landscape; MLP provides valuable information about the contribution of explanatory variables; handles multiple transitions simultaneously rather than modeling each transition separately
Tools/Soft Used: TerrSet software; MODIS sinusoidal projection; Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) neural network
Predictors: Evidence Likelihood of Land Cover (Cramer's V = 0.3592); Altitude from ASTER GDEM (Cramer's V = 0.1836); Mean Annual Precipitation (Cramer's V = 0.1821); Mean Annual Minimum Temperature (Cramer's V = 0.1718); Distance from previous changes (Cramer's V = 0.1546)
Data Sources: MODIS MCD12Q1v006 land cover product (2001-2018) at 500m spatial resolution; ASTER GDEM for elevation data; WorldClim historical climate data (2000-2018) at 2.5 minutes grids; CMIP6 climate data for future projections from ensemble of 4 GCMs (BCC-CSM2-MR, CNRM-ESM2-1, PSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC-ES2L)
Validation Methods: Model performance tested by predicting land cover for 2018 and comparing with observed 2018 land cover; accuracy assessment using Producer's Accuracy, User's Accuracy, Overall Accuracy, and Kappa Coefficient; comparison with CORINE land cover 2018 as reference dataset
Validation Data Sources: MODIS land cover 2018 (observed); CORINE land cover 2018 (reference dataset for accuracy assessment)
Key Findings: Four dominant land cover transformations identified: Savannas to Woody Savannas; Savannas to Grasslands; Grasslands to Savannas; Croplands to Grasslands; model achieved 96.7% predictive accuracy for 2018; major historical land transformations do not correspond to land degradation or desertification; Woody Savannas gain areas constantly while Grasslands and Croplands lose areas; forested areas demonstrate moderate gains; SSP126 accelerates expansion of woody vegetation while SSP585 slows down the rate of changes
Implications: Historical land cover transitions indicate transformation to more natural types of land cover, likely due to land abandonment from economic crisis and population emigration; results do not support previous findings of major land degradation or desertification risk in Greece; direction of historical changes will prevail in next decade; climate change scenarios have different impacts on land cover transition rates
Limitations: Uncertainties in remotely sensed information; lower expected model performance in cases of future abrupt and unpredictable changes induced by natural disasters or geopolitical instabilities; MODIS 500m spatial resolution restrictive for local scale use; model trained on historical data may not handle unprecedented future events
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Model developed at country scale for area with diverse and complex land cover pattern; methodology could potentially be applied to other Mediterranean countries or regions with similar characteristics, though specific validation would be required
Novelty: First land cover model for whole country of Greece simulating all dominant transitions; incorporates socioeconomic scenarios (SSPs) with climate projections; challenges previous findings about land degradation and desertification in Greece; uses ensemble of multiple GCMs for future projections; demonstrates that economic crisis and population decline led to landscape naturalization rather than degradation

Title: Projections of desertification trends in Central Asia under global warming scenarios
Authors: Ma, Xiaofei; Zhu, Jianting; Yan, Wei; Zhao, Chengyi
Country: Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, and Xinjiang of China)
Objective: To quantify desertification in Central Asia; identify main driving forces of desertification; propose the evolution normal form of desertification in Central Asia; and predict future desertification in Central Asia and typical areas under global warming scenarios
LULC Classes: Arable land; grassland; potential desert land; forestland; desert land; water body; built-up land; others
Scenarios: Four Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, RCP 8.5); Global warming scenarios of 1.5°C (GW1.5) and 2.0°C (GW2.0)
Analysis Methods: Actual evapotranspiration (ETa) calculation using advection-aridity (AA) model; CA-Markov model coupling; stepwise regression analysis; Sen's slope method; Mann-Kendall statistical test; correlation analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: CA-Markov model coupled with regression analysis compensates for the inability of traditional CA-Markov models to consider predicted driving factors of desertification; provides spatial computation ability and considers distance to desertification as weight to judge spatial heterogeneity
Tools/Soft Used: Four general circulation models (GCMs) from ISIMIP 2b; bilinear interpolation algorithm; maximum value composite method; object-oriented method for image processing
Predictors: Actual evapotranspiration (ETa); temperature; precipitation; normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI)
Data Sources: Global Meteorological Station data (NOAA); Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP) 2b climate data; GIMMS NDVI data set (AVHRR sensor); European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative Land Cover Maps (CCI-LC); Landsat MSS and TM/ETM images; Google Earth high-resolution images
Validation Methods: Field verification with 136 sample sites in Gurbantunggut Desert; high-resolution QuickBird image analysis using object-oriented method; artificial visual interpretation technology
Validation Data Sources: Field samples from Gurbantunggut Desert (September 2016); QuickBird high-resolution images; Google Earth images
Key Findings: Temperature, precipitation, and NDVI increased during 1980-2015 with sudden changes in 1994; desert land area decreased (5.94 × 10⁴ km²/10 yr) while potential desert land area increased (0.17 × 10⁴ km²/10 yr); under GW2.0, potential increase in desert land equivalent to current Aral Sea water area; ETa correlation with desert land area (R² = 0.43) greater than NDVI correlation (R² = 0.30); Aral Sea plays important role in Central Asia desertification
Implications: Provides policy support for combating desertification in Central Asia and promoting achievement of Sustainable Development Goals; demonstrates need for continued vigilance against desertification despite global greening trends; highlights critical role of Aral Sea in regional desertification processes
Limitations: Study based on linear relationships while human activities may have nonlinear effects on desertification; most field verification points distributed only in Xinjiang, China; some errors may exist in land use classification despite extensive verification; effects of policy and human activities not fully considered in modeling
Future Directions: Establish appropriate models to fully consider effects of human activities on desertification; strengthen investigation and verification of field data from five Central Asian countries; develop nonlinear relationship models for human activity impacts; further optimize desertification monitoring models
Scalability: Methods could be applied to other arid regions globally; AA model calibrated for desert lands in northern China and Tarim Basin; complementary theory and CA-Markov coupling approach transferable to similar ecological contexts
Novelty: Proposed evolution normal form of desertification in Central Asia; coupling of regression analysis with CA-Markov model to improve desertification inversion method; comprehensive use of actual evapotranspiration as key predictor rather than relying solely on NDVI; quantitative assessment linking desertification to specific global warming thresholds (1.5°C and 2.0°C)

Title: Settlement changes after peak population: Land system projections for China until 2050
Authors: Wang, Yuan; van Vliet, Jasper; Debonne, Niels; Pu, Lijie; Verburg, Peter H.
Objective: To simulate land system changes in China until 2050 under different population scenarios after peak population, focusing on settlement system changes and their impacts on urbanization trajectories
LULC Classes: 18 land system classes grouped into four major categories: Urban systems (High-dense urban area, Low dense urban area, Peri-urban area, Sub-urban area); Village systems (Clustered landscapes, Spread landscapes, Agricultural hinterland villages, Grazing hinterland villages, Forest hinterland villages); Agricultural systems (High-intensity, Medium-intensity, Low-intensity agricultural systems); Natural systems (Grassland system, Forest system, Forest-grass mix system, Wetland, Water, Other land)
Scenarios: Four scenarios: S1 (High population projection + Constant density); S2 (High population projection + Gradual decline); S3 (Low population projection + Constant density); S4 (Low population projection + Gradual decline). Population scenarios based on UN projections with high projection peaking at 1518 million (2044) and low projection peaking at 1447 million (2024)
Analysis Methods: CLUMondo land system model; Expert-based classification; Logistic regression analysis; Iterative allocation procedure using conversion rules and empirically derived suitability values
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUMondo simulates land system changes rather than land cover conversions; allows modeling urban development as gradual process; enables separate modeling of urban expansion and urban intensification; represents multiple settlement systems along rural-urban gradient; allows incremental change processes
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo land system model; Google Earth (for population density validation)
Predictors: Population density; Built-up land share; Land cover composition; Agricultural productivity; Socio-economic factors; Biophysical factors (used in logistic regression for suitability values)
Data Sources: Built-up data (Global human settlement layer, European Commission); Population data (Global human settlement layer, European Commission); Cropping frequency (Chinese Academy of Sciences); Land cover data (Chinese Academy of Sciences); Grain production (National Bureau of Statistics of China)
Validation Methods: Simulation of known land system changes between 2000-2015; Assessment of model ability to translate population growth scenarios into urban intensification or expansion; Evaluation using built-up land area changes
Validation Data Sources: Historical land system changes between 2000-2015; Built-up land area changes as validation metric
Key Findings: Under constant density, population decline allows decrease in built-up land saving natural areas; Continuation of declining population density leads to large urban area increase even with low population; High population + gradual decline scenario shows 48% increase in built-up land; Low population + constant density could be accommodated within current built-up land; Maintaining current population densities can avoid loss of 57-73 × 10³ km² of natural land; Urban expansion mostly leads to conversion of agricultural land and decline in natural areas
Implications: Population decline alone doesn't automatically reduce built-up land; Policies needed to avoid further natural area losses; Opportunity for sustainable urban development through density controls; Need for strong land use policies and enforcement; Urban land use efficiency becomes important with population decline
Limitations: Simplified assumptions about drivers of urban density changes; Population density changes included as scenario input rather than modeled from underlying drivers; Economic changes and policy drivers not explicitly modeled; Focus on potential trajectories rather than most likely outcomes; Complete policy analysis beyond scope
Future Directions: Not specified
Scalability: Demonstrates need for nuanced representation of settlement systems for other regions; Methodology could be adapted to other countries experiencing population decline; Approach relevant for regions with strong land use policies
Novelty: First study to simulate settlement changes after peak population in China; Novel representation of multiple settlement systems along rural-urban gradient; Integration of population decline scenarios with land system modeling; Distinction between urban expansion and intensification processes; Application of CLUMondo model to Chinese context with settlement system focus

Title: Spatial identification and scenario simulation of the ecological transition zones under the climate change in China
Authors: Fan, Zemeng
Objective: Develop a spatial model for identifying the boundary of each ETZ type and its distribution; simulate their response to climate scenarios to understand ecosystem response and feedback to global climate change
LULC Classes: 41 ecological transition zone (ETZ) types between various ecosystem types including cool temperate steppe/moist forest/warm temperate dry forest; boreal moist forest/wet forest/cool temperate moist forest; warm temperate dry forest/moist forest/cool temperate moist forest
Scenarios: RCP2.6; RCP4.5; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Improved Holdridge life zone (iHLZ) model; spatial shift of mean center model; High accuracy surface modeling (HASM)
Sim. Method Advantages: HASM overcomes the limits of the IDW, TIN, Kriging, and Spline methods and greatly improves the accuracy of interpolating and downscaling the climate data
Tools/Soft Used: High accuracy surface modeling (HASM)
Predictors: Mean annual biotemperature (MAB); total annual precipitation (TAP); potential evapotranspiration ratio (PER)
Data Sources: 782 weather stations in China; IPCC CMIP5 climate scenario data; Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) digital elevation model
Validation Methods: Accuracy assessment of climate data interpolation and downscaling
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: 41 ETZ types identified in China accounting for 18% of land area; three major ETZ types account for one-third of total ETZ area; ETZ mean centers show significant spatial shifts under climate scenarios; cold ETZ projected to transform to warm humid ETZ; alpine cold and arid ETZ types have higher sensitivity to climate change
Implications: ETZs are most sensitive areas to climate change; ETZs are areas where biodiversity is more vulnerable to climate change; ETZs serve as basic indicators for identifying global change
Limitations: Effects of human activities on ETZ change not evaluated; study focused only on climate change effects
Future Directions: Evaluate effects of human activities on ETZ changes
Scalability: Method can be applied to other regions
Novelty: Novel ETZ spatial identification method; quantitative spatial identification approach; spatial shift of mean center model for ETZ analysis; first study to identify 49 surface terrain ETZ types and overcome limitations of existing models that can only recognize boundaries between two ecosystem types

Title: Spatial optimization of urban land and cropland based on land production capacity to balance cropland protection and ecological conservation
Authors: Wang, Liye; Zheng, Weiwei; Tang, Lanping; Zhang, Siyu; Liu, Yaolin; Ke, Xinli
Objective: To optimize the spatial distribution of urban land and cropland based on land agricultural production capacity to balance cropland protection and ecological conservation requirements
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest; Grassland; River; Wetland; Urban land; Rural settlements; Unused land
Scenarios: Business as usual (BAU) scenario; Compensational optimization (CO) scenario; Occupancy optimization (OO) scenario; Occupancy and compensational optimization (OCO) scenario
Analysis Methods: LAND System Cellular Automata model for Potential Effects (LANDSCAPE); Spatial optimization; Multi-objective optimization; Kappa simulation for validation; Sankey diagrams for visualization
Sim. Method Advantages: LANDSCAPE model can express cascading progress among multiple land use changes; combines spatial and quantitative optimization capabilities; overcomes limitations of mathematical methods that failed in optimizing spatial distribution; widely used in land use change and optimal land use allocation
Tools/Soft Used: LANDSCAPE model; ArcGIS 10.2; GAEZ model
Predictors: Distance raster of seven types of road networks (railways, high-speed ways, national roads, provincial roads, county roads, city main roads, other roads); Precipitation data; Accumulated temperature data; Digital elevation model (DEM); Slope data; Soil pH data; Soil organic matter data; Agricultural production capacity (APC) data
Data Sources: Data Center of Resources and Environment, Chinese Academy of Science; Global Agro-Ecological Zones (GAEZ) model; Traffic Atlas of China; National Meteorological Information Center; Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM); China Soil Database
Validation Methods: Kappa simulation score comparing simulated results with observed land use maps; distinguishes changed and unchanged cells and validates accuracy of changed cells only
Validation Data Sources: Land use maps from 2000 and 2015 for validation comparison
Key Findings: Reduced ecological land loss in compensational, occupancy, and occupancy and compensational optimization scenarios by 7180, 247, and 7277 km² respectively compared to non-optimization scenario; Mean APC of occupied cropland (45712 t/km²) was almost three times higher than compensated cropland (15746 t/km²); Cropland compensation caused 87.1% of ecological land loss compared to urban expansion; Quality of compensated cropland showed significant increase after optimization
Implications: Should prioritize quality of compensated cropland when developing cropland protection strategies; Compensation optimization is more efficient than occupancy optimization; Land use optimization can balance cropland protection and ecological conservation requirements; Spatial allocation based on agricultural production capacity can mitigate conflicts between land uses
Limitations: Assumed land APC remained consistent during 2000-2015 and in 2030, while in reality production capacity varies over time; Did not assess local ecosystem service impacts when high APC regions become major cropland compensation areas; Need to explore whether regions should reclaim more cropland under same urban expansion levels
Future Directions: Consider change in APC over time according to temperature, precipitation, and radiation; Assess local ecosystem service impacts of optimization; Explore optimal cropland reclamation levels in different regions under urban expansion scenarios
Scalability: The optimization method can be applied to other regions facing similar cropland protection and ecological conservation conflicts, though specific parameters would need regional adjustment
Novelty: First study to optimize urban land and cropland spatial distribution based on land agricultural production capacity with cropland protection restrictions; Novel application of LANDSCAPE model combined with APC data for balancing multiple land use objectives; Innovative scenario-based approach comparing compensation vs. occupancy optimization strategies

Title: Spatial-temporal dynamics of deforestation and its drivers indicate need for locally-adapted environmental governance in Colombia
Authors: Gonzalez-Gonzalez, Andres; Camilo Villegas, Juan; Clerici, Nicola; Fernando Salazar, Juan
Objective: To use a spatially-explicit modeling platform to identify the influence of multiple deforestation drivers in different biogeographical and planning regions of Colombia; produce deforestation scenarios for 2030 and 2050; and determine the historical spatial and temporal variation of deforestation in Colombia in the last decade
LULC Classes: Forest; non-forest; deforested areas; agricultural areas; pasturelands; croplands; urban centers; rural centers
Scenarios: Business as Usual (BAU) - maintaining constant historical deforestation rates; Governance (GOV) - implementing environmental policy enforcement with 30% reduction by 2030 and 50% reduction by 2050; National Agricultural Frontier (NAF) incorporation in both scenarios
Analysis Methods: Spatially-explicit modeling; cellular automata; Weights of Evidence (WoE) method; Bayesian conditional probability; transition matrix analysis; spatial metrics calculation; multiple spatial windows validation; stochastic simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Dinamica EGO allows modeling spatial dynamics of change through systematic steps; permits assimilating underlying causes and dynamic processes of land conversion through time; widely used for tropical LULC change studies; incorporates cellular automata rules for realistic spatial patterns
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica EGO platform; QGIS with Lecos plugin v3.0.0; WGS84 UTM zone 18 N projection system
Predictors: Distance to deforested areas; roads (5 categories); mining concessions; urban centers; rural centers; water bodies (rivers, lakes, swamps, wetlands); slope; protected areas; FARC routes (internal conflict proxy)
Data Sources: Hansen Global Forest Change database v.1.6; National Road Institute of Colombia (Invías); Global Forest Watch mining database; Colombian Geographic Institute Agustín Codazzi (IGAC); SRTM digital elevation model v.4.1; Colombian National Natural Parks System (PNNC, SINAP); FIP (Fundación Ideas para la Paz) for FARC routes
Validation Methods: Multiple spatial windows with constant decay function; similarity comparison between historical and simulated landscape maps for 2018; moving windows of size n × n pixels (n = 3 to 13); similarity expressed from 0 to 1 scale
Validation Data Sources: Historical forest loss map 2018 from Hansen Global Forest Change database
Key Findings: Agricultural activities have significant role in deforestation with large regional variation, internal conflict produced contrasting effects; acting as attractor in some areas and deterrent in others, Amazon region shows highest forest loss (6,344 km²), followed by Andean region (3,677 km²), BAU scenario predicts 65,479 km² forest loss by 2050, Governance scenario could preserve about 39,000 km² compared to BAU, deforestation drivers vary considerably among natural regions
Implications: Need for locally-adapted environmental governance; protected areas are effective for forest conservation when properly enforced; current trends could lead to major ecological impacts including fragmentation and loss of connectivity between ecosystems; potential loss of spatial connectivity between Andes and Amazon regions by 2050
Limitations: Only considers direct anthropogenic drivers; does not include indirect drivers like surface-atmosphere feedbacks; model stochasticity creates uncertainty in areas with low transition probabilities; peace agreement effects not fully captured in historical data
Future Directions: Include climate impacts of future deforestation; investigate surface-atmosphere feedbacks; incorporate indirect drivers effects; develop regionally-adapted policy measures; enhance involvement of local, indigenous and afro communities in conservation efforts
Scalability: Results can provide valuable information for development of national policies and strategies in other tropical countries; modeling approach applicable to similar biogeographically diverse nations; methodology transferable to other tropical deforestation contexts
Novelty: First comprehensive spatially-explicit analysis of deforestation drivers across Colombia's five biogeographical regions; demonstrates contrasting effects of internal conflict on deforestation at different spatial scales; integrates National Agricultural Frontier planning with deforestation scenarios; reveals significant regional variation in driver effectiveness challenging generalized approaches

Title: Understanding Complex Relationships between Human Well-Being and Land Use Change in Mozambique Using a Multi-Scale Participatory Scenario Planning Process
Authors: Zorrilla-Miras, Pedro; Lopez-Moya, Estrella; Metzger, Marc J.; Patenaude, Genevieve; Sitoe, Almeida; Mahamane, Mansour; Lisboa, Sa Nogueira; Paterson, James S.; Lopez-Gunn, Elena
Objective: To improve understanding of complex phenomena linking land use and land cover (LULC) change and wellbeing of small-scale farmers in sub-Saharan Africa; identify driving forces of LULC change; contribute to debate about possible futures in Mozambique; illustrate produced scenarios for use in future studies and policy settings
LULC Classes: Agricultural land; forested areas; mined areas; urban areas; woodland areas; protected wildlife areas; areas under private long-term leases and concessions
Scenarios: Three scenarios: Scenario A (Large Private Investments); Scenario B (Small Holder Promotion); Scenario C (Intermediate Scenario)
Analysis Methods: Multi-scale participatory scenario planning; morphological approach combined with intuitive logics methodology; stakeholder workshops; KETSO toolkit for participatory exercises
Sim. Method Advantages: Allows incorporation of stakeholder knowledge and local perspectives; deals with uncertainty through creative thinking; facilitates understanding of complex interactions between drivers; enables cross-scale analysis; supports policy-relevant outcomes
Tools/Soft Used: KETSO toolkit for participatory workshops; qualitative analysis methods; spider diagrams for scenario comparison
Predictors: Empowerment of communities and civil society; effective application of legislation; decentralization and higher involvement of society in politics; changes in rural technologies; economic growth and development; migration patterns
Data Sources: Stakeholder workshops; literature review; government statistics; World Bank data; UN data; national development strategies; previous scenario exercises in Mozambique and neighboring countries
Validation Methods: Stakeholder validation through second round of workshops; evaluation of scenario plausibility by thematic groups; comparison of scenarios with actual pathways since 2015
Validation Data Sources: Workshop participant feedback; actual development trajectories in Mozambique post-2015; comparison with hidden debt crisis impacts and cyclone effects
Key Findings: All scenarios predict large LULC changes by 2035; most important drivers are social empowerment and effective law application; biggest differences arise from policies promoting small vs large-scale agriculture; multi-scale approach reveals hidden differences in local economies; Scenario A leads to higher rural-urban migration; Scenario B promotes food sovereignty through small-scale agriculture; effective law application can produce different results depending on government priorities
Implications: Need for effective protection of natural areas; importance of involving local communities in conservation; potential for payments for ecosystem services; requirement for additional economic resources for nature protection; policy influence on land use planning and rural poverty programs
Limitations: Difficulty in producing quantified results; complex relations between drivers made quantification challenging; lack of expertise from participants in all sectors; insufficient time for rigorous quantitative analysis; contradictory land use change rates in initial quantifications
Future Directions: Need for specific time devoted to producing quantified results; iterative process using modeling tools; application of OLDFAR algorithm for optimally diverse scenarios; inclusion of 'shock event' scenarios; development of Bayesian Belief Networks
Scalability: Method demonstrated as valuable for use in other least developed countries; framework applicable to other Sub-Saharan African contexts; consistent across scales approach allows for regional comparisons
Novelty: Multi-scale participatory scenario planning approach; combination of morphological and intuitive logics methodologies; creation of scenarios not linked to global scenarios for increased local ownership; downscaling from national to provincial level; integration of stakeholder knowledge with scientific analysis

Title: A Declining Trend in China's Future Cropland-N<sub>2</sub>O Emissions Due to Reduced Cropland Area
Authors: Wang, Qingrui; Liu, Ruimin; Zhou, Feng; Huang, Jing; Jiao, Lijun; Li, Lin; Wang, Yifan; Cao, Leiping; Xia, Xinghui
Objective: Predict high-precision cropland‐N₂O emissions in China from 2020 to 2070 using a newly developed land-use prediction model.
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest land; Grassland; Residential land; Water area; Unused land
Scenarios: Harmonized development priority (low population increase, rapid technology innovation_RCP2.6); Socioeconomic development priority (rapid population increase, no technology innovation_RCP8.5); Plus 18 other combinations of population increase rate; technology innovation rate; Grain for Green implementation; RCP2.6; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Distributed system dynamics (DSD) for land‐use count; Distributed cellular automata (DCA) for spatial allocation; Spatial Referenced Nonlinear Model (SRNM) for N₂O emissions
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures spatial heterogeneity via SCUs (provincial/municipal); Improves Kappa coefficient and change trend prediction over conventional SD-CA; Respects permanent basic farmland (PBF) and least cultivated land area (LCLA) constraints
Tools/Soft Used: Vensim; Python
Predictors: Socioeconomic factors: population, GDP, Grain for Green parameter, PBF constraint; Natural drivers: DEM, slope, river network, road network, climate and soil factors for ANN feasibility; Neighborhood effects; change cost matrix; localization factor
Data Sources: Chinese Academy of Sciences (land‐use, population, GDP); National Bureau of Statistics (initial DSD parameter ranges); DEM, slope, river network, road network spatial datasets
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient, Figure of Merit (FOM), Relative Absolute Error (RAE); Monte Carlo calibration, comparison with conventional SD-CA results
Validation Data Sources: Observed land‐use data from 2005 and 2010
Key Findings: Total cropland‐N₂O emissions decline from 0.44±0.03 to 0.39±0.07 Tg N yr⁻¹ (2020–2070); GFG scenarios reduce emissions ~12%; Upland crops contribute >80% of emissions and their rate rises under RCP8.5; Conventional SD-CA underestimates cropland area and N₂O emissions by up to 50% by 2070
Implications: DLUCP model better supports large‐scale N₂O management; Grain for Green aids emission control and reduces nitrogen input costs; Need targeted control in East, Northeast, Southwest, Central South regions
Limitations: PBF and LCLA target changes assumed linear due to data paucity
Future Directions: Model PBF and LCLA target dynamics with dedicated assessment systems; Incorporate more detailed future socioeconomic and policy shifts
Scalability: Applicable to other large regions with heterogeneous socioeconomic drivers
Novelty: Distributed parameterization using provincial/municipal SCUs; Integration of DSD and DCA modules with ANN‐based natural feasibility; Explicit PBF and LCLA constraint implementation for large‐scale land‐use prediction

Title: Assessing biophysical and socio-economic impacts of climate change on regional avian biodiversity
Authors: Kapitza, Simon; Van Ha, Pham; Kompas, Tom; Golding, Nick; Cadenhead, Natasha C. R.; Bal, Payal; Wintle, Brendan A.
Objective: Assess relative influence of biophysical and socio-economic (indirect) climate change impacts on the distribution and extent of suitable ranges for avian species
LULC Classes: urban; cropland; herbaceous ground vegetation; shrubland; open canopy forest; closed canopy forest; wetlands; barren land
Scenarios: RCP2.6; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Computable general equilibrium (GTAP) economic modelling; Spatially explicit land use change modelling (CLUE-S via R ‘lulcc’); Species distribution modelling (MaxEnt via R ‘dismo’)
Sim. Method Advantages: Multistep simulation applying shocks in smaller successive intervals with extrapolation improves accuracy over one-step CGE simulations
Tools/Soft Used: R 3.5.1; ‘lulcc’; CLUE-S; ‘dismo’; MaxEnt 3.3.3k; GTAP; PETSC; HSL
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP 9) database; FAOSTAT urban population projections; Global land use map (reclassified); WorldClim bioclimatic variables (CMIP5 GCM quartiles); GBIF presence records for avian species
Validation Methods: Five-fold cross-validation yielding AUC values for SDMs
Validation Data Sources: GBIF presence records and sampling-effort–weighted background points
Key Findings: Direct biophysical impacts dominate range changes, indirect socio-economic impacts are minor; Under RCP8.5, ~24% of Vietnamese birds lose >50% of suitable range, significant loss also in Australia; Combined direct+indirect predictions mirror direct-only outcomes
Implications: Provides policy-relevant, spatially explicit predictions linking climate change, economy, land use, and biodiversity to inform cross-sectoral adaptation/mitigation strategies
Limitations: Omits other socio-economic processes (e.g. future economic growth, policy changes); No feedback of land use change into CGE model; Assumes unlimited (Vietnam) or bioregion-adjacent (Australia) dispersal; Excludes species with <20 occurrences
Future Directions: Incorporate full Shared Socio-economic Pathways in CGE parameters; Include other taxa and explicit connectivity/dispersal modelling; Simulate specific policy or trade shocks
Scalability: Applicable to other regions and global assessments via same integrated framework
Novelty: First high-resolution, spatially explicit integration of CGE, land use downscaling, and species distribution models under climate change scenarios

Title: ASSESSMENT OF POTENTIAL IMPACTS OF CLIMATE AND SOCIO-ECONOMIC CHANGES ON FUTURE WATER SECURITY IN THE HIMALAYAS, INDIA
Authors: Dau, Quan, V; Kuntiyawichai, Kittiwet
Objective: To assess the combined impacts of climate and socio-economic changes on future water security in the Beas-Sutlej Himalayan basin, India
LULC Classes: Irrigated area; Urban area; Shrub vegetation; Permanent snowfields and glacier; Other ESA-CCI land cover classes
Scenarios: RCP4.5; SSP1
Analysis Methods: Statistical downscaling (Delta Change) of CMIP5 MME under RCP4.5; Markov Chain with MLP neural network for land use projection; WEAP water allocation model with GA-derived rule curves; RRSM rainfall-runoff method; MABIA irrigation demand method
Sim. Method Advantages: MME approach reduces uncertainties across models compared to single-model projections
Tools/Soft Used: WRF model; WEAP; Markov Chain analysis with MLP; GA optimization; Statistical software for Delta Change
Predictors: Elevation; Population density; Slope; Distance to urban centers; Distance to rivers; Distance to roads
Data Sources: ERA-Interim reanalysis; WRF downscaled CMIP5 outputs; ESA-CCI land cover maps; Census of India; Gao (2017) population grids; BBMB reservoir and discharge records
Validation Methods: Kappa Index of Agreement, R² for land use projection; Pearson’s r and Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency for hydrologic simulations
Validation Data Sources: Observed land cover 2010 (ESA-CCI); Observed streamflow and reservoir inflow (BBMB stations)
Key Findings: Future annual precipitation +5–10% downstream, +15–20% upstream, temperature +1–1.55 °C downstream, +3.5–5.0 °C upstream; Glacier volume decline by 14.5% (mid-century) and 37.5% (end-century), increased runoff into Pong/Bhakra reservoirs; Irrigated areas decrease 10–30% in Punjab, 5–10% in Haryana, increase 12–18% in Rajasthan; Irrigation demand decreases ~10% in Punjab, ~5% in Haryana, increases ~13% in Rajasthan
Implications: Provides actionable insights for BBMB and agencies to plan reservoir operations, irrigation, hydropower, and flood control under changing climate and socio-economic conditions
Limitations: Use of only Delta Change downscaling; Reliance on single RCP4.5 and SSP1 scenarios
Future Directions: Apply multiple statistical and dynamical downscaling approaches; Explore additional RCP and SSP scenarios to reduce projection uncertainties
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integration of CMIP5 MME Delta Change, Markov-MLP land use projection, and WEAP GA-optimized reservoir operation for a holistic impact assessment

Title: Desertification risk assessment in Northeast Brazil: Current trends and future scenarios
Authors: Vieira, Rita Marcia D. S. P.; Tomasella, Javier; Barbosa, Alexandre A.; Martins, Minella A.; Rodriguez, Daniel A.; Rezende, Fernanda S. D.; Carriello, Felix; Santana, Marcos D. O.
Objective: Generate future projections of environmentally sensitive areas to desertification by integrating LULC trajectories with downscaled climate-change scenarios and population growth projections
LULC Classes: Evergreen forest; Restinga; Seasonal forest; Fluviomarine (mangrove); Alluvial; Campo Maior complex; Steppe savanna (Caatinga); Baixada Maranhense; Agriculture; Pasture; Water body; Beach; Bare soil; Dunes; Rock outcrops; Salt fields
Scenarios: RCP4.5; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit LULC change modeling; weights-of-evidence; correlation analysis (Cramér’s V, Joint Information Uncertainty); MEDALUS desertification susceptibility mapping
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures spatial feedbacks via cellular automata; Allows expert-knowledge integration; Generates high-resolution, plausible landscape trajectories
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica Environment for Geoprocessing Objects (Dinamica EGO v4.0.9.0); Regional Model Eta; CMIP5 coupling; Bárdossy & Pegram bias correction
Predictors: Population density; Livestock density; Slope; Pedology; Conservation unit status; Hydrological distance; Urban area distance; Roads distance; Aridity index; Vegetation type; Distance to infrastructure
Data Sources: Primary: Dinamica EGO LULC maps (Vieira et al., 2015), bias-corrected downscaled climate data (HadGEM2-ES, MIROC5, CanESM2, 1980–2005 baseline, future slices); Secondary: IBGE demographic census 2010, Brazilian National Water Agency, MMA conservation units, topographic and soil maps
Validation Methods: Fuzzy Similarity Index over multiple window sizes with constant decay function
Validation Data Sources: Historical LULC maps 2000–2010 (Vieira et al., 2015)
Key Findings: Forest area decline up to 75% (HadGEM RCP4.5) by 2040, agriculture +32%, mixed crop-pasture +10%; Moderate susceptibility areas decrease, high susceptibility increase by 12.28% (RCP4.5) and 19.62% (RCP8.5); 96–99% of region remains moderately to highly susceptible to desertification
Implications: Urgent sustainable land-use policies needed; Prioritize soil-conservation, irrigation efficiency, buffer zones, ecological corridors; Enforcement of environmental protection laws in agricultural frontier
Limitations: Business-as-usual LULC scenarios only; Excluded RCP2.6 (“Paris accord”) scenario; Simplified demographic trend (linear to 2040)
Future Directions: Explore low-emissions (RCP2.6) and green-economy LULC alternatives; Include broader indicator sets in simulations; Assess benefits of Land Degradation Neutrality policies
Scalability: Applicable to other dryland regions via Dinamica EGO and MEDALUS integration
Novelty: First integration of downscaled climate scenarios with LULC trajectories and demographic projections for Northeast Brazil’s desertification susceptibility.

Title: Rapid adaptive modelling for policy support towards achieving Sustainable Development Goals: Brexit and the livestock sector in Wales
Authors: Thomas, A.; Cosby, B. J.; Gooday, R.; Lyons, H.; Siriwardena, G.; Kettel, E.; Matthews, R.; Beauchamp, K.; Petr, M.; Emmett, B. A.
Objective: Provide rapid adaptive modelling evidence of potential agricultural sector responses to Brexit trade scenarios to support policy for Sustainable Development Goals
LULC Classes: Agricultural land (dairy, sheep, beef, mixed grazing, various grazing, lowland mixed grazing); Pigs, Poultry, Woodland
Scenarios: EU Deal; No Deal; Multilateral Free Trade Agreements (MFTA)
Analysis Methods: Participatory adaptive scenario modelling; Agri-economic models; Environmental impact models (Farmscoper, BTO bird models, CARBINE, ESC); Capacity-based decision trees; Spatial mapping
Sim. Method Advantages: Rapid linkage of existing models for timely policy input; Transparent assumptions; Spatially explicit outputs for local targeting
Tools/Soft Used: Farmscoper, CARBINE, Ecological Site Classification model; GIS for spatial mapping
Predictors: Livestock numbers, Stocking densities, Livestock composition; Farm survey data, Landscape data, Climate, Soil; Agricultural Land Classification, Glastir Woodland Creation rules
Data Sources: Welsh Government June Agricultural Survey; FAPRI-UK model; AHDB impact assessment; ERAMMP programme data; BTO/JNCC/RSPB Breeding Bird Survey; National farm survey and landscape data
Validation Methods: Cross-checking with stakeholder groups and SWG; Expert judgement comparisons with other projections; Consistency checks of input data and assumptions
Validation Data Sources: Stakeholder reports (SWG); FAPRI-UK and AHDB model outputs; Expert elicitation from Welsh Government specialists
Key Findings: EU Deal affects 3% farmland with small GHG and pollutant changes; No Deal affects 17% with increased NH3 (+11%) and N loads (+3%), job losses; MFTA affects 15% with reduced pollutants (GHG −16%, N −14%), large job losses; Spatial variations concentrate impacts in uplands and polluted areas; Woodland planting potential up to 98 343 ha yields significant GHG mitigation; Mixed biodiversity responses across 54 bird species
Implications: Trade deal choice crucial for agriculture, environment, jobs; Need spatially targeted policies for environmental protections and social safety nets; Opportunity to align post-Brexit agricultural support with SDG via woodland creation; Risk of exporting environmental impacts if production shifts abroad
Limitations: No uncertainty or sensitivity analysis; Biodiversity assessed only via birds; Excludes cross-sector global impact of displaced agriculture; Assumes no regulatory or policy change post-Brexit
Future Directions: Incorporate uncertainty and sensitivity analyses; Extend biodiversity assessment to other taxa; Model global displacement effects; Evaluate policy interventions for targeted woodland planting
Scalability: Approach transferable to other regions with available farm surveys and environmental models
Novelty: First rapid adaptive linkage of agri-economic and environmental models for policy support under dynamic political change; Spatially explicit scenario modelling integrating jobs, environmental, and land use outcomes

Title: Soil erosion in future scenario using CMIP5 models and earth observation datasets
Authors: Maurya, Swati; Srivastava, Prashant K.; Yaduvanshi, Aradhana; Anand, Akash; Petropoulos, George P.; Zhuo, Lu; Mall, R. K.
Objective: Investigate impact of rainfall and land use/land cover changes on soil erosion losses using the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE)
LULC Classes: Waterbody; Forest; Grassland; Cropland; Barren; Urban
Scenarios: Historical baseline; Future scenario under CMIP5 RCP4.5 projections (seven GCMs and ensemble mean)
Analysis Methods: RUSLE spatially distributed modeling; CA-Markov land use/land cover simulation; statistical evaluation of CMIP5 outputs (Taylor diagram, box-whisker analysis); GIS-based terrain and soil mapping
Sim. Method Advantages: CA-Markov combines Cellular Automata and Markov Chain to capture both spatial dynamics and temporal transition probabilities, offering higher consistency and ability to simulate multi-temporal LULC changes than standalone Markov or other models
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.1; ENVI; MATLAB (for CA-Markov implementation implied); statistical software for Taylor diagram
Predictors: Rainfall-runoff erosivity (R); Soil erodibility (K); Topographic factors (LS); Cover-management (C); Conservation practice (P); Land use/land cover transitions
Data Sources: Primary: IMD gridded rainfall, NEX-GDDP-CMIP5 downscaled GCM outputs, Landsat MSS/TM imagery, SRTM DEM, FAO soil map; Secondary: NBSSLUP point-based soil loss validation data
Validation Methods: Accuracy assessment of LULC classification (producer’s and user’s accuracies, overall and Kappa statistics); comparison of modeled soil loss with NBSSLUP datasets
Validation Data Sources: NBSSLUP (National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning) soil loss portal data
Key Findings: Rainfall-runoff erosivity increased from ~475 MJ mm ha⁻¹ h⁻¹ y⁻¹ (1981–1990) to ~661 MJ mm ha⁻¹ h⁻¹ y⁻¹ (2011–2040 ensemble); Soil erosion rose from 55.23 t/ha/y (1981–1990) to 71.46 t/ha/y (2011–2040 ensemble); Forest and cropland show highest per-class erosion rates (up to ~327 t/ha/y and ~313 t/ha/y projected)
Implications: Findings can inform conservation planning, watershed management, and policy-making for soil and water conservation in the Mahi River Basin and similar regions
Limitations: Absence of field-based P-factor measurements; reliance on statistical downscaling; fixed K and LS factors for future scenario
Future Directions: Incorporate finer-scale climate scenarios (RCP8.5); include field surveys for P-factor; extend methodology to other basins; assess socioeconomic drivers
Scalability: Methodology is robust, low-cost, globally applicable using freely available satellite and model datasets
Novelty: Integration of CA-Markov LULC simulation with CMIP5-downscaled rainfall projections in a spatially explicit RUSLE framework for future soil erosion assessment in Mahi River Basin

Title: The Loop Effect: How Climate Change Impacts the Mitigation Potential of the French Forest Sector
Authors: Delacote, Philippe; Lobianco, Antonello; Caurla, Sylvain; Bontemps, Jean-Daniel; Lungarska, Anna; Merian, Pierre; Riviere, Miguel; Barkaoui, Ahmed
Objective: Evaluate the capacity of temperate forest resources to provide climate change mitigation and sustain the downstream timber sector, explicitly considering cascading biophysical and economic drivers and their uncertainty
LULC Classes: Agriculture; Forest; Urban; Other
Scenarios: IPCC SRES A1B; A2; B1; constant climate; variants of management expectation (noexp/fullexp); no active management (nomgm); no risk aversion (nora)
Analysis Methods: Recursive spatialized bio-economic forest sector model (FFSM++); Statistical climate-impact models (GAMs for growth and presence); Agricultural supply model AROPAj; Econometric land-use share model (spatial error model)
Sim. Method Advantages: Endogenous feedbacks between forest dynamics, markets, land use and management; Spatially explicit at 8 km resolution; Captures “loop effects” of climate impacts on mitigation potential
Tools/Soft Used: FFSM++ (bio-economic model); AROPAj (agricultural supply); R package gam (Generalized Additive Models); R package spdep (spatial error model)
Predictors: Agricultural shadow price; Expected forestry returns; Population density; Population revenues; Slope; Soil texture class; Soil C:N; Soil pH; Water-holding capacity; Soil depth; Seasonal precipitation; Temperature; Vapor deficit
Data Sources: National Forest Inventory (NFI); SAFRAN climatic grid; Corine Land Cover 2000; AROPAj v2 & v5; INSEE population & revenue data; IIASA demographic projections; GTOPO30 elevation; European Soil Database
Validation Methods: K-fold cross-validation for GAMs; Moran’s I test and spatial error diagnostics for land-use model
Validation Data Sources: NFI plot data; Corine Land Cover observations
Key Findings: Climate impacts on tree mortality exceed growth changes; Competition with agriculture may reverse forest expansion trends; Rising mean tree size drives declining volume growth, peaking before century’s end; Future climate and socioeconomic drivers already affect today’s forest investment profitability; Exports of primary wood increase, imports of transformed products decrease; Substitution effects gain relative importance over sequestration over time; Climate change and adaptation threaten up to 30% of the sector’s mitigation potential, profit-driven management enhances mitigation
Implications: Need to integrate adaptation-mitigation trade-offs in policy; Active management can bolster both timber supply and climate goals; Land-use competition underscores importance of cross-sectoral strategies
Limitations: Only seven inventoried species modeled; Constant demand/supply elasticities over time; Excludes legal land-use restrictions, biodiversity services, pathogen network effects; Long management strategies fixed until harvest, no dynamic re-planting decisions
Future Directions: Incorporate additional species and genetic adaptation; Model legal/institutional land-use constraints; Integrate biodiversity and ecosystem service valuation; Include disturbance network effects (pests, pathogens); Assess specific policy-induced market shifts
Scalability: Approach transferable to other regions given comparable high-resolution biophysical and socioeconomic data
Novelty: First integration of spatialized forest sector model, agricultural supply, econometric land-use model and statistical climate-impact models to capture cascading “loop effects” under climate change.

Title: Urbanization can benefit agricultural production with large-scale farming in China
Authors: Wang, Sitong; Bai, Xuemei; Zhang, Xiaoling; Reis, Stefan; Chen, Deli; Xu, Jianming; Gu, Baojing
Objective: quantify potential cropland release and its impact on crop production, farm size, and agricultural sustainability with China’s urbanization
LULC Classes: urban built-up land; rural built-up land; cropland; natural land
Scenarios: urbanization level 56% → 70% (2030) with rural land reclamation; 56% → 80% (2050) with and without rural land reclamation; 56% → 90% (2050) with and without reclamation; urban density high/low
Analysis Methods: spatial statistics; scenario analysis; focal statistics on grid priorities; county-level aggregation
Sim. Method Advantages: captures spatially explicit expansion and reclamation priorities; integrates GDP ranking for tie-breaking; reflects rural homestead reclamation potential not addressed by land-use competition models
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.6; Focal Statistics tool
Predictors: proportion of urban grids (10×10 window); proportion of rural and cropland grids (3×3 window); GDP for tie-breaking; elevation ≤3,500 m; slope ≤30°
Data Sources: Resource and Environment Data Cloud Platform land-use and GDP; National Bureau of Statistics urban/rural population; SOC map by Yu et al. (2012); UN World Urbanization Prospects
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: increased cropland by +2.7 Mha (2030) and +5.8 Mha (2050) via rural reclamation; crop production +3.1–4.2% (2050) despite lower fertility; per-capita rural cropland area doubled by 2050; average farm size potential raised from 0.5 ha to 1.35 ha; supports large-scale farming and environmental protection
Implications: integrated urban–rural development can enhance food security; policy reform of Hukou and HCRS needed; land consolidation and rural reclamation vital for sustainable agriculture
Limitations: assumes unlimited migration and development; excludes rural density changes; uncertainty in future yield improvements; ignores socioeconomic barriers to reclamation
Future Directions: assess socioeconomic impacts on land-lost farmers; model yield gains from technology adoption; extend scenarios under trade and climate change pressures
Scalability: applicable to other developing regions undergoing rapid urbanization with rural homestead patterns
Novelty: highlights rural built-up land reclamation potential; integrates urban expansion and rural land release in one spatially explicit framework; linkage of land release to farm size and productivity gains

Title: 1 km land use/land cover change of China under comprehensive socioeconomic and climate scenarios for 2020-2100
Authors: Luo, Meng; Hu, Guohua; Chen, Guangzhao; Liu, Xiaojuan; Hou, Haiyan; Li, Xia
Objective: Develop a 1-km gridded land-use/land-cover (LULC) dataset for China for 2020-2100 under the full matrix of 24 SSP-RCP scenarios, integrating GCAM and FLUS models to provide high-resolution, scenario-rich projections for research and policy assessment.
LULC Classes: Urban; Cropland; Grassland; Shrub; Forest; Water; Bareland; Ice
Analysis Methods: GCAM v5.2 to project regional LULC demand; calibration with ESA CCI-LC and Chen et al. (2020) urban dataset; downscaling with FLUS cellular automata model driven by artificial neural networks; spatio-temporal comparison with LUH2
Sim. Method Advantages: FLUS couples top-down system dynamics with bottom-up CA; captures heterogeneous spatial detail at 1 km; delivers higher accuracy than single CA or CLUE-S; GCAM-FLUS linkage covers full SSP-RCP matrix and explicitly models urban change
Tools/Soft Used: GCAM v5.2; FLUS 2020; Artificial Neural Network module within FLUS; GIS software (ArcGIS/ENVI implied); MATLAB (for FLUS)
Predictors: Annual mean temperature; annual precipitation; soil oxygen availability; soil excess salts; soil workability; DEM; slope; population (POP); GDP; distance to rivers/lakes; distance to main roads; distance to highways; distance to railways; distance to airports; distance to urban centres
Data Sources: GCAM v5.2 outputs; ESA CCI-LC 2010; Chen et al. (2020) 1-km future urban land; WorldClim v2.0; GTOPO30 DEM; Fischer et al. (2008) soil data; Gaughan et al. (2016) population; Kummu et al. (2018) GDP; Huang et al. (2013) transport networks; LUH2 for comparison
Validation Methods: Overall accuracy; Cohen’s Kappa; Figure of Merit; confusion matrix versus CCI-LC 2010; Pearson correlation and RMSD versus LUH2 2010-2100
Validation Data Sources: ESA CCI-LC 2010; LUH2 CMIP6 dataset
Key Findings: Mean Kappa = 0.64 and overall accuracy = 0.79 for China; FoM = 0.13 within accepted range; high spatial (r = 0.66-0.88) and temporal consistency with LUH2; dataset captures finer urban, cropland and forest details than 0.25° LUH2; provides full-scenario coverage at 1 km resolution
Implications: Enables detailed earth-system and ecosystem-service modelling, biodiversity and carbon neutrality studies; supports policy design for 1.5 °C and 2 °C targets; reduces uncertainty from coarse LULC inputs
Limitations: Bareland assumed unchanged except for urban encroachment; water and ice held constant; urban shrinkage disallows conversion back to non-urban; some discrepancies with LUH2 in northwest and southeast China
Future Directions: Incorporate dynamic bareland processes; refine urban shrinkage representation; extend framework to other countries; fuse additional earth-observation data for improved accuracy
Scalability: Approach (GCAM-FLUS integration) is transferable to other regions where GCAM sub-regional outputs and suitable driving factors are available
Novelty: First 1-km Chinese LULC projections covering the complete SSP-RCP matrix with urban-calibrated demands, integrating GCAM v5.2 and FLUS for high-resolution, multi-scenario analysis

Title: Agent-Based Modeling of Alternative Futures in the British Land Use System
Authors: Brown, C.; Seo, B.; Alexander, P.; Burton, V; Chacon-Montalvan, E. A.; Dunford, R.; Merkle, M.; Harrison, P. A.; Prestele, R.; Robinson, E. L.; Rounsevell, M.
Objective: To develop a flexible agent-based modeling framework capable of representing paired SSP-RCP scenarios at national to continental scales and explore potential future land system change in Great Britain prompted by linked climatic and socio-economic conditions
LULC Classes: Arable land uses (intensive arable for food; intensive arable for fodder; sustainable arable; extensive arable); Pastoral land uses (intensive pastoral; extensive pastoral; very extensive pastoral); Forest land uses (productive native conifer; productive non-native conifer; productive native broadleaf; productive non-native broadleaf; multifunctional mixed woodland; native woodland for conservation); Combined classes (bioenergy; agroforestry); Urban areas; Natural vegetation; Conservation management
Scenarios: RCP2.6-SSP1 (Sustainability); RCP4.5-SSP2 (Middle of the Road); RCP4.5-SSP4 (Inequality); RCP6.0-SSP3 (Regional Rivalry); RCP8.5-SSP2 (Middle of the Road with high emissions); RCP8.5-SSP5 (Fossil-fueled Development)
Analysis Methods: Agent-based modeling using CRAFTY framework; Scenario-specific model parameterization; Competition-based land use allocation; Ecosystem service provision modeling; Spatial analysis at 1 km² resolution
Sim. Method Advantages: Flexible framework allows scenario-specific model designs; Accounts for human behavior, social interactions, and societal preferences; Represents land use intensity variations; Integrates multiple capitals (human, social, manufactured, financial, natural); Captures emergent properties of competition between agents; Links global and local dynamics
Tools/Soft Used: CRAFTY agent-based modeling framework; LandSyMM (Land System Modular Model); Ecological Site Classification (ESC) yield class model; Statistical modeling tools
Predictors: Human capital; Social capital; Manufactured capital; Financial capital; Natural capital (yields/suitabilities for arable, pastoral, forest); Climate variables (temperature, precipitation, potential evapotranspiration, growing degree days); Protected area designations; Ecosystem service demands; Agent behavioral characteristics
Data Sources: Land Cover Map 2015 (LCM2015); National Forest Inventory 2010-2015; UK-SSP scenarios; UK-RCP climate projections; CHESS-SCAPE climate dataset; UK Climate Projections 2018 (UKCP18); LandSyMM global modeling framework; Various protected area datasets; EUNIS habitat classification; CEH Land Cover Plus data
Validation Methods: TRACE protocol evaluation; Sensitivity analyses; Expert and stakeholder consultations; Comparison to independent datasets; Agent typology evaluation against habitat and management maps
Validation Data Sources: LCM 2015; EUNIS habitat classification scheme; CEH Land Cover Plus: Fertilisers and Pesticides data; Expert knowledge; Stakeholder input
Key Findings: Substantial differences in land use intensity between scenarios; SSP conditions had greater impact than RCP climate scenarios; UK-SSP1 led to extensification but couldn't meet high ecosystem service demands; UK-SSP5 showed highest intensification and urban expansion; UK-SSP3 resulted in extensive agriculture due to lack of inputs; Social and human capitals can generate impacts comparable to climate change; Large differences in land management intensities, ecosystem service provision, and decision-making motivations across scenarios
Implications: Different scenarios require distinct model components and parameterizations; Social factors are essential for climate policy objectives; Land sparing vs. land sharing strategies produce different environmental outcomes; Current scenario modeling may underestimate the importance of social change and human behavior; Policy pathways need to account for diverse future conditions
Limitations: Climate impacts from extreme events not fully represented; No simulation of land degradation impacts on productivity; Limited representation of biodiversity outcomes; Forest management dynamics need improvement; Feedbacks between national and global models technically challenging; Model restricted to Great Britain rather than full UK
Future Directions: Better alignment with biodiversity outcomes; Improved modeling of forest dynamics; More realistic assessment of land-based climate change mitigation; Enhanced representation of policy interventions; Development of feedbacks between national and global scale models; Application of multi-model ensembles
Scalability: Framework is transferrable and has been applied to other regions (Europe, Sweden, Brazil); Open-access model available for adaptation to other contexts; Generic CRAFTY framework allows for different geographical implementations
Novelty: First comprehensive agent-based model of British land system under multiple RCP-SSP scenarios; Scenario-specific model parameterization approach; Integration of human and social capitals in land use modeling; Explicit representation of land management intensity variations; Comprehensive ecosystem service modeling within agent-based framework; Novel land use intensity mapping approach

Title: C-LLAMA 1.0: a traceable model for food, agriculture, and land use
Authors: Ball, Thomas S.; Vaughan, Naomi E.; Powell, Thomas W.; Lovett, Andrew; Lenton, Timothy M.
Country: Global (162 countries from FAOSTAT database, excluding some due to data limitations)
Objective: Development of C-LLAMA 1.0 (Country-level Land Availability Model for Agriculture), a statistical-empirical model to provide an open and transparent approach to modelling the sensitivity of future agricultural land use to drivers such as diet, crop yields, and food-system efficiency
LULC Classes: Cropland (food crops and fodder crops); Pasture land; Agricultural land (aggregated); Freed land (when land demand decreases)
Baseline Years: 2013 (starting year for projections, using historical data from 1961-2017)
Scenarios: Anchor scenario (business-as-usual with default parameters); Maximum efficiency scenario; Minimum efficiency scenario; Full-vegetarian diet scenario; Various sensitivity scenarios
Analysis Methods: Linear regression projections; Statistical-empirical modeling; Bottom-up approach; Country-level disaggregation; Sensitivity analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Simplicity and high traceability; Open and transparent approach; Easily modifiable and adaptable; Reduced complexity compared to IAMs; Ability to explore specific components independently; Country-level representation of food system differences
Tools/Soft Used: Python programming language; Pickle library for serialized format storage
Predictors: Diet composition and calorie supply; Crop yields; Food-system efficiency parameter; Population trajectories; Processing, distribution, and post-production loss factors; Livestock feed efficiency; Effective pasture yield
Data Sources: FAOSTAT database (food supply, production, crop yield, land use data from 1961-2017); Shared Socio-economic Pathways (SSP) database for population trajectories; Literature values for efficiency parameters
Validation Methods: Comparison with FALAFEL model business-as-usual scenario; Comparison with SSP2 scenarios and AR5 scenario database; Sensitivity analyses; Behavioral testing under prescribed scenarios
Validation Data Sources: FALAFEL model outputs; SSP2 scenario database; AR5 scenario database; Historical FAOSTAT data for calibration
Key Findings: Agricultural land use projected to increase by ~450 Mha by 2050 in anchor scenario; Full-vegetarian scenario reduces land use by 1.8 Gha (34% reduction); Food-system efficiency parameter has greatest impact on land use sensitivity (~500 Mha difference); Cropland projected at 1.64 Gha and pasture at 3.57 Gha by 2050
Implications: Significant potential for land use reduction through dietary changes; Importance of food-system efficiency improvements; Need for sustainable deployment of climate mitigation strategies; Land availability for bioenergy and afforestation depends on food system transitions
Limitations: Limited trade representation (uses historical production snapshots); Coarse livestock and land use representation; Exclusion of countries with poor data quality; No consideration of nutritional implications in dietary scenarios; Simplified approach to land use transitions
Future Directions: Improved trade representation through matrices or forward projections; Enhanced livestock and land use representation with productivity and transition modeling; Inclusion of excluded countries with constructed datasets; Integration of nutritional considerations; Development of more nuanced land use change modeling
Scalability: Good scalability potential due to use of publicly available global datasets; Model structure facilitates regional and country-level modifications; Adaptable to different population projections and efficiency scenarios
Novelty: First country-level disaggregation of FALAFEL model; Transparent and traceable approach using only open-source data; Food-system efficiency parameter based on calorie consumption; Integration of waste streams as livestock feed; Simplified yet comprehensive approach to global food system modeling

Title: Climate Change Impact on Peruvian Biomes
Authors: Zevallos, Jose; Lavado-Casimiro, Waldo
Objective: To analyze the potential distributions of biomes in Peru under the effects of climate change and evaluate the impact of climate change (2035-2065) on the distribution of biomes in Peru using future scenarios based on regional climate models
LULC Classes: 10 biomes: (1) evergreen montane forest (EMF), (2) seasonally dry tropical montane forest (SDTF), (3) humid puna (HP), (4) paramo (P), (5) montane shrubland (MS), (6) xeric pre-puna (PP), (7) glaciers (GC), (8) xeric puna (XP), (9) Yunga forest (YF), and (10) swamp (SW)
Scenarios: RCP 8.5 (high carbon emissions scenario)
Analysis Methods: Random Forest (RF) machine learning algorithm; bioclimatic envelope models (BEMs); delta method for bias correction
Sim. Method Advantages: RF reduces possibility of overtraining since trees have low correlations and high variance; efficient for finding nonlinear patterns frequent in ecology; BEM only requires climate information making it suitable for developing countries where data are limited
Tools/Soft Used: R programming language; dismo package; scikit-learn library; WRF-ARW model version 3; PISCO gridded product
Predictors: Six bioclimatic variables: mean annual temperature; monthly temperature range; isothermality; temperature seasonality; annual precipitation; precipitation seasonality; plus elevation data from SRTM
Data Sources: 654 precipitation stations; 442 temperature stations; SRTM digital elevation model; CHIRPS version 2; MODIS product MOD11A2; National Map of Ecosystems of Peru (MINAM); CMIP5 climate models data
Validation Methods: 5-fold cross-validation; precision and sensitivity indicators; confusion matrix analysis; model performance evaluation using training (80%) and validation (20%) datasets
Validation Data Sources: Training and validation datasets derived from the complete biome database maintaining proportionality of biome distribution
Key Findings: 82% of current biome coverage will remain stable; 6% will change to higher humidity conditions; 4.5% will maintain stable physiognomy with increased humidity; 6% will experience decreased humidity; glaciers and swamps are most vulnerable with >50% probable losses; montane shrubland and xeric puna show area increases
Implications: Need for public policies for adaptation and mitigation of climate effects on biomes at national scale; species migration and extinction risks; agricultural displacement to higher altitudes; conservation challenges for protected areas
Limitations: Model does not consider land use changes; limited number of climate models (3 RCMs); uncertainty in climate projections not properly quantified; subjectivity in biome boundary delimitation; interpretability of RF model is complicated
Future Directions: Improve delimitation of current biomes; enhance classification models with better data quality; include human activity such as land use; expand number of climate change models; better understanding of ecological relationships for predictor variable selection
Scalability: Methodology can be applied to other regions but requires region-specific climate data, biome classifications, and model calibration
Novelty: First study to include entire Peruvian territory for biome estimation and climate change impact evaluation, uses regional climate models specific to Peru for 2035-2065 period; This comprehensive analysis reveals that Peru's biomes face significant challenges from climate change, with glaciers and swamps being the most vulnerable ecosystems. The study's innovative approach of using machine learning with regional climate models provides valuable insights for conservation planning and climate adaptation strategies in Peru. The findings emphasize the urgent need for targeted conservation policies to protect Peru's biodiversity under changing climatic conditions.

Title: Delimiting China's Urban Growth Boundaries Under Localized Shared Socioeconomic Pathways and Various Urban Expansion Modes
Authors: Huang, Miao; Wang, Zichen; Pan, Xinhao; Gong, Binghua; Tu, Mengzhao; Liu, Zhifeng
Objective: Delimit China's urban growth boundaries (UGBs) before 2100 under localized shared socioeconomic pathways and diverse urban expansion modes and evaluate urban shrinkage pressure and impacts on land use/cover and ecosystem services
LULC Classes: Urban land; cropland; forest; grassland; wetland; bare land; rural residential area; other construction land; other land
Scenarios: Localized SSP1; SSP2; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: Linear regression for urban land demand estimation; Patch-based LUSD-urban model for spatial simulation; Morphological opening/closing for UGB delineation; InVEST habitat quality module; NPP-based food production allocation; NPP for carbon sequestration
Sim. Method Advantages: Patch-based cellular automata simulate expansion in patches and diverse organic vs spontaneous growth modes more effectively than pixel-based CA
Tools/Soft Used: Customized patch-based LUSD-urban model; GIS; InVEST; adaptive Monte Carlo calibration
Predictors: Distance to city centers (population <0.5 M, 0.5–1 M, 1–5 M, >5 M); distance to railways; highways; national roads; provincial roads; rivers; DEM; slope; land use inheritances (2015); constrained factors (high-quality cropland; nature reserves)
Data Sources: Urban land (He et al., 2019); Land use/cover (RESDC 2015); DEM (GSCloud); NPP (He, Liu, et al., 2017); GIS auxiliary (NGCC); Nature reserves (RESDC); Provincial census (2005–2015, stats.gov.cn); Localized SSPs (Chen, Guo, et al., 2020)
Validation Methods: Adaptive Monte Carlo parameter calibration; kappa index comparison
Validation Data Sources: Historical urban land data for 2010 and 2020
Key Findings: China's urban land demand peaks in 2042–2048 then declines, UGB extent projected at 121,199–142,982 km² (34.14–58.25% above 2020); Urban land demand in 2100 is 20.83–53.41% lower than UGB extent, implying widespread shrinkage pressure; Future expansion will occupy chiefly cropland (43.28–47.04%), causing declines in habitat quality (0.26–0.43%), food production (0.51–0.97%), and carbon sequestration (0.32–0.69%)
Implications: Mitigation and adaptation measures needed, especially in Heilongjiang, Jilin, Liaoning to address shrinkage; Optimize urban spatial patterns and adopt province-specific expansion modes to reduce ecosystem service losses
Limitations: Excludes farmland-redline and ecological-redline constraints; ULD estimation based solely on population (GDP effects omitted); Coarse 1 km resolution, transit infrastructure and agglomeration effects not incorporated; Other drivers of shrinkage (e.g., economic depression) not spatially simulated
Future Directions: Incorporate farmland-redline and ecological-redline data; Update population SSPs with 2020 census and third-child policy; Develop hierarchical multi-resolution spatial models; Integrate transportation networks and agglomeration processes; Simulate spatial patterns of urban shrinkage and include GDP drivers
Scalability: Study framework applicable across all Chinese provinces; methodology can be adapted to other national or regional scales
Novelty: First national-scale future UGB delimitation under localized SSPs and 11 organic/spontaneous growth modes; Development of a patch-based CA model (LUSD-urban) capturing diverse urban expansion dynamics

Title: Development of a Systems Model for Assessing Pathways to Resilient, Sustainable, and Profitable Agriculture in New Zealand
Authors: Vannier, Clemence; Cochrane, Thomas A.; Zawar-Reza, Peyman; Bellamy, Larry
Objective: To develop a systems model that quantifies agriculture outputs (carbon emissions, water use and quality, food energy, export value) influenced by land use, technology, and other factors, and explore pathways to meet New Zealand’s resilience, sustainability, and profitability goals by 2050
LULC Classes: dairy; beef; sheep; cereals; horticulture; forestry
Scenarios: Business As Usual; Optimisation and technology; Carbon farming; Reduction in dairy demand
Analysis Methods: proxy-based and phenomenological statistical modelling; system dynamics simulation in Stella Architect
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrative national-scale model combining production, market, land, water, energy, and emissions; Customisable parameters for stakeholder scenario building; First model of entire NZ agricultural system enabling disruptive scenario testing
Tools/Soft Used: Stella Architect
Predictors: land area; yield per sector; livestock stocking rate; product market value; irrigation percentage; fertiliser use; energy use; livestock enteric and manure emission factors; technology efficiency improvements
Data Sources: Stats NZ; Ministry for Primary Industries; FAOSTAT; Beef + Lamb NZ; Dairy NZ; Irrigation NZ
Validation Methods: Comparison of model outputs (2010 inputs) against national datasets for irrigation water use, food energy production, GHG emissions, export value
Validation Data Sources: FAOSTAT; Ministry for Primary Industries
Key Findings: Only the optimisation and technology scenario meets all quantitative objectives (GHG reduction, water use, water quality, food calories, export value); Carbon neutrality can be achieved via forestry offsets or native regrowth but may compromise other sustainability goals; Reduction in dairy demand can improve environmental metrics but risks export revenue
Implications: Provides policymakers and industry with a decision support tool to assess trade-offs between environmental, resilience, and profitability objectives; informs targets for technology adoption, land-use change, and carbon offsetting
Limitations: Aggregated national-scale model lacks spatial and temporal specificity; reliance on broad levers (forest planting, land abandonment) to meet targets; indirect treatment of climate change impacts
Future Directions: Incorporate spatial analysis and detailed climate change projections; refine regional parameters; integrate socio-economic and demographic trends
Scalability: Model framework is adaptable for other countries with appropriate data; potential for global application
Novelty: First linear statistical system dynamics model encompassing all NZ agricultural sectors at national scale, integrating production, market values, resources, and emissions for disruptive scenario analysis

Title: Downscaling population and urban land use for socio-economic scenarios in the UK
Authors: Merkle, Magnus; Alexander, Peter; Brown, Calum; Seo, Bumsuk; Harrison, Paula A.; Harmáčková, Zuzana V.; Pedde, Simona; Rounsevell, Mark
Objective: Project fine‐scale (1-km) urban land use and population distributions in the UK under Shared Socioeconomic Pathway narratives to support climate change impact and risk analysis
LULC Classes: Urban; grassland; arable land; mountains/heath/bog; woodland; water/coastal
Scenarios: UK-SSP1; UK-SSP2; UK-SSP3; UK-SSP4; UK-SSP5
Analysis Methods: gravity-based downscaling; Kumaraswamy-derived unimodal neighbourhood function; Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: avoids forced agglomeration by enabling leapfrogging; accommodates scenario narratives for sprawl; integrates land-use masks (flood risk, protected areas)
Tools/Soft Used: R; dIAP/RUG sub-model; Monte Carlo simulation on HPC cluster
Predictors: Distance to nearest urban cell; adjacency of urban cells; urban density in 5 km, 50 km, 150 km radii; land cover suitability; protected/flood risk masks
Data Sources: UKCEH Land Cover Map 2015; WorldPop 2020; UK-SSP regional (10′) urban projections (dIAP-RUG); UK-SSP LAD-level population projections; protected areas; flood risk zones
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: SSP1/2/4 yield dense, compact growth with limited sprawl despite population change; SSP3 and SSP5 exhibit large sprawl even under population decline (SSP3) or growth (SSP5); Rural areas show higher allocation uncertainty than urban centres
Implications: Strong land‐use planning critically reduces unsustainable sprawl; scenario choice influences future infrastructure and environmental risks
Limitations: no explicit climate impact feedback; limited suitability variables (e.g. slope/coastal proximity not included); urban mask based on land‐cover not density
Future Directions: integrate additional suitability factors (elevation, slope, coastal proximity); incorporate socio-cultural attributes; include climate impact–driven migration dynamics
Scalability: Method can be adapted to other regions with SSP narratives and equivalent land-cover/population datasets
Novelty: first UK-SSP-specific 1-km downscaling combining gravity-based leapfrogging; UK-specific land exclusions; Monte Carlo analysis of scenario narrative uncertainties

Title: GOBLIN version 1.0: a land balance model to identify national agriculture and land use pathways to climate neutrality via backcasting
