Authors: Duffy, Colm; Prudhomme, Remi; Duffy, Brian; Gibbons, James; O'Donoghue, Cathal; Ryan, Mary; Styles, David
Objective: Present and demonstrate GOBLIN, a new biophysical land-use model to generate and filter AFOLU scenarios at national scale for climate-neutral pathways via backcasting
LULC Classes: Grassland; cropland; forestry (commercial & conservation); wetlands; drained organic soils; fallow; re-wetted organic soils; mineral soils
Scenarios: 0 – animal reduction only; 1 – animal reduction + organic soil rewetting; 2 – animal reduction + mineral-soil afforestation; 3 – animal reduction + rewetting + afforestation; 4 – animal reduction + increased livestock productivity; 5 – scenario 4 + rewetting + afforestation
Analysis Methods: Integrated land-use modelling; backcasting; Latin hypercube global sensitivity sampling; IPCC Tier 2 & Tier 3 GHG algorithms
Sim. Method Advantages: Unbiased exploration of full parameter ranges via Latin hypercube sampling; Backcasting filters outcomes against explicit neutrality criteria without preconceived feasibility
Tools/Soft Used: GOBLIN model code (archived on Zenodo); Latin hypercube sampling routines; standard IPCC calculation algorithms
Predictors: 65 input parameters including livestock population; milk yield; beef finish weight; grass fertiliser rate; grass utilisation; proportions of spared land allocated to forestry / rewetting; herd cohort coefficients
Data Sources: Ireland’s National Inventory Report; Central Statistics Office herd data; IPCC (2006, 2019) guidelines; national soil and land-cover maps; peer-reviewed literature (e.g. Finneran et al., Donnellan et al.)
Validation Methods: Comparison of GOBLIN outputs with NIR time series for herd numbers and GHG fluxes (1990; 2015), herd module vs CSO/Donellan et al. coefficients
Validation Data Sources: UNFCCC National Inventory Reports; CSO activity data
Key Findings: GOBLIN accurately replicates NIR AFOLU GHG time series; No scenario achieves GWP100 net-zero by 2050, several achieve GWP∗ zero-warming balance; Organic soil rewetting and afforestation essential to offset residual CH₄ / N₂O from livestock
Implications: Provides rigorous, biophysically grounded evidence for national climate policy and AFOLU NDCs; Supports transparent stakeholder engagement via backcasting of neutrality definitions; Highlights need for separate CH₄ targets alongside CO₂/N₂O balance
Limitations: Cropland area held static, no bioenergy or harvested-wood-product modules; Fertiliser response and grass utilisation not spatially explicit; Specific parameterisation for Ireland limits direct global transfer
Future Directions: Integrate harvested-wood-product modules and downstream LCA of wood value chains; Couple bioenergy crop and biogas models for full AFOLU-energy LCA; Enhance spatial explicitness of grassland productivity and soil emissions; Adapt and apply model to other temperate, livestock-intensive regions
Scalability: Modular design allows transfer to similar temperate livestock contexts with moderate refactoring; requires substantial adaptation for divergent agroecologies
Novelty: First national AFOLU model combining livestock energy demand, grass-fertiliser response, detailed forestry dynamics; Randomised backcasting approach to identify all biophysically compatible pathways to climate neutrality

Title: Gridded value-added of primary, secondary and tertiary industries in China under Shard Socioeconomic Pathways
Authors: Jing, Cheng; Su, Buda; Zhai, Jianqing; Wang, Yanjun; Lin, Qigen; Gao, Miaoni; Jiang, Shan; Chen, Ziyan; Jiang, Tong
Objective: Develop high-resolution gridded projections of value-added for primary, secondary and tertiary industries in China under Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
LULC Classes: Cropland (irrigated; rain-fed crops; rice); Managed pasture; Rangeland; Built-up (urban); Natural vegetation (primary/secondary forest; non-forest)
Scenarios: SSP1; SSP2; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: Cobb-Douglas production model; Multidimensional population projection; Generalized Additive Model (GAM) downscaling; Perpetual inventory approach; Trend extrapolation
Sim. Method Advantages: Structural economic modeling captures medium- and long-term dynamics with localized demographic and capital parameters, offering sector-specific insights and higher spatial resolution than purely statistical extrapolation
Tools/Soft Used: Matlab R2014b; R-4.1.2
Predictors: Land use areas (cropland; pasture; rangeland; natural vegetation; urban); Population by age, gender, education; Labour force participation rate; Years of schooling; Capital stock; Total factor productivity
Data Sources: Bureau of Statistics of China (demographics; provincial & county statistical yearbooks); HYDE 3.2; LUH2; IIASA/PIK/OECD SSP databases; RESDC; Kummu et al. gridded GDP
Validation Methods: Relative error analysis against 2011–2019 provincial/ national statistics; Correlation comparisons with RESDC and Kummu et al. gridded GDP
Validation Data Sources: Provincial statistical yearbooks; RESDC GDP dataset; Kummu et al. global GDP dataset
Key Findings: National RE within ±6% for all sectors during 2011–2019; GAM downscaling explains up to R²=0.798 for tertiary sector; Future GDP under SSP5 reaches ~505 trillion yuan by 2100, other SSPs range 150–366 trillion yuan
Implications: Provides sector-level economic projections at climate model scales for impact/vulnerability assessments; informs industrial restructuring and policy planning under different development pathways
Limitations: Model does not account for endogenous land–economy feedbacks; GAM used solely for downscaling, not causal land-use projections
Future Directions: Explore incorporation of additional drivers in downscaling; extend framework to other countries/regions; refine feedback coupling between land use and economy
Scalability: Methods adaptable to other regions with sufficient local demographic, economic and land-use data
Novelty: First high-resolution (5′) sector-specific gridded economic projections for China under SSP framework combining demographic, capital and land-use downscaling.

Title: Modelling Climate Change Impacts on Location Suitability and Spatial Footprint of Apple and Kiwifruit
Authors: Vetharaniam, Indrakumar; Timar, Levente; Stanley, C. Jill; Muller, Karin; van den Dijssel, Carlo; Clothier, Brent
Objective: Develop projections of future location suitability for apple and kiwifruit production and project land-use change and spatial footprints of these industries under climate change scenarios using biologically driven suitability models and econometric land-use simulations.
LULC Classes: Apple; kiwifruit; other horticulture; dairy farming; sheep–beef farming; plantation forestry; scrub (unproductive land)
Scenarios: RCP 2.6 (stringent GHG mitigation); RCP 8.5 (unabated GHG emissions)
Analysis Methods: Continuous sliding-scale crop suitability modelling; bias-variance corrections of RCM data; multinomial logit land-use model; LURNZ partial-equilibrium spatial simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates continuous biological suitability with econometric revealed-preference decisions; preserves climate-change signals in bias correction; models spatial allocation of land use responding to both suitability and economic/policy drivers
Tools/Soft Used: GNU Octave 6.2.0; MATLAB R2020b for LURNZ model
Predictors: Location suitability scores for apples and kiwifruit; land, soil and terrain variables; other drivers implicit in LURNZ (economic incentives, carbon price, water-quality constraints); forest age for plantation constraints
Data Sources: Primary: VCSN land/soil/weather database, NIWA high-resolution RCM outputs forced by six CMIP5 GCMs, orchard location data, forest-age map; Secondary: VCSN observed climate, regional council policy parameters (Freshwater NPS), PCE and Productivity Commission reports
Validation Methods: Comparison of historic RCP-Past suitability maps with VCSN-based historic suitability; RMSE analysis by histogram bins; one-to-one graphs of suitability scores
Validation Data Sources: VCSN observed climate station network; orchard location data
Key Findings: Mid-century suitability change occurs largely by mid-century under RCP 2.6; Under RCP 8.5, apple suitability declines in northern North Island and shifts south; Kiwifruit suitability declines in Northland and Bay of Plenty but increases in central North Island and South Island; Average kiwifruit suitability up 9% (RCP 2.6) or 24% (RCP 8.5) by late century; Apple average suitability up 4% (RCP 2.6) or 2.5% (RCP 8.5)
Implications: Policy and industry must plan adaptation (new cultivars, management) in declining regions; Emerging production opportunities in cooler regions; Local councils should prepare infrastructure, water and land-zoning for shifting horticulture footprint; Carbon pricing and water-quality regulation influence land allocation
Limitations: Excludes market price, demand and other land-use suitability; Does not model yields or cultivar-specific responses; 5 km climate grid may mask microclimates; Uncertainty in future climate signals and residual biases; Other horticultural crops bundled together; Population/demographic trends not considered
Future Directions: Refine bias/variance corrections; Extend suitability modelling to yield and management interventions; Incorporate additional crops and explicit market/demand drivers; Model effectiveness of adaptation strategies; Include grower/social attitudes dynamics
Scalability: Methodology generalisable to other crops and geographic regions given suitable biological and econometric data
Novelty: Bias-variance correction preserving climate signals for biologically driven suitability; Continuous sliding-scale suitability integrated with econometric spatial land-use simulation (LURNZ); First joint projection of apple and kiwifruit spatial footprints under contrasting RCPs using combined suitability and econometric modelling.

Title: New land-usechange scenarios for Brazil: Refining global SSPs with a regional spatially-explicit allocation model
Authors: Silva Bezerra, Francisco Gilney; Von Randow, Celso; Assis, Talita Oliveira; Aguiar Bezerra, Karine Rocha; Tejada, Graciela; Castro, Aline Anderson; de Paula Gomes, Diego Melo; Avancini, Rodrigo; Aguiar, Ana Paula
Objective: Define and generate spatially explicit land-use change scenarios for Brazil aligned with global SSP–RCP frameworks
LULC Classes: Forest vegetation; Grassland vegetation; Planted pasture; Agriculture; Mosaic of occupation; Forestry; Others (artificial areas, water bodies, bare land)
Target Years: 2015–2050 (mapped at annual intervals; scenarios run through 2050)
Scenarios: SSP1/RCP1.9 (sustainable development); SSP2/RCP4.5 (middle of the road); SSP3/RCP7.0 (strong inequality)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit dynamic modeling with LuccME; Spatial lag regression for potential; CLUE-like allocation; PreComputedValues demand; Multi-resolution validation metric (Costanza–Pontius)
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates global IAM projections with regional and local drivers; Spatially explicit allocation at 10×10 km resolution; Dynamic potential incorporates neighborhood effects; Balances global SSP–RCP narratives with local biophysical and institutional contexts
Tools/Soft Used: LuccME (TerraME framework); INLAND; GeoDa (spatial regression); FillCell plugin; NetCDF
Predictors: Agronomic: climatological; geophysical variables; Agrarian structure: proportion of large agricultural establishments; Economic: distances to highways, ports, airports, railways, urban centers, rivers; Restrictive: protected areas, conservation units, indigenous lands, hydropower plants, rural settlements
Data Sources: Primary: IBGE land-use maps (2000, 2010, 2012, 2014); IMAGE model projections for SSP–RCP combinations; INLAND climate/water deficit outputs; Spatial datasets (roads, PAs, ILs, hydroelectric plants)
Validation Methods: Multi-resolution adjustment metric comparing observed vs. simulated maps
Validation Data Sources: IBGE land-use maps for 2014
Key Findings: SSP1: +447,944 km² forest gain (notably Atlantic Forest, Cerrado, Caatinga); SSP2: –805,956 km² forest loss (Amazon and Cerrado driven); SSP3: –933,092 km² forest loss; Grassland declines under all scenarios (–602,847 to –1,346,988 km²); Agriculture and mosaic expand most under SSP2/SSP3; Model achieved 84.44% spatial fit overall, 52.55% in changed areas
Implications: Scenario outputs inform regional policymaking for biodiversity conservation and deforestation reduction; Downscaled global projections enable tailored sustainable development strategies
Limitations: Not specified
Future Directions: Incorporate participatory scenario development; Include qualitative stakeholder inputs; Explore additional SSP–RCP combinations
Scalability: Framework adaptable to other regions by adjusting local drivers and biomes
Novelty: First integration of global SSP–RCP IAM outputs with regional spatially explicit LuccME–INLAND modeling for Brazil; Dynamic incorporation of neighborhood potential via spatial lag regression; Detailed biome-specific driver parameterization maintaining global–local consistency

Title: Rising temperature threatens China's cropland
Authors: Wang, Jianghao; Zhang, Junjie; Zhang, Peng
Objective: Assess the impact of temperature on cropland area in China using climate econometric models
LULC Classes: Cropland (irrigated; non-irrigated); forest land; grassland; waterbody; developed land; barren land
Scenarios: RCP 2.6; RCP 4.5; RCP 6.0; RCP 8.5
Analysis Methods: Distributed-lag model; Period-averaged model; Long-difference model; Kriging spatial interpolation; Downscaling of CMIP5 projections
Sim. Method Advantages: Flexible estimation of long-term cumulative effects; isolation of contemporaneous and lagged weather impacts
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Daily average temperature bins; Precipitation (annual total, quadratic); Relative humidity (annual mean, quadratic); Wind speed (annual mean, quadratic); Sunshine duration (annual mean, quadratic)
Data Sources: China Land-use/Cover Datasets (CLUDs) from Chinese Academy of Sciences; Daily weather data from China Meteorological Data Service Center; Downscaled projections from 39 CMIP5 climate models
Validation Methods: Robustness checks on 50% and 25% subsamples; Censored regression; Alternative temperature measures (max/min bins); Alternative dependent-variable specifications
Validation Data Sources: Subsamples of CLUDs; alternative weather measures derived from China Meteorological Data Service Center
Key Findings: Extremely hot days (>30 °C) reduce cropland by ~1.01% per permanent hot-day shift over ten years; Projected cropland loss of 2.09%–25.51% by 2070–2099 across RCPs; Irrigation mitigates short-term (<5 yr) impacts but not long-term; Lost cropland partly converts to developed land
Implications: Threat to China’s food security and “red line” cropland target; Need for aggressive GHG mitigation; Limited long-term efficacy of irrigation adaptation; Policy support required (subsidies, infrastructure)
Limitations: Excludes CO₂ fertilization effects; Does not account for sea-level rise impacts; Assumes static socioeconomic factors (prices, population, technology)
Future Directions: Incorporate CO₂ fertilization and sea-level rise; Extend framework internationally with fine spatiotemporal data; Integrate price, population, and technological change
Scalability: Generalizable to other regions with high-resolution land and weather data
Novelty: First dynamic assessment of extensive-margin (cropland area) climate impacts in China using matched high-resolution satellite land-use data and daily weather records.

Title: Scenario analysis and land use change modelling reveal opportunities and challenges for sustainable expansion of aquaculture in Nigeria
Authors: Yakubu, Suleiman O.; Falconer, Lynne; Telfer, Trevor C.
Objective: To develop and assess potential futures of freshwater pond aquaculture production in Nigeria to 2035 using scenario analysis and land use change modelling
LULC Classes: No data; Rainfed cropland; Irrigated cropland; Mosaic cropland/vegetation; Mosaic vegetation; Forest; Mosaic forest; Shrubland; Grassland; Marshy areas; Urban areas; Bare areas; Water bodies
Scenarios: A familiar route; Vicious cycle; Nipped in the bud; Autopilot
Analysis Methods: Delphi technique; Morphological analysis; Land Change Modeler (MLP-NN neural network; Markov chain)
Sim. Method Advantages: Combines qualitative narratives with quantitative spatial projections; Captures nonlinear dynamics and multiple uncertainties; Enhances transparency and reproducibility over top-down global models
Tools/Soft Used: TerrSet (Land Change Modeler); SPSS v26; Clark Labs Hammer-Aitoff Grid; GIS tools
Predictors: Distance from urban areas; Distance from rainfed cropland; Population density; Poverty index; Elevation; Slope; Empirical likelihood of change
Data Sources: ESA-CCI land cover maps; SRTM elevation; DIVA-GIS state boundaries; UNDP poverty index; NBS population density; FDF pond area and production data; FAO historical aquaculture data; literature review
Validation Methods: Predictive validation of 2015 land cover via comparison of predicted vs actual maps; success rate (Sr) metric
Validation Data Sources: ESA-CCI 2015 land cover map
Key Findings: Availability/cost of inputs, land use change, government policy, and climate change were critical uncertainties; Baseline production unlikely to reach 2.5 million t by 2035 (projected 0.24–0.38 million t); Scenario “Nipped in the bud” yields highest per capita production (up to 2 kg/person); Urban expansion outpaces rainfed cropland, limiting pond area growth
Implications: Need integration of aquaculture in land use planning; Clustered pond development and evidence-based policies essential; Interventions needed to expand pond area and improve yields to meet potential
Limitations: Use of urban and cropland proxies for pond area change; Limited understanding of climate change impacts; Model uncertainties from input data and assumptions
Future Directions: Develop specialized foresight tools integrating environmental and technological interactions; Improve regulatory frameworks and data collection; Investigate species/system-specific scenarios and consumer preference impacts
Scalability: Approach transferable to other countries with similar data but requires localized expert input and data
Novelty: First application of combined Delphi, morphological analysis, and spatial LULC modelling for national aquaculture foresight; Quantitative linkage of scenario narratives with GIS-based land change and production projections

Title: Shift in the migration trajectory of the green biomass loss barycenter in Central Asia
Authors: Han, Feifei; Ling, Hongbo; Yan, Junjie; Deng, Mingjiang; Deng, Xiaoya; Gong, Yanming; Wang, Wenqi
Country: Central Asia (including Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in northwestern China)
Objective: To quantitatively reveal the change and migration laws of green biomass loss (GBL) caused by drought in historical and future periods using a joint kNDVI-SPEI distribution based on copula theory
LULC Classes: Rangeland; sparse vegetation; cropland; desert areas; bare land
Target Years: Near future period (NFP): 2019-2060; Far future period (FFP): 2061-2100
Scenarios: SSP126 (low radiative forcing); SSP245 (medium radiative forcing); SSP585 (high radiative forcing)
Analysis Methods: Binary probabilistic framework based on copula theory; kNDVI-SPEI joint distribution; Pearson correlation analysis; Hot spots analysis using Getis-Ord G* index; Barycenter migration model
Sim. Method Advantages: Unlike previous deterministic methods, copula function can construct multi-dimensional joint distribution with marginal distribution and correlation structure; can simulate dependency structure of correlated variables; flexible and diverse forms for characterizing dependence structure
Tools/Soft Used: Python programming language; BCC-CSM2-MR climate model
Predictors: kNDVI (kernel normalized difference vegetation index); SPEI (standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index); soil water storage; temperature
Data Sources: SPEI data from Spanish National Research Council (SPEIbase v2.6, 1901-2018); GIMMS-NDVI dataset (8km resolution, 15-day temporal resolution); MODIS NDVI dataset; BCC-CSM2-MR climate model data; GLDAS_NOAH 2.0 dataset (soil water storage); CRU_TS 4.06 dataset (temperature)
Validation Methods: Cross validation between GIMMS-NDVI and MODIS NDVI datasets; Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test for optimal marginal distribution; Goodness-of-fit test based on Rosenblatt's transform for copula function selection
Validation Data Sources: MODIS NDVI dataset for cross validation with GIMMS-NDVI data
Key Findings: 94.4% of regional GBL in May-October was caused by water deficit; 62.6% of regional maximum kNDVI-SPEI correlations reached significant level; GBL probability peaked in August with 80.45%, 73.03%, 62.15%, and 44.66% at different kNDVI quantiles under extreme drought; Under high-emission scenario, 18.16 percentage-point increase in GBL probability in FFP compared to NFP
Implications: Results provide scientific basis for spatial mapping of drought-vulnerable ecosystems; important for drought preparedness and risk management; demonstrates effectiveness of China's proactive climate change strategies; helps decision-makers formulate strategies to deal with GBL caused by global climate change
Limitations: kNDVI-SPEI correlation results could not explain whether water deficit or water surplus caused vegetation dynamic changes; limited understanding of whether water deficit or water surplus plays more critical role in weakening vegetation health
Future Directions: Monthly-scale temporal variation must be considered when conducting vegetation vulnerability assessment; factors of GBL probability variation at monthly scale should be considered in future assessments
Scalability: Method can be applied to other drought-sensitive and ecologically vulnerable regions; provides new idea for vegetation protection research in response to global climate change
Novelty: First study to use copula theory for constructing joint kNDVI-SPEI distribution for GBL assessment; innovative binary probabilistic framework unlike previous deterministic approaches; novel approach to reveal migration laws of vegetation loss barycenter

Title: Spatiotemporal Variations of Chinese Terrestrial Ecosystems in Response to Land Use and Future Climate Change
Authors: Li, Shuaishuai; Zhang, Jiahua; Henchiri, Malak; Cao, Dan; Zhang, Sha; Bai, Yun; Yang, Shanshan
Objective: To examine the spatiotemporal distribution of terrestrial ecosystems under current land use and climate baseline (1970-2000) using the CSCS model and quantitatively project spatiotemporal variations of ecosystems and their succession under future climate scenarios (2030s-2080s)
LULC Classes: Farmland (paddy field, dry land); Forest (forest land, shrub forest, sparse forest land, other forest land); Grassland (high-coverage grassland, medium-coverage grassland, low-coverage grassland); Water area (canals, lakes, reservoirs and ponds, permanent glaciers and snow, tidal flats, beaches); Residential land (urban land, rural residential area, other construction land); Unused land (Gobi, marshland, bare land, bare rock texture, sandy land, saline land, others)
Scenarios: RCP2.6 (very low forcing level mitigation scenario); RCP4.5 (medium stabilization scenario); RCP8.5 (extremely high baseline emission scenario)
Analysis Methods: Comprehensive Sequential Classification System (CSCS) model; Holdridge Life Zone (HLZ) model comparison; Kappa statistic for validation; Sankey diagram for succession analysis; Spatial overlay analysis in ArcGIS
Sim. Method Advantages: CSCS model synthesizes information on bioclimatic variables, edaphic conditions, and vegetation characteristic variables; Has become a critical tool for creating strategies to mitigate climate change consequences on ecosystems; Performs better than HLZ model with higher Kappa index (0.75 vs 0.4); Successfully utilized to model biomes through continuous optimization
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; GIS technology
Predictors: Annual cumulative temperature above 0°C (∑θ/GDD0); Humidity index (K); Mean annual precipitation (MAP); Bioclimatic variables; Edaphic conditions; Vegetation characteristic variables
Data Sources: WorldClim 2.1 (climate data); CMIP5 Meteorological Research Institute Coupled General Circulation Model version 3 (MRI-CGCM3); Resource and Environment Data Cloud Platform of China (RESDC) for land use data; SRTM-DEM data; Vegetation map of China at 1:1,000,000 scale
Validation Methods: Kappa statistic; 750 randomly selected sample points; Comparison between CSCS model, HLZ model, and actual vegetation distribution map
Validation Data Sources: 1:1,000,000 vegetation distribution map of China; 750 randomly selected sample points
Key Findings: Vegetation without human disturbance mainly distributed in high elevation regions covering less than 10% of national area; More than 58% of tundra and alpine steppe would shrink; Semidesert would expand by 39.49 × 10^4 km²; Temperate forest would face considerable shrinkage especially under RCP8.5 (55.06 × 10^4 km²); Warmer and wetter climate would be conducive to CSCS ecosystems occurrence and development
Implications: Offers new insights on potential ecosystem response to land use and climate change; Provides foundation for creating targeted policies for effective adaptation; Supports implementation of ecosystem protection measures; Contributes to understanding climate-vegetation interactions
Limitations: Uncertainties in simulation of PNV due to dataset accuracy limitations; GCMs from CMIP5 still too limited for definite regional climate estimates; Error sources from homogenization and interpolation methods; Some regions with few or scattered observation sites may result in classification accuracy errors
Future Directions: More integrated representation of vegetation in climate models; Comprehensive climate impact assessments; Enhanced understanding of ecosystem-climate feedbacks; Future intercomparison research between different RCPs; Investigation of synergistic effects of climate change and land-use factors
Scalability: CSCS model has wide range of potential applications at global and regional scales; Critical tool for creating strategies to mitigate climate change consequences on ecosystems; Successful utilization for modeling biomes through continuous optimization
Novelty: Few studies have examined contribution of vegetation succession to vegetation dynamics; Few have tried to compare PNV variations under different climate scenarios; Land-use impacts on vegetation are often neglected in terrestrial ecosystem exploration; Deep understanding of land-use impacts on vegetation dynamics is lacking

Title: Valuation of Land-Use/Land-Cover-Based Ecosystem Services in Afghanistan-An Assessment of the Past and Future
Authors: Najmuddin, Omaid; Li, Zhihui; Khan, Rabnawaz; Zhuang, Weiqing
Objective: To assess the ecosystem services value (ESV) changes in response to the changes of LULC in Afghanistan between 2000-2020, and predict likely scenarios of ESV changes by 2030 using the dynamics of the land system (DLS) model coupled with linear programming
LULC Classes: Agricultural land; Forest; Grassland; Water bodies; Built-up land; Unused land
Scenarios: Business-As-Usual (BAU); Rapid Economic Development (RED); Environmental Protection (ENP)
Analysis Methods: Benefits transfer method (BTM); Spatial calculating model (SCM); Change matrix analysis; Binomial logistic regression (BLR); Dynamic Land System (DLS) model; Linear programming; Thornthwaite Memorial model for NPP estimation; Value transfer method with NDVI and GDP adjustments
Sim. Method Advantages: DLS model has two main favorable features: (1) applies a dual strategy to reach a demand balance, and (2) incorporates driving factors into the simulation process; innovatively couples linear programming with LULC simulation modeling to develop more rational scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: Geographic Information System (GIS); DLS (Dynamic Land System) model; Linear programming; Spatial calculating model (SCM); Statistical analysis software for binomial logistic regression
Predictors: Temperature; Precipitation; Soil pH; Soil density; Elevation; Slope; Road distance; City distance; Investment on irrigation; GDP per capita; Population density; NDVI; Actual evapotranspiration
Data Sources: GlobeLand30 land cover products; WorldClim temperature and precipitation data; SoilGrids250m soil data; NASA Earthdata elevation and slope; WorldPop population data; Afghanistan Central Statistics Organization GDP data; MODIS NDVI and evapotranspiration data; DIVA-GIS road network data
Validation Methods: Contingency table analysis; Overall accuracy assessment; Kappa coefficient calculation; Comparison between simulated and actual LULC for 2020
Validation Data Sources: GlobeLand30 land cover images for 2000, 2010, and 2020; actual LULC data for 2020 used to validate predictions
Key Findings: Total ESV decreased from 161 billion USD in 2000 to 152.27 billion USD in 2020 (5.4% decrease); Built-up land increased by 118%, agricultural land by 4.5%; Forest, grassland, and water bodies decreased by 20.6%, 10.2%, and 4.7% respectively; Environmental-oriented LULC types showed severe instability and vulnerability; About 92% of ESV decrease was from supporting and provisioning services; Validation achieved overall accuracy of 89% with Kappa value of 0.78; BAU and RED scenarios predict further ESV decline by 2030 (5.5% and 6.6% respectively); ENP scenario predicts 4.5% increase in ESV by 2030
Implications: Need for balanced approach between economic and environmental development; Urgent need for strict environmental protection measures; Importance of reforestation goals (60,000 ha every 5 years); Water management crucial for both economic and environmental development; International support needed for environmental restoration programs; Population control measures may be necessary while respecting local culture
Limitations: Assumption of ecosystem service value homogeneity within LULC classes, Services may have different values in different areas than original study coefficients, Data scarcity in Afghanistan; much required data either unavailable or low quality, Unavailability of angle coefficient data that could have improved results, BTM approach limitations despite being cost-effective for large geographical scales
Future Directions: Need for more localized ecosystem service valuation coefficients; Integration of angle coefficients when data becomes available; Development of better data collection systems for Afghanistan; More detailed analysis of regional variations in ecosystem services; Integration of climate change impacts on ecosystem services
Scalability: Methodology can be applied to other data-scarce regions; BTM approach suitable for cost-effective assessment at large geographical scales; DLS model framework adaptable to different geographical contexts; Linear programming approach for scenario development transferable to other regions
Novelty: First comprehensive national-level ESV assessment for Afghanistan; Innovative coupling of linear programming with LULC simulation modeling; More rational scenario development process using objective and constraint functions; Integration of scarcity and LULC quality effects in ecosystem service valuation; Application of DLS model in Afghanistan context

Title: Can we avert an Amazon tipping point? The economic and environmental costs
Authors: Banerjee, Onil; Cicowiez, Martin; Macedo, Marcia N.; Malek, Ziga; Verburg, Peter H.; Goodwin, Sean; Vargas, Renato; Rattis, Ludmila; Bagstad, Kenneth J.; Brando, Paulo M.; Coe, Michael T.; Neill, Christopher; Marti, Octavio Damiani; Murillo, Josue Avila
Objective: Assess the economic, natural capital and ecosystem services impacts of moving towards an Amazon tipping point and the costs and benefits of policy strategies to avert it

Scenarios: BASE (business-as-usual); COMBI (tipping point: YIELD, DRGHT, FIR); POLICY (net zero deforestation, YIELD50, NFIR)
Analysis Methods: IEEM Platform (recursive dynamic CGE model linked to UN SEEA); Spatial land use–land cover modeling (Dyna-CLUE); Ecosystem Services Modeling (InVEST sediment delivery, carbon, water yield, nutrient delivery)
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates detailed environmental information with economic accounts consistent with SNA; Generates policy-relevant GDP, wealth, natural capital and ecosystem services indicators; Links CGE outputs to spatially explicit land-cover and service flows
Tools/Soft Used: IEEM Platform; Dyna-CLUE; InVEST models
Predictors: Precipitation; maximum cumulative water deficit; SPI drought index; dry-season length; historical deforestation trends; land demand from IEEM; location factors for Dyna-CLUE
Data Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook (GDP growth); UN DESA population projections; Historical deforestation data, agricultural census, LULC maps, national household and employment surveys; Amazon Climate Source, CMIP climate projections, IPCC RCP8.5 emissions; IEEM databases and UN SEEA
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Approaching tipping point (COMBI) causes cumulative GDP loss of US$256.6 billion and wealth loss of US$81.6 billion by 2050; Policies to avert tipping point (POLICY) yield US$148.9 billion less GDP loss and generate US$339.3 billion additional wealth; Erosion mitigation, carbon storage, water quality and regulation services improve significantly under POLICY
Implications: Coordinated regional policies—net zero deforestation, agricultural intensification, fire management—are economically justified and critical to sustaining natural capital and ecosystem services
Limitations: Lack of detailed costs for policy implementation; Conservative service scope (only four InVEST models); Excludes some Amazon countries and broader global spillovers; Focuses on agriculture–land feedbacks, omitting health and cross-border impacts
Future Directions: Quantify policy implementation costs; Incorporate additional ecosystem services and health impacts; Extend analysis to remaining Amazon countries; Assess global trade and climate spillover effects
Scalability: Framework is transferable to other Amazon countries and potentially other regions with compatible economic and environmental data
Novelty: First high-resolution, whole-economy CGE study integrating spatial LULC and ecosystem services to quantify tipping point impacts and policy trade-offs in the Amazon biome

Title: China's Socioeconomic and CO<sub>2</sub> Status Concerning Future Land-Use Change under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways

Title: Combined effects of predicted climate and land use changes on future hydrological droughts in the Luanhe River basin, China
Authors: Chen, Xu; Han, Ruiguang; Feng, Ping; Wang, Yongjie
Objective: Evaluate combined impacts of future climate change and land-use change on hydrological drought evolution in the Luanhe River basin
LULC Classes: Dry land; Paddy field; Forest; Grassland; Water body; Construction land; Unutilized land
Scenarios: RCP2.6; RCP4.5; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Statistical downscaling (SDSM); Bias correction (Quantile mapping, Distribution mapping); Land-use change modelling (CA–Markov); Hydrological modelling (SWAT); Standardized Runoff Index (SRI)
Sim. Method Advantages: SWAT’s process-based, flexible watershed-scale hydrological simulation offers detailed physical mechanisms and scenario configuration superior to lumped models
Tools/Soft Used: SDSM; ArcGIS CA–Markov module; SWAT; GLDAS; NOAA PSL datasets
Predictors: Large-scale atmospheric variables (NCEP/NCAR reanalysis grid predictors); Socioeconomic and geographical driving factors for land-use transitions
Data Sources: NCEP/NCAR reanalysis (1961–2005), CMIP5 GCMs ensemble, Hydrometeorological station data; GLDAS Noah_2.0 soil moisture, Land-use maps (1990, 2005, 2010)
Validation Methods: Runoff: calibration (1963–1994) and validation (1995–2011) using R², NSE, RMSE; Soil moisture: Spearman correlation; Land-use: area and spatial accuracy metrics
Validation Data Sources: Observed runoff records (1961–2011); GLDAS Noah_2.0 soil moisture (1961–2010); Observed land-use maps (2005, 2010)
Key Findings: SWAT model accurately simulates runoff and soil moisture.; SDSM with bias correction yields acceptable downscaled climate inputs.; Future projections show increasing forest and construction land, decreasing dry land, water bodies, unutilized land.; Mild drought frequency increases under all scenarios except RCP2.6 in 2080s.; Under RCP8.5 by 2080s, severe/extreme drought duration, severity, and frequency rise.; Spatially, extreme drought shifts from upper basin (RCP2.6) to middle/lower reaches (RCP8.5).
Implications: Inform policymakers and resource managers for drought mitigation planning under climate and land-use change
Limitations: Precipitation downscaling performance relatively low despite bias correction; Reservoir operations not considered in runoff simulation; CA–Markov assumes stationary transition probabilities
Future Directions: Incorporate reservoir management in hydrological modelling; Improve precipitation downscaling methods; Extend analysis to agricultural and socioeconomic drought impacts
Scalability: Applicable to other temperate continental basins with similar data but requires local calibration
Novelty: Integrated use of SDSM-bias correction, CA–Markov land-use projection, and SWAT-SRI framework for combined climate and land-use impact on future hydrological droughts

Title: GCAM-USA v5.3_water_dispatch: integrated modeling of subnational US energy, water, and land systems within a global framework
Authors: Binsted, Matthew; Iyer, Gokul; Patel, Pralit; Graham, Neal T.; Ou, Yang; Khan, Zarrar; Kholod, Nazar; Narayan, Kanishka; Hejazi, Mohamad; Kim, Son; Calvin, Katherine; Wise, Marshall

Scenarios: Ref; High Growth; Transition; High Growth + Transition
Analysis Methods: Market equilibrium modeling; recursive dynamic simulation; probabilistic logit technology choice; sub-annual electricity dispatch modeling; HUC-2 basin water market; land–energy–water coupling

Tools/Soft Used: GCAM v5.3_water_dispatch; gcamdata R package; Hector climate model; Xanthos hydrology; Python preprocessing
Predictors: Population; per-capita GDP (economic growth); technology costs / efficiencies; resource endowments (renewable / non-renewable water, fossil resources, renewables); policy costs (carbon price, standards); climate (for building services)

Key Findings: Electricity demand grows 85% by 2100 (Ref), met by increasing gas then renewables; Building and industry electrification varies regionally, deepens under carbon price; Power sector water withdrawals decline as once-through cooling retires, offset by rising irrigation withdrawals; Bioenergy cropland drives large irrigation increase and land-use change under low-carbon transition; Capacity factors for wind / solar decline modestly with marginal site deployment

Scalability: Blueprint for other regionally detailed GCAM variants (e.g., GCAM-China); adaptable global framework for subnational modeling elsewhere
Novelty: First open-source global model with integrated subnational (50 states + DC; 235 water basins; 384 land regions) energy-water-land coupling; sub-annual power dispatch segmentation; endogenous water markets with renewable / non-renewable water supply curves.

Title: Identifying priority regions and territorial planning strategies for conserving native vegetation in the Cerrado (Brazil) under different scenarios of land use changes
Authors: Colman, Carina Barbosa; Guerra, Angelica; Roque, Fabio de Oliveira; Rosa, Isabel M. D.; Sanches de Oliveira, Paulo Tarso
Objective: Explore combined and isolated impacts of Legal Reserves (LRs) and Protected Areas (PAs) arrangements, and evaluate the complementarity between LR compliance and PA cover to reduce deforestation and conserve native vegetation in the Cerrado hotspot
LULC Classes: Native vegetation: Forest Formation, Savanna Formation, Grassland Formation, Wetland; Anthropogenic use: Pasture, Agriculture, Urban Infrastructure, Mining
Scenarios: BAU (Business as usual); LRE (Legal Reserve Elimination); PAE (Protected Area Elimination); PALRE (LR + PA Elimination); LRI (Legal Reserve Increase); CPA (Creation of Protected Areas); CPALRI (Creation of PAs + LR Increase)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit land-change modeling; scenario modeling using Monte Carlo Markov Chain (MCMC)–based parameter estimation; linear model selection for drivers; binary change‐map integration over 100 iterations
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures spatial heterogeneity and temporal trends via multiple calibration periods; Quantifies uncertainty through posterior distributions and MCMC sampling; Enables comparison among multiple policy‐driven scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Land cover; distance to roads; distance to cities; dry season length; elevation; agricultural potential; distance to rivers; cattle density; permanent agriculture
Data Sources: Primary: Land‐cover maps (MapBiomas), Cadastro Ambiental Rural (CAR) registry, input layers for roads, cities, rivers, elevation, climate, cattle and agriculture statistics; Secondary: Native Vegetation Protection Law (Forest Code), Conservation Unit and Indigenous Land boundaries, IBGE agricultural data
Validation Methods: Calculation of AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve); pixel‐by‐pixel comparison yielding perfect match, commission, omission rates
Validation Data Sources: Observed deforestation/land‐cover change data for 2008–2016 (MapBiomas and national land‐use datasets)
Key Findings: BAU projects 30.6 M ha native‐vegetation loss by 2070; LRE increases loss by 34% over BAU, PAE by 7%, PALRE by 54%; LRI reduces loss by 5%, CPA by 35%, CPALRI by 43% vs. BAU; LR elimination causes more loss than PA elimination due to concentration of native vegetation on private lands; CPALRI is the most effective conservation trajectory
Implications: Private properties (via LRs) are essential for efficient land‐use planning; Complementary strengthening of LRs and PAs needed to reconcile WFEE (Water–Food–Energy–Ecosystems) nexus; Scenario outputs can guide territorial planning and policy arbitration
Limitations: Model excludes policy shifts, trade dynamics, socio‐behavioral and technological changes, and climate change; Restoration dynamics not modeled—LR‐deficient properties remain noncompliant; Effects of drivers may vary over coming decades
Future Directions: Assess LR and PA efficacy for water and soil provisioning and broader ecosystem services; Incorporate restoration pathways and small‐farm biodiversity dynamics; Integrate WFEE nexus under climate‐change and global trade scenarios
Scalability: Framework applicable to other regions for policy‐driven land‐use scenario planning, though regional data availability and socio‐political factors may pose challenges
Novelty: First spatially explicit MCMC‐based scenario comparison combining LR and PA policy levers in the Brazilian Cerrado, quantifying their isolated and joint effects on long‐term native‐vegetation conservation.

Title: Integrating IPAT and CLUMondo Models to Assess the Impact of Carbon Peak on Land Use
Authors: Wang, Han; Jin, Yujie; Hong, Xingming; Tian, Fuan; Wu, Jianxian; Nie, Xin
Objective: Integrate IPAT and CLUMondo models to assess how China’s carbon peak policy impacts land use
LULC Classes: Cultivated land; forest land; grassland; building (construction) land; water areas; unused land
Scenarios: natural development scenario (NDS); ideal policy scenario (IPS); reactive carbon emission scenario (RCS)
Analysis Methods: IPAT model for carbon emission forecasts; CLUMondo model for land use simulation; trend extrapolation for built-up area; regression for driving factors
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUMondo incorporates policy stimuli as demand drivers; adjusts land-use intensity via constrained demand; simple parameterization; higher accuracy than cellular automata or CLUE-S
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS (slope, cost-distance, projection); CLUMondo; statistical fitting (regression)
Predictors: Temperature; precipitation; elevation; slope; distance to city (accessibility); population; gross national product (GNP)

Scalability: Applicable to other large regions with sufficient land-use and emissions data, though data harmonization challenges exist
Novelty: First integration of carbon peak scenarios (including reactive emissions) with land-use simulation at national scale; Incorporation of policy-driven carbon constraints into CLUMondo demand module; Comparison of three distinct emission-land-use scenarios

Validation Methods: Overall accuracy and skill measure computed using 50% hold-out testing dataset in TerrSet
Validation Data Sources: Historical MODIS LULC maps (2008, 2018)
Key Findings: Forest cover projected to decline under all deforestation scenarios (e.g., Belize River watershed from 49% in 2018 to 28–36% by 2090); Greater deforestation leads to increased runoff (up to +2.5% in Belize River under Development scenario); SSP126 yields minor runoff decreases (≤6%), SSP585 yields major decreases (up to 80%) due to reduced precipitation; Southern watersheds more sensitive to precipitation changes, northern to LULC changes
Implications: Inform Coastal Zone Management Authority and ICZMP updates; Support long-term planning for water quality and reef conservation; Highlight need for land management policies to mitigate runoff
Limitations: 500 m MODIS resolution leads to misclassification of small tropical agricultural plots; Soil and elevation held constant across scenarios; Annual precipitation rates mask seasonal/runoff event dynamics; N-SPECT sediment estimates unreliable (overestimation)
Future Directions: Update soil and elevation inputs to reflect erosion and sea-level changes; Validate model outputs over time; Monitor coral health and diversity in relation to runoff
Scalability: Approach applicable to other coastal tropical regions with similar data and modeling frameworks
Novelty: First study to employ CMIP-6 climate projections in Belize LULC and hydrologic modeling, and integrate bookend SSP scenarios with TerrSet and N-SPECT for water quality assessment

Title: Modelling Continuous Location Suitability Scores and Spatial Footprint of Apple and Kiwifruit in New Zealand
Authors: Vetharaniam, Indrakumar; Muller, Karin; Stanley, C. Jill; van den Dijssel, Carlo; Timar, Levente; Clothier, Brent
Objective: Develop and apply a continuous sliding‐scale suitability modelling approach to assess current and future location suitability for apple and kiwifruit production and estimate impacts on spatial footprints
LULC Classes: Apple cultivation; kiwifruit cultivation; alternative land uses (from LURNZ baseline)
Target Years: Mid and late 21st century (companion projections)[Not specified exact years]
Scenarios: Different climate-change pathways (Representative Concentration Pathways for mid and late century)
Analysis Methods: Weighted sliding‐scale suitability scoring for individual criteria; Weighted geometric averaging for combined suitability; Multinomial logit econometric modelling of land use probabilities
Sim. Method Advantages: Continuous suitability scores avoid categorical thresholds; Balances multiple criteria holistically; Captures incremental changes in suitability under climate change
Tools/Soft Used: GNU Octave 6.2.0; GIS spatial interpolation tools
Predictors: Climate criteria: Richardson chill units, frost survival rates, growing degree days (GDD10), GDD10 for first 50 days after bloom; Land criteria: Potential rooting depth, drainage class, slope, Land Use Capability (LUC) class; Location factors for logit model: Suitability scores, slope, LUC class, proximity to ports and towns
Data Sources: Primary: NIWA Virtual Climate Station Network daily temperature (1972–2017), New Zealand Fundamental Soil Layer, NZ Land Resource Inventory, LENZ, LURNZ basemap, confidential orchard location data; Secondary: Industry feedback, published literature for physiological parameters

Validation Data Sources: Industry‐supplied maps of apple and kiwifruit orchards; expert review panels
Key Findings: Suitability models aligned well with current orchard locations; Apple suitability highest on current apple sites, kiwifruit suitability highest on current kiwifruit sites; Framework enables projecting incremental changes in suitability and spatial footprints under climate change
Implications: Provides evidence‐based guidance for land‐use policy; supports adaptation strategies for horticultural industries under climate change
Limitations: Microclimate and soil variability within grid cells; Hourly temperature estimates approximated by sinusoidal model; Phytopathology risks not quantified

Title: Oil palm reconciliation in Indonesia: Balancing rising demand and environmental conservation towards 2050
Authors: Xin, Yu; Sun, Laixiang; Hansen, Matthew C.

Analysis Methods: Trade flow analysis; Generalized geo-economic gravity models; Parametric survival analysis; Stock-difference CO₂ emission estimation

Tools/Soft Used: R (flexsurv package); ArcGIS
Predictors: Economic/trade: GDP per capita, Population, Real exchange rate, Tariff rate, Number of RTAs, Number of RTAs with Indonesia, WTO membership, Distance, Colony history, Shared religion, Time; Biophysical/socioeconomic: Attainable oil yield, Distance to existing plantation, Distance to processing mills, Slope, Elevation, Peatland ratio, Access time to large cities, Population density, Protected area ratio, Oil palm concession ratio, 1996 LCLU type

Key Findings: Projected demand of 313–679 Mt oil palm products (fruit equiv.) by 2050 → 18.58–45.59 M ha new plantation; 8–22% secondary forest and 21–54% peatland loss under historical expansion; Shifting expansion to degraded lands reduces CO₂ emissions by 87–142 M t CO₂/year (with higher transport/infrastructure costs)

Title: Optimizing distribution of urban land on the basis of urban land use intensity at prefectural city scale in mainland China
Authors: Wang, Liye; Zhang, Siyu; Tang, Lanping; Lu, Yanchi; Liu, Yanfang; Liu, Yaolin
Objective: Optimize spatial distribution of urban land based on urban land use intensity (ULUI) to increase economic benefits and reduce ecosystem service value (ESV) loss
LULC Classes: cropland; forest; grassland; river; wetland; urban land; rural settlements; unused land (bare land, snow, rocky area)
Scenarios: ULUI scenario; quota (QT) scenario
Analysis Methods: Entropy method for weight calculation; global and local Moran’s I spatial autocorrelation; Sankey diagrams; LISA cluster mapping
Sim. Method Advantages: LANDSCAPE model allows partitioned transition probability and asynchronous rate to set regional optimization goals simultaneously, overcoming limitations of traditional CA models that only optimize overall area
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS (Kriging, slope derivation); LANDSCAPE model; spatial autocorrelation modules; Sankey diagram tools
Predictors: Digital elevation model; slope; soil organic matter; soil pH; soil phosphorus; precipitation; accumulated temperature; transportation accessibility; agricultural production capacity; urban land use intensity components (urban land intensity, input intensity, output intensity, population intensity)
Data Sources: Land use data (RESDC); Soil data (China Soil Database); Meteorological data (CMA); DEM (SRTM); Transportation data (OpenStreetMap); Agricultural production capacity (Global Agro-Ecological Zones); China Statistical Yearbooks (2015)
Validation Methods: Kappa Simulation metric comparing simulated 2015 map against observed 2015 using 2000 baseline
Validation Data Sources: Land use maps of 2000 and 2015 (RESDC)
Key Findings: ULUI shows significant spatial heterogeneity: high in Pearl River, Yangtze River, Cheng-Yu agglomerations; low in northwest and northeast; ULUI-based optimization (ULUI scenario) yields higher total economic benefits and lower ESV loss than quota scenario; 119 prefectural cities achieved both increased economic benefits and reduced ESV loss under ULUI scenario
Implications: ULUI-based allocation offers a reasonable method for planners to balance economic development and ecological conservation; Can inform urban land quota trading and Linkage Policy to control expansion sustainably; Different development strategies recommended by ULUI cluster (e.g., ecological focus in low-ULUI regions, intensive growth in high-ULUI agglomerations)
Limitations: ESV estimation uses province-level standard equivalent values which may not capture within-province biodiversity variations; Some regions experienced increased ESV loss despite overall reduction; LANDSCAPE model may underperform for isolated or outlying urban expansion
Future Directions: Develop methods to increase both total economic benefits and ESV without regional losses; Improve ESV valuation by spatially explicit biodiversity data; Enhance simulation of outlying urban growth patterns
Scalability: Approach applicable at national scale; potential to adapt to other countries with regional ULUI data and land use models
Novelty: Coupling ULUI at prefectural level with LANDSCAPE CA model to optimize urban land distribution nationwide and simultaneously assess economic and ecosystem service outcomes.

Title: Projections of urban built-up area expansion and urbanization sustainability in China?s cities through 2030
Authors: Sun, Zhongchang; Jiang, Huiping; Guo, Huadong; Xing, Qiang; Zhang, Hongsheng; Ma, Yuanxu; Li, Sijia
Objective: Produce annual SSPs-consistent projections of urban built-up area at city level to assess China’s urbanization sustainability through 2030
LULC Classes: Urban built-up area
Scenarios: Shared Socioeconomic Pathways SSP1, SSP2, SSP3, SSP4, SSP5
Analysis Methods: logistic regression; panel data regression; linear extrapolation; exponential extrapolation; compound growth approach; Zipf’s rank-size analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Logistic regression captures nonlinear changes across urbanization stages and aligns more closely with observed dynamics than panel data regression
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: per capita cumulative GDP; per capita GDP; urbanization rate; historical built-up area; provincial urban population growth rates
Data Sources: Provincial SSP-consistent projections (Tsinghua Univ. for population & urbanization, Nanjing Univ. of Information Science & Technology for GDP); National Bureau of Statistics of China; China Urban Construction Statistical Yearbook
Validation Methods: Absolute Percentage Error (APE) against 2020 official statistics; Zipf’s rank-size distribution preservation

Key Findings: Logistic regression outperforms panel regression with mean provincial APE 3.94% vs. 7.87%; National LCRPGR declines toward ideal value (~1) by 2030 under logistic regression across SSPs; Population stagnation in Northeast and allometric expansion in Western China need regulation; Megacities grow slower than super-large and large cities

Scalability: Can be applied in other data-rich countries; may combine national projections and remote sensing for data-poor regions
Novelty: First local-scale SSPs-consistent projections of urban built-up area and population for all county- and prefecture-level cities in mainland China with integrated downscaling approach.

Title: Spatial correlation evolution and prediction scenario of land use carbon emissions in China

Scalability: Not specified

Title: A multi-model approach to explore sustainable food and land use pathways for Argentina
Authors: Frank, Federico; Volante, Jose; Calamari, Noelia; Peri, Pablo L.; Gonzalez Chavez, Baltazar; Garcia Martinez, Pablo; Mosciaro, Maria J.; Martin, Gabriel; Benito Amaro, Ignacio; Guerrero, Ignacio Pace; Casellas, Karina; Zuliani, Melina; Sirimarco, Ximena; Gaitan, Juan; Cristeche, Estela; Barral, Maria P.; Villarino, Sebastian; Zelarayan, Ana L.; Monjeau, Adrian
Objective: To present mid-century food and land-use system pathways to achieve biodiversity, freshwater use, food production and greenhouse gas emission targets, co-developed with government, research and civil society stakeholders; to construct a carbon neutral, actionable food system and land-use scenario by 2050

Analysis Methods: Multi-model approach integrating FABLE calculator, Dinamica EGO land-use allocation model, and NatureMap spatially explicit conservation prioritization; Random forest algorithms for classification; Markov transition matrices; Weights of evidence; Cellular automata model; Linear programming optimization
Sim. Method Advantages: Enables integration of food production and land-use systems with ecological assessments; provides spatially explicit recommendations; allows structured dialogue among stakeholder groups; helps achieve multiple sustainability objectives in tandem; rare integrated approach with high value for cross-sectoral experts and policymakers
Tools/Soft Used: FABLE calculator; Dinamica EGO; NatureMap; Excel; R programming language; prioritizr package; Gurobi solver; Random forest algorithms; Excel's Solver tool
Predictors: Altitude; Slope; Aspect; Mean annual evapotranspiration; Mean annual temperature; Mean annual precipitation; Water balance; Distance to rivers; Distance to water bodies; Effective soil depth; Soil limiting factors; Distance to LULC categories; Distance to urban settlements; Distance to paved roads; Provincial limits; Protected areas; Forest conservation zonification
Data Sources: Landsat and MODIS satellite imagery; SRTM elevation data; CHIRPS climate data; Terraclimate global data; Digital map of Argentina soils (INTA 1990); IGN geographical data; Ministry of Environment databases; Google Earth high-resolution images; IPCC guidelines; FAO data

Implications: Argentina must transition toward more sustainable food and land-use systems to achieve SDGs and Paris Agreement objectives; Success depends on consensus between public and private sectors and inter-sectoral agreements; Multiple sustainability objectives can be achieved simultaneously with proper planning and implementation
Limitations: Used IPCC Tier 1 values for sequestration and emissions coefficients; Lack of information on net carbon fixation of native forest at regional level; Did not consider impacts of dietary changes on food and land-use systems; Findings need discussion, validation and refining; Specific narratives on achieving assumptions need development

Scalability: Methodology is transferable and can be readily adjusted and applied to other countries with similar objectives; Nationally designed transferable methodology presented
Novelty: First attempt at integrated modeling across food production systems, land-use and conservation sectors in Argentina; Novel integration of three unique tools (FABLE calculator, Dinamica EGO, NatureMap); Rare integrated approach for achieving multiple sustainability objectives; Multi-criteria spatial prioritization approach for simultaneous biodiversity, carbon, and water conservation

Title: Cell-level coupling of a mechanistic model to cellular automata for improving land simulation
Authors: Chen, Guangzhao; Zhuang, Haoming; Liu, Xiaoping
Objective: To propose a novel model that couples Lund Potsdam Jena (LPJ), a mechanistic model, and cellular automata (CA) at the cell level to consider the mechanisms and statistics in land use and land cover change (LUCC) simulations, improving accuracy especially for natural vegetation under climate change scenarios
LULC Classes: Forest land; Grassland; Farmland; Urban land; Barren land; Water (considered to remain unchanged)
Scenarios: SSP1-RCP2.6 (sustainable socioeconomic development with low emission concentration); SSP5-RCP8.5 (fossil-fueled development with high emission concentration)
Analysis Methods: Cellular automata (CA) coupled with dynamic global vegetation model (LPJ); Random Forest (RF) algorithm; FLUS (Future Land Use Simulation) model; Cell-level coupling mechanism; Roulette selection mechanism; Self-adaptive inertia mechanism
Sim. Method Advantages: Higher simulation accuracy especially on natural vegetation compared to conventional CA models; Combines strengths of mechanistic and statistical models; Retains high spatial resolution of CA while representing spatial possibilities under different climate scenarios; Enables tight coupling between mechanistic and CA models at cell level; Can simulate LUCC under extreme climate scenarios
Tools/Soft Used: Python with scikit-learn package (Version 0.23); LPJ dynamic global vegetation model; FLUS model; Random Forest algorithm
Predictors: Human influence (population, distance to urban centers, distance to roads); Terrain (DEM, slope); Soil (workability, oxygen availability to roots, excess salts, nutrient availability); Climate (temperature annual range, temperature seasonality, annual mean temperature, precipitation seasonality, annual precipitation)
Data Sources: MODIS Land Cover Type Product (MCD12Q1); LandScan Human Population; ESRI World Cities layer; ESRI World Roads layer; WorldClim; Harmonized World Soil Database v 1.2; Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project; LUH2 dataset; MIROC5 climate data; EWEMBI bias-corrected data
Validation Methods: Figure of Merit (FoM); Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves; Area Under Curve (AUC) values; Pearson correlation analysis; Comparison with historical simulations for 2010 and 2015

Key Findings: LPJ-FLUS model achieved 5% higher overall FoM compared to conventional CA models (23.37% vs 18.23%); Up to 8% improvement for natural vegetation types; Better spatial correlation with LPJ model results; More realistic simulation of natural vegetation distribution under climate change; Successful integration of mechanistic and statistical approaches
Implications: Valuable for high spatial resolution LUCC simulations; Promising for environmental impact analysis under extreme climate scenarios; Contributes to climate change and environmental change studies; Supports sustainable development goals assessment; Enhances interpretability of future LUCC simulations
Limitations: Some driving forces have relatively low spatial resolution (5′ to 30′); Only 2100 data used from LPJ model; RF model only considers historical drivers; Equal weights used for coupling (may not be optimal); Limited to LPJ model for mechanistic component; Resolution constraints from climate model data
Future Directions: Explore variable weight settings for different climate scenarios; Use intermediate year data from LPJ model for multi-year projections; Update RF model with projected future drivers; Optimize and test sensitivity of coupling weights; Explore coupling with other mechanistic models; Investigate tighter coupling mechanisms; Apply to high-resolution small-scale simulations
Scalability: The proposed cell-level coupling mechanism could be used for spatially tight coupling with models of different structures; Can be applied to other regions with sufficient computational resources and appropriate data availability; Model framework is transferable but may require region-specific calibration
Novelty: First study to achieve tight spatial coupling of DGVM and CA models at cell level; Novel integration of mechanistic model spatial information to guide CA simulations; Innovative use of foliage projective cover (FPC) as suitability probability proxy; Cell-level coupling mechanism that goes beyond conventional loose coupling approaches; Integration of biogeographic and biochemical mechanisms with statistical relationships

Title: Contributions of healthier diets and agricultural productivity toward sustainability and climate goals in the United States
Authors: Wu, Grace C.; Baker, Justin S.; Wade, Christopher M.; McCord, Gordon C.; Fargione, Joseph E.; Havlik, Petr
Objective: To explore the GHG emissions impacts of seven scenarios that vary U.S. crop yields and healthier diets in the U.S. and overseas, and examine how impacts vary across assumptions of future ruminant livestock productivity and ruminant stocking density in the U.S.
LULC Classes: Cropland; Pastureland; Natural lands; Forested lands
Scenarios: Baseline; Sustainability; Healthy World; US Sustainability; Healthy US; Healthy ROW; US Yields; BAU Livestock Productivity; High Livestock Productivity; Constant Ruminant Density; Lower Ruminant Density
Analysis Methods: Partial equilibrium modeling; Land use/GHG accounting modeling; Two complementary land use models (US FABLE Calculator and GLOBIOM)
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures market adjustments and industry productivity responses to dietary changes; Accounts for interactions between U.S. land use system and global markets; Enables exploration of exogenous changes to livestock sector; Integrates both endogenous and exogenous factors
Tools/Soft Used: US FABLE Calculator; GLOBIOM (Global Biosphere Management Model); EPIC (for crops); RUMINANT (for livestock)
Predictors: U.S. crop yields; Diet patterns (U.S. and ROW); Livestock productivity; Ruminant density; Population growth; Macroeconomic assumptions
Data Sources: USDA Dietary Guidelines for Americans (2015-2020); FAO data; FAOSTAT; USDA data (2010-2020); U.S. Department of Agriculture Economic Research Service; UN DESA population projections
Validation Methods: Scenario validation of exogenous assumptions with endogenous responses; Cross-model comparison between US FABLE Calculator and GLOBIOM
Validation Data Sources: GLOBIOM endogenous model outputs; Historical USDA data; FAO data
Key Findings: Healthier U.S. diets following Dietary Guidelines for Americans reduce agricultural and land use GHG emissions by 25-57% (120-310 MtCO2e/y) and pastureland area by 28-38%; Pastureland declines more dramatically than cropland in response to healthier diets; U.S. agricultural productivity growth has modest land sparing benefits within the U.S. but significant global benefits; Livestock productivity and ruminant density significantly influence land use and emissions impacts
Implications: Healthy U.S. diets can significantly contribute toward meeting U.S. long-term climate goals for land use sectors; Dietary transitions can complement sustainability and climate change goals through direct and indirect emissions reductions; Market interactions between U.S. and global systems must be considered in sustainability assessments; Government policy has significant influence on dietary patterns
Limitations: Dietary scenarios are not isocaloric; Limited representation of U.S. food systems variety; Models do not account for calories from fish; Limited representation of fruit and vegetable production systems; Minimal differentiation of forest management systems; Does not quantify full suite of benefits and costs of dietary transitions
Future Directions: Improve representation of fruit and vegetable production systems; Better forest management dynamics modeling; Quantify broader economic costs and benefits of dietary transitions; Consider costs of incentive structures for dietary change; Include research and development costs for yield improvements; Develop more comprehensive sustainability policy assessment
Scalability: Limited; study is specifically focused on United States, mentions potential for application to other regions but would require adaptation
Novelty: Use of two complementary land use models (US FABLE Calculator and GLOBIOM); Integration of dietary transitions with agricultural productivity scenarios; Accounting for market interactions between U.S. and global systems; Examination of livestock productivity and ruminant density sensitivity

Title: Downscaling Global Land-Use Scenario Data to the National Level: A Case Study for Belgium

Tools/Soft Used: GLOBIO 4 land‐use allocation module; GIS tools for distance and upscaling; reclassification and accuracy analysis routines
Predictors: Euclidean distance to existing urban areas; Euclidean distance to existing cropland; Protected‐area mask; Ruminant livestock density (converted to tropical livestock units); Distance to roads; Elevation
Data Sources: LUH2 dataset; ESA WorldCover (2020); CORINE Land Cover (2018); FAO Gridded Livestock of the World; Global Roads Inventory Project; Copernicus Global Land Service; WDPA; FAO national statistics
Validation Methods: Overall accuracy; Kappa coefficient; Root Mean Squared Error–observations standard deviation ratio (RSR)

Key Findings: ESA WorldCover at 10 m resolution produced the highest agreement with LUH2 (RSR 0.11–0.24, accuracy 0.94–0.98, Kappa 0.91–0.97), outperforming upscaled WorldCover and CORINE references; Urban areas expand and pasture declines across all scenarios, choice of reference map significantly influences downscaling accuracy
Implications: High‐resolution downscaled maps inform local biodiversity impact assessments, sustainable land management, and stakeholder engagement for planning
Limitations: Use of relatively simple, expert‐based suitability maps; reliance on global IAM‐derived claims not tailored to a single country; limited validation beyond Copernicus data
Future Directions: Develop refined, environmentally driven suitability layers; use country‐specific land‐demand projections with stakeholder input; conduct field‐based validation
Scalability: Methodology can be readily applied to other countries or regions with appropriate input data
Novelty: First application of GLOBIO downscaling to 10 m resolution; systematic comparison of reference land cover maps’ influence on downscaling outcomes

Title: Future land-use change and its impact on terrestrial ecosystem carbon pool evolution along the Silk Road under SDG scenarios
Authors: Cao, Min; Tian, Ya; Wu, Kai; Chen, Min; Chen, Yu; Hu, Xue; Sun, Zhongchang; Zuo, Lijun; Lin, Jian; Luo, Lei; Zhu, Rui; Xu, Zhenci; Bandrova, Temenoujka; Konecny, Milan; Yuan, Wenping; Guo, Huadong; Lin, Hui; Lue, Guonian

Title: Impacts of future urban expansion on natural habitats will intensify in China: scenario analysis with the improved LUSD-urban model

Title: Implications of future land-use/cover pattern change on landslide susceptibility at a national level: A scenario-based analysis in Romania
Authors: Jurchescu, Marta; Kucsicsa, Gheorghe; Micu, Mihai; lteanu, Dan Ba; Sima, Mihaela; Popovici, Elena -Ana
Objective: Conduct a first countrywide assessment of the potential evolution of landslide susceptibility (LS) in response to possible future land-use/cover (LUC) change for the territory of Romania; investigate the possible effect on future LS level of implementing and respecting appropriate land management by comparatively evaluating differences between two LS outcomes
LULC Classes: Artificial areas; arable lands; permanent crops; pastures and natural grasslands; scrubs/herbaceous vegetation; forests; open spaces with little or no vegetation; heterogeneous agricultural areas; wetlands; waters
Baseline Years: 2006 (for landslide susceptibility reference map); 2013 (for LUC scenario modeling)
Scenarios: Two LUC scenarios - LUCS 1 (assumes future LUC dynamics follow registered past linear trend 1990-2012); LUCS 2 (similar to LUCS 1 but considers LUC transitions in agreement with respecting environmental regulations for adequate land management within protected areas)
Analysis Methods: Statistical-heuristic methodological framework; Spatial Multi-Criteria Evaluation (SMCE); Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP); pixel-based difference analysis; overlay analysis; regionally-differentiated susceptibility assessments
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUE-s modeling framework is extremely flexible and versatile for targeted zoning level; proves suitable when landslide inventory data are incomplete and heterogeneous; allows incorporation of expert knowledge alongside statistical analysis
Tools/Soft Used: CLUE-s (Conversion of Land Use and its Effects at Small regional extent) modeling framework; Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) data; Google Earth for imagery
Predictors: Elevation; slope angle; slope aspect; horizontal relief fragmentation; main soil classes; average annual precipitation and temperature (1961-2015); average number of inhabitants (1992-2012) and employees (1991-2012); major protected areas; distance to roads; distance to settlements; distance to towns; lithology; land-use/cover
Data Sources: CORINE Land Cover (CLC) database (1990, 2006, 2012, 2018); SRTM altitudinal model; National lithological map; Three nationwide landslide databases (ELSUS-Romania inventory for training, IGSU and UTCB + URBAN-INCERC for validation); National Geographical Atlas of Romania maps
Validation Methods: Quantitative testing comparing LS estimates with distribution of independent national inventories; Prediction Rate Curves (PRCs); Qualitative expert evaluations; Statistical measures KSimulation, KTransition, and KTransLoc for LUC model validation
Validation Data Sources: Two independent national landslide inventories (IGSU, UTCB + URBAN-INCERC); CLC 2018 dataset for LUC model validation
Key Findings: Overall net slight decrease in landslide susceptibility at national level under both scenarios (average 7.3% of LUC change area); Expected increase in forest-covered area contributes most to LS decrease (44.2% from pastures/grasslands to forests, 11.4% from heterogeneous agricultural areas to forests); Transitions to pastures and natural grasslands result in most important LS increase (52.2%); 24.2% of projected new built-up areas expected to spread over moderate, high and very high LS areas; More appropriate land management in protected areas could significantly reduce landslide occurrences
Implications: Results could direct landslide risk reduction actions toward LUC management and prioritize areas for protective measures; Appropriate land management extension should be encouraged in protected areas and degraded/unstable terrains; Need for more in-depth studies on future landslide exposure of built-up areas; Results support national and regional land planning and sustainable management
Limitations: Reduced number of controlling factors; Incompleteness and spatial heterogeneity of landslide inventories; Classification uncertainties in CLC database; Short historical period (22 years) used to predict long-term trends (63 years); Assumption that determinant factors remain constant; Transient nature of landslide susceptibility changes; Cannot distinguish among different mass movement categories
Future Directions: Improve typological differentiation of susceptibility estimations; Include additional static and dynamic drivers; Extend research to landslide hazard, exposure and risk analyses; Closer examination of predicted landslide exposure of built-up areas; Evaluate stabilizing effects under climate change scenarios
Scalability: The approach could be extended to future investigations in Romania and could be followed for other national territories; Results intended for national and regional purposes; Methodology provides foundation for similar national-scale approaches
Novelty: First national-level exploration of LUC pattern change effects on landslide susceptibility in Romania; First countrywide assessment at this scale; Integration of environmental management scenarios in protected areas analysis; Novel approach combining CLUE-s modeling with landslide susceptibility assessment at national scale

Title: Integrated high-resolution, continental-scale land change forecasting
Authors: Calderon-Loor, Marco; Hadjikakou, Michalis; Hewitt, Richard; Marcos-Martinez, Raymundo; Bryan, Brett A.
Objective: Design and validate an integrated, high-resolution, continental-scale land-change model and forecast Australia’s land change to 2030
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest; Grassland; Built-up; Water; Other
Scenarios: Not specified

Tools/Soft Used: Google Earth Engine; Scikit-learn (Python); R (‘compositions’ package); high-performance computing; GitHub repository
Predictors: Historical path dependencies (1985–2005 land-use history); Neighbourhood dynamics (3×3, 9×9, 81×81 windows); Accessibility (distances to infrastructure and land classes); Environmental factors (elevation, slope, climate, soil, ecoregion, state id)
Data Sources: Calderón-Loor et al. (2021) 30 m land-use dataset; Commonwealth Dept. of Environment connectivity index; ANUCLIM climate layers; Soil and terrain data (Viscarra Rossel et al. 2014, Farr et al. 2007); Facebook HRSL; Terrestrial ecoregions (Olson et al. 2001)

Scalability: Framework transferable to other regions with cloud/HPC infrastructure
Novelty: First integrated, multiclass, 30 m resolution continental-scale land-change forecast; Couples RF suitability, compositional regression demand modelling, and likelihood allocation algorithm

Title: Modeling forest landscape futures: Full scale simulation of realistic socioeconomic scenarios in Estonia
Authors: Kaasik, Ants; Kont, Raido; Lohmus, Asko

Method Advantages: Stand-level spatially explicit ownership and management rule linkage; Whole-population sampling reducing sampling errors; Optimized iterative harvest decision processing (data.table); Middle ground between tree-level yield and grid-based landscape models; Feasible country-scale high-resolution, multi-scenario simulation
Tools/Soft Used: R; NextStand R-script; data.table; sf; terra; University of Tartu HPC
Predictors: Stand composition; Stand age; Site-productivity class; Ownership type; Protection regime; Management intensity; Adjacency constraints; Base clear-cutting probabilities

Validation Methods: Not specified

Key Findings: Intensive management continuation risks national timber supply decline; Strict protection maintains overall old-forest area but increases isolation; Restricted-management zones predicted to see larger and more numerous clear-cut patches; Intensively managing private owners forecast to nearly eliminate ≥ 60 yr stands by 2050; Non-intensive owners buffer age distribution of mid-aged/older stands; Early-successional patch size peaks pre-2035 then declines; Old-forest connectivity remains low despite slight improvement
Implications: Need for governance of adjacency constraints; Conservation reliant on strict protection; Land-sharing (‘restricted management’) may exacerbate landscape contrast; Certification and sustainable yield strategies require reevaluation; Decision support tool potential for policy and spatial planning

Future Directions: Integrate tree-species composition dynamics and disturbance regimes; Refine owner characteristics (estate size, certifications); Model climate-driven land cover change; Incorporate dynamic protected-area policies; Extend as multi-service decision support tool

Title: Multi-target scenario discovery to plan for sustainable food and land systems in Australia
Authors: Navarro Garcia, Javier; Marcos-Martinez, Raymundo; Mosnier, Aline; Schmidt-Traub, Guido; Javalera Rincon, Valeria; Obersteiner, Michael; Perez Guzman, Katya; Thomson, Marcus J.; Penescu, Liviu; Douzal, Clara; Bryan, Brett A.; Hadjikakou, Michalis

Title: Past and projected future patterns of fractional vegetation coverage in China
Authors: Kong, Zijie; Ling, Hongbo; Deng, Mingjiang; Han, Feifei; Yan, Junjie; Deng, Xiaoya; Wang, Zikang; Ma, Yuanzhi; Wang, Wenqi
