Future Directions: Incorporate higher‐resolution seasonal data; Include biotic disturbances and CO₂ effects; Separate ecosystem management interventions explicitly
Scalability: Methods applicable to other heterogeneous ecogeographical regions for vegetation trend assessment
Novelty: Ensemble logistic–Gaussian function framework for full‐process FVC pattern detection; Integration of periodic superposition trend model with stepwise regression to quantify environmental contributions; Combined multi‐algorithm ML prediction under SSPs for mid‐century FVC trends

Title: Projecting Diversity Conflicts of Future Land System Pathways in China Under Anthropogenic and Climate Forcing
Authors: Lin, Xin; Jiao, Xin; Tian, Zhiqiang; Sun, Qiangqiang; Zhang, Yongxiang; Zhang, Ping; Ji, Zhengxin; Chen, Lu; Lun, Fei; Chang, Xiao; Liu, Wen; Liu, Ming; Sun, Danfeng

Tools/Soft Used: PLUS (Patch-generating Land Use Simulation) model; random forest (LEAS module); CA with multi-type random patch seeds (CARS module)
Predictors: DEM; slope; distance to railways; distance to main roads; distance to residences; distance to main rivers; ecological protection zones; soil clay content; soil sand content; soil silt content; GDP distribution; population distribution; average annual precipitation; average annual temperature; Palmer Drought Severity Index

Scalability: Framework transferable to other regions with appropriate calibration of regional drivers and high-resolution land cover data.

Title: Simulating the dynamics of urban land quantity in China from 2020 to 2070 under the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Authors: Hou, Yiming; Li, Yiyu; Li, Jian; Huang, Qingxu; Duan, Xiaoyu; Feng, Xingyun; Zhu, Guoliang

Title: Estimation and simulation of carbon sequestration in typical dryland areas of China under future climate change scenarios
Authors: Zheng, Kai; Shi, Mingjie; Wu, Hongqi; Gu, Haibin; Jiang, Pingan; He, Panxing; Dong, Tong; Liu, Zhuo; Wang, Xiaozhen; Zhang, Nuozhou; Wei, Ruhao

Title: Evaluation and prediction of water conservation of the Yellow river basin in Sichuan Province, China, based on Google Earth Engine and CA-Markov
Authors: Yang, Zhichong; Dai, Xiaoai; Lu, Heng; Liu, Chao; Nie, Ruihua; Zhang, Min; Ma, Lei; Li, Naiwen; Liu, Tiegang; He, Yuxin; Yang, Zhengli; Qu, Ge; Li, Weile; Wang, Youlin

LULC Classes: Evergreen needleleaf forests; Deciduous broadleaf forests; Mixed forests; Woody savannas; Savannas; Grasslands; Permanent wetlands; Croplands; Barren
Scenarios: Original scenario (2001–2002); GFG scenario (2003–2020); Current scenario (2018–2020)

Predictors: Precipitation (PR); Evapotranspiration (ET); Runoff (RO); Land cover change
Data Sources: Primary: MODIS (MOD16A2.006, MCD12Q1.006), CHIRPS precipitation, TerraClimate runoff; Secondary: LUCC dataset from RESDC for LC validation

Key Findings: Total WC rose from 1.93 to 6.77 billion m³ (2001–2020); Precipitation dominates WC variation, runoff shapes spatial patterns, ET stable; Forests highest WC capacity (≈691 mm/km²), grasslands low (≈192 mm/km²), cropland high (≈514 mm/km²), barren negative (≈–310 mm/km²); GFG policy boosted WC by ≈4.53 billion m³ since 2003 but yields diminishing returns; WC in Shiqu County remains negative, EYRS counties similar WC per county

Novelty: First long-term WC study for the Yellow River Basin in Sichuan Province; Integration of multi-source GEE datasets to overcome InVEST data limitations; CA-Markov forecasting of both LC and quantified WC under multiple scenarios

Validation Methods: Pixel-based confusion metrics (hits, misses, false alarms, persistence); Producer’s/user’s accuracy, overall model performance (MP); Degree of correspondence (DoC), mean bias error (MBE) for population; Multiple-resolution (sampling window) validation; Comparison to Null and Random benchmark models
Validation Data Sources: GHSL maps (1990, 2015) for urban land and population; CLC (1990, 2000, 2006, 2012)
Key Findings: Persistence of residential land well captured (>98% in all countries); Weighted producer’s accuracy for change varied (11–59%), higher in compact urban areas; Systematic underestimation of rural residential expansion (−6 pp) and overestimation in cities (+2 pp) and suburbs (+3 pp); Population allocation DoC 75–85% in most countries, better in urban than rural areas; LUISA outperforms Null and Random models at aggregated scales (>1 km²)
Implications: Joint simulation useful for policy support in EU territorial planning; Better suited for compact urban growth scenarios than scattered rural development; Aggregated projections at municipal level reliable
Limitations: Single generic residential class fails to capture diverse housing market segments; Omission of spatial planning regulations and land price variations; Data harmonization errors and model complexity may propagate uncertainty
Future Directions: Segment residential land-use types and population by demographic groups; Incorporate continuous/mosaic land-use representations; Integrate spatial planning regulations where available; Assess data quality impacts on model performance
Scalability: Scalable across EU27+UK; requires calibration of attractiveness and suitability per country
Novelty: First pan-European joint spatial simulation and rigorous validation of population and urban residential land-use change patterns across diverse contexts

Title: Meteorological and Hydrological Drought Risks under Future Climate and Land-Use-Change Scenarios in the Yellow River Basin
Authors: Li, Yunyun; Huang, Yi; Fan, Jingjing; Zhang, Hongxue; Li, Yanchun; Wang, Xuemei; Deng, Qian
Objective: simulate and analyze projected land use changes; construct a copula-based drought risk model; apply an integrated framework to predict sub-seasonal and seasonal meteorological and hydrological drought risks
LULC Classes: Cropland; Woodland; Grassland; Water; Build-up; Bare land
Scenarios: RCP4.5; RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: downscaled climate projections (NEX-GDDP BCC-CSM1-1); CA-Markov land-use modeling; SWAT hydrological simulation; copula-based risk analysis; linear regression
Sim. Method Advantages: CA-Markov couples temporal Markov transitions with spatial cellular automata to accurately predict both magnitude and spatial distribution of land-use change
Tools/Soft Used: IDRISI Andes v17.0 (CA-Markov); SWAT model
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: NEX-GDDP dataset; meteorological data (1970–2015) from China National Climate Center; streamflow data from Yellow River Conservancy Commission; DEM (SRTM); soil map and land-use maps (1980–2020) from Chinese Academy of Sciences
Validation Methods: Kappa statistic for CA-Markov accuracy; Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (Ens), coefficient of determination (R²), and percent bias (PBIAS) for SWAT model
Validation Data Sources: observed land-use maps (2010, 2020); observed streamflow records at five hydrological stations
Key Findings: sub-seasonal meteorological drought risk up by 30–35% in upstream zones (A, B, C); sub-seasonal hydrological drought risk up by 30–35% in Loess Plateau zones (C, E); seasonal meteorological drought remains low (<10% risk); seasonal hydrological drought risk up ~20% in downstream zone (F); urban expansion exacerbates hydrological drought under meteorological drought conditions
Implications: proactive adaptation and mitigation measures required; integrated framework offers decision-support for localized drought risk forecasts
Limitations: no incorporation of future water resource development and utilization (reservoirs, irrigation, withdrawals)
Future Directions: integrate water resource development and utilization projections from socioeconomic scenarios, land-use modeling, and water planning forecasts
Scalability: methodology can be replicated in other climate-vulnerable regions for localized drought risk assessment
Novelty: first integrated coupling of downscaled climate projections, land-use-change simulations, and copula-based risk analysis for future sub-seasonal and seasonal drought risk modeling in the YRB

Title: Pathways to sustainable land use and food systems in Canada
Authors: Zerriffi, Hisham; Reyes, Rene; Maloney, Avery
Objective: Assess three land-use and food‐system pathways to 2050 for Canada, evaluating their ability to meet SDGs and Paris Agreement targets
LULC Classes: Cropland; Grassland; Forest; Urban; Other natural land
Scenarios: Current Trends; Sustainable Medium Ambition; Sustainable High Ambition
Analysis Methods: FABLE Calculator partial‐equilibrium model; Scenario assessment via shared socioeconomic pathways; Iterative national‐global trade balancing
Sim. Method Advantages: No specialized software or licenses required; Flexible, transparent Excel‐based framework; Easily updated with national/subnational data; Supported by Quality Assurance Tool for consistency
Tools/Soft Used: FABLE Calculator; FABLE Quality Assurance Tool
Predictors: Population; GDP; Consumption preferences (diets); Agricultural productivity; Land‐use regulation; Trade flows
Data Sources: FAOSTAT; ESA CCI land cover; Statistics Canada; Environment and Climate Change Canada; Natural Resources Canada; UN DESA; IPCC; FABLE Secretariat
Validation Methods: Consistency checks across tables and formulas using the Quality Assurance Tool
Validation Data Sources: National and global statistical datasets pre‐populated in the FABLE Calculator (e.g., FAOSTAT, ESA); national expert reviews
Key Findings: Medium and high ambition pathways reduce AFOLU GHG by 69% and 88% by 2050 vs. Current Trends; High ambition preserves natural land and increases afforestation (up to +2 M ha); Healthier diets shift reduces livestock emissions and brings kcal intake closer to EAT-Lancet ranges; Canada remains self‐sufficient in major crop and livestock groups, moderate export concentration persists
Implications: Stringent policies on deforestation, afforestation, protected areas critical for meeting SDGs; Diet shifts and efficiency gains essential for GHG mitigation; Trade and production diversity affect resilience and sovereignty
Limitations: Supply management not yet modeled; Wetlands under‐represented; Forest products module incomplete
Future Directions: Integrate supply management constraints; Improve wetland representation and statistics; Develop and integrate Forest Products Module
Scalability: Flexible framework allows adaptation to other countries and subnational regions
Novelty: First application of the FABLE Calculator at national level for Canada, linking SDGs, biodiversity and climate targets in an open, transparent scenario tool.

Title: Projection of Future Fire Emissions Over the Contiguous US Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence and CMIP6 Models
Authors: Wang, Sally S. -C.; Leung, L. Ruby; Qian, Yun
Objective: Predict future fire PM2.5 emissions over the contiguous US and understand their drivers under a high-emissions scenario
LULC Classes: Tree; grass; shrub; crop; bare soil; residual
Analysis Methods: Artificial neural network (ANN) model with five layers; Shapley Additive explanation (SHAP) for variable importance; 10-fold cross-validation
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures non-linear relationships at fine spatial scales; More computationally efficient than DGVMs; Explainable via SHAP compared to black-box ML
Tools/Soft Used: Python; PyTorch; Deep SHAP; NERSC computing platform
Predictors: RH, apcp, wndsp, SPEI, VPD, normalized temperature, normalized RH, normalized apcp, normalized VPD; SVD1_NCA, SVD2_NCA, SVD1_SRM, SVD2_SRM, SVD1_SElag2, SVD2_SElag2, soil moisture, vegetation fraction; LAI, grass fraction, tree fraction, crop fraction, shrub fraction, bare soil fraction, residual fraction, population density
Data Sources: GFED v4 (fire PM2.5 emissions); NARR, gridMET (meteorology); NLDAS-2 (soil moisture, vegetation fraction); MODIS (LAI, land cover); GPW v4, SSP5 projections (population); CMIP6 GCM outputs (ACCESS-ESM1.5, CESM2, CMCC-CM2-SR5, EC-Earth-CC, EC-Earth-Veg, EC-Earth-VegLR; GFDL-ESM4.1, CanESM5)
Validation Methods: 10-fold cross-validation; RMSE; correlation coefficient; index of agreement (IoA)
Validation Data Sources: GFED observations; NARR reanalysis
Key Findings: CONUS fire PM2.5 emissions projected to increase by 4%–75% (median +38%) by mid-century; Western US summer emissions to rise by 67%–186% (median +85% in SWUS); Increases driven by higher normalized temperature (23%–29%) and reduced soil moisture (2%–10%); LULC change adds an extra 58%–83% increase over western US due to vegetation fraction increases
Implications: Future fire impacts on air quality and health will intensify, especially in western US; Land management and prescribed fire planning must account for warming and drying trends
Limitations: Assumes stationarity of predictor–emission relationships; No feedback between fire emissions and climate; Uncertainties in GCM biases and future LULC projections
Future Directions: Improve LULC projections and dynamic vegetation responses; Incorporate fire–climate feedbacks in modeling; Assess antecedent climate influences at finer scales
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First use of explainable AI (SHAP) with CMIP6 outputs to quantify drivers of future fire PM2.5 emissions; Combines process-based and statistical advantages at 1° resolution under SSP5-8.5 scenario

Title: Quantifying the Safe Operating Space for Land-System SDG Achievement via Machine Learning and Scenario Discovery
Authors: Khan, Md Shakil; Moallemi, Enayat A. A.; Nazari, Asef; Thiruvady, Dhananjay; Bryan, Brett A. A.
Objective: Develop a machine-learning surrogate model to replicate the LUTO land-system model and identify policy settings defining a safe operating space for achieving multiple SDG targets
LULC Classes: Agricultural production; Carbon Plantings; Environmental Plantings; Biofuels; Wheat Food/Biofuels; Wheat Food/Bioenergy; Woody Perennials Bioenergy
Scenarios: Original LUTO: 648 scenarios combining four global outlooks (L1, M2, M3, H3), three GCMs, constraint settings, productivity growth, hurdle rates; Surrogate: Latin hypercube sampling of 10,000 inputs × 24 outlook/GCM/constraint combinations (240,000 for 2030 and 240,000 for 2050)
Analysis Methods: Machine-learning surrogate modeling (LR; GBRT; RF; MARS; XGBoost); five-fold cross-validation; scenario discovery; Latin hypercube sampling
Sim. Method Advantages: Surrogate runs 480,000 simulations in minutes vs. 1 hr per run for original LUTO; No proprietary solver requirement; low computational overhead; rapid scenario generation
Tools/Soft Used: Python 3.7; scikit-learn; XGBoost; CPLEX solver (LUTO); grid and random search for hyperparameters; GitHub; Zenodo
Predictors: Yield Increase (Crops); Constraint Settings; Carbon Price; Hurdle Rate; Biodiversity Fund levy; Global Outlook; Yield Increase (Trees); GCM; plus nine other dummy and quantitative inputs (17 total)
Data Sources: LUTO model outputs (Bryan et al., 2015) via CSIRO open data portal; Downscaled SDG targets (Gao & Bryan, 2017); Supporting Information S1
Validation Methods: Five-fold cross-validation comparing surrogate predictions to LUTO outputs
Validation Data Sources: Test subset (4,924 rows) of LUTO projections
Key Findings: XGBoost surrogate achieved 96% accuracy (R² = 0.9694, RMSE = 0.00379); Only 5.82% of 2050 pathways met five weak SDG targets; Safe operating space defined by Yield Increase (Crops) > 1.78×, Carbon Price > 100 AU$/tCO₂, Biodiversity levy > 9%, regulated land-use constraints
Implications: Machine-learning surrogates enable dense uncertainty exploration and policy-relevant scenario discovery for land-system sustainability; Surrogate models can be deployed widely without heavy compute resources
Limitations: Requires extensive hyper-parameter tuning; Must retrain surrogate if original model is modified; Unreliable for inputs beyond original parameter ranges
Future Directions: Evaluate additional ML algorithms and ensemble surrogates; Apply surrogate discovery approach to other land-use models and regions
Scalability: Surrogate approach is open-source, computationally light, and deployable for other regions and process-based models
Novelty: First application of ML-based surrogate modeling of a national-scale land-system model (LUTO) combined with scenario discovery to define a safe operating space for SDG achievement.

Title: Quantity and spatial imbalance of supply and demand for water yield services in terrestrial ecosystems under different future land use scenarios in Xinjiang, China
Authors: Liu, Zhuo; Shi, Mingjie; Wu, Hongqi; Jiang, Pingan; Zhang, Haoyu; He, Panxing; Zheng, Kai; Dong, Tong; Zhang, Yue
Objective: To assess water yield services supply and demand in Xinjiang under multiple future land use scenarios (BAU, RED, ELP, SD) for 2025 and 2030
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest; Grassland; Water; Constructed; Bare land
Scenarios: BAU (business-as-usual); RED (rapid economic development); ELP (ecological land protection); SD (sustainable development)
Analysis Methods: GMOP-PLUS model coupling (PLUS + GMOP); InVEST water yield module; Markov chain; freshwater security index
Sim. Method Advantages: PLUS model improves patch-level LULC prediction via LEAS and CARS over traditional cellular automata; GMOP enables multi-objective optimization (ecological + economic) via gray prediction and linear programming
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.7; LINGO 12.0; GMOP-PLUS; InVEST; Markov module
Predictors: Distance to rail; Distance to major roads; Distance to secondary roads; Distance to water; DEM‐derived slope; Soil type and depth; Plant available water content; Precipitation; Temperature; Potential evapotranspiration; Population density; GDP grid; Night-time lights
Data Sources: RESDC (LULC, administrative divisions, water systems, climate data, socioeconomic grids); FAO and World Harmonized Soil databases; Geospatial Data Cloud (DEM); OpenStreetMap (transport and water distances); Xinjiang Water Resources Bulletin, Xinjiang Statistical Yearbook, China Research Data Service (night-time lights); Zomer et al. (2022) for evapotranspiration
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient and overall accuracy comparison of simulated vs. actual LULC for 2015 and 2020
Validation Data Sources: Actual LULC maps for 2015 and 2020 from RESDC
Key Findings: All scenarios show water yield decline from 2025 to 2030, RED yields highest in 2025 due to impervious expansion; ELP and SD scenarios slow decline via vegetation retention, SD balances cropland growth and ecological protection; FSI indicates persistent water deficit under all scenarios, highest imbalance in RED, closest equilibrium in ELP/SD
Implications: Sustainable planning (SD) can narrow supply–demand gap and spatial imbalance; Policies needed for buffer zones, water-saving agriculture, ecological conservation near oases, industrial water efficiency
Limitations: Only four LULC scenarios considered, lacking climate–land use interaction
Future Directions: Incorporate future climate projections and policy constraints; Model groundwater–surface water coupling and interactive feedbacks; Develop more objective demand estimation methods for scenarios; Expand scenario diversity to reflect uncertainties
Scalability: Potentially scalable to other arid regions via GMOP-PLUS + InVEST framework with region‐specific data
Novelty: Coupling of GMOP-PLUS (multi‐objective optimized spatial LULC) with InVEST water yield; Assessment of water supply–demand under sustainable development scenario balancing ecological and economic objectives

Title: Simulation of China's potential rice yields by coupling land system evolution and climate change
Authors: Li, Manchun; Du, Cong; Jiang, Penghui; Luan, Wenbo; Chen, Dengshuai
Objective: Construct a Grey Prediction Model–Future Land Use Simulation (GM-FLUS) coupled with an improved Global Agro-Ecological Zone (GAEZ) model to simulate China’s land‐system evolution and estimate future potential rice yields under four climate scenarios
LULC Classes: Paddy fields; forestland; grassland; construction land
Analysis Methods: Grey prediction model (GM(1,1)); FLUS spatial simulation; GAEZ potential productivity modelling; Mann-Kendall trend test
Sim. Method Advantages: Macro-scale simulation consistent with actual productivity; Integrates land-system evolution with climate projections; Less data- and computation-intensive than crop growth or machine-learning models
Tools/Soft Used: GM-FLUS model; GAEZ model; Mann-Kendall test
Predictors: Elevation; slope; slope direction; distance to city centre; distance to town centre; distance to expressway; distance to arterial road; distance to railway; GDP; population
Data Sources: Land use: Data Centre for Resources and Environmental Sciences (1990–2020); Climate (2020): TerraClimate and FLDAS datasets, (2030–2060): ScenarioMIP outputs from CAS-ESM; Soil: Harmonised World Soil Database; Topography: Shuttle Radar Topography Mission; Socioeconomic: National Bureau of Statistics, OpenStreetMap; Rice yields (verification): Statistical Yearbook
Validation Methods: Land‐use simulation: 2018→2020 prediction vs. observed (overall accuracy 72.89%, Kappa 0.65)
Validation Data Sources: Remotely sensed land‐use 2020; Statistical Yearbook rice yields 2020
Key Findings: Potential rice yields increase under SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0, decrease under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5; Paddy‐field area stable (net –2,103 km²) due to land‐protection policy; Temperature rise negatively correlates with potential yields, precipitation positively correlates under low‐emission scenarios
Implications: Need heat‐resistant rice and anti‐heat measures; Improve irrigation and drainage infrastructure; Protect paddy fields in vulnerable regions
Limitations: Assumed all paddy fields planted with rice; Focused only on rice, not other major grain crops; Did not address extreme climate‐event uncertainties
Future Directions: Expand to wheat, maize, soybean potential productivity; Incorporate extreme climate‐event simulations; Refine spatial planting distribution data
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Coupling of GM-FLUS land system evolution with GAEZ climatic potential productivity under multiple SSP scenarios

Title: Spatially-explicit assessment of carbon stocks in the landscape in the southern US under different scenarios of industrial wood pellet demand
Authors: Duden, A. S.; Verweij, P. A.; Faaij, A. P. C.; Abt, R. C.; Junginger, M.; van der Hilst, F.
Objective: Determine the impact of increased wood pellet demand on carbon stocks in the landscape in the Southern US in a spatially explicit manner, including both indirect market and land-use change effects
LULC Classes: grassland; cropland; urban area; pine plantation; natural pine forest; mixed forest; upland hardwood forest; lowland hardwood forest; non-forest vegetation; federal land; water; pasture
Scenarios: High housing demand & high wood pellet demand (HhHp); High housing demand & low wood pellet demand (HhLp); Low housing demand & high wood pellet demand (LhHp); Low housing demand & low wood pellet demand (LhLp)
Analysis Methods: SubRegional Timber Supply (SRTS) economic modelling; PCRaster Land-Use Change (PLUC) spatial allocation; IPCC Tier I carbon stock calculations
Sim. Method Advantages: Soft link between market and spatial models allows spatially explicit, high-resolution quantification of indirect market and land-use change effects
Tools/Soft Used: SRTS model; PLUC model; FIA EVALIDator; PCRaster; IPCC guidelines
Predictors: agricultural rent; timber rent; distance to wood pellet mills; distance to other wood-using mills; land-use suitability factors (per land use)
Data Sources: Primary: USDA Forest Service FIA survey data; Secondary: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, IPCC default values, soil data from Domke et al. (2017), previous land-use projections (Duden et al., 2017)
Validation Methods: Comparison of projected wood pellet production, forest area changes, agricultural rent trends with observed data; Regression analysis of historical land-use allocation (2000–2010)
Validation Data Sources: National Land Cover Database (2000–2010); USDA statistics; observed market data
Key Findings: Modest wood pellet demand increase yields 103 Mt additional carbon stock (+0.7%), driven by afforestation/reforestation; Timber market trends exert greater impact on carbon stocks than wood pellet demand; Under low timber demand, wood pellet impact rises to +224 Mt (+1.6%)
Implications: Policies limiting conversion of natural forests to plantations can enhance carbon benefits; Payment for carbon storage could incentivize forest retention; Spatially explicit assessments are critical for identifying carbon hotspots
Limitations: No temporal flux within land-use types, assumes new forests reach average carbon stocks by 2030; Fixed forest productivity, no age-class growth dynamics; Private landowner decision factors beyond market signals not modelled
Future Directions: Include extreme wood pellet demand scenarios; Incorporate temporal flux of forest and soil carbon growth curves; Extend analysis over longer horizons and multiple rotation cycles
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with linked market and land-use dynamics via SRTS-PLUC framework
Novelty: Introduces a spatially explicit methodological framework that integrates indirect market effects and land-use change into landscape-scale carbon calculations using high-resolution field data.

Title: Structural succession of land resources under the influence of different policies: A case study for Shanxi Province, China
Authors: Yu, Ziyue; Deng, Xiangzheng; Cheshmehzangi, Ali; Mangi, Eugenio
Objective: To model future land use demand and spatial distribution under different socio-economic scenarios and government policies using a combined CGELUC–DLS approach
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest land; Grassland; Water area; Construction land; Unused land
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (SSP2); Green Development (SSP1); Economic Priority Development (SSP5)
Analysis Methods: Malmquist index DEA; Computable General Equilibrium of Land Use Change (CGELUC); Dynamics of Land System (DLS); InVEST carbon storage model
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates socio-economic and spatial models to capture both land demand and spatial patterns under policy influences, overcoming single-model limitations
Tools/Soft Used: GAMS; ArcGIS 10.6; InVEST model; DEA software
Predictors: Natural factors; Socio-economic factors (e.g., population pressure; GDP density; distance to roads); Spatial autocorrelation
Data Sources: China Statistical Yearbook (2007–2018), Shanxi Provincial Statistical Yearbook (2007–2018); China Rural Statistical Yearbook (2007–2018), China Finance Yearbook (2018); Shanxi General Public Budget Income and Expenditure Summary, Shanxi Financial Yearbook; Meteorological data (China Meteorological Data Service Center); Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, Harmonized World Soil Database; Land use and socio-economic raster data (Chinese Academy of Sciences RESDC)
Validation Methods: Kappa index comparison of simulated vs. actual 2020 land use patterns
Validation Data Sources: Actual 2020 land use maps
Key Findings: Agricultural land TFP fluctuated 2006–2019 with slow growth overall; Technical efficiency drove productivity gains; Under BAU, cropland −2.43%, forest −5.26%, grassland −1.87%, construction +21.52%; Under EPD, construction +33.02%, unused land −66.33%; Under GDS, slowest ecological land loss and highest carbon sequestration retention (−1.62%)
Implications: Subsidies and green policies can balance economic growth and ecological protection; land policy design critical for sustainable land management and carbon mitigation
Limitations: Major climate and biome context not specified; some local government data estimated; spatial resolution limited to 1 km
Future Directions: Integrate energy–land–environment pathways; refine socio-economic parameter quantification; extend beyond 2030
Scalability: Applicable to other provinces with tailored SAM and DLS parameters
Novelty: Embedded land accounts in SAM; combined CGELUC–DLS modeling under SSP-based policy scenarios

Title: A new assessment framework to forecast land use and carbon storage under different SSP-RCP scenarios in China
Authors: Guo, Wei; Teng, Yongjia; Li, Jing; Yan, Yueguan; Zhao, Chuanwu; Li, Yongxing; Li, Xiang
Objective: Develop a scenario-based coupled framework to forecast land-use/land-cover (LULC) and terrestrial ecosystem carbon storage (CS) under different SSP-RCP scenarios
LULC Classes: forest; grassland; cropland; urban; barren; water
Scenarios: SSP245; SSP370; SSP585
Analysis Methods: Integrated scenario assessment using LUH2 dataset for structural prediction; PLUS (Patch-generating Land Use Simulation) model for 500 m×500 m distribution simulation; InVEST model for carbon storage estimation
Sim. Method Advantages: Higher spatial resolution downscaling from 0.25° to 500 m; Improved spatial heterogeneity capture; Overall simulation accuracy > 90%
Tools/Soft Used: LUH2 dataset; PLUS model; InVEST model; Random Forest algorithm
Predictors: elevation; slope; temperature; precipitation; soil workability; soil oxygen availability; GDP distribution; population distribution; distance to water; distance to airports; distance to railways; distance to primary ways
Data Sources: LUH2C dataset; MCD12Q1 v061 (MODIS land cover); Global Aboveground Biomass Carbon; GSOCmap1.5.0; ecological barrier maps
Validation Methods: Confusion matrix; Kappa coefficient
Validation Data Sources: MCD12Q1 v061 land-cover for 2020
Key Findings: Basic LULC and CS distribution set by natural context; Forest and urban areas increase, grassland decreases under all scenarios; SSP370 yields highest CS growth (0.82%) and greatest spatial heterogeneity; Carbon sources in cropland and urban regions, carbon sinks in grassland and afforested areas
Implications: Strengthen forest conservation; Delineate urban expansion limits and ecological parks; Promote rotational grazing, afforestation in western regions; Explore carbon trading/tax; Accelerate clean-energy technology deployment
Limitations: Classification mismatches between LUH2C and MCD12Q1; Potential bias from multi-source predictor resolution; Ignored within-class carbon density variability
Future Directions: Develop dynamic driving systems incorporating phenology, policies, human activities; Conduct field measurements to capture within-class variability; Forecast CS dynamics at finer temporal and spatial scales
Scalability: Applicable to smaller watersheds or urban scales
Novelty: First integration of LUH2 dataset, PLUS model, and InVEST for 500 m resolution coupled LULC-CS forecasting under multiple SSP-RCP scenarios

Title: An assessment of future rewilding potential in the United Kingdom
Authors: Brown, C.; Prestele, R.; Rounsevell, M.
Objective: An assessment of future rewilding potential in Great Britain
LULC Classes: unmanaged (abandoned or never‐managed); conservation (land managed for non-extractive ecosystem services); very extensive pasture; food crops; fodder crops; grass-fed milk; grass-fed meat; bioenergy fuel; softwood; hardwood
Scenarios: RCP2.6-SSP1; RCP4.5-SSP2; RCP4.5-SSP4; RCP6.0-SSP3; RCP8.5-SSP2; RCP8.5-SSP5
Analysis Methods: High-resolution agent-based land‐use modeling with CRAFTY-GB embedded in the LandSyMM global framework
Sim. Method Advantages: Captures local decision‐making and competition among land users; integrates cross‐sectoral drivers and ecosystem services; operates at 1 km² resolution with annual time steps
Tools/Soft Used: CRAFTY-GB; LandSyMM; R package terra
Predictors: Human capital; social capital; financial capital; manufactured capital; natural capital; societal demands for provisioning, regulating, cultural ecosystem services
Data Sources: UK Land Cover Map 2015; Copernicus HRL Water & Wetness 2015; EUNIS 3.1; CORINE CLC 2012; CHESS-SCAPE climate data; peat maps (BGS, Cranfield, OS); protected-area designations; UK-SSP narratives
Validation Methods: Calibration and evaluation against observed land-use patterns and ecosystem service indicators (File S2)
Validation Data Sources: Observed land-cover maps; protected-area data; ecosystem service assessments
Key Findings: Areas of 5,000–7,000 km² unmanaged and 24,000–42,000 km² under conservation management could be suitable for rewilding by 2080; Total rewilding potential areas (RPAs) reach ~17,000–20,000 km², up to 27,000 km² under low-pressure scenarios; Hotspots often occur near urban centers and cultural landscapes; Priority habitats (peatlands, ancient woodlands, wetlands) largely fall outside RPAs and remain vulnerable to conversion
Implications: Substantial scope exists to meet UK and global restoration targets without compromising food and timber production; Targeted interventions needed to protect high-carbon and high-biodiversity ecosystems; Policy and market instruments can shape the nature and extent of rewilding
Limitations: Aggregated ecological resolution; reliance on scenario narratives (non-probabilistic); no modeling of explicit rewilding policies or carbon/biodiversity market investments; uncertain ecological outcomes of passive rewilding; potential model sensitivity to agent tenacity
Future Directions: Higher‐resolution spatial and ecological modeling of ecological and biological impacts; Assessment of carbon sequestration and biodiversity outcomes under climate change risks; Evaluation of policy and market intervention effects on RPAs
Scalability: Application of CRAFTY-GB and LandSyMM frameworks to other regions with equivalent scenario downscaling and data inputs
Novelty: First integrated assessment of future rewilding potential using an agent-based land-use model under RCP-SSP scenarios; linkage of rewilding opportunity mapping with multiple high-priority habitat overlaps

Title: Broadening the horizon in land use change modelling: Normative scenarios for nature positive futures in Switzerland
Authors: Black, Benjamin; Adde, Antoine; Farinotti, Daniel; Guisan, Antoine; Kuelling, Nathan; Kurmann, Manuel; Martin, Caroline; Mayer, Paula; Rabe, Sven-Erik; Streit, Jan; Zekollari, Harry; Gret-Regamey, Adrienne
Objective: To present an approach to operationalize and quantitatively model normative, nature-positive land use change scenarios using a constrained cellular automata model for Switzerland
LULC Classes: alpine pastures; closed forest; glacier; grassland; intensive agriculture; open forest; shrubland; permanent crops; urban/amenities; static
Target Years: 2060 (simulations at 5-year time steps to produce maps from 2020 to 2060)
Scenarios: EI-NAT (intrinsic value); EI-SOC (instrumental value); EI-CUL (relational value); Business-as-Usual (BAU); Growth and Extinction (GR-EX)
Analysis Methods: Random Forest transition-potential modelling; expert-elicited transition rates; spatial interventions; dynamic predictor updating; landscape metric analysis (Patch Cohesion Index, Effective Mesh Size)
Sim. Method Advantages: Constrained cellular automata abstract actor processes and are easily explained to non-experts; Extensible framework integrating statistical and process-based models (e.g., glacier evolution); Allows spatially explicit scenario operationalization (transition rates, zoning policies, dynamic drivers)
Tools/Soft Used: R (4.2.2); Dinamica EGO (7.2.0); randomForest R package; landscapemetrics R package; Zenodo repository for code/data
Predictors: Land suitability and accessibility variables (biophysical, socio-economic); neighborhood predictors (focal metrics for existing LULC classes); dynamic drivers (climate RCPs, population projections, economic trends)
Data Sources: Swiss area statistics LULC maps (SFSO 1985–2018); climate projections (Broennimann & Guisan 2024); population projections (SFSO 2020); economic projections (Cretegny & Müller 2020); glacier evolution model (Zekollari et al. 2019)
Validation Methods: Hold-out validation (70:30 splits); multiple performance metrics for Random Forest TP models (“stage 1”); expert feedback on spatial patterns
Validation Data Sources: Historical LULC maps from SFSO calibration periods; expert stakeholder feedback via interactive web platform
Key Findings: Normative scenarios constrained urban sprawl and fragmentation compared to BAU and GR-EX; EI-NAT increased closed forest via natural succession, EI-CUL preserved pastures and permanent crops, EI-SOC prioritized ecosystem-service-oriented land uses; All scenarios showed forest expansion and major glacial loss, spatial metrics generally concurred with narrative expectations
Implications: Provides decision-makers with spatially explicit comparisons of normative futures for Switzerland’s Ecological Infrastructure; Highlights trade-offs between cultural landscapes, biodiversity, and ecosystem services; Suggests that PA siting based on Nature Contributions to People may better limit urban encroachment
Limitations: De-glaciated areas defaulted to static class due to limited data on post-glacial trajectories; Expert elicitation of numerous transition rates introduced aggregation challenges; High-resolution maps hindered stakeholder interpretation of broad landscape patterns
Future Directions: Ensemble simulations sampling expert-elicited rate uncertainties and system shocks; Develop interpretable metrics for ecosystem service outcomes rather than LULC patterns alone; Investigate utilization of newly de-glaciated lands under differing scenarios
Scalability: The modelling framework and open-source code/data are replicable for other regions and SES contexts
Novelty: Deep operationalization of normative scenario components (dynamic drivers, spatial policies, expert elicitation); Integration of machine-learning TP models with process-based glacier projections; Multi-region, participatory approach linking local data-driven methods with global narrative frameworks

Title: Carbon potential of China's Grain to Green Program and its contribution to the carbon target
Authors: Ma, Yinqiu; Huang, Lin; Li, Jiahui; Cao, Wei; Cai, Yumei
Objective: Estimate the impact of China’s Grain for Green Program (GFGP) on carbon storage and carbon sink capacity from 2000 to 2020, and project its carbon potential under expansion and management scenarios for 2030 and 2060
LULC Classes: Forest; Grassland; Cropland; Barren hills and wasteland
Scenarios: SSP1-RCP2.6; SSP2-RCP4.5; SSP5-RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: Coupling Land Use and Land Cover Change (LULCC) data with net ecosystem productivity (NEP) estimation using the CASA model; Linear regression of future NDVI on temperature, precipitation, solar radiation; Calculation of soil heterotrophic respiration and net ecosystem productivity
Sim. Method Advantages: Accounts for temporal–spatial heterogeneity in NEP; integrates field-scale GFGP plot identification with remote-sensing-driven productivity models, avoiding overreliance on area-only proxies
Tools/Soft Used: CASA model; LUCCC model; statistical regression (unspecified software)
Predictors: Mean monthly temperature; Mean monthly precipitation; Solar radiation; NDVI; Simple Ratio (SR)
Data Sources: Globeland30 land use/land cover dataset (2000–2020); CASA model inputs: SOL (solar radiation), FPAR, NDVI, meteorological data (temperature, precipitation); County-level carbon emission inventories
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: GFGP contributed 1,482.62 Tg C sink from 2000 to 2020, 60.7% from forests and 39.3% from grasslands; Annual sinks in 2030: 47.49–75.70 Tg C, in 2060: 38.57–73.53 Tg C, offsetting up to 1.87% of national CO₂ emissions; Strong spatial heterogeneity: highest sinks in Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau, Sichuan-Chongqing-Hunan-Hubei subregion, Lower–Middle Yangtze
Implications: Large-scale ecological restoration can measurably offset national emissions; GFGP serves as a model for nature-based negative emissions strategies in other countries; Need to integrate forest management and mixed-species planting to optimize carbon and ecosystem service co-benefits
Limitations: Land cover data resolution (30 m for 2000–2020, 1 km/5 km for future) may misclassify early-stage regrowth; CASA model omits CO₂ fertilization and detailed management effects; Underestimation of cropland carbon sink baseline, overestimation from ignoring grazing/harvest emissions
Future Directions: Incorporate detailed agricultural baseline carbon sink and harvest/grazing scenarios; Expand observation networks and reconcile top-down/bottom-up estimates; Integrate chemical weathering carbon sinks and microbial respiration dynamics; Develop multifunctional cost-benefit frameworks for mixed-species restoration
Scalability: Demonstrated framework applicable to other large-scale national restoration programs, subject to local land-cover and climate data availability
Novelty: Coupling high-resolution LULCC mapping of GFGP plots with process-based CASA NEP modeling to reveal actual temporal-spatial heterogeneity and scenario-based carbon potential beyond area-only estimates

Title: Decadal analysis and simulation of land use and land cover changes in Taiwan using machine learning and markov chain models
Authors: Liu, Chun-ya; Arora, Aman
Objective: Decadal analysis of Land Use Land Cover (LULC) changes (1990–2020) in Taiwan and simulation of future LULC for 2030 and 2050 using Support Vector Machine–Markov Chain integration
LULC Classes: Barren; Uncultivated; Water Shallow; Water Deep; Built-up; Forest; Cultivated
Scenarios: 2-variables; 3-variables; 5-variables; 6-variables
Analysis Methods: Supervised classification (Maximum Likelihood Classifier); Support Vector Machine; CA-Markov simulation; accuracy assessment (confusion matrix, Cohen’s Kappa, RMSE)
Sim. Method Advantages: Combines precise ML‐based LULC classification (SVM) with probabilistic future prediction (Markov); Captures non-linear spatial drivers; Improves simulation validity by integrating multiple environmental predictors
Tools/Soft Used: Google Earth Engine; GIS (for resampling, Euclidean distance); SVM module with grid search
Predictors: Elevation; Distance to roads; Distance to rivers; Aspect; Hillshade; Slope
Data Sources: Landsat 5/7/8 Surface Reflectance Tier 1 imagery; SRTM DEM; OpenStreetMap; Google Earth Engine
Validation Methods: Confusion matrix; Producer’s and User’s Accuracy; Overall Accuracy; Cohen’s Kappa; RMSE
Validation Data Sources: Ground Control Points (GCPs); actual 2020 Landsat LULC map
Key Findings: Built-up area expanded by ~140% (1990–2020) and projected +209% (2030), +223% (2050); Barren and deep-water classes declined ~49–54%; Forest and cultivated lands increased slightly; 3-variable and 6-variable scenarios yielded most consistent simulations
Implications: Continued urbanization despite negative population growth; Need for infill and green-space planning; Critical balance between development and environmental protection
Limitations: Moderate spatial resolution of pre-2000 Landsat data; Exclusion of socio-economic and fine‐scale demographic variables due to data format mismatches
Future Directions: Incorporate socio-economic and population datasets; Apply object-based classification for higher urban accuracy; Explore dynamic transition probabilities
Scalability: Applicable to other mid-sized, rapidly urbanizing regions with complex topography
Novelty: First national-scale decadal LULC simulation for Taiwan; Integration of SVM classification with CA-Markov modeling under multiple predictor scenarios; Consideration of negative population growth in LULC projection

Title: Divergent urban land trajectories under alternative population projections within the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
Authors: Mcmanamay, Ryan A.; Raad, Alen; Vernon, Chris R.; Thurber, Travis; Gao, Jing; Powers, Stephen; O'Neill, Brian
Objective: Compare how two alternative spatially explicit US population projections (state-specific vs national-level) influence long-term urban land trajectories under SSP2, SSP3, and SSP5
LULC Classes: Urban land (impervious surfaces); rural areas
Scenarios: SSP2; SSP3; SSP5
Analysis Methods: SELECT spatially explicit urban land model; Country-Level Urban Building Scenario (CLUBS);  Gravity-based downscaling; Ward’s hierarchical agglomerative clustering; Loess smoothing
Sim. Method Advantages: Accounts for spatial heterogeneity and temporal non-stationarity; Operates at multiple scales with dynamic feedbacks; Locally calibrated sub-models for 20 subnational regions; Avoids static per-capita coefficients and rigid historical constraints
Tools/Soft Used: R 4.2.1; SELECT model; CLUBS model; empirical gravity model; spatial scaling algorithms
Predictors: Population size; population growth rate; urban maturity; environmental variables (e.g., topography, proximity to urban); spatial autocorrelative surrogates; socioeconomic variables
Data Sources: Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL); NP projections (Jones & O’Neill 2016); SP projections (Jiang et al. 2020, Zoraghein & O’Neill 2020b); US Census Bureau urban area definitions
Validation Methods: Empirical calibration against GHSL; Parametric uncertainty analysis; Visual inspection of clustering dendrograms
Validation Data Sources: GHSL time-series built-up data
Key Findings: Total US urban land totals remain constant, but spatial distribution diverges dramatically between population inputs; State-specific projections yield increased urban land in rural areas (1–3% higher) and decreased infilling in urban cores (1–6% lower); Spatial heterogeneity at sub-state scales—neighboring areas can show opposite trends; No linear relationship between population delta and urban land delta
Implications: Local demographic processes (domestic/international migration) critically shape urban sprawl patterns; Projections must incorporate spatially varying population inputs to improve realism; Land-use planning should account for potential rural extensification
Limitations: Fixed static urban/rural boundaries ignore peri-urban transition zones; Results subject to SELECT model structure and parameter choices; SP projections based on pre-COVID migration trends
Future Directions: Incorporate dynamic boundary definitions and transition gradients; Test alternative urban expansion models under the same SSPs; Assess post-2020 migration shifts (e.g., COVID-19 effects); Integrate economic and governance variables more explicitly
Scalability: SELECT framework applicable to other countries or regions with recalibrated subnational models
Novelty: First experiment isolating effects of spatially explicit state vs national population projections—under identical SSP land-budget constraints—on high-resolution urban land trajectories.

Title: High-resolution land use/cover forecasts for Switzerland in the 21st century
Authors: Butikofer, Luca; Adde, Antoine; Urbach, Davnah; Tobias, Silvia; Huss, Matthias; Guisan, Antoine; Randin, Christophe
Objective: Forecast high-resolution land-use/land-cover (LULC) change in Switzerland for the 21st century
LULC Classes: Modelled: Industry, Building, Special urban, Urban green, Horticulture, Arable, Grassland, Alpine grassland, Forest, Brush, Trees, Unproductive vegetation, Bare land, Glacier; Static: Lakes, Rivers, Transportation (and nine sub-classes from NOAS04_72)
Scenarios: RCP 4.5; RCP 8.5; baseline LULC demand with policy-driven modifications
Analysis Methods: Neural network for environmental suitability; linear extrapolation for demand; transition-matrix rules; CLUE-S allocation algorithm; mechanistic glacier-lake model
Sim. Method Advantages: Improved prediction accuracy via data augmentation for underrepresented classes; Compatibility with past maps at 100 m resolution; Integration of policy scenarios beyond purely data-driven trends
Tools/Soft Used: R (terra, covsel, lulcc, Himsc, RS-BID); Python (TensorFlow/Keras); CLUE-S algorithm
Predictors: Past LULC maps (three time-steps); LULC neighbourhood proportions; dominant land-use in 5 km×5 km; Cantons; distance to roads (five classes); distance to urban areas (three classes); Population density; one- and nine-kilometre neighbourhood densities; 19 climatic variables; 10 soil variables; 14 hydrology variables; elevation; slope; Distance to lakes/rivers (three size classes); bed-rock type; noise from transportation
Data Sources: Swiss Federal Statistical Office aerial-survey LULC maps; GeoStat CSV; climate projections (CH2018); glacier model outputs; policy documents (Spatial Planning Act; biodiversity strategy; cropland protection plan; adaptation strategy)
Validation Methods: Neural network cross-validation (80–20 split); Quantity and allocation disagreement metrics; Comparison of requested vs. obtained class prevalence after CLUE-S allocation
Validation Data Sources: GeoStat LULC products (2012–18)
Key Findings: Overall NN accuracy 0.79, quantity disagreement 0.053, allocation disagreement 0.15; Class-wise balanced accuracy average 0.89 (range 0.72–0.98); CLUE-S allocations matched demand within 0.2% error
Implications: Provides policy-relevant LULC forecasts for land-use planning, resource management, ecological and hydraulic modelling, and conservation
Limitations: Static classes not modelled; Reliance on GeoStat map accuracy; Single scenario for demand and transition rules
Future Directions: Enable alternative management scenarios by varying demand/transition parameters; apply to other policy contexts
Scalability: Yes; methodology compatible with other regions given comparable input data and policy rules
Novelty: First LULC forecast for Switzerland at thematic resolution matching past maps; integration of NN-based suitability with policy-driven modules at 100 m resolution

Title: Identifying resource-conscious and low-carbon agricultural development pathways through land use modelling
Authors: Deo, Aniket; Shirsath, Paresh B.; Aggarwal, Pramod K.
Objective: Examine potential of producing more food from available agricultural land with low-carbon (reduced GHG emissions) and resource-conscious (optimal resource use) options
LULC Classes: cereals (rice, wheat, maize, sorghum, pearl millet); legumes (pigeon pea, chickpea); oilseeds (groundnut, mustard, soybean)
Scenarios: Calories-nation; Calories-group; Calories-crop; Emissions-nation; Emissions-group; Emissions-crop
Analysis Methods: Linear programming land-use optimization (simplex via MATLAB linprog)
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates calorie production, emissions, resource constraints simultaneously; Operates at multiple spatial scales (district, state, national); Uses realized yields for realistic planning
Tools/Soft Used: MATLAB 2016b (linprog); Cool Farm Tool; FAO-56 crop coefficient method; Hargreaves evapotranspiration
Predictors: District-level yields; calorie content; GHG emissions; irrigation requirement; cost of cultivation; harvest prices; land, water, capital availability
Data Sources: Primary: Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES) district-level crop data (2017–2019), India Meteorological Department rainfall/temperature, Cool Farm Tool emission factors; Secondary: Longvah et al. (2017), USDA calorie values, DES cost of cultivation and prices
Validation Methods: Rigid boundary test replicating baseline land use under strict constraints
Validation Data Sources: Baseline DES district-level production and resource data
Key Findings: Calories-nation can increase calorie production by 11% while reducing emissions by 2.5% and sparing 2–3% land and water; Emissions-group can reduce GHG by ~30% with no calorie loss and spare 15% land, 18% water; State-level crop targets limit redistribution benefits, food-group targets offer greater gains; Maize and oilseed redistribution drive improvements in resource and emission efficiencies
Implications: Spatial crop redistribution enables low-carbon, resource-efficient agricultural development; Policy design should allow inter-state crop reallocation and food-group targets; Spared resources could support carbon sinks or alternative land uses
Limitations: Static, deterministic model, ignores future climate, population, price dynamics; Only ten crops considered, excludes other land uses; Does not assess actual conservation or post-redistribution land use
Future Directions: Incorporate climate change effects via dynamic crop simulation coupling; Extend to include demand-side, market pricing, population projections; Evaluate spared land conversion to carbon sinks or biodiversity habitats
Scalability: Applicable to regions with similar fine-scale agricultural data; data availability may limit transfer
Novelty: Combines calorie and emission objectives with resource constraints across multiple spatial scales; Uses realized district-level yields for realistic land-use optimization in India; Introduces food-group vs. crop-level state targets in scenario design

Title: Integrating national integrated assessment model and land-use intensity for estimating China's terrestrial ecosystem carbon storage
Authors: Wang, Yuanhui; Song, Changqing; Gao, Yifan; Ye, Sijing; Gao, Peichao
Objective: Estimate potential effects of land‐use changes on China’s terrestrial ecosystem carbon storage (TECS) from 2000 to 2050 under China‐specified policies
LULC Classes: Forestland; Agricultural land; Settlement land; Grassland; Wetland; Water; Bareland; Artificial surfaces
Scenarios: Base scenario; Balanced scenario; Narrowly focused scenario
Analysis Methods: Logistic regression for local suitability; “Many‐to‐many” land service balancing in CLUMondo; Overlay analysis for biomass and soil carbon density; Kappa statistic for validation
Sim. Method Advantages: CLUMondo’s ability to handle many‐to‐many relationships between multiple land service demands and multiple land system types, and incorporation of land‐use intensity via land system taxonomy
Tools/Soft Used: CLUMondo; Threshold21‐China; Logistic regression; Spatial resampling and sliding‐window aggregation
Predictors: Market access index; Market influence index; Market density index; Nighttime lights; Distance to river; Distance to road; Distance to railway; Time to nearest city; Travel time; GDP; Gridded population; Crop yield; GPP (Mar, Jun, Sep, Dec); Elevation; Elevation variance; Slope; Aspect; Annual and monthly precipitation; Annual and monthly temperature; NDVI (Apr, Jun, Sep, Dec); Livestock densities (buffaloes, cattle, goats, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens, ducks)
Data Sources: GlobeLand30 land‐cover data; Threshold21‐China IAM outputs; CLUMondo; GlobeLand30; International Soil Reference and Information Centre soil data; FAO statistical data; National vegetation and soil maps; GPP and NDVI datasets; Natural Earth; DMSP‐OLS nighttime lights; CIESIN population; Monfreda et al. crop data
Validation Methods: Kappa statistic comparison of simulated 2010 land system map versus observed; Comparison of TECS estimates in 2010 against literature values
Validation Data Sources: GlobeLand30 2010 land‐cover map; Xu et al. (2018) TECS estimates; Field study by Zheng et al. (2018)
Key Findings: TECS increases by 846.7–865.5 Tg C under base/balanced scenarios and 739.1 Tg C under narrowly focused by 2050; Forest conversions contribute 83.3–90.3% of TECS gains, cultivated-to-artificial conversions cause 53–65% of TECS losses; Balanced scenario reduces cultivated-to-artificial loss by 82 Tg C and adds 73 Tg C via forest densification; Mountainous and rapidly urbanizing regions show highest sensitivity to policy scenarios
Implications: Implementation of sustainable development policies can significantly enhance carbon storage; targeted land‐change management needed in mountainous and urbanizing regions; framework applicable for policy planning
Limitations: No explicit climate and biome details; land‐use intensity levels subjectively set to three; reliance on 1 km resolution may miss fine‐scale changes
Future Directions: Develop more detailed land‐use intensity classification; downscale global IAMs; refine national IAMs; incorporate finer resolution remote sensing data
Scalability: Applicable to other countries given available national IAM and land system data
Novelty: Integration of a Chinese national IAM (Threshold21‐China) with CLUMondo; incorporation of land‐use intensity, vegetation types, and soil types into carbon density coefficients for TECS estimation

Title: Land Use Changes and Future Land Use Scenario Simulations of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor under the Belt and Road Initiative
Authors: Deng, Yuanjie; Chen, Hang; Hai, Yifeng
Country: China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (encompassing Kashgar region, China, and entire Pakistan including Pakistani-administered Kashmir)
Objective: Analyze spatial–temporal land use changes in the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) from 2000 to 2020 and simulate future land use patterns in 2040 under four scenarios using a coupled Markov–FLUS model
LULC Classes: Farmland; forest land; grassland; water body; urban land; unutilized land
Scenarios: Natural development; investment priority; ecological protection; harmonious development
Analysis Methods: GIS spatial–temporal analysis; land use dynamic degree; land use transfer matrix; Sankey diagram; Markov chain forecasting; FLUS (Future Land Use Simulation) model integrating ANN–neighborhood effect–inertia coefficients–conversion cost
Sim. Method Advantages: Integrates human and natural drivers; Supports multi-scenario simulation; High predictive accuracy (Kappa = 0.88, overall accuracy = 0.889); Applicable at regional scale of CPEC
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; Markov model; FLUS model (ANN-based); GIS software for preprocessing; Google Earth Engine; GIS spatial analysis tools
Predictors: Elevation; slope; slope direction; temperature; precipitation; GDP (night-time lights); population distribution; road network proximity
Data Sources: Land use (ESA CCI 2000–2020); Population distribution (WorldPop 2015–2020); GDP proxy (NPP-VIIRS night lights via Google Earth Engine 2015–2020); Constructions, roads, rivers (OpenStreetMap 2020); DEM, slope, aspect (SRTM 2020); Soil pH, sediment, organic carbon (HWSD 2020); Temperature, precipitation (NOAA NCDC 2015–2020)
Validation Methods: Confusion matrix; Kappa coefficient; overall accuracy by comparing simulated 2020 map with actual 2020 land use
Validation Data Sources: Observed land use maps for 2010 and 2015 used to forecast 2020 and validate against actual 2020 data
Key Findings: Urban land, forest land, and grassland increased (2000–2020) while farmland, unutilized land, and water bodies decreased; Unutilized land most frequently converted to grassland; FLUS model achieved high simulation accuracy (Kappa = 0.88); Harmonious development scenario best balances infrastructure, economic growth, and ecological protection
Implications: Provides scientific basis for land planning and policy in CPEC; informs trade-offs between urbanization, agriculture, and ecological conservation; supports sustainable development under Belt and Road Initiative
Limitations: Lacks in-depth analysis of driving mechanisms; Top-down macro focus without micro decision-making behavior; Does not explicitly incorporate extreme climate events in simulations
Future Directions: Integrate system dynamics for feedback mechanisms; Introduce agent-based models to capture stakeholder behaviors; Incorporate climate scenarios (e.g., CMIP) and extreme weather impacts
Scalability: Demonstrated applicability in CPEC; model framework transferable to other Central Asian or Belt and Road regions with similar data inputs
Novelty: First application of FLUS multi-scenario simulation specifically to the CPEC region; coupling of Markov chain forecasting with FLUS for integrated human–natural driver modeling

Title: Mapping the future afforestation distribution of China constrained by a national afforestation plan and climate change
Authors: Song, Shuaifeng; Zhang, Xuezhen; Yan, Xiaodong
Objective: Map future afforestation distribution in China by integrating a national afforestation plan and climate-driven suitability
LULC Classes: IGBP 17-class scheme including evergreen needleleaf forests; evergreen broadleaf forests; deciduous needleleaf forests; deciduous broadleaf forests; mixed forests; woodland savannas; savannas; grasslands; croplands; urban; wetlands; water bodies; barren; snow/ice; shrublands; woody savannas; open shrublands
Analysis Methods: Dynamical downscaling with WRF; bias correction of MPI-ESM1-2-HR via ERA5; Holdridge life zone model; grid-level allocation by HLZ value constrained by provincial afforestation quotas
Sim. Method Advantages: Physically based dynamical downscaling ensures physical consistency among variables and captures fine‐scale surface features, improving upon coarse GCM (~100–300 km) and overcoming statistical downscaling’s instability under novel climates
Tools/Soft Used: WRF v4.2; Holdridge life zone classification; bias-correction algorithms; MATLAB for data processing
Predictors: Annual average biotemperature; annual total precipitation; potential evapotranspiration ratio; land cover class
Data Sources: CN05.1 ground meteorology; MODIS MCD12Q1 land cover; National Forest Management Planning (2016–2050) afforestation targets; bias-corrected MPI-ESM1-2-HR climate projections; ERA5 reanalysis; Chinese vegetation regionalization map
Validation Methods: Comparison of WRF outputs (HIS_ERA vs. HIS_MPI) against CN05.1 observations; scatterplots of AT, TP, PE; spatial correlation, bias, MAE; kappa statistic for PVD maps
Validation Data Sources: CN05.1 temperature and precipitation; MODIS land cover (for PVD comparison)
Key Findings: Future potential forestation domain (PFD) increases by 3.49% (~17.5×10⁴ km²); Largest vegetation shift: warm temperate to subtropical forests (~30.6×10⁴ km²); Future afforestation (~73.64×10⁴ km²) prioritized east of Hu Line; Dominant land conversions: grassland→deciduous broadleaf in north (40%), savannas→evergreen broadleaf in southwest (42%)
Implications: Provides grid-level dataset for assessing carbon, ecosystem services, water resources, and climate impacts; Guides strategic afforestation planning under climate change and policy constraints
Limitations: Single GCM driving WRF limits uncertainty quantification; precipitation biases in WRF; coarse 25 km resolution in complex terrain; omission of socioeconomic, soil, and governance factors
Future Directions: Use multi-model CMIP6 ensembles for downscaling; explore other SSPs; incorporate socioeconomic, soil, and policy variables; apply convection-permitting modeling or high-resolution statistical downscaling
Scalability: Method transferable for gridded afforestation planning in other countries with suitable data
Novelty: First integration of national-level afforestation quotas with future climate-driven suitability at 25 km resolution; use of bias-corrected dynamical downscaling combined with Holdridge model for allocation pacing

Title: Projections of future spatiotemporal urban 3D expansion in China under shared socioeconomic pathways
Authors: Wang, Kechao; He, Tingting; Xiao, Wu; Yang, Runjia
Objective: Integrate urban building height predictions with horizontal sprawl projections to forecast China’s three-dimensional urban expansion under five Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs)
LULC Classes: Construction land; non-construction land
Scenarios: SSP1; SSP2; SSP3; SSP4; SSP5
Analysis Methods: Regression model (panel data linear regression for building volume demand); Cellular Automata with ANN (conversion probability); Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) for building height prediction; Evolutionary algorithm (elite selection) for spatiotemporal simulation
Sim. Method Advantages: Combines top-down macro constraints (SSP-based volume demand) with bottom-up spatial processes; Includes vertical growth (height) not just horizontal sprawl; High spatial granularity (1 km resolution) and temporal continuity (10-year steps)
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Per capita GDP; urbanization rate (for volume demand); Seven spatial variables for CNN (e.g., gridded GDP, population density, distance to roads, proximity to urban land, provincial capital location, water bodies, elevation-derived slope/aspect excluded due to collinearity)
Data Sources: National Bureau of Statistics (historic GDP, population, urban rate 1990–2010); SSP database (projected GDP, population, urban rate 2010–2100); Global 30 m spatiotemporal 3D urban expansion dataset (He et al., 2023); CNBH-10 m building height dataset (Wu et al., 2023); NASADEM (terrain); RESDC (provincial capitals); National Earth System Science Data Center (water bodies); GRIP dataset (roads)
Validation Methods: Comparison of predicted building heights (2010–2020) with reference CNBH-10 m dataset; Scatterplots and R² metrics in Zhejiang, Beijing, Guangdong, and nationwide
Validation Data Sources: CNBH-10 m dataset (Wu et al., 2023)
Key Findings: China’s building volume demand peaks 2040–2050 at ~4500–6500 km³, then declines to ~60% by 2100; Conversion probability high east of Heihe-Tengchong line, corridor-style and neighborhood expansion patterns; CNN effectively predicts building heights (national R² = 0.664, regional up to 0.814); Future spatiotemporal 3D expansion shows intensified density in eastern clusters and new settlements in south/southwest; Volume Building Density (VBD) exhibits east-west gradient, exponential growth in volume 2010–2050
Implications: Need for incremental and stock-focused urban planning to address post-2050 contraction and avoid “ghost cities”; Policy differentiation under stagnation (SSP3) vs. aggressive expansion (SSP5) scenarios, emphasizing regional cooperation, green innovation, and sprawl control
Limitations: Panel regression limited to GDP and urbanization rate, excludes technological, policy, environmental factors; Assumes spatial drivers and model parameters constant over century; Relies on accuracy of SSP database projections
Future Directions: Integrate time-series models (RNN, LSTM) to capture dynamic predictors; Validate at finer resolution and extend to global contexts
Scalability: Applicable to other regions with appropriate socio-economic and spatial data inputs
Novelty: First large-scale 3D urban expansion projection combining horizontal sprawl and building height under SSPs; Fine spatial (1 km) and temporal (decadal) resolution over 2010–2100

Title: Spatio-temporal evolution, driving mechanisms, and simulation of land use and cover in China from 2000 to 2060
Authors: Chen, Jiandong; Liu, Miaomiao; Chen, Xingyu; Li, Zhiwen
Objective: Investigate the spatio-temporal evolution of land use and cover in China from 2000 to 2060, analyze driving mechanisms, and simulate future scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest; Grassland; Water; Built-up land; Unused land
Scenarios: Baseline; Cropland protection; Green development
Analysis Methods: Patch-generated Land Use Simulation (PLUS) model (LEAS + CARS); Markov chains; Random Forest Classifier; ArcGIS spatial analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Fully reflects and quantifies contributions of driving factors; accurately identifies multi-temporal and diverse land patches; simulates multiple land types under different policy scenarios; outperforms FLUS in accuracy
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; PLUS model; Random Forest Classifier; Markov chain analysis
Predictors: Elevation; Slope; Aspect; Precipitation; Temperature; GDP; Population density; Euclidean distance to county-level cities; Distance to roads; Distance to railways
Data Sources: Resource and Environment Science and Data Center (land, GDP, population density); National Data Center for Science (Qinghai-Tibet Plateau climate); National Center for Basic Geographic Information (roads); ASTER GDEM V3 (DEM); government administrative data
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient; Overall accuracy (OA); Figure of Merit (FOM); bootstrap significance testing; comparison with FLUS model
Validation Data Sources: Observed land‐cover data for 2000, 2010, and 2020 from Resource and Environment Science and Data Center
Key Findings: Forest and grassland dominated land cover but experienced significant change (especially 2000–2010); cropland steadily decreased while forest, water, and built-up areas expanded; socioeconomic factors (GDP, population) were primary drivers; under baseline scenario cropland and unused land increase while forest and grassland decrease; cropland protection scenario shifts built-up expansion toward grassland; green development scenario preserves forest/grass but leads to cropland degradation
Implications: Need to maintain cropland protection and ecological restoration policies; tailor land-use planning to local driving factors; balance agricultural production with ecological preservation; control built-up land scale and promote redevelopment of idle urban land
Limitations: Long-term simulation accuracy may decline due to uncertainties; model resolution limited to 1000 m; static driving factors from 2000–2020 may reduce prediction accuracy
Future Directions: Introduce additional models for higher-resolution simulation; incorporate dynamic changes in driving factors for more accurate long-term projections
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First national-scale, multi-scenario PLUS model simulation analyzing multiple land types with quantified driving mechanisms under diverse policy scenarios.

Title: Spatiotemporal variations of non-farming use of cropland in China under different SSP-RCP scenarios
Authors: Linghu, Linna; Sun, Peijun; Zhang, Meng; Sun, Zhangli; Wu, Yue
Objective: Project spatiotemporal variations of non-farming use of cropland in China under different SSP-RCP scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forestland; Grassland; Construction land; Unused land; Water area
Scenarios: SSP126; SSP245; SSP585
Analysis Methods: Ensembled strategy based on Majority Voting; Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) model; System Dynamics (SD) model; center of gravity analysis; spatial autocorrelation; dynamic degree; transfer matrix
Sim. Method Advantages: Mitigates uncertainty and reduces errors inherent in individual models through ensemble majority voting
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS 10.5; Vensim PLE ×64; FLUS; ANN within FLUS; Interactive Digital Language v8.5; Python (for calibration formulas)
Predictors: Population; GDP; fixed assets investment in agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry; annual mean temperature; driving factors (socioeconomic and natural)
Data Sources: Primary: GLC30 (2000, 2010, 2020), LUH2, GCAM LU products, China Statistical Yearbook (2000–2020), SSP database, CMIP6 climate models, future grid population under SSPs; Secondary: Protected areas, future urban land expansion datasets, “Added tree cover” correction data
Validation Methods: Overall accuracy; Kappa coefficient; Figure-of-Merit (FoM); correlation coefficients (Pearson; Spearman)
Validation Data Sources: Observed GLC30 2020 land use map; LUH2 products
Key Findings: Cropland area increases by 51,088 km² under SSP126, decreases by 113,642 km² under SSP245, and by 48,699 km² under SSP585; NFUC shows fluctuating uptrend under SSP126, continuous uptrend under SSP245 & SSP585
Implications: Need proactive cultivated land protection, balance ecological restoration with food security; Adopt sustainable SSP126 pathway, implement stricter land-transfer regulations; Enhance agricultural innovation and targeted machinery for complex terrains
Limitations: Limited SSP-RCP combinations; divergent IAM outputs causing LU demand uncertainty; classification system inconsistencies across data sources
Future Directions: Expand to additional SSP-RCP combinations; adopt unified modeling frameworks; refine classification harmonization; analyze agricultural land occupation decoupling
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integrated ensemble majority voting of three LU demand models (SD, LUH2, GCAM) in FLUS to enhance projection accuracy and reliability

Title: Substantial increase in future land exposure to compound droughts and heatwaves in China dominated by climate change
Authors: Liu, Taizheng; Zhang, Yuqing; Guo, Bin; Zhang, Shuming; Li, Xin
Objective: Explore changes in cropland, forest, grassland, urban, and bare land exposure to compound droughts and heatwaves (CDH) frequency and magnitude in China under multiple emission scenarios in the far-future (2070–2099)
LULC Classes: Cropland; forest; grassland; urban; bare land
Analysis Methods: CMIP6 multi-model ensemble; LUH2 land-use data; 1-month SPEI for drought; 95th percentile Tmax heatwave detection; normalization to CDH magnitude index; bilinear interpolation to 0.5° grid; land exposure calculation (km²-events, km²-CDHMI); decomposition of exposure change into climate, land-area, and joint effects
Sim. Method Advantages: CMIP6 provides more reliable simulation of climate extremes and future projections than CMIP5
Tools/Soft Used: Not specified
Predictors: Not specified
Data Sources: CN05.1 gridded precipitation and temperature observations; 12 CMIP6 model outputs; LUH2 land-use harmonization data
Validation Methods: Taylor diagrams comparing model outputs with CN05.1 observations (correlation coefficients, normalized standard deviation)
Validation Data Sources: CN05.1 gridded dataset
Key Findings: CDH frequency increases by 151.30%–515.48% and magnitude by 102.00%–386.81% under scenarios; Cropland, forest, grassland, urban, and bare land exposures to CDH events all rise sharply, especially under SSP5-8.5; Climate change effect drives >50% of exposure changes (up to 74%–92% under SSP5-8.5), joint effects dominate urban exposure changes; Regional hotspots of exposure increase in Northwestern and Southern China
Implications: Urgent need for emission mitigation and adaptation policies; strengthen agricultural risk management (irrigation upgrades, heat- and drought-tolerant crops, insurance); region-specific resilience strategies
Limitations: Use of Thornthwaite method may misestimate evapotranspiration; reliance on model simulations with inter-model uncertainties; MME underestimation of observed CDH metrics
Future Directions: Incorporate Penman-Monteith evapotranspiration; apply bias correction to model data; refine risk assessments with improved observational constraints
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: First comprehensive assessment of CDH exposure across five land-use types in China under multiple CMIP6 scenarios

Title: Understanding Japan's Land-use Dynamics between 1987 and 2050 using Land Accounting and Scenario Analysis
Authors: Huang, Wanhui; Hashimoto, Shizuka; Yoshida, Takehito; Saito, Osamu; Meraj, Gowhar
Objective: Assess historical patterns and project future shifts in land use dynamics from 1987 to 2050 across Japan using high-resolution land use and land cover datasets, land change simulations, and land accounting
LULC Classes: Residential land; paddy fields; croplands; other agricultural land; abandoned farmland; grassland; natural forest; secondary forest; plantation forest; other land uses
Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BaU)
Analysis Methods: Land accounting (stock and flow); scenario analysis

Predictors: Distance to each land use category (log-transformed); Density of each land use category (100 m radius); Elevation; slope

Title: Unearthing Agricultural Land Use Dynamics in Indonesia: Between Food Security and Policy Interventions
Authors: Faoziyah, Uly; Rosyaridho, Muhammad Faruk; Panggabean, Romauli

Title: A nature-inclusive future with healthy soils? Mapping soil organic matter in 2050 in the Netherlands
Authors: Helfenstein, Anatol; Mulder, Vera L.; Hack-ten Broeke, Mirjam J. D.; Breman, Bas C.
Objective: explore whether a nature-inclusive scenario for 2050 is conducive to enhancing soil organic matter (SOM)-related soil health

Scenarios: nature-inclusive scenario
Analysis Methods: digital soil mapping; quantile regression forest; 3D + T space-time modelling
Sim. Method Advantages: higher spatial prediction accuracy than mechanistic soil carbon models
Tools/Soft Used: quantile regression forest implementation; 3D + T soil mapping platform
Predictors: static covariates (climate, topography, parent material); dynamic covariates (land use; peat classes; peat occurrence)
Data Sources: soil point data (869 094 SOM observations from 339 231 locations); national soil map (De Vries et al., 2003, updated 2021); land use maps (Hazeu et al., 2023, Breman et al., 2022); peatscape data (Delft & Maas, 2022)

Key Findings: SOM decreases (> 1%) on 22% of land, increases (> 1%) on 14% under nature-inclusive scenario; up to 25% SOM increase in rewetted peatlands (0–40 cm); up to 5% SOM decrease in grasslands converted to cropland; major SOM losses in non-rewetted deep peat (> 25% in reclaimed land subsoils)

Limitations: static climate covariates; oversimplified land use classes and management practices; peat growth rate and rewetting assumptions; inability to quantify ΔSOM uncertainty
Future Directions: incorporate dynamic climate covariates; include agroecological management practices; develop geostatistical methods to quantify ΔSOM uncertainty; field monitoring for practice effectiveness
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: first application of 3D + T digital soil mapping to simulate a future national-scale SOM scenario

Title: A novel flood risk management approach based on future climate and land use change scenarios
Authors: Nguyen, Huu Duy; Nguyen, Quoc-Huy; Dang, Dinh Kha; Van, Chien Pham; Truong, Quang Hai; Pham, Si Dung; Bui, Quang-Thanh; Petrisor, Alexandru-Ionut

Analysis Methods: Machine learning (XGBoost; CatBoost; LightGBM; ExtraTree) for flood susceptibility; Hydrodynamic modeling (MIKE Flood integrating MIKE 11 & MIKE 21); Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP) to weight hazard, exposure, vulnerability
Sim. Method Advantages: Integration of 1D (river network) and 2D (floodplain) hydrodynamic modeling for higher accuracy and flexibility; ability to model overflow links and GIS integration surpassing standalone MIKE 11 or MIKE 21
Tools/Soft Used: MIKE Flood (MIKE 11, MIKE 21, NAM); ArcGIS 10.6; Google Earth Engine; IDRISI; R (for CA-Markov); Python-based ML frameworks (implied)
Predictors: Elevation; Curvature; Aspect; Slope; Distance to road; Distance to river; LULC; Rainfall; Topographic Wetness Index; Soil type; NDVI; NDBI; NDWI; Sediment Transport Index; Flow Direction
