Validation Methods: Hydrodynamic: Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency, water-level peak error; Machine learning: AUC, RMSE, MAE, R², ROC curves
Validation Data Sources: Observed water levels at Le Thuy and downstream stations; 30% hold-out flood inventory points
Key Findings: High/very high flood hazard areas increase by ~200 km² from 2005 to 2050; Very high flood risk zones grow from 2.3 km² (2005) to 83.5 km² (2050); Urban expansion and population growth concentrate in high-risk zones
Implications: Need integrated flood risk management combining structural and nature-based solutions; Spatial planning must account for future climate and LULC changes
Limitations: Poverty data for 2005 approximated by 2015 rates; 2005 flood hazard modeled using 2010 event; Dikes/dams not explicitly incorporated; CA-Markov assumed homogeneous urban expansion
Future Directions: Evaluate multiple climate/LULC scenarios (beyond RCP8.5); Incorporate CMIP6 ScenarioMIP projections; Integrate future infrastructure (dikes/dams) effects
Scalability: Easily adjustable to other regions with different climate and land-use scenarios; all models freely available
Novelty: First integration of ensemble ML flood-susceptibility with linked 1D–2D hydrodynamic modeling under future climate/LULC scenarios; Use of AHP to combine susceptibility, depth, velocity into hazard index

Title: Amazonian vegetation types and indigenous lands threatened by upcoming climate change: Forecast impact for Brazilian biomes
Authors: Arruda, Daniel M.; Schaefer, Carlos E. G. R.; Fonseca, Rubia S.; Fernandes-Filho, Elpidio I.; Veloso, Gustavo V.; Gomes, Lucas C.; Oliveira, Fabio S.; Correa, Guilherme R.; Espirito-Santo, Mario M.; Oliveira, Guilherme C.; Solar, Ricardo R. C.

Future Directions: Integrate deforestation and land‐use feedback loops into dynamic models; Model pedogenesis to refine soil predictors over longer timescales
Scalability: Method transferable to other continental‐scale regions with climate and soil data availability
Novelty: First continental‐scale biome modeling in Brazil combining high-resolution soil and climate predictors; Use of soil layer as a “brake” on GCM variability to improve ecotone predictions

Title: An Optimization Strategy for Provincial “Production-Living-Ecological” Spaces under the Guidance of Major Function-Oriented Zoning in China

Scalability: Methodology applicable to other provinces or regions with similar zonation frameworks (requires local functional zoning data)

Title: Assessment of Carbon Storage in a Multifunctional Landscape: A Case Study of Central Asia
Authors: Dong, Xinyue; Cao, Zeyu; Guo, Yi; Lin, Jingyuan; Yan, Hanze; Li, Mengyu; Yao, Peng

Title: Availability of the current and future water resources in Central Africa, case of the large Sanaga catchment in Cameroon

Title: Balancing urbanization, agricultural production and ecological integrity: A cross-scale landscape functional and structural approach in China
Authors: Wang, Yafei; He, Yao; Fan, Jie; Olsson, Lennart; Scown, Murray

Method Advantages: Integrates top-down (national strategic targets) and bottom-up (local suitability) constraints; Captures cross-scale interactions among national, provincial, and sub-regional levels; Adapts driving factors dynamically via adaptive cellular automata, improving robustness over single-scale or purely trend-based methods

Data Sources: Primary:; CLCD Landsat‐based annual land-cover (1990–2020); DEM, precipitation, temperature, water resources, environmental monitoring, disaster survey, ecological monitoring (CAS ResDC); Secondary:; Statistical yearbooks, government planning documents (Major Functional Zoning, Territory Spatial Planning); SSP population, GDP, urbanization projections

Title: Coupling analysis of land use change with landscape ecological risk in China: A multi-scenario simulation perspective
Authors: Zeng, Jie; Wu, Jianhua; Chen, Wanxu

Title: Evaluating and simulating the impacts of land use patterns on carbon emissions in coal resource-based regions: A case study of shanxi province, China

Data Sources: GlobeLand30 LULC data; ResDC socioeconomic/environmental data (temperature, precipitation, GDP density, population density, nighttime light); GSCloud DEM and soil; webmap.cn residential distance; road network from webmap.cn
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient comparison of simulated 2020 LULC vs actual (Kappa = 0.840)
Validation Data Sources: Actual 2020 GlobeLand30 LULC dataset
Key Findings: Cropland decreased by 4.85 × 10^5 ha (2000–2020) while construction land increased by 4.38 × 10^5 ha, mainly at cropland expense; Net carbon emissions rose from 3.17 × 10^7 t (2000) to 6.38 × 10^7 t (2020), spatially higher in west/south; In 2030 BAUs, highest total CE, EEBs yield stronger decoupling of land use mix and CE; Decoupling state shifted from expansionary negative decoupling to weak/strong decoupling under optimized scenarios
Implications: Inform land-use policy to balance economic development with carbon peaking; EEB scenario suited for sustainable land allocation in coal resource regions
Limitations: Uncertainty in future economic benefit predictions (GM(1,1), smoothing, regression); Ecosystem service value equivalence uncertainties due to data gaps; Indirect carbon emission estimation for construction land omitted some energy types
Future Directions: Refine economic benefit prediction methods; Improve spatially explicit ESV assessments; Develop more comprehensive CE calculation for construction land
Scalability: Provides theoretical framework and case study applicable to other coal resource–based regions
Novelty: Integrates PLUS patch-generating simulation with multi-objective planning (MOP) and decoupling analysis to assess land-use pattern impacts on carbon emissions under multiple scenarios.

Title: Evaluating future flood risk mitigation capacities in major cities across China
Authors: Dai, Kaixuan; Cheng, Changxiu; Shen, Shi; Geng, Jiachen; Zhang, Tianyuan
Objective: Evaluate future urban flood risk mitigation capacity changes under urban expansion and climate change scenarios
LULC Classes: Cropland; Forest; Grass; Water; Urban; Unused land
Scenarios: SSP126; SSP245; SSP585
Analysis Methods: Urban expansion simulation using FUTURES model; Precipitation projection via RegCM4.6 downscaled GFDL-ESM2M; Urban Flood Risk Mitigation (UFRM) evaluation via SCS-CN model
Sim. Method Advantages: High-resolution (30 m) spatial allocation; Couples observed urban growth demand (LUH) with fine-scale LULC patterns; Stratified sampling and multilevel logistic regression optimize potential estimation over purely cellular automata
Tools/Soft Used: FUTURES model; RegCM4.6; USDA SCS-CN method; multilevel logistic regression
Predictors: DEM; Climate data; GDP distribution; Night light; Road networks; Point of Interest data
Data Sources: Primary: RESDC 30 m LULC (1990–2015), LUH 0.25° LULC (2015–2050), CN05.1 precipitation dataset, RegCM4.6 projections, Oak Ridge soil group map; Secondary: DEM, GDP, night lights, roads, POI
Validation Methods: Calibration to 2015 LULC; Kappa coefficient
Validation Data Sources: RESDC 2015 land use map
Key Findings: City sizes expand ~30% by 2050, primarily in north and east China; Precipitation intensity +0.4% (SSP126), –5.4% (SSP245), –2.3% (SSP585); UFRM decreases 2.7% (SSP126), 2.1% (SSP585), increases 0.2% (SSP245)
Implications: Inform targeted “Sponge City” and NbS strategies; Promote LID in rapidly expanding regions; Prioritize urban renewal and green infrastructure in areas with declining UFRM
Limitations: Difficulty isolating quantitative contributions of urbanization vs. precipitation; Simplified secondary effects of urbanization on climate (e.g., urban heat island)
Future Directions: Apply spatiotemporal statistical methods to isolate factor contributions; Integrate urban climate projections mechanistically with expansion models; Use multiple GCM ensembles for precipitation projections
Scalability: Method framework applicable to other major cities/regions with available LULC and climate projection data
Novelty: First nationwide quantification of future urban flood mitigation capacity evolution under combined urban expansion and climate scenarios; Coupling of high-resolution FUTURES simulation with UFRM SCS-CN evaluation in major Chinese cities

Title: Evaluating the impact of various driving factors on future water supply and demands
Authors: Wang, Hongxiang; Yuan, Weiqi; Ma, Yajuan; Ye, Handong; Li, Yanhua; Bai, Xiangyu; Cheng, Siyuan; Guo, Wenxian
Journal: JOURNAL OF WATER AND CLIMATE CHANGE
Objective: Analyze temporal characteristics of climate and land use/land cover (LULC) from 2000 to 2020; predict spatiotemporal changes in LULC in the Han River Basin under future scenarios; assess water supply–demand evolution and quantify the water security index; explore quantitative attribution of social-natural factors to water provisioning services
LULC Classes: Cropland; forest land; grassland; construction land; water bodies; barren land; six primary types and 25 secondary types
Scenarios: Natural Increase Scenario (NIS); Economic Development Scenario (EDS); Ecological Protection Scenario (EPS)
Analysis Methods: PLUS model; InVEST model; geographic detector; Markov chain; material quality assessment; FDM (geographical detector interaction module)
Sim. Method Advantages: Multi-class random patch seeding simulates patch-level LULC changes; better depicts multi-type land patch evolution; supports multi-scenario policy constraints compared to traditional CA models (e.g., CA-Markov, FLUS)
Tools/Soft Used: PLUS model; InVEST model; ArcGIS 10.7
Predictors: Precipitation; potential evapotranspiration; DEM; slope (gradient); soil erosion; population; GDP; distances to rivers, roads (national, provincial, rural, primary, motorways); distance to county government; distance to railway
Data Sources: Primary: Resource and Environmental Science Data Center of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (LULC), China Meteorological Data Service Centre (meteorological), Yangtze River Basin and Southwest Rivers Water Resources Bulletin (water use); Secondary: National Geographic Information Resources Catalog Service System (vector boundaries), statistical yearbooks for GDP, population
Validation Methods: Calibration of InVEST Z parameter; comparison of simulated water yield with reported water resources; relative error assessment
Validation Data Sources: Yangtze River Basin and Southwest Rivers Water Resources Bulletin (2010 actual water resources)
Key Findings: Precipitation increased slowly, potential evapotranspiration decreased slightly (2000–2020); Cropland decreased by 1.29%, forest and grassland increased, construction land expanded by 0.54%; Future LULC impact on water supply minor (0.17–0.45%), impact on water demand ~10%; WSI declined from 0.118 (2000) to 0.078 (2030 NIS), improves to 0.103 under EPS, lowest (0.068) under EDS; Precipitation, LULC, elevation are primary drivers of water yield, precipitation–LULC interaction contributes >90%
Implications: Inform LULC spatial planning and watershed management; balance ecological protection, agricultural needs, and economic growth; guide policy for sustainable water resource allocation
Limitations: Parameter selection bias in PLUS model based on literature; constant climate assumption for future scenarios; social policy impacts on water demand not modeled
Future Directions: Refine socio-economic factor composition and dynamics; incorporate future climate scenario impacts; model multifactor water demand services
Scalability: Not specified
Novelty: Integration of PLUS and InVEST models with geographic detector for future WSI analysis; multi-scenario LULC prediction with policy constraints; quantitative attribution of social-natural interactions on water provisioning services

Title: Forecast urban ecosystem services to track climate change: Combining machine learning and emergy spatial analysis
Authors: Liu, Gengyuan; Meng, Fanxin; Huang, Xiaoxiao; Han, Yang; Chen, Yu; Huo, Zhaoman; Chiaka, Jeffrey Chiwuikem; Yang, Qing
Objective: Use LSTM to simulate future precipitation and combine land use change projection with emergy spatial analysis to predict urban ecosystem services dynamics

Scenarios: SSP1-RCP2.6; SSP5-RCP8.5
Analysis Methods: emergy spatial analysis; machine learning (LSTM); distributed land-use change prediction (DLUCP) model (distributed system dynamics; distributed cellular automaton); emergy-based ES accounting
Sim. Method Advantages: ML processes high-dimensional data and identifies non-linear trends automatically; LSTM captures long-term dependencies in time-series data and improves efficiency over manual spreadsheets
Tools/Soft Used: Python; MySQL; ArcGIS; MATLAB LSTM package; PyTorch-based LSTM
Predictors: precipitation; land use area; solar energy; thermal energy; tidal energy; wind energy; rain chemical potential energy; runoff geopotential energy; runoff chemical potential energy; socioeconomic factors; spatial heterogeneity of government planning; land use suitability; neighborhood effects; cost of change; localization factors

Scalability: Not specified

Title: Future urban ecological land transition and its implications for high-heat exposure in China
Authors: Feng, Rundong; Liu, Shenghe; Wang, Fuyuan; Wang, Kaiyong; Zhengchen, Rouyu; Wang, Disheng
Objective: Quantify impacts of future urban ecological land (UEL) transitions on high-heat exposure (HHE) in Chinese cities
LULC Classes: Forest; grassland; shrub; cropland; water; construction land; barren; ice
Analysis Methods: Population-weighted exposure modeling; Pearson and partial correlation; ordinary least squares multiple linear regression; random forest; paired t-test; Mann–Kendall trend; Theil–Sen slope estimation
Sim. Method Advantages: High spatial resolution (30 m) captures detailed land-cover transitions; integrates SSP-RCP scenarios for long-term projections; outperforms prior 1 km products in Figure of Merit
Tools/Soft Used: FLUS model; GCAM; Fragstats; random forest (scikit-learn or equivalent)
Predictors: Latitude; mean temperature; construction land ratio; UEL coverage rate (CR); landscape evolution index (LEI)
Data Sources: GLC_FCS30; Landsat surface reflectance; China 1 km monthly temperature; WorldClim CMIP6 projections; WorldPop; SSP population forecasts
Validation Methods: Figure of Merit for land-cover simulation; accuracy metrics (overall accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score) for vegetation classification; correlation analysis between temperature datasets
Validation Data Sources: Observed 2020 land cover; multi-temporal training samples; 17 675 validation samples; overlapping period temperature comparison (China dataset vs. WorldClim)
Key Findings: Infilling expansion dominates UEL under SSP1-2.6, enclosing shrinkage under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5; UEL transitions influence 0.12–0.26 °C of HHE and dominate HHE in 10.2–22.8% of cities (95.1–181.2 million people); LEI more influential than area, patterns differ between urban cores and expansion surfaces
Implications: Prioritize optimizing UEL landscape pattern (connectivity, infilling) over simply increasing area; tailor urban greening strategies by region and urbanization stage; follow sustainable SSP1-2.6/SSP2-4.5 pathways
Limitations: UEL component–specific cooling effects not differentiated; HHE model does not capture individual-level interactions; static driving factors and transition rules in FLUS; no policy constraints considered
Future Directions: Incorporate anthropogenic/policy elements into FLUS; explore synergistic cooling among UEL types; integrate demographic attributes for exposure equity; compare across city types and regions
Scalability: Dataset and framework adaptable to other regions with available high-resolution land-cover and climate projections
Novelty: Development of 30 m, SSP-RCP–based future urban land dataset for China; integration of landscape evolution patterns (LEI) into HHE analysis; differentiation between urban core and expansion surface impacts

Title: Historical Changes and Multi-scenario Prediction of Land Use and Terrestrial Ecosystem Carbon Storage in China
Authors: An, Yue; Tan, Xuelan; Ren, Hui; Li, Yinqi; Zhou, Zhou

Analysis Methods: Future Land Use Simulation (FLUS) model; Markov model; inverse distance weighted interpolation for carbon density; scenario setting under SSPs-RCPs and PCS
Sim. Method Advantages: Robust simulation capability evidenced by high Kappa (0.92), FOM (0.68), and overall accuracy (0.94); Chunked parallel computing for efficiency; Integration of socioeconomic, natural, and climatic factors improves realism
Tools/Soft Used: FLUS model; backpropagation neural network algorithm; IDW interpolation; Markov model
Predictors: Elevation; Soil conditions; Climate variables; Population; GDP; Road network; Neighbourhood effects; Inertia coefficient; Policy control inputs
Data Sources: Primary: China Land Cover Dataset (CLCD) Wuhan University; LUH2 dataset; WCRP-CMIP6 climate scenarios; Harmonized World Soil Database; Resources and Environmental Sciences and Data Center of Chinese Academy of Sciences; National Geographic Information Resources; Ministry of Natural Resources; National Science and Technology Infrastructure platform for carbon density
Validation Methods: Kappa coefficient; Figure of Merit (FOM); Overall accuracy (OA)
Validation Data Sources: Historical land-use maps from CLCD (1990–2020) used as training and validation data
Key Findings: From 1990 to 2020, cropland and grassland proportions declined by 0.93% and 1.08% respectively, while forest and impervious surfaces increased; Total carbon storage peaked at 102.85×10¹² kg in 2005, then declined by 0.53×10¹² kg by 2020; Under PCS, carbon storage continues a modest decline (0.83×10¹² kg by 2060); Under SSPs-RCPs, pronounced losses occur—up to 8.07×10¹² kg in SSP4-RCP3.4—driven by urbanisation and forest/grassland conversion
Implications: Protect forests and grasslands; stabilise cropland; improve urban land-use intensity; delineate ecological red lines to mitigate carbon loss and support dual-carbon targets

Scalability: Not specified

Title: How much carbon storage will loss in a desertification area? Multiple policy scenario analysis from Gansu Province
Authors: Liu, Jiamin; Pei, Xiutong; Yu, Weijie; Nan, Jiangfan; Fang, Hongwei; Wang, Kaizhong; Jiao, Jizong
Objective: To delineate ecological red lines and simulate land use and carbon storage changes under multiple policy scenarios in a desertification-prone region

Validation Data Sources: GlobeLand30 land use 2020
Key Findings: Baseline scenario yields 1.62×10^7 t carbon loss (2000–2050); Ecological red line scenario reverses declining carbon trend, achieving 61.7% of global ecological scenario effect by 2050; Natural factors dominate in southeast, human factors dominate central region

Limitations: Uncertainties in land use conversion rules and carbon density coefficients; Reliance on interpolated statistical data; Static ecological red line delineation may require updates

Title: Implications of landscape changes for ecosystem services and biodiversity: A national assessment in Ecuador
Authors: Koo, Hongmi; Kleemann, Janina; Cuenca, Pablo; Noh, Jin Kyoung; Fuerst, Christine
Objective: Spatial assessment of ecosystem and land‐use capacities to provide biodiversity and ecosystem services (BES) under current conditions and future deforestation and climate change scenarios

Scenarios: deforestation; climate change RCP 2.6 (ΔT ≤ 2 °C); climate change RCP 6.0 (ΔT ≤ 4 °C)
Analysis Methods: Spatially explicit modeling (GISCAME) integrating GIS and Cellular Automaton modules; Expert‐based assessment matrix (Likert‐scale); Participatory surveys and workshops

Tools/Soft Used: GISCAME (GIS + CA); ArcGIS; expert elicitation; statistical processing in GIS
Predictors: slope; water balance (availability); SNAP protection status; elevation; population density; water supply > demand
Data Sources: MAATE ecosystem map (2012); MAATE land cover map (2018); National Statistics and Census Institute population density map (2018); SNAP map (2018); Water balance map (2019); RCP maps (2019) from MAATE; DEM (30 m, 2018) from Military Geographical Institute; Expert surveys and workshops
Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Deforestation scenario → BES ↓ 20–25%, food provision ↑ ~ 5% due to agricultural expansion; Agricultural area expands by 14.3% nationally, key forest types decline by 1–5%; RCP 6.0 scenario → slight decreases in most BES, food provision trade‐off ↑, impacts more visible than RCP 2.6; Páramo ecosystems deliver highest multi‐service and biodiversity capacities
Implications: Supports BES‐informed decision‐making and priority‐area planning; Recommends Páramo conservation incentives and alternative livelihoods (ecotourism, education); Framework can inform national BES monitoring and regional planning

Future Directions: Biome‐specific BES assessments and scenarios (degradation vs. conservation); Integrate remote sensing, field data, and Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs); Apply and adapt framework in other megadiverse countries (e.g., Peru)
Scalability: Applicable to other national or megadiverse regions; adaptable to biome‐level assessments
Novelty: First national‐scale, integrative BES assessment in Ecuador combining participatory expert knowledge with spatially explicit GIS–CA modeling for future scenario analysis.

Title: Machine learning-based surrogate modelling of a robust, sustainable development goal (SDG)-compliant land-use future for Australia at high spatial resolution
Authors: Khan, Md Shakil; Moallemi, Enayat A.; Thiruvady, Dhananjay; Nazari, Asef; Bryan, Brett A.
Objective: Develop a high-resolution machine learning surrogate model (ML-LUTO Spatial) to identify a robust, SDG-compliant land-use future for Australia
LULC Classes: Agriculture; Carbon Plantings; Environmental Plantings; Wheat (Biofuels); Wheat (Food, Biofuels); Wheat (Food, Bioenergy); Woody Perennials (Bioenergy); Woody Perennials (Biofuels)
Scenarios: 648 global/domestic LUTO scenarios; 252 SDG-compliant “pathways” within safe operating space
Analysis Methods: Process-based LUTO modelling; machine learning surrogate modelling; hyperparameter tuning (random/grid search); five-fold cross-validation; spatial overlay; uncertainty quantification (frequency, margin of victory, Shannon’s entropy)
Sim. Method Advantages: 50× faster than original LUTO (3 s vs. 2.5 min per projection); Runs on standard laptop without high-performance computing; Enables exploration of hundreds of scenarios and spatial uncertainty at 1.1 km resolution
Tools/Soft Used: Scikit-Learn (ANNs, CNN, RNN, GRU); Python; ML-LUTO Spatial surrogate; original LUTO model; high-performance computing (for baseline)
Predictors: Scenario settings (RCP; temperature increase; global outlook; population outlook; GDP; carbon price; commodity prices; bioenergy demand constraints; productivity growth; hurdle rate; capacity constraints); spatial data layers (yield; prices; costs; irrigation; emissions; biodiversity score; biomass/establishment rates; fire risk)
Data Sources: LUTO model inputs and outputs; spatial socioeconomic and climatic raster layers; scenario discovery results from Gao & Bryan (2017); supplementary tables
Validation Methods: Five-fold cross-validation across five random train/test splits; evaluation metrics (Accuracy; Precision; Recall; F1-Score; Figure of Merit; Specificity; Prevalence)
Validation Data Sources: Test subsets of LUTO output dataset (400 M rows per split)
Key Findings: MLP with batch normalization achieved highest accuracy (0.95) and balanced precision/recall (0.87); Surrogate model reproduced spatial land-use patterns with 95% accuracy
Implications: Accelerates land-use planning and policy analysis under deep uncertainty; Empowers rapid exploration of SDG scenarios without HPC; Supports evidence-based decision-making for sustainable land management
Limitations: Lower prediction skill for rare classes (Environmental Plantings, Wheat Biofuels) due to low prevalence; Surrogate inherits biases and uncertainties of original LUTO model; Extrapolation beyond training parameter ranges untested
Future Directions: Extend surrogate approach to other land-use models (MAgPIE, GLOBIOM) or regions; Test model performance outside experienced parameter space; Explore additional ML architectures and sensitivity analyses
Scalability: Yes; methods transferable to national/regional/global land-use models
Novelty: First high-resolution (1.1 km) ML surrogate replicating a complex process-based land-use model; Enables hundreds of SDG-compliant scenario projections on a standard laptop; Integrates spatial uncertainty quantification (frequency, margin, entropy) for robust land-use futures

Title: Mapping and assessing the future provision of lake ecosystem services in Lithuania
Authors: Inacio, Miguel; Baltranaite, Egle; Bogdzevic, Katazyna; Kalinauskas, Marius; Pinto, Luis Valenta; Barcelo, Damia; Pereira, Paulo
Objective: Map and assess the future supply of three lake ecosystem services—maintenance of nursery conditions, nutrient regulation, and recreation—under combined land use and climate change scenarios

Scenarios: A0 – Business as usual; A1 – Urbanisation; A2 – Land abandonment and afforestation; A3 – Agricultural intensification
Analysis Methods: Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA; Dunn post-hoc test; Spearman correlation; Principal Component Analysis with Varimax rotation; Moran’s I spatial autocorrelation; Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis
Sim. Method Advantages: Quantitative CA modelling via Dinamica EGO yields more robust and reliable spatially explicit results than qualitative expert-elicitation methods; incorporates Bayesian weights of evidence to preserve spatial patterning
Tools/Soft Used: Dinamica EGO; ArcGIS Pro; InVEST Habitat Quality model; JASP Software
Predictors: Socio-economic variables; Proximity variables (distance to primary/secondary/residential roads, motorways, railways); Environmental/climatic variables (mean annual precipitation, temperature); Land use regulation variables (protected areas)

Key Findings: A0 yields highest nursery ES supply; A1 yields lowest nutrient regulation ES; A2 yields highest recreation ES; eastern and northeastern regions show consistently high ES supply while central region shows low supply; PCA reveals nursery and recreation ES covary, nutrient regulation is distinct

Novelty: First integrated mapping and assessment of future lake ecosystem services in Lithuania under combined land use and climate scenarios using Dinamica EGO and spatial ES models

Title: Monitoring forest cover and land use change in the Congo Basin under IPCC climate change scenarios
Authors: Yuh, Yisa Ginath; N'Goran, Kouame Paul; Kross, Angela; Heurich, Marco; Matthews, H. Damon; Turner, Sarah E.

Objective: Generate accurate land cover maps for the Congo Basin (1990–2020) and project LULC to 2050 under socioeconomic, demographic, and IPCC climate scenarios
LULC Classes: Dense forest; woody savanna; grassland savanna; open savanna/bareland; cropland; built-up areas; wetland; water bodies
Analysis Methods: Random Forest classification; MLP-ANN; Markov chain; change detection via GIS geometry
Sim. Method Advantages: Ensemble of MLP-ANN & Markov chain captures nonlinear transition potentials and stochastic change dynamics better than single models
Tools/Soft Used: Google Earth Engine; TerrSet ILCM; ArcGIS; R; Excel
Predictors: Logging & forest clearing; distance to built-up areas; human population density; slope; elevation; precipitation; max/min temperature; wildland fires
Data Sources: Primary: Landsat 5/7/8 surface reflectance (GEE), NOAA DMSP-OLS night lights, MODIS fire, SRTM DEM, CMIP6 climate projections, WorldPop SSP projections, Tyukavina et al. socioeconomic maps, Potapov et al. built-up & cropland data; Secondary: FAO, MODIS global land cover, Hansen et al. global forest cover, Potapov et al. validation datasets
Validation Methods: Confusion/error matrix (OA, PA, UA); Pearson’s correlation with existing global LULC products; back-prediction validation of ILCM outputs
Validation Data Sources: MODIS global land cover; Hansen et al. Forest Cover; Potapov et al. built-up & cropland datasets
Key Findings: Dense forest loss: 8.5% (1990–2020); projected 3.7–4.0% more by 2050 (total ~12.3–12.6% loss); Woody savanna gain: +4.8% (1990–2020); projected +5.9% by 2050; Built-up expansion: +0.4→1.1% (1990–2020); projected +1.2–1.5% by 2050; Cropland expansion: +0.8→2.1% (1990–2020); projected +2.3–2.6% by 2050
Implications: Data support REDD+ planning; highlight urgent need for sustainable forest management, community tenure, afforestation, equitable benefit sharing, and rural socioeconomic support to curb deforestation and accommodate urban growth

Scalability: Applicable to other large tropical regions with available satellite and socioeconomic data, pending local validation
Novelty: First integration of RF, MLP-ANN, Markov chain for Congo Basin 30-year LULC mapping and IPCC-scenario projections; combined socioeconomic, demographic, biophysical, and climate change drivers in LULCC modeling

Title: Nature-based solutions still result in unfairness in carbon emissions
Authors: Yin, Yitong; Lin, Gang; Li, Xiuhong; Yang, Rongjin
Objective: Explore the carbon neutrality situation of 395 county-level cities under business-as-usual and nature-based solutions scenarios for 2060
LULC Classes: Cultivated land; Woodland; Grassland; Water area; Construction land; Unused land
Scenarios: BAU (Business-As-Usual) scenario; NbS (Nature-based Solutions) scenario
Analysis Methods: System dynamics (SD) model; Patch-level land use simulation (PLUS) model; InVEST carbon storage model; Spatial superposition analysis in ArcGIS
Sim. Method Advantages: Considers coupling of social-economic subsystems and land-use interactions; Integrates patch-level spatial dynamics for high-resolution land-use change
Tools/Soft Used: ArcGIS; SD model; PLUS model; InVEST; GIS spatial analysis
Predictors: Population; GDP; Water resources; Energy consumption; Current land use; DEM; Slope; Aspect; Topographic position index; Temperature; Precipitation; Distance to roads; Distance to water bodies; Distance to town centers; Distance to schools and hospitals; Ecological redline; Natural reserves
Data Sources: Ministry of Ecology and Environment; National Bureau of Statistics; Ministry of Water Resources; Ministry of Natural Resources; National Energy Administration; World Energy Outlook 2022/2060; Scientific Data Center of Chinese Academy of Sciences (DEM, climate, carbon density); InVEST China land-use dataset; PLUS DEM; National Geographic Science Data Center
Validation Methods: Model testing of LUCC simulation accuracy
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: Under NbS, China as a whole can achieve carbon neutrality by 2060 with surplus sinks, but 395 county-level cities still exhibit 90 Mt of net emissions and spatial hysteresis; NbS increases neutral cities from 128 to 152, reduces emissions by 54 Mt and increases sinks by 21 Mt; Spatial unfairness persists across six regions, with the northwestern region losing neutrality and the southeastern region showing lowest conversion to neutrality
Implications: Highlights need for region-specific integration of NbS with socio-economic planning, resource and land-use management; Informs targeted policy to address spatial unfairness in carbon neutrality at subnational scales
Limitations: Raster data unification may misclassify small units; SD model lacks coupling with biophysical climate processes; Uniform carbon density inputs ignore regional heterogeneity
Future Directions: Integrate dynamic climate–land surface process models; Incorporate additional adaptation measures in NbS scenarios; Develop finer-resolution carbon density data for county-level analyses

Title: Predictive modeling of regional carbon storage dynamics in response to land use/land cover changes: An InVEST-based analysis

Title: Soil erosion in the United States: Present and future (2020-2050)

Predictors: Rainfall erosivity inputs (PPT, Eref, RH, PAS, 30-min intensity I30); Soil properties (clay, silt, sand, SOM, permeability, bulk density); Vegetation cover (NDVI, NBR2, FCOVER, BSf); Landscape metrics (Sobel filter on NIR band); NPP, GPP, NAIP imagery for sustainability factor interpolation.

Title: SooSim, a landscape model for assessing mire habitat degradation and restoration
Authors: Lohmus, Asko; Kont, Raido; Kaasiku, Triin; Kohv, Marko; Arumae, Tauri; Kaasik, Ants

Scenarios: Business-as-usual (BAU); NULL (no management); NAT (doubled annual restoration); INT (intensive restoration without restoration)
Analysis Methods: Cellular automaton landscape simulation; statistical modeling of tree-cover and height dynamics (orthogonal polynomials, linear regression); spatial autocorrelation analysis; sensitivity analysis; validation against national forest survey, aerial photo studies, Copernicus TCD
Sim. Method Advantages: Explicit spatial organization at 25×25 m resolution; linkage of natural processes, spatial autocorrelation, and management interventions; strategic time-frame suitability; transferable structure with parameterization
Tools/Soft Used: R script implementing SooSim; SAGA GIS (wetness index); orthogonal polynomial functions (R poly); national GIS databases
Predictors: Initial tree cover; initial tree height; distance to wooded area; total ditch length; SAGA wetness index; vegetation height quantiles; canopy closure; peatland type; patch-edge status
Data Sources: Estonian Fund for Nature mire maps; Estonian Topographic Database; State Forest Management Centre restoration maps; Estonian soil map; national Lidar-derived vegetation height and closure maps; Estonian Forest Registry; Agricultural Registry; Copernicus Land Cover Monitoring Service; National Forest Inventory; local aerial photograph studies

Key Findings: Woody encroachment is dominant driver; BAU predicts ∼12% reduction of open and wooded mires by 2050; Afforestation probabilities vary by mire class (10% in ombrotrophic bogs to 33% in fens); Restoration interventions yield limited short-term gains due to time lags and prioritization thresholds; Ditch renovation mainly occurs in forested peatlands and has minor mire benefit

Scalability: Transferable to other regions with appropriate parameterization of local ecological and management variables
Novelty: First high‐resolution (25×25 m) coupled cellular automaton model linking tree-cover dynamics, mire-type transitions, and sequential management interventions for national-scale peatland futures modeling.

Title: Stakeholder-based modelling in climate change planning for the agriculture sector in Argentina
Authors: Gutman, Veronica; Frank, Federico; Monjeau, Adrian; Peri, Pablo L.; Ryan, Daniel; Volante, Jose; Apaza, Luciana; Scardamaglia, Virginia
Objective: Synthesize findings of the AFOLU LTS Project by integrating stakeholder inputs into long-term scenario modelling for the agriculture, forestry and other land-use sector in Argentina, and explore trade-offs concerning biophysical, economic and political feasibility of achieving carbon neutrality by 2050
LULC Classes: crops; pastures; natural forests; implanted forests; protected areas
Scenarios: Business as Usual; Carbon Neutrality; seven intermediate stakeholder-driven scenarios
Analysis Methods: Participatory backcasting; stakeholder workshops and semi-structured interviews; multi-model integration using FABLE Calculator, Dinamica EGO and Nature Map
Sim. Method Advantages: Provides a holistic, spatially explicit integration of food and land-use systems with biodiversity and water prioritization; Enables linkage of accounting and allocation models to capture land-use dynamics under multiple objectives

Predictors: rainfall; temperature; soil quality; slope; distance to roads; and other biophysical and socioeconomic explanatory variables (total ~20)

Validation Methods: Not specified
Validation Data Sources: Not specified
Key Findings: BAU and Carbon Neutrality scenarios diverge sharply in emissions trajectories and land-use distributions; Achieving carbon neutrality requires halting deforestation, increasing natural forest by ≥11% and planted forest by ~300%; Priority conservation of ≥80% of currently threatened species’ distributions would avoid 147 Gt CO₂ and protect 177,694 Mm³ / year of water; Stakeholder-based scenarios project 59–79 Mt CO₂ eq / year by 2050, well above neutrality threshold; Multiple economic, political and governance barriers exist, including lack of incentives, macroeconomic instability and policy fragmentation
Implications: Participatory modelling enhances understanding and informs policy but alone cannot achieve consensus or drive systemic transformation; Institutionalized public-private dialogue spaces are needed to translate scenario insights into actionable roadmaps

Scalability: Not specified

Title: The importance of natural land carbon sinks in modelling future emissions pathways and assessing individual country progress towards net-zero emissions targets
Authors: van der Ploeg, Robin; Haigh, Martin

Predictors: Forest land area per country; Primary forest fraction; Regional forest trends

Scalability: Applicable to any country or region with forest area data; method extendable to global coverage
Novelty: First-order, country-level allocation of global natural land sink projections using forest cover proxy without additional ESM runs

Title: The interplay of future solar energy, land cover change, and their projected impacts on natural lands and croplands in the US
Authors: Diffendorfer, Jay E.; Sergi, Brian; Lopez, Anthony; Williams, Travis; Gleason, Michael; Ancona, Zach; Cole, Wesley
Objective: Integrate projected land use–land cover (LULC) dynamics with capacity expansion modeling to explore interactions between future solar photovoltaic (PV) deployment and impacts on natural lands and croplands in the conterminous United States

Scenarios: IPCC-SRES A1B; A2; B1; B2; Baseline (2010 land cover under B2) combined with two solar deployment scenarios (Business-As-Usual; High Solar)
Analysis Methods: FORE-SCE LULC projections downscaled from 250 m to 90 m; NREL reV model to generate renewable energy supply curves; NREL ReEDS capacity expansion modeling at county resolution; Comparison of PV technical potential, deployed capacity, and land requirements across scenarios; Raster-based quantification of LULC transitions
Sim. Method Advantages: High spatial resolution integration of dynamic LULC with capacity expansion; Ability to quantify PV impacts on specific land cover types by leveraging raster supply curves; County-level resolution enables detailed spatial downscaling of build-out
Tools/Soft Used: GDAL (gdalwarp) for resampling; NREL reV model; NREL ReEDS model; R (for analysis and mapping); High-performance computing (NREL Kestrel)
Predictors: Land cover class; Solar resource quality (capacity factor); Development cost (site + transmission); Exclusion criteria (water, wetlands, developed)
Data Sources: FORE-SCE LULC projections (Sohl et al., 2014); IPCC SRES storylines; NREL reV model inputs; NREL ReEDS model; NLCD-derived land cover for 2010; EIA PV capacity data for 2023

Validation Data Sources: Original FORE-SCE 250 m projections (Sohl et al., 2014)
Key Findings: LULC dynamics had minimal impact on national solar technical potential (<1.4% change); Deployed PV capacity varied by –16.5% to +11.6% from baseline depending on scenario and deployment assumptions; New PV requires 14,000–35,000 km², accounts for 0.3%–0.7% of natural lands and 1.1%–2.4% of croplands by 2050; PV land requirements are small relative to gross LULC change (7–43× larger); Integration of LULC reveals scenarios where high solar deployment coincides with net natural land gains
Implications: Solar deployment under deep decarbonization can be accommodated with relatively small impacts on agriculture and natural systems; integrated land-energy modeling is critical for contextualizing net land cover outcomes and informing siting strategies
Limitations: Single static supply curve per scenario (no annual LULC updates); No alignment of socioeconomic assumptions between LULC and energy models; Assumed uniform PV capacity density; Excluded floating PV and small-scale rooftop beyond ReEDS defaults
Future Directions: Develop annual dynamic supply curves reflecting year-by-year LULC; Align LULC socioeconomic storylines with energy model assumptions; Incorporate agrivoltaics and land-management practices; Extend integration to other regions and renewable technologies
Scalability: Conceptually scalable to other regions; requires region-specific LULC projections and capacity expansion models
Novelty: First integration of dynamic LULC projections with capacity expansion modeling at high spatial resolution to quantify land cover impacts of future solar PV deployment

LULC Classes: Built and road; savannah, bare soil and farmland; water; forest
Scenarios: RCP4.5; RCP8.5; combined CV + LULCC; CV only; LULCC only
Analysis Methods: SWAT hydrological modeling; CA-Markov for LULC prediction; bias correction via CMhyd distribution mapping; statistical evaluation (R², NSE, PBIAS, Taylor diagrams); sensitivity analysis; Kappa for LULC map validation
Sim. Method Advantages: Semi-distributed (SWAT) captures physical heterogeneity of complex forest watershed better than global lumped models
Tools/Soft Used: SWAT; CMhyd (distribution mapping bias correction); CA-Markov
Predictors: Past land use maps (1984, 2006); transition probability matrices; conditional probability images (CA-Markov)
Data Sources: Spatial: SRTM DEM, FAO DSMW soil map, Landsat 5 (1984), Landsat 7 (2006), Landsat 8 (2015); Meteorological: GPCP precipitation, MERRA-2 temperature, humidity, wind, radiation, CORDEX RCM outputs (HIRHAM5, REMO, RCA4, CCCma); Hydrological: Observed flows from Hydrological Research Center
Validation Methods: Hydrological: calibration/validation using R², NSE, PBIAS, Taylor diagrams; LULC: Kappa coefficient comparison of simulated vs observed 2015 map
Validation Data Sources: Observed flow records (2005–2018); 2015 Landsat-derived LULC map
Key Findings: SWAT simulated flows satisfactorily (R² > 0.64; NSE > 0.64; bias < −7.9%); Future precipitation: decrease in CCCma, RCA4, REMO; large increases in HIRHAM5 (unrealistic); RCA4 forecasts most reliable (historical R² = 0.67; NSE = 0.56); Significant future LULC changes: built/road +54%; forest −50% by 2037; Under RCA4, SURQ and WYLD increase despite precipitation drop; CV reduces GW_RCH and PET; Impact scores show LULCC dominates variability of SURQ, WYLD, GW_RCH, except PET
Implications: Results inform water-resource management and infrastructure planning (dams, bridges) under combined urbanization and climate change
Limitations: Scarcity of observed hydro-meteorological stations; Biases in RCM outputs; Static non-meteorological variables for future; Uncertainty in CA-Markov projections
Future Directions: Incorporate additional observed gauges; Extend approach to other basins; Integrate socio-economic drivers beyond LULC; Explore multi-model ensembles for RCMs
Scalability: Applicable to poorly gauged, forested Central African basins undergoing urbanization
Novelty: First separation of LULCC vs CV impacts in Mefou basin; Identification of most reliable RCM (RCA4) for hydro-climatic forecasts; Combined use of SWAT and CA-Markov for future water-resource prediction
